0.title: In the Beginning: The Book of Origins
0.overview:
The message. Genesis tells where everything came from, what went wrong, and how God began to put it right. The one God made a good world by his word, and made man and woman in his image to know him and rule the world under him. They turned from him, and sin and death spread through the whole human race. Yet God did not give up on his world. He promised that the woman’s offspring would crush the serpent (3:15), and he called one man, Abraham, promising that in him “all the families of the earth shall be blessed” (12:3). The rest of the book shows God keeping that promise through a flawed, often faithless family, by grace alone, until Joseph sums up the whole: “you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good” (50:20).

Background: the writer. Genesis does not name its author, but it is the first of the five books of the Law, which Jews and Christians have always received as the books of Moses. They say that Moses wrote at God’s command (Exodus 17:14; 24:4; Numbers 33:2; Deuteronomy 31:9), and Jesus said, “For if you believed Moses, you would believe me; for he wrote of me” (John 5:46). A few small notes seem to have been added later, such as the list of Edom’s kings who reigned “before any king reigned over the Israelites” (36:31); inspiration covers those too.

Did Moses write it? Many modern scholars hold that the five books were stitched together long after Moses from several sources (the “documentary hypothesis”), citing the change between “God” and “the LORD” and to stories that seem to be told twice. Others answer that the divine names change with the meaning (God as Creator of all, the LORD as Israel’s covenant God), that retelling is a deliberate habit of Hebrew storytelling, and that since the 1970s critical scholars themselves have heavily questioned the theory. This commentary’s view: Moses wrote Genesis in substance, using older records, with a few later inspired notes.

When and where. The patriarchs probably lived early in the second millennium BC, Abraham about 2000 BC. He came from Ur, a great city of southern Mesopotamia (modern Iraq), by way of Harran in the north, to Canaan, where he lived in tents among the Canaanites. The story ends in Egypt, where Joseph ruled under Pharaoh and Jacob’s family settled in the eastern Nile Delta. Moses wrote after the exodus, in the fifteenth or the thirteenth century BC (faithful scholars differ on its date).

The first hearers. Picture Israel in the wilderness: former slaves, freshly out of Egypt and its many gods. Genesis told them who their God was, why Canaan was theirs by promise, and how they came to be in Egypt. Their neighbours told of creation and flood too: in the Babylonian Enuma Elish the world is made from a slain goddess and humans are made to do the gods’ work; in the Atrahasis epic the gods send a flood because humans have grown too noisy. Genesis answers with the truth: one good God, who makes the world by his word and humans in his image to bless them, judges real wickedness, and saves by grace.

The kind of book. Genesis is narrative history told with great artistry: a family story set inside the story of the world. The heading “These are the generations of …” (2:4; 5:1; 37:2) opens each of its ten sections and binds the early chapters and the patriarchs into one account. The narrator seldom comments; the reader must weigh what the patriarchs do against what God says, not simply copy them.

How the book makes its case. The first part tells the story of the whole human race (chapters 1–11). God creates a good world (chapters 1–2); man falls (chapter 3); sin spreads from Cain to a world of violence (chapters 4–6); God judges by the flood and saves Noah (chapters 7–9); the nations unite in pride at Babel (chapters 10–11). Each time judgment falls, grace follows: garments of skins (3:21), a mark to protect Cain (4:15), an ark. After Babel none comes, until God speaks to Abram (12:1). The second part narrows to one family (chapters 12–50). God’s promise to Abraham of land, offspring and blessing is threatened by barrenness, famine and Abraham’s own lies, until on Moriah he is asked to give up the son of promise (chapters 12–25). With Isaac and Jacob, God chooses the younger over the older and wrestles the grasping Jacob into Israel (chapters 25–36). In the story of Joseph God is almost hidden, yet he turns the brothers’ evil into the saving of many lives, and Judah, who once sold his brother, offers himself for Benjamin and is promised the sceptre (chapters 37–50). The book ends with a coffin in Egypt and Joseph’s confidence that “God will visit you” (50:24).

Is Genesis 1–11 history? Some read these chapters as myth or as a theological frame. But they are written as ordered narrative, not poetry, joined to Abraham’s story by the same “generations” headings, and the New Testament treats Adam, Abel and Noah as real men (Luke 3:38; Romans 5:12–19; Matthew 24:37–39; Hebrews 11:4–7). This commentary’s view: they are history, in carefully shaped prose. Adam and Eve were real people, specially created (2:7, 22). God made all things in six ordinary days, each numbered and closed with evening and morning, the pattern for Israel’s week: “For in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth” (Exodus 20:11). With the genealogies, these point to a young creation. The flood was a real judgment on the world; how far the waters reached is left to good conscience. Many faithful Christians read the days as long ages, as a literary framework or as God’s workdays described by analogy with ours,, with an old earth, usually out of reverence for Scripture; they are brothers, not enemies of the text.

Where it leads: to Christ. Genesis leads to Christ by promise and by pattern. The promise of 3:15, a bruised heel for a crushed head, is the first sounding of the gospel. Scripture “preached the gospel beforehand to Abraham” (Galatians 3:8), and its promised offspring is one, “who is Christ” (Galatians 3:16). Judah’s sceptre (49:10) looks past every king of Israel to the one to whom “shall be the obedience of the peoples”. Adam “was a type of the one who was to come” (Romans 5:14). Abraham “believed the LORD, and he counted it to him as righteousness” (15:6), and sinners are justified by that same faith (Romans 4:3). On Moriah, “God will provide for himself the lamb” (22:8) points to the God who “did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all” (Romans 8:32). Jacob’s stairway finds its meaning in Jesus, on whom the angels ascend and descend (John 1:51). The New Testament never calls Joseph a type, but the likeness is hard to miss: the beloved son, rejected and sold by his brothers, raised to power, saving the very men who betrayed him.

For us. Genesis tells you who you are: made in God’s image, like everyone you meet, with a dignity no one can take away; fallen in Adam, needing far more than self-improvement; and, if you trust Christ, a child of Abraham: “if you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to promise” (Galatians 3:29). It shows a God who keeps his promises through liars and failures, and who rules even the evil done against his people. At the cross the worst deed ever done became the salvation of the world. Genesis ends with a coffin in Egypt; the gospel ends with an empty tomb, for “all the promises of God find their Yes in him” (2 Corinthians 1:20).

1.title: In the Beginning, God
1.text: <sup>1</sup>In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.<sup>2</sup>The earth was without form and void, and darkness was over the face of the deep. And the Spirit of God was hovering over the face of the waters.<sup>3</sup>And God said, "Let there be light," and there was light.<sup>4</sup>And God saw that the light was good. And God separated the light from the darkness.<sup>5</sup>God called the light Day, and the darkness he called Night. And there was evening and there was morning, the first day.<sup>6</sup>And God said, "Let there be an expanse in the midst of the waters, and let it separate the waters from the waters."<sup>7</sup>And God made the expanse and separated the waters that were under the expanse from the waters that were above the expanse. And it was so.<sup>8</sup>And God called the expanse Heaven. And there was evening and there was morning, the second day.<sup>9</sup>And God said, "Let the waters under the heavens be gathered together into one place, and let the dry land appear." And it was so.<sup>10</sup>God called the dry land Earth, and the waters that were gathered together he called Seas. And God saw that it was good.<sup>11</sup>And God said, "Let the earth sprout vegetation, plants yielding seed, and fruit trees bearing fruit in which is their seed, each according to its kind, on the earth." And it was so.<sup>12</sup>The earth brought forth vegetation, plants yielding seed according to their own kinds, and trees bearing fruit in which is their seed, each according to its kind. And God saw that it was good.<sup>13</sup>And there was evening and there was morning, the third day.<sup>14</sup>And God said, "Let there be lights in the expanse of the heavens to separate the day from the night. And let them be for signs and for seasons, and for days and years,<sup>15</sup>and let them be lights in the expanse of the heavens to give light upon the earth." And it was so.<sup>16</sup>And God made the two great lights—the greater light to rule the day and the lesser light to rule the night—and the stars.<sup>17</sup>And God set them in the expanse of the heavens to give light on the earth,<sup>18</sup>to rule over the day and over the night, and to separate the light from the darkness. And God saw that it was good.<sup>19</sup>And there was evening and there was morning, the fourth day.<sup>20</sup>And God said, "Let the waters swarm with swarms of living creatures, and let birds fly above the earth across the expanse of the heavens."<sup>21</sup>So God created the great sea creatures and every living creature that moves, with which the waters swarm, according to their kinds, and every winged bird according to its kind. And God saw that it was good.<sup>22</sup>And God blessed them, saying, "Be fruitful and multiply and fill the waters in the seas, and let birds multiply on the earth."<sup>23</sup>And there was evening and there was morning, the fifth day.<sup>24</sup>And God said, "Let the earth bring forth living creatures according to their kinds—livestock and creeping things and beasts of the earth according to their kinds." And it was so.<sup>25</sup>And God made the beasts of the earth according to their kinds and the livestock according to their kinds, and everything that creeps on the ground according to its kind. And God saw that it was good.<sup>26</sup>Then God said, "Let us make man in our image, after our likeness. And let them have dominion over the fish of the sea and over the birds of the heavens and over the livestock and over all the earth and over every creeping thing that creeps on the earth."<sup>27</sup>So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them.<sup>28</sup>And God blessed them. And God said to them, "Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth and subdue it, and have dominion over the fish of the sea and over the birds of the heavens and over every living thing that moves on the earth."<sup>29</sup>And God said, "Behold, I have given you every plant yielding seed that is on the face of all the earth, and every tree with seed in its fruit. You shall have them for food.<sup>30</sup>And to every beast of the earth and to every bird of the heavens and to everything that creeps on the earth, everything that has the breath of life, I have given every green plant for food." And it was so.<sup>31</sup>And God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good. And there was evening and there was morning, the sixth day.
1.overview:
Where we are. Genesis 1 is the first page of the Bible and the foundation of everything after it. Before anything else, we are told who God is and what kind of world he made.

The message. There is one God, and he made everything. He made it by his word alone, without struggle or helper; he made it good; and he made man and woman in his own image, to know him and to rule his world under him. The world is not an accident, not divine and not evil: it is a gift, and we are not its owners but its stewards.

Why it was said. Israel had just left Egypt’s gods of sun, river and beast, and was heading for Canaan, where the powers of nature were worshipped (see the introduction). Genesis 1 told them the truth: the sun is a lamp, the sea monster a creature, and every human being God’s image.

How the chapter makes its case. After the opening statement that God created everything (v. 1), the earth is “without form and void” (v. 2). In days one to three God gives it form, separating light from darkness (vv. 3–5), the waters above from the waters below (vv. 6–8), and the seas from the dry land, which he clothes with plants (vv. 9–13). In days four to six he fills what he has formed: lights for day and night (vv. 14–19), fish and birds for sea and sky (vv. 20–23), animals for the land, and finally man and woman in his image (vv. 24–31). Ten times “God said”, and it was so; six times God saw that it was good, and the seventh time, looking at everything with humanity at its head, “very good” (v. 31).

Where it leads. Genesis 1 leads to Christ not by a promise but by revealing the Creator whom Christ makes known, and by a pattern he fulfils. The word by which God spoke the world into being is the Son, through whom “all things were made” (John 1:3), who “upholds the universe by the word of his power” (Hebrews 1:3). Adam was made in God’s image; Christ “is the image of the invisible God” (Colossians 1:15), the true man who will rule all things. In him God begins a new creation, speaking light into dark hearts as once into the dark deep (2 Corinthians 4:6).

For us. You are not an accident, and neither is anyone you will meet today: each bears the image of God. The world is God’s good gift, to be received with thanks, worked and cared for, never worshipped. And if your own life feels formless and dark, the God who said “Let there be light” has not lost his voice; in Christ he still speaks it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — Creation Days One through Three
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God alone made the world, and in three days he gives the formless earth its shape. The section opens with the foundation of the whole Bible: before anything was, God was, and he created all things (v. 1). The earth begins unformed and empty, with the Spirit hovering over the dark waters (v. 2). Then God speaks, and the account settles into its steady rhythm: God said, it was so, God saw that it was good, evening and morning. On day one he makes light (vv. 3–5); on day two, the sky that separates the waters (vv. 6–8); on day three, the dry land and the plants that clothe it (vv. 9–13). There is no struggle and no rival, only a word that is obeyed.
verseByVerse.theology: Light is divided from darkness, the waters above from the waters below, the sea from the dry land, and the land is clothed with plants. God creates by speaking, and each thing he makes he calls good.
verseByVerse.examples: Israel's neighbours told of gods battling chaos; here one God speaks and the chaos obeys. And the same Spirit who hovered over the dark deep is the one who makes a new creation in Christ (2 Cor. 5:17).

verseByVerse.quote: In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything that exists was made by God, who was there before it and depends on nothing. The Bible’s first sentence names its main character and sets everything else beneath him.

In the beginning. Time itself starts here, and God is already there.

Created. In the Old Testament the verb bara (“create”) is used only of God’s work. The word does not by itself mean “out of nothing” (v. 27 uses it of man, formed from dust in 2:7), but here, with nothing before God, it describes creation from nothing: what is seen was not made from things visible (Hebrews 11:3).

The heavens and the earth. This is a Hebrew way of saying “everything”. The universe is not eternal, not divine and not an accident, and the sun and sea are things made, not gods to be feared as in the myths of Israel’s neighbours.

Through the Son. John opens his Gospel with the same words, “In the beginning”, and tells us who was there: the Word, through whom “all things were made” (John 1:1–3). The Maker did not stay a distant cause at the edge of the universe. The Word became flesh (John 1:14), so that he could be seen, heard and touched.

In everyday life. Everything you touch today was made by God and belongs to him, and so do you.

Hasn’t science made the Creator unnecessary? Many thoughtful people assume so. Each century science explains something once put down to God, and God seems to retreat into shrinking gaps. But Genesis 1 was never competing with physics. Its rivals were the gods: the sun, the moon and the sea that Israel’s neighbours feared. By turning them into lamps and waters, made things that obey a word, it took the divinity out of nature and left a world that is orderly, good and open to study. The philosopher Alfred North Whitehead, no orthodox believer himself, argued in Science and the Modern World that the confidence that nature can be understood grew out of the medieval belief in a rational Creator. Science can tell us a great deal about how the world runs. It cannot tell us why there is a world at all, or why it should make sense to minds like ours. (On the age of the earth, see v. 5.)

Uncertain wording. The opening Hebrew words can be read two ways. Most translations, including the ESV, make v. 1 a complete statement. Some modern versions make it a lead-in to what follows: “When God began to create”. Both are grammatically possible. The traditional reading is the more natural, and it best fits creation from nothing, which Scripture teaches elsewhere (Romans 4:17).
verseByVerse.note: Genesis means “origin.” Jewish and Christian tradition credits Moses with the five books of the Law.

verseByVerse.quote: The earth was without form and void, and darkness was over the face of the deep. And the Spirit of God was hovering over the face of the waters.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At first the earth was unshaped and empty, but not abandoned: the Spirit of God was already there, ready to bring order and life.

Without form and void. The Hebrew tohu wabohu means unformed and unfilled, and the six days answer both: the first three give the world form, the last three fill it.

The deep. In the Babylonian story the deep was a goddess, Tiamat, defeated in battle (see the introduction). Here the deep (tehom) is only water, dark and waiting for God’s word.

The Spirit of God was hovering. The Spirit of God hovers over the waters like a bird over its young (Deuteronomy 32:11).

The Spirit of new creation. The same Spirit came down “like a dove” on Jesus at the Jordan (Matthew 3:16), and by the Spirit people are born again (John 3:5). No life is so dark and shapeless that he cannot hover over it.

Where Christians differ: the gap theory. Some taught a ruined first creation between vv. 1 and 2, to make room for long ages. This commentary’s view: the grammar does not support a gap; v. 2 describes the state of the earth God had just made, not a ruin.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew ruach can mean spirit, wind or breath, so some translate “a mighty wind” or “a wind from God”. But elsewhere this phrase regularly means “the Spirit of God” (Exodus 31:3), and a wind does not hover like a bird. The ESV’s reading is the likelier.

verseByVerse.quote: And God said, "Let there be light," and there was light. And God saw that the light was good. And God separated the light from the darkness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God speaks, and light exists: he creates by his word alone, and what he makes is good.

Let there be light. Creation comes by word (Psalm 33:6, 9): no struggle with chaos, only command. Light exists before the sun and moon are made on day four, for God, not the sun, is the source of light (Revelation 22:5). The text does not explain how the first days had evening and morning without a sun; it says only that God gave them.

The light was good. God calls what he has made good. Matter is not evil, though some later thinkers taught that it was.

Light in our hearts. Paul sees conversion as this verse happening again: “For God, who said, ‘Let light shine out of darkness,’ has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6). The light of the first day was a sign of the one who would say, “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12).

verseByVerse.quote: God called the light Day, and the darkness he called Night. And there was evening and there was morning, the first day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God names day and night, and with the first evening and morning the first day is complete: time itself is his creation and under his rule.

God called the light Day. To name something in the ancient world was to show authority over it: by naming day and night, God shows that time is his. Evening comes first because the Hebrew day began at evening.

Where Christians differ: the days of creation. Some hold six literal 24-hour days; others see long ages (day-age); others a literary framework (days 1–3 matching 4–6); others God’s workdays described by analogy to ours. This commentary’s view: God made all things in six ordinary 24-hour days. Each day is numbered and closed with evening and morning, the plain marks of an ordinary day, and elsewhere in the Old Testament a numbered day is almost always an ordinary day. Exodus 20:11 grounds Israel’s six days of work and one of rest in God’s own six days and seventh, a comparison that holds only if the days are of the same kind. And Jesus places man and woman from the beginning of creation (Mark 10:6), not at the end of long ages. With the genealogies of chapters 5 and 11, true history even if they leave small gaps (see on 5:6–17), these days point to a young creation, thousands rather than billions of years old. This view has a cost, plainly stated: it rejects the settled judgment of most scientists that the earth is billions of years old, with long ages of life and death in the rocks. This commentary judges the text the surer guide, while granting that those questions are real. Faithful Christians read the days otherwise, and their reasons deserve a hearing. The day-age view notes that day can mean a longer period (2:4) and that much happens on day six. The framework view sees days 1–3 matched by days 4–6 and takes the week as a literary arrangement of God’s works by topic. The analogical view takes them as God’s workdays, like ours but not the same. And many hold an old earth because of what they see in the world God made. Those who hold these views are brothers, not enemies of the text. All must affirm that God created all things from nothing, by his word, that Adam and Eve were real people specially created, and that creation was very good before the fall. The text’s chief aim is to show who made the world and why.

verseByVerse.quote: And God said, "Let there be an expanse in the midst of the waters, and let it separate the waters from the waters." And God made the expanse and separated the waters that were under the expanse from the waters that were above the expanse. And it was so.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God makes the sky, separating the waters above from the waters below, so that the world has room for life.

Let there be an expanse. The expanse is the sky, pictured as a canopy stretched over the earth (Psalm 104:2). Genesis describes the sky as it appears to an observer, not as a science textbook would. Why then take the days plainly? Because the days, unlike the sky, are numbered and made the pattern of Israel’s week (see v. 5).

Uncertain wording. The word for “expanse” (raqia) comes from a verb used for beating metal thin (Exodus 39:3), so some think it means a solid dome. But birds fly “across the expanse of the heavens” (v. 20), and Scripture freely uses picture language for the sky. The likeliest meaning is simply the visible sky. The “waters above” are probably the waters of cloud and rain (compare 7:11; Psalm 148:4), though the text does not say exactly how.

verseByVerse.quote: And God called the expanse Heaven. And there was evening and there was morning, the second day.
verseByVerse.commentary: God names the sky, showing that it is his, and the second day ends. Day two alone lacks “it was good”, probably because the separating of the waters is finished only on day three, where the phrase comes twice.

verseByVerse.quote: And God said, "Let the waters under the heavens be gathered together into one place, and let the dry land appear." And it was so. God called the dry land Earth, and the waters that were gathered together he called Seas. And God saw that it was good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God gathers the seas into their place and brings up the dry land, preparing a home for living creatures and for people.

Let the dry land appear. God sets the sea its limits (Job 38:8–11). In the myths the sea was a rival power; here it goes where it is told.

The wind and the sea obey him. When Jesus rebuked the storm on Galilee, the disciples asked, “Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?” (Mark 4:41). Genesis 1 had already given the answer: only the one who set the sea its bounds.

verseByVerse.quote: And God said, "Let the earth sprout vegetation, plants yielding seed, and fruit trees bearing fruit in which is their seed, each according to its kind, on the earth." And it was so. The earth brought forth vegetation, plants yielding seed according to their own kinds, and trees bearing fruit in which is their seed, each according to its kind. And God saw that it was good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God makes the land fruitful, with plants that carry their own seed, so that life will go on and multiply.

Each according to its kind. Plants come in ordered variety, each reproducing after its kind and carrying its seed, so creation is built to continue and multiply. “Kinds” is not a technical term for modern species; the point is order and fruitfulness.

verseByVerse.quote: And there was evening and there was morning, the third day.
verseByVerse.commentary: The third day closes with the world formed: what it lacks now is inhabitants. The first three days have answered “without form” (v. 2); the next three answer “void”, filling each realm in turn.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–31 — Creation Days Four through Six: Lights, Living Creatures, and the Image of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God fills the world he has shaped, and crowns it with humanity made in his image. Each of days four to six fills a realm formed on days one to three: lights for the day and the night (vv. 14–19), fish and birds for the sea and the sky (vv. 20–23), animals for the land (vv. 24–25). Then the pace slows. God deliberates, “Let us make man in our image”, and creates man and woman to represent him and rule the earth under him (vv. 26–28). He gives food to every creature (vv. 29–30) and surveys the whole: “very good” (v. 31). The things the nations feared as gods are only creatures; ordinary man and woman bear the image of God.
verseByVerse.theology: The lights fill the day and the night, birds and fish the sky and the sea, animals and people the land. The making of man and woman in God's image, blessed to fill and rule the earth, is the climax of the week.
verseByVerse.examples: The sun, moon and sea monsters the nations feared are simply God's creatures. Every human being, of whatever age or ability, bears God's image, and ordinary work obeys God’s sixth-day charge to fill and rule the earth.

verseByVerse.quote: And God said, "Let there be lights in the expanse of the heavens to separate the day from the night. And let them be for signs and for seasons, and for days and years, and let them be lights in the expanse of the heavens to give light upon the earth." And it was so.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God sets lights in the sky to divide day from night and to mark out time for his creatures.

Let there be lights. Day four fills what day one made: the light now has its lights.

Seasons. The same word names Israel’s appointed feasts, so time itself is ordered for worship.

Not astrology. The stars mark time; they do not rule anyone’s destiny (Jeremiah 10:2).
verseByVerse.note: “Seasons” can also be rendered “appointed times” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: And God made the two great lights—the greater light to rule the day and the lesser light to rule the night—and the stars. And God set them in the expanse of the heavens to give light on the earth,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sun, moon and stars that the nations worshipped are simply lamps that God made and hung in place.

The two great lights. The sun and moon are not even named, perhaps because Israel’s neighbours worshipped them as gods; here they are lamps.

And the stars. Billions of galaxies are mentioned in three words. If God made them so easily, nothing is too hard for him (Isaiah 40:26).

verseByVerse.quote: to rule over the day and over the night, and to separate the light from the darkness. And God saw that it was good. And there was evening and there was morning, the fourth day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The lights rule only as God’s appointees, and he calls their work good. They are a small picture of the rule he will give to humanity in v. 26.

No need of sun or moon. The lights serve for now. In the new creation “the city has no need of sun or moon to shine on it, for the glory of God gives it light, and its lamp is the Lamb” (Revelation 21:23).

verseByVerse.quote: And God said, "Let the waters swarm with swarms of living creatures, and let birds fly above the earth across the expanse of the heavens." So God created the great sea creatures and every living creature that moves, with which the waters swarm, according to their kinds, and every winged bird according to its kind. And God saw that it was good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God fills sea and sky with teeming life, and even the creatures the nations feared are his.

Let the waters swarm. Day five fills what day two made, as sea and sky teem with life.

Great sea creatures. The tanninim were monsters feared in pagan myth. Here they are simply God’s creatures, and bara is used again, for the first animal life.

verseByVerse.quote: And God blessed them, saying, "Be fruitful and multiply and fill the waters in the seas, and let birds multiply on the earth." And there was evening and there was morning, the fifth day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God blesses the creatures of sea and sky with fruitfulness: his first blessing in the Bible falls on fish and birds. He delights in his creatures and wills that life should spread.

Not one forgotten. Jesus drew the same lesson: sparrows are sold cheaply, “and not one of them is forgotten before God” (Luke 12:6). If God blesses birds, he will not forget you.

verseByVerse.quote: And God said, "Let the earth bring forth living creatures according to their kinds—livestock and creeping things and beasts of the earth according to their kinds." And it was so. And God made the beasts of the earth according to their kinds and the livestock according to their kinds, and everything that creeps on the ground according to its kind. And God saw that it was good.
verseByVerse.commentary: God fills the land with animals of every kind, and calls them good. Day six fills what day three made, with livestock and wild animals alike. Because they are God’s creatures, caring for them is part of godliness (Proverbs 12:10).

verseByVerse.quote: Then God said, "Let us make man in our image, after our likeness. And let them have dominion over the fish of the sea and over the birds of the heavens and over the livestock and over all the earth and over every creeping thing that creeps on the earth." So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God makes humanity, male and female, in his own image, to represent him and rule his world under him: this is the summit of creation.

In our image, after our likeness. Every other creature comes by command; man alone is made after God deliberates (“Let us make man”), and in God’s own likeness.

The image of God. To bear God’s image is to represent him on earth and reflect him in rule, relationship, reason and moral nature. In the ancient Near East a king set up statues of himself to mark the lands he ruled, and a king might be called the “image” of his god; Genesis gives that dignity not to a king alone but to every man and woman. The fall damaged the image but did not destroy it (Genesis 9:6; James 3:9).

Male and female he created them. Man and woman are both fully in God’s image, equal in dignity and different by design. Bara comes three times in v. 27, marking the climax of creation.

The true image. What Adam was made to be, Christ is: “He is the image of the invisible God” (Colossians 1:15). In him the damaged image is being restored, as believers put on the new self, “which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator” (Colossians 3:10), until they are conformed to the image of the Son (Romans 8:29).

In everyday life. Every person you meet today bears God’s image, the unborn child and the dying, the disabled, the difficult and the stranger; treat them so.

Where Christians differ: “Let us”. Some take the plural as a plural of majesty, some as God speaking to his heavenly court of angels, some as a hint of the Trinity. This commentary’s view: angels are never said to create or to share God’s image. In the light of the New Testament, this is a first hint of the plurality within the one God (John 1:3).
verseByVerse.note: The Hebrew for man (adam) is the general word for mankind; it later becomes the proper name Adam (ESV notes).

verseByVerse.quote: And God blessed them. And God said to them, "Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth and subdue it, and have dominion over the fish of the sea and over the birds of the heavens and over every living thing that moves on the earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God blesses man and woman and gives them their work: to fill the earth, and to rule it under him for its good.

The creation mandate. God blessed before he commanded. Family, work and culture are his calling, and your daily work is part of it.

Subdue and rule. People are to rule as stewards, not tyrants: Genesis 2:15 speaks of working and keeping the garden. This is no licence to exploit or destroy creation. We are to rule as God rules, for the good of what he has made.

The man who will rule. We do not yet see everything subject to man, “But we see him who for a little while was made lower than the angels, namely Jesus” (Hebrews 2:9). The rule Adam lost, Christ has taken up, and his people will reign with him.

What it does not mean. “Be fruitful” is a blessing on humanity, not a verdict on every person. Single people and childless couples have not failed God’s design; Jesus himself was unmarried, and Paul calls singleness a gift (1 Corinthians 7:7).

verseByVerse.quote: And God said, "Behold, I have given you every plant yielding seed that is on the face of all the earth, and every tree with seed in its fruit. You shall have them for food. And to every beast of the earth and to every bird of the heavens and to everything that creeps on the earth, everything that has the breath of life, I have given every green plant for food." And it was so.
verseByVerse.commentary: God gives plants as food to people and animals alike: he provides for every creature he has made (Psalm 104:27–28). Before the fall, people and animals are given plants to eat; permission to eat meat comes after the flood (9:3).

verseByVerse.quote: And God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good. And there was evening and there was morning, the sixth day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God looks over everything he has made, with humanity at its head, and pronounces it very good.

It was very good. Only here is the verdict “very good”: creation is complete. Sin, death and suffering are intruders, not part of God’s first design (Romans 5:12). On the young-creation reading taken at v. 5, the death recorded in the rocks came after the fall.

Why this matters. The body is good, and so are matter, sex and food (1 Timothy 4:4). Praise God for his creation, which he will one day make new through Christ: “Behold, I am making all things new” (Revelation 21:5).

1.theology:
The Trinity in Creation. The Spirit hovers (v. 2); God speaks his Word (v. 3); the Father creates (v. 1). John 1:1–3 identifies the creative Word with the eternal Son, and Colossians 1:16 and Hebrews 1:2 confirm that the universe was made through and for Christ.

The Image of God and Human Dignity. The image of God (vv. 26–27) is the foundation of human dignity: not achievement, intelligence, beauty or usefulness, but God's image stamped on every human being, the unborn included (Psalm 139:13–16). That is why taking human life is an assault on God himself (Gen. 9:6). In an age of competing accounts of human value, Genesis 1:27 makes the most radical claim of all: every person bears the image of the Creator of the cosmos.
1.examples:
Then: Israel's neighbours had elaborate creation myths; the Babylonian Enuma Elish featured warring gods and humanity made as slave labour for them. Genesis 1 quietly answers them all: one God, sovereign speech, ordered goodness, and humanity as image-bearers rather than slaves.

Now: Cosmology traces the universe to a beginning (on its dating, see v. 5). Science cannot tell us whether the beginning had a Maker behind it; Genesis answers with confidence, because God himself has told us. And since everyone bears God’s image, no one’s worth lies in their output, genes or usefulness.

keyVerse.quote: So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them.
keyVerse.note: Everything in the chapter climbs to this verse: humanity is the only creature made after God deliberates, and the only one made in his likeness. It gives every man and woman a dignity that no age, illness or failure can remove, and it prepares for Christ, the perfect image of God, in whom that image is being restored in his people (Colossians 3:10).

1.reflection:
Genesis 1 told Israel that the sun, the sea and the beasts were not gods but creatures. What does our culture treat as a power to be feared or served, and how does this chapter cut it down to size?

Every person is made in God’s image (vv. 26–27). Whom do you find it hardest to treat that way, and what would change this week if you did?

God gave man and woman work before sin entered the world (v. 28). How does that change the way you see your daily work, paid or unpaid, and your care for the world God made?

John 1 and 2 Corinthians 4:6 take the language of this chapter and apply it to Christ and to conversion. Where do you most need the God who said “Let there be light” to speak into darkness now?

2.title: The LORD God Formed the Man
2.text: <sup>1</sup>Thus the heavens and the earth were finished, and all the host of them.<sup>2</sup>And on the seventh day God finished his work that he had done, and he rested on the seventh day from all his work that he had done.<sup>3</sup>So God blessed the seventh day and made it holy, because on it God rested from all his work that he had done in creation.<sup>4</sup>These are the generations of the heavens and the earth when they were created, in the day that the LORD God made the earth and the heavens.<sup>5</sup>When no bush of the field was yet in the land and no small plant of the field had yet sprung up—for the LORD God had not caused it to rain on the land, and there was no man to work the ground,<sup>6</sup>and a mist was going up from the land and was watering the whole face of the ground—<sup>7</sup>then the LORD God formed the man of dust from the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and the man became a living creature.<sup>8</sup>And the LORD God planted a garden in Eden, in the east, and there he put the man whom he had formed.<sup>9</sup>And out of the ground the LORD God made to spring up every tree that is pleasant to the sight and good for food. The tree of life was in the midst of the garden, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.<sup>10</sup>A river flowed out of Eden to water the garden, and there it divided and became four rivers.<sup>11</sup>The name of the first is the Pishon. It is the one that flowed around the whole land of Havilah, where there is gold.<sup>12</sup>And the gold of that land is good; bdellium and onyx stone are there.<sup>13</sup>The name of the second river is the Gihon. It is the one that flowed around the whole land of Cush.<sup>14</sup>And the name of the third river is the Tigris, which flows east of Assyria. And the fourth river is the Euphrates.<sup>15</sup>The LORD God took the man and put him in the garden of Eden to work it and keep it.<sup>16</sup>And the LORD God commanded the man, saying, "You may surely eat of every tree of the garden,<sup>17</sup>but of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat, for in the day that you eat of it you shall surely die."<sup>18</sup>Then the LORD God said, "It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him a helper fit for him."<sup>19</sup>Now out of the ground the LORD God had formed every beast of the field and every bird of the heavens and brought them to the man to see what he would call them. And whatever the man called every living creature, that was its name.<sup>20</sup>The man gave names to all livestock and to the birds of the heavens and to every beast of the field. But for Adam there was not found a helper fit for him.<sup>21</sup>So the LORD God caused a deep sleep to fall upon the man, and while he slept took one of his ribs and closed up its place with flesh.<sup>22</sup>And the rib that the LORD God had taken from the man he made into a woman and brought her to the man.<sup>23</sup>Then the man said, "This at last is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh; she shall be called Woman, because she was taken out of Man."<sup>24</sup>Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.<sup>25</sup>And the man and his wife were both naked and were not ashamed.
2.overview:
Where we are. Genesis 1 has shown God making the whole world in six days and calling it very good. Chapter 2 completes the week with God’s rest (vv. 1–3), then opens the book’s first “generations” section (v. 4) and comes down from the sky to a garden and a man made from dust.

The message. The God who made the universe is also the LORD who shapes a man with his own hands, breathes life into him, and gives him everything he needs: a home in his presence, work, freedom, a word to live by, and a wife. This is life as God meant it: lived before his face, received as gift, ordered by his word and shared in love.

Why it was said. Israel was learning to keep the Sabbath, serve God at a tabernacle and live by his commands (see the introduction). Genesis 2 showed them that rest, sanctuary, priestly service, God’s word and marriage were not inventions of Moses but the shape of the world God made.

How the chapter makes its case. God finishes his work and blesses the seventh day (vv. 1–3). The LORD God forms the man from dust and breathes life into him (vv. 4–7), plants a garden with the tree of life at its centre and a river flowing out to the world (vv. 8–14), and sets the man there to work and keep it, free to eat from every tree but one (vv. 15–17). Then comes the one thing “not good”: the man alone (v. 18). He names the animals, but none is fit for him (vv. 19–20); God builds the woman and brings her to him, and he sings for joy (vv. 21–23). The narrator draws out the pattern of marriage (v. 24) and leaves them naked and unashamed (v. 25).

Where it leads. This chapter leads to Christ by pattern. Paul quotes v. 7 to set “the first man Adam”, who became a living being, beside “the last Adam”, who “became a life-giving spirit” (1 Corinthians 15:45). The garden where God dwelt with man points to Christ, the true meeting place of God and man, and to the new creation where the tree of life grows again (Revelation 22:2). God’s rest is opened to his people in Christ (Hebrews 4:9–10). And Paul says that the marriage of v. 24 was always pointing to “Christ and the church” (Ephesians 5:32).

For us. You were shaped by God’s hand and given breath by him; you did not invent yourself and cannot complete yourself. Work is a calling, rest is a gift, God’s word is freedom rather than a cage, and loneliness is something God himself calls “not good”. What was lost in Eden, God is restoring in Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–17 — The Seventh Day and the Garden
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God completes his work and rests, then shows how he made the man and gave him a home with himself. The seventh day crowns the week: God ceases from finished work, and blesses and sets apart the day (vv. 1–3). A new heading (v. 4) then turns from the wide view of chapter 1 to a close-up, using God’s covenant name. Before there were fields or anyone to work them (vv. 5–6), the LORD God shapes the man from dust and breathes life into him (v. 7), plants a garden of good trees (vv. 8–9), and waters it with a river that flows out to the world (vv. 10–14). He sets the man there to work it and keep it (v. 15), with generous freedom and one command (vv. 16–17).
verseByVerse.theology: God rests on the seventh day and blesses it, the first thing in Scripture he makes holy. Then the LORD God forms the man, breathes life into him, and sets him in the garden to work it and keep it under one prohibition.
verseByVerse.examples: Work is a gift given before the fall, and rest is a gift given before any work was done.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus the heavens and the earth were finished, and all the host of them. And on the seventh day God finished his work that he had done, and he rested on the seventh day from all his work that he had done.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s work of creation is complete, and he rests, not from weariness, but because nothing is missing. God rests, or ceases (the verb shabat lies behind the word Sabbath), not because he is tired (Isaiah 40:28), but because the work is done.

No evening and morning. The seventh day has no closing formula, and Hebrews 4 sees God’s rest as still open for his people to enter. Some take this to mean the creation days too were long ages; but the six working days each do close with evening and morning, and Exodus 20:11 counts them with the seventh as a week, so this commentary reads them as ordinary days (see on 1:5).

verseByVerse.quote: So God blessed the seventh day and made it holy, because on it God rested from all his work that he had done in creation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God blesses the seventh day and sets it apart, building a rhythm of work and rest into time itself.

God blessed the seventh day. To bless the day and make it holy is to set it apart. The first thing in Scripture that God makes holy is not a place or a person but a time.

Rest in Christ. Jesus called himself “lord even of the Sabbath” (Mark 2:28) and offered the weary rest (Matthew 11:28). The rest God entered at creation is the rest he opens to his people in Christ (Hebrews 4:9–10).

In everyday life. Man’s first full day was God’s day of rest. If you find yourself working as though everything depends on you, this day says otherwise: you began by receiving, not achieving.

Where Christians differ: a creation ordinance. Sabbatarians (the Westminster tradition) see here a weekly Sabbath binding on all people for all time, now kept on the Lord’s Day. Others note that no command is given until Exodus 16 and 20. This commentary’s view: the pattern of work and rest is built into creation and is good for all people. For Christians, the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ’s rest (Hebrews 4:9–10), and the Lord’s Day is a privilege for worship and rest, not a set of rules binding the conscience. Hold the view charitably.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the generations of the heavens and the earth when they were created, in the day that the LORD God made the earth and the heavens. When no bush of the field was yet in the land and no small plant of the field had yet sprung up—for the LORD God had not caused it to rain on the land, and there was no man to work the ground, and a mist was going up from the land and was watering the whole face of the ground—
verseByVerse.commentary:
A new heading turns from the whole universe to the making of man, and the Creator is now named the LORD God, Israel’s covenant God. The land waits, with no rain and no one to work it, for its gardener.

These are the generations. The Hebrew toledot (“what came of” someone or something) is a heading that divides Genesis into ten sections.

The LORD God. God’s covenant name, Yahweh, is joined to Elohim: the Creator of chapter 1 is Israel’s covenant God.

Where Christians differ: two creation accounts? Critical scholars have seen two contradictory sources (the documentary hypothesis). This commentary’s view: chapter 1 gives the wide view of all creation; chapter 2 zooms in on the making of man and woman and the garden. They complement each other, as Jesus treated them together (Matthew 19:4–5).

Uncertain wording. The word translated “mist” (ed) is rare: it may be a mist, or water welling up from below. Either way the land is watered, but not yet worked.

verseByVerse.quote: then the LORD God formed the man of dust from the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and the man became a living creature.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God shapes the man from dust with his own hands and breathes his own breath into him: we are humble earth and God-given life together.

Formed the man of dust. God forms the man as a potter shapes clay (Jeremiah 18:6), with personal, hands-on care. The dust speaks of our humble origin (3:19; Psalm 103:14); the breath of life, given directly by God, shows that we are both earthly and spiritual.

The last Adam. Paul quotes this verse: “The first man Adam became a living being”; “the last Adam became a life-giving spirit” (1 Corinthians 15:45). Adam received breath; Christ gives it, breathing on his disciples, “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20:22).

Where Christians differ: a historical Adam? Some today accept that humans evolved, with Adam as a symbol or a representative chosen from among early humans. This commentary’s view: Scripture treats Adam as a real, specially created first man, from whom all humanity descends (Luke 3:38; Acts 17:26; Romans 5:12–19). The gospel’s logic of the first and last Adam depends on it. Eve too was a real woman, specially made from Adam’s side (vv. 21–22; 1 Timothy 2:13), and Jesus speaks of the two as made from the beginning of creation (Mark 10:6). Christians who accept human evolution usually want to honour both Scripture and the evidence they see in the world, and should be answered with patience, not scorn.
verseByVerse.note: “Man” (adam) and “ground” (adamah) sound alike in Hebrew: man is made from the earth.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD God planted a garden in Eden, in the east, and there he put the man whom he had formed. And out of the ground the LORD God made to spring up every tree that is pleasant to the sight and good for food. The tree of life was in the midst of the garden, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God plants a garden where he will live with the man, full of good trees, with life at its centre and one tree that tests trust.

A garden in Eden. Eden is a sanctuary where God dwells with man, the first temple: like the tabernacle it is entered from the east and guarded by cherubim (3:24), and God walks in it (3:8; Leviticus 26:12). Its trees are both pleasant and good: beauty and usefulness alike come from God.

The knowledge of good and evil. The forbidden tree stands for deciding good and evil for oneself, apart from God (3:5, 22).

The tree of life restored. The tree of life returns in the new creation (Revelation 22:2), and the way back to it runs through the tree where Christ “bore our sins in his body” (1 Peter 2:24).

Uncertain wording. The exact sense of “the knowledge of good and evil” is debated: moral independence, as taken here; the wisdom of maturity (compare 1 Kings 3:9); or knowledge of everything. Clearly it was to be received from God, not seized against his word.
verseByVerse.note: “Eden” sounds like a Hebrew word for delight.

verseByVerse.quote: A river flowed out of Eden to water the garden, and there it divided and became four rivers. The name of the first is the Pishon. It is the one that flowed around the whole land of Havilah, where there is gold. And the gold of that land is good; bdellium and onyx stone are there. The name of the second river is the Gihon. It is the one that flowed around the whole land of Cush. And the name of the third river is the Tigris, which flows east of Assyria. And the fourth river is the Euphrates.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A river flows out of Eden to water the world, and the garden is set on a real map, rich in good things.

A river flowed out of Eden. Eden is placed in the real world, in the region of Mesopotamia, and its gold and onyx are materials later used in the tabernacle.

Rivers of living water. The river of Eden flows again from Ezekiel’s temple (Ezekiel 47) and in the city of God, “from the throne of God and of the Lamb” (Revelation 22:1), and Jesus promised “rivers of living water” to all who believe in him (John 7:38).

Uncertain wording. The Pishon and Gihon cannot now be identified, nor certainly the lands they encircle (Cush usually means the land south of Egypt, but here may lie further east). Bdellium is probably a fragrant resin, and the stone called “onyx” is uncertain. Where exactly Eden lay is lost; that it lay in the real world is not.
verseByVerse.note: The Tigris and Euphrates are known rivers of Mesopotamia; the Pishon and Gihon cannot now be identified.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD God took the man and put him in the garden of Eden to work it and keep it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God gives the man work in a perfect world: to tend and guard the garden as service to God.

Work and keep. These verbs later describe the priests’ service in the tabernacle: Adam is a priest-gardener, and tending the garden is itself his service to God. “Keep” can also mean guard, a hint that something may threaten the garden, and that Adam is responsible to protect it.

Work before the fall. Work comes before the fall. It is not a curse; the curse makes it toilsome (3:17–19). Your work is a calling from God, not merely a way to pay bills.
verseByVerse.note: The same pair of verbs is used of the Levites’ service in Numbers 3:7–8.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD God commanded the man, saying, "You may surely eat of every tree of the garden, but of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat, for in the day that you eat of it you shall surely die."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God gives the man lavish freedom and a single command, and warns plainly that disobedience will bring death.

You may surely eat of every tree. God gives generous freedom first: every tree but one. The single prohibition is a test of trust and obedience. “You shall surely die” meant spiritual death at once, the loss of fellowship with God, and physical death in time.

The obedient one. Adam, with every tree to enjoy, refused the one limit. Christ, hungry in a wilderness, would not take bread the Father had not given (Matthew 4:1–4), and in another garden prayed, “not as I will, but as you will” (Matthew 26:39). By his obedience many are made righteous (Romans 5:19).

What it does not mean. Not that God is stingy, as the serpent will suggest (3:1): his first word is “surely eat”, and the limit guards the gift.

Where Christians differ: a covenant of works? Reformed theology has seen here a covenant of works: life promised for obedience, death threatened for disobedience, with Adam as the head of humanity. Some object that “covenant” is not used. This commentary’s view: the elements of a covenant are present (Hosea 6:7), and Romans 5:12–21 treats Adam as a representative head, as Christ is.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–25 — The Creation of Woman and the First Marriage
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The one thing not good in God’s good world is the man alone, and God answers it with the woman and the first marriage. God names the need (v. 18), then lets the man discover it as he names the animals and finds no partner among them (vv. 19–20). God builds the woman from the man’s side and brings her to him (vv. 21–22), and the man’s first recorded words are a song of delight (v. 23). The narrator draws out the lasting pattern: a man leaves his parents, holds fast to his wife, and the two become one flesh (v. 24). They stand together, naked and unashamed, with nothing to hide (v. 25).
verseByVerse.theology: God builds the woman from the man's side and brings her to him. Marriage, given before sin, becomes a picture of Christ and the church (Eph. 5:31–32).
verseByVerse.examples: Jesus settled the divorce question by going back to this chapter. Loneliness is a need God named before sin entered, and the answer he gives is marriage for many and his people for all.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD God said, "It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him a helper fit for him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In a world God called good, the one thing “not good” is the man alone, so God promises a partner who corresponds to him. This is the first “not good” in a very good world.

A helper. The Hebrew ezer is used often of God himself (Psalm 121:1–2), so it implies no inferiority. Fit for him means corresponding to him: like him, yet different.

The myth of the self-sufficient self. Our culture tells us to become complete on our own: know yourself, love yourself, need no one. There is some wisdom in not making another person your saviour. But in 2023 the Surgeon General of the United States issued a public warning that loneliness had become an epidemic, with effects on health he compared to smoking. Genesis would not be surprised. Here is a man with a sound body, meaningful work, an unspoiled world and God himself walking with him, and God says it is “not good” that he is alone. We were not made to be self-contained, because the God who made us is not. Before there was a world the Father loved the Son (John 17:24), and we are made in the image of that love. So the cure for loneliness is not a stronger self but being taken into love. And that is what Christ secured when he was left utterly alone on the cross, crying, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46). He was abandoned so that “God settles the solitary in a home” (Psalm 68:6) could be true of anyone who comes to him.

In everyday life. If you are lonely, God calls it “not good” too. Seek friendship and the family of the church. This does not mean that a single person is incomplete: God’s answer to loneliness is marriage for many, and the family of his people for all (Mark 10:29–30).

Where Christians differ: roles in marriage. Egalitarians read equality without distinct roles. Complementarians see equality of worth with a loving headship given to the husband, as Paul argues from this order (1 Corinthians 11:8–9; 1 Timothy 2:13). This commentary’s view: complementarian, held with care: men and women equal in dignity, different by design, with servant headship in marriage and the church.
verseByVerse.note: “Fit for him” can be rendered “corresponding to him” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: Now out of the ground the LORD God had formed every beast of the field and every bird of the heavens and brought them to the man to see what he would call them. And whatever the man called every living creature, that was its name. The man gave names to all livestock and to the birds of the heavens and to every beast of the field. But for Adam there was not found a helper fit for him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As the man names the animals he exercises the rule God gave him, and discovers for himself that none of them is a partner fit for him. The animals are good, but none can stand beside him as an equal.

In everyday life. God let Adam feel the need before he met it. A longing God allows us to feel is often where he is preparing a gift.

verseByVerse.quote: So the LORD God caused a deep sleep to fall upon the man, and while he slept took one of his ribs and closed up its place with flesh. And the rib that the LORD God had taken from the man he made into a woman and brought her to the man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God makes the woman from the man’s side and brings her to him: she shares his nature, and she is God’s gift.

One of his ribs. The woman is taken from beside the man: not from his head to rule him nor his feet to be trampled, as Matthew Henry observed, but from his side to be his equal. And God himself brings her to him, as a father gives away the bride.

From the side of the last Adam. Many Christians since the early church have seen a picture here: as the first Adam slept and his bride was taken from his side, so from the pierced side of the last Adam, in the sleep of death, came blood and water (John 19:34), and from his death the church was born. Scripture does not draw this link directly, though Paul does say the first marriage points to Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:31–32).

Uncertain wording. The word translated “rib” (tsela) elsewhere usually means “side”, as of the tabernacle (Exodus 26:20). It may mean a rib or a larger part of his side; either way, she is made of his own substance.
verseByVerse.note: “Made into a woman” is literally “built” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the man said, "This at last is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh; she shall be called Woman, because she was taken out of Man."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man greets the woman with a song of delight: at last, one who shares his own nature.

This at last is bone of my bones. The first recorded human words are a poem of delight: at last, what the animals could not supply. Ishshah (woman) sounds like ish (man), a wordplay that shows their unity.

His own flesh. Paul uses this verse to show how Christ loves his church: no one hates his own flesh, “but nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ does the church” (Ephesians 5:29).

In everyday life. If you are married, does your husband or wife still hear delight from you, or only requests?
verseByVerse.note: “This at last” stresses the man’s relief and delight after naming the animals.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Marriage is God’s design from creation: a man leaves his parents, holds fast to his wife, and the two become one flesh for life.

Hold fast to his wife. Marriage creates a new first loyalty, and one flesh is a lifelong, exclusive, sexual union. Jesus quotes this verse against easy divorce (Matthew 19:4–6). God’s design is one man and one woman; the church holds the historic view of sexuality, speaking it with compassion to all who struggle.

Christ and the church. Paul quotes this verse and adds, “This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church” (Ephesians 5:32). Every faithful marriage is a small picture of the one who holds fast to his people and will never let them go (John 10:28).

In everyday life. If you are married, ask what holding fast would look like today. Leaving does not mean abandoning your parents, whom you must still honour (Mark 7:10–13), only that they are no longer your first loyalty.

verseByVerse.quote: And the man and his wife were both naked and were not ashamed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man and woman lived in complete openness before God and each other, with nothing to hide and nothing to be ashamed of.

Naked and were not ashamed. They felt no shame because they had nothing to hide from God or each other. The word for naked (arummim) sounds like the word for the serpent’s craftiness (arum) in the next verse (3:1), and the verse prepares for what follows, when they hide (3:7–10).

Shame covered. In Christ, who endured the cross, “despising the shame” (Hebrews 12:2), our shame is covered, and one day we will stand before God with nothing to hide.

2.theology:
The Garden as Temple. Eden is the original sacred space, where heaven and earth overlap and God walks with humanity. Its imagery returns in the tabernacle and temple, and Revelation 21–22 closes the canon with a garden-city whose temple is the Lord God himself: God and humanity dwelling together without barrier, the vision of Eden restored and surpassed.

The Second Adam. Paul's argument in Romans 5 and 1 Corinthians 15 turns on Adam and Christ. Adam, given every permission and one prohibition, failed and brought death to all. Christ faced every temptation, obeyed perfectly in our place, and brought life to all who are in him; his obedience is counted to all who trust him (Romans 5:19). In Eden Adam chose his own will; in Gethsemane Christ chose his Father’s, praying, “not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42).
2.examples:
Then: Israel would recognise Eden in the tabernacle: cherubim guarding the way (3:24) and woven into the veil, gold and onyx (2:11–12) among its materials. The priesthood would seek to restore, through ritual, the access to God lost at the fall.

Now: Against a culture that either deifies career or despises it, Genesis 2 says work is a gift before it is a burden, a calling before it is a job. And the chapter’s account of man and woman, the one-flesh covenant, and the goodness of the body comes from how God made us, not from human custom.

keyVerse.quote: Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.
keyVerse.note: This is the chapter’s climax and the foundation of marriage in all of Scripture. Jesus went back to it to settle the question of divorce (Matthew 19:4–6), and Paul to show what marriage is finally for: a picture of Christ, who holds fast to his church and will never let her go (Ephesians 5:31–32).

2.reflection:
God rested and blessed the seventh day before the man had done any work at all (vv. 2–3). What does it mean for you that human life began with receiving rather than achieving? How do you practise rest?

The man was given work in a perfect world (v. 15). How would seeing your work, paid or unpaid, as a calling from God change your attitude to it on an ordinary Monday?

God gave lavish freedom and one limit (vv. 16–17). Why are God’s commands a gift rather than a cage? Where do you find that hardest to believe?

God calls loneliness “not good” (v. 18). Who in your church or neighbourhood is alone, and how could your group be part of God’s answer?

3.title: The Fall
3.text: <sup>1</sup>Now the serpent was more crafty than any other beast of the field that the LORD God had made. He said to the woman, "Did God actually say, 'You shall not eat of any tree in the garden'?"<sup>2</sup>And the woman said to the serpent, "We may eat of the fruit of the trees in the garden,<sup>3</sup>but God said, 'You shall not eat of the fruit of the tree that is in the midst of the garden, neither shall you touch it, lest you die.'"<sup>4</sup>But the serpent said to the woman, "You will not surely die.<sup>5</sup>For God knows that when you eat of it your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil."<sup>6</sup>So when the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise, she took of its fruit and ate, and she also gave some to her husband who was with her, and he ate.<sup>7</sup>Then the eyes of both were opened, and they knew that they were naked. And they sewed fig leaves together and made themselves loincloths.<sup>8</sup>And they heard the sound of the LORD God walking in the garden in the cool of the day, and the man and his wife hid themselves from the presence of the LORD God among the trees of the garden.<sup>9</sup>But the LORD God called to the man and said to him, "Where are you?"<sup>10</sup>And he said, "I heard the sound of you in the garden, and I was afraid, because I was naked, and I hid myself."<sup>11</sup>He said, "Who told you that you were naked? Have you eaten of the tree of which I commanded you not to eat?"<sup>12</sup>The man said, "The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit of the tree, and I ate."<sup>13</sup>Then the LORD God said to the woman, "What is this that you have done?" The woman said, "The serpent deceived me, and I ate."<sup>14</sup>The LORD God said to the serpent, "Because you have done this, cursed are you above all livestock and above all beasts of the field; on your belly you shall go, and dust you shall eat all the days of your life.<sup>15</sup>I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring; he shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel."<sup>16</sup>To the woman he said, "I will surely multiply your pain in childbearing; in pain you shall bring forth children. Your desire shall be for your husband, and he shall rule over you."<sup>17</sup>And to Adam he said, "Because you have listened to the voice of your wife and have eaten of the tree of which I commanded you, 'You shall not eat of it,' cursed is the ground because of you; in pain you shall eat of it all the days of your life;<sup>18</sup>thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you; and you shall eat the plants of the field.<sup>19</sup>By the sweat of your face you shall eat bread, till you return to the ground, for out of it you were taken; for you are dust, and to dust you shall return."<sup>20</sup>The man called his wife's name Eve, because she was the mother of all living.<sup>21</sup>And the LORD God made for Adam and for his wife garments of skins and clothed them.<sup>22</sup>Then the LORD God said, "Behold, the man has become like one of us in knowing good and evil. Now, lest he reach out his hand and take also of the tree of life and eat, and live forever—"<sup>23</sup>therefore the LORD God sent him out from the garden of Eden to work the ground from which he was taken.<sup>24</sup>He drove out the man, and at the east of the garden of Eden he placed the cherubim and a flaming sword that turned every way to guard the way to the tree of life.
3.overview:
Where we are. Genesis 2 ended with the man and woman naked and unashamed in God’s garden, free to eat from every tree but one. Chapter 3 is the hinge of the whole Bible: without it there would be no need for a covenant, a law, a temple, a Messiah or a cross.

The message. Sin began with distrust: believing a voice that said God could not be trusted and his word need not be obeyed. It brought shame, fear, blame, pain and death, and cut humanity off from God’s presence. Yet God came looking for the sinners, promised a son of the woman who would crush the serpent, and clothed them before he sent them out. Judgment is real, but in this chapter the promise is spoken before the sentence.

Why it was said. Israel would live under God’s word in a good land, surrounded by voices that made other gods seem more generous (see the introduction). This chapter explained why their world was full of toil, pain and death, and why they could come near God only through priests and sacrifices, past cherubim woven into a curtain.

How the chapter makes its case. The serpent twists God’s word and slanders his goodness (vv. 1–5); the woman eats, and her husband with her (v. 6). Their eyes open to shame; they cover themselves and hide (vv. 7–8). God seeks them with questions, and each passes the blame (vv. 9–13). Then God speaks in reverse order: he curses the serpent and promises its defeat by the woman’s offspring (vv. 14–15), and sentences the woman to pain and conflict (v. 16) and the man to toil and death (vv. 17–19). Adam names his wife Eve in faith (v. 20), God clothes them (v. 21), and they are sent out, with the way to the tree of life guarded (vv. 22–24).

Where it leads. This chapter leads to Christ by promise, by pattern and by the need it exposes. The offspring of v. 15 is Christ, born of a woman (Galatians 4:4), who through death destroyed “the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil” (Hebrews 2:14). Where Adam fell in a garden of plenty, Christ stood firm in a wilderness and obeyed in Gethsemane: “For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive” (1 Corinthians 15:22). Through his torn flesh the way back to God stands open (Hebrews 10:19–20).

For us. Every temptation still whispers that God is holding out on you; the cross is his answer. Stop sewing fig leaves and stop passing blame, and answer God’s “Where are you?” with plain confession. The God who clothed Adam and Eve clothes everyone who trusts his Son.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — The Temptation and the Fall
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Sin enters the world through distrust of God’s goodness, and at once it breaks every relationship. The serpent questions God’s word, then denies it and slanders God’s motive (vv. 1–5). The woman looks, desires, takes and eats, and her husband beside her eats too (v. 6). Their eyes open, not to glory but to shame, and they cover themselves and hide from God (vv. 7–8). Yet God comes looking, with questions that make room for confession (vv. 9–11). Instead, the man blames the woman and God who gave her, and the woman blames the serpent (vv. 12–13). Trust in God, openness with each other and peace with creation are all torn in a moment.
verseByVerse.theology: The serpent questions God's word, denies his warning and slanders his motive. The woman sees, desires, takes and eats; the man beside her eats too. They hide, and under God's questions each passes the blame while still admitting, "and I ate."
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the three appeals of verse 6 are the ones Jesus refused in the wilderness. Now: the lie at the root of every sin is still that God is withholding something good.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the serpent was more crafty than any other beast of the field that the LORD God had made. He said to the woman, "Did God actually say, 'You shall not eat of any tree in the garden'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The serpent opens his attack by twisting God’s word, making the generous God sound stingy.

Crafty. The Hebrew arum plays on arummim, “naked” (2:25): the couple who had nothing to hide meet a creature that hides everything.

Did God actually say? The first attack is on God’s word, by doubt and distortion: God gave every tree but one, and the question makes him sound as if he gave none.

Who is the serpent? The serpent is a creature, but the voice behind it is Satan, “that ancient serpent” (Revelation 12:9; John 8:44).

It is written. Temptation still often starts by making God seem stingy and his word unclear. When the same tempter came to Jesus, he answered each time from what God had actually said: “It is written” (Matthew 4:4).
verseByVerse.note: In Hebrew, “you” in vv. 1–5 is plural: the serpent speaks to both (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: And the woman said to the serpent, "We may eat of the fruit of the trees in the garden, but God said, 'You shall not eat of the fruit of the tree that is in the midst of the garden, neither shall you touch it, lest you die.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: The woman answers, but she blurs God’s word, adding to his command and softening his warning. “Neither shall you touch it” was not in God’s command (2:17), and she leaves out “surely” and “every”. It matters to know exactly what God has said, neither adding nor subtracting.

verseByVerse.quote: But the serpent said to the woman, "You will not surely die. For God knows that when you eat of it your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The serpent now flatly contradicts God and slanders his motive, offering as a prize what they already had: likeness to God.

You will not surely die. This is the first lie. God, the serpent suggests, is holding them back. The bait is to be like God, and that is the root of sin: to be one’s own god. Yet they were already made in his image (1:27).

Why would anyone trust that God is good? The serpent’s suggestion has become the common sense of the modern world: whoever claims authority over you is probably holding you back, and you will only flourish when you decide good and evil for yourself. It is not a foolish suspicion. Kings, priests and parents have often used authority to crush people. But Genesis puts a startling claim at the start of the Bible: this suspicion is not the cure for evil; it is how evil came in. The world is not broken because God made it badly (it was “very good”, 1:31), or because we lack education. It is broken because creatures made for love decided their Maker could not be trusted, and that distrust has run through every heart since. This takes evil more seriously than the optimist does, and gives more hope than the cynic can. Evil is an intruder, so it can be driven out. And how can we know God is not holding out on us? In the garden he withheld one tree. At Calvary he did not withhold his Son: “He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?” (Romans 8:32).

verseByVerse.quote: So when the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise, she took of its fruit and ate, and she also gave some to her husband who was with her, and he ate.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The woman takes the fruit and eats, and her husband, standing beside her, eats too.

Three appeals. The fruit appeals to appetite, beauty and wisdom, the same three John names: “the desires of the flesh and the desires of the eyes and pride of life” (1 John 2:16).

Her husband who was with her. Adam was with her, and said nothing.

Where Adam fell, Christ stood. Adam fell with a full stomach in a garden of plenty. Jesus, hungry in a wilderness, faced the same tempter offering bread, splendour and a shortcut to glory, and refused every time (Matthew 4:1–11).

Where Christians differ: history or myth? Some read the fall as a symbol of every person’s story. This commentary’s view: Scripture treats it as a real event that brought sin and death into the world (Romans 5:12; 1 Timothy 2:14). It is also every person’s story.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the eyes of both were opened, and they knew that they were naked. And they sewed fig leaves together and made themselves loincloths.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Their eyes are opened, as promised, but to shame, not glory, and they try to cover it themselves. The fig leaves are the first attempt to cover one’s own guilt, and every such attempt since has failed as they did. Only God can truly cover sin.
