Two kinds of fig leaves. We are still sewing. Some of us cover our shame with goodness: a clean record, a respectable life, causes we can point to, a moral ledger kept in our favour. Others cover it by denying there is anything to cover: shame is only conditioning, guilt is a hangover from religion, and the answer is to accept yourself. The first is the fig leaf of the moralist, the second of the free spirit, and both are ways of being our own saviour. Both wither. The moralist is anxious, because the record is never quite good enough. The free spirit finds that the sense of being exposed does not go away by being renamed, and social media has made curators of us all, polishing a self we hope no one sees behind. Genesis does not tell Adam and Eve to sew better, or to stop minding. It shows God making clothes for them himself (v. 21). The gospel is not a better fig leaf. It is being clothed by someone else: “Blessed is the one whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered” (Psalm 32:1).

verseByVerse.quote: And they heard the sound of the LORD God walking in the garden in the cool of the day, and the man and his wife hid themselves from the presence of the LORD God among the trees of the garden. But the LORD God called to the man and said to him, "Where are you?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sinners hide from God, but God comes looking for them. His presence in the garden had been their delight; now they hide from it, because sin breaks fellowship.

Where are you? God does not ask for information. The question is an invitation to come out, and it shows that God seeks the sinner first.

The seeking God. The question of the garden is answered in the incarnation: “For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost” (Luke 19:10).

Uncertain wording. “The cool of the day” is literally “the wind (or spirit) of the day”. Most take it as the breezy part of the day, the evening; some suggest a storm-like coming of God in judgment. The usual reading is the more natural, but either way the sound of God’s coming now brings fear.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "I heard the sound of you in the garden, and I was afraid, because I was naked, and I hid myself." He said, "Who told you that you were naked? Have you eaten of the tree of which I commanded you not to eat?"
verseByVerse.commentary: Guilt makes Adam afraid of God, but God answers with questions that give him room to confess.

verseByVerse.quote: The man said, "The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit of the tree, and I ate."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Adam blames his wife, and God who gave her: sin has already turned husband against wife, and man against God.

In everyday life. We are quick to do the same, but the God who came looking for Adam welcomes plain confession (1 John 1:9).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD God said to the woman, "What is this that you have done?" The woman said, "The serpent deceived me, and I ate."
verseByVerse.commentary: The woman blames the serpent: she was truly deceived, but deception does not excuse her. She was deceived (2 Corinthians 11:3). Yet though she ate first, Paul says sin came into the world through Adam, who stood for us all (Romans 5:12).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–24 — The Curse and the Expulsion from the Garden
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God judges, but inside the judgment he plants the first promise of redemption. He curses the serpent and declares lasting war between its offspring and the woman’s, ending in a crushed head and a bruised heel (vv. 14–15). The woman will bear children in pain and know conflict in marriage (v. 16); the man will toil against a cursed ground until he returns to the dust (vv. 17–19). Yet Adam names his wife Eve, “the mother of all living”, believing the promise (v. 20), and God himself clothes them with skins (v. 21). Then he sends them out of the garden, and cherubim guard the way to the tree of life (vv. 22–24).
verseByVerse.theology: The serpent is cursed, the woman's pain and the man's toil are multiplied, and death is pronounced. Yet God himself clothes them before barring the way to the tree of life.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the promise of verse 15 is traced through the whole Old Testament until God sends his Son. Now: the sword that closed the garden fell on Christ, and through him the way to the tree of life is open again (Rev. 22:2).

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD God said to the serpent, "Because you have done this, cursed are you above all livestock and above all beasts of the field; on your belly you shall go, and dust you shall eat all the days of your life. I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring; he shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God curses the serpent and promises that a son of the woman will crush him, at the cost of a wound to himself: the first announcement of the gospel.

Cursed are you. The serpent is cursed without being questioned, and without mercy. God himself puts hostility between the serpent and the woman, between the serpent’s offspring and hers. To crawl on the belly and lick the dust was a picture of utter defeat in Israel’s world (Psalm 72:9; Micah 7:17), and Isaiah 65:25 says that in the new creation “dust shall be the serpent’s food.”

The first gospel. This verse has long been called the first gospel (in Latin, the protoevangelium). One offspring of the woman will crush the serpent, at the cost of a wound to himself. It is fulfilled in Christ’s death and victory (Galatians 4:4; Hebrews 2:14; Romans 16:20). The offspring is both a people (the godly line) and one person (“he”). And the promise came at the very moment of the fall: before God spoke a word of sentence to Adam and Eve, he promised the one who would crush the serpent.

How Jewish readers take it. Rashi and many Jewish interpreters take the plain sense: a lasting hostility between people and snakes, and more widely humanity’s long struggle with evil. Yet the old Aramaic Targums (Pseudo-Jonathan and Neofiti) already looked further, promising a remedy for the wounded heel in the days of King Messiah. This commentary agrees that the verse speaks of a long conflict, but reads the one offspring who deals the decisive blow as Christ, born of a woman (Galatians 4:4), who by his death destroyed the devil’s power (Hebrews 2:14).

Where Christians differ: “she shall bruise”? The Latin Vulgate read “she shall crush”, applied to Mary. This commentary’s view: the Hebrew reads “he” (or “it”), the offspring. It points to Christ, not Mary.

Uncertain wording. The verb translated “bruise” (shuph) is rare, and the same word is used for both blows; it may mean crush, strike or snap at. The ESV keeps one verb, as the Hebrew does. The difference lies in the target: a heel wounded, a head crushed.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “offspring” is literally “seed.”

verseByVerse.quote: To the woman he said, "I will surely multiply your pain in childbearing; in pain you shall bring forth children. Your desire shall be for your husband, and he shall rule over you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The woman’s sentence touches her calling as mother and wife: pain enters childbirth, and conflict enters marriage.

I will surely multiply your pain in childbearing. The curse falls not on childbirth itself, but on the pain in it.

He shall rule over you. This is no command for men to dominate women. It describes the curse, which Christ came to undo, and no husband may appeal to it to excuse harshness. Abuse is sin; anyone in danger at home should seek safety at once and tell someone who can help.

Where Christians differ: her desire. Some read sexual or emotional longing; others a desire to master him, as in 4:7, where the same words describe sin’s desire. This commentary’s view: the parallel with 4:7 suggests a sinful struggle for control between the sexes, answered by harsh rule. Both distort the good order of chapter 2. In Christ, marriage is restored to loving headship and glad help (Ephesians 5:22–33).
verseByVerse.note: “For your husband” can also be rendered “to,” “toward” or “against” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: And to Adam he said, "Because you have listened to the voice of your wife and have eaten of the tree of which I commanded you, 'You shall not eat of it,' cursed is the ground because of you; in pain you shall eat of it all the days of your life; thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you; and you shall eat the plants of the field.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because Adam listened to his wife instead of God, the ground is cursed: work becomes painful, and creation groans with humanity.

Cursed is the ground because of you. Adam listened to his wife over God’s voice, and creation now suffers with humanity (Romans 8:20–22).

A crown of thorns. Christ would one day wear a crown made from the cursed ground’s thorns (Matthew 27:29), bearing the curse to lift it.

In everyday life. When work is frustrating, this is why, and there is hope of renewal (Revelation 22:3).

verseByVerse.quote: By the sweat of your face you shall eat bread, till you return to the ground, for out of it you were taken; for you are dust, and to dust you shall return."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Toil will last until death, and the man made from dust will return to it: the warning of 2:17 is carried out. Work becomes hard toil, and they will die and return to the dust, words spoken at funerals ever since.

Made alive in Christ. Christ tasted death so that those who return to dust will rise: “For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive” (1 Corinthians 15:22).

verseByVerse.quote: The man called his wife's name Eve, because she was the mother of all living.
verseByVerse.commentary: Under the sentence of death, Adam names his wife for life: an act of faith in God’s promise. The name Eve, Chawwah, sounds like the word for “life”. Adam believes v. 15: the human race will go on, and through it the promised offspring will come. And all humanity descends from this one couple (Acts 17:26).
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “Eve” resembles the Hebrew for “living.”

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD God made for Adam and for his wife garments of skins and clothed them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before sending them out, God himself clothes the guilty pair, with garments that cost a life.

God clothes them. Adam and Eve had tried to cover themselves with fig leaves, which would wither in a day. Now God does it for them, with something that will last, like a father getting his children ready for a long journey.

Skins. To make garments of skin, an animal had to die. Genesis does not explain it, but it is the first death in the Bible, and it falls on an innocent creature so that the guilty can be covered: a first hint of the sacrifices to come, and of the Lamb of God who would die so that sinners could be clothed (John 1:29).

Mercy in the midst of judgment. The sentence stands: they will toil, suffer and die. Yet God’s last act before the exile is not a blow but a kindness. Even when he disciplines his children, he does not stop caring for them. So he clothes us in Christ’s righteousness: “he has clothed me with the garments of salvation” (Isaiah 61:10).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD God said, "Behold, the man has become like one of us in knowing good and evil. Now, lest he reach out his hand and take also of the tree of life and eat, and live forever—" therefore the LORD God sent him out from the garden of Eden to work the ground from which he was taken.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God sends the man out of the garden and bars him from the tree of life: a sentence, but also a mercy.

Like one of us. The plural “one of us” returns from 1:26. Man now decides good and evil for himself. Barring the tree is a mercy as well as a sentence: God will not let him live for ever in a fallen state. He is sent out, exiled from God’s presence.

verseByVerse.quote: He drove out the man, and at the east of the garden of Eden he placed the cherubim and a flaming sword that turned every way to guard the way to the tree of life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God drives the man out and sets cherubim to guard the way back to the tree of life.

To guard the way to the tree of life. The guarded way back is on the garden’s east side. Winged guardian figures stood at the doors of palaces and temples across the ancient Near East; here real cherubim guard the entrance to God’s own garden-sanctuary. Later the tabernacle and temple faced east, with cherubim embroidered on the veil (Exodus 26:31).

The way opened. The way into God’s presence stayed closed until Christ opened it: when he died the curtain was torn in two (Matthew 27:51), and we now enter “by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh” (Hebrews 10:20). In the new creation the tree of life is regained (Revelation 22:14).

In everyday life. You were made for Eden, and only Christ brings you home.
verseByVerse.note: Cherubim are angelic guardians of God’s holy presence.

3.theology:
The Anatomy of Sin. Sin begins with doubt about God's word (v. 1), moves to distrust of his character (vv. 4–5), leads to action against his will (v. 6), and produces shame, fear and broken relationship (vv. 7–13). Its root is the claim, in practice if not in theory, that I am a better judge of my good than my Creator.

The First Gospel and the Story It Starts. Verse 15 is the seed from which the rest of the Bible's story grows. The call of Abraham, the exodus, the covenant with David, the prophets and the incarnation all unfold this one promise, and the conflict between the two offspring is resolved at the cross and the empty tomb.
3.examples:
Then: Other ancient stories, such as the Gilgamesh epic and the Adapa myth, made human misery a cosmic accident or the work of rival gods. Genesis 3 says sin is the free act of creatures made in God's image, and it explained the thorns and the pain of childbirth Israel knew every day, with a hint that the curse could be reversed.

Now: What is wrong with us? Not ignorance, environment or psychology, but rebellion against the Creator, a will set against him that needs not improvement but redemption. We are not basically good people who sometimes do bad things, but fallen image-bearers who need a new creation. And the seed of the woman has come, and the serpent’s head is crushed.

keyVerse.quote: I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring; he shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel.
keyVerse.note: This is the first promise of the gospel, spoken in the middle of the curse and before the man and woman hear their own sentence. The rest of the Bible traces the line of the woman’s offspring until the one comes who crushes the serpent’s head and is wounded in doing it, at the cross (Romans 16:20; Hebrews 2:14).

3.reflection:
The serpent made God seem stingy and his word uncertain (vv. 1–5). In what forms does that suspicion come to you, and how does the cross answer it (Romans 8:32)?

Adam blamed Eve and God; Eve blamed the serpent (vv. 12–13). Why does blame come so naturally, and what would plain confession look like in your marriage, family or church?

Fig leaves were the first attempt at self-covering (v. 7). What are the fig leaves of respectable people today, and of those who reject religion? What does it mean to be clothed by God instead (v. 21)?

God’s first promise of rescue comes in the middle of judgment (v. 15). How does that shape the way you face the consequences of your own sin and the brokenness of the world?

4.title: Am I My Brother's Keeper?
4.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Adam knew Eve his wife, and she conceived and bore Cain, saying, "I have gotten a man with the help of the LORD."<sup>2</sup>And again, she bore his brother Abel. Now Abel was a keeper of sheep, and Cain a worker of the ground.<sup>3</sup>In the course of time Cain brought to the LORD an offering of the fruit of the ground,<sup>4</sup>and Abel also brought of the firstborn of his flock and of their fat portions. And the LORD had regard for Abel and his offering,<sup>5</sup>but for Cain and his offering he had no regard. So Cain was very angry, and his face fell.<sup>6</sup>The LORD said to Cain, "Why are you angry, and why has your face fallen?<sup>7</sup>If you do well, will you not be accepted? And if you do not do well, sin is crouching at the door. Its desire is for you, and you must rule over it."<sup>8</sup>Cain spoke to Abel his brother. And when they were in the field, Cain rose up against his brother Abel and killed him.<sup>9</sup>Then the LORD said to Cain, "Where is Abel your brother?" He said, "I do not know; am I my brother's keeper?"<sup>10</sup>And the LORD said, "What have you done? The voice of your brother's blood is crying to me from the ground.<sup>11</sup>And now you are cursed from the ground, which has opened its mouth to receive your brother's blood from your hand.<sup>12</sup>When you work the ground, it shall no longer yield to you its strength. You shall be a fugitive and a wanderer on the earth."<sup>13</sup>Cain said to the LORD, "My punishment is greater than I can bear.<sup>14</sup>Behold, you have driven me today away from the ground, and from your face I shall be hidden. I shall be a fugitive and a wanderer on the earth, and whoever finds me will kill me."<sup>15</sup>Then the LORD said to him, "Not so! If anyone kills Cain, vengeance shall be taken on him sevenfold." And the LORD put a mark on Cain, lest any who found him should attack him.<sup>16</sup>Then Cain went away from the presence of the LORD and settled in the land of Nod, east of Eden.<sup>17</sup>Cain knew his wife, and she conceived and bore Enoch. When he built a city, he called the name of the city after the name of his son, Enoch.<sup>18</sup>To Enoch was born Irad, and Irad fathered Mehujael, and Mehujael fathered Methushael, and Methushael fathered Lamech.<sup>19</sup>And Lamech took two wives. The name of the one was Adah, and the name of the other Zillah.<sup>20</sup>Adah bore Jabal; he was the father of those who dwell in tents and have livestock.<sup>21</sup>His brother's name was Jubal; he was the father of all those who play the lyre and pipe.<sup>22</sup>Zillah also bore Tubal-cain; he was the forger of all instruments of bronze and iron. The sister of Tubal-cain was Naamah.<sup>23</sup>Lamech said to his wives: "Adah and Zillah, hear my voice; you wives of Lamech, listen to what I say: I have killed a man for wounding me, a young man for striking me.<sup>24</sup>If Cain's revenge is sevenfold, then Lamech's is seventy-sevenfold."<sup>25</sup>And Adam knew his wife again, and she bore a son and called his name Seth, for she said, "God has appointed for me another offspring instead of Abel, for Cain killed him."<sup>26</sup>To Seth also a son was born, and he called his name Enosh. At that time people began to call upon the name of the LORD.
4.overview:
Where we are. Adam and Eve have been sent out of Eden under the sentence of death, holding God’s promise of an offspring who will crush the serpent (3:15). Chapter 4 shows what sin does in the very next generation, and how God keeps that promise alive.

The message. Sin, once let in, spreads and grows: from distrust of God to the murder of a brother, and from one murder to a boast of limitless revenge. Yet God keeps speaking to sinners, warning before the crime, questioning after it, and protecting even the murderer. And through it all he preserves a line that calls on his name, so that the promised offspring will come.

Why it was said. Israel would bring offerings to God and live as brothers under his law, which would forbid murder and limit vengeance (see the introduction). Cain showed them that offerings mean nothing without faith, and that hatred of a brother is the seed of murder.

How the chapter makes its case. Eve bears Cain and Abel (vv. 1–2). Both bring offerings, and God accepts Abel’s but not Cain’s (vv. 3–5). God warns the angry Cain that sin is crouching at his door (vv. 6–7), but Cain kills his brother (v. 8). God questions him, hears Abel’s blood, and sends him out as a wanderer, yet marks him for protection (vv. 9–16). Cain’s line builds a city and develops herding, music and metalwork, and ends in Lamech’s boast of seventy-sevenfold revenge (vv. 17–24). Then God gives Seth in Abel’s place, and people begin to call on the name of the LORD (vv. 25–26).

Where it leads. This chapter leads to Christ by pattern and by the need it exposes. Abel, the shepherd who offered his best by faith and was murdered by his brother, is the first of the righteous dead (Matthew 23:35). Jesus, the good shepherd, was handed over by his own people out of envy (Matthew 27:18), and his blood “speaks a better word than the blood of Abel” (Hebrews 12:24), crying for mercy, not vengeance. Lamech’s seventy-sevenfold revenge is answered by Jesus’ seventy-sevenfold forgiveness (Matthew 18:22). And the line of Seth, preserved by God, runs on to Jesus, “the son of Seth, the son of Adam, the son of God” (Luke 3:38).

For us. Sin is crouching at your door too, and it wants you; resentment and envy are where it usually gets in. Do not answer God’s questions with a sneer but with confession, and the God who heard Abel’s blood will hear you. Above all, call on the name of the LORD, for “everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved” (Romans 10:13).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — Cain and Abel: The First Murder
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Sin, once let in, grows from resentment to murder, yet God keeps speaking to the sinner. Eve bears two sons (vv. 1–2), and both bring offerings; God accepts Abel, who gave his best in faith, but not Cain (vv. 3–5). God warns the angry Cain that sin is crouching at his door, and offers him acceptance (vv. 6–7). Cain refuses, and kills his brother in the field (v. 8). God questions him as he questioned Adam, and hears Abel’s blood crying from the ground (vv. 9–10). Cain is cursed and sent out a wanderer, yet God marks him for protection, and he goes away from the LORD’s presence (vv. 11–16).
verseByVerse.theology: God regards Abel and his offering, not Cain and his. He warns Cain that sin is crouching at the door, but Cain kills his brother, denies he is his keeper, and is sent out a wanderer, yet marked by God for protection.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: John warns the church not to be like Cain (1 John 3:12). Now: God still hears the blood of the wronged, and the blood of Jesus speaks a better word than Abel's (Heb. 12:24).

verseByVerse.quote: Now Adam knew Eve his wife, and she conceived and bore Cain, saying, "I have gotten a man with the help of the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eve bears her first son and names him with thanks to the LORD, perhaps hoping he is the promised offspring.

Adam knew Eve his wife. “Knew” is the Bible’s word for sexual union, and it implies personal knowledge, not mere contact.

I have gotten a man. Eve names her son Cain with thanks for the LORD’s help; perhaps she hoped he was the offspring promised in 3:15. If so, the first son born into the world was a bitter disappointment: the promise would not be kept by ordinary human hopes.

Uncertain wording. “With the help of the LORD” is literally “with the LORD”, and the sense is uncertain. Most read it as the ESV does. Luther read “I have gotten a man, the LORD”, as though Eve thought her son was the promised deliverer himself. The ESV’s reading is the likelier.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “Cain” sounds like the Hebrew for “gotten.”

verseByVerse.quote: And again, she bore his brother Abel. Now Abel was a keeper of sheep, and Cain a worker of the ground.
verseByVerse.commentary: A second son is born, and the two brothers take up different but honourable work. Abel’s name means breath or vapour, the word the ESV renders “vanity” in Ecclesiastes 1:2: his life will be short. The brothers’ two callings, shepherd and farmer, are both honourable; the difference between them is not in their work.

verseByVerse.quote: In the course of time Cain brought to the LORD an offering of the fruit of the ground, and Abel also brought of the firstborn of his flock and of their fat portions. And the LORD had regard for Abel and his offering, but for Cain and his offering he had no regard. So Cain was very angry, and his face fell.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God accepts Abel and his offering but not Cain and his, because he looks first at the heart of the worshipper.

The firstborn and the fat portions. Abel brought the best: the firstborn of the flock and the fat, which Israel’s law would later reserve for God (Leviticus 3:16). Cain brought “an offering of the fruit of the ground”, with no mark of the first or the best.

His face fell. Cain’s fallen face shows anger and resentment, directed at God and soon at his brother.

The offering God accepts. We do not come to God with Abel’s lamb but by faith in the Lamb God provided, the one offering that makes any worshipper acceptable (Hebrews 10:10–14).

In everyday life. The story asks whether we give God our best or our leftovers, and it asks this of people to whom God gave his own Son.

Where Christians differ: why was Abel accepted? Some say because his offering was a blood sacrifice. This commentary’s view: Hebrews 11:4 says Abel offered by faith. He gave the firstborn and the best; Cain simply brought an offering. God looked at the offerer first, then the offering. Grain offerings were acceptable later (Leviticus 2).

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Cain, "Why are you angry, and why has your face fallen? If you do well, will you not be accepted? And if you do not do well, sin is crouching at the door. Its desire is for you, and you must rule over it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before Cain sins, God warns him: sin is crouching like a beast at his door, and he must master it.

Sin is crouching at the door. God reasons with Cain before he sins: the warning itself is grace. Sin crouches like a predator at the door. As in 3:16, “desire” here is a desire to master, and Cain must “rule” it instead. Sin wants to master you.

You must rule over it. Anger left unchecked opens the door to worse sin (Ephesians 4:26–27), and the believer masters it not by willpower but by the Spirit now living in him (Romans 8:13).

Uncertain wording. Two phrases are hard. “Be accepted” is literally “a lifting up”, perhaps of the face that has fallen (v. 5), or of acceptance and forgiveness. And a word related to “crouching” names, in Akkadian, a demon lurking at doorways; here it pictures sin as a beast waiting to spring. The overall sense is clear.

verseByVerse.quote: Cain spoke to Abel his brother. And when they were in the field, Cain rose up against his brother Abel and killed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Cain lures his brother into the field and kills him: within one generation of the fall, sin has become murder.

Cain rose up against his brother Abel. The victim is a brother: the word “brother” comes seven times in this chapter.

Why? John gives the reason: because Cain’s own deeds were evil and his brother’s righteous (1 John 3:12).

Does religion make people violent? Many people think so, and the first murder seems to agree: it follows an act of worship. Cain is no atheist. He brings an offering, and when his brother is accepted and he is not, he kills him. The Bible is honest that religion can turn deadly. But notice what kind of religion this is. Cain treats worship as a transaction: I bring something, so God owes me approval. When God does not pay, the brother who received grace becomes an insult, and resentment does the rest. Take God away and the pattern does not vanish. A few verses later Lamech boasts of killing with no religion in sight (v. 23), and the twentieth century’s godless regimes proved as murderous as any age of faith. The root is a heart that must win, before God or without him. What answers it is not less religion but grace, which cannot be earned and so need not be envied. In the gospel Cain’s story is turned inside out: the brother God accepts, Jesus, lets himself be killed by those who resent him, and his death becomes the very means by which they are welcomed (Romans 5:10).

Textual note. The Hebrew does not say what Cain said. The Samaritan Pentateuch, the Greek and other ancient versions add, “Let us go out to the field.” The ESV follows the Hebrew.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV gives the ancient versions’ reading in its note.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Cain, "Where is Abel your brother?" He said, "I do not know; am I my brother's keeper?" And the LORD said, "What have you done? The voice of your brother's blood is crying to me from the ground.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God confronts Cain with a question, and when Cain lies, God declares that he has heard Abel’s blood crying out.

Where is Abel your brother? The question echoes “Where are you?” (3:9): again God gives room to confess.

I do not know. Cain answers with a lie and a sneer, “am I my brother’s keeper?”, a sign of how fast sin hardens. The answer is yes: God expects us to care for one another.

The voice of your brother’s blood. Spilt blood cries out, and God hears injustice. No one who has been wronged goes unheard by him.

A better word. Jesus’ blood “speaks a better word than the blood of Abel” (Hebrews 12:24): Abel’s cried for justice; Christ’s cries for mercy, even for those who shed it.

verseByVerse.quote: And now you are cursed from the ground, which has opened its mouth to receive your brother's blood from your hand. When you work the ground, it shall no longer yield to you its strength. You shall be a fugitive and a wanderer on the earth."
verseByVerse.commentary: Cain is cursed: the ground that drank his brother’s blood will no longer yield to him, and he will be a restless wanderer. This time it is not the ground that is cursed, as in 3:17, but Cain himself, driven from the ground that witnessed his crime.

verseByVerse.quote: Cain said to the LORD, "My punishment is greater than I can bear. Behold, you have driven me today away from the ground, and from your face I shall be hidden. I shall be a fugitive and a wanderer on the earth, and whoever finds me will kill me." Then the LORD said to him, "Not so! If anyone kills Cain, vengeance shall be taken on him sevenfold." And the LORD put a mark on Cain, lest any who found him should attack him. Then Cain went away from the presence of the LORD and settled in the land of Nod, east of Eden.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Cain grieves his punishment, not his sin; yet God shows him mercy, marking him for protection, before he goes away from the LORD’s presence.

My punishment is greater than I can bear. Cain’s complaint is self-pity, not repentance: he grieves the penalty, not the sin. Yet the mark God gives him is protection, mercy even for a murderer.

Away from the presence of the LORD. The deepest punishment is the last: to go away from the presence of the LORD himself.

What it does not mean. The “mark of Cain” has been grievously misused to justify racism and slavery. The text says nothing of skin or race.

Uncertain wording. The word translated “punishment” can also mean guilt (the ESV margin gives “My guilt is too great to bear”), but the context, which speaks of what God has done to him, favours the ESV text. Nor are we told what the mark was: a sign on his body, or a sign given to him as a pledge. What matters is its purpose, protection.
verseByVerse.note: “Nod” means wandering (ESV note).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–26 — The Lines of Cain and Seth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Two lines go out from Adam: one builds a world without God, the other calls on his name. Cain’s line builds the first city and brings herding, music and metalwork into the world, real goods given by God’s kindness even to those who have turned from him (vv. 17–22). But it ends in Lamech, who takes two wives and sings of killing a young man and of revenge seventy-sevenfold (vv. 23–24). Then God gives Eve another son, Seth, in Abel’s place, and in the days of Seth’s son Enosh people begin to call on the name of the LORD (vv. 25–26). The promise of 3:15 is still alive.
verseByVerse.theology: Cain's line builds the first city and brings music and metalwork into the world. Seth is born in Abel's place.
verseByVerse.examples: Culture flourished even in the line under judgment, a gift of God's common kindness to the undeserving. And everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved (Rom. 10:13).

verseByVerse.quote: Cain knew his wife, and she conceived and bore Enoch. When he built a city, he called the name of the city after the name of his son, Enoch. To Enoch was born Irad, and Irad fathered Mehujael, and Mehujael fathered Methushael, and Methushael fathered Lamech. And Lamech took two wives. The name of the one was Adah, and the name of the other Zillah. Adah bore Jabal; he was the father of those who dwell in tents and have livestock. His brother's name was Jubal; he was the father of all those who play the lyre and pipe. Zillah also bore Tubal-cain; he was the forger of all instruments of bronze and iron. The sister of Tubal-cain was Naamah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Cain’s line builds the first city and gives the world herding, music and metalwork: real gifts, developed by people who have turned from God.

Cain knew his wife. Cain’s wife was a sister or other relative (5:4); marriage between close relatives was not yet forbidden (Leviticus 18).

He built a city. Sentenced to wander, Cain builds a city and names it after his son: security and a name of his own making, without God.

Culture in Cain’s line. Cities, music and technology are developed by Cain’s line. Culture is good, but it can be used without God. These are gifts of God’s common kindness to the undeserving (Matthew 5:45), and Christians may thank him for good music and fine craftsmanship whoever made them.

verseByVerse.quote: Lamech said to his wives: "Adah and Zillah, hear my voice; you wives of Lamech, listen to what I say: I have killed a man for wounding me, a young man for striking me. If Cain's revenge is sevenfold, then Lamech's is seventy-sevenfold."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lamech boasts to his wives of killing a man for a mere wound, and multiplies revenge beyond all limit.

Lamech’s is seventy-sevenfold. Lamech’s two wives are the first polygamy, a departure from God’s design (2:24). His song celebrates violence and multiplies revenge to seventy-seven times, turning God’s protection of Cain into a licence for himself.

Seventy-seven times. Jesus reverses Lamech, telling his people to forgive seventy-seven times (Matthew 18:22). The forgiven stop keeping score, forgiving “as God in Christ forgave you” (Ephesians 4:32).

verseByVerse.quote: And Adam knew his wife again, and she bore a son and called his name Seth, for she said, "God has appointed for me another offspring instead of Abel, for Cain killed him." To Seth also a son was born, and he called his name Enosh. At that time people began to call upon the name of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God gives Eve another son in Abel’s place, and in Seth’s line people begin to call on the name of the LORD: the promise lives on.

Another offspring. Eve calls Seth “another offspring”, using the word of the promise in 3:15. Cain has not destroyed God’s plan.

Call upon the name of the LORD. With Seth the godly line continues, and public worship begins as people call on the name of the LORD. Cain’s line ends in violence; Seth’s in prayer.

The line that leads to Christ. Luke traces Jesus’ ancestry back through this line, “the son of Seth, the son of Adam, the son of God” (Luke 3:38), and the prayer that began here is answered in him: “everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved” (Romans 10:13).
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “Seth” sounds like the Hebrew for “he appointed.”

4.theology:
Worship and the Heart. Acceptable worship is never merely formal. The problem with Cain was not his work or the material of his offering but his heart. The sacrificial law, the prophets' critique of hollow ritual (Amos 5:21–24; Isa. 1:11–17) and Jesus's own teaching (John 4:24) all flow from this: you cannot separate the offering from the offerer.

The Spread of Sin. Genesis 4 shows what theologians call total depravity: not that fallen humanity is as bad as it could be, but that sin corrupts every part of life. Broken fellowship with God (ch. 3) produces broken human relationships, and those produce an ever more violent culture (vv. 23–24). The flood is the end of a road this chapter has already mapped.
4.examples:
Then: For a people who had watched the righteous suffer in Egypt, the story answered real questions: God sees the heart, God protects even the guilty, and the line of faith survives every catastrophe.

Now: "Am I my brother's keeper?" Individualism answers no; the gospel answers yes, for Christ became our keeper at the cost of his life. The mark of Cain reminds us that even the guilty bear God's image and cannot simply be discarded. And verse 26 shows what the church is in every generation: not a triumphant majority but a people calling on the name of the One who alone can heal what Cain began.

keyVerse.quote: If you do well, will you not be accepted? And if you do not do well, sin is crouching at the door. Its desire is for you, and you must rule over it.
keyVerse.note: God speaks to Cain before the murder, warning him and offering him acceptance. The verse shows both how sin works, crouching and waiting to master us, and how patient God is with sinners; Cain’s refusal of this word is the turning point of the chapter. What Cain would not master, believers master not by willpower but by the Spirit of Christ (Romans 8:13).

4.reflection:
God accepted Abel and his offering but not Cain and his (vv. 3–5; Hebrews 11:4). What does this teach about the heart behind worship and giving? What would it look like for you to give God your best rather than your leftovers?

God warned Cain that sin was crouching at the door (v. 7). Where do resentment or envy crouch at your door, and how does the Spirit help us master them?

“Am I my brother’s keeper?” (v. 9). In what ways does God expect us to keep our brothers and sisters, in the church and beyond?

Lamech multiplies revenge; Jesus multiplies forgiveness (vv. 23–24; Matthew 18:22). Whom are you keeping score against, and how does the blood of Christ, which speaks a better word than Abel’s, free you to forgive?

5.title: The Book of the Generations of Adam
5.text: <sup>1</sup>This is the book of the generations of Adam. When God created man, he made him in the likeness of God.<sup>2</sup>Male and female he created them, and he blessed them and named them Man when they were created.<sup>3</sup>When Adam had lived 130 years, he fathered a son in his own likeness, after his image, and named him Seth.<sup>4</sup>The days of Adam after he fathered Seth were 800 years; and he had other sons and daughters.<sup>5</sup>Thus all the days that Adam lived were 930 years, and he died.<sup>6</sup>When Seth had lived 105 years, he fathered Enosh.<sup>7</sup>Seth lived after he fathered Enosh 807 years and had other sons and daughters.<sup>8</sup>Thus all the days of Seth were 912 years, and he died.<sup>9</sup>When Enosh had lived 90 years, he fathered Kenan.<sup>10</sup>Enosh lived after he fathered Kenan 815 years and had other sons and daughters.<sup>11</sup>Thus all the days of Enosh were 905 years, and he died.<sup>12</sup>When Kenan had lived 70 years, he fathered Mahalalel.<sup>13</sup>Kenan lived after he fathered Mahalalel 840 years and had other sons and daughters.<sup>14</sup>Thus all the days of Kenan were 910 years, and he died.<sup>15</sup>When Mahalalel had lived 65 years, he fathered Jared.<sup>16</sup>Mahalalel lived after he fathered Jared 830 years and had other sons and daughters.<sup>17</sup>Thus all the days of Mahalalel were 895 years, and he died.<sup>18</sup>When Jared had lived 162 years, he fathered Enoch.<sup>19</sup>Jared lived after he fathered Enoch 800 years and had other sons and daughters.<sup>20</sup>Thus all the days of Jared were 962 years, and he died.<sup>21</sup>When Enoch had lived 65 years, he fathered Methuselah.<sup>22</sup>Enoch walked with God after he fathered Methuselah 300 years and had other sons and daughters.<sup>23</sup>Thus all the days of Enoch were 365 years.<sup>24</sup>Enoch walked with God, and he was not, for God took him.<sup>25</sup>When Methuselah had lived 187 years, he fathered Lamech.<sup>26</sup>Methuselah lived after he fathered Lamech 782 years and had other sons and daughters.<sup>27</sup>Thus all the days of Methuselah were 969 years, and he died.<sup>28</sup>When Lamech had lived 182 years, he fathered a son<sup>29</sup>and called his name Noah, saying, "Out of the ground that the LORD has cursed, this one shall bring us relief from our work and from the painful toil of our hands."<sup>30</sup>Lamech lived after he fathered Noah 595 years and had other sons and daughters.<sup>31</sup>Thus all the days of Lamech were 777 years, and he died.<sup>32</sup>After Noah was 500 years old, Noah fathered Shem, Ham, and Japheth.
5.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 4 ended with two lines of descent: Cain’s, ending in Lamech’s song of vengeance (4:17–24), and Seth’s, in whose days “people began to call upon the name of the LORD” (4:26). Chapter 5 opens the second “generations” section of the book (see the introduction) and follows Seth’s line through ten generations to Noah.

The message. Death now reigns over everyone, exactly as God said it would, but it does not have the last word. The chapter tolls “and he died” eight times over men made in God’s likeness, so that no one can call death natural. Yet through it God keeps the line of promise unbroken, takes one man who walked with him without his dying, and gives a father hope that relief from the curse is coming.

Why it was said. Israel’s neighbours told of kings before the flood who reigned for tens of thousands of years; Genesis gives real men long lives and then buries every one of them but the man who walked with God. Israel in the wilderness, where a whole generation would die (Numbers 14:29), needed to know that death is the judgment on sin, and that their God had kept his promised line alive through it (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. The heading recalls creation: man made in God’s likeness and blessed (vv. 1–2). Then the refrain begins: he lived, he fathered, he died (vv. 3–20). Enoch, the seventh from Adam, breaks the pattern: he walks with God and is taken (vv. 21–24). Methuselah, the longest-lived of all, dies in the year of the flood (vv. 25–27). Lamech names his son Noah in hope of rest from the curse (vv. 28–31), and the list ends with Noah’s three sons, the fathers of the nations (v. 32).

Where it leads. The chapter does not prophesy Christ; it leads to him by the need it exposes and by the promise it carries. Only someone stronger than death can answer it. This is the line of the woman’s offspring promised in 3:15: Luke traces Jesus back through these very names to “the son of Seth, the son of Adam, the son of God” (Luke 3:38). Enoch’s taking is a first glimpse that God can bring a man past death, and Lamech’s longing for rest is answered in the one who gives rest to the weary (Matthew 11:28). The funeral bell is finally silenced by the one who died and rose: “For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive” (1 Corinthians 15:22).

For us. Every name here was a real life, and every one ended; yours will too, unless Christ returns first. Do not avoid the subject; let it send you to the one who has beaten death. And Enoch shows that an ordinary family life can be a daily walk with God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–32 — The Generations from Adam to Noah
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Death reigns over everyone descended from Adam, yet God keeps his line of promise alive through it. The genealogy bridges the first stories and the flood, moving from Adam to Noah in ten generations. Its refrain tolls like a funeral bell: he lived, he fathered, and he died (vv. 3–20). Twice the rhythm breaks. Enoch walks with God and is taken without dying (vv. 21–24), and Lamech names his son Noah in hope that relief from the curse is coming (vv. 28–31). Between them Methuselah, the longest-lived of all, dies in the year of the flood (vv. 25–27), and the list ends with Noah’s three sons, from whom the nations will come (v. 32).
verseByVerse.theology: Ten generations run from Adam to Noah. Enoch walks with God and is taken, and the list ends on Noah, whose father hoped he would bring relief from the cursed ground.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the long lives of the first generations did not outrun the sentence of 2:17. Now: Enoch's exception points to a God who is stronger than the drumbeat of death.

verseByVerse.quote: This is the book of the generations of Adam. When God created man, he made him in the likeness of God. Male and female he created them, and he blessed them and named them Man when they were created.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Human beings remain God’s image-bearers after the fall, which is why the deaths that follow are a tragedy and not simply nature.

The book of the generations of Adam. “The book” is a written record, and this heading opens the second of the book’s “generations” sections (see the introduction), linking Adam to Noah. Its opening recalls that God made man in his likeness and blessed him (1:27–28), and the image remains after the fall (9:6; James 3:9).

Named them Man. The name Adam means humanity, both male and female: what is said of the first man is said of the race he heads.

verseByVerse.quote: When Adam had lived 130 years, he fathered a son in his own likeness, after his image, and named him Seth. The days of Adam after he fathered Seth were 800 years; and he had other sons and daughters. Thus all the days that Adam lived were 930 years, and he died.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Adam passes on God’s image to his son, marred now by his own fall, and then he dies exactly as God had warned.

In his own likeness, after his image. The words of 1:26 return, but now it is Adam’s likeness: Seth bears his father’s image, fallen nature included (Romans 5:12).

And he died. The refrain of the chapter begins: God’s word in 2:17 has come true. Adam lived 930 years, but the serpent’s “You will not surely die” (3:4) was a lie all the same; the long delay was mercy, not escape.

Where Christians differ: the long lifespans. Some take them as symbolic, or as the reigns of clans. This commentary’s view: the text presents them as real lives, gradually shortening after the flood as the effects of sin take hold. We need not explain how.

verseByVerse.quote: When Seth had lived 105 years, he fathered Enosh. Seth lived after he fathered Enosh 807 years and had other sons and daughters. Thus all the days of Seth were 912 years, and he died. When Enosh had lived 90 years, he fathered Kenan. Enosh lived after he fathered Kenan 815 years and had other sons and daughters. Thus all the days of Enosh were 905 years, and he died. When Kenan had lived 70 years, he fathered Mahalalel. Kenan lived after he fathered Mahalalel 840 years and had other sons and daughters. Thus all the days of Kenan were 910 years, and he died. When Mahalalel had lived 65 years, he fathered Jared. Mahalalel lived after he fathered Jared 830 years and had other sons and daughters. Thus all the days of Mahalalel were 895 years, and he died.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Generation after generation lives, raises children and dies: the sentence of death reaches everyone.

And he died. Each entry has the same pattern: he lived, he fathered, he died. Each life matters to God, and each ends. “Death reigned from Adam to Moses” (Romans 5:14), and the chapter makes you hear it reign.

Where Christians differ: gaps and dates. Archbishop Ussher used these numbers to date creation to 4004 BC. Others note that Hebrew genealogies sometimes skip generations (compare Matthew 1:8 with 1 Chronicles 3:11–12). This commentary’s view: the genealogies are true history, but may not be complete chronologies. Gaps of a few generations do not stretch the line across vast ages, and with the six ordinary days of Genesis 1 they point to a young creation (see on 1:5). Faithful Christians who hold an old earth differ here in good conscience, and are brothers.

Textual note. The Greek Old Testament and Samaritan Pentateuch give different ages from the Hebrew in this chapter. The ESV follows the Hebrew.

verseByVerse.quote: When Jared had lived 162 years, he fathered Enoch. Jared lived after he fathered Enoch 800 years and had other sons and daughters. Thus all the days of Jared were 962 years, and he died. When Enoch had lived 65 years, he fathered Methuselah. Enoch walked with God after he fathered Methuselah 300 years and had other sons and daughters. Thus all the days of Enoch were 365 years. Enoch walked with God, and he was not, for God took him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In a world under death, Enoch lived in close friendship with God, and God took him to himself without his dying.

Enoch walked with God. Enoch is the only man in the list described by his relationship with God and not just his years, and the phrase comes twice. To walk with God is close, daily fellowship. Enoch did it “after he fathered Methuselah”, while raising sons and daughters: it is possible in ordinary family life, not only in withdrawal from it.

The seventh from Adam. Jude calls Enoch “the seventh from Adam” (Jude 14). Cain’s line also had a seventh, Lamech, who boasted that he had killed a man and would be avenged seventy-sevenfold (4:23–24). The two show the two ways: one man taking vengeance for himself, the other walking with God. Jude adds that Enoch prophesied judgment on the ungodly (Jude 14–15).

God took him. Then the pattern breaks. There is no “and he died”: God took him without dying, as later he took Elijah (2 Kings 2:11). “By faith Enoch was taken up so that he should not see death”, and before that he was commended as having pleased God, which no one does without faith (Hebrews 11:5–6). Enoch is a sign that death will not have the last word.

Better than Enoch’s escape. Christ went down into death and came out again, so for those who belong to him death has become what it was for Enoch: being taken by God to be with him (Philippians 1:23).

What it does not mean. Not a spectacular life: we are told nothing about Enoch except that he walked with God and had children. Most faithful lives look like that from the outside.
verseByVerse.note: The Greek Old Testament reads “pleased God” and “was not found” (ESV notes), the wording Hebrews uses.

verseByVerse.quote: When Methuselah had lived 187 years, he fathered Lamech. Methuselah lived after he fathered Lamech 782 years and had other sons and daughters. Thus all the days of Methuselah were 969 years, and he died.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even the longest life ends in death, and Methuselah’s ended in the year God’s long patience ran out.

All the days of Methuselah were 969 years. Methuselah lives longest of all, and still “he died”. By the Hebrew numbers he died in the year of the flood: God’s patience had been long, and Methuselah’s life measures it.

Does his name predict the flood? The popular claim that his name means “when he dies, it will come” is not well founded; the point rests on the numbers, not the name.
verseByVerse.note: The year follows from adding the ages given in vv. 25–28 and 7:6.

verseByVerse.quote: When Lamech had lived 182 years, he fathered a son and called his name Noah, saying, "Out of the ground that the LORD has cursed, this one shall bring us relief from our work and from the painful toil of our hands." Lamech lived after he fathered Noah 595 years and had other sons and daughters. Thus all the days of Lamech were 777 years, and he died.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lamech names his son Noah in hope that God will bring relief from the curse on the ground, a hope God will begin to answer through him.

Called his name Noah. Lamech names his son Noah, which sounds like “rest”, and explains it with a similar-sounding word, “relief” or “comfort”: he longs for the curse on the ground to be lifted (3:17). This is a different Lamech from the violent man of 4:23: that one boasted of what he would do; this one hopes in what the LORD will do.

Rest for the weary. Noah did not end the curse, though through him God promised never again to curse the ground because of man (8:21). Lamech’s longing for rest from toil is everyone’s, and it is fully answered only in Christ: “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28). One day the creation itself “will be set free from its bondage to corruption” (Romans 8:21).
verseByVerse.note: The name may also echo the Hebrew for “relief” or “comfort”.

verseByVerse.quote: After Noah was 500 years old, Noah fathered Shem, Ham, and Japheth.
verseByVerse.commentary: Through Noah’s three sons the whole human race will continue after the flood. Shem, Ham and Japheth are the ancestors of all the nations listed in chapter 10, so every reader of Genesis descends from one of them. Shem is named first, and through him the line of promise runs on to Abraham (11:10–26).

5.theology:
Death as Theological Fact. The genealogy is history that makes an argument: death is real, universal and unnatural, not the way things were meant to be. That is the ground of the Christian hope: death is not merely hard but wrong, and Christ's resurrection begins its reversal, for "the last enemy to be destroyed is death" (1 Cor. 15:26).

Walking with God. Enoch's walk (vv. 22, 24) is the Old Testament’s shortest description of the life of faith: not spectacular achievement but a whole life turned toward God, by faith (Heb. 11:5–6). The New Testament calls it walking "by the Spirit" (Gal. 5:16), "in the light" (1 John 1:7) and "worthy of the Lord" (Colossians 1:10). His being taken does not show that such a life earns immortality, but that the God with whom he walked is the God who raises the dead.
5.examples:
Then: Ancient king lists gave pre-flood kings reigns of tens of thousands of years as a mark of divine favour. Genesis 5 uses the form and overturns it: the long-lived patriarchs all die.

Now: A culture invested in anti-ageing and in outrunning death is told plainly: you cannot. The only way past death runs through the One who walked into it and out the other side.

keyVerse.quote: Enoch walked with God, and he was not, for God took him.
keyVerse.note: In a chapter that tolls “and he died” eight times, this is the one life that ends differently. It shows that the life of faith is a daily walk with God, and that the God who walks with his people can carry them beyond death. It is the chapter’s window onto the hope Christ has opened for all who belong to him.

5.reflection:
The chapter repeats “and he died” eight times. Why do you think Genesis wants us to feel the weight of death rather than hurry past it? How does our culture avoid thinking about death, and how do you?

Enoch walked with God while raising a family, through years of ordinary days. What would walking with God look like in your actual week, at home and at work?

The two Lamechs (4:23–24; 5:29) show two ways of living in a cursed world: taking vengeance for yourself, or hoping in God for relief. Where are you tempted to take matters into your own hands rather than wait for God?

Jesus said, “everyone who lives and believes in me shall never die” (John 11:26). How does his resurrection change the way you face your own death, or grieve for someone else?

6.title: Noah Found Favor in the Eyes of the LORD
6.text: <sup>1</sup>When man began to multiply on the face of the land and daughters were born to them,<sup>2</sup>the sons of God saw that the daughters of man were attractive. And they took as their wives any they chose.<sup>3</sup>Then the LORD said, "My Spirit shall not abide in man forever, for he is flesh: his days shall be 120 years."<sup>4</sup>The Nephilim were on the earth in those days, and also afterward, when the sons of God came in to the daughters of man and they bore children to them. These were the mighty men who were of old, the men of renown.<sup>5</sup>The LORD saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every intention of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually.<sup>6</sup>And the LORD regretted that he had made man on the earth, and it grieved him to his heart.<sup>7</sup>So the LORD said, "I will blot out man whom I have created from the face of the land, man and animals and creeping things and birds of the heavens, for I am sorry that I have made them."<sup>8</sup>But Noah found favor in the eyes of the LORD.<sup>9</sup>These are the generations of Noah. Noah was a righteous man, blameless in his generation. Noah walked with God.<sup>10</sup>And Noah had three sons, Shem, Ham, and Japheth.<sup>11</sup>Now the earth was corrupt in God's sight, and the earth was filled with violence.<sup>12</sup>And God saw the earth, and behold, it was corrupt, for all flesh had corrupted their way on the earth.<sup>13</sup>And God said to Noah, "I have determined to make an end of all flesh, for the earth is filled with violence through them. Behold, I will destroy them with the earth.<sup>14</sup>Make yourself an ark of gopher wood. Make rooms in the ark, and cover it inside and out with pitch.<sup>15</sup>This is how you are to make it: the length of the ark 300 cubits, its breadth 50 cubits, and its height 30 cubits.<sup>16</sup>Make a roof for the ark, and finish it to a cubit above, and set the door of the ark in its side. Make it with lower, second, and third decks.<sup>17</sup>For behold, I will bring a flood of waters upon the earth to destroy all flesh in which is the breath of life under heaven. Everything that is on the earth shall die.<sup>18</sup>But I will establish my covenant with you, and you shall come into the ark, you, your sons, your wife, and your sons' wives with you.<sup>19</sup>And of every living thing of all flesh, you shall bring two of every sort into the ark to keep them alive with you. They shall be male and female.<sup>20</sup>Of the birds according to their kinds, and of the animals according to their kinds, of every creeping thing of the ground, according to its kind, two of every sort shall come in to you to keep them alive.<sup>21</sup>Also take with you every sort of food that is eaten, and store it up. It shall serve as food for you and for them."<sup>22</sup>Noah did this; he did all that God commanded him.
6.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 5 ended with Noah, born to a father who hoped he would bring relief from the curse. Chapter 6 shows why relief is needed: sin, which began with one act in a garden and one murder in a field, now fills the earth. Verses 1–8 close the “generations of Adam”, and verse 9 opens “the generations of Noah”.

The message. God sees the whole truth about the human heart, is grieved by it to his own heart, and will judge it; yet in the same breath he shows grace to one man and provides a way of rescue. Judgment and grace are not rival moods in God. The holy God who will not shrug at violence is the God who builds an ark into his judgment.

Why it was said. Israel knew flood stories in which the gods destroyed mankind for being too noisy (see the introduction). Genesis tells it differently: one God, grieved by real wickedness, judging justly and saving by covenant grace. Israel, about to enter a land full of corruption, needed to know that God sees, that he judges, and that he keeps a people for himself by grace.

How the chapter makes its case. Boundaries are broken as the sons of God take the daughters of man, and God sets a limit to his patience (vv. 1–4). God’s verdict follows: every intention of the human heart is evil, and he is grieved and resolves to blot out what he made (vv. 5–7). “But Noah found favor” (v. 8): grace comes first, and Noah’s righteous walk stands out against a world filled with violence (vv. 9–12). God tells Noah of the ark that will carry him through the coming end, binds himself by covenant and gathers the animals (vv. 13–21), and Noah does all that God commands (v. 22).

Where it leads. The chapter leads to Christ by pattern and by revealing the character of God. Jesus took “the days of Noah” as the pattern of his own coming (Matthew 24:37–39), and Peter saw in the ark, which carried eight people safely through the waters, the pattern of salvation in Christ (1 Peter 3:20–21). God’s grief and justice meet finally at the cross, where in his Son he went under his own judgment. Noah found grace in the eyes of the LORD; sinners find it in Jesus, the one door to safety: “I am the door. If anyone enters by me, he will be saved” (John 10:9).

For us. Verse 5 is a verdict on us as well as on Noah’s world, and no programme of self-improvement answers it. The answer is to go where Noah went, into the refuge God has provided, which is Christ. And then, like Noah, to live by God’s word before the world sees it proved, even when the world thinks you foolish.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — The Corruption of the Earth and the Call of Noah
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Sin has filled the earth and God will judge it, but he shows grace to Noah and provides a way of rescue. The chapter opens with boundaries broken, as the sons of God take the daughters of man and God limits man’s days (vv. 1–4). Then comes God’s verdict: every intention of the human heart is evil, and he is grieved to his heart and resolves to blot out what he made (vv. 5–7). “But Noah found favor” (v. 8): grace comes first, and Noah’s righteous walk stands out against a world of violence (vv. 9–12). God tells him of the ark and his covenant (vv. 13–21), and Noah does all that God commands (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: The earth fills with corruption and violence until the LORD is grieved to his heart and resolves to blot out man. But God covenants with Noah and commands the ark.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Noah built for years for a judgment nobody else believed in. Now: grace comes first and righteousness follows, as verse 8 comes before verse 9.

verseByVerse.quote: When man began to multiply on the face of the land and daughters were born to them, the sons of God saw that the daughters of man were attractive. And they took as their wives any they chose. Then the LORD said, "My Spirit shall not abide in man forever, for he is flesh: his days shall be 120 years." The Nephilim were on the earth in those days, and also afterward, when the sons of God came in to the daughters of man and they bore children to them. These were the mighty men who were of old, the men of renown.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As humanity multiplied, the boundaries God had set were broken, and God set a limit to how long he would bear with it. The passage is hard, but its point is clear: evil was growing, and judgment was coming.

Saw … took. The words echo Eve in the garden, who “saw that the tree was good” and took (3:6). Desire, not God’s word, decides.

His days shall be 120 years. The 120 years are either a shortened lifespan or a countdown to the flood. Many think the second fits better, since people lived far longer than 120 years after the flood (11:10–25), and Peter speaks of God’s patience waiting “in the days of Noah, while the ark was being prepared” (1 Peter 3:20). Either way, God will not bear with sin for ever.

The mighty men … the men of renown. Literally “men of the name”. They made a name for themselves, as the builders of Babel will try to do (11:4); God will give Abraham a great name as a gift (12:2). Their fame is forgotten; the name above every name belongs to the one who humbled himself (Philippians 2:8–9).

Where Christians differ: the sons of God. Some see fallen angels (Jude 6; 2 Peter 2:4); some the godly line of Seth marrying into Cain’s ungodly line; some tyrant kings, since “sons of God” could be a title for rulers and “any they chose” sounds like a royal harem. This commentary’s view: the question is genuinely hard, and this commentary gives no verdict. The angel view is ancient and has New Testament support; the Sethite view fits these chapters’ focus on two lines and avoids angels marrying (Matthew 22:30). Either way, the boundaries God set were broken, and evil grew.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew verb in v. 3 is uncertain: “abide in”, “strive with” or “contend with” man. “Nephilim” may mean “fallen ones” or simply “giants” (see the verse note); who they were is unknown beyond this verse and the spies’ report in Numbers 13:33, where the name is used of giants in Canaan.
verseByVerse.note: “Nephilim” is rendered “giants” in the ESV note.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every intention of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually. And the LORD regretted that he had made man on the earth, and it grieved him to his heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God sees the whole truth about the human heart, that it is bent on evil all the time, and it grieves him to his heart.

The LORD saw. In chapter 1 God saw all he had made and it was very good (1:31); now he sees wickedness everywhere. The words pile up: every intention, of the thoughts, of his heart, only evil, continually. Sin reaches every part of a person, which is what theologians mean by total depravity (Jeremiah 17:9; Romans 3:10–18): not that people are as bad as they could be, but that nothing in us is untouched.

It grieved him to his heart. God is not indifferent to sin; he is grieved by it. The word translated “regretted” is the word behind “relief” in Noah’s name (5:29), a wordplay that ties the two chapters together: Lamech hoped for comfort, and it is God who grieves.

Would a loving God ever judge? To many people the flood is the clearest case against the God of the Old Testament: surely love would let things go. (On the wider question of “the angry God”, see the note on Exodus 34:6–7.) But look at what provokes it: the earth “filled with violence” (v. 11). We do not admire a judge who shrugs at violence, or a parent who watches a child being harmed and feels nothing. A love that is never angry at what destroys the beloved is not a deeper love but a thinner one, and our own outrage at cruelty is a small reflection of God’s grief. What we really struggle with is that he judges us too, not only the people we would put in the dock; Genesis will not let anyone stand outside verse 5. Yet the same chapter has an ark. And Jesus spoke of his coming death as “a baptism to be baptized with” (Luke 12:50): the waters of judgment would close over him. The God who grieved over the flood went under it himself, so that all who are in him pass through.

Where Christians differ: did God change his mind? Open theists, who hold that God does not know the future choices of free creatures, take “regretted” to mean God did not know what would happen. This commentary’s view: God does not change his mind as humans do (Numbers 23:19; 1 Samuel 15:29). Scripture speaks of God in human terms to show his real grief at sin, without denying his knowledge or purpose.

verseByVerse.quote: So the LORD said, "I will blot out man whom I have created from the face of the land, man and animals and creeping things and birds of the heavens, for I am sorry that I have made them." But Noah found favor in the eyes of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God resolves to wipe out the world he made, but one man receives his undeserved favour.

I will blot out man. God resolves to blot out the world in judgment, and the animals with it, because man was set over them (1:28) and what he ruled shares his fall (Romans 8:20).

But Noah. The turning point. Noah found favour, literally “found grace”, and grace is named before Noah’s righteousness is described (v. 9). He was not spared because he was better than others; he became what he was because grace had found him. Every rescue in Scripture turns on a “but” like this one, down to “But God, being rich in mercy” (Ephesians 2:4).
verseByVerse.note: This is the first time the Bible uses the word “favor” (grace).

verseByVerse.quote: These are the generations of Noah. Noah was a righteous man, blameless in his generation. Noah walked with God. And Noah had three sons, Shem, Ham, and Japheth. Now the earth was corrupt in God's sight, and the earth was filled with violence. And God saw the earth, and behold, it was corrupt, for all flesh had corrupted their way on the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Noah lived a righteous life with God in a world that had become corrupt and violent.

Righteous … blameless … walked with God. Righteous means right with God and living rightly; blameless means whole, a man of integrity, not sinless (9:21 will show that). Noah is righteous by faith (Hebrews 11:7), and like Enoch he walks with God (5:22). Grace found him first (v. 8), and the same grace lets you walk with God in a corrupt world.

Corrupt … filled with violence. “Corrupt” comes three times in two verses: the earth was spoiled, ruined. When God says “I will destroy them” (v. 13), it is the same Hebrew verb: he will ruin what they have already ruined. Judgment fits the crime. And the sin named is violence: Cain’s murder has become the way of the world.

verseByVerse.quote: And God said to Noah, "I have determined to make an end of all flesh, for the earth is filled with violence through them. Behold, I will destroy them with the earth. Make yourself an ark of gopher wood. Make rooms in the ark, and cover it inside and out with pitch. This is how you are to make it: the length of the ark 300 cubits, its breadth 50 cubits, and its height 30 cubits. Make a roof for the ark, and finish it to a cubit above, and set the door of the ark in its side. Make it with lower, second, and third decks.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God tells Noah plainly that judgment is coming, and in the same breath tells him how to be saved from it.

Make yourself an ark. God warns before he strikes, and the years of building made Noah “a herald of righteousness” to his neighbours (2 Peter 2:5). The ark is a huge box built to float, not to sail: no rudder, no mast, its course in God’s hands (on its size see the verse note and Cubit). The Hebrew word appears only once more in the Bible, for the basket that carried the baby Moses on the Nile (Exodus 2:3): both times God brings his chosen one safely through the waters in a box sealed with pitch.

Pitch. The word comes from a root meaning to cover, the same root later used for atonement, God’s covering of sin. The ark is not said to be a symbol of atonement, but the picture is apt: it was covered so that the waters could not get in, and Christ covers his people so that judgment cannot reach them.

Uncertain wording. “Gopher wood” occurs only here, and no one knows what tree it was; perhaps cypress. The word translated “roof” in v. 16 is also rare: it may mean a roof, or an opening for light beneath it, as older translations took it (“window”).
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that a cubit was about 18 inches, so the ark was about 450 by 75 by 45 feet.

verseByVerse.quote: For behold, I will bring a flood of waters upon the earth to destroy all flesh in which is the breath of life under heaven. Everything that is on the earth shall die. But I will establish my covenant with you, and you shall come into the ark, you, your sons, your wife, and your sons' wives with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will send a flood that destroys every living thing, but he binds himself by covenant to save Noah and his family.

I will bring a flood of waters. In Hebrew the “I” is emphatic: the flood is no natural disaster but God’s own act of judgment.

I will establish my covenant. This is the first time the word “covenant” appears in the Bible.

What a covenant is. We tend to hear “covenant” as an old word for a contract, and contracts are about protecting yourself: if you fail to deliver, I am released. A covenant in Scripture is a binding relationship in which someone pledges himself by solemn promise, and here it is God who binds himself. Noah has signed nothing and bargained for nothing; God simply says, “I will establish my covenant with you.” Most of us relate to God like a nervous party to a contract, wondering whether we have done enough. The covenant runs the other way, and it reaches its full meaning at a supper table, when Jesus lifts the cup and says, “This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood” (Luke 22:20). God did not only promise; he paid. So at the Lord’s Supper, or lying awake unsure where you stand, rest on what he has bound himself to, not on how well you have kept your side. See Covenant in the Theological Dictionary.

Where Christians differ: global or local? Some hold a worldwide flood; others a regional one covering the world known to Noah. This commentary’s view: the language of the text is universal, and the New Testament treats the flood as a real judgment on the world (2 Peter 3:6). Christians differ in good conscience on its extent, but all must affirm it as a real event.
verseByVerse.note: In Scripture a covenant is a binding promise God makes and keeps.

verseByVerse.quote: And of every living thing of all flesh, you shall bring two of every sort into the ark to keep them alive with you. They shall be male and female. Of the birds according to their kinds, and of the animals according to their kinds, of every creeping thing of the ground, according to its kind, two of every sort shall come in to you to keep them alive. Also take with you every sort of food that is eaten, and store it up. It shall serve as food for you and for them." Noah did this; he did all that God commanded him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God preserves the animals with Noah, and Noah obeys every word before he has seen a drop of rain.

Two of every sort. Two of every sort go in, male and female, to keep life going, and seven pairs of the clean animals (7:2). God is saving his creation, not only humanity, and he brings the animals himself: they “shall come in to you” (v. 20).

He did all that God commanded him. Noah does all that God commands without having seen a flood: “warned by God concerning events as yet unseen”, he built (Hebrews 11:7). Faith acts on God’s word. There is one ark, with one door, and safety only in what God has provided (1 Peter 3:20–21). Obey God’s word even when the world thinks you foolish.

How could they all fit? The ark was very large (see on vv. 13–16), and “according to their kinds” need not mean every species we name today. The text does not explain the logistics; it presents the gathering and keeping of the animals as God’s work.

6.theology:
The Grief of God. Verse 6 shows a personal God whose fellowship with humanity involves real pain when it is violated. Christian teaching rightly says both that God is not driven or overcome by passions as we are, and that he truly responds to his creation. The cross is the final statement: God's answer to sin was not detached judgment but the Father's gift and the Son's suffering.

The Ark as a Picture of Christ. Peter treats the ark as a pattern (1 Pet. 3:20–21): as Noah's family was saved through water while the world perished, so baptism, the sign of union with Christ, points to salvation through the death and resurrection of the One who bore judgment for us. The ark does not escape judgment but carries its passengers through it; Christ goes through death with his people and out the other side.
6.examples:
Then: Memory of a great flood was widespread in the ancient world (notably the Gilgamesh epic). In Genesis the flood is not the whim of gods disturbed by human noise but the just response of the one holy God to universal corruption, tempered by grace for one family.

Now: Verse 5 sounds extreme to people taught to think well of human nature, but the twentieth century's genocides and gulags bear it out. And verse 8 is what every generation needs: not a better plan for self-improvement but a God who steps in with grace.

keyVerse.quote: But Noah found favor in the eyes of the LORD.
keyVerse.note: After God’s verdict on the whole race (vv. 5–7), this short sentence turns the story. Grace is named before anything is said of Noah’s goodness (v. 9): God’s favour found him first. Every rescue that follows in Scripture, and finally the gospel itself, keeps that order.

6.reflection:
Verse 5 says every intention of the human heart was only evil continually. Do you find that hard to believe, about the world or about yourself? Why does it matter that we take this diagnosis seriously?

God is grieved to his heart by sin (v. 6), and he also judges it (v. 7). Why do we need a God who does both? What would be lost if he did only one?

“Noah found favor” (v. 8) comes before “Noah was a righteous man” (v. 9). How does that order shape the way you think about your own obedience?

Noah built for years on God’s word alone while his neighbours carried on as normal. Where does following Christ make you look foolish to the people around you, and what helps you keep building?

7.title: The Flood
7.text: <sup>1</sup>Then the LORD said to Noah, "Go into the ark, you and all your household, for I have seen that you are righteous before me in this generation.<sup>2</sup>Take with you seven pairs of all clean animals, the male and his mate, and a pair of the animals that are not clean, the male and his mate,<sup>3</sup>and seven pairs of the birds of the heavens also, male and female, to keep their offspring alive on the face of all the earth.<sup>4</sup>For in seven days I will send rain on the earth forty days and forty nights, and every living thing that I have made I will blot out from the face of the ground."<sup>5</sup>And Noah did all that the LORD had commanded him.<sup>6</sup>Noah was six hundred years old when the flood of waters came upon the earth.<sup>7</sup>And Noah and his sons and his wife and his sons' wives with him went into the ark to escape the waters of the flood.<sup>8</sup>Of clean animals, and of animals that are not clean, and of birds, and of everything that creeps on the ground,<sup>9</sup>two and two, male and female, went into the ark with Noah, as God had commanded Noah.<sup>10</sup>And after seven days the waters of the flood came upon the earth.<sup>11</sup>In the six hundredth year of Noah's life, in the second month, on the seventeenth day of the month, on that day all the fountains of the great deep burst forth, and the windows of the heavens were opened.<sup>12</sup>And rain fell upon the earth forty days and forty nights.<sup>13</sup>On the very same day Noah and his sons, Shem and Ham and Japheth, and Noah's wife and the three wives of his sons with them entered the ark,<sup>14</sup>they and every beast, according to its kind, and all the livestock according to their kinds, and every creeping thing that creeps on the earth, according to its kind, and every bird, according to its kind, every winged creature.<sup>15</sup>They went into the ark with Noah, two and two of all flesh in which there was the breath of life.<sup>16</sup>And those that entered, male and female of all flesh, went in as God had commanded him. And the LORD shut him in.<sup>17</sup>The flood continued forty days on the earth.
