The waters increased and bore up the ark, and it rose high above the earth.<sup>18</sup>The waters prevailed and increased greatly on the earth, and the ark floated on the face of the waters.<sup>19</sup>And the waters prevailed so mightily on the earth that all the high mountains under the whole heaven were covered.<sup>20</sup>The waters prevailed above the mountains, covering them fifteen cubits deep.<sup>21</sup>And all flesh died that moved on the earth, birds, livestock, beasts, all swarming creatures that swarm on the earth, and all mankind.<sup>22</sup>Everything on the dry land in whose nostrils was the breath of life died.<sup>23</sup>He blotted out every living thing that was on the face of the ground, man and animals and creeping things and birds of the heavens. They were blotted out from the earth. Only Noah was left, and those who were with him in the ark.<sup>24</sup>And the waters prevailed on the earth 150 days.
7.overview:
Where we are. In chapter 6 God announced the flood, gave Noah the plan of the ark and bound himself by covenant, and Noah did all he was told. Now comes the flood itself: seven days’ warning, the entry into the ark, and the waters rising over the earth, until the story turns at 8:1.

The message. God’s judgment on sin is real, total and on time, and his salvation in the middle of it is just as real: the waters that destroy everything outside the ark lift those inside. Salvation is God’s work from start to finish. He calls Noah in, brings the animals, and with his own hand shuts the door.

Why it was said. In the Babylonian flood stories the gods are frightened by the flood they have unleashed and regret it when they go hungry for offerings (see the introduction). Here the one God sends the waters at the hour he named and rules them throughout. Israel, who would pass through the Red Sea and watch Egypt’s army drown, needed to know this God: he controls the waters, judges at his appointed time, and keeps his own safe.

How the chapter makes its case. God calls Noah into the ark and gives the world seven days (vv. 1–5). The entry is told twice, with Noah’s age and the very day, as real history (vv. 6–16): the fountains of the deep burst and the windows of heaven open, creation runs backwards, and “the LORD shut him in” (v. 16). The waters rise above the mountains, and the ark rises with them (vv. 17–20). Everything outside dies; only Noah and those with him are left (vv. 21–23), while the waters prevail 150 days (v. 24).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern, a pattern Jesus and the apostles drew themselves. “As were the days of Noah, so will be the coming of the Son of Man” (Matthew 24:37): the flood is a preview of the final judgment. Peter saw the eight brought safely through water as corresponding to baptism, which saves “through the resurrection of Jesus Christ” (1 Peter 3:20–21). The deepest likeness is this: the ark took the full force of the waters, and those inside were safe. At the cross Christ took the full force of judgment, so that those in him are safe, held by the same hand that shut Noah in (John 10:28).

For us. The flood came on people “eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage” (Matthew 24:38). Ordinary life was not their danger; ignoring God’s warning in the middle of it was. Make sure you are in Christ. And if you are, rest: the one who shut the door is holding it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–24 — The Flood: Judgment and Preservation
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s judgment on sin falls exactly as he said, and in the midst of it he keeps safe those he has shut in. Noah is called into the ark and given seven days’ warning (vv. 1–5). The entry is told twice, with Noah’s age and the very day, as real history, and that history is the ground of the flood’s meaning throughout Scripture (vv. 6–16). The fountains of the deep burst and the windows of heaven open, undoing the order of creation, and the LORD himself shuts the door. The waters rise above the highest mountains, lifting the ark as they destroy (vv. 17–20). Everything outside dies; only Noah and those with him remain (vv. 21–24).
verseByVerse.theology: Noah goes in with his family and the animals, and the waters prevail for 150 days. Everything outside the ark dies.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the same waters that destroyed the world bore up the ark. Now: Jesus warned that his coming will be like the days of Noah (Matt. 24:37–39), and safety lies in being in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Noah, "Go into the ark, you and all your household, for I have seen that you are righteous before me in this generation. Take with you seven pairs of all clean animals, the male and his mate, and a pair of the animals that are not clean, the male and his mate, and seven pairs of the birds of the heavens also, male and female, to keep their offspring alive on the face of all the earth. For in seven days I will send rain on the earth forty days and forty nights, and every living thing that I have made I will blot out from the face of the ground." And Noah did all that the LORD had commanded him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God calls Noah and his household into the ark, gives the world one last week, and Noah again obeys.

Go into the ark, you and all your household. The Hebrew verb can mean “come” as well as “go”, and older translations have “Come into the ark”: the God who sends the flood calls his people into safety.

You are righteous before me. God counts Noah righteous, with the righteousness “that comes by faith” (Hebrews 11:7). The difference between clean and unclean animals is known before Sinai, and the extra clean animals will be needed for sacrifice (8:20).

In seven days. The seven days of waiting are a last week of grace. And Noah does all he is told: obedience again, the fruit of the grace he had found (6:8).

Does this contradict 6:19? There God gave the basic rule, a pair of every kind to keep it alive; here he adds the detail that clean animals go in by sevens. A summary followed by fuller instructions is a normal way of telling a story, not a sign of two conflicting accounts (see the introduction).

Uncertain wording. “Seven pairs” is literally “seven seven”. It may mean seven pairs, or seven of each kind (see the verse note). Either way, there are more of the clean animals than of the others.
verseByVerse.note: “Seven pairs” may mean seven of each kind (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: Noah was six hundred years old when the flood of waters came upon the earth. And Noah and his sons and his wife and his sons' wives with him went into the ark to escape the waters of the flood. Of clean animals, and of animals that are not clean, and of birds, and of everything that creeps on the ground, two and two, male and female, went into the ark with Noah, as God had commanded Noah. And after seven days the waters of the flood came upon the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Noah and his family enter the ark as God commanded, and after seven days the flood begins, just as God said.

Two and two, male and female. God brings the animals two by two; Noah does not have to round them up (6:20). Then come seven days in a closed ark before a drop falls. Faith waits, and God keeps his word to the day.

verseByVerse.quote: In the six hundredth year of Noah's life, in the second month, on the seventeenth day of the month, on that day all the fountains of the great deep burst forth, and the windows of the heavens were opened. And rain fell upon the earth forty days and forty nights. On the very same day Noah and his sons, Shem and Ham and Japheth, and Noah's wife and the three wives of his sons with them entered the ark, they and every beast, according to its kind, and all the livestock according to their kinds, and every creeping thing that creeps on the earth, according to its kind, and every bird, according to its kind, every winged creature. They went into the ark with Noah, two and two of all flesh in which there was the breath of life. And those that entered, male and female of all flesh, went in as God had commanded him. And the LORD shut him in.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the day God had fixed, the waters above and below burst in on the earth, undoing creation, and the LORD himself shut Noah safely inside.

The fountains of the great deep burst forth. The precise date presents this as history. On the second day God separated the waters above from the waters below, and on the third he gathered the seas so that dry land appeared (1:6–9). Now both burst open, and the world returns towards the watery chaos of 1:2. Judgment is creation running backwards: not chaos winning, but God withdrawing the order that he alone holds in place (Colossians 1:17).

The LORD shut him in. Noah did not close the door; God did. Verse 16 has just said that the animals went in “as God had commanded him”, but for this act the narrator uses God’s covenant name, the LORD. Salvation is God’s work, and his people are kept safe by him: “no one will snatch them out of my hand” (John 10:28). If your safety depended on your holding the door shut, you would never sleep; it depends on the one who closed it.

The shut door. The door that shut Noah in also shut the world out. Jesus warned of a day when “the door was shut” (Matthew 25:10). Today the door of the ark God has provided stands open; it will not stand open for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: The flood continued forty days on the earth. The waters increased and bore up the ark, and it rose high above the earth. The waters prevailed and increased greatly on the earth, and the ark floated on the face of the waters. And the waters prevailed so mightily on the earth that all the high mountains under the whole heaven were covered. The waters prevailed above the mountains, covering them fifteen cubits deep.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The waters that destroyed the world lifted the ark above it.

Bore up the ark. The same waters that judged the world lifted the ark. “Prevailed” comes four times (vv. 18, 19, 20, 24): the waters triumph over everything except the ark. Fifteen cubits is about twenty-two feet above the peaks. On whether this covered the whole globe, see the note on 6:17–18.

A picture of baptism. Peter sees a picture of baptism here: eight people brought safely through water by the means God appointed (1 Peter 3:20–21).

Where Christians differ: does baptism save? Some read 1 Peter 3:21 as baptismal regeneration. This commentary’s view: Peter adds, “not as a removal of dirt… but as an appeal to God for a good conscience, through the resurrection of Jesus Christ.” Baptism signifies salvation through Christ; it does not save by itself.

verseByVerse.quote: And all flesh died that moved on the earth, birds, livestock, beasts, all swarming creatures that swarm on the earth, and all mankind. Everything on the dry land in whose nostrils was the breath of life died. He blotted out every living thing that was on the face of the ground, man and animals and creeping things and birds of the heavens. They were blotted out from the earth. Only Noah was left, and those who were with him in the ark. And the waters prevailed on the earth 150 days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything outside the ark died; only those God had shut in were left alive.

All flesh died. The list runs back through creation: birds, livestock, beasts, swarming creatures and mankind, everything “in whose nostrils was the breath of life” (2:7). Judgment unmakes what God made. It is real (2 Peter 2:5).

Only Noah was left. Only Noah and those with him remain, a remnant, the few God preserves, saved by grace. Jesus warned that as it was in the days of Noah, so it will be at his coming (Luke 17:26–27). The ark pictures the only safety there will be on that day, and that safety is Christ.

What it does not mean. Not that every flood or disaster is God’s judgment on its victims; Jesus forbade that reasoning (Luke 13:1–5). The flood was a unique event, announced beforehand, preceded by long patience, and given as a pattern of the final judgment.

7.theology:
Judgment and Grace. The flood holds together what modern minds separate: God's holiness judges sin, and his love provides salvation within judgment. The cross brings them together: the judgment the flood foreshadowed falls on the Son, and those in him are shut into safety. Judgment with no rescue would leave us without hope; rescue with no judgment would treat sin as a small thing.

Undoing and New Creation. Judgment undoes creation, and salvation is new creation. The pattern returns at the Red Sea, in the exile, and supremely in the death and resurrection of Christ. The resurrection is the new creation the flood dimly foreshadowed.
7.examples:
Then: The forty days and nights of rain (v. 4) became a number Israel would meet again: Moses was on the mountain forty days (Exod. 24:18), the spies searched Canaan forty days (Num. 13:25), Israel wandered forty years, and Jesus fasted forty days (Matt. 4:2). The number marks a time of trial, cleansing, and preparation for what comes next.

Now: Jesus’s use of the flood in Matthew 24:37–39 warns against spiritual complacency: the world before the flood did not see it coming because it was busy with ordinary life. The point is not that Christians should be anxious about the end but that they should be alert, watching in the faith that marked Noah. And verse 23 speaks to every small church in a hostile culture: you are not a failed majority but a preserved remnant, held by the same God who shut Noah in.

keyVerse.quote: And the LORD shut him in.
keyVerse.note: In a chapter of rising waters and universal death, these few words carry the gospel of the flood. Noah did not save himself or even close his own door; the LORD did, and no one could open it. Those who are in Christ are kept by the same hand (John 10:28).

7.reflection:
The flood is creation running backwards (vv. 11–12). What does it tell us about sin that God’s judgment on it looks like the world coming apart? Where do you see sin unmaking things today?

“And the LORD shut him in” (v. 16). How does it change the Christian life to know that your safety rests on God’s hand, not your grip? Which of your anxieties does that answer?

Jesus said that before the flood people were eating and drinking and marrying until the day it came (Matthew 24:38). None of those things is wrong. What made their ordinary life dangerous, and what would being ready look like for you?

Peter sees the eight brought safely through the water as a picture of salvation through Christ (1 Peter 3:20–21). How does the ark, carried through the waters that destroyed the world, help you understand what Christ has done for you?

8.title: God Remembered Noah
8.text: <sup>1</sup>But God remembered Noah and all the beasts and all the livestock that were with him in the ark. And God made a wind blow over the earth, and the waters subsided.<sup>2</sup>The fountains of the deep and the windows of the heavens were closed, the rain from the heavens was restrained,<sup>3</sup>and the waters receded from the earth continually. At the end of 150 days the waters had abated,<sup>4</sup>and in the seventh month, on the seventeenth day of the month, the ark came to rest on the mountains of Ararat.<sup>5</sup>And the waters continued to abate until the tenth month; in the tenth month, on the first day of the month, the tops of the mountains were seen.<sup>6</sup>At the end of forty days Noah opened the window of the ark that he had made<sup>7</sup>and sent forth a raven. It went to and fro until the waters were dried up from the earth.<sup>8</sup>Then he sent forth a dove from him, to see if the waters had subsided from the face of the ground.<sup>9</sup>But the dove found no place to set her foot, and she returned to him to the ark, for the waters were still on the face of the whole earth. So he put out his hand and took her and brought her into the ark with him.<sup>10</sup>He waited another seven days, and again he sent forth the dove out of the ark.<sup>11</sup>And the dove came back to him in the evening, and behold, in her mouth was a freshly plucked olive leaf. So Noah knew that the waters had subsided from the earth.<sup>12</sup>Then he waited another seven days and sent forth the dove, and she did not return to him anymore.<sup>13</sup>In the six hundred and first year, in the first month, the first day of the month, the waters were dried from off the earth. And Noah removed the covering of the ark and looked, and behold, the face of the ground was dry.<sup>14</sup>In the second month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month, the earth had dried out.<sup>15</sup>Then God said to Noah,<sup>16</sup>"Go out from the ark, you and your wife, and your sons and your sons' wives with you.<sup>17</sup>Bring out with you every living thing that is with you of all flesh—birds and animals and every creeping thing that creeps on the earth—that they may swarm on the earth, and be fruitful and multiply on the earth."<sup>18</sup>So Noah went out, and his sons and his wife and his sons' wives with him.<sup>19</sup>Every beast, every creeping thing, and every bird, everything that moves on the earth, went out by families from the ark.<sup>20</sup>Then Noah built an altar to the LORD and took some of every clean animal and some of every clean bird and offered burnt offerings on the altar.<sup>21</sup>And when the LORD smelled the pleasing aroma, the LORD said in his heart, "I will never again curse the ground because of man, for the intention of man's heart is evil from his youth. Neither will I ever again strike down every living creature as I have done.<sup>22</sup>While the earth remains, seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, day and night, shall not cease."
8.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 7 left the earth under water for 150 days, with only Noah and those with him alive. Chapter 8 is the turning point of the flood story and its unwinding: the waters go down as precisely as they rose, Noah steps out into a washed world, and God makes a promise that still holds every time the seasons turn.

The message. God remembers his people, and his remembering means action: judgment gives way to new creation. Then, on the ground of an accepted sacrifice, God binds himself to patience with a race whose heart has not changed. The evil of the human heart, which brought the flood (6:5), is now the reason God gives for holding back (8:21). What has changed is not man; an offering has gone up.

Why it was said. In the Babylonian flood story the gods, hungry for offerings, crowd round the survivor’s sacrifice (see the introduction). Here the LORD needs nothing and freely promises. Israel, about to receive the law of burnt offerings and to live by rain and harvest in Canaan, needed to know that the seasons are the gift of the God who remembers, not the whim of the storm gods their neighbours served.

How the chapter makes its case. God remembers Noah, sends a wind, and the waters recede until the ark rests on the mountains of Ararat (vv. 1–5). Noah waits and tests, with a raven and then a dove, until the olive leaf, and then the dove that does not return (vv. 6–12). The ground dries, a year after the flood began (vv. 13–14). God calls Noah out and renews the blessing of creation (vv. 15–19). Noah builds an altar, and the LORD accepts the offering and promises to keep the seasons while the earth remains (vv. 20–22).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern and by the character of God. The God who “remembered Noah” is the God to whom a dying thief prayed, “Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom”, and was answered that same day (Luke 23:42–43). Noah’s offering, a pleasing aroma that turned judgment into promise, foreshadows the one sacrifice that truly does so: Christ “gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God” (Ephesians 5:2). Because of that sacrifice God can be patient with sinners without ceasing to be just (Romans 3:25–26).

For us. In the long silences, when God seems to have forgotten you, remember the months the ark drifted before the wind came: he has not forgotten. And let every harvest and sunrise remind you that God is holding back judgment so that more may come to him (2 Peter 3:9). Use the time he gives.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — The Recession of the Flood and Noah's Worship
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God remembers Noah, and judgment gives way to a new beginning sealed by a sacrifice and a promise. The flood turns at verse 1: God sends a wind, and the waters recede as precisely as they came, until the ark rests on the mountains of Ararat (vv. 1–5). Noah waits and tests, sending out a raven and a dove, until the olive leaf and the dove’s last flight tell him the earth is coming back to life (vv. 6–12). When the ground is dry, God calls him out and renews the blessing of creation (vv. 13–19). The chapter ends with Noah’s altar and God’s promise to keep the seasons while the earth remains (vv. 20–22).
verseByVerse.theology: Noah waits for the raven, the dove and the olive leaf, and then for God's word to go out. God promises never again to cut off every living creature.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: God's remembering is always God acting, as it was for Israel in Egypt and for Hannah. Now: seedtime and harvest, day and night, still keep the promise of 8:22.

verseByVerse.quote: But God remembered Noah and all the beasts and all the livestock that were with him in the ark. And God made a wind blow over the earth, and the waters subsided. The fountains of the deep and the windows of the heavens were closed, the rain from the heavens was restrained, and the waters receded from the earth continually. At the end of 150 days the waters had abated, and in the seventh month, on the seventeenth day of the month, the ark came to rest on the mountains of Ararat. And the waters continued to abate until the tenth month; in the tenth month, on the first day of the month, the tops of the mountains were seen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God had not forgotten Noah: he acted on his promise, and the waters began to go down.

God remembered Noah. In Scripture, for God to remember is to act on his covenant (Exodus 2:24), as when he “remembered Rachel” and opened her womb (30:22). He remembered the animals too: his care reaches every creature he made (Psalm 36:6). This verse is the hinge of the flood story: before it the waters rise, after it they fall.

A wind. The wind he sends is the same Hebrew word as “Spirit” in 1:2, where the Spirit hovered over the waters: a new creation begins. The fountains of the deep and the windows of the heavens are closed, reversing 7:11.

The mountains of Ararat. The phrase names a region, the ancient land of Urartu around Lake Van in what is now eastern Turkey and Armenia, rather than one particular peak. Claims to have found the ark on the modern Mount Ararat have never been confirmed. The date, the seventeenth day of the seventh month, is exactly five months after the flood began (7:11).

In the long silence. Five months on the water with no recorded word from God: Noah’s faith was tested by silence as well as storm. But God’s remembering came, as it does for his people: “Even these may forget, yet I will not forget you” (Isaiah 49:15).
verseByVerse.note: Ararat is the region of eastern Turkey and Armenia; the text speaks of its mountains, not a single peak.

verseByVerse.quote: At the end of forty days Noah opened the window of the ark that he had made and sent forth a raven. It went to and fro until the waters were dried up from the earth. Then he sent forth a dove from him, to see if the waters had subsided from the face of the ground. But the dove found no place to set her foot, and she returned to him to the ark, for the waters were still on the face of the whole earth. So he put out his hand and took her and brought her into the ark with him. He waited another seven days, and again he sent forth the dove out of the ark. And the dove came back to him in the evening, and behold, in her mouth was a freshly plucked olive leaf. So Noah knew that the waters had subsided from the earth. Then he waited another seven days and sent forth the dove, and she did not return to him anymore.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Noah waits patiently and tests the earth, until the dove’s olive leaf shows that life is returning.

A raven … a dove. The raven, a scavenger, could live off what floated on the waters and did not come back. The dove needs dry ground and trees, so she is the better test, and Noah gathers her back in his hand (v. 9).

A freshly plucked olive leaf. Noah tests before he moves. The olive leaf brings news of new life, and has been a symbol of peace ever since. Many Christians have also heard an echo when the Spirit descends like a dove on Jesus as he comes up from the water (Mark 1:10), though the Gospels do not draw the link.

He waited another seven days. Twice Noah waits. Waiting for God’s timing is part of faith: he remembered Noah, and he remembers his own. Even when the dove does not return, Noah does not leave until God tells him to (vv. 15–16). He uses ordinary means to learn what God is doing, but God’s word, not a sign he has set, is what moves him.

verseByVerse.quote: In the six hundred and first year, in the first month, the first day of the month, the waters were dried from off the earth. And Noah removed the covering of the ark and looked, and behold, the face of the ground was dry. In the second month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month, the earth had dried out.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The earth is dry on New Year’s Day, a new beginning for a renewed world, a year after the flood began.

The face of the ground was dry. The earth is dry on the first day of the first month: a new year and a new beginning. Noah “looked, and behold”, as God had looked on the corrupt earth (6:12); now he sees a washed one. The surface is dry first, and nearly two months later the earth is dried out. Noah has been in the ark a year and ten days (7:11), a long trial of faith.
verseByVerse.note: Compare 7:11: the flood began in the second month of Noah’s six hundredth year.

verseByVerse.quote: Then God said to Noah, "Go out from the ark, you and your wife, and your sons and your sons' wives with you. Bring out with you every living thing that is with you of all flesh—birds and animals and every creeping thing that creeps on the earth—that they may swarm on the earth, and be fruitful and multiply on the earth." So Noah went out, and his sons and his wife and his sons' wives with him. Every beast, every creeping thing, and every bird, everything that moves on the earth, went out by families from the ark.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At God’s word Noah leaves the ark, and God renews his blessing on the creatures to fill the earth again.

Go out from the ark. Noah waits for God’s word to leave the ark, as he did to enter it. The creation blessing, “Be fruitful”, is renewed (1:22, 28), the animals go out “by families”, and Noah becomes a new Adam, starting humanity again.

A new Adam who falls. Within a chapter Noah lies drunk and exposed in his tent (9:20–21): a new start does not give a new heart. The world needed a better Adam than Noah, “the last Adam”, who became “a life-giving spirit” (1 Corinthians 15:45).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Noah built an altar to the LORD and took some of every clean animal and some of every clean bird and offered burnt offerings on the altar. And when the LORD smelled the pleasing aroma, the LORD said in his heart, "I will never again curse the ground because of man, for the intention of man's heart is evil from his youth. Neither will I ever again strike down every living creature as I have done. While the earth remains, seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, day and night, shall not cease."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Noah’s first act in the new world is worship, and on the ground of his offering God freely promises patience with a race whose heart has not changed.

Noah built an altar to the LORD. Before building a house, Noah builds an altar: this is the proper order of a restored life, and the first response to salvation is praise. From the few creatures saved he gives some of every clean kind back to God.

The pleasing aroma. In the Babylonian flood story the gods, hungry after the flood, crowd “like flies” round the survivor’s sacrifice; here the LORD needs nothing, and “pleasing aroma” is the phrase the law later uses for an offering God accepts (Leviticus 1:9). The Hebrew word for “pleasing” means soothing or restful, and sounds like Noah’s name: the rest Lamech longed for (5:29) comes through a sacrifice. Its pleasing aroma points forward to Christ’s sacrifice (Ephesians 5:2).

Evil from his youth. The flood did not change the human heart: man is still evil from his youth, and only grace can change him (Ezekiel 36:26). The reason given for judgment in 6:5 is now the reason given for patience, and what has come between is the offering. That is the gospel in miniature: God does not wait for us to improve; he deals with us on the ground of a sacrifice.

Seedtime and harvest. God promises seedtime and harvest, his kindness to all people alike (Acts 14:17): every harvest, gathered by believer or unbeliever, is God keeping this word. But “while the earth remains” hints at an end. God promises no second flood (9:11), not that there will be no final judgment; the present world is “being kept until the day of judgment” (2 Peter 3:7), and his patience is the time to repent.
verseByVerse.note: The first altar in the Bible.

8.theology:
New Creation. Genesis 8 echoes Genesis 1: the wind over the waters, dry land appearing, living creatures coming out. The flood unmade the world; its going down is a new creation, a pattern that runs through the exodus, the return from exile and the resurrection of Christ, to the new heavens and earth (Revelation 21).

The Patience of God. In verse 21 God commits to patience with a race whose heart is evil from youth. Peter links "the patience of our Lord" with salvation (2 Pet. 3:15): God waits so that more might be saved. The cross is how he can be patient without compromising his justice.
8.examples:
Then: Israelites who knew the burnt offerings would notice that the father of the renewed world was, above all, a worshipper. The olive leaf (v. 11) became a symbol of peace far beyond Israel because of this story.

Now: “God remembered Noah” (v. 1) is the chapter’s great comfort. In the long silences, the unanswered prayer, the drawn-out suffering, the season in which God seems absent, the promise is that he has not forgotten. His remembering is always the turn of the tide. And verse 21 keeps Christian mission realistic: we do not expect the gospel to improve the old nature but to make people new.

keyVerse.quote: But God remembered Noah and all the beasts and all the livestock that were with him in the ark.
keyVerse.note: This sentence is the hinge of the flood story: before it the waters rise, after it they fall. When God remembers, it is not a jog to a forgetful memory but the moment he acts on his promise. It is the hope of every believer who waits, and the prayer of the dying thief, “Jesus, remember me”, was answered the same way (Luke 23:42–43).

8.reflection:
Noah spent months in the ark with no recorded word from God before “God remembered Noah” (v. 1). How do you tend to respond when God seems silent? What does this chapter give you to hold on to?

Noah sent out the birds to learn what was happening, but left the ark only when God told him to (vv. 15–16). How do you hold together using ordinary wisdom and waiting on God?

Noah’s first act in the new world was to build an altar (v. 20). After God has brought you through something hard, what would it look like to put worship first?

The evil of the human heart is the reason for the flood (6:5) and then the reason for God’s patience (8:21). What made the difference, and how does that point to Christ?

9.title: The Covenant with Noah
9.text: <sup>1</sup>And God blessed Noah and his sons and said to them, "Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth.<sup>2</sup>The fear of you and the dread of you shall be upon every beast of the earth and upon every bird of the heavens, upon everything that creeps on the ground and all the fish of the sea. Into your hand they are delivered.<sup>3</sup>Every moving thing that lives shall be food for you. And as I gave you the green plants, I give you everything.<sup>4</sup>But you shall not eat flesh with its life, that is, its blood.<sup>5</sup>And for your lifeblood I will require a reckoning: from every beast I will require it and from man. From his fellow man I will require a reckoning for the life of man.<sup>6</sup>"Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed, for God made man in his own image.<sup>7</sup>And you, be fruitful and multiply, increase greatly on the earth and multiply in it."<sup>8</sup>Then God said to Noah and to his sons with him,<sup>9</sup>"Behold, I establish my covenant with you and your offspring after you,<sup>10</sup>and with every living creature that is with you, the birds, the livestock, and every beast of the earth with you, as many as came out of the ark; it is for every beast of the earth.<sup>11</sup>I establish my covenant with you, that never again shall all flesh be cut off by the waters of the flood, and never again shall there be a flood to destroy the earth."<sup>12</sup>And God said, "This is the sign of the covenant that I make between me and you and every living creature that is with you, for all future generations:<sup>13</sup>I have set my bow in the cloud, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and the earth.<sup>14</sup>When I bring clouds over the earth and the bow is seen in the clouds,<sup>15</sup>I will remember my covenant that is between me and you and every living creature of all flesh. And the waters shall never again become a flood to destroy all flesh.<sup>16</sup>When the bow is in the clouds, I will see it and remember the everlasting covenant between God and every living creature of all flesh that is on the earth."<sup>17</sup>God said to Noah, "This is the sign of the covenant that I have established between me and all flesh that is on the earth."<sup>18</sup>The sons of Noah who went forth from the ark were Shem, Ham, and Japheth. (Ham was the father of Canaan.)<sup>19</sup>These three were the sons of Noah, and from these the people of the whole earth were dispersed.<sup>20</sup>Noah began to be a man of the soil, and he planted a vineyard.<sup>21</sup>He drank of the wine and became drunk and lay uncovered in his tent.<sup>22</sup>And Ham, the father of Canaan, saw the nakedness of his father and told his two brothers outside.<sup>23</sup>Then Shem and Japheth took a garment, laid it on both their shoulders, and walked backward and covered the nakedness of their father. Their faces were turned backward, and they did not see their father's nakedness.<sup>24</sup>When Noah awoke from his wine and knew what his youngest son had done to him,<sup>25</sup>he said, "Cursed be Canaan; a servant of servants shall he be to his brothers."<sup>26</sup>He also said, "Blessed be the LORD, the God of Shem; and let Canaan be his servant.<sup>27</sup>May God enlarge Japheth, and let him dwell in the tents of Shem, and let Canaan be his servant."<sup>28</sup>After the flood Noah lived 350 years.<sup>29</sup>All the days of Noah were 950 years, and he died.
9.overview:
Where we are. The flood is over. Noah has come out of the ark, offered his sacrifice, and heard God promise that seedtime and harvest will not cease while the earth remains (8:20–22). Chapter 9 turns that promise into a covenant, and then shows the first family of the new world falling, as the first family of the old one did.

The message. God binds himself to keep this world going, and he does it for a race that has not changed. He renews the blessing of creation, guards human life because every person bears his image, and swears by a sign in the sky that the waters will never again destroy all flesh. The God who keeps this promise is utterly reliable; the man he keeps it for is not, as Noah’s tent soon shows.

Why it was said. Israel heard this on the way to a land where life hung on the rains, among neighbours who feared that the gods might wipe out mankind again on a whim (see the introduction). Genesis tells them that the world stands under a sworn promise of the one God. It also explains the curse on Canaan, whose land Israel was about to enter.

How the chapter makes its case. God renews Adam’s blessing, now giving animals for food (vv. 1–3), and guards life, because man is made in his image (vv. 4–7). He covenants with every living creature never again to destroy the earth by flood (vv. 8–11), and sets his bow in the cloud as the sign (vv. 12–17). Then Noah lies drunk and uncovered; Ham shames him while Shem and Japheth cover him (vv. 18–23). Noah’s words over his sons curse Canaan, bless the God of Shem and make room for Japheth in Shem’s tents (vv. 24–29).

Where it leads. To Christ by covenant, by the need exposed and by promise. This covenant keeps the world standing so that God’s saving purpose can run its course. Noah, the new Adam, falls at once, and the world still waits for a man who will not. And the blessing on “the God of Shem” narrows the story to the line that leads to Abraham and on to Jesus, “the son of Shem” in Luke’s genealogy (Luke 3:36), in whose tents the nations of Japheth have now come to live (Ephesians 2:13, 19). The bow God hung up in the sky was finally laid down at the cross, where the judgment the flood pictured fell on his Son.

For us. Every rainbow is a promise kept to a world that does not deserve it: God is patient, so that people may repent. Every human being you meet bears God’s image, so life is to be guarded and honoured. And when a believer falls, as Noah did, the right response is the covering love that Shem and Japheth showed, not the gossip of Ham.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God makes a covenant with the whole living world, binding himself to preserve it. First he renews the blessing of creation, now giving animals as food (vv. 1–3), but he guards life: blood is not to be eaten, and the life of a man, made in God’s image, is to be answered for, even by the hand of man (vv. 4–7). Then he establishes his covenant with Noah, his offspring and every creature: never again a flood to destroy the earth (vv. 8–11). The rainbow is its sign, a bow set in the cloud for God himself to see and remember (vv. 12–17). The promise rests on God alone; nothing is asked of Noah in return.
verseByVerse.theology: God blesses Noah as he blessed Adam, gives the animals for food but forbids eating blood, and requires the life of any who sheds man's blood. He covenants with every living creature never again to flood the earth.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the first covenant in Scripture has no conditions and includes the animals. Now: the sign is put where God will see it and remember, as the Passover blood was (Exod. 12:13); assurance rests on what God has undertaken, not on how well we remember.

verseByVerse.quote: And God blessed Noah and his sons and said to them, "Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth. The fear of you and the dread of you shall be upon every beast of the earth and upon every bird of the heavens, upon everything that creeps on the ground and all the fish of the sea. Into your hand they are delivered. Every moving thing that lives shall be food for you. And as I gave you the green plants, I give you everything.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God starts the world again with the same blessing he gave Adam, and now he gives animals as well as plants for food.

Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth. The words of 1:28 are spoken again, almost exactly. After the flood God has not changed his purpose for humanity: he still wants the earth filled with people who bear his image. Noah and his sons stand where Adam stood, at the head of the human race.

The fear of you and the dread of you. Something has changed, though. Adam ruled the animals in peace; now they will fear man. The relationship is spoiled by sin and by the killing that the new permission will bring. Man’s rule over creation remains (“into your hand they are delivered”), but it is a rule in a fallen world.

I give you everything. In 1:29 God gave plants for food; now he adds “every moving thing that lives”. The plain sense is that people did not eat meat before the flood, or at least had no permission to, and that eating meat is a new gift. Later Israel would distinguish clean and unclean animals (Leviticus 11), but Jesus declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19).

Received with thanksgiving. Food is a gift, not a right: “everything created by God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving” (1 Timothy 4:4). Christians are free to eat meat or not, but not to despise one another over it (Romans 14:3).

verseByVerse.quote: But you shall not eat flesh with its life, that is, its blood. And for your lifeblood I will require a reckoning: from every beast I will require it and from man. From his fellow man I will require a reckoning for the life of man. "Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed, for God made man in his own image. And you, be fruitful and multiply, increase greatly on the earth and multiply in it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Life belongs to God: blood, which stands for life, is not to be eaten, and whoever takes a human life must answer for it, because man is made in God’s image.

Flesh with its life, that is, its blood. The permission to eat meat has one limit. Blood stands for life, and life belongs to God (Leviticus 17:11), so even in killing an animal for food man must acknowledge that he did not give its life. The rule passed into Israel’s law, and the Jerusalem council asked Gentile believers to abstain from blood out of care for Jewish fellow believers (Acts 15:20).

I will require a reckoning. Three times God says he will “require” the life of man. Even an animal that kills a person must answer for it (Exodus 21:28). After the violence that filled the earth before the flood (6:11), God puts a guard around human life.

By man shall his blood be shed. Verse 6 is a carefully balanced line of poetry in Hebrew: shed blood, man; man, blood shed. God now gives to human beings the task of answering murder. Before the flood, God himself protected the murderer Cain (4:15); now, in a world where violence must be restrained, human justice is appointed. This is the beginning of what Paul later calls the God-given authority that “does not bear the sword in vain” (Romans 13:4).

For God made man in his own image. This is the reason for the whole command. Murder is not just a crime against a person but an attack on God’s image in him, like defacing a king’s portrait. The image is not lost in the fall: it is the ground of every person’s dignity, believer or not (see the comment on 1:26–27; James 3:9). To strike a person is to strike at God.

Be fruitful and multiply. The command to multiply returns to close the paragraph: the God who forbids the taking of life wants life to fill the earth.

The blood that speaks better. Abel’s blood cried out from the ground for justice (4:10), and this verse answers that cry. But Scripture has a blood that “speaks a better word than the blood of Abel” (Hebrews 12:24). Jesus, the true image of God, let his blood be shed by men, not to demand vengeance but to bring forgiveness to the very people who shed it.

For life today. Every human life, from conception to old age, bears God’s image and is guarded by God himself. That lies beneath the Christian concern for the unborn, the disabled and the dying, and beneath Jesus’ teaching that anger and contempt are already murder in the heart (Matthew 5:21–22).

Where Christians differ: capital punishment. Some Christians see this verse as a lasting mandate for the state to punish murder with death; others hold it a permission now superseded by the mercy of the gospel, or reject the death penalty because of the risk of punishing the innocent. This commentary’s view: given to all humanity before Israel, it grounds the state’s right to use the sword for murder (Romans 13:4), to be exercised justly and with great care.

Where Christians differ: blood transfusions. Jehovah’s Witnesses forbid them from this verse. This commentary’s view: the command concerns eating blood, as a way of honouring life. Giving blood to save a life honours the same principle.

verseByVerse.quote: Then God said to Noah and to his sons with him, "Behold, I establish my covenant with you and your offspring after you, and with every living creature that is with you, the birds, the livestock, and every beast of the earth with you, as many as came out of the ark; it is for every beast of the earth. I establish my covenant with you, that never again shall all flesh be cut off by the waters of the flood, and never again shall there be a flood to destroy the earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God binds himself by covenant to every living creature: never again will a flood destroy the earth.

I establish my covenant. This is the covenant God promised Noah before the flood (6:18). A covenant is a solemn, binding commitment. Here God alone makes the promise and asks nothing in return: it does not depend on Noah’s faithfulness, or anyone’s. That is just as well, given verse 21.

With every living creature. The circle is as wide as it could be: Noah, his offspring “after you”, and every bird and beast. This is not a covenant of salvation for believers but God’s commitment to preserve the whole created order. Reformed theology calls this common grace: the kindness God shows to all, which does not save but keeps the world going, restrains evil and makes ordinary life possible (Matthew 5:45). Every sunrise and harvest since has been God keeping it.

Never again. God has kept this promise for thousands of years. Floods still come and still bring grief, but never again one that destroys all flesh. The promise does not mean there will be no final judgment: Peter says that the present heavens and earth are “stored up for fire, being kept until the day of judgment” (2 Peter 3:7). The God who promised Noah has never failed; his promises of mercy and of judgment are equally sure. Isaiah used this covenant to comfort exiles: as God swore that the waters of Noah would not return, so he swears that his steadfast love will not depart from his people (Isaiah 54:9–10).

verseByVerse.quote: And God said, "This is the sign of the covenant that I make between me and you and every living creature that is with you, for all future generations: I have set my bow in the cloud, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and the earth. When I bring clouds over the earth and the bow is seen in the clouds, I will remember my covenant that is between me and you and every living creature of all flesh. And the waters shall never again become a flood to destroy all flesh. When the bow is in the clouds, I will see it and remember the everlasting covenant between God and every living creature of all flesh that is on the earth." God said to Noah, "This is the sign of the covenant that I have established between me and all flesh that is on the earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The rainbow is the sign of God’s covenant, set in the cloud as a reminder to God himself, and so as an assurance to us.

I have set my bow in the cloud. The Hebrew word for “bow” is the ordinary word for a warrior’s bow. Many interpreters see a picture here: God hangs up his weapon of judgment in the sky, laid down after the storm. The rainbow may already have existed in nature; God now gives it a new meaning, as he would later give meaning to water, bread and wine.

I will see it and remember. Strikingly, the sign is first for God. He does not need reminding, but he binds himself in terms we can grasp: whenever the clouds gather and the bow appears, God is pledged to remember. To “remember” in Scripture is to act on a commitment (8:1). So when believers see the rainbow, they are seeing what God sees, and can rest in the promise he keeps.

The everlasting covenant. The covenant is called everlasting and is for “all future generations”. It is the first covenant in the Bible sealed with a sign, as later covenants will be: circumcision for Abraham (17:11), the Sabbath for Israel (Exodus 31:13), and the cup of the new covenant in Christ’s blood (Luke 22:20).

The bow and the cross. The rainbow promises that the flood will not return; the cross shows how God can keep that promise without ignoring sin, for there the judgment the flood pictured fell on the Son of God. Ezekiel saw the glory of God shining “like the appearance of the bow that is in the cloud on the day of rain” (Ezekiel 1:28), and John saw a rainbow around God’s throne (Revelation 4:3): the God who rules is the God who keeps his promise of mercy.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–29 — The Sin of Ham and the Prophecy over the Sons of Noah
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The first story of the new world is a fall, and its outcome reaches far into Israel’s history. Noah, the new Adam, plants a vineyard, gets drunk and lies uncovered in his tent (vv. 18–21). Ham sees and tells; Shem and Japheth walk in backwards and cover their father (vv. 22–23). When Noah wakes, he curses Canaan, Ham’s son, blesses the LORD as the God of Shem, and prays that Japheth may be enlarged and live in Shem’s tents (vv. 24–27). The words set the course of the nations in chapter 10 and point the line of promise through Shem toward Abraham. Noah dies at 950, the last of the long-lived fathers (vv. 28–29).
verseByVerse.theology: Noah plants a vineyard, gets drunk and lies uncovered. Ham sees and tells; Shem and Japheth cover their father without looking. Noah curses Canaan, blesses the God of Shem, and prays that Japheth may dwell in Shem's tents.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the curse concerns the Canaanite nations Israel was about to meet, not any race alive today. Now: love still covers a multitude of sins.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Noah who went forth from the ark were Shem, Ham, and Japheth. (Ham was the father of Canaan.) These three were the sons of Noah, and from these the people of the whole earth were dispersed. Noah began to be a man of the soil, and he planted a vineyard. He drank of the wine and became drunk and lay uncovered in his tent. And Ham, the father of Canaan, saw the nakedness of his father and told his two brothers outside. Then Shem and Japheth took a garment, laid it on both their shoulders, and walked backward and covered the nakedness of their father. Their faces were turned backward, and they did not see their father's nakedness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first story of the new world is a fall: Noah gets drunk and lies uncovered, and his sons show the difference between exposing a father’s shame and covering it.

Ham was the father of Canaan. The narrator says it twice (vv. 18, 22), preparing for the curse that falls on Canaan. From these three sons “the people of the whole earth were dispersed”, which chapter 10 will spell out. See Shem, Ham and Japheth.

He planted a vineyard. Noah, “a man of the soil”, is the new Adam, and like Adam he falls in a garden of his own, a vineyard. Wine is a good gift that gladdens the heart (Psalm 104:15), and Scripture never says Noah sinned by making it. His sin is drunkenness, which Scripture consistently condemns (Ephesians 5:18). The man who “walked with God” (6:9) and survived the flood is not safe from one evening’s excess. The Bible tells the sins of its heroes honestly, and so warns us: past faithfulness is no guarantee against present failure.

Ham saw … and told. Whatever exactly Ham did (see the box below), the contrast is plain. Ham saw his father’s shame and spread it. Shem and Japheth took a garment, walked in backwards, and covered him without looking. In a culture where honouring a father was a sacred duty (Exodus 20:12), Ham dishonoured his father at his weakest moment.

Covering, not exposing. We are to cover others’ shame rather than expose it, for “love covers a multitude of sins” (1 Peter 4:8). That is how God has dealt with us. From the garments of skins in Eden (3:21) to the righteousness of Christ, God has always covered his people’s shame rather than displaying it.

What it does not mean. Covering is not covering up. Love does not broadcast a brother’s fall for entertainment, but neither does it hide serious wrongdoing from those responsible for dealing with it. Where someone is being harmed, above all where there is abuse, the matter must be brought into the light, to the church’s leaders and, where a crime has been committed, to the police. Shem and Japheth protected their father’s dignity; they did not shelter a danger to others.

Uncertain wording. What Ham did is not fully clear. “Saw the nakedness of his father” could be literal looking; elsewhere “uncover the nakedness” is a way of speaking of sexual relations (Leviticus 18:6–8), and so some think of a sexual act, or even of incest with Noah’s wife. But the text says Ham “saw”, not “uncovered”, and the brothers’ remedy, a garment and averted eyes, matches a sin of looking. Most likely Ham gazed on his father’s shame and mocked it to his brothers.

verseByVerse.quote: When Noah awoke from his wine and knew what his youngest son had done to him, he said, "Cursed be Canaan; a servant of servants shall he be to his brothers." He also said, "Blessed be the LORD, the God of Shem; and let Canaan be his servant. May God enlarge Japheth, and let him dwell in the tents of Shem, and let Canaan be his servant." After the flood Noah lived 350 years. All the days of Noah were 950 years, and he died.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Noah’s words over his sons set the course of the nations: Canaan is cursed, the LORD is blessed as the God of Shem, and Japheth is given room in Shem’s tents.

Cursed be Canaan. Noah speaks as a prophet, and his words reach far beyond his family. The curse falls not on Ham but on Canaan, Ham’s son, ancestor of the Canaanites. Why Canaan is named is not explained. Perhaps a son who dishonoured his father is answered through his own son, or perhaps Noah foresaw in Canaan’s line the same contempt for moral boundaries that Israel would later meet in the land (Leviticus 18:3, 24–25). “A servant of servants” means the lowest of servants. The words were fulfilled when Israel came into Canaan and the Canaanites were subdued (Joshua 9:23; Judges 1:28).

Blessed be the LORD, the God of Shem. Noah does not bless Shem directly; he blesses the LORD as Shem’s God. Shem’s privilege is that the LORD is his God. From this point the line of promise runs through Shem (11:10–26) to Abraham (11:26), and on through Israel to Christ (Luke 3:36). The word “Shem” means “name”, and Babel’s builders will try to make a name for themselves (11:4); God will give a great name to Shem’s descendant Abram (12:2).

May God enlarge Japheth. As the ESV notes, “Japheth” sounds like the Hebrew for “enlarge”. Japheth’s descendants spread widely, to the north and west (10:2–5). That they should “dwell in the tents of Shem” is a hint of the nations sharing in the blessing God gives to Shem’s line. Christians have long heard here the gospel coming to the Gentiles, who were once “far off” and have now “been brought near by the blood of Christ” (Ephesians 2:13), and who are “no longer strangers and aliens, but … fellow citizens with the saints” (Ephesians 2:19).

All the days of Noah were 950 years, and he died. Noah’s death closes his story with the refrain of chapter 5, “and he died”. Even the man who came through the flood could not escape death. The world still awaits a deliverer who will not merely survive judgment but conquer death itself.

What it does not mean. The so-called curse of Ham was used for centuries to justify the enslavement of Africans. This is a grievous misuse. The curse names Canaan, not Ham, and certainly not Ham’s other descendants such as Cush, Egypt and Put (10:6); it was fulfilled when Israel subdued the Canaanites; and it says nothing about race or skin colour. Scripture teaches that God made every nation from one man (Acts 17:26), and in Christ “there is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free” (Galatians 3:28).

Uncertain wording. Two phrases are unclear. Noah’s “youngest son” is literally “his small son”. Ham is listed second (v. 18), so some take the word as “younger” rather than “youngest”, and a few suggest it refers to Canaan, a grandson called a son; most take it to mean Ham was the youngest. And in “let him dwell in the tents of Shem” (v. 27) the Hebrew “he” could refer to God, “may God dwell in the tents of Shem”, rather than to Japheth. Both readings fit what follows: God did make his dwelling among Shem’s descendants, and the nations have been welcomed there. The ESV’s reading, that Japheth will share Shem’s blessing, is the more natural.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “Japheth” sounds like the Hebrew for “enlarge.”

9.theology:
Common Grace. The covenant with Noah introduces what Reformed theology calls common grace: God's kindness to all people, which does not save but preserves the created order and makes civilisation possible. The regular seasons (8:22), the restraint of evil, and the beauty and justice found even among unbelievers flow from it. It keeps the world going while saving grace does its work.

The Rainbow and the Cross. The rainbow promises that the flood will not return; the cross explains how God can keep that promise without ignoring sin, for there the judgment the flood represented fell on the Son of God.
9.examples:
Then: Verse 6 underlies the rule that punishment must fit the crime, and the bow was a covenant sign written in the sky for every generation, in an age with few written documents.

Now: The chapter’s real message is that the covenant covers everyone: every dawn and harvest is a gift of God's faithfulness to a world that does not deserve it, which makes care for creation a matter of faith, not only of policy.

keyVerse.quote: I have set my bow in the cloud, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and the earth.
keyVerse.note: The whole chapter rests on this sign: the God who judged the earth now pledges never to destroy it by flood again, and he binds the promise to something every generation can see. The bow points to a God who remembers his word, and finally to the cross, where the judgment it held back fell on Christ.

9.reflection:
God renews the blessing of creation (vv. 1, 7) to a family that has just seen the world judged. What does it tell you about God that he still wants the earth filled with people who bear his image?

Verse 6 grounds the value of every human life in the image of God. Whom do people around you, or you yourself, find it easiest to treat as less than fully human? How would this verse change that?

The covenant in vv. 8–17 depends entirely on God and covers every living creature. Where do you see God’s common kindness to all people today, and how should it shape the way you speak about and treat those who do not believe?

Ham exposed his father’s shame; Shem and Japheth covered it (vv. 22–23). How can we cover one another’s failures in love without covering up wrongdoing that needs to be dealt with?

10.title: The Table of Nations
10.text: <sup>1</sup>These are the generations of the sons of Noah, Shem, Ham, and Japheth. Sons were born to them after the flood.<sup>2</sup>The sons of Japheth: Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, Meshech, and Tiras.<sup>3</sup>The sons of Gomer: Ashkenaz, Riphath, and Togarmah.<sup>4</sup>The sons of Javan: Elishah, Tarshish, Kittim, and Dodanim.<sup>5</sup>From these the coastland peoples spread in their lands, each with his own language, by their clans, in their nations.<sup>6</sup>The sons of Ham: Cush, Egypt, Put, and Canaan.<sup>7</sup>The sons of Cush: Seba, Havilah, Sabtah, Raamah, and Sabteca. The sons of Raamah: Sheba and Dedan.<sup>8</sup>Cush fathered Nimrod; he was the first on earth to be a mighty man.<sup>9</sup>He was a mighty hunter before the LORD. Therefore it is said, "Like Nimrod a mighty hunter before the LORD."<sup>10</sup>The beginning of his kingdom was Babel, Erech, Accad, and Calneh, in the land of Shinar.<sup>11</sup>From that land he went into Assyria and built Nineveh, Rehoboth-Ir, Calah, and<sup>12</sup>Resen between Nineveh and Calah; that is the great city.<sup>13</sup>Egypt fathered Ludim, Anamim, Lehabim, Naphtuhim,<sup>14</sup>Pathrusim, Casluhim (from whom the Philistines came), and Caphtorim.<sup>15</sup>Canaan fathered Sidon his firstborn and Heth,<sup>16</sup>and the Jebusites, the Amorites, the Girgashites,<sup>17</sup>the Hivites, the Arkites, the Sinites,<sup>18</sup>the Arvadites, the Zemarites, and the Hamathites. Afterward the clans of the Canaanites dispersed.<sup>19</sup>And the territory of the Canaanites extended from Sidon in the direction of Gerar as far as Gaza, and in the direction of Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboiim, as far as Lasha.<sup>20</sup>These are the sons of Ham, by their clans, their languages, their lands, and their nations.<sup>21</sup>To Shem also, the father of all the children of Eber, the elder brother of Japheth, children were born.<sup>22</sup>The sons of Shem: Elam, Asshur, Arpachshad, Lud, and Aram.<sup>23</sup>The sons of Aram: Uz, Hul, Gether, and Mash.<sup>24</sup>Arpachshad fathered Shelah; and Shelah fathered Eber.<sup>25</sup>To Eber were born two sons: the name of the one was Peleg, for in his days the earth was divided, and his brother's name was Joktan.<sup>26</sup>Joktan fathered Almodad, Sheleph, Hazarmaveth, Jerah,<sup>27</sup>Hadoram, Uzal, Diklah,<sup>28</sup>Obal, Abimael, Sheba,<sup>29</sup>Ophir, Havilah, and Jobab; all these were the sons of Joktan.<sup>30</sup>The territory in which they lived extended from Mesha in the direction of Sephar to the hill country of the east.<sup>31</sup>These are the sons of Shem, by their clans, their languages, their lands, and their nations.<sup>32</sup>These are the clans of the sons of Noah, according to their genealogies, in their nations, and from these the nations spread abroad on the earth after the flood.
10.overview:
Where we are. Noah’s family has come out of the ark, God has renewed the command to “fill the earth” (9:1), and Noah’s words over his sons have hinted at the future of their descendants (9:25–27). Chapter 10, the Table of Nations, now traces those descendants across the known world before chapter 11 tells how they came to be scattered at Babel.

The message. Every nation on earth belongs to one human family, and every nation stands before the one God. The list is no dry catalogue: it declares that God keeps his word (the earth is being filled), that no people is outside his concern, and that the line of promise through Shem is chosen for the sake of all the rest. Before God calls one man, he shows us the whole world he means to bless through him.

Why it was said. Israel lived among the peoples named here: Egypt, which had enslaved them, the Canaanites whose land they were to enter, Assyria and Babylon, the great powers of the east (see the introduction). Genesis 10 tells Israel that all of them are relatives, all made by the LORD, and that Israel’s own calling is to be understood against this map of the world.

How the chapter makes its case. After a heading (v. 1), the sons of Japheth spread north and west to the coastlands (vv. 2–5). The sons of Ham fill the south and Canaan (vv. 6–20), with Nimrod, the first empire-builder, founding Babel and Nineveh (vv. 8–12), and the Canaanites’ territory marked out (vv. 15–19). The sons of Shem come last, because the story will follow them: through Eber and Peleg, in whose days the earth was divided, toward Abraham (vv. 21–31). A closing line gathers the whole: from these the nations spread abroad on the earth (v. 32).

Where it leads. To Christ by promise. Abraham will be called so that “all the families of the earth” shall be blessed (12:3), and this chapter has just named those families. The promise is kept in Christ: at Pentecost Elamites, Medes, Cretans and Arabians hear the gospel in their own languages (Acts 2:9–11); a Cushite is baptised on the road to Gaza (Acts 8:27–38); and the redeemed in heaven come “from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages” (Revelation 7:9). The Table of Nations is the guest list of the gospel.

For us. Every person you meet is a relative, descended from the same family and made by the same God. No nation or ethnic group may claim to be more human than another, and no people is beyond the reach of the gospel. The church’s mission to every nation is not a modern idea; it is written into the first map of the world.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The whole known world is traced back to the three sons of Noah, showing that humanity is one family in all its diversity. Japheth’s descendants spread to the north and west, to the coastlands and islands (vv. 2–5). Ham’s fill the south, from Cush and Egypt to the Canaanites, and among them Nimrod founds the first great kingdoms in Babylonia and Assyria (vv. 6–20). Shem’s are listed last, because the story will follow them, narrowing through Eber and Peleg toward Abraham (vv. 21–31). About seventy nations are named, a number that stands for the whole world. The list fulfils the command to fill the earth (9:1) and sets out the families God means to bless through Abraham (12:3).
verseByVerse.theology: The descendants of Japheth, Ham and Shem spread into the nations of the known world, and Shem's line is traced through Eber and Peleg towards Abram.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel heard in this list every nation it would meet, all of them cousins. Now: the multitude before the throne comes from every one of them (Rev. 7:9).

verseByVerse.quote: These are the generations of the sons of Noah, Shem, Ham, and Japheth. Sons were born to them after the flood. The sons of Japheth: Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, Meshech, and Tiras. The sons of Gomer: Ashkenaz, Riphath, and Togarmah. The sons of Javan: Elishah, Tarshish, Kittim, and Dodanim. From these the coastland peoples spread in their lands, each with his own language, by their clans, in their nations.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The nations of the world begin with Noah’s sons, and Japheth’s descendants spread north and west to the coastlands, each with its own land, language and clans.

These are the generations. This is the fourth of the “generations” headings that structure Genesis (see the introduction). It introduces the descendants of all three sons “after the flood”: God’s command to be fruitful and fill the earth (9:1) is being obeyed.

The sons of Japheth. Many of these names can be matched with peoples known from history, mostly to the north and west of Israel. Madai is the Medes, in what is now Iran; Javan is the Ionians, the Greeks; Gomer, Tubal and Meshech belong to the region of modern Turkey and the Black Sea; Tarshish lay far to the west, probably in Spain, and Kittim is Cyprus. Some of these names reappear in the prophets: Gog “of the land of Magog”, with Meshech and Tubal, in Ezekiel 38:2.

Each with his own language. Each list ends with the same formula: lands, languages, clans, nations (vv. 5, 20, 31). The table is not arranged purely by race: it groups peoples by descent, but also by geography, language and political ties. Peoples are something richer than bloodlines.

Seventy nations. The Hebrew text names seventy nations (the Greek Old Testament, seventy-two). The number seems deliberate, standing for the whole world. Israel too went down to Egypt as seventy persons (46:27): a small nation set among the nations for their sake. Many have also seen a link with the seventy-two whom Jesus sent out ahead of him (Luke 10:1), a sign that his mission was for all the nations.

One human family. All nations come from one family, and so from one man: God “made from one man every nation of mankind” (Acts 17:26). There is no basis here for any idea of racial superiority. Every person you meet, of whatever nation, is your relative, made in the same image (9:6). See Shem, Ham and Japheth.

Uncertain wording. Several of these names cannot now be identified with confidence. Magog, Riphath and Tiras are uncertain, Ashkenaz is perhaps the Scythians, and Elishah may be part of Cyprus. Dodanim appears as Rodanim in the parallel list (1 Chronicles 1:7), which would point to Rhodes. The general picture, the peoples to the north and west, is clear even where single names are not.
verseByVerse.note: The Greek Old Testament counts seventy-two names.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Ham: Cush, Egypt, Put, and Canaan. The sons of Cush: Seba, Havilah, Sabtah, Raamah, and Sabteca. The sons of Raamah: Sheba and Dedan. Cush fathered Nimrod; he was the first on earth to be a mighty man. He was a mighty hunter before the LORD. Therefore it is said, "Like Nimrod a mighty hunter before the LORD." The beginning of his kingdom was Babel, Erech, Accad, and Calneh, in the land of Shinar. From that land he went into Assyria and built Nineveh, Rehoboth-Ir, Calah, and Resen between Nineveh and Calah; that is the great city.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ham’s descendants fill the south, and among them Nimrod becomes the first great empire-builder, founding the cities of Babylonia and Assyria.

The sons of Ham. Cush is the land south of Egypt, roughly modern Sudan; Egypt is Egypt; Put is probably Libya; Canaan is the land Israel would enter. The sons of Cush include peoples of Arabia, such as Sheba and Dedan. Africa receives a central place in God’s map of the world, and long before the gospel reached Europe it reached Cush, when the Ethiopian official believed and was baptised (Acts 8:27–38; see the Ethiopian eunuch).

He was the first on earth to be a mighty man. Nimrod is the only person in the chapter given a story. “Mighty man” is the word used for the “mighty men” before the flood (6:4): a warrior, a man of power. He was famous enough to become a proverb, and Micah calls Assyria “the land of Nimrod” (Micah 5:6).

The beginning of his kingdom was Babel. Nimrod is the first named king in the Bible, and the first to build an empire. His cities are the great centres of Mesopotamia: Babel (Babylon), Erech (Uruk) and Accad in Shinar, the plain of Babylonia, and then Nineveh and Calah in Assyria. These would become the two powers that destroyed Israel and Judah. Babel’s founding here prepares for the story of its tower in chapter 11.

Power under God’s eye. Whatever Nimrod thought of the LORD, he lived “before the LORD”, under his eye. The empires that later seemed to rule the world were known to God from their beginning, and the Bible ends with the fall of the last “Babylon” (Revelation 18). Human power, however impressive, is never out of God’s sight or beyond his reach; only Christ’s kingdom has no end.

Uncertain wording. Three things are uncertain here. “A mighty hunter before the LORD” may simply mean a very great hunter (“before the LORD” as a way of saying “in God’s eyes”, that is, “extraordinary”); some take it as approval and others, following ancient Jewish tradition, as defiance “in the face of” the LORD. The text itself makes no judgment. Second, Nimrod’s name may echo the Hebrew for “we will rebel”, but that is a guess, and no attempt to identify him with a known king has won agreement. Third, it is unclear whether “that is the great city” (v. 12) refers to Resen, Calah, or Nineveh and its region together; Jonah calls Nineveh “that great city” (Jonah 1:2).
verseByVerse.note: Shinar is the old name for the plain of Babylonia.

verseByVerse.quote: Egypt fathered Ludim, Anamim, Lehabim, Naphtuhim, Pathrusim, Casluhim (from whom the Philistines came), and Caphtorim. Canaan fathered Sidon his firstborn and Heth, and the Jebusites, the Amorites, the Girgashites, the Hivites, the Arkites, the Sinites, the Arvadites, the Zemarites, and the Hamathites. Afterward the clans of the Canaanites dispersed. And the territory of the Canaanites extended from Sidon in the direction of Gerar as far as Gaza, and in the direction of Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboiim, as far as Lasha. These are the sons of Ham, by their clans, their languages, their lands, and their nations.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The peoples descended from Egypt and Canaan are listed, and the borders of Canaan, the land God will give Abraham, are marked out.

From whom the Philistines came. The Philistines, Israel’s great enemy in the days of Samson, Saul and David, were sea peoples from the Aegean, and here they are listed among the descendants of Egypt. Even Israel’s worst enemies have their place on God’s map. Amos can say that the LORD brought “the Philistines from Caphtor” as surely as he brought Israel from Egypt (Amos 9:7).

Canaan fathered Sidon his firstborn and Heth. Sidon is the Phoenician coast, Heth the Hittites (Abraham will buy a grave from the Hittites, 23:3–20), and the Jebusites held Jerusalem until David took it. These are the peoples of the land God would promise to Abraham’s offspring (15:18–21). The curse on Canaan (9:25) stands in the background.

The territory of the Canaanites. Their land runs from Sidon in the north to Gaza in the south-west and to the cities of the plain in the south-east, among them Sodom and Gomorrah, whose story is still to come (chapter 19). These are the borders of the land the story is heading toward.

Not a racial map. The Canaanites spoke a language very close to Hebrew, yet they are listed under Ham, while the Elamites, whose language was quite different, are listed under Shem (v. 22). Genesis is not classifying languages or races but tracing family and political ties as God saw them.

Uncertain wording. Elsewhere Scripture says the Philistines came from Caphtor, probably Crete (Amos 9:7; Jeremiah 47:4), so many think the note “from whom the Philistines came” belongs with the Caphtorim, the last name in v. 14, and has been placed one name early, or that both peoples were linked. Lasha (v. 19) cannot now be located.

verseByVerse.quote: To Shem also, the father of all the children of Eber, the elder brother of Japheth, children were born. The sons of Shem: Elam, Asshur, Arpachshad, Lud, and Aram. The sons of Aram: Uz, Hul, Gether, and Mash. Arpachshad fathered Shelah; and Shelah fathered Eber. To Eber were born two sons: the name of the one was Peleg, for in his days the earth was divided, and his brother's name was Joktan.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Shem’s line is listed last because it is the chosen line, running through Eber and Peleg toward Abraham.

To Shem also. Shem is introduced as “the father of all the children of Eber”, though Eber is his great-grandson. The narrator is already looking ahead: Eber may be the source of the name “Hebrew” (14:13). The order of the chapter, Japheth, Ham, then Shem, is the pattern of Genesis: the line that is not followed is dealt with first, and the chosen line is kept until last, because the story will follow it.

The sons of Shem. Elam lay east of Babylonia, in what is now south-western Iran; Asshur is Assyria; Aram is the Arameans of Syria, whose language, Aramaic, Jesus would speak. Uz, among Aram’s sons, is probably the land of Job (Job 1:1).

In his days the earth was divided. “Peleg” means “division” (ESV note). The most natural reading is that it refers to the dividing of humanity at Babel (11:8–9), which would then have happened in Peleg’s lifetime. Chapter 10 describes the result of Babel before chapter 11 tells the story: Genesis often gives the outcome first and then goes back to explain it.

The line that leads to Christ. Luke traces Jesus’ genealogy back through “the son of Peleg, the son of Eber” to Shem, Noah and Adam (Luke 3:35–38). The quiet names of this list are the steps by which God was bringing his Son into the world.

Uncertain wording. Verse 21 can be read as the ESV has it, Shem “the elder brother of Japheth”, or, as the ESV note allows, as “the brother of Japheth the elder”, making Japheth the eldest. The Hebrew allows both. And the division in Peleg’s days is not explained: most take it as the scattering at Babel, some as a division of land or the digging of canals (“peleg” can mean a water channel, as in “streams of water”, Psalm 1:3). The suggestion that it refers to the splitting of the continents finds little support in the text.
verseByVerse.note: “Peleg” means division (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: Joktan fathered Almodad, Sheleph, Hazarmaveth, Jerah, Hadoram, Uzal, Diklah, Obal, Abimael, Sheba, Ophir, Havilah, and Jobab; all these were the sons of Joktan. The territory in which they lived extended from Mesha in the direction of Sephar to the hill country of the east. These are the sons of Shem, by their clans, their languages, their lands, and their nations. These are the clans of the sons of Noah, according to their genealogies, in their nations, and from these the nations spread abroad on the earth after the flood.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The table closes by listing Joktan’s Arabian tribes and then gathering all the nations together: from Noah’s sons the nations spread abroad on the earth.

Joktan fathered Almodad. Joktan, Peleg’s brother, is the father of tribes in southern Arabia. Hazarmaveth is probably Hadramaut in modern Yemen; Ophir was later famous for its gold (1 Kings 9:28), and Sheba gave its name to the queen who visited Solomon (1 Kings 10:1). Joktan’s line is listed here and then left: chapter 11 will follow Peleg’s line to Abram.

Sheba and Havilah again. Sheba and Havilah appear among the sons of Cush (v. 7) and the sons of Joktan (vv. 28–29). Peoples mixed, moved and married; the table reflects real history, not tidy categories.

The nations spread abroad on the earth. The closing verse sums up: “the clans of the sons of Noah … in their nations”. The nations spread, fulfilling “fill the earth” (9:1), though Babel will try to resist it (11:4). Abraham’s call will be for “all the families of the earth” (12:3), the very families listed here.

The nations gathered in. Scripture never forgets this list. Isaiah foresaw God sending messengers “to Tarshish, Pul, and Lud, … to Tubal and Javan, to the coastlands far away”, who “shall declare my glory among the nations” (Isaiah 66:19). The Lamb is praised because by his blood he “ransomed people for God from every tribe and language and people and nation” (Revelation 5:9). The scattered families of Genesis 10 are gathered at last around Christ.

For us. God’s concern for the nations rebukes every nationalism that claims his backing for one people’s superiority, and every indifference to peoples far away. The diversity of nations is a gift, not a problem. Praise God that the gospel is reaching every one of these families, and pray for those still waiting to hear it.

Uncertain wording. Many of Joktan’s sons cannot now be located, and Mesha and Sephar (v. 30) are unknown places, though the region is clearly Arabia.

10.theology:
The Unity of Humanity. All human diversity, ethnic, linguistic and cultural, flows from one source. Racism is therefore not only a social wrong but a denial of God’s truth, the common humanity this chapter affirms. And in Christ the dividing wall between peoples is broken down at the cross (Eph. 2:14–16).
