Election and Mission. Because chapter 10 surveys all the nations first, the narrowing to one man in chapter 12 is plainly for their sake, not favouritism. God chooses Abraham not to exclude the nations but to bless them through him.
10.examples:
Then: No other ancient text attempts a map of all known humanity. In a world where different nations had different gods, Genesis 10 declares that one God made all peoples.

Now: The chapter rebukes every nationalism that claims God’s backing for one people’s superiority. All nations descend from the same family, are preserved by the same grace, and are meant in God's purpose to be blessed through the same seed (Rev. 5:9). The diversity of nations is a gift, not a problem: the filling of the earth that God commanded and Genesis 10 maps.

keyVerse.quote: These are the clans of the sons of Noah, according to their genealogies, in their nations, and from these the nations spread abroad on the earth after the flood.
keyVerse.note: This closing line gathers up the whole map: every nation on earth comes from one family preserved by God’s grace in the ark. It prepares for the call of Abraham, through whom these same families are to be blessed (12:3), and for the gospel that gathers people from every nation to Christ.

10.reflection:
Genesis 10 traces every nation back to one family (v. 32; Acts 17:26). How should that shape the way you think about people of other nations and ethnic backgrounds, including those your culture looks down on?

Nimrod built great cities and empires (vv. 8–12), yet he lived “before the LORD”. How does it help to know that the powers of our own day are under God’s eye?

Before God calls Abraham, he shows the whole world he means to bless through him. Why does it matter that God’s choice of one family was for the sake of all the others? How does that shape the church’s mission?

Which peoples or nations do you know least about, or find it hardest to care for? How could you pray for them this week?

11.title: The Tower of Babel
11.text: <sup>1</sup>Now the whole earth had one language and the same words.<sup>2</sup>And as people migrated from the east, they found a plain in the land of Shinar and settled there.<sup>3</sup>And they said to one another, "Come, let us make bricks, and burn them thoroughly." And they had brick for stone, and bitumen for mortar.<sup>4</sup>Then they said, "Come, let us build ourselves a city and a tower with its top in the heavens, and let us make a name for ourselves, lest we be dispersed over the face of the whole earth."<sup>5</sup>And the LORD came down to see the city and the tower, which the children of man had built.<sup>6</sup>And the LORD said, "Behold, they are one people, and they have all one language, and this is only the beginning of what they will do. And nothing that they propose to do will now be impossible for them.<sup>7</sup>Come, let us go down and there confuse their language, so that they may not understand one another's speech."<sup>8</sup>So the LORD dispersed them from there over the face of all the earth, and they left off building the city.<sup>9</sup>Therefore its name was called Babel, because there the LORD confused the language of all the earth. And from there the LORD dispersed them over the face of all the earth.<sup>10</sup>These are the generations of Shem. When Shem was 100 years old, he fathered Arpachshad two years after the flood.<sup>11</sup>And Shem lived after he fathered Arpachshad 500 years and had other sons and daughters.<sup>12</sup>When Arpachshad had lived 35 years, he fathered Shelah.<sup>13</sup>And Arpachshad lived after he fathered Shelah 403 years and had other sons and daughters.<sup>14</sup>When Shelah had lived 30 years, he fathered Eber.<sup>15</sup>And Shelah lived after he fathered Eber 403 years and had other sons and daughters.<sup>16</sup>When Eber had lived 34 years, he fathered Peleg.<sup>17</sup>And Eber lived after he fathered Peleg 430 years and had other sons and daughters.<sup>18</sup>When Peleg had lived 30 years, he fathered Reu.<sup>19</sup>And Peleg lived after he fathered Reu 209 years and had other sons and daughters.<sup>20</sup>When Reu had lived 32 years, he fathered Serug.<sup>21</sup>And Reu lived after he fathered Serug 207 years and had other sons and daughters.<sup>22</sup>When Serug had lived 30 years, he fathered Nahor.<sup>23</sup>And Serug lived after he fathered Nahor 200 years and had other sons and daughters.<sup>24</sup>When Nahor had lived 29 years, he fathered Terah.<sup>25</sup>And Nahor lived after he fathered Terah 119 years and had other sons and daughters.<sup>26</sup>When Terah had lived 70 years, he fathered Abram, Nahor, and Haran.<sup>27</sup>Now these are the generations of Terah. Terah fathered Abram, Nahor, and Haran; and Haran fathered Lot.<sup>28</sup>Haran died in the presence of his father Terah in the land of his kindred, in Ur of the Chaldeans.<sup>29</sup>And Abram and Nahor took wives. The name of Abram's wife was Sarai, and the name of Nahor's wife, Milcah, the daughter of Haran the father of Milcah and Iscah.<sup>30</sup>Now Sarai was barren; she had no child.<sup>31</sup>Terah took Abram his son and Lot the son of Haran, his grandson, and Sarai his daughter-in-law, his son Abram's wife, and they went forth together from Ur of the Chaldeans to go into the land of Canaan, but when they came to Haran, they settled there.<sup>32</sup>The days of Terah were 205 years, and Terah died in Haran.
11.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 10 has mapped the nations spreading over the earth. Chapter 11 goes back to tell how that scattering began, at Babel, and then narrows the whole human story to one family: Shem’s line runs down to Terah, and Terah’s family sets out from Ur. It closes the story of the whole human race (chapters 1–11).

The message. Humanity united without God is humanity united against God, and God will not let it succeed. The builders of Babel try to make a name for themselves and secure their future by their own achievement; God comes down, confuses their language and scatters them. Then, where no word of grace follows the judgment, God quietly begins his answer: a genealogy that leads to a barren couple, through whom he will give the name and the blessing that Babel tried to grab.

Why it was said. Babylon was the oldest and proudest city of the world Israel knew, and would later destroy Jerusalem (see the introduction). Genesis tells Israel what Babylon really is: a monument to human pride that God laughed at and brought down. It also tells them where they came from: their father Abraham was called out of this very region, from a family that “served other gods” (Joshua 24:2).

How the chapter makes its case. Humanity settles in Shinar and resolves to build a city and a tower to make a name and avoid being scattered (vv. 1–4). The LORD comes down to see it, confuses their language and disperses them, and the city is called Babel (vv. 5–9). Shem’s genealogy follows, ten generations to Terah, lifespans shrinking as it goes (vv. 10–26). Terah’s family is introduced, with Sarai, who “was barren; she had no child” (vv. 27–30). They leave Ur for Canaan but stop at Haran, where Terah dies (vv. 31–32).

Where it leads. To Christ by the need exposed, by promise and by pattern. Babel shows that humanity cannot climb to heaven or make itself a name; the gap must be bridged from God’s side. Jesus is the true way between heaven and earth (John 1:51), and the name above every name is not seized but given to him by the Father because he humbled himself (Philippians 2:9). At Pentecost the Spirit undoes Babel’s curse, as people from many nations hear the gospel each “in his own language” (Acts 2:6). And Sarai’s barren womb is the first of many in Scripture through which God brings life where there was none, until the promised Son is born of a virgin.

For us. Babel is not only an ancient city; it is the human heart wherever we try to secure our future and make our name without God, in careers, nations, churches or technology. The gospel calls us to stop building towers and receive a name and a city as a gift (Hebrews 11:10). And where life looks barren, God often begins there.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Humanity unites to make a name for itself without God, and God scatters it. With one language and new building skills, the people settle in Shinar and resolve to build a city and a tower reaching to the heavens, so that they will not be dispersed (vv. 1–4). The LORD “came down” to see their tower, a sharp irony, and confuses their language so that they cannot work together; the building stops and they are scattered over the earth (vv. 5–9). In nine verses the story explains the diversity of languages, lays bare the pride at the root of human civilisation without God, and shows that God will not let humanity build its way to independence from him. His judgment is also a mercy, restraining evil.
verseByVerse.theology: With one language, the people settle in Shinar, Babylonia, and build a city and a tower to make a name for themselves and avoid being scattered. The LORD comes down, confuses their language, and scatters them.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel would meet Babel again as Babylon, the empire that carried it into exile. Now: what sin scattered, grace gathers into one people in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the whole earth had one language and the same words. And as people migrated from the east, they found a plain in the land of Shinar and settled there. And they said to one another, "Come, let us make bricks, and burn them thoroughly." And they had brick for stone, and bitumen for mortar. Then they said, "Come, let us build ourselves a city and a tower with its top in the heavens, and let us make a name for ourselves, lest we be dispersed over the face of the whole earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
United by one language and new technology, humanity sets out to build a city and a tower to make a name for itself and avoid being scattered: a project of pride against God’s command.

The whole earth had one language. This story goes back before the spreading of chapter 10, which already speaks of each nation with “his own language” (10:5). Genesis often gives the outcome first and then explains it (see the comment on 10:21–25).

As people migrated from the east. They settle in Shinar, the plain of Babylonia (10:10). In Genesis moving east often means moving away from God: Adam and Eve were driven out east of Eden (3:24), Cain settled east of Eden (4:16), and Lot “journeyed east” toward Sodom (13:11).

They had brick for stone, and bitumen for mortar. Southern Mesopotamia has little building stone, so its cities were built of mud brick, baked hard and set in bitumen (natural tar). For Israel, who built with stone, the detail places the story firmly in Babylonia. The new technology is not wrong in itself; the problem is what they use it for. The tower was probably a ziggurat, a stepped temple-tower of the kind found in every Mesopotamian city, meant to be a link between the gods and the earth.

With its top in the heavens. The phrase can describe a very tall building (Deuteronomy 1:28 speaks of cities “fortified up to heaven”), but here it also reveals the builders’ ambition: to reach God’s realm on their own terms. Compare Jacob’s dream, where a stairway reaches heaven, but God sets it up and comes down it to speak (28:12–13).

Let us make a name for ourselves. This is the heart of the sin: self-glory, security and fame without God. The next chapter shows the contrast: God tells Abram, “I will … make your name great” (12:2), as a gift. Their other motive, “lest we be dispersed”, defies God’s command to fill the earth (9:1). They want safety in numbers and in walls rather than in God.

Our own Babels. It is worth asking where we too are building a name for ourselves: through work, reputation, a nation, a church or a cause, looking to our achievements to give us significance and protect us from being “scattered”. Every such tower is too small, and every such name fades. The only lasting name is the one God gives.
verseByVerse.note: Ziggurats were common in Mesopotamia; the best preserved is at Ur, Abram’s home city.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD came down to see the city and the tower, which the children of man had built. And the LORD said, "Behold, they are one people, and they have all one language, and this is only the beginning of what they will do. And nothing that they propose to do will now be impossible for them. Come, let us go down and there confuse their language, so that they may not understand one another's speech." So the LORD dispersed them from there over the face of all the earth, and they left off building the city. Therefore its name was called Babel, because there the LORD confused the language of all the earth. And from there the LORD dispersed them over the face of all the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD comes down to see the tall tower, confuses their language and scatters them: the city of human pride is left unfinished, and is called Babel.

The LORD came down to see. The irony is sharp: their tower “to the heavens” was so small that God had to come down to see it. God does not need to come down to know (he sees all things); the language pictures him as the true King inspecting a rebel city before passing judgment, as he will at Sodom (18:21).

This is only the beginning. God is not threatened by human achievement. His concern is that a humanity united in pride and rebellion would have no limit to the evil it could do: “nothing that they propose to do will now be impossible for them.” The flood showed what unrestrained human evil becomes (6:5, 11); God now acts to restrain it before it gets that far. What is “impossible” for proud humanity is a question God answers later: “nothing will be impossible with God” (Luke 1:37).

Come, let us go down. The builders said, “Come, let us” three times (vv. 3, 4); now God answers with his own “Come, let us”, echoing the creation of man (1:26). On the plural, see the comment on 1:26–27.

Therefore its name was called Babel. The builders wanted to make a name; they got one. The Babylonians said their city’s name meant “gate of god”. As the ESV notes, “Babel” sounds like the Hebrew for “confused”. Genesis answers Babylon’s boast with a pun: not the gate of heaven but the place of confusion.

The LORD dispersed them. The scattering is judgment, but it is also mercy: it limits united rebellion and pushes humanity to fill the earth as God commanded. Babylon becomes in Scripture the symbol of proud human power set against God. Nebuchadnezzar boasts, “Is not this great Babylon, which I have built by my mighty power … ?” (Daniel 4:30), and in Revelation the last Babylon falls (Revelation 18:2), replaced by “the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God” (Revelation 21:2). The city we cannot build up, God brings down.

Babel reversed. At Pentecost Babel is reversed. The Spirit comes down, and people from many nations hear the gospel, “each one … in his own language” (Acts 2:6). God does not undo the variety of languages; he unites them in praise. The goal is a great multitude “from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages” worshipping the Lamb together (Revelation 7:9). The unity Babel tried to build around its own name, God gives around the name of Jesus.

A reader’s question: is this the origin of all languages? Genesis presents Babel as the decisive moment when God divided human speech, and sees all the world’s languages as coming from that event. It does not say how quickly the many languages developed or how they relate to one another, and it is not written to answer the questions of modern linguistics. Its concern is why humanity is divided, and how God means to bring it together.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “Babel” sounds like the Hebrew for “confused.”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–26 — The Genealogy from Shem to Abram
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After the judgment at Babel, God’s answer begins quietly, with a family tree. Shem’s line is traced through ten generations to Terah, in the same pattern as Adam’s line in chapter 5, so that the story narrows from all the nations to the one family through whom God will bless them. The lifespans shrink, from Shem’s 600 years to Terah’s 205, and unlike chapter 5 no one’s death is recorded: the list is pressing forward. Its last verse names Abram, and the whole of Genesis turns on him.
verseByVerse.theology: The line of promise is kept in order through ordinary fathers and sons.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: God was keeping a family tree while Babel was building. Now: Luke traces Jesus back through these names (Luke 3:34–36); each name is a link in a line that ends in a manger.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the generations of Shem. When Shem was 100 years old, he fathered Arpachshad two years after the flood. And Shem lived after he fathered Arpachshad 500 years and had other sons and daughters. When Arpachshad had lived 35 years, he fathered Shelah. And Arpachshad lived after he fathered Shelah 403 years and had other sons and daughters. When Shelah had lived 30 years, he fathered Eber. And Shelah lived after he fathered Eber 403 years and had other sons and daughters. When Eber had lived 34 years, he fathered Peleg. And Eber lived after he fathered Peleg 430 years and had other sons and daughters. When Peleg had lived 30 years, he fathered Reu. And Peleg lived after he fathered Reu 209 years and had other sons and daughters. When Reu had lived 32 years, he fathered Serug. And Reu lived after he fathered Serug 207 years and had other sons and daughters. When Serug had lived 30 years, he fathered Nahor. And Serug lived after he fathered Nahor 200 years and had other sons and daughters. When Nahor had lived 29 years, he fathered Terah. And Nahor lived after he fathered Terah 119 years and had other sons and daughters. When Terah had lived 70 years, he fathered Abram, Nahor, and Haran.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Shem’s line is traced through ten generations to Abram: after Babel, God’s answer begins with a family tree.

These are the generations of Shem. This is the fifth of the “generations” headings (see the introduction). Babel ended with no word of grace, as earlier judgments had (3:21; 4:15; 6:8). This list is the grace: God is already at work in a family line, quietly preparing the man through whom he will bless the scattered nations.

Ten generations. There are ten generations from Shem to Terah, as from Adam to Noah (chapter 5). Each list ends with a father with three sons (Noah: Shem, Ham and Japheth; Terah: Abram, Nahor and Haran), and in each the first son named carries the line. The pattern suggests the lists are shaped, and perhaps selective, for teaching and memory (see the textual note below).

Lifespans shorten. Shem lives 600 years, the next three over 400, from Peleg on between about 150 and 240, and Terah 205. By Abraham’s time (175 years) and Moses’ (120), lives are much nearer our own. Death is tightening its grip on the human race after the flood.

No “and he died”. Unlike chapter 5, the list does not end each entry with “and he died”. The focus is not on death but on moving forward: the list is hurrying to Abram, and to the promise.

Steps toward Christ. Luke traces Jesus’ ancestry back through these names: “the son of Terah, the son of Nahor, the son of Serug, the son of Reu, the son of Peleg, the son of Eber, the son of Shelah, the son of Cainan, the son of Arphaxad, the son of Shem” (Luke 3:34–36). Names that seem to mean nothing were the generations through which God was bringing his Son into the world. God is often at work in long stretches of ordinary, unremarkable lives.

Gaps in the genealogy? If the list has no gaps, Shem would still have been alive in Abraham’s old age, and the flood would have come only three or four centuries before Abraham. Some take the figures straightforwardly; many think, given the patterned ten generations and Luke’s extra name, that the list may be selective, as some biblical genealogies are (compare Matthew 1:8, which leaves out three kings). This commentary takes the genealogies as true history, perhaps with small gaps.

Textual note. The Greek Old Testament adds a Cainan between Arpachshad and Shelah, which Luke follows (Luke 3:36), and gives different ages. The Hebrew omits him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Terah’s family is introduced, and with it the great obstacle to God’s promise: “Sarai was barren; she had no child” (v. 30). Terah’s son Haran dies in Ur, leaving his son Lot, and Abram and Nahor marry (vv. 27–29). Then Terah sets out from Ur of the Chaldeans with Abram, Sarai and Lot, heading for Canaan, but they stop at Haran and settle there, and Terah dies (vv. 31–32). The scene is set for God’s call: a family far from the land, worshipping other gods (Joshua 24:2), with no child and no future except what God will give.
verseByVerse.theology: Terah's family is introduced: Abram, Nahor, Haran (who dies in Ur), Lot, Milcah, and Sarai. Terah sets out for Canaan but settles in Haran and dies there.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the promise of offspring is about to be given to a man whose wife cannot conceive. Now: many lives set out for the right place and settle halfway; God's purpose goes on to the one he calls.

verseByVerse.quote: Now these are the generations of Terah. Terah fathered Abram, Nahor, and Haran; and Haran fathered Lot. Haran died in the presence of his father Terah in the land of his kindred, in Ur of the Chaldeans. And Abram and Nahor took wives. The name of Abram's wife was Sarai, and the name of Nahor's wife, Milcah, the daughter of Haran the father of Milcah and Iscah. Now Sarai was barren; she had no child.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Terah’s family is introduced, living in Ur among other gods, and the great obstacle to God’s promise is named at once: Sarai was barren.

These are the generations of Terah. This sixth “generations” heading introduces the story of Abraham, which runs to 25:11. Terah’s three sons are named: Abram, Nahor, whose granddaughter Rebekah will marry Isaac (24:15), and Haran, the father of Lot. Haran dies young, “in the presence of his father”, which helps explain why Lot travels with Abram.

Ur of the Chaldeans. Ur was a great and ancient city in southern Mesopotamia, near the Euphrates in what is now southern Iraq, with a large ziggurat to its chief god, the moon god. Abram did not grow up as a worshipper of the LORD: Terah’s family “served other gods” (Joshua 24:2). God’s call came to an idolater, by grace, not because Abram had found God first.

Sarai was barren; she had no child. The narrator says it twice, for emphasis. In a world where a family’s future depended on children, this was a grief and a dead end. The promised line seems to end before it begins. This sets up the whole Abraham story: the promise will come where it seems impossible, and will depend on God alone. Paul says that Abraham faced “the barrenness of Sarah’s womb” and still believed (Romans 4:19). See Sarah.

The barren women of Scripture. Sarai is the first of several barren women through whom God brings the line of promise: Rebekah (25:21), Rachel (29:31), Hannah (1 Samuel 1:2) and Elizabeth (Luke 1:7). Each time the child is plainly God’s gift. The pattern reaches its climax when the promised Son is born not from a barren womb but from a virgin’s, by the power of the Spirit (Luke 1:35–37). Where life is impossible, God gives it; that is the shape of the gospel, and finally of the resurrection.

For those who long for a child. This verse does not mean that every childless couple will be given children, or that childlessness is a sign of God’s disfavour. Sarai’s story is about God keeping his promise of a Saviour, and he has kept it. For those who grieve childlessness today, the hope Scripture offers is not a guaranteed pregnancy but a God who sees, who gives his people a family in the church (Mark 10:29–30), and whose purposes are bigger than our lineage (Isaiah 56:4–5).

Uncertain wording. “Of the Chaldeans” uses the name of a people who became prominent in southern Mesopotamia later than Abraham, so it probably identifies the city for later readers. Most locate Ur at the famous site in southern Iraq; a few have argued for a northern Ur near Haran, but the southern city remains the likelier.
verseByVerse.note: Ur’s chief god was the moon god.

verseByVerse.quote: Terah took Abram his son and Lot the son of Haran, his grandson, and Sarai his daughter-in-law, his son Abram's wife, and they went forth together from Ur of the Chaldeans to go into the land of Canaan, but when they came to Haran, they settled there. The days of Terah were 205 years, and Terah died in Haran.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Terah sets out from Ur toward Canaan with Abram, Sarai and Lot, but they stop at Haran and settle there, and Terah dies.

They went forth together from Ur. Stephen tells us that God had already appeared to Abram in Ur: “The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham when he was in Mesopotamia, before he lived in Haran” (Acts 7:2). So the move from Ur was a response to God’s call, though Genesis records Terah as leading it. They “went … to go into the land of Canaan”: the destination was set.

When they came to Haran, they settled there. Haran lay far to the north-west, on the great trade route that ran from Mesopotamia round the Fertile Crescent to Canaan. (In Hebrew the city’s name is spelled differently from that of Abram’s brother.) Like Ur, it was a centre of the worship of the moon god, so the move had not yet taken the family away from the gods of Joshua 24:2. The family stopped halfway.

Terah died in Haran. Stephen says that “after his father died, God removed him from there into this land” (Acts 7:4). Since Terah was seventy when his first son was born (v. 26), and Abram left at seventy-five (12:4), it seems Abram was not the eldest son but is named first because of his importance, as Shem is named first among Noah’s sons. Terah would then have been about 130 when Abram was born.

Stopping halfway. Terah’s family set out for Canaan and settled short of it. Many begin to follow God and stop at a comfortable halfway place. God’s call is not only to leave but to arrive: Abram will have to go on from Haran too (12:1–4).
verseByVerse.note: Haran lay in northern Mesopotamia, on the route from Ur to Canaan.

11.theology:
Babel and Pentecost. At Pentecost "each one was hearing them speak in his own language" (Acts 2:6). The church of every tribe and tongue is the new humanity Babel failed to produce, united not by self-glory but by one Spirit and one Lord. Babel sought unity by making everyone the same; the gospel unites different peoples by reconciling them to God and to each other.

The City of God. Augustine's great work draws the line this text draws: the City of Man built on self-love, and the City of God built on love of God. Every empire is a version of Babel; the City of God is the New Jerusalem, built by God, filled with the redeemed of every nation, with the Lamb as its temple and light.
11.examples:
Then: The ziggurats of Mesopotamia were built as places where heaven and earth met. Genesis turns that idea upside down: the meeting place between heaven and earth cannot be built from below; it must be given from above.

Now: Every age builds its Babel: the plan for a perfect society, the dream of unlimited human power, the nation that makes its name at the expense of others. The twentieth century's most ambitious Babels, Soviet communism and National Socialism, showed what Genesis 11 warns: unlimited human power directed by a godless vision ends in catastrophe. The answer is not better planning but the fear of the LORD, the recognition that every civilisation depends on, and must answer to, the God who came down to see what we were building.

keyVerse.quote: Come, let us build ourselves a city and a tower with its top in the heavens, and let us make a name for ourselves, lest we be dispersed over the face of the whole earth.
keyVerse.note: This verse lays bare the root of human rebellion: to reach heaven by our own effort, make our own name and secure our own future without God. Everything that follows answers it: God scatters the builders, then calls Abram and promises, “I will … make your name great” (12:2), the gift that Babel tried to seize, and in Christ he gives the name above every name.

11.reflection:
The builders of Babel wanted to “make a name” for themselves and avoid being scattered (v. 4). In what ways do people today, and we ourselves, try to find significance and security through our own achievements?

Babel’s scattering was a judgment, but also a mercy that restrained evil (vv. 6–8). Where have you seen God’s frustration of human plans, including your own, turn out to be kind?

At Pentecost the gospel was heard in many languages (Acts 2:6–11). What does it tell us about God’s purposes that he unites people across languages and cultures rather than making them all the same? How should that shape your church?

The chapter ends with a family far from God, stopped halfway, and a woman who “had no child” (vv. 30–31). Why do you think God so often begins his work where things look most hopeless?

12.title: Go from Your Country
12.text: <sup>1</sup>Now the LORD said to Abram, "Go from your country and your kindred and your father's house to the land that I will show you.<sup>2</sup>And I will make of you a great nation, and I will bless you and make your name great, so that you will be a blessing.<sup>3</sup>I will bless those who bless you, and him who dishonors you I will curse, and in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed."<sup>4</sup>So Abram went, as the LORD had told him, and Lot went with him. Abram was seventy-five years old when he departed from Haran.<sup>5</sup>And Abram took Sarai his wife, and Lot his brother's son, and all their possessions that they had gathered, and the people that they had acquired in Haran, and they set out to go to the land of Canaan. When they came to the land of Canaan,<sup>6</sup>Abram passed through the land to the place at Shechem, to the oak of Moreh. At that time the Canaanites were in the land.<sup>7</sup>Then the LORD appeared to Abram and said, "To your offspring I will give this land." So he built there an altar to the LORD, who had appeared to him.<sup>8</sup>From there he moved to the hill country on the east of Bethel and pitched his tent, with Bethel on the west and Ai on the east. And there he built an altar to the LORD and called upon the name of the LORD.<sup>9</sup>And Abram journeyed on, still going toward the Negeb.<sup>10</sup>Now there was a famine in the land. So Abram went down to Egypt to sojourn there, for the famine was severe in the land.<sup>11</sup>When he was about to enter Egypt, he said to Sarai his wife, "I know that you are a woman beautiful in appearance,<sup>12</sup>and when the Egyptians see you, they will say, 'This is his wife.' Then they will kill me, but they will let you live.<sup>13</sup>Say you are my sister, that it may go well with me because of you, and that my life may be spared for your sake."<sup>14</sup>When Abram entered Egypt, the Egyptians saw that the woman was very beautiful.<sup>15</sup>And when the princes of Pharaoh saw her, they praised her to Pharaoh. And the woman was taken into Pharaoh's house.<sup>16</sup>And for her sake he dealt well with Abram; and he had sheep, oxen, male donkeys, male servants, female servants, female donkeys, and camels.<sup>17</sup>But the LORD afflicted Pharaoh and his house with great plagues because of Sarai, Abram's wife.<sup>18</sup>So Pharaoh called Abram and said, "What is this you have done to me? Why did you not tell me that she was your wife?<sup>19</sup>Why did you say, 'She is my sister,' so that I took her for my wife? Now then, here is your wife; take her, and go."<sup>20</sup>And Pharaoh gave men orders concerning him, and they sent him away with his wife and all that he had.
12.overview:
Where we are. Chapters 1–11 have traced sin from the garden to Babel, where the nations were scattered with no word of grace. Chapter 11 ended with Terah’s family stalled in Haran and Sarai barren. Now, into that darkness, God speaks to one man, and the whole Bible turns on what he says.

The message. God answers the curse that has spread through the world with a promise of blessing, and he begins it with one undeserving man. He calls Abram to leave everything and promises him a land, a great nation, a name and a blessing that will reach all the families of the earth. Abram believes and goes. But within the same chapter he fails badly, and the promise survives only because God keeps it. The blessing of the world rests on God’s faithfulness, not Abram’s.

Why it was said. Israel heard this as the story of their own beginning: they were Abraham’s offspring, on their way to the land promised here, called to be a blessing to the nations (see the introduction). They had just come out of Egypt, and Abram’s trip there, with famine, a threatened wife, plagues on Pharaoh and a departure with wealth, was a foretaste of their own story.

How the chapter makes its case. The LORD calls Abram to go and gives him a sevenfold promise of blessing (vv. 1–3). Abram goes, at seventy-five, with Sarai and Lot, and enters Canaan, though “the Canaanites were in the land” (vv. 4–6). The LORD appears and promises the land to his offspring, and Abram builds altars and calls on the LORD’s name as he moves through the land (vv. 7–9). Then famine drives him to Egypt, where in fear he passes Sarai off as his sister, and she is taken into Pharaoh’s house (vv. 10–16). The LORD strikes Pharaoh with plagues, and Abram is rebuked and sent away (vv. 17–20).

Where it leads. To Christ by promise, above all. Paul says that in “all the families of the earth shall be blessed” Scripture “preached the gospel beforehand to Abraham” (Galatians 3:8), and that the offspring to whom the promise was made is Christ (Galatians 3:16). Jesus himself said, “Your father Abraham rejoiced that he would see my day” (John 8:56). The chapter also exposes a need: the father of the faithful puts his wife in danger to save himself. The blessing will come through a better offspring, the husband who “gave himself up” for his bride (Ephesians 5:25).

For us. God’s call still comes before we have anything to offer, and it comes with promises. Faith means trusting God enough to go where he leads, and the blessing we receive is always meant to flow on to others. When we fail, as Abram did, the promise does not fail with us: God keeps his word and brings us back.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — The Call of Abram and the Covenant Promise
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After eleven chapters of spreading ruin, God calls one man and gives him a promise for all humanity. The LORD tells Abram to leave his country, kindred and father’s house, and promises him a great nation, a great name and a blessing that will reach all the families of the earth (vv. 1–3). Abram goes, as the LORD told him, and enters Canaan, though the Canaanites are still there (vv. 4–6). The LORD appears and promises the land to his offspring, and Abram answers by building altars and calling on the LORD’s name as he journeys south (vv. 7–9). Abram’s departure is the pattern of biblical faith: trusting God’s word and going.
verseByVerse.theology: The LORD calls Abram to leave country, kindred and father's house, and promises a great nation, a great name, and blessing for all the families of the earth. Abram goes, and builds altars in a land the Canaanites still hold.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Abram had no map, only a promise. Now: every believing Gentile is the fulfilment of this promise.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the LORD said to Abram, "Go from your country and your kindred and your father's house to the land that I will show you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God calls Abram to leave everything familiar and go to a land he has not seen, trusting only God’s word.

Now the LORD said to Abram. After Babel, God starts again with one man. The call is pure grace: Abram came from a family that “served other gods” (Joshua 24:2), and nothing in him explains why God chose him (see the comment on 11:27–30). Stephen says that God first appeared to him in Ur (Acts 7:2); here the call is repeated, or recalled, in Haran.

Go from your country and your kindred and your father’s house. Each step is harder than the last: the land, then the clan, then the household he grew up in. In the ancient world your family and land were your security, identity and future. Abram is to leave them all for a land he has not seen: “he went out, not knowing where he was going” (Hebrews 11:8).

To the land that I will show you. God gives a direction and a Caller, not a detailed plan. Abram must trust God for each step.

The command comes wrapped in promise. Notice that the call of verse 1 is surrounded by the promises of verses 2–3. What God asks us to leave, he asks as one who means to give. Jesus calls his disciples in the same way, to leave, follow and receive “a hundredfold” (Mark 10:29–30).

verseByVerse.quote: And I will make of you a great nation, and I will bless you and make your name great, so that you will be a blessing. I will bless those who bless you, and him who dishonors you I will curse, and in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God promises Abram a great nation, a great name and his blessing, and promises that through him all the families of the earth will be blessed: this is the gospel announced in advance.

I will make of you a great nation. The promises pile up: a nation, blessing, a name, blessing for others, protection, judgment on those who curse him, and blessing for all families. They are spoken to a man of seventy-five with a barren wife (11:30). The great name that Babel grasped for (11:4), God gives.

What God’s blessing is. “Bless” and “blessing” come five times in two verses, answering the five times “curse” has appeared in chapters 3–11. When God blesses, he gives life, fruitfulness and good, and above all he gives himself: it is the reverse of the curse. We often treat blessing as the reward for a life well managed. Here it is pure gift, spoken to a man who has done nothing yet. Timothy Keller often pointed out, following Kierkegaard, that sin is trying to build an identity for yourself apart from God; that is Babel. Blessing is the identity God gives instead. It comes to us the same way: Christ became a curse for us “so that in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles” (Galatians 3:14). See Bless in the Theological Dictionary.

So that you will be a blessing. The blessing is never meant to stop with Abram. God chooses one man for the sake of all the others: election is for mission. The same is true of the church, chosen in Christ to make him known. Ask where God’s blessing to you is meant to overflow this week.

Him who dishonors you I will curse. The Hebrew uses two different words: whoever treats Abram lightly or with contempt, God will curse. And “those who bless” is plural, while “him who dishonors” is singular: God expects the blessing to be wide and the curse to be the exception.

In you all the families of the earth shall be blessed. These are the families just listed in chapter 10. Paul calls this promise the gospel preached “beforehand to Abraham” (Galatians 3:8), and finds its focus in one offspring, Christ (Galatians 3:16). Peter told the crowds in Jerusalem that God had sent his risen servant Jesus to bless them in fulfilment of it (Acts 3:25–26). Everyone, from any nation, who trusts in Christ is “blessed along with Abraham, the man of faith” (Galatians 3:9).

How Jewish readers take it. Many Jewish interpreters, following Rashi, read the last promise as people blessing themselves by Abraham: a father will say to his son, may you be like Abraham. Jewish tradition also hears here Israel’s calling to make the one God known among the nations, a theme the prophets take up (Isaiah 49:6). Both readings agree that Abraham’s family was chosen for the sake of the world. This commentary follows Paul, who hears in the promise the gospel announced in advance and finds its focus in one offspring, Christ (Galatians 3:8, 16).

Where Christians differ: bless Israel today? Some Christian Zionists apply “I will bless those who bless you” to support for the modern state of Israel. This commentary’s view: the promise is fulfilled in Christ and in all who belong to him by faith (Galatians 3:7–9, 29). Christians should love the Jewish people and pray for their salvation, and judge any nation’s actions by God’s justice.

Uncertain wording. As the ESV notes, “shall be blessed” can also be translated “will bless themselves”: the Hebrew verb form can be read either way, and the related promises later in Genesis (22:18; 26:4) use a form that is just as open. The Greek Old Testament and the New Testament take it as “shall be blessed” (Galatians 3:8; Acts 3:25). Even on the other reading, Abraham is the measure of blessing for the nations, and they find it by being joined to him. The ESV’s main reading is the likelier, and it is the one the apostles relied on.
verseByVerse.note: “Will be blessed” can also be rendered “will bless themselves” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: So Abram went, as the LORD had told him, and Lot went with him. Abram was seventy-five years old when he departed from Haran. And Abram took Sarai his wife, and Lot his brother's son, and all their possessions that they had gathered, and the people that they had acquired in Haran, and they set out to go to the land of Canaan. When they came to the land of Canaan, Abram passed through the land to the place at Shechem, to the oak of Moreh. At that time the Canaanites were in the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abram obeys at once and enters Canaan, but finds the land already occupied: the promise faces real obstacles.

So Abram went, as the LORD had told him. No argument, no recorded reply: faith obeys. Abram is seventy-five, and it is never too late for God’s call. He takes Sarai, Lot, the possessions and the household servants gathered in Haran (see slavery in the ancient world), a large household on the move, some 400 miles from Haran to Canaan.

Lot went with him. Lot, his orphaned nephew, comes too. His presence will bring both kindness and trouble (chapters 13–14, 19).

The oak of Moreh. Shechem lay in the hill country at the heart of Canaan, and would become a key place in Israel’s story: Jacob settled there (33:18–20), Joshua renewed the covenant there (Joshua 24:1), and Jesus sat at Jacob’s well nearby and offered living water to a Samaritan woman (John 4:5–6). “Moreh” means “teacher”, and the great tree may have been a place where Canaanites sought guidance from their gods; if so, Abram’s altar to the LORD nearby (v. 7) is a quiet claim on the land.

At that time the Canaanites were in the land. The land God promised was not empty. Abram arrives with nothing but a promise, as a guest in someone else’s country. Faith often has to hold on to God’s word while the circumstances seem to contradict it. Abram lived “in the land of promise, as in a foreign land, living in tents” (Hebrews 11:9).
verseByVerse.note: Shechem lay in the hill country at the heart of Canaan. The “oak” may be a terebinth (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD appeared to Abram and said, "To your offspring I will give this land." So he built there an altar to the LORD, who had appeared to him. From there he moved to the hill country on the east of Bethel and pitched his tent, with Bethel on the west and Ai on the east. And there he built an altar to the LORD and called upon the name of the LORD. And Abram journeyed on, still going toward the Negeb.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD appears and promises the land to Abram’s offspring, and Abram answers by building altars and calling on the LORD’s name across the land.

The LORD appeared to Abram. This is the first time in the Bible that God is said to “appear” to someone. He meets Abram in the land and confirms the promise just where its fulfilment looks least likely, with the Canaanites all around.

To your offspring I will give this land. The land is promised to Abram’s offspring, not to Abram himself, who will own only a grave in it (23:19; Acts 7:5). The promise looks beyond his lifetime. Paul notes that the word “offspring” is singular and finds its focus in Christ (Galatians 3:16), and he widens the promise: Abraham and his offspring are “heir of the world” (Romans 4:13).

He built there an altar. Abram answers God’s word with worship. His altars, at Shechem and between Bethel and Ai, mark the land as the LORD’s. Wherever we live can be made a place of worship.

Called upon the name of the LORD. This is what people began to do in Seth’s day (4:26): to pray to and worship the LORD by name, and probably to proclaim him. The contrast with Babel is pointed: the builders tried to make a name for themselves (11:4); Abram calls on the name of the LORD.

A tent and an altar. Abram pitches a tent and builds an altar: the tent shows he is a pilgrim, the altar that his heart is fixed on God. That is the shape of the Christian life: “here we have no lasting city, but we seek the city that is to come” (Hebrews 13:14). He journeys on toward the Negeb, the dry south country.

Where Christians differ: the land promise. Dispensationalists expect its future fulfilment to ethnic Israel. This commentary’s view: it was fulfilled in Joshua’s day (Joshua 21:43–45), and points beyond Canaan to the whole world (Romans 4:13) and the new earth that Abraham himself looked for (Hebrews 11:10, 16).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–20 — Abram in Egypt: Faith and Failure
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The first test of the promise brings the patriarch’s first failure. Famine drives Abram to Egypt, and fearing for his life he tells Sarai to say she is his sister (vv. 10–13). She is taken into Pharaoh’s house, and Abram grows rich because of her (vv. 14–16). The mother of the promised offspring is in a foreign king’s harem, and the promise seems lost. But the LORD strikes Pharaoh with plagues, Pharaoh rebukes Abram and sends him away with his wife and all he has (vv. 17–20). This sets a pattern for Genesis: faith falters, the promise is endangered, and God preserves what man cannot.
verseByVerse.theology: Famine drives Abram to Egypt, where fear makes him pass Sarai off as his sister. Pharaoh takes her, and the LORD strikes Pharaoh's house with plagues until she is returned and Abram is sent away.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the episode rehearses the exodus: famine, Egypt, plagues, and a departure with wealth. Now: the promise rests not on the faithfulness of the man carrying it but on the God who made it (2 Tim. 2:13).

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was a famine in the land. So Abram went down to Egypt to sojourn there, for the famine was severe in the land. When he was about to enter Egypt, he said to Sarai his wife, "I know that you are a woman beautiful in appearance, and when the Egyptians see you, they will say, 'This is his wife.' Then they will kill me, but they will let you live. Say you are my sister, that it may go well with me because of you, and that my life may be spared for your sake."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Famine follows the promise, and the man of faith acts in fear: he goes down to Egypt and asks Sarai to pose as his sister to save his own life.

There was a famine in the land. Famine comes right after the promise: the land God promised cannot even feed him. Canaan depends on rain, but Egypt is watered by the Nile, so in drought years people from Canaan went down to Egypt for food, as Jacob’s sons later will (42:1–2). Abram goes “to sojourn”, to live as a resident foreigner, without legal protection. The text does not say whether going was wrong; it does show that Abram went without asking God, and that fear soon took over.

Say you are my sister. Abram reasons that a powerful man will kill a foreign husband to take a beautiful wife. His solution protects himself and leaves Sarai exposed. The story is a half-truth: Sarai was his half-sister (20:12), but the aim was to deceive. He even hopes it will “go well with me because of you”.

Faith has weak points. The man who left everything at God’s word now cannot trust God to protect him in Egypt. Faith in one area does not guarantee it in another, and Abram will repeat this same sin years later (chapter 20), as Isaac will after him (26:6–11). Watch your weak points, and when you fail, return to the God who kept his promise to Abram in spite of him.

Is this like Rahab’s lie? This commentary holds that deceiving those bent on murder, as Rahab did to protect the spies, is not the lie the ninth commandment forbids. Abram’s case is different: there was no actual threat, only his fear of one, and his deceit protected himself by putting another in danger. Scripture does not commend it; it lets a pagan king rebuke him (vv. 18–19).
verseByVerse.note: Egypt, watered by the Nile, was the usual refuge when rain failed in Canaan.

verseByVerse.quote: When Abram entered Egypt, the Egyptians saw that the woman was very beautiful. And when the princes of Pharaoh saw her, they praised her to Pharaoh. And the woman was taken into Pharaoh's house. And for her sake he dealt well with Abram; and he had sheep, oxen, male donkeys, male servants, female servants, female donkeys, and camels. But the LORD afflicted Pharaoh and his house with great plagues because of Sarai, Abram's wife.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sarai is taken into Pharaoh’s house and Abram grows rich because of her, but the LORD steps in with plagues to protect her and his promise.

The woman was taken into Pharaoh’s house. What Abram feared happens, in a different way: Sarai is taken into the royal harem. The mother of the promised line is now in a foreign king’s household, and the promise seems lost. Pharaoh is a title, “great house”, not a personal name; this king is not named.

For her sake he dealt well with Abram. Abram is paid, in effect, for his wife: sheep, oxen, donkeys, servants and camels. It is a shameful profit, and some of it may have come back to trouble the family; Hagar, Sarai’s Egyptian servant (16:1), may have been acquired here.

But the LORD afflicted Pharaoh. God steps in where Abram failed. He protects Sarai and his promise when his servant does not. The psalm remembers it: “he rebuked kings on their account, saying, ‘Touch not my anointed ones, do my prophets no harm!’” (Psalm 105:14–15). God’s faithfulness does not depend on ours.

A rehearsal of the exodus. Abram goes down to Egypt because of famine, his family is endangered, the LORD strikes Pharaoh with “great plagues”, and Abram leaves with great wealth. Israel’s story will follow the same path, on a larger scale: famine, Egypt, plagues, and an exodus with the Egyptians’ gold and silver (Exodus 11:1–2; 12:35–36). The God who rescued Sarai from Pharaoh’s house will rescue her descendants from Pharaoh’s land, and, in the greater exodus, his people from sin and death through Christ.

What it does not mean. Abram’s failure as a husband is not a model. He put his wife in danger to save himself, the opposite of the love a husband owes his wife, which is modelled on Christ, who “gave himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:25). No wife is obliged to go along with a husband’s plan that exposes her to harm or requires her to sin. Anyone being placed in danger by a spouse should seek help from church leaders, and where there is danger, from the authorities.

verseByVerse.quote: So Pharaoh called Abram and said, "What is this you have done to me? Why did you not tell me that she was your wife? Why did you say, 'She is my sister,' so that I took her for my wife? Now then, here is your wife; take her, and go." And Pharaoh gave men orders concerning him, and they sent him away with his wife and all that he had.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pharaoh rebukes Abram for his deceit and sends him away: the man of God is put to shame by a pagan king, but leaves with his wife and the promise intact.

What is this you have done to me? The man of God is rebuked by a pagan king, a humiliating moment. Pharaoh behaves more honourably than Abram: he did not know Sarai was married, and when he finds out he restores her at once. Abram has no reply. Scripture does not approve Abram’s lie; it records it honestly, and lets the outsider speak the truth.

Here is your wife; take her, and go. Pharaoh’s words, “take her, and go”, echo God’s “Go” in verse 1. Abram is sent back to the land of promise, with his wife and all he has. God has kept his promise in spite of Abram.

When believers bring shame on God’s name. Christians can be rightly rebuked by unbelievers whose conduct is better than theirs. The right response is not self-defence but honest confession: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins” (1 John 1:9).

The blessing does not rest on Abram. The chapter that began with the greatest promise in the Old Testament ends with its first bearer disgraced. That is the point: the promise rests on God’s faithfulness, not Abram’s. The blessing of all the families of the earth will come through Abram’s offspring, but not because Abram was good enough to deserve it. It will come through the one offspring who never failed, Jesus Christ.

12.theology:
Election and Mission. Genesis 12:1–3 is the Bible’s foundational text on election, God’s free choice of a people for himself: he chooses Abram not for his merit but in his sovereign purpose. And election is always for mission: Abram is chosen so that all the families of the earth may be blessed. The church, chosen in Christ (Eph. 1:4), exists for the same end.

The Gospel in Seed. The blessing for all nations was always, at root, this: God counts sinners righteous through faith in the offspring by whom the blessing comes. Genesis 12 is not a preface to the gospel but the gospel announced in advance (Galatians 3:8).
12.examples:
Then: Abram left one of the most advanced civilisations of the ancient world for a wandering life in an unknown land: he traded security for a promise. In Egypt a powerful Pharaoh could take whatever he wanted, and a foreign visitor had no one to appeal to. Only God's intervention (v. 17) could protect the powerless.

Now: The call of Abram is the pattern for every Christian calling: not a detailed plan but a direction and a Caller. The three promises find their fulfilment in Christ and the new creation: the land is the new earth (Abraham is “heir of the world”, Rom. 4:13), the offspring is Christ and all in him (Gal. 3:29), and the blessing is the gospel offered to all nations. Every Sunday the church gathers around Abraham's heir, receiving a blessing promised before any of us existed.

keyVerse.quote: I will bless those who bless you, and him who dishonors you I will curse, and in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed.
keyVerse.note: This promise is the hinge between the story of the nations (chapters 1–11) and the story of Abraham’s family, and the thread that runs through the rest of the Bible. Paul calls it the gospel preached beforehand to Abraham (Galatians 3:8): God’s answer to the curse is a blessing for all the families of the earth, fulfilled in Abraham’s offspring, Christ.

12.reflection:
God called Abram to leave his country, his kindred and his father’s house (v. 1). What has following Christ asked you to leave behind, or what might it be asking now? How do the promises of vv. 2–3 help?

Abram was blessed “so that you will be a blessing” (v. 2). How is God’s blessing to you meant to reach others, in your family, church, neighbourhood and beyond?

Abram trusted God enough to leave Haran, but not enough to tell the truth in Egypt (vv. 10–13). Where are your weak points of faith? What fears tend to push you toward compromise?

God kept his promise in spite of Abram’s failure (vv. 17–20). How does that encourage you when you fail, and why does it matter that the blessing finally comes through Christ rather than through Abram?

13.title: Lot and Abram Part Ways
13.text: <sup>1</sup>So Abram went up from Egypt, he and his wife and all that he had, and Lot with him, into the Negeb.<sup>2</sup>Now Abram was very rich in livestock, in silver, and in gold.<sup>3</sup>And he journeyed on from the Negeb as far as Bethel to the place where his tent had been at the beginning, between Bethel and Ai,<sup>4</sup>to the place where he had made an altar at the first. And there Abram called upon the name of the LORD.<sup>5</sup>And Lot, who went with Abram, also had flocks and herds and tents,<sup>6</sup>so that the land could not support both of them dwelling together; for their possessions were so great that they could not dwell together,<sup>7</sup>and there was strife between the herdsmen of Abram's livestock and the herdsmen of Lot's livestock. At that time the Canaanites and the Perizzites were dwelling in the land.<sup>8</sup>Then Abram said to Lot, "Let there be no strife between you and me, and between your herdsmen and my herdsmen, for we are kinsmen.<sup>9</sup>Is not the whole land before you? Separate yourself from me. If you take the left hand, then I will go to the right, or if you take the right hand, then I will go to the left."<sup>10</sup>And Lot lifted up his eyes and saw that the Jordan Valley was well watered everywhere like the garden of the LORD, like the land of Egypt, in the direction of Zoar. (This was before the LORD destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah.)<sup>11</sup>So Lot chose for himself all the Jordan Valley, and Lot journeyed east. Thus they separated from each other.<sup>12</sup>Abram settled in the land of Canaan, while Lot settled among the cities of the valley and moved his tent as far as Sodom.<sup>13</sup>Now the men of Sodom were wicked, great sinners against the LORD.<sup>14</sup>The LORD said to Abram, after Lot had separated from him, "Lift up your eyes and look from the place where you are, northward and southward and eastward and westward,<sup>15</sup>for all the land that you see I will give to you and to your offspring forever.<sup>16</sup>I will make your offspring as the dust of the earth, so that if one can count the dust of the earth, your offspring also can be counted.<sup>17</sup>Arise, walk through the length and the breadth of the land, for I will give it to you."<sup>18</sup>So Abram moved his tent and came and settled by the oaks of Mamre, which are at Hebron, and there he built an altar to the LORD.
13.overview:
Where we are. Abram has just come back from Egypt, where fear drove him to pass Sarai off as his sister and Pharaoh sent him away loaded with gifts (12:10–20). He is back in the land of promise, but the wealth he brought out of Egypt is about to split his family.

The message. God’s promise sets his people free from grasping. Lot chooses by sight the ground that looks like paradise and drifts towards Sodom; Abram, resting on what God has said, gives the choice away, and God at once gives him the whole land again, more fully than before. Faith loses nothing by letting go, because the inheritance is in God’s hand, not ours.

Why it was said. Israel in the wilderness (see the introduction) was travelling to this same land and would soon need to share it out among its tribes without tearing itself apart. Sodom was already a name for wickedness and ruin. The chapter shows them their father living by the promise, and what became of the man who chose the best-looking ground.

How the chapter makes its case. Abram returns to his first altar between Bethel and Ai and calls on the LORD (vv. 1–4): after failure, the way home is worship. Wealth brings strife, and Abram, the senior man, offers Lot first choice for the sake of peace (vv. 5–9). Lot lifts up his eyes, sees a valley like Eden and like Egypt, chooses it for himself and moves his tent towards Sodom, whose men are great sinners (vv. 10–13). Then the LORD tells Abram to lift up his eyes: all the land is his and his offspring’s for ever, and his offspring will be as countless as dust. He settles at Hebron and builds another altar (vv. 14–18).

Where it leads. Chiefly by promise. The land and the offspring promised here “forever” are fulfilled in Christ, the offspring to whom the promises were made (Galatians 3:16), and through him Abraham becomes “heir of the world” (Romans 4:13), and the meek inherit the earth (Matthew 5:5). There is also a faint likeness, which the New Testament does not draw but which is hard to miss: the elder who gives up his right for the sake of peace, as the Son “did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped” (Philippians 2:6), and was given the name above every name.

For us. Because our inheritance is secure in Christ, we can afford to give way in a family quarrel or a church dispute. Watch the choices you make only with your eyes, and see where they are moving your tent. And when you have failed, go back to the place where you first called on the Lord.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–18 — Abram and Lot Separate; the Promise Renewed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The one who does not grasp receives everything; the one who grasps ends up in Sodom. Abram comes back from Egypt to his first altar and calls on the LORD (vv. 1–4). When the land cannot hold both households, he lets Lot choose rather than quarrel (vv. 5–9). Lot chooses by sight, a valley like Eden, and moves towards a city of great sinners (vv. 10–13). Then, as soon as Lot is gone, God tells Abram to look in every direction: all of it is his and his offspring’s for ever, and his offspring will be beyond counting (vv. 14–17). Abram moves to Hebron and builds an altar (v. 18). Faith loses nothing by being generous.
verseByVerse.theology: Abram returns from Egypt to his first altar. When the land cannot hold both households, he lets Lot choose, and Lot moves his tent towards Sodom. Then God gives Abram all the land he can see and offspring like the dust of the earth.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Lot's choice of Eden-like ground comes six chapters before the fire. Now: the believer who is sure of his inheritance can afford to give way, because what God gives will not run out.

verseByVerse.quote: So Abram went up from Egypt, he and his wife and all that he had, and Lot with him, into the Negeb. Now Abram was very rich in livestock, in silver, and in gold. And he journeyed on from the Negeb as far as Bethel to the place where his tent had been at the beginning, between Bethel and Ai, to the place where he had made an altar at the first. And there Abram called upon the name of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abram comes back from Egypt rich, and goes straight back to the altar where he first worshipped: after failure, the way home is the place where God is called upon.

Went up from Egypt … into the Negeb. The Negeb is the dry south of Canaan. “Went up” reverses 12:10, where Abram “went down” to Egypt in a famine. The whole household comes back, Sarai too, whom Abram had put at risk to save himself (12:11–20), and Lot, who will soon matter.

Very rich. The Hebrew says, literally, “very heavy” with livestock, silver and gold, much of it Pharaoh’s gifts (12:16). The wealth is real blessing, yet it came by way of a lie, and it is about to cause the first quarrel in the family of promise (v. 6). Wealth brings its own trouble.

To the place where his tent had been at the beginning. The narrator piles up the phrases, “at the beginning”, “at the first”, to show Abram retracing his steps to the altar he built between Bethel and Ai (12:8). There he “called upon the name of the LORD”, the same words as before: open worship and prayer to the God who had appeared to him. No speech of repentance is recorded, and Genesis records no altar in Egypt, but the journey itself is a picture of repentance: after failure, the way back is to the place of worship.

The way home. Abram did not have to earn his way back to the altar; the God who had called him was still there to be called on. That is the welcome the gospel holds out to every believer who has wandered: the father runs to meet the son while he is still a long way off (Luke 15:20), and “if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins” (1 John 1:9). When you have failed, do not wait until you feel worthy to pray again. Go back to where you first called on the Lord, and call on him.

verseByVerse.quote: And Lot, who went with Abram, also had flocks and herds and tents, so that the land could not support both of them dwelling together; for their possessions were so great that they could not dwell together, and there was strife between the herdsmen of Abram's livestock and the herdsmen of Lot's livestock. At that time the Canaanites and the Perizzites were dwelling in the land. Then Abram said to Lot, "Let there be no strife between you and me, and between your herdsmen and my herdsmen, for we are kinsmen. Is not the whole land before you? Separate yourself from me. If you take the left hand, then I will go to the right, or if you take the right hand, then I will go to the left."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When prosperity sets the family quarrelling, Abram, the senior man who holds the promise, gives up his right to choose, because peace with his kinsman matters more to him than the best land.

The land could not support both of them. Pasture and water in the hill country were limited, and large flocks need wide range. Lot, who had come with Abram (12:4), has grown rich alongside him. The blessing itself becomes the problem: “their possessions were so great that they could not dwell together.”

Strife between the herdsmen. The quarrel starts among the servants, at the wells and the grazing grounds, as family quarrels often start among those who work for the family. Abram goes straight to the top: “between you and me”.

The Canaanites and the Perizzites. The note probably explains both the shortage of pasture and the danger: the best land was already held by others, and a small family of outsiders was quarrelling over wells in full view of the people who owned the land. It also reminds the reader that the promise is still only a promise (12:6–7).

For we are kinsmen. Literally, we are men, brothers; Lot is his nephew, but family is family. Relationship outranks rights, and Abram cares about the harm the quarrel would do as much as about who wins it: “Behold, how good and pleasant it is when brothers dwell in unity!” (Psalm 133:1).

Is not the whole land before you? As the elder and head of the clan, Abram had every right to choose first. Instead he offers Lot the choice: left or right, which may mean north or south of where they stood. Faith can afford to be generous, because Abram’s security is not in the land but in the God who promised it. The same freedom is ours in Christ, who “though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor” (2 Corinthians 8:9), and in whom believers already have every spiritual blessing (Ephesians 1:3).

What it does not mean. Not that believers must always give way or never press a just claim. Abram proposes a fair and peaceful separation, not surrender to bullying, and he will soon fight to rescue the captured (14:14–16). Where giving way would leave others harmed or wrong unchecked, love may need to stand firm; Paul himself appealed to Caesar (Acts 25:11). But where only my own advantage is at stake, Paul’s question stands: “Why not rather suffer wrong?” (1 Corinthians 6:7). It is a fair question for us where we could give up our rights for the sake of peace.

verseByVerse.quote: And Lot lifted up his eyes and saw that the Jordan Valley was well watered everywhere like the garden of the LORD, like the land of Egypt, in the direction of Zoar. (This was before the LORD destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah.) So Lot chose for himself all the Jordan Valley, and Lot journeyed east. Thus they separated from each other. Abram settled in the land of Canaan, while Lot settled among the cities of the valley and moved his tent as far as Sodom. Now the men of Sodom were wicked, great sinners against the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lot chooses by sight alone, takes the richest ground for himself, and moves step by step towards a city of great sinners.

Lot lifted up his eyes. The phrase will come back in v. 14, when God tells Abram to lift up his eyes. Lot looks at what he can take; Abram will look at what God gives.

Well watered everywhere. The plain of the Jordan near the Dead Sea was then rich and green. Lot sees it as “like the garden of the LORD, like the land of Egypt”: beautiful, fertile and watered without depending on rain, as Egypt was watered by the Nile (Deuteronomy 11:10–11). But both comparisons are ominous: Eden is where humanity fell, and Egypt is where Abram’s faith had just failed.

This was before the LORD destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah. The narrator’s aside casts a shadow over the view. The first readers knew this region as the desolate country round the Salt Sea. What looked like paradise was under sentence.

Lot chose for himself … and Lot journeyed east. “For himself” says it all: no altar, no prayer, no thought of his uncle’s kindness. In Genesis the eastward road has already been the road away from God’s presence (3:24; 4:16). Then the slide goes step by step: among the cities of the valley, his tent pitched as far as Sodom, then living in Sodom (14:12), then sitting in its gate (19:1).

The men of Sodom were wicked, great sinners against the LORD. The verse is placed right after Lot’s move, without comment, and the reader is left to draw the conclusion. Their sin is first of all “against the LORD”; chapters 18 and 19 will show what it was.

A righteous man’s costly choice. Lot was not an unbeliever. Peter calls him “righteous Lot, greatly distressed by the sensual conduct of the wicked” (2 Peter 2:7). But he chose his home by the “desires of the eyes” (1 John 2:16), and it cost him his home, his possessions and his wife (19:26). Jesus held up “the days of Lot” as a warning of how ordinary life goes on until judgment comes (Luke 17:28–32). It was not wrong to want good land. It was wrong to choose it with no thought for God, his kinsman or the moral danger. The moves we make for a job, a house or a school are rarely only about money; God’s values, not only what looks good, should decide our choices.

Uncertain wording. “Jordan Valley” translates a word meaning “circle” or “round area”, the plain of the Jordan; “the cities of the valley” are the cities of that plain. Where exactly Sodom and its neighbours stood is not known. Many have placed them near the southern end of the Dead Sea, near Zoar; some archaeologists argue for a site north-east of it, near where the Jordan enters the sea. The point of the story does not depend on the answer.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Abram, after Lot had separated from him, "Lift up your eyes and look from the place where you are, northward and southward and eastward and westward, for all the land that you see I will give to you and to your offspring forever. I will make your offspring as the dust of the earth, so that if one can count the dust of the earth, your offspring also can be counted. Arise, walk through the length and the breadth of the land, for I will give it to you." So Abram moved his tent and came and settled by the oaks of Mamre, which are at Hebron, and there he built an altar to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As soon as Lot has gone, God tells Abram to lift up his eyes and promises him all the land he can see and offspring beyond counting: what Abram let go, God gives back enlarged.

After Lot had separated from him. God speaks at the moment Abram seems to have lost out. Lot, who may well have seemed Abram’s likely heir, is gone; the promise will be kept God’s way.

Lift up your eyes and look. Now God tells Abram to lift up his eyes too, but to look at what God promises, “northward and southward and eastward and westward”, the valley Lot chose included.

To you and to your offspring forever. For the first time the land is promised “forever”, and to Abram himself as well as his offspring. Yet Abram never owned more of it than a field with a tomb, bought to bury Sarah (23:17–20; Acts 7:5). The promise was bigger than his lifetime, and he knew it: he lived in tents, looking for “the city that has foundations” (Hebrews 11:9–10). On how the land promise was fulfilled, see the note on 12:7–9.

As the dust of the earth. Offspring beyond counting, from a man who has no child at all. The picture will grow: stars (15:5), then sand on the seashore (22:17).

Arise, walk through the length and the breadth of the land. Walking a land was a way of laying claim to it, as God later told Joshua, “Every place that the sole of your foot will tread upon I have given to you” (Joshua 1:3). Abram walks it as its heir, by faith, while others hold it.

The oaks of Mamre … at Hebron. Mamre was also the name of an Amorite ally of Abram (14:13), and Hebron, about twenty miles south of Jerusalem, becomes his main home. Abram’s life is marked by two things: the tent, which shows he is a sojourner, and the altar, which shows whose he is. This is his third altar in the land (12:7, 8).

The heir of the world. The promise to Abram’s offspring finds its focus in one offspring, Christ (Galatians 3:16), and in him it widens from Canaan to the world: “the promise to Abraham and his offspring that he would be heir of the world” (Romans 4:13). Jesus put it in a sentence: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth” (Matthew 5:5). The man who let Lot take the best ground is the meek man of that beatitude, and everyone who belongs to Christ shares his inheritance. God gives more than we give up.
verseByVerse.note: Hebron, about 20 miles south of Jerusalem, became Abraham’s main home.

13.theology:
Walking by Faith, Not by Sight. Abram and Lot are the Old Testament's sharpest illustration of 2 Corinthians 5:7: "we walk by faith, not by sight." Faith trusts God's word over the evidence of the eyes and holds the present loosely for the promised future. Abram gave away the visible and received the promise: invisible, future, vast.

Generosity and the Covenant. Abram's generosity is the freedom of a man whose security is in God, not in possessions. The gospel creates the same freedom: because we are already blessed "with every spiritual blessing" in Christ (Eph. 1:3), we can be generous with earthly blessings, holding them as stewards rather than owners.
13.examples:
Then: Grazing land was scarce and fiercely contested, and in a culture that took seniority and clan rights very seriously, Abram's offer to let Lot choose first was remarkable. The mention of Sodom (v. 13) would have warned the first readers at once: it was already a byword for wickedness.

Now: Lot's drift toward Sodom is a lasting warning: the most dangerous moral slides are rarely sudden. The gradual acceptance of what once seemed clearly wrong, the slow move closer to what we know is destructive, the reasonable-sounding series of small choices that ends where we never meant to be: this is Lot's journey. And Abram's generosity challenges every instinct toward self-protection: the one who gives the first choice away, trusting the promise, receives a promise that makes the land he gave up look small.

keyVerse.quote: The LORD said to Abram, after Lot had separated from him, “Lift up your eyes and look from the place where you are, northward and southward and eastward and westward, for all the land that you see I will give to you and to your offspring forever.
keyVerse.note: God speaks at the very moment Abram seems to have lost out, and he uses Lot’s words: Lot lifted up his eyes to take (v. 10), Abram lifts up his eyes to receive. The verse holds the chapter’s message: what faith lets go, God gives back enlarged, and the promise it makes reaches its full size only in Christ, in whom believers inherit the earth.

13.reflection:
Abram goes back to the altar where he first called on the LORD before his failure in Egypt (vv. 3–4). When you have failed, what tempts you to stay away from God, and what helps you come back?

Abram had the right to choose first, and he gave it away for the sake of peace (vv. 8–9). Where in your family, work or church could you give up a right for the sake of peace? When would doing so be wrong?

Lot chose by what he could see, and his choice took him step by step towards Sodom (vv. 10–13). What decisions in our lives (a job, a house, a school, a friendship) are most easily made by sight alone? What questions should we ask before we move our tent?

God gives Abram more than he gave up (vv. 14–17). How does knowing that believers are heirs of the world in Christ (Romans 4:13) make it easier to be generous now?

14.title: Melchizedek King of Salem
14.text: <sup>1</sup>In the days of Amraphel king of Shinar, Arioch king of Ellasar, Chedorlaomer king of Elam, and Tidal king of Goiim,<sup>2</sup>these kings made war with Bera king of Sodom, Birsha king of Gomorrah, Shinab king of Admah, Shemeber king of Zeboiim, and the king of Bela (that is, Zoar).<sup>3</sup>And all these joined forces in the Valley of Siddim (that is, the Salt Sea).<sup>4</sup>Twelve years they had served Chedorlaomer, but in the thirteenth year they rebelled.<sup>5</sup>In the fourteenth year Chedorlaomer and the kings who were with him came and defeated the Rephaim in Ashteroth-karnaim, the Zuzim in Ham, the Emim in Shaveh-kiriathaim,<sup>6</sup>and the Horites in their hill country of Seir as far as El-paran on the border of the wilderness.<sup>7</sup>Then they turned back and came to En-mishpat (that is, Kadesh) and defeated all the country of the Amalekites, and also the Amorites who were dwelling in Hazazon-tamar.<sup>8</sup>Then the king of Sodom, the king of Gomorrah, the king of Admah, the king of Zeboiim, and the king of Bela (that is, Zoar) went out, and they joined battle in the Valley of Siddim<sup>9</sup>with Chedorlaomer king of Elam, Tidal king of Goiim, Amraphel king of Shinar, and Arioch king of Ellasar, four kings against five.<sup>10</sup>Now the Valley of Siddim was full of bitumen pits, and as the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah fled, some fell into them, and the rest fled to the hill country.<sup>11</sup>So the enemy took all the possessions of Sodom and Gomorrah, and all their provisions, and went their way.<sup>12</sup>They also took Lot, the son of Abram's brother, who was dwelling in Sodom, and his possessions, and went their way.<sup>13</sup>Then one who had escaped came and told Abram the Hebrew, who was living by the oaks of Mamre the Amorite, brother of Eshcol and of Aner. These were allies of Abram.<sup>14</sup>When Abram heard that his kinsman had been taken captive, he led forth his trained men, born in his house, 318 of them, and went in pursuit as far as Dan.<sup>15</sup>And he divided his forces against them by night, he and his servants, and defeated them and pursued them to Hobah, north of Damascus.<sup>16</sup>Then he brought back all the possessions, and also brought back his kinsman Lot with his possessions, and the women and the people.<sup>17</sup>After his return from the defeat of Chedorlaomer and the kings who were with him, the king of Sodom went out to meet him at the Valley of Shaveh (that is, the King's Valley).<sup>18</sup>And Melchizedek king of Salem brought out bread and wine.
