(He was priest of God Most High.)<sup>19</sup>And he blessed him and said, "Blessed be Abram by God Most High, Possessor of heaven and earth;<sup>20</sup>and blessed be God Most High, who has delivered your enemies into your hand!" And Abram gave him a tenth of everything.<sup>21</sup>And the king of Sodom said to Abram, "Give me the persons, but take the goods for yourself."<sup>22</sup>But Abram said to the king of Sodom, "I have lifted my hand to the LORD, God Most High, Possessor of heaven and earth,<sup>23</sup>that I would not take a thread or a sandal strap or anything that is yours, lest you should say, 'I have made Abram rich.'<sup>24</sup>I will take nothing but what the young men have eaten, and the share of the men who went with me. Let Aner, Eshcol, and Mamre take their share."
14.overview:
Where we are. Lot has moved his tent to Sodom (13:12), and Abram has settled at Hebron with God’s renewed promise of the land ringing in his ears (13:14–18). Now the great powers of the day march through that land, and Abram is drawn into their war.

The message. The God who promised Abram the land is “God Most High, Possessor of heaven and earth” (v. 19), and kings and armies are in his hand. So Abram can use real strength to rescue a kinsman who does not deserve it, bow before God’s priest-king, and refuse to let the king of Sodom make him rich. His victory and his wealth must be credited to God alone.

Why it was said. Israel would enter Canaan as a small people facing kings, fortified cities and the descendants of feared giants (see the introduction). This chapter shows their father defeating an army that had crushed those giants, and it teaches them that victory is God’s gift, to be acknowledged in worship and not turned into plunder that compromises them. It also brings onto the stage for the first time Salem, the city that would one day be Jerusalem.

How the chapter makes its case. Four kings from the east crush a rebellion of five city-kings of the plain and carry off Lot with the goods of Sodom (vv. 1–12). Abram pursues with 318 trained men and his allies, attacks by night, and brings back Lot, the people and the goods (vv. 13–16). Then two kings come out to meet him. Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, brings bread and wine and blesses him, and Abram gives him a tenth (vv. 17–20). The king of Sodom offers him the goods, and Abram refuses even a thread (vv. 21–24).

Where it leads. By a pattern that Scripture itself draws. Melchizedek appears once and vanishes, and a thousand years later David hears God swear to his Lord, “You are a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 110:4). Hebrews shows that this priest-king, greater than Abraham, foreshadows Jesus, king of righteousness and peace, priest not by descent but “by the power of an indestructible life” (Hebrews 7:16). And Abram, setting out at once to free a kinsman who had taken the best for himself, gives a glimpse of the greater deliverer who came for us while we were his enemies.

For us. Our great priest-king has already blessed us, so we need nothing from Sodom. Decide before the offer comes which gains you will not take, honour God first with what he gives, and go after the people who have wandered into trouble, even when they chose it themselves.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — The Battle of the Kings and the Rescue of Lot
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A man who makes his home in Sodom shares its troubles, and a man who lives by faith goes to his rescue. Four kings from the east crush a rebellion of the five cities of the plain, sweeping through the peoples of the region on their way (vv. 1–7). The rebel kings are routed, and Lot, now living in Sodom, is carried off with its goods (vv. 8–12). When Abram hears, he sets out at once with 318 trained men of his household and his Amorite allies, attacks by night, pursues the invaders far beyond Damascus and brings back Lot, the people and the goods (vv. 13–16). The man who would not grasp uses his strength for a kinsman who owed him nothing.
verseByVerse.theology: Four eastern kings crush a rebellion of the five cities of the plain and carry off Lot, who is now living in Sodom. Abram pursues with 318 trained men and his Amorite allies, attacks by night, and brings back Lot, the people and the goods.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: a man who makes his home in Sodom shares its troubles. Now: Abram rescued a nephew who owed him nothing, the fruit of grace doing its slow work in him.

verseByVerse.quote: In the days of Amraphel king of Shinar, Arioch king of Ellasar, Chedorlaomer king of Elam, and Tidal king of Goiim, these kings made war with Bera king of Sodom, Birsha king of Gomorrah, Shinab king of Admah, Shemeber king of Zeboiim, and the king of Bela (that is, Zoar). And all these joined forces in the Valley of Siddim (that is, the Salt Sea). Twelve years they had served Chedorlaomer, but in the thirteenth year they rebelled.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A war of great kings sweeps into the land God has promised Abram, and Genesis tells it as real history, with names, places and dates.

In the days of Amraphel king of Shinar. Four kings come from the east. Shinar is Babylonia, the land of Babel (11:2). Elam lay east of Babylonia, in what is now south-western Iran, and its king Chedorlaomer leads the alliance (v. 4). Goiim simply means “nations”. Against them stand the city-kings of the plain round the southern Jordan: Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, Zeboiim and Bela.

The Valley of Siddim (that is, the Salt Sea). The Salt Sea is the Dead Sea. The narrator explains the old name for later readers, as he does with Bela (“that is, Zoar”).

Twelve years they had served Chedorlaomer. The cities of the plain were vassals, paying tribute to a distant overlord. In the thirteenth year they stopped paying, and in the fourteenth the overlord came to punish them. This was the ordinary politics of the ancient world, and Abram lives in the middle of it. The promise does not lift him out of history; it carries him through it.

The Most High rules. The kings of the earth seem to decide everything here, marching and counter-marching while the man with the promise lives in a tent. By the end of the chapter it will be clear who rules: “God Most High, Possessor of heaven and earth” (v. 19). Daniel learned the same lesson in Babylon, “that the Most High rules the kingdom of men and gives it to whom he will” (Daniel 4:17), and Jesus told Pilate, “You would have no authority over me at all unless it had been given you from above” (John 19:11). The headlines of our own day are no different.

Uncertain wording. None of the four eastern kings can be identified with certainty in other ancient records. Amraphel was once often identified with Hammurabi of Babylon, but that is now largely abandoned. The names themselves fit the period and the regions named: Chedorlaomer has the form of an Elamite royal name, and Tidal resembles a name borne by several Hittite kings.

verseByVerse.quote: In the fourteenth year Chedorlaomer and the kings who were with him came and defeated the Rephaim in Ashteroth-karnaim, the Zuzim in Ham, the Emim in Shaveh-kiriathaim, and the Horites in their hill country of Seir as far as El-paran on the border of the wilderness. Then they turned back and came to En-mishpat (that is, Kadesh) and defeated all the country of the Amalekites, and also the Amorites who were dwelling in Hazazon-tamar.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before it reaches the rebel cities, the eastern army sweeps through the whole region and crushes every people in its path, including the giant peoples Israel would later fear.

The route. The army comes south down the country east of the Jordan: Ashteroth-karnaim in Bashan, then the lands that would later be Ammon and Moab, then Seir, the hill country later called Edom, down to El-paran at the edge of the wilderness. It then turns back north-west to Kadesh, through the land later held by the Amalekites, and to Hazazon-tamar, which is En-gedi on the shore of the Dead Sea (2 Chronicles 20:2). The rebel cities are left surrounded.

The Rephaim … the Zuzim … the Emim. Deuteronomy remembers these peoples as giants: the Emim were “a people great and many, and tall as the Anakim”, and the Zuzim seem to be the people the Ammonites called Zamzummim (Deuteronomy 2:10–11, 20–21). It was fear of such giants that would keep Israel out of the land at Kadesh (Numbers 13:33). Here those very giants are crushed by Chedorlaomer, and Chedorlaomer is crushed by Abram with God’s help. Israel had no reason to fear.

The country of the Amalekites. Amalek was a grandson of Esau (36:12), not yet born, so the region is named by the people who later lived there, as a modern writer might speak of Roman soldiers marching through France.

En-mishpat (that is, Kadesh). The name means “spring of judgment”. Kadesh would become the place where Israel refused to enter the land and spent long years in the wilderness (Numbers 13–14; 20:1).

For us. The powers that frighten us are not the final powers. The giants of Genesis 14 fell to a king who fell to Abram, and the God who gave Abram the victory has “disarmed the rulers and authorities” at the cross (Colossians 2:15).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king of Sodom, the king of Gomorrah, the king of Admah, the king of Zeboiim, and the king of Bela (that is, Zoar) went out, and they joined battle in the Valley of Siddim with Chedorlaomer king of Elam, Tidal king of Goiim, Amraphel king of Shinar, and Arioch king of Ellasar, four kings against five. Now the Valley of Siddim was full of bitumen pits, and as the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah fled, some fell into them, and the rest fled to the hill country. So the enemy took all the possessions of Sodom and Gomorrah, and all their provisions, and went their way. They also took Lot, the son of Abram's brother, who was dwelling in Sodom, and his possessions, and went their way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The five kings of the plain are routed, and Lot, who has made his home in Sodom, is carried off with its goods: his choice has caught up with him.

Four kings against five. The numbers do not decide the battle. The rebels fight on home ground and still lose.

Full of bitumen pits. Bitumen, a natural tar or asphalt, is still found round the Dead Sea, and lumps of it float to the surface; Greek and Roman writers called the Dead Sea the asphalt lake. The fleeing kings fall into the pits, and the rest run for the hills. The king of Sodom appears again in v. 17, so “fell” may mean that some dived into the pits to hide, or that their men fell there.

They also took Lot. The narrator names Lot carefully: “the son of Abram’s brother, who was dwelling in Sodom.” The first phrase prepares for the rescue; the second marks how far Lot has gone. In 13:12 he pitched his tent near Sodom; now he lives in it, and he shares its disaster. The choice made with the eyes (13:10–11) has delivered him, with all the possessions he chose it for, into an enemy’s hands. Scripture’s later call to God’s people about the world’s great city applies here: “Come out of her, my people, lest you take part in her sins, lest you share in her plagues” (Revelation 18:4).

What it does not mean. Not that every disaster is a punishment for a particular choice. Jesus refused that reasoning (Luke 13:1–5; John 9:2–3), and Abram does not stop to say “I told you so”. But compromising choices carry consequences, and the place we choose for its advantages can become the place that holds us captive.

verseByVerse.quote: Then one who had escaped came and told Abram the Hebrew, who was living by the oaks of Mamre the Amorite, brother of Eshcol and of Aner. These were allies of Abram. When Abram heard that his kinsman had been taken captive, he led forth his trained men, born in his house, 318 of them, and went in pursuit as far as Dan. And he divided his forces against them by night, he and his servants, and defeated them and pursued them to Hobah, north of Damascus. Then he brought back all the possessions, and also brought back his kinsman Lot with his possessions, and the women and the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Abram hears that Lot has been taken, he goes after him at once with his own trained men and his allies, defeats the invaders by a night attack, and brings back everyone and everything.

Abram the Hebrew. This is the first time anyone in the Bible is called a Hebrew. The word marks Abram as an outsider among the peoples of the land, and it is often used later by foreigners speaking of Israelites (39:14; Exodus 2:6).

Allies of Abram. Literally, masters of Abram’s covenant: Mamre, Eshcol and Aner were bound to him by treaty. Abram lives at peace with his Amorite neighbours and keeps faith with them (v. 24).

His trained men, born in his house, 318 of them. Men born into his household and trained to fight: Abram is a powerful chief, not a lone shepherd. Yet 318 men against the armies of four kings is still a small force. He divides it and attacks by night, a sound tactic for a smaller army, and Melchizedek will say plainly who gave the victory (v. 20).

As far as Dan … to Hobah, north of Damascus. Dan is in the far north of the land; the town had another name until the tribe of Dan took it (Judges 18:29), so the narrator uses the name later readers knew (see the introduction on such later notes). The pursuit runs from Hebron to beyond Damascus, well over a hundred miles.

He brought back all. Everything and everyone: the goods, Lot and his possessions, “and the women and the people.” Abram fights not for gain, as vv. 22–24 will show, but to free the captured.

A deliverer for the undeserving. Lot had taken the best for himself and walked into captivity; Abram owed him nothing and went anyway, at risk to his life. The New Testament does not draw the likeness, but it is hard to miss. We too chose for ourselves and were taken captive, and Christ came “to proclaim liberty to the captives” (Luke 4:18). “While we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son” (Romans 5:10). So we are to help even those who have treated us poorly, or brought their trouble on themselves, as God helped us.

What it does not mean. Abram’s war is not a licence for private revenge or for advancing God’s cause by force. It was a rescue: lawful force used to free the captured, the kind of protection of the weak that Scripture allows, while Christ’s kingdom itself is never spread by the sword (John 18:36).

Uncertain wording. Where the word “Hebrew” comes from is not certain. It may come from Eber, an ancestor of Abram (10:21; 11:14–17), or from a root meaning “to cross over”, one who came from beyond the river. Some link it to the habiru or apiru of ancient texts, a name for people living outside the settled order, but the connection is debated. “Trained men” translates a word found only here in the Bible; it probably means men trained for war or retainers.
verseByVerse.note: Dan lay in the far north of Canaan.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–24 — Melchizedek and the King of Sodom
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Two kings meet Abram on his return, and how he treats each shows where his trust lies. Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, brings bread and wine and blesses Abram in the name of the God who owns heaven and earth and gave him the victory, and Abram gives him a tenth of everything (vv. 17–20). The king of Sodom offers Abram the goods, but Abram has sworn to the LORD, God Most High, to take nothing, so that no one but God can say he made Abram rich (vv. 21–24). The priest-king of Salem points ahead to Christ (Psalm 110:4; Hebrews 7).
verseByVerse.theology: Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, brings bread and wine, blesses Abram and receives a tenth of everything. The king of Sodom offers Abram the goods; Abram refuses, having sworn to God Most High that no one should say, "I have made Abram rich."
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Hebrews 7 finds the promised priest-king of Psalm 110 in Jesus. Now: a tempting gain is best refused by a decision made before the offer comes.

verseByVerse.quote: After his return from the defeat of Chedorlaomer and the kings who were with him, the king of Sodom went out to meet him at the Valley of Shaveh (that is, the King's Valley). And Melchizedek king of Salem brought out bread and wine. (He was priest of God Most High.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two kings come out to meet the returning Abram: the king of Sodom, and Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, who brings bread and wine.

The king of Sodom went out to meet him. He is mentioned first and then made to wait while Melchizedek speaks. The contrast between the two kings is the point of the scene: one comes with blessing, the other with an offer (v. 21).

The Valley of Shaveh (that is, the King’s Valley). Near Jerusalem; much later, Absalom set up a monument to himself there (2 Samuel 18:18).

Melchizedek king of Salem. Melchizedek’s name means “king of righteousness”, and Salem means “peace” (Hebrews 7:2). Salem is almost certainly Jerusalem: “His abode has been established in Salem, his dwelling place in Zion” (Psalm 76:2). He is a priest of the true God from outside Abraham’s family. Abram is not the only man left in the world who knows God, though he is the one through whom God will bless the world.

Brought out bread and wine. Food and drink for exhausted soldiers: a king’s hospitality and a sign of friendship, given by one who also acts as God’s priest.

Priest of God Most High. “God Most High” translates El Elyon, a title Abram himself takes up in v. 22. Before Aaron, before the law, before the tabernacle, there was a priest of the true God in Jerusalem who was also its king. Israel’s kings would later be forbidden to act as priests (2 Chronicles 26:16–21). The two offices meet again only in the one David foresaw: “You are a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 110:4). Hebrews says Melchizedek appears without recorded father, mother or genealogy, “resembling the Son of God he continues a priest forever” (Hebrews 7:3). The silence of Genesis about where he came from and where he went is itself part of the picture.

Where Christians differ: bread and wine. Roman Catholic tradition sees a sacrifice here, prefiguring the Mass. This commentary’s view: Melchizedek gives a meal of refreshment and blessing; Scripture does not call it a sacrifice. Hebrews, which says much about him, says nothing of the bread and wine, and sees him as a type of Christ’s priesthood, not of the Mass. Christians may still be glad that the priest-king of Salem set a table for the weary, as our priest-king does.
verseByVerse.note: “God Most High” translates El Elyon, a title Abram himself takes up in v. 22.

verseByVerse.quote: And he blessed him and said, "Blessed be Abram by God Most High, Possessor of heaven and earth; and blessed be God Most High, who has delivered your enemies into your hand!" And Abram gave him a tenth of everything.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Melchizedek blesses Abram in the name of God Most High, maker and owner of all, and gives God the glory for the victory; Abram gives him a tenth of everything, honouring him as God’s priest.

Blessed be Abram by God Most High. The blessing promised in 12:2–3 is spoken over Abram by God’s own priest. Hebrews draws the lesson: “It is beyond dispute that the inferior is blessed by the superior” (Hebrews 7:7).

Possessor of heaven and earth. The whole universe belongs to God, so the spoils of war do too, and so does the land the kings have been fighting over.

Who has delivered your enemies into your hand. Melchizedek blesses God as well as Abram, and names who really won the battle. The 318 men did the fighting; God gave the victory.

A tenth of everything. The first tithe in the Bible. A tenth of the spoil was a customary gift to a king or a sanctuary in that world; Abram gives it to honour the God whose priest has just blessed him. By giving it he recognises Melchizedek’s priesthood. The Hebrew says only he gave him a tenth, but Hebrews 7:4 makes clear it was Abram who gave.

Greater than Abraham. Hebrews builds a careful argument on these two verses. Melchizedek blessed Abraham and received a tenth from him, so he is greater than Abraham, and so greater than Levi, Abraham’s descendant, who in a sense paid the tithe “through Abraham” (Hebrews 7:4–10). If God later swore that the coming king would be a priest after Melchizedek’s order, not Aaron’s (Psalm 110:4), then the Levitical priesthood was never the final word. Jesus is that priest: from Judah, not Levi, made priest by God’s oath, holding his priesthood “permanently, because he continues forever”, and so “able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him” (Hebrews 7:24–25).

How Jewish readers take it. The Targums and the Talmud (Nedarim 32b) identify Melchizedek with Shem, son of Noah; the Talmud teaches that the priesthood passed from him to Abraham’s line, and reads Psalm 110 as addressed to Abraham. Jewish and Christian readers agree that he was a real priest of the one true God, and the Qumran community even saw him as a heavenly figure of the last days. This commentary follows Hebrews, which reads him through Psalm 110:4 as the sign of a priesthood greater than Aaron’s, fulfilled in Christ (Hebrews 7:1–17).

For us. Abram’s first act after victory is to bless God and give. Giving to God first is a confession that all we have is his, received, not achieved.

Where Christians differ: who was Melchizedek? Some think he was a pre-incarnate appearance of Christ, since he is described as “having neither beginning of days nor end of life” (Hebrews 7:3); others have thought him an angel. This commentary’s view: he was a real, historical king-priest whose life God arranged, and whose lack of recorded genealogy makes him a type of Christ, the priest for ever (Psalm 110:4). Hebrews says he resembled the Son of God, not that he was the Son.

Where Christians differ: tithing. Some argue that the tithe comes before the law of Moses and so still binds Christians to exactly a tenth. This commentary’s view: this was a voluntary gift; the New Testament calls for regular, proportionate, generous and cheerful giving (2 Corinthians 9:7), for which a tenth is a helpful guide, and many should give more.

Uncertain wording. The word translated “Possessor” can mean either “owner” or “maker”; some translations have Creator of heaven and earth. Both are true of God, and each implies the other: he owns all things because he made them.
verseByVerse.note: The first tithe in the Bible.

verseByVerse.quote: And the king of Sodom said to Abram, "Give me the persons, but take the goods for yourself." But Abram said to the king of Sodom, "I have lifted my hand to the LORD, God Most High, Possessor of heaven and earth, that I would not take a thread or a sandal strap or anything that is yours, lest you should say, 'I have made Abram rich.' I will take nothing but what the young men have eaten, and the share of the men who went with me. Let Aner, Eshcol, and Mamre take their share."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king of Sodom offers Abram the goods, and Abram refuses even a thread, because he has sworn to God Most High that no one but God will be able to say he made Abram rich.

Give me the persons, but take the goods. After Melchizedek’s blessing comes Sodom’s offer, and it is a test. The king of Sodom brings nothing and blesses no one; his first words are “Give me”. By the customs of war the rescuer could keep the spoil, so the offer looks generous. But it would have tied Abram’s wealth to Sodom.

I have lifted my hand to the LORD, God Most High. Raising the hand was the gesture of an oath. Abram has already sworn, before the offer came. And he puts the name of the LORD, Israel’s covenant God, beside Melchizedek’s title: the God Most High whom Melchizedek serves is the LORD who called Abram.

Not a thread or a sandal strap. Nothing at all, down to the smallest things. “Lest you should say, ‘I have made Abram rich.’” Abram will owe his wealth to God alone. Perhaps the gifts of Pharaoh, gained by a lie (12:16), had taught him something.

Let Aner, Eshcol, and Mamre take their share. Abram’s vow binds himself, not others. His young men have eaten what they needed, and his allies, who risked their lives with him, may take their lawful share. Abram does not make his own conscience a rule for everyone else.

All things are yours. Abram can refuse Sodom’s goods because he has just been blessed by God Most High, Possessor of heaven and earth. Believers have far more: God “did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all; how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?” (Romans 8:32). We do not need what the world offers on its own terms.

For us. A tempting gain is best refused by a decision made before the offer comes: the gift with strings, the deal that would mean keeping quiet, the money that would make us beholden to wrong. Refuse gains that would compromise your witness, and thank God, Possessor of heaven and earth, as the source of all you have.

What it does not mean. Not that believers may never receive help, wages or trade from unbelievers. Abram let his allies take their share, and later paid the Hittites a fair price for a field (23:16). The question is whether a gain would obscure God’s glory or tie us to evil.

14.theology:
The Order of Melchizedek. Each element of Melchizedek's description finds its fulfilment in Jesus: king and priest at once (Heb. 4:14), king of peace (Eph. 2:14–15), Son of the Most High God (Mark 5:7), and bringer of bread and wine, which Christ gives at the Last Supper as signs of the new covenant. To read Genesis 14 in the light of the whole Bible is to see Christ foreshadowed in Abram’s world.

The Superiority of Christ's Priesthood. The Levitical priesthood, though ordained by God, was never the final word; it ranked below an older, greater order of priesthood, not handed from father to son and with no repeated sacrifices. Jesus fulfils that order: priest by oath ("The LORD has sworn and will not change his mind," Ps. 110:4), priest for ever, and his sacrifice once for all (Heb. 7:27).
14.examples:
Then: City-states in the ancient Near East formed and broke alliances constantly. That Abram, a single clan chief with 318 trained men, defeated a coalition of kings is presented as God's doing (v. 20), not military strategy. And Salem appears here for the first time: the city that will house the temple and the throne of David, where the Son of David will be crucified and rise.

Now: Employers, governments, markets and benefactors can come to seem the source of our prosperity, until their claims on us feel as strong as God's. Abram's refusal of Sodom's goods is the act of someone who knows that all he has comes from God and will not let that be obscured. And Melchizedek's bread and wine still speak: the eternal priest-king sets the table, and every Lord's Supper is a meeting with the one who is greater than Abraham.

keyVerse.quote: And he blessed him and said, “Blessed be Abram by God Most High, Possessor of heaven and earth; and blessed be God Most High, who has delivered your enemies into your hand!”
keyVerse.note: Melchizedek’s blessing tells the truth about the whole chapter: the battle was won not by Abram’s 318 men but by God Most High, who owns heaven and earth. That is why Abram gives a tenth to God’s priest and refuses Sodom’s goods. And the priest who speaks the blessing points ahead to Jesus, the priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek.

14.reflection:
Abram went after Lot at once, though Lot had chosen Sodom for himself (vv. 12–16). Is there someone in trouble of their own making whom God may be calling you to help? What would that look like, and what would keep it from becoming mere rescuing that changes nothing?

Melchizedek appears for three verses, yet Psalm 110 and Hebrews 7 see Christ in him. What does it mean for you that Jesus is both king and priest, and a priest “forever”?

Abram gave a tenth to God’s priest and refused anything from the king of Sodom (vv. 20–23). What do our giving and our refusing say about where we think our wealth comes from?

Abram had sworn before the offer came (v. 22). Which gains, gifts or opportunities would compromise your witness, and how could you decide about them now, before they are offered?

15.title: The LORD Your Shield and Reward
15.text: <sup>1</sup>After these things the word of the LORD came to Abram in a vision: "Fear not, Abram, I am your shield; your reward shall be very great."<sup>2</sup>But Abram said, "O Lord GOD, what will you give me, for I continue childless, and the heir of my house is Eliezer of Damascus?"<sup>3</sup>And Abram said, "Behold, you have given me no offspring, and a member of my household will be my heir."<sup>4</sup>And behold, the word of the LORD came to him: "This man shall not be your heir; your very own son shall be your heir."<sup>5</sup>And he brought him outside and said, "Look toward heaven, and number the stars, if you are able to number them." Then he said to him, "So shall your offspring be."<sup>6</sup>And he believed the LORD, and he counted it to him as righteousness.<sup>7</sup>And he said to him, "I am the LORD who brought you out from Ur of the Chaldeans to give you this land to possess."<sup>8</sup>But he said, "O Lord GOD, how am I to know that I shall possess it?"<sup>9</sup>He said to him, "Bring me a heifer three years old, a female goat three years old, a ram three years old, a turtledove, and a young pigeon."<sup>10</sup>And he brought him all these, cut them in half, and laid each half over against the other. But he did not cut the birds in half.<sup>11</sup>And when birds of prey came down on the carcasses, Abram drove them away.<sup>12</sup>As the sun was going down, a deep sleep fell on Abram. And behold, dreadful and great darkness fell upon him.<sup>13</sup>Then the LORD said to Abram, "Know for certain that your offspring will be sojourners in a land that is not theirs and will be servants there, and they will be afflicted for four hundred years.<sup>14</sup>But I will bring judgment on the nation that they serve, and afterward they shall come out with great possessions.<sup>15</sup>As for you, you shall go to your fathers in peace; you shall be buried in a good old age.<sup>16</sup>And they shall come back here in the fourth generation, for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete."<sup>17</sup>When the sun had gone down and it was dark, behold, a smoking fire pot and a flaming torch passed between these pieces.<sup>18</sup>On that day the LORD made a covenant with Abram, saying, "To your offspring I give this land, from the river of Egypt to the great river, the river Euphrates,<sup>19</sup>the land of the Kenites, the Kenizzites, the Kadmonites,<sup>20</sup>the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Rephaim,<sup>21</sup>the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Girgashites and the Jebusites."
15.overview:
Where we are. Abram has just defeated four kings, given a tenth to Melchizedek and refused every thread of Sodom’s goods (chapter 14). He has turned down wealth, may fear reprisal, and is still childless, ten years after God first promised him offspring (12:2, 7; 16:3).

The message. God answers Abram’s fear and doubt with himself, his word and his oath. Abram trusts the promise of a son and offspring like the stars, and God counts that faith to him as righteousness: a sinner is right with God not by what he does but by trusting what God has promised. Then God binds himself by a covenant in which he alone walks between the pieces, so that the whole weight of the promise rests on God, not on Abram.

Why it was said. Israel, newly brought out of Egypt (see the introduction), could read here that its slavery, its rescue “with great possessions” and the long wait before entering the land had all been foretold to Abraham. Their history was no accident, their hope rested on God’s oath, and they belonged to him the way their father did, by believing him.

How the chapter makes its case. In two movements. First, the offspring (vv. 1–6): God promises to be Abram’s shield and reward; Abram pours out his complaint that a servant will be his heir; God promises a son of his own body and offspring as many as the stars; and Abram believes, and it is counted to him as righteousness. Second, the land (vv. 7–21): Abram asks how he can know; God has him lay out animals cut in two (vv. 7–11), tells him in a dreadful darkness of four centuries of slavery, judgment on Egypt and return (vv. 12–16), and then passes alone between the pieces as a smoking fire pot and flaming torch, sealing the gift of the land by covenant (vv. 17–21).

Where it leads. By promise and by covenant, both drawn out in the New Testament. Verse 6 is the text on which Paul builds justification by faith: the words “it was counted to him” were written “for ours also”, who believe in the God who raised Jesus (Romans 4:23–24). And the God who walked alone between the pieces, taking the covenant’s curse upon himself, bore that curse in his Son, so that “in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles” (Galatians 3:13–14).

For us. Bring God your honest fears and disappointments, as Abram did. Your standing with God does not depend on your record but on trusting his promise in Christ, and your hope does not rest on your grip on him but on his oath to you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–21 — The Covenant Confirmed: Abram's Faith and God's Oath
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God answers fear and doubt with his word and his oath, and the man who believes him is counted righteous. The chapter has two movements. In the first (vv. 1–6), God promises to be Abram’s shield and reward; Abram complains that he is still childless; God promises a son of his own and offspring as many as the stars; and Abram believes, and God counts it to him as righteousness. In the second (vv. 7–21), Abram asks how he can know he will possess the land. God has him cut animals in two, foretells four hundred years of slavery and the exodus, and then passes alone between the pieces, binding himself by covenant to give the land to Abram’s offspring.
verseByVerse.theology: God answers Abram's complaint of childlessness with the stars, and Abram believes. Then God makes a covenant for the land and foretells four hundred years of affliction.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul notes that verse 6 comes before circumcision (Rom. 4:9–12). Now: God took both sides of the covenant on himself, and in Christ he bore its curse (Gal. 3:13).

verseByVerse.quote: After these things the word of the LORD came to Abram in a vision: "Fear not, Abram, I am your shield; your reward shall be very great." But Abram said, "O Lord GOD, what will you give me, for I continue childless, and the heir of my house is Eliezer of Damascus?" And Abram said, "Behold, you have given me no offspring, and a member of my household will be my heir."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God tells Abram not to be afraid, because God himself is his protection and his reward; Abram answers honestly that nothing God gives can matter much while he has no son.

After these things … in a vision. After the battle and the refused spoils of chapter 14. The phrase “the word of the LORD came” is the way the prophets later describe God speaking to them, and Abram is later called a prophet (20:7).

Fear not, Abram. Abram may well fear reprisal from the kings he has defeated, and he has just turned down the riches of Sodom. God speaks to both fears.

I am your shield; your reward shall be very great. God himself is his protection, as the psalms later sing: “But you, O LORD, are a shield about me” (Psalm 3:3). And his reward is not the spoil he refused (14:23) but what God will give, and above all God himself.

O Lord GOD. Abram addresses God as “Lord” (master) and by his covenant name, the LORD; this is the first time the two are joined in the Bible. Abram speaks to God as a servant to his master, but a servant who may speak freely.

I continue childless. Abram answers with an honest complaint. Ancient documents show that a childless man could adopt a trusted servant to inherit his estate, so Abram is naming the future custom left him: everything would pass to Eliezer, and the promise to a household servant. Faith can voice its questions to God, and we may bring him our real disappointment; God does not rebuke Abram for it.

God himself as your reward. Like most of us, Abram may be wondering whether faith has left him poorer. Underneath his question about an heir is the question every heart asks: what will finally make my life worth it? We usually answer with something God gives: a child, a marriage, a career, security. Those are good gifts, but when one of them becomes the reward we live for, it cannot carry the weight, and we hold it with clenched fists. God’s answer to Abram is first of all himself. That is what Christ died to secure: he “suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God” (1 Peter 3:18), not merely to God’s benefits. So when a good thing is withheld this week, pray with the psalmist, “Whom have I in heaven but you? And there is nothing on earth that I desire besides you” (Psalm 73:25).

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of v. 2b is one of the hardest phrases in Genesis. Literally it reads something like the son of the meshek of my house is Dammesek Eliezer, with a play on sounds between meshek, a rare word whose meaning is uncertain, and Dammesek, Damascus. The general sense is clear from v. 3, and the ESV gives it: a member of Abram’s household, Eliezer, probably from Damascus, stands to inherit. Whether this Eliezer is the unnamed senior servant of chapter 24 is not said.
verseByVerse.note: Damascus was a city of Syria, north of Canaan.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, the word of the LORD came to him: "This man shall not be your heir; your very own son shall be your heir." And he brought him outside and said, "Look toward heaven, and number the stars, if you are able to number them." Then he said to him, "So shall your offspring be."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God answers Abram’s complaint with a specific and humanly impossible promise: not a servant but a son of his own body will be his heir, and his offspring will be as countless as the stars.

This man shall not be your heir. God answers Abram’s words directly, phrase for phrase. The alternative Abram feared is ruled out.

Your very own son. Literally, one who will come out of your own body. The same expression is used centuries later in God’s promise to David of the son whose kingdom he would establish (2 Samuel 7:12). Both promises run on to Christ.

He brought him outside. God takes Abram out of the tent into the night. “Number the stars, if you are able to number them.” Before city lights, the night sky over the Judean hills was crowded with stars, and the point is plain: you cannot count them. The promise once pictured by the dust (13:16) is now written across the sky, and Abram can look up at it every clear night.

So shall your offspring be. Moses could tell Israel, “you are today as numerous as the stars of heaven” (Deuteronomy 1:10). But the promise reaches further. All who belong to Christ are Abraham’s offspring (Galatians 3:29), and John saw “a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation” (Revelation 7:9). Paul says Abram “in hope … believed against hope” (Romans 4:18), and Hebrews marvels that these descendants came “from one man, and him as good as dead” (Hebrews 11:12).

For us. God’s promises often outrun every human possibility. Faith does not pretend the obstacles are not there; it looks up from them to the God who made the stars and keeps his word.

verseByVerse.quote: And he believed the LORD, and he counted it to him as righteousness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abram trusted God’s promise, and God credited righteousness to him: here Scripture first states plainly that a sinner is right with God through faith, not by what he does.

He believed the LORD. The Hebrew verb comes from the same root as “amen”: to lean on, rely on, count as firm. Abram trusts God’s word, though nothing he can see has changed; he is still old and childless. And he believes the LORD himself, not just a statement about the future: faith rests its weight on a person.

He counted it to him as righteousness. Counted means credited, put to his account. Righteousness here is a right standing before God the judge. Abram was not righteous in himself: he had lied in Egypt (12:10–20) and would soon take Hagar (16:1–4). God declares him right with himself because he trusts the promise.

Was Abram not a believer already? Yes. By faith he had left his country years before (Hebrews 11:8). Verse 6 is not necessarily the moment Abram was first justified; it is Scripture’s verdict on the faith he lived by, set at the point where that faith is most plainly tested and most plainly answered.

Before circumcision and before the law. Paul builds justification by faith on this verse (Romans 4:3; Galatians 3:6). He points out that it was said before Abram was circumcised (Romans 4:10), and 430 years before the law was given (Galatians 3:17), so neither circumcision nor law-keeping can be the way anyone is made right with God. It is “to the one who does not work but believes in him who justifies the ungodly” that “his faith is counted as righteousness” (Romans 4:5).

Written for us. “But the words ‘it was counted to him’ were not written for his sake alone, but for ours also. It will be counted to us who believe in him who raised from the dead Jesus our Lord” (Romans 4:23–24). The promise Abram believed was the promise of the offspring through whom all nations would be blessed, and that offspring is Christ (Galatians 3:16); Jesus said, “Your father Abraham rejoiced that he would see my day” (John 8:56). Abram believed God would bring life from his own dead body (Romans 4:19); we believe God brought life from the dead body of his Son. It is the same faith in the same God.

Paul and James. James quotes the same verse and says it was “fulfilled” when Abraham offered Isaac, decades later (James 2:21–23). They do not contradict each other. Paul shows how Abraham was counted righteous, by faith apart from works; James shows what kind of faith that was, a living faith that obeyed.

Where Christians differ: what is counted? Some read Abram’s faith itself as the righteous act that God rewards; Roman Catholic teaching includes inner renewal and good works in justification. This commentary’s view: faith is the instrument, not the ground. God counts righteous the one who trusts him, apart from works (Romans 4:4–5), on the ground of Christ’s righteousness credited to him (2 Corinthians 5:21). Faith adds nothing of its own; it receives.
verseByVerse.note: “Counted” is a bookkeeping word: entered to his account.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to him, "I am the LORD who brought you out from Ur of the Chaldeans to give you this land to possess." But he said, "O Lord GOD, how am I to know that I shall possess it?" He said to him, "Bring me a heifer three years old, a female goat three years old, a ram three years old, a turtledove, and a young pigeon." And he brought him all these, cut them in half, and laid each half over against the other. But he did not cut the birds in half. And when birds of prey came down on the carcasses, Abram drove them away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God reminds Abram that he brought him out to give him this land, and when Abram asks for assurance, God has him prepare the animals for a solemn covenant ceremony.

I am the LORD who brought you out from Ur. God’s past rescue is the pledge of his future gift. The words anticipate the opening of the Ten Commandments: “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt” (Exodus 20:2).

How am I to know? This is a request for assurance, not unbelief; Abram has just believed (v. 6). God does not rebuke him but answers with a covenant.

A heifer three years old, a female goat, a ram, a turtledove and a young pigeon. Animals in their prime, and exactly the kinds that the law would later prescribe for Israel’s sacrifices: cattle, goats, sheep, doves and pigeons (Leviticus 1).

Cut them in half. This was a known covenant ritual. In Hebrew one “cuts” a covenant (the verb behind “made a covenant” in v. 18). The animals were cut in two and the parties walked between the halves, calling death on themselves if they broke their word. Jeremiah describes the rite and its curse: those who broke the covenant would be made like the calf they cut in two (Jeremiah 34:18–20). An Aramaic treaty from the eighth century BC uses the same picture of a calf cut in two. Abram knows what is about to happen: a solemn oath, sworn on pain of death.

Abram drove them away. Birds of prey descend on the carcasses, and Abram keeps them off while he waits. Many see a hint of the threats that would come against the promise before it was fulfilled; at the least, it shows Abram waiting, guarding what God has told him to prepare.

The time of day. The stars are visible in v. 5, and the sun is only going down in v. 12. Either the scene stretches over a night and a day, or vv. 7–21 record a later occasion. The text does not say.

verseByVerse.quote: As the sun was going down, a deep sleep fell on Abram. And behold, dreadful and great darkness fell upon him. Then the LORD said to Abram, "Know for certain that your offspring will be sojourners in a land that is not theirs and will be servants there, and they will be afflicted for four hundred years. But I will bring judgment on the nation that they serve, and afterward they shall come out with great possessions. As for you, you shall go to your fathers in peace; you shall be buried in a good old age. And they shall come back here in the fourth generation, for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In a dreadful darkness God tells Abram the hard road ahead: four hundred years of slavery for his offspring, judgment on their oppressors and a rescue with great wealth, a peaceful death for Abram himself, and a return to the land only when the Amorites’ sin is full.

A deep sleep fell on Abram. The same word is used of the deep sleep God sent on Adam (2:21). Abram is put out of action; God will act alone (v. 17). “Dreadful and great darkness” is the awe of God’s presence, and perhaps also a shadow of the dark years about to be described.

Know for certain. This answers Abram’s question “how am I to know?” (v. 8). The assurance God gives includes hard truth: the promise is sure, but the road to it runs through suffering.

Sojourners … servants … afflicted for four hundred years. Israel’s time in Egypt, foretold in three words: strangers, slaves, oppressed. “Afflicted” is the verb used of Egypt’s oppression in Exodus 1:11–12.

I will bring judgment on the nation that they serve. The plagues of Egypt, and then “they shall come out with great possessions”, as they did when the Egyptians gave them silver, gold and clothing: “Thus they plundered the Egyptians” (Exodus 12:36).

You shall go to your fathers in peace. Abram himself will not see any of this; he will die in a good old age (25:8). His fathers were buried far away in Mesopotamia, so “go to your fathers” seems to mean more than sharing a grave. Jesus drew on God’s covenant with the patriarchs to prove the resurrection: “He is not God of the dead, but of the living” (Matthew 22:32).

For the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete. “Amorites” stands for the peoples of Canaan. God will not give their land to Abram’s offspring until their judgment is fully deserved. God’s delay in judgment is patience, not indifference. He waited four centuries for the Amorites, as he waits now: “The Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise as some count slowness, but is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish” (2 Peter 3:9).

Suffering before glory. Abram’s family must go down into Egypt and be afflicted before it inherits. That pattern runs through Scripture and reaches its centre in Christ: “Was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory?” (Luke 24:26). Those who belong to him walk the same road, and God tells them so in advance.

Where Christians differ: the conquest. How can God give one people’s land to another? This commentary’s view: the conquest was God’s judgment on centuries of wickedness, delayed in patience (Leviticus 18:24–25). It was a unique act of God, never a pattern or licence for violence by nations today.

Uncertain wording. How “four hundred years” fits with “the fourth generation” is not certain. The word “generation” may here mean a full lifetime of about a century, as lives then were long; or the four generations may be counted from those who went down to Egypt, as in the line Levi, Kohath, Amram, Moses (Exodus 6:16–20). Either way the promise is clear: the return would come, and at God’s time.
verseByVerse.note: “Four hundred years” is a round figure; Exodus gives 430 years.

verseByVerse.quote: When the sun had gone down and it was dark, behold, a smoking fire pot and a flaming torch passed between these pieces. On that day the LORD made a covenant with Abram, saying, "To your offspring I give this land, from the river of Egypt to the great river, the river Euphrates, the land of the Kenites, the Kenizzites, the Kadmonites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Rephaim, the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Girgashites and the Jebusites."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God alone passes between the pieces, in smoke and fire, binding himself by oath to give the land to Abram’s offspring: the whole weight of the covenant rests on God.

A smoking fire pot and a flaming torch. Smoke and fire mark God’s presence, as in the pillar of cloud and fire (Exodus 13:21) and on Sinai, which was “wrapped in smoke because the LORD had descended on it in fire” (Exodus 19:18).

Passed between these pieces. In the usual form both parties walked between the halves. Here only God does. Abram is asleep (v. 12). God takes the whole obligation on himself: if the covenant is broken, the curse pictured by the divided animals will fall on him. This is a covenant of grace. Hebrews says that when God made his promise to Abraham, “since he had no one greater by whom to swear, he swore by himself” (Hebrews 6:13).

The cost God took on. The covenant was broken many times, not by God but by Abraham’s children, and by us. The death the ritual pictured did fall, at the cross, on God the Son: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13). So Christians have rightly seen in this silent night a preview of the gospel. And it gives believers solid ground: God guaranteed his purpose with an oath “so that by two unchangeable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we who have fled for refuge might have strong encouragement to hold fast to the hope set before us” (Hebrews 6:18). Your security does not rest on your grip on God, but on his oath to you.

From the river of Egypt to the great river. The land is described at its widest, from the edge of Egypt to the Euphrates. On how this promise was fulfilled, and what it points to, see the note on 12:7–9.

The land of the Kenites … and the Jebusites. Ten peoples hold the land. The promise is made while it belongs to others; Abram must still live by faith.

Uncertain wording. “The river of Egypt” is probably not the Nile but the Wadi el-Arish, the seasonal stream in northern Sinai that elsewhere marks Canaan’s south-western border (Numbers 34:5, where it is called “the Brook of Egypt”). Some think the eastern arm of the Nile delta is meant. The Euphrates is certain.
verseByVerse.note: The borders in vv. 18–21 were reached, at least as a realm of subject kingdoms, under Solomon (1 Kings 4:21).

15.theology:
Justification by Faith. Genesis 15:6 is the Old Testament's clearest statement of what the Reformation recovered: righteousness before God comes through faith, not works. Paul's argument in Romans 4 is that it was always so: Abraham was justified before circumcision, before the law, before any achievement, and righteousness "will be counted to us who believe in him who raised from the dead Jesus our Lord" (Rom. 4:24).

A Covenant God Keeps Alone. God swears by himself, for there is no one greater (Heb. 6:13–14), and takes the whole burden of the covenant on himself. Abram's obedience still matters, but the security of the promise rests on God’s faithfulness, not Abram’s. At the cross God kept that undertaking: God the Son bore the curse his own covenant required.
15.examples:
Then: Ancient readers would have recognised the ceremony as a known treaty form. What was startling was that only one party walked. And in a world where the stars were linked with divine power and destiny, God takes them up to promise a childless man a family.

Now: The honesty of Abram's complaint (vv. 2–3) gives Christians lasting permission to lament, to pour out grief to God in prayer. A faith that must always look cheerful and hide its doubts has no support in the Bible: Abram brought his pain directly to God, and God met him there. The church that makes room for honest lament is more faithful than one that expects its members to act contented. And verse 6 remains every sinner's only hope: not what I have done, but whom I have trusted.

keyVerse.quote: And he believed the LORD, and he counted it to him as righteousness.
keyVerse.note: This is one of the most important sentences in the Bible. Paul builds his teaching on justification on it (Romans 4; Galatians 3): a man who had not yet been circumcised, had received no law and had done nothing to earn it was counted righteous because he trusted God’s promise. It was written, Paul says, for us also, who believe in him who raised Jesus from the dead.

15.reflection:
Abram is told, “Fear not … I am your shield; your reward shall be very great” (v. 1), and he answers with an honest complaint (vv. 2–3). What do you most want from God? How does it help to know that God offers himself as the reward, and that he welcomes honest complaint?

Verse 6 says Abram believed the LORD, and it was counted to him as righteousness. In your own words, what did Abram contribute to his righteousness, and what did God? Why does Paul say this was written for us too (Romans 4:23–24)?

God told Abram plainly that his offspring would suffer for four hundred years before the promise was fulfilled (vv. 13–16). How does it help or trouble you that God’s plans for his people include long waiting and hardship?

Only God passed between the pieces while Abram slept (vv. 12, 17). How should that shape the way you think about your assurance of salvation on days when your faith feels weak?

16.title: Hagar and Ishmael
16.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Sarai, Abram's wife, had borne him no children. She had a female Egyptian servant whose name was Hagar.<sup>2</sup>And Sarai said to Abram, "Behold now, the LORD has prevented me from bearing children. Go in to my servant; it may be that I shall obtain children by her." And Abram listened to the voice of Sarai.<sup>3</sup>So, after Abram had lived ten years in the land of Canaan, Sarai, Abram's wife, took Hagar the Egyptian, her servant, and gave her to Abram her husband as a wife.<sup>4</sup>And he went in to Hagar, and she conceived. And when she saw that she had conceived, she looked with contempt on her mistress.<sup>5</sup>And Sarai said to Abram, "May the wrong done to me be on you! I gave my servant to your embrace, and when she saw that she had conceived, she looked on me with contempt. May the LORD judge between you and me!"<sup>6</sup>But Abram said to Sarai, "Behold, your servant is in your power; do to her as you please." Then Sarai dealt harshly with her, and she fled from her.<sup>7</sup>The angel of the LORD found her by a spring of water in the wilderness, the spring on the way to Shur.<sup>8</sup>And he said, "Hagar, servant of Sarai, where have you come from and where are you going?" She said, "I am fleeing from my mistress Sarai."<sup>9</sup>The angel of the LORD said to her, "Return to your mistress and submit to her."<sup>10</sup>The angel of the LORD also said to her, "I will surely multiply your offspring so that they cannot be numbered for multitude."<sup>11</sup>And the angel of the LORD said to her, "Behold, you are pregnant and shall bear a son. You shall call his name Ishmael, because the LORD has listened to your affliction.<sup>12</sup>He shall be a wild donkey of a man, his hand against everyone and everyone's hand against him, and he shall dwell over against all his kinsmen."<sup>13</sup>So she called the name of the LORD who spoke to her, "You are a God of seeing," for she said, "Truly here I have seen him who looks after me."<sup>14</sup>Therefore the well was called Beer-lahai-roi; it lies between Kadesh and Bered.<sup>15</sup>And Hagar bore Abram a son, and Abram called the name of his son, whom Hagar bore, Ishmael.<sup>16</sup>Abram was eighty-six years old when Hagar bore Ishmael to Abram.
16.overview:
Where we are. God has just promised Abram a son of his own body and sworn a covenant to him (chapter 15). But Sarai is still barren, Abram has lived ten years in Canaan, and both are growing old.

The message. Faith grows impatient and tries to help God keep his promise, and the shortcut brings contempt, cruelty and flight. Yet God does not abandon the people hurt by it. He goes after the runaway Egyptian slave, hears her misery, gives her son a name and a future, and she discovers that the God of Abram is “a God of seeing” (v. 13). The promised child cannot be produced by human strategy; and the God who chose Abram sees the overlooked.

Why it was said. Israel knew Ishmael’s descendants as neighbours in the desert to the south and east (see the introduction), and needed to know both why the promise did not pass through them and that God had cared for their mother too. Israel would also know slavery and affliction in Egypt, and here an Egyptian slave woman, afflicted in Abram’s house, is the one whom God hears.

How the chapter makes its case. Sarai, believing God has closed her womb, gives her Egyptian servant Hagar to Abram, and he agrees (vv. 1–3). Hagar conceives and despises her mistress; Sarai blames Abram, Abram hands Hagar over, and Sarai treats her so harshly that she runs away (vv. 4–6). The angel of the LORD finds her by a spring on the road to Egypt and sends her back (vv. 7–9), with a promise of countless offspring and a son named Ishmael, “God hears” (vv. 10–12). Hagar names the God who sees her, and Ishmael is born to Abram at eighty-six (vv. 13–16).

Where it leads. By the need it exposes, and by the character of God revealed in Christ. The child of the flesh is not the child of promise (Galatians 4:23): God’s promise would be kept only by God’s own power, in Isaac and finally in the Son born of a virgin. And the God who sought out Hagar is the God we meet in Jesus, who went out of his way to find a woman at a well in Samaria and tell her all that she had ever done. This commentary takes the angel of the LORD, who speaks as God, to be the Son himself, appearing before his incarnation.

For us. Impatience with God’s timing produces arrangements that outlive us, and calling our plan God’s will does not make it so. But the God who sees finds us in the wilderness of our own making, and finds the people our choices have hurt. If no one else sees you, he does.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — Hagar and Ishmael: Faith's Impatience
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The attempt to help God keep his promise ends in contempt, cruelty and flight, but the God who sees goes after the one who was wronged. Sarai gives her Egyptian slave Hagar to Abram, a step her culture accepted (vv. 1–3). The household falls apart: Hagar despises Sarai, Sarai blames Abram, Abram steps back, and Sarai’s harshness drives Hagar into the desert (vv. 4–6). The angel of the LORD finds her, sends her back with a promise of countless offspring, and names her son Ishmael, because the LORD has heard her (vv. 7–12). Hagar names the God who sees her, and Ishmael is born, the child of impatience, not of promise (vv. 13–16).
verseByVerse.theology: Sarai gives Hagar to Abram, and the household falls apart. The angel of the LORD finds Hagar in the wilderness, sends her back with a promise, and names her son.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul reads the two mothers as two covenants, slavery and freedom. Now: impatience with God's timetable produces arrangements that outlive us, and the God who sees still finds the overlooked.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Sarai, Abram's wife, had borne him no children. She had a female Egyptian servant whose name was Hagar. And Sarai said to Abram, "Behold now, the LORD has prevented me from bearing children. Go in to my servant; it may be that I shall obtain children by her." And Abram listened to the voice of Sarai. So, after Abram had lived ten years in the land of Canaan, Sarai, Abram's wife, took Hagar the Egyptian, her servant, and gave her to Abram her husband as a wife.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Still childless after ten years in the land, Sarai gives her Egyptian slave Hagar to Abram to bear a child for her, and Abram agrees: faith grows impatient and tries to help God keep his promise.

Sarai, Abram’s wife, had borne him no children. Genesis has said so since 11:30. God has promised Abram a son of his own body (15:4), but he has not yet said it will be Sarai’s son; that comes in 17:16. Her reasoning is understandable.

A female Egyptian servant whose name was Hagar. Hagar was Sarai’s personal slave, perhaps one of those Abram received from Pharaoh (12:16). She is never asked what she wants; in this chapter she is spoken about, given and handed back, until God speaks to her by name (v. 8). On slavery in that world, see Slavery in the Ancient World.

The LORD has prevented me from bearing children. Sarai sees God’s hand in her barrenness, rightly, but takes matters into her own hands. “It may be that I shall obtain children by her” (literally “be built up”, see the note): a child born to her slave would legally count as hers. Ancient marriage contracts and laws record exactly this arrangement, so Sarai is doing what her world considered reasonable. Rachel and Leah will do the same (30:3–9).

Abram listened to the voice of Sarai. The words echo God’s verdict on Adam: “Because you have listened to the voice of your wife” (3:17). And as Eve “took” and “gave” to her husband (3:6), so Sarai “took Hagar … and gave her to Abram”. The narrator does not comment, but the echoes say it: a second fall in miniature, with a husband following where he should have led.

As a wife. Hagar becomes a secondary wife, a concubine. Genesis records the polygamy of the patriarchs without approving it; God’s pattern is one man and one woman (2:24), and every divided household in Genesis is full of rivalry and pain, this one first.

For us. It is worth asking where we too try to force God’s promise by our own methods, especially methods our culture finds perfectly normal. Waiting for God is not doing nothing, but it does mean refusing to do wrong to get what God has promised.

What it does not mean. Not that childless couples who seek medical help are faithless like Sarai, or that infertility is a sign of God’s displeasure. Hannah, Elizabeth and others carried that grief and were dearly loved by God. The longing for a child is good, and its grief is real and should be met with tenderness, not advice. But Sarai’s shortcut brought a third person into the making of a child within a marriage, and that is why this commentary counsels against donor eggs or sperm and surrogacy, while holding that IVF within marriage, using the couple’s own eggs and sperm and treating every embryo as a child, is permissible.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes a wordplay: “obtain children” is literally “be built up.”

verseByVerse.quote: And he went in to Hagar, and she conceived. And when she saw that she had conceived, she looked with contempt on her mistress. And Sarai said to Abram, "May the wrong done to me be on you! I gave my servant to your embrace, and when she saw that she had conceived, she looked on me with contempt. May the LORD judge between you and me!" But Abram said to Sarai, "Behold, your servant is in your power; do to her as you please." Then Sarai dealt harshly with her, and she fled from her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The shortcut works and the household falls apart: Hagar despises her mistress, Sarai blames Abram, Abram washes his hands of it, and Sarai treats Hagar so harshly that she runs away.

She looked with contempt on her mistress. Literally, her mistress became “light” in her eyes. In a world that measured a woman’s worth by her children, the pregnant slave now looks down on the barren wife. Proverbs knows the scene: the earth trembles under “a maidservant when she displaces her mistress” (Proverbs 30:23).

May the wrong done to me be on you! Sarai blames Abram for an arrangement that was her idea. “May the LORD judge between you and me!” She calls on God to judge the very scheme that bypassed him.

Your servant is in your power; do to her as you please. Abram gives up his responsibility. The woman carrying his child is handed back to an angry mistress with no protection. He does not pray, decide or defend anyone. Passivity is not peace.

Sarai dealt harshly with her. The same verb is used of Egypt’s oppression of Israel (15:13; Exodus 1:11–12). With a bitter irony, Abram’s house treats an Egyptian as Egypt would one day treat Abram’s children. The shortcut bears its fruit: contempt, blame, passivity and cruelty.

The way of the flesh. Paul reads the story this way: “the son of the slave was born according to the flesh, while the son of the free woman was born through promise” (Galatians 4:23). What we produce by our own strength to secure God’s blessing always ends in bondage and conflict. What God gives by promise brings freedom. Every attempt to earn by our own effort what God has promised to give by grace is a kind of Hagar arrangement.

No one comes out well. Scripture tells this story about the father of the faithful and his wife without excusing either. The heroes of Genesis are sinners saved by grace, and their failures are recorded so that we will not trust in them, but in the God who kept his promise in spite of them.

verseByVerse.quote: The angel of the LORD found her by a spring of water in the wilderness, the spring on the way to Shur. And he said, "Hagar, servant of Sarai, where have you come from and where are you going?" She said, "I am fleeing from my mistress Sarai." The angel of the LORD said to her, "Return to your mistress and submit to her."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The angel of the LORD seeks out the runaway slave in the desert, calls her by name, asks where she is going, and sends her back to her mistress.

The angel of the LORD found her. This is the first time the angel of the LORD appears in the Bible, and he comes not to Abram but to an Egyptian slave. He does not stumble on her; he finds her, as a shepherd finds a lost sheep.

By a spring of water … on the way to Shur. Shur lay in the desert towards Egypt: Hagar is heading home. A pregnant woman alone in that wilderness was in danger of her life; a spring was the difference between life and death.

Hagar, servant of Sarai. For the first time someone speaks to Hagar by name. “Where have you come from and where are you going?” God’s questions, like his question to Adam (“Where are you?”, 3:9), are not for his information but to draw her out. She can answer the first but not the second: “I am fleeing from my mistress Sarai.”

Return to your mistress and submit to her. The command is hard. But God did not send Hagar back into the same household unchanged: she returned carrying God’s promise for her son and God’s own word, which Abram and Sarai could not ignore, and she returned to the household where her son would be safely born and claimed by his father (v. 15). Alone in the desert, she and her child would probably have died.

The Son who seeks. The angel of the LORD speaks as God, promising what only God can promise (v. 10), and Hagar recognises that she has seen God (v. 13). The One who sought out a runaway slave by a desert spring is the same Lord who, in the flesh, sat by a well in Samaria and spoke with a woman everyone else avoided (John 4:6–29), and who came “to seek and to save the lost” (Luke 19:10).

What it does not mean. This was a particular word to Hagar in her situation, not a rule that the oppressed must return to those who mistreat them. Scripture elsewhere commands God’s people to rescue the oppressed (Proverbs 24:11), and Paul himself escaped those who sought his life (Acts 9:23–25). Anyone who is being abused, in a home, a church or a workplace, should get to safety, tell someone they trust and, where there is danger, contact the police the same day. Church leaders should protect the vulnerable, never send them back to harm.

Where Christians differ: who is the angel of the LORD? Some see a created angel speaking in God’s name, as an ambassador speaks for his king. Others see a pre-incarnate appearance of the Son of God. This commentary’s view: he speaks as God and is called God (v. 13), so he is best read as the Son appearing before his incarnation, as many Reformed interpreters have held.
verseByVerse.note: Shur lay on the way to Egypt.

verseByVerse.quote: The angel of the LORD also said to her, "I will surely multiply your offspring so that they cannot be numbered for multitude." And the angel of the LORD said to her, "Behold, you are pregnant and shall bear a son. You shall call his name Ishmael, because the LORD has listened to your affliction. He shall be a wild donkey of a man, his hand against everyone and everyone's hand against him, and he shall dwell over against all his kinsmen."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God gives Hagar a promise of countless offspring and a son whose name will always remind her that the LORD heard her misery, a son who will be free and untamed, living at odds with his neighbours.

I will surely multiply your offspring. The promise to Hagar echoes the one given to Abram (13:16; 15:5). The angel speaks in the first person, “I will”, as only God can.

You shall call his name Ishmael. Ishmael means “God hears”. “Because the LORD has listened to your affliction”: the word “affliction” comes from the same root as Sarai’s harsh treatment (v. 6). The suffering inflicted on her in Abram’s house did not go unheard. Every time she called her son, she would be saying what God had done.

A wild donkey of a man. The wild donkey roamed the desert, free and impossible to tame (Job 39:5–8). Ishmael will be free, untamed and independent, a man of the open country, not anyone’s slave as his mother was. It is not simply an insult. But it also foretells conflict: “his hand against everyone and everyone’s hand against him.” Ishmael’s descendants became the desert tribes south and east of Israel (25:12–18).

God cares for the outsider. The promise is given to an outsider: an Egyptian, a slave, a woman with no standing. God cares for Hagar too. Later, when she and her son are sent away, God hears again: “God has heard the voice of the boy where he is” (21:17). The God who chose Abraham’s family never stopped caring for those outside it, and in Christ his blessing reaches “all the families of the earth” (12:3).

Uncertain wording. “He shall dwell over against all his kinsmen” could mean “alongside”, “in defiance of” or “to the east of” his relatives; the Hebrew phrase allows each. The ESV keeps the ambiguity. It may suggest both: Ishmael’s people would live near their kin, to the east, and often in conflict with them.
verseByVerse.note: The promise to Hagar echoes the one given to Abram (13:16; 15:5).

verseByVerse.quote: So she called the name of the LORD who spoke to her, "You are a God of seeing," for she said, "Truly here I have seen him who looks after me." Therefore the well was called Beer-lahai-roi; it lies between Kadesh and Bered. And Hagar bore Abram a son, and Abram called the name of his son, whom Hagar bore, Ishmael. Abram was eighty-six years old when Hagar bore Ishmael to Abram.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hagar names the LORD “a God of seeing”, because the God who looks after her has met her; then she returns, bears Abram a son, and Abram names him Ishmael, as God had said.

The God who sees. In Hebrew, El Roi. Hagar is the only person in Scripture to give God a name, and she is a slave, an Egyptian, a social nobody. When no one else sees you, he does.

The hunger to be seen. Few things hurt like being invisible. The psychologist William James wrote that hardly any punishment could be crueller than to be turned loose in society and remain unnoticed by everyone in it. Our age has turned that hunger into an industry: we post, and count who saw, and the count never satisfies, because being watched is not the same as being seen. Hagar had no audience at all. She was a slave, a foreigner and a pawn in other people’s plans, and when she ran, nobody came after her, except God. Notice what kind of seeing it is. God does not look at her as a spectator scores a performance; she calls him the one “who looks after me”.

Seen in Christ. Jesus kept stopping for people the crowd never noticed, the woman who touched his cloak, the small man up a tree, and he told his disciples that their “Father who sees in secret” (Matthew 6:4) is enough. If the One whose opinion matters most sees you with kindness, you can stop performing for everyone else.

Beer-lahai-roi … between Kadesh and Bered. The spring was named for what happened there, and it was still known in Israel’s day; Isaac later lived near it (24:62; 25:11). Bered is otherwise unknown.

Abram called the name of his son … Ishmael. Hagar went back, and she must have told Abram what God had said, for he gives the boy the name God chose. God’s word to a slave woman directs the head of the household.

Eighty-six years old. Abram was seventy-five when he left Harran (12:4). Thirteen more years will pass before God speaks of the promised son again (17:1). Ishmael is a real son, loved and blessed, but he is not the child of promise.

Ishmael and Islam. Muslim tradition traces the Arabs, and Muhammad, to Ishmael. God’s promise of blessing to Ishmael was real (17:20), but the covenant line is through Isaac (17:21), and the promise of blessing for all nations is fulfilled in Christ, offered to Ishmael’s children as to Isaac’s.

Uncertain wording. The end of v. 13 is very compressed in Hebrew, and it can be understood in several ways: “Truly here I have seen him who looks after me” (ESV); or, as a question, have I really seen the One who sees me?; or, with a small change to the Hebrew, have I seen God and remained alive after seeing him? What is clear is that Hagar knows she has been seen by God, and that she has, in some way, seen him.
verseByVerse.note: “Beer-lahai-roi” means the well of the Living One who sees me (ESV note).

16.theology:
The Two Sons as Allegory. In Galatians 4:21–31 Hagar and Ishmael stand for the covenant of Sinai treated as a way to earn righteousness by keeping the law, which is slavery; Sarah and Isaac stand for the covenant of promise and the freedom of the children of grace. Those who seek to be justified by law are slaves, not sons; those who trust the promise are free heirs.

The God Who Sees the Overlooked. The God of Israel is also the God of the outsider, the slave and the forgotten. He "lifts the needy from the ash heap" (Ps. 113:7); the prophets rebuke Israel for forgetting the widow, the orphan and the foreigner; and Jesus' ministry turns again and again to those whom society counted as nobodies.
16.examples:
Then: Surrogacy through a female slave was legally recognised in the ancient Near East (the Code of Hammurabi and the Nuzi tablets record it). Sarai's contemporaries would have seen reasonable problem-solving; Genesis quietly calls it a failure of faith.

Now: Many Christians have grown impatient with God's timing and put their own solution in place: a decision that got ahead of his leading, a strategy that substituted cleverness for his direction. Such solutions bring their own conflicts, and calling our own plan God’s will does not make it the promised child. Yet God did not abandon Ishmael or Hagar, and he does not abandon us in the consequences of our shortcuts; he meets us in them. And the God who found Hagar in the wilderness still sees what no one else notices.

keyVerse.quote: So she called the name of the LORD who spoke to her, “You are a God of seeing,” for she said, “Truly here I have seen him who looks after me.”
keyVerse.note: In a chapter full of human scheming and cruelty, the one person everyone else used and then drove away is the one who meets God and gives him a name. The God of Abraham is not only the God of the chosen family but the God who sees the overlooked slave, and his seeing is care, not mere watching. In Christ that same God came looking for the lost and the unnoticed.

16.reflection:
Sarai and Abram tried to bring about God’s promise by a method their culture accepted (vv. 1–3). Where are you tempted to force an outcome God has promised, or that you want, by your own methods? How can you tell the difference between wise action and impatient grasping?

Trace how the shortcut went wrong: contempt, blame, passivity, harshness, flight (vv. 4–6). Which of these do you recognise in yourself when things go badly, and what would it have looked like for Abram to act rightly here?

The angel of the LORD sought Hagar out and asked her, “where have you come from and where are you going?” (v. 8). How would you answer those questions today? What does it mean to you that God comes looking for people before they look for him?

Hagar calls God “a God of seeing” (v. 13). Who in your church, workplace or neighbourhood is easily overlooked, and how could you share God’s way of seeing them?

17.title: Walk Before Me and Be Blameless
17.text: <sup>1</sup>When Abram was ninety-nine years old the LORD appeared to Abram and said to him, "I am God Almighty; walk before me, and be blameless,<sup>2</sup>that I may make my covenant between me and you, and may multiply you greatly."<sup>3</sup>Then Abram fell on his face.
