And God said to him,<sup>4</sup>"Behold, my covenant is with you, and you shall be the father of a multitude of nations.<sup>5</sup>No longer shall your name be called Abram, but your name shall be Abraham, for I have made you the father of a multitude of nations.<sup>6</sup>I will make you exceedingly fruitful, and I will make you into nations, and kings shall come from you.<sup>7</sup>And I will establish my covenant between me and you and your offspring after you throughout their generations for an everlasting covenant, to be God to you and to your offspring after you.<sup>8</sup>And I will give to you and to your offspring after you the land of your sojournings, all the land of Canaan, for an everlasting possession, and I will be their God."<sup>9</sup>And God said to Abraham, "As for you, you shall keep my covenant, you and your offspring after you throughout their generations.<sup>10</sup>This is my covenant, which you shall keep, between me and you and your offspring after you: Every male among you shall be circumcised.<sup>11</sup>You shall be circumcised in the flesh of your foreskins, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and you.<sup>12</sup>He who is eight days old among you shall be circumcised. Every male throughout your generations, whether born in your house or bought with your money from any foreigner who is not of your offspring,<sup>13</sup>both he who is born in your house and he who is bought with your money, shall surely be circumcised. So shall my covenant be in your flesh an everlasting covenant.<sup>14</sup>Any uncircumcised male who is not circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin shall be cut off from his people; he has broken my covenant."<sup>15</sup>And God said to Abraham, "As for Sarai your wife, you shall not call her name Sarai, but Sarah shall be her name.<sup>16</sup>I will bless her, and moreover, I will give you a son by her. I will bless her, and she shall become nations; kings of peoples shall come from her."<sup>17</sup>Then Abraham fell on his face and laughed and said to himself, "Shall a child be born to a man who is a hundred years old? Shall Sarah, who is ninety years old, bear a child?"<sup>18</sup>And Abraham said to God, "Oh that Ishmael might live before you!"<sup>19</sup>God said, "No, but Sarah your wife shall bear you a son, and you shall call his name Isaac. I will establish my covenant with him as an everlasting covenant for his offspring after him.<sup>20</sup>As for Ishmael, I have heard you; behold, I have blessed him and will make him fruitful and multiply him greatly. He shall father twelve princes, and I will make him into a great nation.<sup>21</sup>But I will establish my covenant with Isaac, whom Sarah shall bear to you at this time next year."<sup>22</sup>When he had finished talking with him, God went up from Abraham.<sup>23</sup>Then Abraham took Ishmael his son and all those born in his house or bought with his money, every male among the men of Abraham's house, and he circumcised the flesh of their foreskins that very day, as God had said to him.<sup>24</sup>Abraham was ninety-nine years old when he was circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin.<sup>25</sup>And Ishmael his son was thirteen years old when he was circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin.<sup>26</sup>That very day Abraham and his son Ishmael were circumcised.<sup>27</sup>And all the men of his house, those born in the house and those bought with money from a foreigner, were circumcised with him.
17.overview:
Where we are. Thirteen years have passed since Hagar bore Ishmael (16:16), the heir Abram and Sarai had tried to secure by their own plan, and heaven has been silent. Now, with Abram ninety-nine and Sarai long past bearing, the LORD appears again.

The message. God Almighty binds himself in an everlasting covenant to be God to Abraham and to his offspring, and he will keep that promise by his own power, not by human contrivance. The heir will not be the son Abraham arranged but a son Sarah herself will bear, within a year, against all nature. God puts his promise into new names and a sign in the flesh, and he calls the man who receives it to live his whole life before his face.

Why it was said. Israel in the wilderness (see the introduction) bore this sign, and the chapter told them what it meant: not that they had earned God, but that he had claimed them by promise and called them to walk before him wholeheartedly. It also explained why Ishmael’s descendants, their desert neighbours, were blessed by God and yet were not the covenant people.

How the chapter makes its case. God names himself and calls Abram to walk before him (vv. 1–3). He sets out his side: nations, kings, a new name, the land, and above all himself as God to Abraham’s offspring for ever (vv. 4–8). Then Abraham’s side: every male is to bear the sign of circumcision (vv. 9–14). Then Sarah: a new name and the promise that she will bear the son (vv. 15–18). Abraham laughs and pleads for Ishmael; God blesses Ishmael but fixes the covenant on Isaac (vv. 19–22). Abraham obeys that very day (vv. 23–27).

Where it leads. To Christ by covenant and by promise. The heart of the covenant, “to be God to you and to your offspring after you” (v. 7), runs through Scripture to its last page, where “he will dwell with them, and they will be his people” (Revelation 21:3). The offspring to whom the promises were made is, as Paul says, one, “who is Christ” (Galatians 3:16), and through him the father of a multitude gains children from every nation (Romans 4:16–17). Circumcision pointed beyond itself to the heart circumcised by the Spirit and to “the circumcision of Christ” (Colossians 2:11), the Son cut off for his people. And a son born from a body “as good as dead” (Romans 4:19) points to the God who raises the dead.

For us. Your standing with God rests on his promise, not your arrangements, so stop trying to secure by your own schemes what only he can give. And the God who has made you his calls you to live all of life before his face, not flawlessly but wholeheartedly, trusting Christ’s blameless life in your place.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God confirms his covenant with Abram, renames him Abraham and gives the covenant its sign. He first names himself God Almighty and calls Abram to walk before him blameless (vv. 1–3). Then he sets out what he will do: make Abraham the father of a multitude of nations and of kings, be God to him and his offspring for ever, and give them Canaan (vv. 4–8). Finally he tells Abraham what he must do: circumcise every male of his household, from infants of eight days to slaves bought from foreigners, as the sign of the covenant in their flesh (vv. 9–14). The word “covenant” comes again and again, and the order matters: God’s promise first, then the life that answers it.
verseByVerse.theology: God promises to be God to Abraham and his offspring, and gives circumcision as the sign of the covenant, for every male of the household at eight days old.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel's sign was in the flesh, but it always pointed beyond the flesh. Now: no outward rite can supply the circumcised heart God looks for (Rom. 2:28–29).

verseByVerse.quote: When Abram was ninety-nine years old the LORD appeared to Abram and said to him, "I am God Almighty; walk before me, and be blameless, that I may make my covenant between me and you, and may multiply you greatly." Then Abram fell on his face. And God said to him,
verseByVerse.commentary:
After thirteen years of silence God reveals himself as God Almighty and calls Abram to live his whole life in his presence with an undivided heart, so that God may carry out the covenant he has promised.

When Abram was ninety-nine years old. He was eighty-six when Ishmael was born (16:16), and thirteen years pass without a word from God. Abram may have settled into thinking Ishmael was the answer. God lets the human solution run its course and speaks when only he can fulfil the promise: Abram is ninety-nine and Sarai eighty-nine.

I am God Almighty. The Hebrew is El Shaddai, the first time the name appears in the Bible. It belongs especially to the age of the patriarchs (28:3; 35:11; 48:3), and God later tells Moses, “I appeared to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, as God Almighty” (Exodus 6:3). In Genesis it comes again and again where God promises to make his people fruitful against all odds, and so it fits this moment exactly: the God who speaks is able to give a child to the dead womb of an old woman.

Walk before me, and be blameless. To walk before someone is to live in his sight, as a servant goes about his master’s business with his master watching. Enoch and Noah walked with God (5:22, 24; 6:9). “Blameless” (tamim) means whole, complete, with integrity; the same word describes a sacrificial animal without blemish, and Noah was “blameless in his generation” (6:9). It is not sinless perfection, but a life wholly given to God, not divided between God and other loyalties. After the Hagar scheme, the call is pointed: no more half-trust.

That I may make my covenant. The covenant was made in chapter 15, when God passed alone between the pieces; here he confirms it and puts it into effect. God speaks his name first and the command follows: the obedience he asks is the shape of life with a God who has already bound himself, not the price of his favour. Yet it is no bare promise: God gives himself, and he claims the whole man in return.

Abram fell on his face. He bows to the ground in awe and worship, and he stays there while God speaks (v. 3; again v. 17). This is the right posture before the God of the impossible.

The blameless one. No son of Abraham ever walked before God perfectly blameless, Abraham included, as chapter 20 will show. One did. Jesus said of his Father, “I always do the things that are pleasing to him” (John 8:29), and he offered himself as the Lamb “without blemish or spot” (1 Peter 1:19). His obedience is counted to all who trust him: “For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God” (2 Corinthians 5:21). And his Spirit now enables his people to “walk by the Spirit” (Galatians 5:16), so that the call to Abram becomes possible for us, not to earn God’s favour, but because we already have it.

Living before his face. Walking before God means no part of life is hidden from him: the private screen, the tax return, the tone of voice at home. For those who know him as God Almighty that is a comfort, not a threat: the one who sees everything can also do anything. If you have run ahead of him, as Abram did with Hagar, the way back is the same: fall on your face, hear his promise again, and start walking.

What it does not mean. “Be blameless” does not mean that only the sinless can belong to God, or that God keeps his covenant only as long as we keep ours perfectly. Abraham will fail again (chapter 20), and God does not cancel the covenant. Wholehearted is not the same as flawless.

Uncertain wording. The meaning of Shaddai is uncertain. Suggestions include a link with a word for “mountain” (God as the mighty one, like a mountain), with the Hebrew word for “breasts” (God as the giver of fruitfulness, compare 49:25), or with a phrase meaning “the one who is sufficient”. None is certain. The traditional rendering “Almighty” follows ancient translations, and it fits how the name is used: the God who is able to do what he promises.
verseByVerse.note: The meaning of Shaddai is uncertain; “Almighty” follows the ancient translations.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, my covenant is with you, and you shall be the father of a multitude of nations. No longer shall your name be called Abram, but your name shall be Abraham, for I have made you the father of a multitude of nations. I will make you exceedingly fruitful, and I will make you into nations, and kings shall come from you. And I will establish my covenant between me and you and your offspring after you throughout their generations for an everlasting covenant, to be God to you and to your offspring after you. And I will give to you and to your offspring after you the land of your sojournings, all the land of Canaan, for an everlasting possession, and I will be their God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God spells out his side of the covenant: Abraham will be the father of a multitude of nations and of kings, God will be God to him and his offspring for ever, and Canaan will be their everlasting possession; and he seals it with a new name.

Behold, my covenant is with you. In Hebrew v. 4 begins with an emphatic “As for me”, and the chapter is built on it: first what God will do (vv. 4–8), then “As for you” (v. 9), then “As for Sarai” (v. 15). God’s side comes first and is by far the largest.

Your name shall be Abraham. Abram means “exalted father”, a name that must have stung a childless man; Abraham sounds like the Hebrew for “father of a multitude”. A name given by God marks a new identity and calling, as when Jacob becomes Israel (32:28) and Simon becomes Peter (Matthew 16:18). Every time anyone addressed him, Abraham heard God’s promise, and he had to introduce himself as “father of a multitude” while he had one son, by a slave woman.

For I have made you. God speaks of the promise as already done, for he “gives life to the dead and calls into existence the things that do not exist” (Romans 4:17).

Nations, and kings shall come from you. In a first sense this came true in Abraham’s many descendants: Israel, the Ishmaelites (25:12–18), the Edomites through Esau (chapter 36), and the peoples descended from Keturah (25:1–4). Kings came from him in Israel, above all David. But the New Testament sees a larger fulfilment. Abraham is “the father of us all”, Jew and Gentile alike, who share his faith (Romans 4:16), and the King who comes from him is the Messiah.

An everlasting covenant, to be God to you. Here is the heart of the covenant, and of every covenant God makes: not first the land or the children, but God himself. “I will be their God” (v. 8) is repeated through the whole Bible (Exodus 6:7; Jeremiah 31:33) until its final fulfilment: “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God” (Revelation 21:3). The promise is also for Abraham’s “offspring after you throughout their generations”: God’s purpose reaches beyond one lifetime.

The land of your sojournings. Abraham lived in Canaan as a foreigner; the only land he ever owned there was a burial cave (chapter 23). The promise of “all the land of Canaan” as “an everlasting possession” was fulfilled in Joshua’s day (Joshua 21:43–45), yet the patriarchs were looking further: “he was looking forward to the city that has foundations, whose designer and builder is God” (Hebrews 11:10). Paul can even call Abraham “heir of the world” (Romans 4:13).

Every promise, Yes in Christ. The offspring to whom the promises were made, Paul says, is not many but one, “who is Christ” (Galatians 3:16), and those who belong to him are “Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to promise” (Galatians 3:29). So the father of a multitude gains children in every nation as the gospel goes out, and “to be God to you” is what Christ calls eternal life: to know “the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17:3). Abraham’s name was given when his family was almost nothing; it is being filled out today wherever someone believes.

Named by God. God tells Abraham who he is before Abraham sees any evidence. Christians are named in the same way: “child of God”, “saint”, “beloved”, while still struggling and unfinished. Live by the name God gives you, not by the evidence of your feelings or your past.

Where Christians differ: the land. Dispensational Christians hold that “everlasting possession” requires a future possession of Canaan by the nation of Israel, often in a coming millennial kingdom, and some see the modern state of Israel as part of that fulfilment. Others read the land promise as fulfilled in Joshua’s day and enlarged in Christ to the whole renewed earth. This commentary’s view: the land promise was fulfilled under Joshua and points to the whole new earth that Abraham’s children in Christ will inherit (Romans 4:13; Matthew 5:5); the modern state is not the fulfilment of these promises, though Christians should love the Jewish people and pray for their salvation.
verseByVerse.note: Abram means “exalted father”; Abraham means “father of a multitude” (ESV notes).

verseByVerse.quote: And God said to Abraham, "As for you, you shall keep my covenant, you and your offspring after you throughout their generations. This is my covenant, which you shall keep, between me and you and your offspring after you: Every male among you shall be circumcised. You shall be circumcised in the flesh of your foreskins, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and you. He who is eight days old among you shall be circumcised. Every male throughout your generations, whether born in your house or bought with your money from any foreigner who is not of your offspring, both he who is born in your house and he who is bought with your money, shall surely be circumcised. So shall my covenant be in your flesh an everlasting covenant. Any uncircumcised male who is not circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin shall be cut off from his people; he has broken my covenant."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abraham and his offspring are to keep the covenant by bearing its sign: every male in the household, from infants of eight days to slaves bought from foreigners, is to be circumcised, and a male who refuses it has broken the covenant and is cut off.

As for you, you shall keep my covenant. To keep the covenant is not to earn it but to guard and honour it, receiving the sign God gives and living as one who belongs to him. God has already made the promises; this is the response of the people who receive them.

Every male among you shall be circumcised. Circumcision, the removal of the foreskin, was known among Israel’s neighbours, Egypt included (Jeremiah 9:25–26), usually as a rite at puberty or before marriage. What is new is its meaning: “a sign of the covenant between me and you” (v. 11). The rainbow was set in the sky (9:12–17); this sign is set in the body, on the organ of generation, in a covenant all about offspring. After the Hagar scheme it was a lasting reminder that the promised seed would come by God’s gift, not human strength, and that every child of the family belonged to God.

He who is eight days old. In infancy, before the child could do or understand anything: the sign spoke of God’s claim and promise, not the child’s achievement. The eighth day followed the mother’s seven days of uncleanness after childbirth (Leviticus 12:2–3).

Born in your house or bought with your money. The household included servants and slaves, and they too received the sign, even “any foreigner who is not of your offspring”. From the start the covenant family was not a closed race: outsiders could be brought in. This is a first glimpse of the nations who would come in through Abraham’s greater offspring.

Cut off from his people. In Hebrew there is a grim play on words: covenants were “cut”, the foreskin was cut, and the one who refused to be cut would be “cut off”. To despise the sign was to despise the God who gave it: “he has broken my covenant.” Being cut off meant exclusion from the covenant people, and probably death at God’s hand; God came close to putting Moses to death for neglecting to circumcise his son (Exodus 4:24–26).

A circumcised heart. Even in the Old Testament the sign pointed beyond the flesh. Moses commanded, “Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart” (Deuteronomy 10:16), and promised that God himself would do it (Deuteronomy 30:6). Paul draws the line out: “circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit, not by the letter” (Romans 2:29). And he insists that Abraham was counted righteous before he was circumcised: “He received the sign of circumcision as a seal of the righteousness that he had by faith while he was still uncircumcised” (Romans 4:11). The sign followed faith; it did not create it.

The circumcision of Christ. Jesus was circumcised on the eighth day (Luke 2:21), placed under the covenant and its law for his people. Paul tells believers that “in him also you were circumcised with a circumcision made without hands, by putting off the body of the flesh, by the circumcision of Christ” (Colossians 2:11). Many take this “circumcision of Christ” to be his death: the covenant curse of being cut off fell on him, for “he was cut off out of the land of the living” (Isaiah 53:8), so that his people might never be cut off. Through him the sign is fulfilled, and outward circumcision no longer counts before God: “For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything, but only faith working through love” (Galatians 5:6).

Is circumcision required today? No. The apostles decided that Gentile believers must not be required to be circumcised (Acts 15), and Paul warned that to make it necessary for salvation was to abandon grace (Galatians 5:2–4). Whether parents circumcise a son for medical or family reasons is a matter of Christian liberty; it has no spiritual weight either way.

Where Christians differ: circumcision and baptism. Paedobaptists (Presbyterians and many others) argue that God’s covenant of grace has always included believers’ children, that baptism is the New Testament counterpart of circumcision (Colossians 2:11–12), and that infants of believers should therefore receive it, as Abraham’s sons received the sign. Credobaptists reply that the Abrahamic covenant had two strands, a physical family marked by circumcision and a spiritual offspring of faith, and that the new covenant is made with those who know the Lord (Jeremiah 31:34), so its sign belongs to those who profess faith. This commentary’s view: credobaptist, following the 1689 Confession’s reading of the covenants as less continuous than Westminster’s: baptism is for believers. Paedobaptists are honoured brothers in the Reformed tradition, and Christians differ here in good conscience.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–27 — Sarah's New Name and the Promise of Isaac
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The promise reaches its sharpest point: not merely an heir, but a son from Sarah herself, named in advance and due within a year. God renames Sarai as Sarah, mother of nations and kings (vv. 15–16). Abraham falls on his face and laughs at the thought of parents aged a hundred and ninety, and asks that Ishmael might be enough (vv. 17–18). God answers with patience and firmness: Ishmael will be blessed and become a great nation, but the covenant goes on through Isaac (vv. 19–22). The section closes with Abraham’s prompt obedience: that very day he, Ishmael and every male in his house are circumcised (vv. 23–27).
verseByVerse.theology: Sarai becomes Sarah. Abraham laughs and pleads for Ishmael; God blesses Ishmael but establishes his covenant with Isaac, and that same day Abraham circumcises his whole household.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul says Abraham did not weaken in faith though he considered his body as good as dead (Rom. 4:19). Now: God may refuse what we ask for someone and still bless that person, as he blessed Ishmael.

verseByVerse.quote: And God said to Abraham, "As for Sarai your wife, you shall not call her name Sarai, but Sarah shall be her name. I will bless her, and moreover, I will give you a son by her. I will bless her, and she shall become nations; kings of peoples shall come from her." Then Abraham fell on his face and laughed and said to himself, "Shall a child be born to a man who is a hundred years old? Shall Sarah, who is ninety years old, bear a child?" And Abraham said to God, "Oh that Ishmael might live before you!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God renames Sarai as Sarah and promises that she herself will bear Abraham a son and become the mother of nations and kings; Abraham bows, laughs inwardly at the impossibility, and asks God to let Ishmael be the heir.

Sarah shall be her name. Sarah receives a new name too. Sarai and Sarah are two forms of a word meaning “princess”; the change marks a new beginning and a royal destiny: “kings of peoples shall come from her.” She is not a bystander in the covenant. For the first time the promise names her as the mother of the heir, and the plan of chapter 16 is set aside.

I will bless her … she shall become nations. Twice God says “I will bless her.” The barren woman who had given up and given her servant to her husband (16:2) is to be the mother of the promised line.

Abraham fell on his face and laughed. He bows in reverence and laughs “to himself”, doing the sums: a father of a hundred, a mother of ninety. Was it the laugh of faith or of doubt? Probably something of both: wonder that God should say such a thing, and an honest sense of how impossible it was. God does not rebuke him, as he will question Sarah’s laughter (18:13), but his next words show that he is not yet expecting what God has promised.

Oh that Ishmael might live before you! This is a father’s love for the boy he has raised for thirteen years, and it is a real prayer. But it also settles for less. Abraham asks God to bless the son he has already got rather than give the son God has promised. Ishmael is real and loved; he is also the fruit of a plan made without God.

Faith that grows. Paul describes Abraham’s faith in these years: “He did not weaken in faith when he considered his own body, which was as good as dead (since he was about a hundred years old), or when he considered the barrenness of Sarah’s womb” (Romans 4:19). Abraham looked squarely at the facts and laughed, and yet he went on believing. Faith is not pretending that the obstacles are small; it is trusting that God is greater.

A son from a body as good as dead. God chose to give the son of promise only when it was impossible, so that the child would be plainly his gift. Paul draws the line to the gospel: the faith that trusted God to bring life from Abraham’s and Sarah’s bodies is the same faith that believes “in him who raised from the dead Jesus our Lord” (Romans 4:24). The God of Isaac’s birth is the God of the empty tomb.

For us. We often pray as Abraham did, asking God to bless what we have arranged. It is not wrong to love what we have, or to pray for it, and God hears such prayers (v. 20). But faith learns to want what God has promised more than what we have managed, and to let him do it his way.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that both forms of the name mean “princess.”

verseByVerse.quote: God said, "No, but Sarah your wife shall bear you a son, and you shall call his name Isaac. I will establish my covenant with him as an everlasting covenant for his offspring after him. As for Ishmael, I have heard you; behold, I have blessed him and will make him fruitful and multiply him greatly. He shall father twelve princes, and I will make him into a great nation. But I will establish my covenant with Isaac, whom Sarah shall bear to you at this time next year." When he had finished talking with him, God went up from Abraham.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God refuses to transfer the promise to Ishmael: Sarah will bear a son called Isaac within a year, and the covenant will continue through him; yet God hears Abraham’s prayer and promises Ishmael a great blessing of his own.

No, but Sarah your wife shall bear you a son. God gently overrules the prayer of v. 18. The heir will be Sarah’s son, and God names him before he is conceived.

You shall call his name Isaac. Isaac means “he laughs”. God takes Abraham’s laughter and turns it into the boy’s name, so that every time the parents called Isaac, they would remember that they had laughed at the impossible and God had done it. Sarah will say at his birth, “God has made laughter for me” (21:6).

I will establish my covenant with him. The covenant passes to Isaac and his offspring by God’s free choice, not by birth order or by Abraham’s preference. Paul draws on this: “not all are children of Abraham because they are his offspring, but “Through Isaac shall your offspring be named”” (Romans 9:7). The children of promise are counted as offspring (Romans 9:8).

As for Ishmael, I have heard you. There is a play on Ishmael’s name, which means “God hears” (16:11). God hears again. Ishmael receives a rich blessing: fruitfulness, twelve princes (listed in 25:13–16, a counterpart to Jacob’s twelve sons) and a great nation. God is kind to those outside the covenant line, and his ear is open to a father praying for his son.

At this time next year. After twenty-four years of waiting since the first promise (12:4), God now sets a date. The promise is not vague: God works to an appointed time.

God went up from Abraham. The appearance ends as it began, by God’s initiative (compare 35:13). Abraham has not climbed up to God; God has come down to him and now returns.

The son of promise. The covenant goes forward through a son who is born at God’s appointed time, by God’s power, named before his birth and bringing laughter to his parents. All of that is a pattern of a greater birth. “When the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son, born of woman, born under the law” (Galatians 4:4), named before his birth (Luke 1:31), the true offspring of Abraham in whom the covenant is established for ever. And Paul tells believers, “Now you, brothers, like Isaac, are children of promise” (Galatians 4:28): we belong to God not by natural birth or effort, but by his promise and his power.

Blessing and covenant. God’s generous blessing on Ishmael shows that God does good to many who are not his covenant people, in common kindness, children and prosperity. But such blessing is not the same as salvation. Earthly blessing is real, but only the promise in Christ brings a person into the covenant.

Where are Ishmael’s descendants today? Genesis places Ishmael’s sons among the peoples of the northern Arabian desert (25:13–18), and many Arab peoples have traditionally traced their ancestry to him. Whatever the exact lines of descent, this chapter forbids contempt: God heard Ishmael’s father, blessed Ishmael, and the gospel is offered to his children as to all the nations (Isaiah 60:7).

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew word translated “No, but” (abal) can mark a contrast (“No, rather”) or a strong affirmation (“Truly” or “Yes, indeed”). The ESV reads it as gently correcting Abraham’s wish for Ishmael; some other translations read “Yes, but” or “Indeed”, as God confirming the promise Abraham had laughed at. The sense is the same either way: Sarah, not Hagar, will bear the heir.
verseByVerse.note: The twelve princes are listed in 25:13–16.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Abraham took Ishmael his son and all those born in his house or bought with his money, every male among the men of Abraham's house, and he circumcised the flesh of their foreskins that very day, as God had said to him. Abraham was ninety-nine years old when he was circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin. And Ishmael his son was thirteen years old when he was circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin. That very day Abraham and his son Ishmael were circumcised. And all the men of his house, those born in the house and those bought with money from a foreigner, were circumcised with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abraham obeys at once and completely: that very day he, his son Ishmael and every male of his household receive the covenant sign.

That very day. There is no delay and no negotiation. Abraham had laughed in v. 17; now he acts. The narrator repeats the details (his age, Ishmael’s age, “that very day”, all the men of his house) to underline that he did exactly “as God had said to him”. At ninety-nine, the rite was painful and humbling, and it involved every man who depended on him.

Ishmael his son was thirteen years old. Ishmael is circumcised too and so belongs to Abraham’s household. Yet he is not the heir of the covenant (vv. 19–21). The sign is given, but the sign does not make anyone a child of promise. As Paul says, “not all who are descended from Israel belong to Israel” (Romans 9:6).

All the men of his house. Servants born in the house and slaves bought from foreigners receive the sign with their master. Abraham’s faith shapes his whole household (compare 18:19).

Obedience that answers grace. Abraham’s quick obedience is the fruit of his faith, not a payment for the promise; it is what James means when he says faith is shown by works (James 2:22). It points ahead to the one Son of Abraham whose whole life was prompt and perfect obedience: “Behold, I have come to do your will, O God” (Hebrews 10:7). Because he obeyed in our place, our obedience can be the glad answer of children, not the anxious labour of servants trying to earn a place.

For us. When God’s word is clear, delayed obedience is a quiet form of disobedience. And Ishmael’s circumcision is a warning against trusting an outward sign. Baptism, church membership and Christian upbringing are good gifts, but none of them alone makes a person a child of promise: “circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit, not by the letter” (Romans 2:29). Ask whether you trust the promise itself, Christ, and not only the sign.

17.theology:
Covenant Sign and Seal. Circumcision was a permanent mark of belonging in the body, given before the child could do anything. Paul calls it a sign (pointing to the righteousness of faith) and a seal (confirming what faith has received), not the thing itself. The Reformers used this to explain baptism as the sign and seal of the new covenant. Baptists agree, but give it only to those who profess faith, the view this commentary takes (see on vv. 9–14).

The God Who Renames. God renames Jacob, Simon and Saul as well. The new name does not describe what the person is now; it declares what God will make of him, spoken before it is lived out: "I will give him a white stone, with a new name written on the stone that no one knows except the one who receives it" (Rev. 2:17). We are most truly who God says we are.
17.examples:
Then: Thirteen years pass between 16:16 and 17:1 without a word. Israel knew that pattern of long silence and then a fuller promise: silence in Egypt, then the burning bush; silence in exile, then the return. God's silence is not absence.

Now: "Walk before me, and be blameless" (v. 1) sums up the Christian life: not occasional acts of obedience but a life lived in the continual awareness of God's presence, before his face. Such a person does not need an audience for virtue, because the one who sees everything is always there. And Abraham's laughter (v. 17) gives permission for an honest response to grace: the promise is so good it seems laughable, and God is not offended.

keyVerse.quote: And I will establish my covenant between me and you and your offspring after you throughout their generations for an everlasting covenant, to be God to you and to your offspring after you.
keyVerse.note: This is the heart of the covenant and of the chapter: before land, children or kings, God promises himself. The words “I will be their God” run through the whole Bible until they are fulfilled when God dwells with his people in the new creation (Revelation 21:3), and they come to us through Abraham’s one offspring, Christ (Galatians 3:16, 29).

17.reflection:
God waited thirteen years after Ishmael’s birth and then introduced himself as “God Almighty” (v. 1; compare 16:16). Where have you tried to secure by your own plans something only God can give, and what does this name of God say to that?

“Walk before me, and be blameless” (v. 1). What would it look like for you to live more consciously in God’s presence this week? How does Christ’s blameless life in our place change the way we hear that command?

Abraham received a new name before he saw any sign of it coming true (vv. 5, 15). What names does God give his people in Christ, and how can they shape the way you see yourself when the evidence seems against them?

Ishmael received the sign but not the covenant (vv. 19–25). What is the right place for outward signs such as baptism and church membership, and how can we make sure we are trusting the promise and not only the sign?

18.title: Is Anything Too Hard for the LORD?
18.text: <sup>1</sup>And the LORD appeared to him by the oaks of Mamre, as he sat at the door of his tent in the heat of the day.<sup>2</sup>He lifted up his eyes and looked, and behold, three men were standing in front of him. When he saw them, he ran from the tent door to meet them and bowed himself to the earth<sup>3</sup>and said, "O Lord, if I have found favor in your sight, do not pass by your servant.<sup>4</sup>Let a little water be brought, and wash your feet, and rest yourselves under the tree,<sup>5</sup>while I bring a morsel of bread, that you may refresh yourselves, and after that you may pass on— since you have come to your servant." So they said, "Do as you have said."<sup>6</sup>And Abraham went quickly into the tent to Sarah and said, "Quick! Three seahs of fine flour! Knead it, and make cakes."<sup>7</sup>And Abraham ran to the herd and took a calf, tender and good, and gave it to a young man, who prepared it quickly.<sup>8</sup>Then he took curds and milk and the calf that he had prepared, and set it before them. And he stood by them under the tree while they ate.<sup>9</sup>They said to him, "Where is Sarah your wife?" And he said, "She is in the tent."<sup>10</sup>The LORD said, "I will surely return to you about this time next year, and Sarah your wife shall have a son." And Sarah was listening at the tent door behind him.<sup>11</sup>Now Abraham and Sarah were old, advanced in years. The way of women had ceased to be with Sarah.<sup>12</sup>So Sarah laughed to herself, saying, "After I am worn out, and my lord is old, shall I have pleasure?"<sup>13</sup>The LORD said to Abraham, "Why did Sarah laugh and say, 'Shall I indeed bear a child, now that I am old?'<sup>14</sup>Is anything too hard for the LORD? At the appointed time I will return to you, about this time next year, and Sarah shall have a son."<sup>15</sup>But Sarah denied it, saying, "I did not laugh," for she was afraid. He said, "No, but you did laugh."<sup>16</sup>Then the men set out from there, and they looked down toward Sodom. And Abraham went with them to set them on their way.<sup>17</sup>The LORD said, "Shall I hide from Abraham what I am about to do,<sup>18</sup>seeing that Abraham shall surely become a great and mighty nation, and all the nations of the earth shall be blessed in him?<sup>19</sup>For I have chosen him, that he may command his children and his household after him to keep the way of the LORD by doing righteousness and justice, so that the LORD may bring to Abraham what he has promised him."<sup>20</sup>Then the LORD said, "Because the outcry against Sodom and Gomorrah is great and their sin is very grave,<sup>21</sup>I will go down to see whether they have done altogether according to the outcry that has come to me. And if not, I will know."<sup>22</sup>So the men turned from there and went toward Sodom, but Abraham still stood before the LORD.<sup>23</sup>Then Abraham drew near and said, "Will you indeed sweep away the righteous with the wicked?<sup>24</sup>Suppose there are fifty righteous within the city. Will you then sweep away the place and not spare it for the fifty righteous who are in it?<sup>25</sup>Far be it from you to do such a thing, to put the righteous to death with the wicked, so that the righteous fare as the wicked! Far be that from you! Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?"<sup>26</sup>And the LORD said, "If I find at Sodom fifty righteous in the city, I will spare the whole place for their sake."<sup>27</sup>Abraham answered and said, "Behold, I have undertaken to speak to the Lord, I who am but dust and ashes.<sup>28</sup>Suppose five of the fifty righteous are lacking. Will you destroy the whole city for lack of five?" And he said, "I will not destroy it if I find forty-five there."<sup>29</sup>Again he spoke to him and said, "Suppose forty are found there." He answered, "For the sake of forty I will not do it."<sup>30</sup>Then he said, "Oh let not the Lord be angry, and I will speak. Suppose thirty are found there." He answered, "I will not do it, if I find thirty there."<sup>31</sup>He said, "Behold, I have undertaken to speak to the Lord. Suppose twenty are found there." He answered, "For the sake of twenty I will not destroy it."<sup>32</sup>Then he said, "Oh let not the Lord be angry, and I will speak again but this once. Suppose ten are found there." He answered, "For the sake of ten I will not destroy it."<sup>33</sup>And the LORD went his way, when he had finished speaking to Abraham, and Abraham returned to his place.
18.overview:
Where we are. Only a short time has passed since God renamed Abraham and Sarah and promised a son “at this time next year” (17:21). Abraham is camped by the oaks of Mamre, near Hebron (13:18); his nephew Lot lives inside Sodom, down in the valley (13:12; 14:12).

The message. The LORD who comes to Abraham’s tent as a guest is the God for whom nothing is too hard and the Judge of all the earth who always does what is just. He gives life where there is none, and he judges evil only after full inquiry. And he draws his friend into his plans, so that Abraham’s prayer becomes part of how God works.

Why it was said. Israel was to be the people who would “keep the way of the LORD by doing righteousness and justice” (v. 19), and they were about to enter the land of the Canaanites, whose iniquity God had said he would judge when it was complete (15:16; see the introduction). They needed to know that God’s judgments are never careless, that he can keep his promises against all nature, and that he listens when his servants plead, as he listened to Moses.

How the chapter makes its case. Abraham runs to welcome three travellers and serves them a feast (vv. 1–8). They ask for Sarah, and the LORD promises her a son within the year; she laughs behind the tent door, and he answers, “Is anything too hard for the LORD?” (vv. 9–15). As the men leave, the LORD resolves to share with Abraham his plan for Sodom (vv. 16–21). Abraham stays before the LORD and pleads, from fifty righteous down to ten, appealing to the justice of the Judge of all the earth (vv. 22–33).

Where it leads. To Christ by the character of God revealed in him, and by pattern. The LORD who eats under Abraham’s tree foreshadows the Word who “became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). The question “Is anything too hard for the LORD?” is answered to Mary: “For nothing will be impossible with God” (Luke 1:37). And Abraham’s plea that the righteous should not die with the wicked is answered in the most unexpected way at the cross, where the one righteous man was “numbered with the transgressors” (Isaiah 53:12) so that the wicked might be spared, and where he now “always lives to make intercession” for his people (Hebrews 7:25).

For us. Bring God the promises you have stopped believing, for nothing he has promised is too hard for him. Trust his justice when the world’s evil seems unanswered. And pray for your city and your neighbours with Abraham’s mix of humility and boldness, because God delights to be asked.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — The Three Visitors and the Promise to Sarah
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The LORD comes to Abraham as a guest and renews the promise of a son, this time in Sarah’s hearing. Abraham, seeing three travellers in the midday heat, runs to welcome them and turns a promised morsel into a feast, standing by to serve while they eat (vv. 1–8). The visitors ask for Sarah by name, and the LORD promises that she will have a son by this time next year (vv. 9–10). Sarah, old and long past bearing, laughs to herself behind the tent door (vv. 11–12). The LORD, who hears her silent laughter, answers with the question at the heart of the chapter, “Is anything too hard for the LORD?”, and gently refuses her denial (vv. 13–15).
verseByVerse.theology: Abraham serves his guests a feast, standing by them as they eat. The LORD promises that Sarah will have a son by this time next year; Sarah laughs to herself and denies it.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Abraham's welcome is the pattern of hospitality the whole Bible commends. Now: God hears even the laugh of a hope long buried. He does not promise to grant every request, but nothing he has promised is beyond him.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD appeared to him by the oaks of Mamre, as he sat at the door of his tent in the heat of the day. He lifted up his eyes and looked, and behold, three men were standing in front of him. When he saw them, he ran from the tent door to meet them and bowed himself to the earth and said, "O Lord, if I have found favor in your sight, do not pass by your servant. Let a little water be brought, and wash your feet, and rest yourselves under the tree, while I bring a morsel of bread, that you may refresh yourselves, and after that you may pass on— since you have come to your servant." So they said, "Do as you have said."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD comes to Abraham’s tent in the form of three travellers, and Abraham, not yet knowing who they are, runs in the heat of the day to welcome them with generous hospitality.

The LORD appeared to him. The narrator tells us at once who the visitor is, but Abraham does not yet know. He sees only “three men”. The scene is set at the oaks of Mamre near Hebron, Abraham’s home for many years (13:18; 14:13), and “in the heat of the day”, the hour when everyone rests in the shade.

He ran from the tent door to meet them. A man of ninety-nine runs, which in that culture was hardly dignified for an elder, and bows to the ground. Desert hospitality was a sacred duty: travellers could die without water, shade and food, and a host was honoured to protect and refresh them. Abraham does far more than duty requires. He begs them not to pass by, as if they would be doing him a favour by stopping.

Let a little water be brought, and wash your feet. Washing the dust of the road from a guest’s sandalled feet was the first courtesy of welcome. Abraham modestly offers “a morsel of bread”; what he actually provides is a feast (vv. 6–8). “Since you have come to your servant” means: you have come my way, so let me serve you.

Three men were standing in front of him. The three are the LORD and two others whom the next chapter calls angels (19:1). Abraham addresses them sometimes as one and sometimes as all three, and later the LORD remains with Abraham while “the men” go on to Sodom (v. 22).

The God who comes as a guest. The Maker of heaven and earth comes to a nomad’s tent, sits under a tree and receives a meal. Here, long before Bethlehem, God takes on human form for a while to meet his friend. It is a foreshadowing of the day when “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14), and when that Word came to his own, his own people did not receive him (John 1:11). Abraham, without knowing it, welcomed the Lord; we are told plainly who knocks at our door.

Welcome the stranger. The New Testament draws on this scene: “Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers, for thereby some have entertained angels unawares” (Hebrews 13:2). Hospitality to strangers, the lonely, the newcomer at church, the overseas student, is not an optional extra for the naturally sociable; it is a reflection of God’s own welcome: “welcome one another as Christ has welcomed you, for the glory of God” (Romans 15:7). Use wisdom and keep your family safe, but do not let caution become an excuse for a closed door.

Where Christians differ: a picture of the Trinity? Many church fathers saw in the three visitors a revelation of the Trinity, and Rublev’s famous icon paints them so. Others note that the text clearly distinguishes the LORD from the two who go on to Sodom and are called angels (18:22; 19:1). This commentary’s view: the visitors are the LORD and two angels, and the LORD who appears in human form here is best understood, like the angel of the LORD (16:7–13), as the Son appearing before his incarnation. The Trinity is not pictured here, but the Son who would one day take flesh for good is already coming to meet his people.

Uncertain wording. In v. 3 Abraham’s address can be read either as “my lord”, a polite title for a human superior, or as “Lord”, the title used for God. The Hebrew letters allow both; the traditional Hebrew vowels read it as the divine title, and the ESV follows that, noting “my lord” as an alternative. Abraham may well have spoken more than he knew: he greeted an honoured guest, and it was in fact the Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: And Abraham went quickly into the tent to Sarah and said, "Quick! Three seahs of fine flour! Knead it, and make cakes." And Abraham ran to the herd and took a calf, tender and good, and gave it to a young man, who prepared it quickly. Then he took curds and milk and the calf that he had prepared, and set it before them. And he stood by them under the tree while they ate.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abraham turns his modest offer into a lavish feast, hurrying his whole household, and stands by as a servant while his guests eat; and the LORD himself eats at his table.

Quick! Three seahs of fine flour! The words tumble out: “went quickly”, “Quick!”, “ran”, “prepared it quickly”. Three seahs was a very large amount of flour (the ESV note gives about 22 litres), far more than three guests could eat, and fine flour was the best. Sarah kneads and bakes the bread herself.

A calf, tender and good. Herding people rarely killed their animals for meat; they lived on milk, curds and bread, and meat was for great occasions. To kill a choice calf for strangers was a royal welcome. Jesus’ parable uses the same gesture for a father’s joy: “bring the fattened calf and kill it, and let us eat and celebrate” (Luke 15:23).

He stood by them under the tree while they ate. The host does not sit with his guests but stands, ready to serve, as a servant waits at table. The great man of the region takes the servant’s place.

And the LORD eats. The text is plain: they ate. God took a real human form for this visit, not a vision or an illusion. The risen Jesus would do the same, taking broiled fish and eating it before his disciples to show that he was no ghost (Luke 24:42–43).

The guest who became the servant. At Mamre the Lord was served by Abraham. When he came in the flesh, he reversed the order: “For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45). He knelt to wash his disciples’ feet (John 13:5), and he still offers to be the guest of anyone who will open the door: “If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in to him and eat with him, and he with me” (Revelation 3:20). Abraham gave his best calf; Christ gave himself.

Generous and glad. Abraham’s hospitality is eager, costly and personal. Generosity does not wait to be asked twice, and it gives the best, not the leftovers. Notice too that the whole household works together, and that the head of the house serves rather than presides.
verseByVerse.note: Three seahs was about 23 quarts (22 liters) of flour (ESV note), a lavish meal.

verseByVerse.quote: They said to him, "Where is Sarah your wife?" And he said, "She is in the tent." The LORD said, "I will surely return to you about this time next year, and Sarah your wife shall have a son." And Sarah was listening at the tent door behind him. Now Abraham and Sarah were old, advanced in years. The way of women had ceased to be with Sarah. So Sarah laughed to herself, saying, "After I am worn out, and my lord is old, shall I have pleasure?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The visitors ask for Sarah by name, and the LORD promises that she will have a son by this time next year; Sarah, listening behind the tent door and long past childbearing, laughs to herself at the impossibility.

Where is Sarah your wife? Strangers know her name, and her new name at that. The question shows that the promise is meant for her ears too. Whatever Abraham had told her after chapter 17, she must hear it from the LORD himself.

I will surely return to you about this time next year. The visitor speaks as only God can: he will “return”, and Sarah will have a son. The promise of 17:21 is repeated, now in her hearing.

The way of women had ceased to be with Sarah. The narrator states the medical facts plainly: both are old, and Sarah has passed the menopause. There is no natural way this can happen.

After I am worn out … shall I have pleasure? The word “worn out” is used of old clothes. “Pleasure” is the delight of married love and perhaps the joy of a child; both seem long gone. Her laugh is not mockery but the laugh of a woman who has been disappointed too many times to hope again. Decades of barrenness, the humiliation with Hagar (16:4–5), and now this.

And my lord is old. Sarah speaks of Abraham respectfully, even in a private thought. Peter takes this as an example for Christian wives, “as Sarah obeyed Abraham, calling him lord” (1 Peter 3:6), and adds that they are her daughters when they do good and “do not fear anything that is frightening”.

Life from barrenness. Sarah is the first of a line of barren women in Scripture to whom God gives a son: Rebekah, Rachel, Hannah, Elizabeth. Each time God shows that the promised line depends on his power, not human fertility. The line reaches its climax when a virgin conceives, with no human father at all (Luke 1:34–35). The prophet even sings over Zion, “Sing, O barren one, who did not bear”, and Paul applies the song to the church, the free children of promise (Isaiah 54:1; Galatians 4:27).

For the weary. If you have stopped hoping because the disappointment has been long, notice that God comes to Sarah in her weariness. He does not wait for her to feel hopeful before he speaks his promise. What God says can revive a heart that has given up.

Uncertain wording. The phrase translated “about this time next year” (vv. 10, 14) is literally something like “according to the time of life”. Most take it to mean “when the season comes round again”, a year from now; some take it as “when the time of pregnancy is complete”. Either way it points to the birth within about a year (17:21).

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Abraham, "Why did Sarah laugh and say, 'Shall I indeed bear a child, now that I am old?' Is anything too hard for the LORD? At the appointed time I will return to you, about this time next year, and Sarah shall have a son." But Sarah denied it, saying, "I did not laugh," for she was afraid. He said, "No, but you did laugh."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD, who heard Sarah’s silent laugh, answers it with the question that rebukes all unbelief, “Is anything too hard for the LORD?”, sets a date for his promise, and gently but firmly refuses her frightened denial.

Why did Sarah laugh? She laughed “to herself” (v. 12), inside the tent, unseen. The visitor knows. He hears thoughts no human guest could hear, and by now Abraham must know who is at his table. Jewish interpreters noticed long ago that the LORD reports her words kindly: he repeats “now that I am old”, but leaves out her remark that “my lord is old”.

Is anything too hard for the LORD? The word means too wonderful, too extraordinary, beyond what is possible. The question is not asking for information; it calls Sarah, and every reader, to measure the promise by the power of the one who made it. It echoes through Scripture: Jeremiah prays, “Nothing is too hard for you” (Jeremiah 32:17), and God answers, “Is anything too hard for me?” (Jeremiah 32:27).

At the appointed time. God has a date in mind. His promises are not vague hopes but appointments he will keep.

I did not laugh … No, but you did laugh. Fear makes Sarah lie, and the LORD will not let the lie stand. But there is no anger, no punishment and no withdrawal of the promise: only the truth, spoken plainly. God corrects his children in order to restore them. And her laugh of unbelief will become a laugh of joy, for her son will be called “he laughs”, and she will say, “God has made laughter for me; everyone who hears will laugh over me” (21:6). In the end she believed: “By faith Sarah herself received power to conceive, even when she was past the age, since she considered him faithful who had promised” (Hebrews 11:11).

Nothing will be impossible with God. The angel Gabriel almost repeats this question to Mary, telling her of Elizabeth’s pregnancy in old age and of her own child: “For nothing will be impossible with God” (Luke 1:37). The God who gave a son to a woman of ninety gave his own Son through a virgin, and raised him from the dead. The deepest answer to “Is anything too hard for the LORD?” is the empty tomb.

What it does not mean. This question is not a promise that God will give us anything we ask if we only believe hard enough. It concerns what God has promised. Many faithful couples long for children and are not given them, and many sick believers are not healed in this life; that is not a sign of weak faith or of God’s displeasure. What God has promised in Christ, forgiveness, his presence, resurrection, a new creation, is never too hard for him, and he will do it at the appointed time.

For us. What are we laughing off as impossible that God has in fact promised? That he could change a hardened heart, forgive a long-buried sin, or raise the dead? And when we are caught out, as Sarah was, it is better to admit the truth than to hide it in fear. The God who corrects her keeps his promise to her.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Judge of all the earth takes his friend into his confidence, and Abraham intercedes for Sodom. As the visitors look toward the city, the LORD resolves not to hide his plan from the man he has chosen to teach righteousness and justice (vv. 16–19). He tells Abraham of the great outcry against Sodom and Gomorrah and that he will go down to see (vv. 20–21). Abraham remains before the LORD and pleads, appealing to God’s own justice: will he sweep away the righteous with the wicked? Six times he asks, from fifty to ten, humble and bold together, and six times the LORD agrees (vv. 22–33). Not even ten will be found, but the prayer is not wasted (19:29).
verseByVerse.theology: The LORD tells Abraham, his friend, that he is going down to see Sodom's sin. Abraham draws near and pleads on the ground of God's justice.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the prayer did not save the city, but it brought Lot out. Now: a few righteous people are salt in a place (Matt. 5:13), and one righteous man at Calvary was enough.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the men set out from there, and they looked down toward Sodom. And Abraham went with them to set them on their way. The LORD said, "Shall I hide from Abraham what I am about to do, seeing that Abraham shall surely become a great and mighty nation, and all the nations of the earth shall be blessed in him? For I have chosen him, that he may command his children and his household after him to keep the way of the LORD by doing righteousness and justice, so that the LORD may bring to Abraham what he has promised him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
As the visitors set out toward Sodom, the LORD resolves to share his plan with Abraham, because he has chosen him to be the father of a great nation, a blessing to all the earth, and the head of a household that keeps the way of the LORD by doing righteousness and justice.

They looked down toward Sodom. From the hills near Hebron one looks down and east toward the valley of the Dead Sea. Abraham walks with his guests a little way, as a courteous host would, to “set them on their way”.

Shall I hide from Abraham what I am about to do? The LORD speaks his thoughts aloud, and the reader overhears. He will not keep his friend in the dark. Abraham is called God’s friend (2 Chronicles 20:7; Isaiah 41:8), and James adds, “and he was called a friend of God” (James 2:23). A prophet is one who stands in God’s counsel: “For the Lord GOD does nothing without revealing his secret to his servants the prophets” (Amos 3:7), and Abraham will soon be called a prophet (20:7).

All the nations of the earth shall be blessed in him. God recalls his promise of 12:3. Because Abraham is to be a blessing to the nations, he must understand how God deals with the nations, both in judgment and in mercy.

For I have chosen him. The Hebrew is literally “I have known him”: God set his love on him and chose him, as he later says to Israel, “You only have I known of all the families of the earth” (Amos 3:2). God chose Abraham for a purpose: “that he may command his children and his household after him to keep the way of the LORD by doing righteousness and justice”. Righteousness and justice are what Sodom lacks. The family of Abraham is to be a living contrast with the city of the plain.

So that the LORD may bring to Abraham what he has promised. This does not make the promise depend on Abraham’s performance, as if he could earn it. God’s choice comes first; the godly household is the way God has chosen to carry the promise forward through the generations. God ordains the end and the means together.

Friends of God. Jesus says the same to his disciples: “No longer do I call you servants, for the servant does not know what his master is doing; but I have called you friends, for all that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John 15:15). In Christ, ordinary believers are taken into God’s confidence through his word, so that they understand his purposes and pray in line with them.

Teach your household. Abraham’s calling was not only private faith but a household shaped by God’s ways. Parents, grandparents and all who lead others are to teach and model “the way of the LORD”, not as a set of rules for children only, but as a life of righteousness and justice that the children can see in the adults.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said, "Because the outcry against Sodom and Gomorrah is great and their sin is very grave, I will go down to see whether they have done altogether according to the outcry that has come to me. And if not, I will know."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD announces that the outcry against Sodom and Gomorrah is great and their sin very grave, and that he will go down to see for himself, so that his judgment will rest on full and fair inquiry.

The outcry against Sodom and Gomorrah. The word is the cry of the oppressed calling for help, the same word used of Israel crying out under slavery in Egypt (Exodus 3:7, 9). Like Abel’s blood crying from the ground (4:10), it is the cry of victims. Scripture names Sodom’s sins: “Behold, this was the guilt of your sister Sodom: she and her daughters had pride, excess of food, and prosperous ease, but did not aid the poor and needy” (Ezekiel 16:49), and Jude says the cities “indulged in sexual immorality and pursued unnatural desire” (Jude 7). The next chapter shows a whole town ready to commit gang rape on strangers (19:4–9).

Their sin is very grave. Literally “very heavy”. The weight of evil has built up until it can no longer be ignored.

I will go down to see. As at Babel (11:5), the LORD “comes down” to look. This does not mean that God is ignorant and needs to find out. It is a way of saying, in human terms, that his judgment is never hasty or based on hearsay; he examines the evidence fully before he acts. Israel’s judges were to do the same (Deuteronomy 13:14).

Does God not know? Some, especially those called open theists, take verses like this to mean that God does not know the future or even the present fully. But the God who knew Sarah’s silent laugh (v. 13) knows Sodom. Scripture often speaks of God in human terms, so that we may understand him; here the point is the fairness of his judgment, not a gap in his knowledge.

The cry is heard. God hears the cry of those who are trampled. James warns the rich who defraud their workers: “the cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord of hosts” (James 5:4). God “has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed” (Acts 17:31), and that man is Jesus Christ. He knows every hidden abuse.

For us. If you have been wronged and no one seems to hear, God hears; your cry has reached him, and justice will be done. And if we are comfortable, we should ask whether the pride, excess and neglect of the poor that Ezekiel names are growing in us and in our communities. Sodom’s sins were not only the ones that shock us.

verseByVerse.quote: So the men turned from there and went toward Sodom, but Abraham still stood before the LORD. Then Abraham drew near and said, "Will you indeed sweep away the righteous with the wicked? Suppose there are fifty righteous within the city. Will you then sweep away the place and not spare it for the fifty righteous who are in it? Far be it from you to do such a thing, to put the righteous to death with the wicked, so that the righteous fare as the wicked! Far be that from you! Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?" And the LORD said, "If I find at Sodom fifty righteous in the city, I will spare the whole place for their sake."
verseByVerse.commentary:
While the two men go on toward Sodom, Abraham stays before the LORD and, appealing to God’s own justice, asks whether he will destroy the righteous with the wicked; the LORD agrees to spare the whole city for fifty righteous.

Abraham still stood before the LORD. The two angels go on toward Sodom (19:1), and Abraham does not let the LORD leave without speaking. To “stand before” someone can mean to wait on him as a servant, or to plead before a judge.

Abraham drew near. He comes close to speak. His concern is surely partly for Lot and his family in the city, but he does not name Lot; he argues from God’s justice for all the righteous there.

Will you indeed sweep away the righteous with the wicked? Abraham is not accusing God. He appeals to what he knows God to be. “Far be it from you” is a strong expression, almost “It would be unthinkable for you”, said twice.

Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just? This is the centre of the chapter. The God of Abraham is not a local deity but the Judge of the whole earth, and he will act in keeping with his own character. God accepts Abraham’s appeal at once: “I will spare the whole place for their sake.” A few righteous people can be a blessing to a whole city, like salt that preserves the meal (compare Jeremiah 5:1).

Why does God let Abraham argue? God had told Abraham his plan in order to draw this prayer out of him (vv. 17–19). Abraham is not more merciful than God, wresting a concession from a reluctant judge. God is shaping the heart of his friend to share his own justice and mercy, and he has made his people’s prayers part of how he works. God ordains the means as well as the end, so the prayers are real.

The prayer God answered upside down. Abraham’s plea rests on something we all feel: justice is not a matter of taste. Even people who believe morality is a human invention protest when the innocent are crushed along with the guilty, as though there really were a Judge of all the earth who ought to do right. Abraham asks that the righteous should never fare as the wicked. Centuries later God did exactly what Abraham said he never would. At the cross the righteous one was put to death with the wicked; Jesus “was numbered with the transgressors” (Isaiah 53:12), crucified between two criminals. As men’s act it was the worst injustice in history. But it was also the Judge of all the earth doing what is just in the most unexpected way: letting the righteous fare as the wicked, so that the wicked might fare as the righteous (2 Corinthians 5:21). Abraham could bargain God down to ten. In Christ God found one righteous man, and for his sake he spares a multitude.

Textual note. An ancient Jewish scribal tradition says that v. 22 originally read “the LORD remained standing before Abraham”, and that the scribes reversed it out of reverence. The ESV notes this reading. The sense of the passage is unchanged: Abraham and the LORD remain together, and Abraham pleads.

verseByVerse.quote: Abraham answered and said, "Behold, I have undertaken to speak to the Lord, I who am but dust and ashes. Suppose five of the fifty righteous are lacking. Will you destroy the whole city for lack of five?" And he said, "I will not destroy it if I find forty-five there." Again he spoke to him and said, "Suppose forty are found there." He answered, "For the sake of forty I will not do it." Then he said, "Oh let not the Lord be angry, and I will speak. Suppose thirty are found there." He answered, "I will not do it, if I find thirty there." He said, "Behold, I have undertaken to speak to the Lord. Suppose twenty are found there." He answered, "For the sake of twenty I will not destroy it." Then he said, "Oh let not the Lord be angry, and I will speak again but this once. Suppose ten are found there." He answered, "For the sake of ten I will not destroy it." And the LORD went his way, when he had finished speaking to Abraham, and Abraham returned to his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With deep humility and growing boldness Abraham presses on, from forty-five to ten, and each time the LORD agrees; then the conversation ends, leaving the reader to discover whether even ten righteous will be found.

I who am but dust and ashes. Abraham remembers what he is, a creature of dust (3:19), and Job uses the same words in his repentance (Job 42:6). He knows he has no right to instruct God. Yet he keeps asking. Humility and boldness belong together in prayer: humility because of who we are, boldness because of who God is and what he has promised.

Oh let not the Lord be angry. Twice Abraham asks God not to be angry at his persistence (vv. 30, 32). God never is. He never refuses, never rebukes, and never sets a limit; it is Abraham who stops.

Suppose ten are found there. Why ten? Perhaps Abraham counted Lot’s household and hoped there would be at least that many; perhaps ten seemed the smallest group that could make a community. The text does not say. In the event not even ten righteous are found, and the city falls. But God goes beyond what Abraham asked: he rescues Lot and his daughters, “God remembered Abraham” (19:29).

And the LORD went his way. The LORD ends the conversation when he has finished speaking; Abraham returns home. He has prayed, and he leaves the outcome with the Judge of all the earth.

The one who stands in the breach. Abraham is the first great intercessor in Scripture; Moses will plead for Israel in the same way (Exodus 32:11–14). Later God laments, “I sought for a man among them who should build up the wall and stand in the breach before me for the land, that I should not destroy it, but I found none” (Ezekiel 22:30). That man came. Jesus prayed for his enemies from the cross (Luke 23:34), and now “he is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him, since he always lives to make intercession for them” (Hebrews 7:25). Our prayers for others rest on his.

Pray for your city. Abraham prayed for a city that was not his and for people who were not his family, except Lot. Pray for your town, its leaders and its hidden sufferers, and for the believers in it. Jesus taught that we “ought always to pray and not lose heart” (Luke 18:1). Pray persistently, specifically and humbly, and thank God that he hears the prayers of his friends, often giving more than we know to ask.

18.theology:
God Coming Down. The LORD at Mamre, eating food and sitting in a tent in the heat of the day, is one of the Old Testament's most striking anticipations of the incarnation: "the Word became flesh and dwelt among us" (John 1:14). The God who fills the heavens stoops to one place, one meal, a bodily form. The incarnation is not foreign to the God of Genesis; in it he shows himself most fully.

Intercessory Prayer. Abraham argues from God's justice, not sentiment; he persists without presuming ("Oh let not the Lord be angry, and I will speak," v. 30). The New Testament develops this in the persistent widow (Luke 18:1–8) and in Jesus' own intercession: "he always lives to make intercession for them" (Heb. 7:25). Our prayers are carried by the prayers of Christ, who is both the friend who pleads and the LORD who hears.
18.examples:
Then: Hospitality to strangers was a sacred duty in the ancient Near East. Sodom's treatment of Lot's guests in chapter 19 is therefore not only a sexual sin but a gross violation of the code that held ancient society together. Abraham's extravagant welcome is the opposite picture: God’s people are to be marked by generous welcome, not hostility.

Now: "Is anything too hard for the LORD?" (v. 14) is a good question to begin every prayer with. When we are tempted to trim our prayers to fit what seems possible, it calls us back to the God of the impossible. And Abraham's bold intercession gives permission for passionate, specific, persistent prayer for those who are perishing. To stand before the LORD and plead for a lost city is not presumption; it is friendship with God.

keyVerse.quote: Is anything too hard for the LORD? At the appointed time I will return to you, about this time next year, and Sarah shall have a son.
keyVerse.note: This question holds the chapter together: the God who will give a son to a woman of ninety is the same Judge of all the earth who hears Abraham’s prayer for Sodom. It is echoed in Jeremiah 32 and answered to Mary in Luke 1:37, and its deepest answer is the resurrection of Jesus.

18.reflection:
Abraham ran to welcome strangers and served them his best without knowing who they were (vv. 1–8; Hebrews 13:2). Who are the strangers around you, and what would generous hospitality to them look like this month?

Sarah laughed because the promise seemed impossible after years of disappointment (vv. 11–15). Is there a promise of God you have quietly stopped believing? How does the question “Is anything too hard for the LORD?” speak to it, and what does it not promise?

God took Abraham into his confidence and chose him to teach his household “righteousness and justice” (v. 19). What does it look like for your home or church to be a living contrast with the world around it?

Abraham pleaded for Sodom, humbly and boldly, appealing to God’s justice (vv. 23–32). How does Jesus’ intercession for us encourage you to pray for your own town or city? What will you pray for this week?

19.title: The Destruction of Sodom
19.text: <sup>1</sup>The two angels came to Sodom in the evening, and Lot was sitting in the gate of Sodom. When Lot saw them, he rose to meet them and bowed himself with his face to the earth<sup>2</sup>and said, "My lords, please turn aside to your servant's house and spend the night and wash your feet. Then you may rise up early and go on your way." They said, "No; we will spend the night in the town square."<sup>3</sup>But he pressed them strongly; so they turned aside to him and entered his house. And he made them a feast and baked unleavened bread, and they ate.<sup>4</sup>But before they lay down, the men of the city, the men of Sodom, both young and old, all the people to the last man, surrounded the house.<sup>5</sup>And they called to Lot, "Where are the men who came to you tonight? Bring them out to us, that we may know them."<sup>6</sup>Lot went out to the men at the entrance, shut the door after him,<sup>7</sup>and said, "I beg you, my brothers, do not act so wickedly.<sup>8</sup>Behold, I have two daughters who have not known any man. Let me bring them out to you, and do to them as you please. Only do nothing to these men, for they have come under the shelter of my roof."<sup>9</sup>But they said, "Stand back!" And they said, "This fellow came to sojourn, and he has become the judge! Now we will deal worse with you than with them." Then they pressed hard against the man Lot, and drew near to break the door down.<sup>10</sup>But the men reached out their hands and brought Lot into the house with them and shut the door.<sup>11</sup>And they struck with blindness the men who were at the entrance of the house, both small and great, so that they wore themselves out groping for the door.<sup>12</sup>Then the men said to Lot, "Have you anyone else here? Sons-in-law, sons, daughters, or anyone you have in the city, bring them out of the place.<sup>13</sup>For we are about to destroy this place, because the outcry against its people has become great before the LORD, and the LORD has sent us to destroy it."<sup>14</sup>So Lot went out and said to his sons-in-law, who were to marry his daughters, "Up! Get out of this place, for the LORD is about to destroy the city." But he seemed to his sons-in-law to be jesting.<sup>15</sup>As morning dawned, the angels urged Lot, saying, "Up! Take your wife and your two daughters who are here, lest you be swept away in the punishment of the city."<sup>16</sup>But he lingered. So the men seized him and his wife and his two daughters by the hand, the LORD being merciful to him, and they brought him out and set him outside the city.<sup>17</sup>And as they brought them out, one said, "Escape for your life. Do not look back or stop anywhere in the valley. Escape to the hills, lest you be swept away."<sup>18</sup>And Lot said to them, "Oh, no, my lords.<sup>19</sup>Behold, your servant has found favor in your sight, and you have shown me great kindness in saving my life. But I cannot escape to the hills, lest the disaster overtake me and I die.<sup>20</sup>Behold, this city is near enough to flee to, and it is a little one. Let me escape there—is it not a little one?—and my life will be saved!"<sup>21</sup>He said to him, "Behold, I grant you this favor also, that I will not overthrow the city of which you have spoken.<sup>22</sup>Escape there quickly, for I can do nothing till you arrive there." Therefore the name of the city was called Zoar.<sup>23</sup>The sun had risen on the earth when Lot came to Zoar.<sup>24</sup>Then the LORD rained on Sodom and Gomorrah sulfur and fire from the LORD out of heaven.<sup>25</sup>And he overthrew those cities, and all the valley, and all the inhabitants of the cities, and what grew on the ground.<sup>26</sup>But Lot's wife, behind him, looked back, and she became a pillar of salt.<sup>27</sup>And Abraham went early in the morning to the place where he had stood before the LORD.<sup>28</sup>And he looked down toward Sodom and Gomorrah and toward all the land of the valley, and he looked and, behold, the smoke of the land went up like the smoke of a furnace.<sup>29</sup>So it was that, when God destroyed the cities of the valley, God remembered Abraham and sent Lot out of the midst of the overthrow when he overthrew the cities in which Lot had lived.<sup>30</sup>Now Lot went up out of Zoar and lived in the hills with his two daughters, for he was afraid to live in Zoar. So he lived in a cave with his two daughters.<sup>31</sup>And the firstborn said to the younger, "Our father is old, and there is not a man on earth to come in to us after the manner of all the earth.<sup>32</sup>Come, let us make our father drink wine, and we will lie with him, that we may preserve offspring from our father."<sup>33</sup>So they made their father drink wine that night. And the firstborn went in and lay with her father.
