He did not know when she lay down or when she arose.<sup>34</sup>The next day, the firstborn said to the younger, "Behold, I lay last night with my father. Let us make him drink wine tonight also. Then you go in and lie with him, that we may preserve offspring from our father."<sup>35</sup>So they made their father drink wine that night also. And the younger arose and lay with him, and he did not know when she lay down or when she arose.<sup>36</sup>Thus both the daughters of Lot became pregnant by their father.<sup>37</sup>The firstborn bore a son and called his name Moab. He is the father of the Moabites to this day.<sup>38</sup>The younger also bore a son and called his name Ben-ammi. He is the father of the Ammonites to this day.
19.overview:
Where we are. On the evening after Abraham’s plea for Sodom (18:22–33), the two angels reach the city. Lot, who chose the well-watered valley and pitched his tent toward Sodom (13:10–13), and whom Abraham had already rescued once (14:12–16), now lives inside it and sits in its gate.

The message. The Judge of all the earth does what is just. Sodom’s violence proves the outcry true, and God destroys the cities with fire from heaven. Yet on the same night he drags a hesitant, compromised believer out by the hand, because he is merciful and because he remembered Abraham. The chapter also shows the cost of settling in Sodom: Lot is saved, but he loses his wife, his home and his daughters’ innocence, and ends in a cave.

Why it was said. Israel was about to enter Canaan, and the dead, salt-crusted land by the Dead Sea stood as a lasting warning of what God’s anger leaves behind (Deuteronomy 29:23; see the introduction). The chapter also explained the origins of Moab and Ammon, Israel’s relatives and frequent enemies across the Jordan, whose land God gave them for Lot’s sake (Deuteronomy 2:9, 19).

How the chapter makes its case. Lot welcomes the angels (vv. 1–3). The whole city comes to rape the guests; Lot offers his daughters, and the angels strike the mob blind (vv. 4–11). Lot’s sons-in-law laugh at his warning (vv. 12–14). At dawn he lingers, and the angels drag him out; he bargains for Zoar (vv. 15–22). Fire falls, Lot’s wife looks back, and Abraham sees the smoke: God had remembered him (vv. 23–29). In a cave Lot’s daughters bear Moab and Ammon (vv. 30–38).

Where it leads. To Christ by the need it exposes and by the character of God revealed in him. Jesus takes the days of Lot as a picture of his own return: life going on as usual until “fire and sulfur rained from heaven and destroyed them all” (Luke 17:29). Sodom’s fire is “an example of what is going to happen to the ungodly” (2 Peter 2:6), and the only shelter is the one who bore God’s judgment in our place. Lot is rescued because the LORD is merciful, not because he is eager, and Christ rescues the same way, from “the present evil age” (Galatians 1:4). And from the shame of the cave come Ruth the Moabite and Naamah the Ammonite, both in the line of Jesus.

For us. Do not linger where God has called you out, and do not look back with longing at what he has judged. Ask what your surroundings are doing to your heart and your family. And if you are slow and weak in faith, take comfort: the God who seized Lot by the hand holds on to his own.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–29 — The Destruction of Sodom and the Rescue of Lot
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God judges Sodom and rescues Lot. The city’s response to two strangers proves the outcry true: every man in Sodom gathers to rape Lot’s guests, and Lot, too much at home there, offers his own daughters instead (vv. 1–11). The angels reveal their mission, but Lot’s warning means nothing to his future sons-in-law (vv. 12–14). At dawn he lingers, and the angels drag him and his family out by the hand, “the LORD being merciful to him”; even then he bargains for a small town to flee to (vv. 15–22). Fire falls from heaven, Lot’s wife looks back and becomes a pillar of salt, and Abraham sees the smoke from afar. The section ends with the reason Lot was saved: “God remembered Abraham” (vv. 23–29).
verseByVerse.theology: The whole city surrounds Lot's house demanding his guests. The angels strike the mob blind, warn Lot's family, and bring them out before the fire falls.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Ezekiel names Sodom's pride and neglect of the poor, Jude its sexual immorality. Now: it is possible to leave the city and still long for it, as Lot’s wife did.

verseByVerse.quote: The two angels came to Sodom in the evening, and Lot was sitting in the gate of Sodom. When Lot saw them, he rose to meet them and bowed himself with his face to the earth and said, "My lords, please turn aside to your servant's house and spend the night and wash your feet. Then you may rise up early and go on your way." They said, "No; we will spend the night in the town square." But he pressed them strongly; so they turned aside to him and entered his house. And he made them a feast and baked unleavened bread, and they ate.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The two angels reach Sodom at evening, and Lot, now a leading man sitting in the city gate, insists that they stay in his house rather than in the open square, because he knows how dangerous Sodom’s streets are.

The two angels came to Sodom in the evening. These are the two “men” who left Abraham at midday (18:2, 22). The LORD himself does not come with them; he stayed with Abraham. Now they are called angels, messengers sent from God.

Lot was sitting in the gate of Sodom. Step by step $Lot has moved closer: he pitched his tent “as far as Sodom” (13:12), then lived in it (14:12), and now sits in the gate, where the city’s elders met, judged cases and did business. He has become a leading citizen of Sodom.

He rose to meet them and bowed himself. The parallels with Abraham’s welcome are deliberate. Like Abraham, Lot rises, bows, calls himself “your servant”, offers water to wash their feet and a meal. But the differences are telling. Abraham ran to them at his tent door in the heat of the day; Lot meets them at the city gate as night falls. Abraham’s meal was lavish and leisurely; Lot’s is a hurried feast with unleavened bread, quick to bake. Abraham’s guests stay to talk with him; Lot is anxious to send his on their way early.

No; we will spend the night in the town square. Travellers without a host might sleep in the open square. But Lot “pressed them strongly”. He knows exactly what Sodom does to strangers after dark.

A righteous man in a wicked city. Lot’s hospitality is a real mark of goodness in a dark place. Peter calls him “righteous Lot, greatly distressed by the sensual conduct of the wicked” (2 Peter 2:7). He was not at home in Sodom’s sins. But he was very much at home in Sodom’s comfort and influence, and the chapter shows what that cost him.

What it does not mean. The story does not teach that Christians should not live in cities, hold public office, or have influence. Daniel and Joseph served in pagan courts. Lot’s problem was not where he lived but what he loved: he chose Sodom for its prosperity (13:10–11) and stayed long after he knew what it was. The question for us is whether we are in the world as salt and light, or slowly being shaped by it.
verseByVerse.note: Lot is now living inside the city; compare 13:12 and 14:12.

verseByVerse.quote: But before they lay down, the men of the city, the men of Sodom, both young and old, all the people to the last man, surrounded the house. And they called to Lot, "Where are the men who came to you tonight? Bring them out to us, that we may know them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before bedtime the whole male population of Sodom surrounds Lot’s house and demands that he hand over his guests so that they can rape them: the outcry against Sodom is proved true.

Both young and old, all the people to the last man. The narrator piles up the words to show that the whole city is involved. Abraham had asked whether ten righteous might be found (18:32); here is the answer. Not one man stays away.

That we may know them. In Hebrew “know” is often used of sexual intercourse (4:1), and Lot’s reply makes the meaning plain (v. 8). The men of Sodom intend gang rape of two strangers who have come under a citizen’s protection: violence, humiliation and a violation of the most basic duty of hospitality, all at once. A later chapter of Israel’s history repeats the scene almost word for word, with a terrible outcome, to show how far Israel itself had sunk (Judges 19:22–25).

Worse than Sodom. Jesus uses Sodom as the measure of guilt, and then says something startling. Of a town that refuses to receive his messengers he says, “it will be more bearable on the day of judgment for the land of Sodom and Gomorrah than for that town” (Matthew 10:15), and of Capernaum, where he had done his mighty works, that if those works had been done in Sodom, “it would have remained until this day” (Matthew 11:23). To hear the gospel and reject the Son of God is more serious than Sodom’s sins. No one can read this chapter and feel superior.

For us. The sins of Sodom are not distant. A crowd can make cruelty seem normal, and a culture can lose all sense of shame. Christians are called to be the few who refuse to join the crowd, and who protect the vulnerable rather than exploit them.

Where Christians differ: the sin of Sodom. Some argue that Sodom’s sin was only inhospitality, or the violence of attempted rape, and that the chapter has nothing to say about same-sex relations as such. Others hold that while the scene is about violence, Scripture’s wider description of Sodom includes sexual sin of a same-sex kind. This commentary’s view: Scripture names Sodom’s pride, excess and neglect of the poor (Ezekiel 16:49–50), and Jude says the cities “indulged in sexual immorality and pursued unnatural desire” (Jude 7). This passage describes attempted gang rape, and it is not the main text for the question of same-sex relationships; that rests on creation (see Romans 1). With the historic Christian church this commentary holds that same-sex sexual relationships are contrary to God’s will. That must be spoken with compassion. The word “sodomite” has often been used as a weapon, and people who experience same-sex attraction are not to be identified with the mob at Lot’s door. All of us are sinners who need the same grace.

verseByVerse.quote: Lot went out to the men at the entrance, shut the door after him, and said, "I beg you, my brothers, do not act so wickedly. Behold, I have two daughters who have not known any man. Let me bring them out to you, and do to them as you please. Only do nothing to these men, for they have come under the shelter of my roof."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lot goes out to shield his guests and pleads with the mob, but, calling them his brothers, he offers them his two virgin daughters instead: a shocking betrayal that Scripture records but never approves.

Lot went out … shut the door after him. There is courage here. Lot faces the mob alone to protect his guests.

I beg you, my brothers. But he calls the would-be rapists “my brothers”. He is too at home in Sodom to see clearly. He calls their plan wicked, yet he cannot break with them.

Let me bring them out to you. Then comes the most shocking line in Lot’s story. To protect men who have come “under the shelter of my roof”, he offers to hand over his own daughters to be raped. The duty to protect guests was sacred in that world, but it could never justify sacrificing one’s children. The narrator adds no comment; he lets the horror speak, and the rest of the chapter shows the bitter fruit in the same family (vv. 30–36).

Scripture records; it does not approve. Many things in Genesis are reported, not commended. The narrator expects us to weigh what people do against what God is like. Lot is called “righteous” (2 Peter 2:7), but that does not mean everything he did was right. Here he was gravely wrong.

The protector who gave himself. Lot tried to protect his guests by giving up others. Christ protects his own by giving up himself: “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10:11). He is the father and husband that Lot failed to be, the one who stands at the door and takes the violence on himself.

If you have been failed by those meant to protect you. Any reader who has been failed or harmed by a father, a husband or anyone meant to protect them should know that God does not stand behind Lot here. Abuse is never acceptable and never your fault. If you are in danger, seek safety now and tell someone you trust; abuse must be reported to the authorities. Ask your church for help, and seek out a biblical counsellor who will care for you with Scripture and with wisdom.

verseByVerse.quote: But they said, "Stand back!" And they said, "This fellow came to sojourn, and he has become the judge! Now we will deal worse with you than with them." Then they pressed hard against the man Lot, and drew near to break the door down. But the men reached out their hands and brought Lot into the house with them and shut the door. And they struck with blindness the men who were at the entrance of the house, both small and great, so that they wore themselves out groping for the door.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The mob rejects Lot’s plea, sneers at the foreigner who presumes to judge them, and moves to break down the door, until the angels pull Lot inside and strike the men at the door with blindness.

This fellow came to sojourn, and he has become the judge! After all his years in Sodom, Lot is still an outsider to them, “this fellow” who came as a resident foreigner. The world never fully accepts the believer who compromises with it, and despises him the moment he objects. There is bitter irony in their words: judgment is indeed about to fall on Sodom, but not from Lot.

Now we will deal worse with you than with them. The mob turns on Lot himself and presses to break down the door.

The men reached out their hands. Lot had tried to rescue his guests; now his guests rescue him. The same hands will drag him out of the city in the morning (v. 16).

They struck with blindness the men. Even struck blind, “both small and great”, they keep groping for the door until they are worn out. Their physical blindness matches the blindness of their hearts. Sin, once it has its grip, does not easily let go; Paul describes those who suppress the truth as having their “foolish hearts” darkened (Romans 1:21).

Sight and blindness. Jesus said, “For judgment I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9:39). Those who will not see the light are left in their darkness; those who know they are blind may ask him for sight. The question is not whether we are sinners but whether we will let him open our eyes.

For us. When believers speak of right and wrong, they may be mocked as people who have “become the judge”. Speak humbly, as one sinner to another, but do not be silenced. The real Judge is not the believer but God, and his verdict is the one that will stand.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew word for “blindness” here is rare, used elsewhere only of the Syrian army struck blind at Elisha’s prayer (2 Kings 6:18). It may mean a sudden dazzling or confusion, a blindness that left the men unable to find what was in front of them, rather than a permanent loss of sight. Either way it was God’s doing, and it stopped them.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the men said to Lot, "Have you anyone else here? Sons-in-law, sons, daughters, or anyone you have in the city, bring them out of the place. For we are about to destroy this place, because the outcry against its people has become great before the LORD, and the LORD has sent us to destroy it." So Lot went out and said to his sons-in-law, who were to marry his daughters, "Up! Get out of this place, for the LORD is about to destroy the city." But he seemed to his sons-in-law to be jesting.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The angels reveal that the LORD has sent them to destroy the city and urge Lot to bring out his whole family; but when he warns the men engaged to his daughters, they think he is joking.

Have you anyone else here? The angels’ mercy reaches out to Lot’s whole family, sons-in-law, sons and daughters. God would have saved them all.

The outcry against its people has become great. The LORD had gone down “to see” (18:21). Now the verdict is in: the outcry was true. “The LORD has sent us to destroy it.”

Up! Get out of this place. Lot does go, in the dark, to warn the men who were to marry his daughters. Give him credit: he tries.

He seemed to his sons-in-law to be jesting. The Hebrew word for “jesting” comes from the same root as “laugh”, the word behind Isaac’s name. Sarah laughed at God’s promise (18:12); Lot’s sons-in-law laugh at God’s warning. After years of living comfortably in Sodom, Lot’s words about judgment carry no weight with them. They have never seen him live as if God’s judgment were real.

As it was in the days of Lot. Jesus warns that his return will come in the same way. In the days of Lot “they were eating and drinking, buying and selling, planting and building, but on the day when Lot went out from Sodom, fire and sulfur rained from heaven and destroyed them all” (Luke 17:28–29). Peter adds that scoffers will mock the promise of his coming (2 Peter 3:3–4). God’s warnings are not a joke, and his patience is meant to lead us to repentance.

Does your life give weight to your words? It is a searching question. If we speak of eternity but live entirely for comfort and success, our family and friends will hear our warnings as Lot’s sons-in-law did. Our lives will not save anyone, but they can make our words believable.

Uncertain wording. The phrase “who were to marry his daughters” can also be read “who had married his daughters”. If the men were already married, Lot may have had other, married daughters who stayed in the city and perished, and the angels’ words in v. 15, “your two daughters who are here”, may hint at this. If they were only engaged, the two daughters of v. 8 were their brides-to-be. The ESV takes the second view, which fits the description of the daughters as having “not known any man” (v. 8).

verseByVerse.quote: As morning dawned, the angels urged Lot, saying, "Up! Take your wife and your two daughters who are here, lest you be swept away in the punishment of the city." But he lingered. So the men seized him and his wife and his two daughters by the hand, the LORD being merciful to him, and they brought him out and set him outside the city. And as they brought them out, one said, "Escape for your life. Do not look back or stop anywhere in the valley. Escape to the hills, lest you be swept away."
verseByVerse.commentary:
At dawn the angels urge Lot to flee, but he lingers, so they seize him, his wife and his daughters by the hand and bring them out of the city, because the LORD was merciful to him; then they tell him to run for the hills and not look back.

Lest you be swept away in the punishment of the city. The Hebrew word for “punishment” is the usual word for “iniquity”: the city’s sin and its punishment are bound together. To stay is to share its fate.

But he lingered. One of the saddest lines in Genesis. Lot hesitates, even with angels urging him and judgment hours away. Perhaps it was his possessions, his house, his position, perhaps family members who would not come. Whatever held him, he could not make himself leave.

The men seized him … the LORD being merciful to him. So the angels take him by the hand, and his wife and daughters too, and pull them out. The reason is stated plainly: “the LORD being merciful to him.” It was not Lot’s readiness, but God’s compassion, that brought him out.

Escape for your life. The commands are urgent: do not look back, do not stop anywhere in the valley, run to the hills. Salvation from judgment is no time for sightseeing.

Rescued by another’s hand. Here is salvation in miniature. Lot does not save himself; he cannot even make himself leave. God reaches in and pulls him out. That is what Christ does: he “gave himself for our sins to deliver us from the present evil age” (Galatians 1:4), and his people are those he has taken by the hand. Peter draws the lesson: “the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials, and to keep the unrighteous under punishment until the day of judgment” (2 Peter 2:9). If your faith is slow and weak, your hope is not the strength of your grip on him but the strength of his grip on you.

Do not linger. Yet the story is also a warning. God was merciful, but Lot’s lingering nearly cost him his life, and it cost him much else. When God calls us away from a sin or a place that is ruining us, the time to go is now.

Was Lot really saved? Peter calls him “righteous” and says “he was tormenting his righteous soul over their lawless deeds that he saw and heard” (2 Peter 2:8). He was a true believer, but a compromised one. Some have used Lot as an example of a “carnal Christian”, a believer who need not follow Christ wholeheartedly. This commentary holds that there is no acceptable class of half-hearted Christians: one call to discipleship applies to all. Lot is a warning, not a model. His story shows that real faith can be weak and that its compromises carry real costs.

verseByVerse.quote: And Lot said to them, "Oh, no, my lords. Behold, your servant has found favor in your sight, and you have shown me great kindness in saving my life. But I cannot escape to the hills, lest the disaster overtake me and I die. Behold, this city is near enough to flee to, and it is a little one. Let me escape there—is it not a little one?—and my life will be saved!" He said to him, "Behold, I grant you this favor also, that I will not overthrow the city of which you have spoken. Escape there quickly, for I can do nothing till you arrive there." Therefore the name of the city was called Zoar.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even while being rescued Lot argues: afraid of the hills, he asks to flee to a small town nearby instead, and the angel grants this too, waiting until Lot is safe before the judgment falls.

Oh, no, my lords. Lot thanks the angels for saving his life, then in the same breath refuses their instruction. He fears that disaster will catch him in the hills. Having been told where safety is, he wants a safety of his own choosing.

Is it not a little one? He pleads for a small town nearby, as if its smallness made his request smaller. The name Zoar means “little” (the ESV note), from this very plea. It is probably the town earlier called Bela (14:2), at the southern end of the Dead Sea.

I grant you this favor also. Literally, “I have lifted up your face”, a Hebrew way of showing favour. God is astonishingly patient with weak faith. He even spares a city for Lot’s sake.

I can do nothing till you arrive there. Judgment is held back until the righteous man is safe. God will not sweep away the righteous with the wicked (18:25). In the same way his present patience with the world gives time for his people to be gathered in: he “is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance” (2 Peter 3:9).

A bruised reed. This is the gentleness of Christ, of whom it was said, “a bruised reed he will not break, and a smoldering wick he will not quench” (Matthew 12:20). He bears with our fears and our bargaining far more than we deserve.

Our bargains do not bring peace. Yet Lot’s chosen refuge did not give him rest. Soon he is too afraid to stay in Zoar and ends up in the hills after all (v. 30), in a cave. The safety we negotiate for ourselves rarely satisfies. It is better to trust God’s word the first time.
verseByVerse.note: “Zoar” means little (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: The sun had risen on the earth when Lot came to Zoar. Then the LORD rained on Sodom and Gomorrah sulfur and fire from the LORD out of heaven. And he overthrew those cities, and all the valley, and all the inhabitants of the cities, and what grew on the ground.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As the sun rises over Zoar, the LORD rains sulfur and fire from heaven on Sodom and Gomorrah and overthrows the cities, the whole valley, all its people and everything that grew there.

The sun had risen on the earth. A new day begins as an ordinary morning in the valley, and it is the day of judgment.

The LORD rained … from the LORD out of heaven. The repetition stresses that this is God’s direct act, not chance. Some early Christian writers saw in the double “LORD” a hint of two divine persons, the LORD who had stood with Abraham and the LORD in heaven; most interpreters take it as emphasis. Either way, the fire comes from God.

Sulfur and fire. The cities probably lay near the southern end of the Dead Sea, a region of bitumen pits (14:10) and salt. Some suggest that God used natural means, such as an earthquake igniting bitumen and gases. The text does not say, and it does not matter to its point: whatever means God used, the fire came at his word and his time. Israel knew the waste land as the standing picture of what the LORD’s anger leaves behind: “burned out with brimstone and salt… an overthrow like that of Sodom and Gomorrah” (Deuteronomy 29:23). The prophets repeat the image again and again (Isaiah 1:9; Amos 4:11).

An example of what is coming. The New Testament treats this as a real event and a preview of the last judgment. Peter writes that by turning the cities to ashes God made them “an example of what is going to happen to the ungodly” (2 Peter 2:6), and Jude speaks of “a punishment of eternal fire” (Jude 7). Jesus says that his own coming will be like this: “so will it be on the day when the Son of Man is revealed” (Luke 17:30). God’s patience with sin has an end.

The fire that fell on Christ. There is one place to shelter from that fire: at the cross, where the judgment of God fell on his Son in the place of sinners. The refuge is open now: “Behold, now is the favorable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Corinthians 6:2).

Why were the children destroyed? This is a real and painful question, and Scripture does not answer it in detail. We do know that God would have spared the whole city for ten righteous (18:32), that he went to great lengths to rescue those who would come, and that “the Judge of all the earth” does what is just (18:25). We can leave the little ones of Sodom in the hands of that Judge, who is also the God who gave his Son for sinners.

What it does not mean. This was a unique judgment, announced by God and carried out by him. It does not mean that every earthquake, fire or disaster is God’s verdict on the particular people who suffer it; Jesus explicitly rejected that conclusion (Luke 13:1–5). Hard providences are never a verdict on the sufferer. They are a call to all of us to repent.

verseByVerse.quote: But Lot's wife, behind him, looked back, and she became a pillar of salt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lot’s wife, lagging behind, looks back toward the city she loved and becomes a pillar of salt, a lasting warning against a heart that cannot let go of what God has judged.

Lot’s wife, behind him. She is following, but lagging. She is never named; she is remembered only for this.

Looked back. The angels had said plainly, “Do not look back” (v. 17). Her look was more than a glance. Her heart was still in Sodom, with the home, the comforts, perhaps the married daughters she had left behind, and she disobeyed a direct command at the moment of rescue.

She became a pillar of salt. The area around the southern Dead Sea is full of salt, including a ridge of rock salt whose pillars local people have long linked with Lot’s wife. She was caught in the judgment she had been rescued from.

Remember Lot’s wife. Jesus made her one of the shortest sermons in the Bible: “Remember Lot’s wife. Whoever seeks to preserve his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life will keep it” (Luke 17:32–33). He also said, “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke 9:62). Jesus himself never looked back: “he set his face to go to Jerusalem” (Luke 9:51), to the cross, for us.

What it does not mean. This is not about a moment of nostalgia or a sad memory. It is about a heart that loved what God had condemned more than the rescue God had given. Many believers look back with regret or weakness, and the same God who took Lot by the hand holds on to his own. But we should ask what we are still looking back to.

verseByVerse.quote: And Abraham went early in the morning to the place where he had stood before the LORD. And he looked down toward Sodom and Gomorrah and toward all the land of the valley, and he looked and, behold, the smoke of the land went up like the smoke of a furnace. So it was that, when God destroyed the cities of the valley, God remembered Abraham and sent Lot out of the midst of the overthrow when he overthrew the cities in which Lot had lived.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Early next morning Abraham goes back to the place where he had prayed and sees the smoke of the whole valley rising like a furnace; and the narrator explains that God rescued Lot because he remembered Abraham.

Abraham went early in the morning to the place where he had stood before the LORD. He returns to the place of his prayer, to see what God has done. From the hills near Hebron he can look down toward the valley.

The smoke of the land went up like the smoke of a furnace. There is no sign that ten righteous were found. All Abraham sees is smoke. He does not yet know that Lot has been saved.

God remembered Abraham. In the Bible, when God “remembers” someone, it does not mean he had forgotten; it means he acts on his commitment to them, as when he “remembered Noah” (8:1) and “remembered his covenant with Abraham” in Egypt (Exodus 2:24). Abraham’s prayer was answered, but not in the form he asked. The city was not spared, but Lot was, and the rescue is credited to God’s remembering Abraham.

Saved for another’s sake. Lot was rescued not for his own merits but because of his relationship with the one God loved and listened to. That is a picture of our salvation. We are accepted not for our sake but for Christ’s sake, because God remembers his Son and the intercession he makes for his people (Hebrews 7:25).

For us. Pray, and leave the answer with God. His answers often look different from our requests, and we may not see the full result for a long time. Abraham saw only smoke; the rescue of Lot was hidden from him that morning. Your prayers for others are not wasted.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Lot’s story ends in darkness. Afraid to stay in Zoar, he lives in a cave in the hills with his two daughters, who believe no man is left to give them children (vv. 30–31). On two nights they make their father drunk and lie with him, and both conceive (vv. 32–36). Their sons become the fathers of Moab and Ammon, Israel’s neighbours east of the Jordan (vv. 37–38). The narrator adds no comment; the facts speak. The man who chose Sodom for its prosperity ends with nothing, and his daughters show how deeply Sodom’s ways have shaped them. Yet the story of these peoples is not finished, for grace will reach even Moab.
verseByVerse.theology: Afraid to stay in Zoar, Lot lives in a cave with his two daughters, who make him drunk and conceive by him.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the choice by sight that began in 13:10 ends in a cave. Now: no one is shut out of God’s grace by where they came from.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Lot went up out of Zoar and lived in the hills with his two daughters, for he was afraid to live in Zoar. So he lived in a cave with his two daughters. And the firstborn said to the younger, "Our father is old, and there is not a man on earth to come in to us after the manner of all the earth. Come, let us make our father drink wine, and we will lie with him, that we may preserve offspring from our father." So they made their father drink wine that night. And the firstborn went in and lay with her father. He did not know when she lay down or when she arose. The next day, the firstborn said to the younger, "Behold, I lay last night with my father. Let us make him drink wine tonight also. Then you go in and lie with him, that we may preserve offspring from our father." So they made their father drink wine that night also. And the younger arose and lay with him, and he did not know when she lay down or when she arose.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Afraid even in Zoar, Lot ends up living in a cave in the hills with his two daughters, who, believing no man is left to give them children, make their father drunk on two nights and lie with him.

He was afraid to live in Zoar. The town he begged for gives him no peace. He ends up in the very hills he was afraid to flee to (v. 19), living in a cave. The man who chose the rich valley of the Jordan for its prosperity (13:10–11) now has nothing: no wife, no home, no flocks, no sons-in-law.

There is not a man on earth to come in to us. The daughters may have believed that the whole world had been destroyed, or simply that no man would marry them now, isolated in the hills as the daughters of a ruined family. “After the manner of all the earth” means the normal way of marriage. Their desire for children was not wrong in itself; their method was a grave sin, later explicitly forbidden (Leviticus 18:6–7).

Let us make our father drink wine. Like Sarah with Hagar (16:1–4), they try to secure offspring by their own scheme. They have been raised in Sodom, and they have just heard their father offer them to a mob. The story shows how deeply Sodom’s values have entered the family.

He did not know when she lay down or when she arose. The narrator stresses Lot’s drunken stupor. It does not excuse him: drunkenness is itself sin, and as with Noah (9:21) it leads to shame. The once leading citizen of Sodom is now so far gone that he does not know what is happening in his own family.

Scripture records without comment. The narrator adds no moral judgment. He does not need to; the facts condemn. This is the last we hear of Lot in Genesis. The man who started out with Abraham ends in a cave, in drunkenness and shame.

The heart that needs a new birth. Lot was rescued from Sodom, but Sodom was not rescued from his family. Changing a person’s surroundings cannot change the heart. That is the need this chapter exposes, and it is why Jesus said, “You must be born again” (John 3:7). Only the Spirit of God can make a new heart, and he does so through Christ.

If you have suffered abuse in your family. This is a story of a family destroyed by sin, and some readers will find it painfully close to home. If you have suffered sexual abuse within your family, it is not your fault, and it is not something to be hidden. If you are in danger, get to safety now and tell someone you trust; abuse must be reported to the authorities. Ask your church for help and seek a biblical counsellor who will walk with you. The God who sees all things sees you.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus both the daughters of Lot became pregnant by their father. The firstborn bore a son and called his name Moab. He is the father of the Moabites to this day. The younger also bore a son and called his name Ben-ammi. He is the father of the Ammonites to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Both daughters become pregnant by their father, and their sons, Moab and Ben-ammi, become the ancestors of the Moabites and the Ammonites, Israel’s neighbours east of the Jordan.

The firstborn bore a son and called his name Moab. The name sounds like the Hebrew for “from father”, and Ben-ammi means “son of my people” (the ESV notes). The names themselves carry the memory of how they were conceived.

To this day. The narrator writes when Moab and Ammon are known nations, living east of the Jordan and the Dead Sea.

Moab and Ammon in Israel’s story. They were Israel’s relatives, and God gave them their lands for Lot’s sake, forbidding Israel to attack them (Deuteronomy 2:9, 19). But they often opposed Israel: Moab hired Balaam to curse Israel and led Israel into idolatry (Numbers 22–25), and so the Moabite and the Ammonite were excluded from the LORD’s assembly (Deuteronomy 23:3–4). Their gods, Chemosh of Moab and Molech of the Ammonites, became snares to Israel (1 Kings 11:7).

Grace beyond shame. Yet the story does not end there. Ruth the Moabite came to trust the God of Israel, married Boaz and became the great-grandmother of David, and Matthew names her in the genealogy of Jesus: “Boaz the father of Obed by Ruth” (Matthew 1:5). Naamah the Ammonite was the mother of King Rehoboam (1 Kings 14:21), and so she too stands in that line. From the shame of a cave come ancestors of the Messiah. Even the prophets who announce Moab’s judgment look beyond it: “Yet I will restore the fortunes of Moab in the latter days” (Jeremiah 48:47).

For us. No family history is so shameful that God’s grace cannot reach it, and no people is beyond his welcome in Christ. If your family story is marked by sin and pain, the gospel says your story can be rewritten. Christ came from a line that included the descendants of Lot’s daughters, and he is not ashamed to call sinners his brothers (Hebrews 2:11).
verseByVerse.note: Moab sounds like the Hebrew for “from father”; Ben-ammi means “son of my people” (ESV notes).

19.theology:
Divine Judgment. God’s patience with a whole society’s wickedness is real but not infinite. The outcry against Sodom (18:20) was the accumulated weight of pride, contempt for the weak and violence against the stranger, and when it was full, judgment fell. The New Testament does not soften this: "It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God" (Heb. 10:31). The gospel does not abolish judgment; it gives the only refuge from it, the one who bore its fire so that those in him are not consumed.

Saved Through Another's Intercession. Lot is saved because of Abraham's intercession, a clear picture of the gospel: we are saved not by our own righteousness but by another's. "While we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son" (Rom. 5:10). We were lingering in the city of destruction, and the Son came to bring us out.
19.examples:
Then: Some archaeologists argue for a violent destruction near the Dead Sea in this period, though the evidence is debated. For Israel, Sodom was the destroyed city above all others, and the prophets used it as the measure of total judgment (Isa. 1:9; Jer. 49:18; Amos 4:11).

Now: Lot moved toward Sodom gradually, settled in fully, and then found himself unable to leave freely. The church in every generation is tempted to blend so thoroughly into the surrounding culture that, when the moment of choice comes, it finds itself lingering. Jesus' warning about Lot's wife is a warning against half-hearted discipleship: the grace that drags you out of destruction also turns you to face your salvation, not the city you were rescued from.

keyVerse.quote: So it was that, when God destroyed the cities of the valley, God remembered Abraham and sent Lot out of the midst of the overthrow when he overthrew the cities in which Lot had lived.
keyVerse.note: This verse sums up the chapter: judgment and rescue on the same day. Lot is saved not because of his own faithfulness, which was weak, but because God remembered Abraham and his prayer. So believers are saved for the sake of another, Jesus Christ, whose intercession never fails.

19.reflection:
Lot moved step by step from pitching his tent near Sodom to sitting in its gate (13:12; 14:12; 19:1). What are the subtle ways your surroundings may be shaping your heart and your family, and what would it look like to be in the world without being of it?

Lot’s sons-in-law thought he was joking (v. 14). Why might people around us not take our faith seriously, and how can our lives give weight to our words?

“But he lingered. So the men seized him … the LORD being merciful to him” (v. 16). How does this verse encourage those whose faith feels weak? And how does Lot’s wife (v. 26; Luke 17:32) warn us?

Moab came from the shame of the cave, yet Ruth the Moabite became an ancestor of Jesus (vv. 36–38; Matthew 1:5). How does this give hope to people whose family history is marked by sin and pain?

20.title: Abraham and Abimelech
20.text: <sup>1</sup>From there Abraham journeyed toward the territory of the Negeb and lived between Kadesh and Shur; and he sojourned in Gerar.<sup>2</sup>And Abraham said of Sarah his wife, "She is my sister." And Abimelech king of Gerar sent and took Sarah.<sup>3</sup>But God came to Abimelech in a dream by night and said to him, "Behold, you are a dead man because of the woman whom you have taken, for she is a man's wife."<sup>4</sup>Now Abimelech had not approached her. So he said, "Lord, will you kill an innocent people?<sup>5</sup>Did he not himself say to me, 'She is my sister'? And she herself said, 'He is my brother.' In the integrity of my heart and the innocence of my hands I have done this."<sup>6</sup>Then God said to him in the dream, "Yes, I know that you have done this in the integrity of your heart, and it was I who kept you from sinning against me. Therefore I did not let you touch her.<sup>7</sup>Now then, return the man's wife, for he is a prophet, so that he will pray for you, and you shall live. But if you do not return her, know that you shall surely die, you and all who are yours."<sup>8</sup>So Abimelech rose early in the morning and called all his servants and told them all these things. And the men were very much afraid.<sup>9</sup>Then Abimelech called Abraham and said to him, "What have you done to us? And how have I sinned against you, that you have brought on me and my kingdom a great sin? You have done to me things that ought not to be done."<sup>10</sup>And Abimelech said to Abraham, "What did you see, that you did this thing?"<sup>11</sup>Abraham said, "I did it because I thought, 'There is no fear of God at all in this place, and they will kill me because of my wife.'<sup>12</sup>Besides, she is indeed my sister, the daughter of my father though not the daughter of my mother, and she became my wife.<sup>13</sup>And when God caused me to wander from my father's house, I said to her, 'This is the kindness you must do me: at every place to which we come, say of me, "He is my brother."'"<sup>14</sup>Then Abimelech took sheep and oxen, and male servants and female servants, and gave them to Abraham, and returned Sarah his wife to him.<sup>15</sup>And Abimelech said, "Behold, my land is before you; dwell where it pleases you."<sup>16</sup>To Sarah he said, "Behold, I have given your brother a thousand pieces of silver. It is a sign of your innocence in the eyes of all who are with you, and before everyone you are vindicated."<sup>17</sup>Then Abraham prayed to God, and God healed Abimelech, and also healed his wife and female slaves so that they bore children.<sup>18</sup>For the LORD had closed all the wombs of the house of Abimelech because of Sarah, Abraham's wife.
20.overview:
Where we are. Sodom lies in ruins, and Abraham moves south into the Negeb and settles for a time in Gerar. God has promised that Sarah will bear a son within the year (18:10, 14), and in the next chapter Isaac is born (21:1–2). Between the promise and the birth, the great intercessor of chapter 18 falls back into his oldest sin.

The message. God keeps his promise even when his chosen servant fails. Out of fear Abraham repeats the lie he told in Egypt and hands Sarah, the promised mother, into a foreign king’s household. God steps in: he warns the king in a dream, keeps him from touching her, and lets a pagan rebuke the patriarch. Yet he still calls Abraham his prophet and answers his prayer. The promise rests on God’s faithfulness, not Abraham’s.

Why it was said. Israel needed to know that God had not chosen them because they were better than the nations (Deuteronomy 9:4–6; see the introduction). Their father had been put to shame by a foreign king’s integrity. They also needed to know that God guards the people he has chosen: “he rebuked kings on their account, saying, “Touch not my anointed ones, do my prophets no harm!”” (Psalm 105:14–15).

How the chapter makes its case. Abraham settles in Gerar, says Sarah is his sister, and King Abimelech takes her (vv. 1–2). God warns Abimelech in a dream; the king pleads his innocence, and God says he himself kept him from sin, and tells him to return Sarah and ask Abraham to pray (vv. 3–7). Abimelech confronts Abraham (vv. 8–10), and Abraham gives his excuses (vv. 11–13). The king returns Sarah with gifts and clears her name (vv. 14–16). Abraham prays, and God opens the wombs he had closed (vv. 17–18).

Where it leads. To Christ by the need it exposes and by the character of God revealed in him. God guards the line of promise from Abraham’s own folly, so that Isaac is born unmistakably Abraham’s and Sarah’s son, as later he would guard the line to Bethlehem. And the chapter shows the need for a better mediator. Abraham the prophet lies, then prays for the man he wronged. Jesus is the prophet in whose mouth “neither was deceit found” (1 Peter 2:22), who prayed for those who wronged him, “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34), and who protects his bride by giving himself for her.

For us. Watch for your old sins; they return when you are tired or afraid. Do not assume there is “no fear of God” in people who do not share your faith. And take heart: God’s purposes for you do not depend on your consistency, though he will lovingly expose and correct your failures.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–18 — Abraham and Abimelech: The Sister-Wife Repeated
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Straight after the judgment on Sodom, the father of the faithful repeats his old lie, and God protects his promise in spite of him. Abraham settles in Gerar and again calls Sarah his sister, and the king takes her into his household, endangering the promised birth just before it happens (vv. 1–2). God warns Abimelech in a dream, keeps him from touching Sarah, and sends him back to Abraham as to a prophet who must pray for him (vv. 3–7). The pagan king rebukes the patriarch, and Abraham’s excuses expose his fear and his misjudgment (vv. 8–13). Abimelech restores Sarah with gifts and publicly clears her name (vv. 14–16), and at Abraham’s prayer God heals the king’s household (vv. 17–18).
verseByVerse.theology: In Gerar Abraham again calls Sarah his sister, and Abimelech takes her. God warns the king in a dream; the king rebukes Abraham and returns Sarah with gifts, and Abraham prays for his household to be healed.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: God shut every womb in Gerar so that no question could hang over Isaac's birth. Now: habitual sins return under the same conditions, and much of our integrity is God's restraint rather than our strength.

verseByVerse.quote: From there Abraham journeyed toward the territory of the Negeb and lived between Kadesh and Shur; and he sojourned in Gerar. And Abraham said of Sarah his wife, "She is my sister." And Abimelech king of Gerar sent and took Sarah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abraham moves south to Gerar and, as in Egypt years before, tells people that Sarah is his sister; the king of Gerar takes her into his household, just when she is about to conceive the promised son.

From there Abraham journeyed toward the territory of the Negeb. He moves from Mamre, near Hebron, into the dry south. “Between Kadesh and Shur” is desert country on the way toward Egypt, the region where Hagar fled (16:7). He then “sojourned”, lived as a resident foreigner, in Gerar, a town in the western Negeb near Gaza.

She is my sister. The same half-truth as in Egypt (12:10–20). Sarah really was his half-sister (v. 12), but the aim was to deceive. Abraham will admit that this was a standing arrangement (v. 13). Years have passed, God has appeared to him again and again, he has just interceded boldly for Sodom, and still he falls back into the old fear.

Abimelech king of Gerar sent and took Sarah. The name Abimelech means “my father is king” and may have been a royal title; a king of Gerar with the same name appears in Isaac’s day (chapter 26). Kings took women into their households not only for beauty but for alliance, and Abraham was a wealthy and powerful chief (23:6). Unlike chapter 12, this chapter says nothing about Sarah’s beauty.

The promise in danger. The timing is what makes this so serious. God has just promised that Sarah will bear a son within the year (18:10). If she is now taken into another man’s household, the promised child is in danger, and if she conceived there, no one could be sure whose son Isaac was. God’s intervention (vv. 3–6) guarantees that Isaac is beyond doubt the son of Abraham and Sarah.

God guards the line. Ever since the promise of the woman’s offspring (3:15), the line of promise has been threatened: by barrenness, famine, kings and the patriarchs’ own sins. Again and again God guards it, until the offspring comes: Jesus, whose own life was threatened at birth by a king (Matthew 2:13–16) and kept safe by God through a dream. Nothing, not even the failures of God’s own people, can stop the promise that ends in Christ.

For us. Old sins return. The temptation we thought we had left behind years ago can reappear in a new place, especially under fear or pressure. It is wise to know our own repeated weaknesses and to watch and pray against them (Matthew 26:41).
verseByVerse.note: Gerar lay in the western Negeb, near Gaza.

verseByVerse.quote: But God came to Abimelech in a dream by night and said to him, "Behold, you are a dead man because of the woman whom you have taken, for she is a man's wife." Now Abimelech had not approached her. So he said, "Lord, will you kill an innocent people? Did he not himself say to me, 'She is my sister'? And she herself said, 'He is my brother.' In the integrity of my heart and the innocence of my hands I have done this."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God warns Abimelech in a dream that he is a dead man for taking a married woman, and the king, who has not touched her, protests that he acted innocently because both Abraham and Sarah told him she was Abraham’s sister.

God came to Abimelech in a dream by night. God speaks directly to a pagan king to protect his promise, as he later warns the magi in a dream to protect his Son (Matthew 2:12). He is the God of all the earth, not only of Abraham’s tent.

You are a dead man … for she is a man’s wife. God treats adultery as a capital offence, and Abimelech understands at once. Marriage is not a private religious custom for Abraham’s family; it is God’s order for all peoples, and he holds every nation to it.

Now Abimelech had not approached her. The narrator makes it clear at once: Sarah has not been touched. The reason is given in v. 6, and it seems to be connected with the illness that God had sent on Abimelech’s household (vv. 17–18).

Lord, will you kill an innocent people? Here is a striking echo. At Sodom Abraham asked, “Will you indeed sweep away the righteous with the wicked?” (18:23). Now a pagan king asks God Abraham’s question, and this time it is Abraham who has put the innocent in danger.

In the integrity of my heart and the innocence of my hands. Abimelech claims a clean conscience and clean hands: he did not know, and he did nothing wrong in intention. Both Abraham and Sarah had told him the same story (v. 5); Sarah went along with her husband’s plan.

A conscience among the nations. Abimelech has no Bible and no covenant, yet he knows that taking another man’s wife is wrong. Paul says that the Gentiles “show that the work of the law is written on their hearts, while their conscience also bears witness” (Romans 2:15). Christians should not be surprised to find real moral seriousness in people outside the church, and should respect it.

Does God still speak through dreams? In the Bible God sometimes spoke to people in dreams, before his word was written down. Now that he has spoken finally in his Son (Hebrews 1:1–2), he guides his people through Scripture, prayer, wisdom and godly counsel. We should not steer our lives by dreams; any dream or impression must be tested by the word God has already given.

verseByVerse.quote: Then God said to him in the dream, "Yes, I know that you have done this in the integrity of your heart, and it was I who kept you from sinning against me. Therefore I did not let you touch her. Now then, return the man's wife, for he is a prophet, so that he will pray for you, and you shall live. But if you do not return her, know that you shall surely die, you and all who are yours."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God agrees that Abimelech acted in integrity, but tells him that it was God himself who kept him from sinning; he must return Sarah to Abraham, who is a prophet and will pray for him, or he and all his household will die.

Yes, I know that you have done this in the integrity of your heart. God acknowledges the truth of Abimelech’s claim. He did not knowingly take a married woman.

It was I who kept you from sinning against me. But God claims the credit for Abimelech’s innocence: “Therefore I did not let you touch her.” Behind the king’s good conscience was God’s restraining hand, perhaps through the illness of v. 17. Notice too that adultery is a sin “against me”: every wrong done to another person is first of all an offence against God, as David confessed, “Against you, you only, have I sinned” (Psalm 51:4).

Restraining grace. God restrains sin, even in those who do not know him. If he did not, the world would be far worse than it is. This is part of his common kindness to all people, and of his providence, by which he governs all things, working through ordinary means such as conscience, illness and circumstance. We have reason to thank him not only for the sins he has forgiven us but for the sins he has kept us from, often without our knowing it.

Return the man’s wife, for he is a prophet. This is the first time the Bible calls anyone a prophet. Here the word stresses not prediction but a special relationship with God: a prophet speaks for God and stands before him to pray for others. Moses (Numbers 21:7), Samuel (1 Samuel 12:23) and Jeremiah were all intercessors. It is astonishing that God calls Abraham this at the very moment when he has lied. God’s choice of Abraham rests on grace, not on Abraham’s record. The psalmist remembers this: “Touch not my anointed ones, do my prophets no harm!” (Psalm 105:15).

So that he will pray for you, and you shall live. The innocent king must go to the guilty prophet to be healed. God honours the office he has given Abraham, even when Abraham does not honour it.

The prophet who never lied. Abraham was a prophet with deceit in his mouth. Christ is the true prophet: “He committed no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Peter 2:22). He alone speaks God’s word perfectly and prays for others without needing prayer for himself. Our prayers for one another are real and powerful, but they rest on his.
verseByVerse.note: A prophet here is one who speaks for God and prays for others (v. 7).

verseByVerse.quote: So Abimelech rose early in the morning and called all his servants and told them all these things. And the men were very much afraid. Then Abimelech called Abraham and said to him, "What have you done to us? And how have I sinned against you, that you have brought on me and my kingdom a great sin? You have done to me things that ought not to be done." And Abimelech said to Abraham, "What did you see, that you did this thing?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abimelech acts at once: he tells his servants, who are terrified, and then confronts Abraham with a just rebuke for bringing guilt on him and his kingdom.

Abimelech rose early in the morning. The pagan king obeys at once. His servants are “very much afraid”: they fear God, which is exactly what Abraham assumed they would not do (v. 11).

What have you done to us? For the second time in Abraham’s story a pagan king rebukes him for this same lie (12:18–19). Abimelech asks how he has wronged Abraham to deserve this.

A great sin. Abimelech calls adultery “a great sin”, and other ancient texts use the same expression for it. He recognises that the guilt would have fallen not only on him but on “my kingdom”: a ruler’s sin affects his people.

Things that ought not to be done. Abimelech speaks as one who knows that there is a moral order everyone is bound by. The man of God is rebuked by a man who does not know the covenant, and the outsider shows a clearer conscience than the patriarch.

What did you see, that you did this thing? In effect: what were you thinking? What did you see in us to make you act like this? Abraham has to give an account.

When the world rebukes the church. It is humbling when unbelievers rightly rebuke believers, and it happens often. When Christians deceive, exploit or behave worse than their neighbours, Paul’s words come true: “The name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you” (Romans 2:24). When an outsider rebukes us justly, the right response is not defensiveness but repentance. Jesus could ask his enemies, “Which one of you convicts me of sin?” (John 8:46), and no one could answer. We cannot ask that, but we can follow him in honesty.

verseByVerse.quote: Abraham said, "I did it because I thought, 'There is no fear of God at all in this place, and they will kill me because of my wife.' Besides, she is indeed my sister, the daughter of my father though not the daughter of my mother, and she became my wife. And when God caused me to wander from my father's house, I said to her, 'This is the kindness you must do me: at every place to which we come, say of me, "He is my brother."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abraham explains himself: he assumed there was no fear of God in Gerar and that he would be killed for his wife; Sarah is in fact his half-sister; and from the start of his travels they had agreed to tell this story wherever they went.

There is no fear of God at all in this place. Abraham misjudged them. He assumed the worst about people who did not share his faith, and he was wrong: the king and his servants feared God more readily than he did (v. 8). Prejudice and fear went together.

They will kill me because of my wife. His concern was for his own life. Fear of man made him put his wife at risk to protect himself. “The fear of man lays a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is safe” (Proverbs 29:25).

She is indeed my sister. Sarah was his half-sister, “the daughter of my father though not the daughter of my mother”. Such marriages were later forbidden in Israel’s law (Leviticus 18:9), but this was long before the law. Abraham’s statement was technically true, but it was meant to deceive. A half-truth told to mislead is a lie.

This is the kindness you must do me. The word “kindness” (hesed) is the great word for loyal, covenant love. Abraham turned it into a demand that his wife cover for him and bear the risk. And this was no sudden panic: “at every place to which we come”. Fear had become a habit, planned in advance.

Is this like Rahab’s lie? This commentary holds that deceiving those bent on murder, as Rahab did to protect the spies (Joshua 2), is not the lie the ninth commandment forbids. Abraham’s case is different. There was no actual threat, only his fear of one, and he did not deceive to protect the innocent but to protect himself, by putting his wife in danger. Scripture does not commend it; it lets a pagan king rebuke him.

The husband who gave himself. Abraham used his wife as a shield. The gospel calls husbands to the opposite, because of Christ: “Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:25). Christ did not protect himself at his bride’s expense; he protected his bride at his own.

For us. Do our fears lead us to sacrifice others to protect ourselves? Do we assume the worst of those who do not share our faith? And do we ask others to cover for our sins? The way out is not better excuses but trust in the God who has promised to protect his people, and honest confession when we fail.

Uncertain wording. In v. 13 the verb in “when God caused me to wander” is plural in Hebrew. Since the Hebrew word for God is plural in form, this can still mean the one God, and the ESV takes it so. But some think Abraham was speaking in terms a pagan king would understand, “when the gods caused me to wander”. The plural verb is unusual, but the sense of Abraham’s explanation is clear either way.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Abimelech took sheep and oxen, and male servants and female servants, and gave them to Abraham, and returned Sarah his wife to him. And Abimelech said, "Behold, my land is before you; dwell where it pleases you." To Sarah he said, "Behold, I have given your brother a thousand pieces of silver. It is a sign of your innocence in the eyes of all who are with you, and before everyone you are vindicated."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abimelech returns Sarah to Abraham with generous gifts and an open invitation to settle in his land, and he publicly clears Sarah’s honour with a large gift of silver.

Then Abimelech took sheep and oxen, and male servants and female servants. In Egypt Pharaoh gave Abraham gifts before discovering the truth and then sent him away (12:16, 20). Abimelech gives gifts after discovering it, by way of compensation, and he does not expel Abraham.

Behold, my land is before you; dwell where it pleases you. Abimelech offers Abraham the same generous freedom Abraham once offered Lot (13:9). The pagan king who was wronged is more generous than the believer who wronged him.

Your brother. There may be a note of irony in the king’s words to Sarah: he gives the money to “your brother”, the very lie that caused the trouble.

A thousand pieces of silver. A thousand shekels of silver was a very large sum, probably far more than a labourer could earn in many years. It was a public declaration that Sarah had done nothing wrong and had not been wronged.

Before everyone you are vindicated. Sarah’s honour is publicly restored. This mattered greatly, because she is about to conceive and bear Isaac. No one must be able to suggest that the promised son was the king’s child, or that Sarah had been shamed.

God cares for the vulnerable. Sarah was caught in her husband’s fear and a king’s power, with little say in either. God saw her, kept her and vindicated her. He is the God who defends those who cannot defend themselves, and in Christ he will one day vindicate his people fully before all: “Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies” (Romans 8:33).

Uncertain wording. The phrase translated “a sign of your innocence” is literally “a covering of the eyes”. It probably means a public gesture that settles the matter so that no one can look at her with suspicion or contempt, but the exact sense of the idiom is uncertain. The rest of the verse makes the general meaning clear: “before everyone you are vindicated.”

verseByVerse.quote: Then Abraham prayed to God, and God healed Abimelech, and also healed his wife and female slaves so that they bore children. For the LORD had closed all the wombs of the house of Abimelech because of Sarah, Abraham's wife.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abraham prays for Abimelech, and God heals the king, his wife and his female servants, opening the wombs he had closed because of Sarah.

Then Abraham prayed to God. This is the first time Genesis uses the usual Hebrew verb for prayer (see also v. 7). The prophet who caused the trouble now prays for the man he wronged, and God hears him.

God healed Abimelech. The healing shows that the trouble in Abimelech’s house had been God’s doing, part of how he “did not let” the king touch Sarah (v. 6).

The LORD had closed all the wombs. Here the narrator uses God’s covenant name, the LORD: the God of Abraham was acting for his promise. There is a quiet irony. Abraham, whose own wife is barren, prays for the opening of wombs in another man’s house, and in the very next verses the LORD visits Sarah and she conceives (21:1–2).

A flawed intercessor and a perfect one. God works through imperfect servants. Abraham’s failure did not cancel his calling, and Job would later pray for the friends who had wronged him (Job 42:8–10). But the chapter also makes us long for a mediator who does not need forgiving himself. Jesus prayed for those who wronged him, “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34), and he now prays for his people at the Father’s right hand.

Pray for those you have wronged, and those who wronged you. Jesus told his disciples, “Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you” (Matthew 5:44). Abraham shows the other side: pray for those you have harmed, and seek to make things right. The fact that God uses us in spite of our sin is not an excuse for sin but a reason for humble gratitude.

20.theology:
Common Grace and Moral Conscience. Abimelech's integrity shows common grace, God’s kindness to all people, at work in conscience: the image of God, though distorted by sin, still works as a moral compass. He acted rightly not because he had the law of Moses but because God had written the law's work on the heart (Rom. 2:14–15) and restrained him (v. 6). The church has no monopoly on conscience; it has the gift of the Spirit, who enables what conscience alone cannot sustain.

The Irrevocability of Calling. God calls Abraham "a prophet" (v. 7) straight after his failure as husband and honest man. "The gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable" (Rom. 11:29): a comfort, for our failures do not revoke our calling, and a warning, for our calling does not excuse them. The cracked vessel is still in the Potter's hands.
20.examples:
Then: In the ancient Near East a foreign woman travelling with a stranger was effectively unprotected, and a king could take her without fear of punishment. Abraham's deception was cowardice with a practical motive. But God protected Sarah through a Philistine king's conscience, working through someone no one would have expected.

Now: Many Christians have been dismayed to find they are still open to sins they thought were behind them. A persistent sin does not cancel our place in God's family or our calling, but it needs to be faced, confessed, and brought again and again to the God who holds his people not by their grip on him but by his grip on them. And Abimelech's integrity should keep the church humble: God’s people are not the only ones who take right and wrong seriously.

keyVerse.quote: Then God said to him in the dream, “Yes, I know that you have done this in the integrity of your heart, and it was I who kept you from sinning against me. Therefore I did not let you touch her.”
keyVerse.note: This verse reveals who is really at work in the chapter. Abraham’s fear endangered the promise, but God restrained the king’s sin and guarded Sarah, so that the promised son would be born without doubt as Abraham’s. It also teaches us to thank God for the sins he keeps us from, often unseen.

20.reflection:
Abraham repeated a sin he had committed years before (vv. 1–2; 12:10–20). What are your recurring weak points, and how can you watch and pray against them, especially under fear or pressure?

Abraham assumed there was “no fear of God at all in this place” (v. 11), and he was wrong. How might we misjudge people outside the church, and what can we learn from the integrity of an outsider like Abimelech?

God said, “it was I who kept you from sinning against me” (v. 6). Can you think of times when God may have kept you from sin through circumstances? How should that shape your gratitude and humility?

Abraham, the one who had done wrong, prayed for the king he had wronged, and God healed him (v. 17). How does Jesus’ prayer for those who crucified him shape the way you pray for people you have hurt or who have hurt you?

21.title: God Has Made Laughter for Me
21.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD visited Sarah as he had said, and the LORD did to Sarah as he had promised.<sup>2</sup>And Sarah conceived and bore Abraham a son in his old age at the time of which God had spoken to him.<sup>3</sup>Abraham called the name of his son who was born to him, whom Sarah bore him, Isaac.<sup>4</sup>And Abraham circumcised his son Isaac when he was eight days old, as God had commanded him.<sup>5</sup>Abraham was a hundred years old when his son Isaac was born to him.<sup>6</sup>And Sarah said, "God has made laughter for me; everyone who hears will laugh over me."<sup>7</sup>And she said, "Who would have said to Abraham that Sarah would nurse children? Yet I have borne him a son in his old age."<sup>8</sup>And the child grew and was weaned. And Abraham made a great feast on the day that Isaac was weaned.<sup>9</sup>But Sarah saw the son of Hagar the Egyptian, whom she had borne to Abraham, laughing.<sup>10</sup>So she said to Abraham, "Cast out this slave woman with her son, for the son of this slave woman shall not be heir with my son Isaac."<sup>11</sup>And the thing was very displeasing to Abraham on account of his son.<sup>12</sup>But God said to Abraham, "Be not displeased because of the boy and because of your slave woman. Whatever Sarah says to you, do as she tells you, for through Isaac shall your offspring be named.<sup>13</sup>And I will make a nation of the son of the slave woman also, because he is your offspring."<sup>14</sup>So Abraham rose early in the morning and took bread and a skin of water and gave it to Hagar, putting it on her shoulder, along with the child, and sent her away. And she departed and wandered in the wilderness of Beersheba.<sup>15</sup>When the water in the skin was gone, she put the child under one of the bushes.<sup>16</sup>Then she went and sat down opposite him a good way off, about the distance of a bowshot, for she said, "Let me not look on the death of the child." And as she sat opposite him, she lifted up her voice and wept.<sup>17</sup>And God heard the voice of the boy, and the angel of God called to Hagar from heaven and said to her, "What troubles you, Hagar? Fear not, for God has heard the voice of the boy where he is.<sup>18</sup>Up! Lift up the boy, and hold him fast with your hand, for I will make him into a great nation."<sup>19</sup>Then God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water. And she went and filled the skin with water and gave the boy a drink.<sup>20</sup>And God was with the boy, and he grew up. He lived in the wilderness and became an expert with the bow.<sup>21</sup>He lived in the wilderness of Paran, and his mother took a wife for him from the land of Egypt.<sup>22</sup>At that time Abimelech and Phicol the commander of his army said to Abraham, "God is with you in all that you do.<sup>23</sup>Now therefore swear to me here by God that you will not deal falsely with me or with my descendants or with my posterity, but as I have dealt kindly with you, so you will deal with me and with the land where you have sojourned."<sup>24</sup>And Abraham said, "I will swear."<sup>25</sup>When Abraham reproved Abimelech about a well of water that Abimelech's servants had seized,<sup>26</sup>Abimelech said, "I do not know who has done this thing; you did not tell me, and I have not heard of it until today."<sup>27</sup>So Abraham took sheep and oxen and gave them to Abimelech, and the two men made a covenant.<sup>28</sup>Abraham set seven ewe lambs of the flock apart.<sup>29</sup>And Abimelech said to Abraham, "What is the meaning of these seven ewe lambs that you have set apart?"<sup>30</sup>He said, "These seven ewe lambs you will take from my hand, that this may be a witness for me that I dug this well."<sup>31</sup>Therefore that place was called Beersheba, because there both of them swore an oath.<sup>32</sup>So they made a covenant at Beersheba. Then Abimelech and Phicol the commander of his army rose up and returned to the land of the Philistines.<sup>33</sup>Abraham planted a tamarisk tree in Beersheba and called there on the name of the LORD, the Everlasting God.<sup>34</sup>And Abraham sojourned many days in the land of the Philistines.
21.overview:
Where we are. Twenty-five years have passed since God first promised Abraham offspring (12:2–4), and a year since he said, “about this time next year … Sarah shall have a son” (18:14). Chapter 20 has just shown Abraham once more putting Sarah, and the promise with her, at risk.

The message. God does exactly what he said, at exactly the time he said, and the impossible child is born: the promise rests on God’s faithfulness, not on human strength. The son of promise must stand alone as heir, so the son of the slave woman is sent away; yet even in the desert God hears that boy and keeps his word to him too. And outsiders begin to see it: “God is with you in all that you do” (v. 22).

Why it was said. Israel in the wilderness was itself a people born of promise, alive only because God had kept his word (see the introduction). They needed to know why the line ran through Isaac and not Ishmael, whose descendants they met in the deserts to the south, and that the LORD who chose them also cared for those he did not choose.

How the chapter makes its case. The LORD visits Sarah, and Isaac is born, named and circumcised (vv. 1–5); Sarah’s laughter of disbelief turns to joy (vv. 6–7). At the weaning feast Sarah demands that Ishmael go, and God tells a grieving Abraham to agree, for through Isaac his offspring will be named, though Ishmael too will be a nation (vv. 8–13). In the wilderness the water runs out and Hagar weeps, but God hears the boy, opens her eyes to a well and stays with Ishmael as he grows (vv. 14–21). Then Abimelech seeks a sworn peace, Abraham settles a dispute over a well, the place is named Beersheba, and Abraham calls on the Everlasting God (vv. 22–34).

Where it leads. By promise and by pattern. Isaac is the child God gave when nature had given up, and the line of such births leads to the Son born of a virgin: “nothing will be impossible with God” (Luke 1:37; compare 18:14). Paul reads the two sons as a pattern: those who trust Christ are “children of promise”, like Isaac (Galatians 4:28), heirs by grace and not by birth or effort. And the God who heard Ishmael “where he is” is the God we meet in Jesus, who came looking for outcasts.

For us. Every Christian is an Isaac, alive because God kept a promise, so faith can laugh with Sarah. And if you are the one sent out, with the water gone, God hears you where you are, not where you ought to be.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–21 — The Birth of Isaac and the Expulsion of Hagar
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God keeps his word to the letter, and the son of promise must stand alone as heir, yet God does not forget the son who is sent away. Three times in two verses the narrator says God did “as he had said” (vv. 1–2), and Abraham names and circumcises the boy as he was told (vv. 3–5). Sarah’s laughter of disbelief becomes the laughter of joy (vv. 6–7). At the weaning feast the old conflict breaks out; God confirms that the line runs through Isaac, and promises a nation for Ishmael too (vv. 8–13). Sent into the wilderness, Hagar gives up hope, but God hears the boy, opens her eyes to water and is with Ishmael as he grows (vv. 14–21).
verseByVerse.theology: Isaac is born to Abraham at a hundred. At the weaning feast Sarah demands that Hagar and her son be cast out; God tells a grieving Abraham to do it, then hears the boy in the wilderness.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul calls the Galatians children of promise, like Isaac (Gal. 4:28). Now: God hears a child "where he is", not where he ought to be.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD visited Sarah as he had said, and the LORD did to Sarah as he had promised. And Sarah conceived and bore Abraham a son in his old age at the time of which God had spoken to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD did exactly what he had said, at exactly the time he had said: the promised son is born because God keeps his word.

The LORD visited Sarah. To “visit” in the Old Testament is for God to come and act, in judgment or in blessing; here it is a visit of grace. Joseph will use the same word as the book closes, “God will visit you” (50:24), and Israel in Egypt will hear it again (Exodus 4:31).

As he had said … as he had promised … of which God had spoken. Three times in two verses the narrator presses the point. After twenty-five years of waiting, two occasions when Abraham let Sarah be taken by a foreign king (12:10–20; 20:1–18) and one shortcut through Hagar (16:1–4), the child comes not because anyone finally got it right but because God said so. “At the time” recalls “At the appointed time I will return to you” (18:14): God was never late.

In his old age. Abraham is a hundred and Sarah ninety (17:17). This is no medical curiosity but new life where there was none: Paul says Abraham’s body was “as good as dead” and Sarah’s womb barren (Romans 4:19). Hebrews credits Sarah’s own faith: “she considered him faithful who had promised” (Hebrews 11:11).

The God who keeps his word. Isaac’s birth begins a line of children God gave to women who could not conceive, Rebekah, Rachel, Hannah, Elizabeth, each one saying that the promised offspring comes by God’s power and not by man’s. The line ends in a birth more impossible still, to a virgin, announced with words that echo 18:14: “nothing will be impossible with God” (Luke 1:37). “All the promises of God find their Yes in him” (2 Corinthians 1:20).

For us. God’s delays are not his denials. A long wait does not mean he has forgotten. “As he had said” will one day be written over every promise he has made in Christ, including the last ones: the Lord’s return and the raising of the dead.

verseByVerse.quote: Abraham called the name of his son who was born to him, whom Sarah bore him, Isaac. And Abraham circumcised his son Isaac when he was eight days old, as God had commanded him. Abraham was a hundred years old when his son Isaac was born to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abraham names the boy Isaac, as God had told him, and circumcises him on the eighth day, as God had commanded: the gift of grace is received with obedience.

Isaac. God chose the name before the boy was conceived (17:19). Isaac, Yitsḥaq, means “he laughs”, and every laugh in these chapters gathers round it: Abraham fell on his face and laughed (17:17), Sarah laughed to herself behind the tent door (18:12), and now God makes laughter for her (v. 6). The name keeps the memory of their doubt, transformed.

When he was eight days old, as God had commanded him. Circumcision was the sign of the covenant (17:9–14), and Isaac is the first child to receive it on the eighth day, as 17:12 laid down; Ishmael had been circumcised at thirteen (17:25). Abraham’s obedience is prompt and exact: grace has not made him careless. On circumcision and baptism, see the note on 17:9–14.

A hundred years old. Twenty-five years after he left Harran at seventy-five (12:4). The number is given so that no one could think the child came by Abraham’s strength.

The sign and what it pointed to. Circumcision marked Isaac as belonging to the covenant people, and pointed to what God always wanted, a circumcised heart (Deuteronomy 10:16; 30:6). In Christ that inward work is done: “In him also you were circumcised with a circumcision made without hands” (Colossians 2:11).
