verseByVerse.quote: And Sarah said, "God has made laughter for me; everyone who hears will laugh over me." And she said, "Who would have said to Abraham that Sarah would nurse children? Yet I have borne him a son in his old age."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sarah’s laughter of disbelief has become the laughter of joy, and she invites everyone to laugh with her at what God has done.

God has made laughter for me. A year before, Sarah laughed to herself at the promise and then denied it (18:12–15). Now she laughs openly and gives God the credit: he “made” the laughter, as he made the child. Laughter is the right response to grace, a joy too large to keep quiet: “When the LORD restored the fortunes of Zion, we were like those who dream. Then our mouth was filled with laughter” (Psalm 126:1–2).

Everyone who hears will laugh over me. She means laugh with her in delight. An old woman nursing a baby is a comic sight, and she does not mind; the joke is on everyone who said it could not happen.

Who would have said …? Nobody would have said it, except God, who did (18:10). Her little poem marvels that what no one could have predicted is now at her breast. She nurses the child herself, at ninety.

Joy out of impossibility. Scripture’s great songs of joy come from places like this: Hannah’s (1 Samuel 2:1–10), Mary’s (Luke 1:46–55), the women running from the empty tomb “with fear and great joy” (Matthew 28:8). The gospel is God’s last laugh over sin and death, and those who once doubted are invited to share it.

What it does not mean. Not that every longing for a child will be answered as Sarah’s was. Isaac’s birth was a unique link in the line of promise. Many faithful women have prayed and waited and not conceived, and they are no less loved, nor is their faith weaker than Sarah’s. God promised those who could have no children “a name better than sons and daughters” (Isaiah 56:5), and his yes to them in Christ is no smaller.

verseByVerse.quote: And the child grew and was weaned. And Abraham made a great feast on the day that Isaac was weaned. But Sarah saw the son of Hagar the Egyptian, whom she had borne to Abraham, laughing. So she said to Abraham, "Cast out this slave woman with her son, for the son of this slave woman shall not be heir with my son Isaac." And the thing was very displeasing to Abraham on account of his son.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the feast for Isaac’s weaning, Ishmael’s laughing exposes the rivalry in the household, and Sarah demands that Hagar and her son be driven out so that Isaac alone will inherit; Abraham is deeply distressed, because Ishmael is his son too.

The child grew and was weaned. Children were usually weaned at two or three (compare 1 Samuel 1:22–24), and in a world where many infants died the day was worth a great feast. Ishmael, fourteen years older (16:16; 21:5), was now about sixteen, old enough to understand what Isaac’s birth meant for his own future.

Laughing. The Hebrew word is a form of Isaac’s own name: Ishmael is “Isaac-ing”, laughing at the laughter-child. Paul reads it as mockery, even persecution: “he who was born according to the flesh persecuted him who was born according to the Spirit” (Galatians 4:29). See the box below.

Cast out this slave woman with her son. Sarah does not use Hagar’s name, or Ishmael’s: “this slave woman”, “her son”. Her concern is the inheritance: he “shall not be heir with my son Isaac”. Ishmael was Abraham’s firstborn, and by the customs of the day a slave wife’s son could share in his father’s estate (see Inheritance and the Firstborn). Sarah wants the matter settled for good.

Very displeasing to Abraham on account of his son. Literally “very evil in Abraham’s eyes”. Ishmael is “his son”, loved for sixteen years, and the narrator does not hide the father’s pain. The arrangement of chapter 16 has come home: a household with two mothers and two heirs cannot hold together, and those who pay most are the slave woman and her boy.

Was Sarah right? Her words are harsh, and her motives were probably mixed, with jealousy and fear among them. Yet God tells Abraham to do as she says (v. 12), and Paul quotes her words as Scripture: “Cast out the slave woman and her son, for the son of the slave woman shall not inherit with the son of the free woman” (Galatians 4:30). God can carry out his purpose through words spoken in a poor spirit without approving the spirit. What Sarah saw was true: the inheritance belongs to the child of promise alone.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew metsaḥeq can mean “laughing”, “playing” or “mocking”. The same verb describes Lot seeming to his sons-in-law to be “jesting” (19:14) and Isaac “laughing” with Rebekah in a way that showed she was his wife (26:8). The early Greek translation adds that Ishmael was playing with Isaac her son. What he was doing is not certain, but Sarah’s alarm and Paul’s reading (Galatians 4:29) favour mockery: the older son making fun of the younger, and of what he stood for.
verseByVerse.note: “Laughing” may mean laughing in mockery (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: But God said to Abraham, "Be not displeased because of the boy and because of your slave woman. Whatever Sarah says to you, do as she tells you, for through Isaac shall your offspring be named. And I will make a nation of the son of the slave woman also, because he is your offspring."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God tells Abraham to do what Sarah asks, because the promised line runs through Isaac alone; but he promises that Ishmael, as Abraham’s son, will also become a nation.

Be not displeased. God speaks into the father’s grief. He does not scold Abraham for loving Ishmael; he gives him a reason to let go, and a promise for the son he is losing.

Do as she tells you. Literally “listen to her voice”, the very phrase used when “Abram listened to the voice of Sarai” and took Hagar (16:2). Then it led him astray; now God commands it. What matters is not whose voice speaks but whether it agrees with what God has said.

Through Isaac shall your offspring be named. Abraham’s true family will be reckoned through Isaac. Paul draws out the lesson: “not all are children of Abraham because they are his offspring, but ‘Through Isaac shall your offspring be named.’ This means that it is not the children of the flesh who are the children of God, but the children of the promise are counted as offspring” (Romans 9:7–8). God’s family is made by his promise, not by descent or effort. Hebrews sets this word at the heart of Abraham’s test on Moriah (Hebrews 11:17–18): the son God now names as heir is the son he will ask Abraham to offer.

I will make a nation of the son of the slave woman also. Because he is Abraham’s offspring, Ishmael shares in a blessing (17:20), and his twelve princes are listed in 25:12–18. Being chosen for the covenant line was Isaac’s; God’s care was not withdrawn from Ishmael.

Children of promise. Paul reads the two sons as a picture of two ways of seeking God’s blessing: by our own effort, which is slavery, or by God’s promise, which is freedom (Galatians 4:21–31). “Now you, brothers, like Isaac, are children of promise” (Galatians 4:28). Every Christian is an Isaac, born, as it were, of the impossible, an heir not by right but by grace.

What it does not mean. Paul’s reading does not put Ishmael’s descendants, or any people, beyond God’s mercy. It is a picture of two ways of relating to God, not of two races. The promise that in Abraham “all the families of the earth shall be blessed” (12:3) is offered in Christ to Ishmael’s children as to Isaac’s.

verseByVerse.quote: So Abraham rose early in the morning and took bread and a skin of water and gave it to Hagar, putting it on her shoulder, along with the child, and sent her away. And she departed and wandered in the wilderness of Beersheba. When the water in the skin was gone, she put the child under one of the bushes. Then she went and sat down opposite him a good way off, about the distance of a bowshot, for she said, "Let me not look on the death of the child." And as she sat opposite him, she lifted up her voice and wept.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abraham obeys early the next morning and sends Hagar and the boy away with bread and water; when the water runs out in the desert, Hagar lays the boy down and weeps, unable to watch him die.

Abraham rose early in the morning. As he will on the morning he sets out for Moriah (22:3). The two chapters belong together. In each Abraham is told to give up a son, rises early and goes; in each the boy comes close to death; in each the angel calls from heaven, eyes are opened or lifted, and God provides, water here and a ram there. Abraham let go of both sons into God’s hands, and God kept both.

Bread and a skin of water. It seems meagre from a rich man. Perhaps he expected her to reach a camp or a settlement; the text does not say. A skin was a goat’s hide sewn into a bag, enough for a day or two in the heat. The separation is final.

Wandered in the wilderness of Beersheba. The dry Negeb in the far south, where water was found only in wells. Last time Hagar ran away by herself (16:6); this time she is sent, and she has nowhere to go.

Let me not look on the death of the child. She lays him in the thin shade of a desert bush and sits a bowshot away, far enough not to see, near enough to keep watch. Then “she lifted up her voice and wept”. Few verses in Genesis show grief so plainly: a mother who cannot save her child and cannot bear to watch.

When hope runs out. Scripture does not tidy away Hagar’s despair, and we should not tidy away other people’s. Despair is not the end of faith; it is often where God is met. If you are near the end of your strength, tell someone today, a pastor or a trusted friend, and if anyone’s life is in danger, get help the same day.

What it does not mean. This is no pattern for fathers. Abraham acted on a particular command of God, in a situation his own taking of a second wife had created. Scripture binds a father to provide for his children, “if anyone does not provide for his relatives, and especially for members of his household, he has denied the faith” (1 Timothy 5:8), and nothing here excuses abandoning a woman or a child.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of v. 14 is awkward. It may mean that Abraham put the bread and water on Hagar’s shoulder and gave her the boy, or that he set the boy on her shoulder too, as some ancient translations take it. Since Ishmael was about sixteen, the ESV’s sense is the likely one: the provisions on her shoulder and the boy with her. “Child” and “boy” are used of youths as well as infants.

verseByVerse.quote: And God heard the voice of the boy, and the angel of God called to Hagar from heaven and said to her, "What troubles you, Hagar? Fear not, for God has heard the voice of the boy where he is. Up! Lift up the boy, and hold him fast with your hand, for I will make him into a great nation."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God hears the boy where he lies and calls to Hagar from heaven, “Fear not”; he tells her to lift up her son and renews the promise that Ishmael will become a great nation.

God heard the voice of the boy. It was Hagar who wept aloud, but God heard the boy, whose name means “God hears” (16:11). Ishmael was named for this moment. Whatever he had done at the feast, God’s ear is open to the cry of the dying.

The angel of God called to Hagar from heaven. In chapter 16 the angel met Hagar on the ground by a spring; now the voice comes from heaven, as it will to Abraham on Moriah (22:11). As before, he speaks as God (“I will make him into a great nation”), and this commentary takes him to be the Son before his incarnation (see the note on 16:7–9).

What troubles you, Hagar? Fear not. For the second time God calls her by name (16:8). He is not asking for information; he is inviting her to look up from her despair.

Where he is. Not where he ought to be: not in Abraham’s tent, not in the covenant line, but under a bush in the desert. God meets the outcast where he is.

Hold him fast with your hand. Literally “make your hand strong on him”. The mother who set her son down at a distance is told to take hold of him again. God does not only rescue; he gives back what despair had let go.

The God who hears the outcast. This is the character of God that comes fully into view in Jesus. He heard the blind beggar shouting by the road when the crowd told him to be quiet (Mark 10:46–52). And he himself cried out in thirst on the cross (John 19:28), cast out of the city, so that those far off might be brought near (Ephesians 2:13).

verseByVerse.quote: Then God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water. And she went and filled the skin with water and gave the boy a drink. And God was with the boy, and he grew up. He lived in the wilderness and became an expert with the bow. He lived in the wilderness of Paran, and his mother took a wife for him from the land of Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God opens Hagar’s eyes to a well she had not seen, the boy is saved, and God is with Ishmael as he grows into a desert archer with an Egyptian wife.

God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water. The well was there before she saw it. Her need was not for God to make water but to show her what he had already provided. Despair narrows our sight; God widens it, as when Elisha prayed for his frightened servant, “O LORD, please open his eyes that he may see” (2 Kings 6:17).

And God was with the boy. A remarkable sentence about someone outside the covenant line. The same will be said of Isaac (26:3, 24), Jacob (28:15) and Joseph (39:2). God’s choice of Isaac never meant indifference to Ishmael.

An expert with the bow. The boy laid down “about the distance of a bowshot” from his mother (v. 16) grows up to master the bow, a man of the open country, as the angel had said (16:12).

The wilderness of Paran … a wife … from the land of Egypt. Paran is the desert of north-eastern Sinai, where Israel later wandered (Numbers 10:12). Hagar, an Egyptian, finds her son an Egyptian wife, and Ishmael’s line grows apart from Abraham’s faith. His descendants became the desert peoples Israel knew (25:12–18).

For us. Ask God to open your eyes to what he has already provided: the promises in his word, the people he has put near you, help that was there all along. Then do what Hagar did: go, fill the skin, and give a drink to the one in your care.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–34 — The Covenant with Abimelech at Beersheba
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The outsiders now see what Abraham’s family is: “God is with you in all that you do” (v. 22). Abimelech, the king Abraham deceived in chapter 20, comes seeking a sworn peace (vv. 22–24). Abraham agrees, but first raises honestly the matter of a well that Abimelech’s servants have seized (vv. 25–26). A covenant is made with gifts, and seven ewe lambs witness that Abraham dug the well, so the place is called Beersheba, the well of the oath (vv. 27–31). Abraham plants a tamarisk and calls on the LORD, the Everlasting God: still a sojourner, but putting down roots in God’s promise (vv. 32–34).
verseByVerse.theology: Abimelech asks Abraham to swear not to deal falsely. Abraham raises the matter of a seized well, gives seven ewe lambs as witness that he dug it, and calls on the name of the LORD.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the Philistine king sees the blessing of 12:2–3 at work. Now: a grievance should be raised with the one who caused it, who may not even know (Matt. 18:15).

verseByVerse.quote: At that time Abimelech and Phicol the commander of his army said to Abraham, "God is with you in all that you do. Now therefore swear to me here by God that you will not deal falsely with me or with my descendants or with my posterity, but as I have dealt kindly with you, so you will deal with me and with the land where you have sojourned." And Abraham said, "I will swear."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king whom Abraham once deceived now comes seeking a sworn peace, because he can see that God is with him; Abraham agrees to swear.

Abimelech and Phicol the commander of his army. Abimelech is the king of Gerar from chapter 20, and he comes with his general: this is a state visit. A king and a commander with the same names meet Isaac in 26:26, so “Abimelech” may have been a royal title, like Pharaoh, and Phicol a title or family name.

God is with you in all that you do. The outsider sees it. He has watched Abraham for years: the plague on his own household (20:17–18), Abraham’s wealth, and now a son born to a woman of ninety. The promise that in Abraham “all the families of the earth shall be blessed” (12:3) begins to work as the nations seek peace with his family because of his God.

That you will not deal falsely with me. A pointed request, since the last time they met Abraham had lied to him (20:2). Abimelech appeals to his own kindness (the word is ḥesed, loyal love) in letting Abraham live wherever he pleased in his land (20:15). The man of faith must promise an unbeliever to be honest, and the unbeliever has reason to ask.

For us. Outsiders notice when God is with his people, and they also notice when we cannot be trusted. A Christian’s plain yes or no should be as good as an oath (Matthew 5:37), so that the world can say what Abimelech said.

verseByVerse.quote: When Abraham reproved Abimelech about a well of water that Abimelech's servants had seized, Abimelech said, "I do not know who has done this thing; you did not tell me, and I have not heard of it until today."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before he swears, Abraham raises a grievance: Abimelech’s servants have seized a well he dug; Abimelech says he knew nothing of it.

A well of water. In the dry Negeb a well was life for people and flocks, and digging one was hard labour; to seize it was to take a livelihood. Isaac will face the same quarrels (26:15–22). On wells in that world, see Wells and Cisterns.

Abraham reproved Abimelech. He does not swallow the wrong or nurse it in silence. He names it, to the one responsible, before entering a covenant with him. Peace built on unspoken grievances is not peace. Jesus gives the same order: “If your brother sins against you, go and tell him his fault, between you and him alone” (Matthew 18:15).

I do not know who has done this thing. Abimelech had not heard. Many grievances are held against people who do not know they have given offence; raising the matter openly gave him the chance to put it right.

verseByVerse.quote: So Abraham took sheep and oxen and gave them to Abimelech, and the two men made a covenant. Abraham set seven ewe lambs of the flock apart. And Abimelech said to Abraham, "What is the meaning of these seven ewe lambs that you have set apart?" He said, "These seven ewe lambs you will take from my hand, that this may be a witness for me that I dug this well." Therefore that place was called Beersheba, because there both of them swore an oath.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abraham and Abimelech make a covenant, and Abraham gives seven ewe lambs as public proof that the well is his, so the place is named Beersheba, the well of the oath.

Sheep and oxen. Abraham, the one asked to swear, gives the gifts: generosity seals the peace.

Seven ewe lambs. A separate gift with a separate purpose. By accepting them in front of witnesses, Abimelech publicly acknowledges that Abraham dug the well. In a world without written deeds, a living receipt was evidence anyone could remember.

Beersheba. Be’er means “well” and sheva “seven”, and the verb “swear” comes from the same root as “seven”, so the name keeps both the lambs and the oath. Beersheba became the southern limit of Israel’s land, as in the phrase “from Dan to Beersheba” (Judges 20:1).

Honest dealing. Abraham, who once lied to this king, now insists on a clear, witnessed agreement. Faith does not make contracts unnecessary; it makes them honest. A clear agreement made before witnesses protects both sides and keeps the peace for generations.
verseByVerse.note: “Beersheba” means “well of seven” or “well of the oath” (ESV note). It marked the southern edge of the land.

verseByVerse.quote: So they made a covenant at Beersheba. Then Abimelech and Phicol the commander of his army rose up and returned to the land of the Philistines. Abraham planted a tamarisk tree in Beersheba and called there on the name of the LORD, the Everlasting God. And Abraham sojourned many days in the land of the Philistines.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With the treaty made, Abraham plants a tamarisk tree and worships the LORD as the Everlasting God: still a sojourner, he puts down roots in the land on the strength of God’s promise.

The land of the Philistines. The Philistines best known from Israel’s later history settled on the coast centuries after Abraham. Gerar’s people may have been an earlier group from the same sea peoples, or the narrator uses the name the region bore in his own day, much as a modern writer says that Abraham came from Iraq. Either way, Abraham lived among people who were not his own.

A tamarisk tree. A hardy desert tree that grows slowly, roots deep to find water and gives shade for generations. Planting one is a quiet act of faith: Abraham owns no land, yet he plants as one who expects his children to sit in its shade.

The LORD, the Everlasting God. In Hebrew, El Olam. Abraham has known God Most High (14:19), the God who sees (16:13) and God Almighty (17:1). Now, after a treaty between two mortal men, he calls on the God who does not die. Kings and treaties pass; the promise rests on the One who is God “from everlasting to everlasting” (Psalm 90:2). Isaiah uses the same title: “The LORD is the everlasting God, the Creator of the ends of the earth” (Isaiah 40:28).

Sojourned many days. Still a guest in someone else’s land. Hebrews sees the patience of faith in it: “By faith he went to live in the land of promise, as in a foreign land … For he was looking forward to the city that has foundations, whose designer and builder is God” (Hebrews 11:9–10).

For us. Christians live as sojourners too (1 Peter 2:11), yet we plant trees: we build, marry, work and invest in places that are not our final home, because our God is everlasting and nothing done for him is lost.

21.theology:
The Children of Promise. Isaac’s birth is central to Paul’s teaching in Romans 9 on election, God’s choosing of his people: "it is not the children of the flesh who are the children of God, but the children of the promise are counted as offspring" (Rom. 9:8). Membership in God's family is determined not by bloodline or merit but by the promise of God. Every believer is an Isaac: a child of the impossible, born of promise, belonging to a family made by God’s grace, not by anything in themselves.

The God Who Hears the Voiceless. Here, as in chapter 16, the God who chose Abraham is also the God who hears Ishmael and sees Hagar. His choice of the covenant line does not exhaust his care for those outside it. The widow, the orphan, the foreign slave-woman abandoned in the wilderness are the special concern of God, and his people are meant to share that concern.
21.examples:
Then: Israel knew long waiting: four hundred years in Egypt, forty in the wilderness, centuries for the promised king. God's faithfulness to Sarah was the pattern and pledge of his faithfulness to Israel. A son for a ninety-year-old woman was the same kind of impossible as redemption from Egypt or return from Babylon.

Now: Sarah's laughter (v. 6) is the right response to every promise God keeps, and the Christian life gathers one “as he had said” after another. The church gathers weekly to celebrate the promise kept: the Son of promise has come, has died, has risen. Isaac's weaning feast is a distant shadow of the marriage supper of the Lamb (Rev. 19:9), the celebration that will make every earlier joy look small.

keyVerse.quote: The LORD visited Sarah as he had said, and the LORD did to Sarah as he had promised.
keyVerse.note: After twenty-five years of waiting and more than one failure by Abraham and Sarah, the chapter opens by saying the same thing twice: God did what he said. Everything in Abraham’s story, and in ours, hangs on that sentence, and its final fulfilment is Christ, in whom all God’s promises are “Yes”.

21.reflection:
Sarah’s laughter changed from disbelief (18:12) to joy (21:6). Is there a promise of God you find hard to believe right now? What would help you keep trusting him while you wait?

Abraham was grieved by Sarah’s demand, yet God told him to let Ishmael go (vv. 11–13). When have you had to let go of something or someone you loved because of God’s purposes, and what did you learn of God in it?

God heard the boy “where he is” and opened Hagar’s eyes to a well that was already there (vv. 17–19). Who do you know who feels sent away or forgotten, and how could you help them see what God has provided?

Abraham raised his grievance about the well openly before making peace with Abimelech (vv. 25–30). Is there a grievance you are nursing in silence? What would it look like to raise it honestly and graciously?

22.title: The LORD Will Provide
22.text: <sup>1</sup>After these things God tested Abraham and said to him, "Abraham!" And he said, "Here I am."<sup>2</sup>He said, "Take your son, your only son Isaac, whom you love, and go to the land of Moriah, and offer him there as a burnt offering on one of the mountains of which I shall tell you."<sup>3</sup>So Abraham rose early in the morning, saddled his donkey, and took two of his young men with him, and his son Isaac. And he cut the wood for the burnt offering and arose and went to the place of which God had told him.<sup>4</sup>On the third day Abraham lifted up his eyes and saw the place from afar.<sup>5</sup>Then Abraham said to his young men, "Stay here with the donkey; I and the boy will go over there and worship and come again to you."<sup>6</sup>And Abraham took the wood of the burnt offering and laid it on Isaac his son. And he took in his hand the fire and the knife. So they went both of them together.<sup>7</sup>And Isaac said to his father Abraham, "My father!" And he said, "Here I am, my son." He said, "Behold, the fire and the wood, but where is the lamb for a burnt offering?"<sup>8</sup>Abraham said, "God will provide for himself the lamb for a burnt offering, my son." So they went both of them together.<sup>9</sup>When they came to the place of which God had told him, Abraham built the altar there and laid the wood in order and bound Isaac his son and laid him on the altar, on top of the wood.<sup>10</sup>Then Abraham reached out his hand and took the knife to slaughter his son.<sup>11</sup>But the angel of the LORD called to him from heaven and said, "Abraham, Abraham!" And he said, "Here I am."<sup>12</sup>He said, "Do not lay your hand on the boy or do anything to him, for now I know that you fear God, seeing you have not withheld your son, your only son, from me."<sup>13</sup>And Abraham lifted up his eyes and looked, and behold, behind him was a ram, caught in a thicket by his horns. And Abraham went and took the ram and offered it up as a burnt offering instead of his son.<sup>14</sup>So Abraham called the name of that place, "The LORD will provide"; as it is said to this day, "On the mount of the LORD it shall be provided."<sup>15</sup>And the angel of the LORD called to Abraham a second time from heaven<sup>16</sup>and said, "By myself I have sworn, declares the LORD, because you have done this and have not withheld your son, your only son,<sup>17</sup>I will surely bless you, and I will surely multiply your offspring as the stars of heaven and as the sand that is on the seashore. And your offspring shall possess the gate of his enemies,<sup>18</sup>and in your offspring shall all the nations of the earth be blessed, because you have obeyed my voice."<sup>19</sup>So Abraham returned to his young men, and they arose and went together to Beersheba. And Abraham lived at Beersheba.<sup>20</sup>Now after these things it was told to Abraham, "Behold, Milcah also has borne children to your brother Nahor:<sup>21</sup>Uz his firstborn, Buz his brother, Kemuel the father of Aram,<sup>22</sup>Chesed, Hazo, Pildash, Jidlaph, and Bethuel."<sup>23</sup>(Bethuel fathered Rebekah.) These eight Milcah bore to Nahor, Abraham's brother.<sup>24</sup>Moreover, his concubine, whose name was Reumah, bore Tebah, Gaham, Tahash, and Maacah.
22.overview:
Where we are. Isaac, the son of promise, has been born and Ishmael sent away (chapter 21), and Abraham lives at Beersheba at peace with his neighbours, his long wait over. “After these things” God gives him the hardest command of his life.

The message. God tests Abraham by asking for the son through whom every promise must come, and Abraham trusts God enough to give him up, reckoning that God could raise him from the dead. God stops his hand and provides a ram in Isaac’s place. The God who has the right to ask for everything is the God who provides the sacrifice himself.

Why it was said. Israel would live among peoples who burned their children to their gods, and would be tempted to copy them (see the introduction). Here they learned that their God has a right to everything they love, yet does not want their children on an altar: he provides the substitute. And the place became the hill where Israel’s own sacrifices were offered (2 Chronicles 3:1).

How the chapter makes its case. God commands Abraham to offer Isaac (vv. 1–2), and Abraham rises early and travels three days to the place (vv. 3–5). Father and son climb together, the son carrying the wood, and Abraham answers Isaac’s question: “God will provide” (vv. 6–8). Abraham binds Isaac and takes the knife (vv. 9–10); the angel of the LORD stops him (vv. 11–12), a ram dies instead of the son, and the place is named “The LORD will provide” (vv. 13–14). God swears by himself to bless Abraham and all nations through his offspring (vv. 15–19). A family note names Rebekah, preparing for chapter 24 (vv. 20–24).

Where it leads. By pattern and by promise, more plainly than anywhere else in Genesis. A father offers his only beloved son; the son carries the wood up the hill; a substitute dies in his place. But on Calvary no voice stopped the Father’s hand: God “did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all” (Romans 8:32). The lamb Abraham said God would provide is “the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world” (John 1:29), and the sworn blessing for the nations comes through the one offspring, Christ (Galatians 3:16).

For us. Begin with grace: God did not spare his own Son for you. Then ask whether anything you love has quietly moved from gift to god, and open your hands to the God who provides. Our losses are not God testing whether we loved someone too much; Abraham received Isaac back, and in Christ we shall receive our own.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Abraham’s faith reaches its summit when he is ready to give up the son of promise, and God shows himself as the One who provides the sacrifice. God commands the unthinkable (vv. 1–2); Abraham obeys at once, telling his servants that he and the boy will come back (vv. 3–5). Isaac carries the wood and asks where the lamb is, and Abraham answers that God will provide (vv. 6–8). At the last moment the angel of the LORD stops the knife (vv. 9–12), and a ram is offered instead of the son (vv. 13–14). God swears by himself to bless the nations through Abraham’s offspring (vv. 15–19). It is real history, and a picture of the cross, where God himself provides the sacrifice his justice requires.
verseByVerse.theology: God tests Abraham, and Abraham goes at once. On the mountain the angel stops his hand, a ram is offered instead of his son, and God swears by himself to bless him.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Abraham reckoned that God could raise the dead. Now: "He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all" (Rom. 8:32). Abraham was stopped, and God was not.

verseByVerse.quote: After these things God tested Abraham and said to him, "Abraham!" And he said, "Here I am." He said, "Take your son, your only son Isaac, whom you love, and go to the land of Moriah, and offer him there as a burnt offering on one of the mountains of which I shall tell you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God tests Abraham by commanding him to offer Isaac, the son of promise whom he loves, as a burnt offering: the gift is asked back, and the promise itself seems to be laid on the altar.

After these things God tested Abraham. The reader is told that it is a test; Abraham is not. God tempts no one to sin (James 1:13), but he tests, as fire tests gold, to prove and strengthen faith (1 Peter 1:7). Abraham has already given up his past (12:1) and his firstborn (21:14); now he is asked for his future.

Abraham! … Here I am. In Hebrew, hinneni: the answer of someone fully present and ready. Abraham says it three times in the chapter, to God (v. 1), to his son (v. 7) and to the angel (v. 11).

Your son, your only son Isaac, whom you love. Each phrase tightens the pain. Ishmael lives, but has been sent away; Isaac is the only son of the promise, and Hebrews calls him Abraham’s “only son” in that sense (Hebrews 11:17). This is the first time the word “love” appears in the Bible: a father’s love for his son.

The land of Moriah … as a burnt offering. A burnt offering was wholly burned on the altar, nothing kept back (Leviticus 1:9). The name Moriah appears again only in 2 Chronicles 3:1, where Solomon builds the temple “on Mount Moriah”, so Israel heard this as the hill where its own sacrifices would later be offered.

A command in a world of child sacrifice. Such a command would not have sounded unthinkable in Abraham’s world, where peoples round about did offer their children to their gods (2 Kings 3:27). What is new is the God who stops the knife and provides the sacrifice himself. Israel’s law later forbade child sacrifice outright (Deuteronomy 12:31).

The Father’s beloved Son. “Your only son … whom you love” is heard again over the Jordan: “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17). “For God so loved the world, that he gave his only Son” (John 3:16). Abraham was asked for what God himself would one day give.

What kind of God asks for everything? This is the chapter that makes many readers close the Bible, and the instinct is healthy: we have seen what happens when people believe God wants them to kill. Most of us would prefer a modest God who supports our plans and asks for a reasonable share. But we do not actually live without ultimate demands; we hand them to other masters. Career, success, a cause or a nation can ask for everything, and they take children too: the evenings, the marriages, the young sent to die for an ideology. Those gods never stop the knife, and they never give back what they took. The God of Genesis 22 asks Abraham for everything, then stays his hand and provides the lamb himself. He is the one God who asks for all and gives back more than he asked. And when at last a Father’s hand was not stayed, the Son who died was God’s own, not ours. He has the right to ask for everything, because he has given everything.

Where Christians differ: how could God command this? The difficulty is real. Abraham did not know God would stop him, Isaac lay bound on the wood, and the chapter commends Abraham’s readiness. It says nothing of Isaac’s fear, and that silence is part of the story’s weight. The philosopher Kierkegaard concluded that faith here sets ethics aside. This commentary’s view: God, the giver of life, had the right to require it, and never intended it to happen (v. 12); he later forbids child sacrifice absolutely (Deuteronomy 12:31). The test showed that Abraham trusted God above his dearest gift, and trusted him to keep his promise of life through this very son. It was real because Abraham did not know the ending; it was not cruel because God did.
verseByVerse.note: Only 2 Chronicles 3:1 links the name Moriah with the temple hill.

verseByVerse.quote: So Abraham rose early in the morning, saddled his donkey, and took two of his young men with him, and his son Isaac. And he cut the wood for the burnt offering and arose and went to the place of which God had told him. On the third day Abraham lifted up his eyes and saw the place from afar. Then Abraham said to his young men, "Stay here with the donkey; I and the boy will go over there and worship and come again to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abraham obeys at once and without a recorded word, travels three days to the place, and tells his servants that he and the boy will worship and come back, because he trusts God to give Isaac back to him.

Abraham rose early in the morning. His obedience is prompt, not grudging, as when he sent Hagar away (21:14). He saddles the donkey and splits the wood himself. The man who argued with God for the strangers of Sodom (18:22–33) does not argue for his son; he had learned what kind of God he was dealing with.

On the third day. Three days gave time to think, and to turn back. Abraham’s obedience held for three days of walking beside the son he expected to lose. On the third day he sees the place where his son will be given back to him, and Christian readers have long heard in it the third day of Christ’s rising.

I and the boy will go over there and worship and come again to you. In Hebrew every verb is plural: we will worship, we will come back. It is not a lie to the servants, nor wishful thinking. Abraham reasoned from the promise: God had said, “through Isaac shall your offspring be named” (21:12), so if Isaac died, God would have to raise him. “He considered that God was able even to raise him from the dead, from which, figuratively speaking, he did receive him back” (Hebrews 11:19).

Worship. Here worship means sacrifice: giving God what is dearest. Abraham has never been more a worshipper than on this road.

For us. Faith does not need to see how God will keep his word in order to keep obeying him. Abraham did not know how; he knew who.

verseByVerse.quote: And Abraham took the wood of the burnt offering and laid it on Isaac his son. And he took in his hand the fire and the knife. So they went both of them together. And Isaac said to his father Abraham, "My father!" And he said, "Here I am, my son." He said, "Behold, the fire and the wood, but where is the lamb for a burnt offering?" Abraham said, "God will provide for himself the lamb for a burnt offering, my son." So they went both of them together.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Father and son climb together, the son carrying the wood and the father the fire and the knife; when Isaac asks where the lamb is, Abraham answers in faith that God will provide it himself.

Laid it on Isaac his son. The son carries the wood up the hill on which he is to be offered, as Christ went out “bearing his own cross” (John 19:17). Isaac was probably a young man, strong enough to carry a load of wood uphill, and strong enough to resist an old father.

The fire and the knife. The fire was probably carried as live coals in a pot. The word for knife is the one used for a butcher’s knife (also in v. 10). Abraham carries the instruments of death; the son carries the fuel.

So they went both of them together. Said twice (vv. 6, 8), before and after the only conversation the chapter records. They walk in step, in silence, all the way.

My father! … Here I am, my son. The tenderest words in the chapter. Abraham is as present to his son as he is to God.

Where is the lamb for a burnt offering? The question of the whole Old Testament. Every lamb on every altar in Israel would ask it again, until John the Baptist answered it: “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!” (John 1:29).

God will provide for himself the lamb. Faith speaking before it can see. Abraham did not know how. The Hebrew is literally “God will see for himself the lamb”, that is, see to it, the same verb that gives the place its name (v. 14). The words can also be heard as God providing himself as the lamb: not what Abraham meant, but what God would one day do.

verseByVerse.quote: When they came to the place of which God had told him, Abraham built the altar there and laid the wood in order and bound Isaac his son and laid him on the altar, on top of the wood. Then Abraham reached out his hand and took the knife to slaughter his son.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abraham builds the altar, binds Isaac and lays him on the wood, and takes the knife to kill his son: he holds nothing back from God.

Built … laid … bound … laid … reached out … took. The narrator slows to the pace of dread, one action at a time, with no word of feeling. The silence lets the reader feel what is not said.

Bound Isaac his son. The binding, akedah in Hebrew, gives the chapter its Jewish name. The young man lets himself be bound by an old father, and says nothing. Christ too went willingly: “No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord” (John 10:18); “like a lamb that is led to the slaughter … so he opened not his mouth” (Isaiah 53:7).

How Jewish readers take it. In Jewish worship the Akedah is read at the New Year, and the Talmud links the ram’s horn blown then to the ram caught in the thicket (Rosh Hashanah 16a). Prayers ask God to remember Isaac’s binding for his children’s sake; rabbinic tradition prizes Abraham’s obedience and Isaac’s willing consent, and many also see here God’s rejection of child sacrifice. One midrash (Genesis Rabbah 56:3) even likens Isaac carrying the wood to a man carrying his cross. This commentary sees in the father who did not spare his son the God who did not spare his own Son (Romans 8:32; Hebrews 11:17–19).

What it does not mean. Nothing here gives anyone licence to harm a child in God’s name, or to treat an inner voice as God’s command to do what his word forbids. This was a unique moment in the history of redemption, ended by God himself, and he has since spoken plainly against such acts (Deuteronomy 12:31; Jeremiah 7:31). A voice that commands harm is not God’s voice; anyone who hears one should get help the same day.

verseByVerse.quote: But the angel of the LORD called to him from heaven and said, "Abraham, Abraham!" And he said, "Here I am." He said, "Do not lay your hand on the boy or do anything to him, for now I know that you fear God, seeing you have not withheld your son, your only son, from me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the last moment the angel of the LORD calls Abraham’s name twice and stops his hand: Abraham has shown that he fears God, for he has not withheld his only son.

Abraham, Abraham! The doubled name is urgent and tender, as God calls “Jacob, Jacob” (46:2), “Moses, Moses” (Exodus 3:4) and “Saul, Saul” (Acts 9:4). Once again Abraham answers, “Here I am.”

The angel of the LORD … from me. The angel speaks as God himself: “you have not withheld your son … from me.” This commentary takes the angel of the LORD who speaks and acts as God to be the Son appearing before his incarnation (see the note on 16:7–9). The Son who stopped Abraham’s knife would one day go to his own altar unspared.

Now I know that you fear God. “Now I know” does not mean God learned something; it means Abraham’s faith has been shown for what it is, in an act. To fear God is not terror but reverent trust that puts him above everything, even his best gifts.

Not withheld … your only son. Paul echoes this verse, in words that follow the Greek translation of Genesis closely: “He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?” (Romans 8:32). Abraham was stopped; God was not.

Where Christians differ: justified by works? James 2:21 says Abraham was justified by works when he offered Isaac; Paul says he was justified by faith (Romans 4:2–3). This commentary’s view: Abraham was counted righteous by faith (15:6) years before; here his faith was shown to be real by obedience. James speaks of faith demonstrated; Paul of faith as the means of being right with God.

verseByVerse.quote: And Abraham lifted up his eyes and looked, and behold, behind him was a ram, caught in a thicket by his horns. And Abraham went and took the ram and offered it up as a burnt offering instead of his son. So Abraham called the name of that place, "The LORD will provide"; as it is said to this day, "On the mount of the LORD it shall be provided."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God provides a ram caught in a thicket, Abraham offers it instead of his son, and he names the place “The LORD will provide”, a saying that lived on in Israel.

Abraham lifted up his eyes and looked. As God opened Hagar’s eyes to the well (21:19), so Abraham looks up and sees what God has provided, “behind him”, already there.

A ram, caught in a thicket by his horns. Abraham had said God would provide a lamb; God provides a ram. The ram serves for that day, but Isaac’s question, “where is the lamb?”, is left hanging over the rest of the Old Testament until the Lamb of God comes.

Instead of his son. The ram dies in Isaac’s place: one life given in the place of another, the heart of the chapter. Isaac was no worse than other boys, but like every child of Adam he had no claim to life before God, and he went down the mountain alive because another died. So do all who trust in Christ, “a lamb without blemish or spot” (1 Peter 1:19).

The LORD will provide. In Hebrew, Yahweh Yireh. The name became a saying in Israel, “On the mount of the LORD it shall be provided”, pointing ahead to what God would yet provide on that mountain. The temple stood there (2 Chronicles 3:1), and Christian tradition places Calvary nearby, though the text does not say so.

For us. The God who provides is not a vending machine for what we want, but the One who sees our deepest need and meets it, in the end with his own Son. The rest of his provision follows from that (Romans 8:32).

Uncertain wording. The verb ra’ah means “see”, and in v. 8 and here it means “see to it”, “provide”; the ESV note gives “the LORD will see”. The saying at the end of v. 14 can be read “it shall be provided” or, with a different vowel, “he will be seen” or “he will appear”. All agree on the main sense: on this mountain God himself sees to what is needed, and makes himself known in doing so.
verseByVerse.note: “The LORD will provide” can also be rendered “the LORD will see” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel of the LORD called to Abraham a second time from heaven and said, "By myself I have sworn, declares the LORD, because you have done this and have not withheld your son, your only son, I will surely bless you, and I will surely multiply your offspring as the stars of heaven and as the sand that is on the seashore. And your offspring shall possess the gate of his enemies, and in your offspring shall all the nations of the earth be blessed, because you have obeyed my voice." So Abraham returned to his young men, and they arose and went together to Beersheba. And Abraham lived at Beersheba.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God swears by himself to bless Abraham, to multiply his offspring, to give them victory and to bless all nations through them, because Abraham has obeyed; then Abraham returns to Beersheba.

By myself I have sworn, declares the LORD. God now seals his promise with an oath, the oath he will recall to Isaac (26:3). There is no stronger oath: “since he had no one greater by whom to swear, he swore by himself” (Hebrews 6:13).

Because you have done this. The promise was not earned here. It was given freely (12:1–3) and sealed by God alone (15:17–18) long before. But God now confirms it by oath and binds it to the obedience his grace has produced. Faith and obedience were never rivals in Abraham’s life.

As the stars of heaven and as the sand that is on the seashore. Two pictures of the uncountable, one looking up and one looking down (13:16; 15:5).

Possess the gate of his enemies. The city gate was where its defence and its government were; to hold the gate was to hold the city. Rebekah’s family will bless her in the same words (24:60). Jesus promised that “the gates of hell shall not prevail” against his church (Matthew 16:18).

Your offspring. The word is collective, meaning many descendants, as the stars and sand show. Yet the pronoun “his enemies” is singular, and Paul finds the promise’s focus in one offspring, Christ, in whom all the rest are gathered (Galatians 3:16, 29).

In your offspring shall all the nations of the earth be blessed. Peter preached this verse to the crowds in Jerusalem, telling them that God had raised up his servant Jesus and sent him to bless them first (Acts 3:25–26). The blessing that began with one family reaches every people through Abraham’s greater Son.

So Abraham returned to his young men. Isaac is not mentioned on the way down, and readers have wondered why. The text keeps its eyes on Abraham; Isaac’s next appearance is in the Negeb, waiting for his bride (24:62).

For us. Our hope rests on the same oath: “we who have fled for refuge might have strong encouragement to hold fast to the hope set before us” (Hebrews 6:18).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: While Abraham has been on the mountain, God has been preparing the future in a distant city. News comes that Abraham’s brother Nahor, far away in Mesopotamia, has twelve sons, eight by his wife Milcah and four by his concubine Reumah, as Ishmael and Jacob will each have twelve. One name in the list is singled out: “Bethuel fathered Rebekah” (v. 23). The short family record links the mountain of God’s provision to the search for Isaac’s wife in chapter 24. The woman who will carry the promise into the next generation is born and named before anyone has asked the question.
verseByVerse.theology: News comes that Nahor's wife Milcah has borne him eight sons, and, as an aside: “Bethuel fathered Rebekah.”
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the wife for Isaac is born and named before the question is asked. Now: God's provision is generally in place long before we look up.

verseByVerse.quote: Now after these things it was told to Abraham, "Behold, Milcah also has borne children to your brother Nahor: Uz his firstborn, Buz his brother, Kemuel the father of Aram, Chesed, Hazo, Pildash, Jidlaph, and Bethuel." (Bethuel fathered Rebekah.) These eight Milcah bore to Nahor, Abraham's brother. Moreover, his concubine, whose name was Reumah, bore Tebah, Gaham, Tahash, and Maacah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
News of Nahor’s twelve sons reaches Abraham, and among the grandchildren one name is singled out, Rebekah: God has already prepared the wife through whom the promise will continue.

Milcah also has borne children to your brother Nahor. “Also”: as Sarah has borne Isaac, so Milcah has borne sons. Nahor and Milcah were last mentioned in 11:29, when the family still lived in Ur; Nahor did not set out with Terah and Abraham (11:31).

Uz his firstborn, Buz his brother. Several of these names reappear later as peoples or places: Job lived “in the land of Uz” (Job 1:1), and Elihu was a Buzite (Job 32:2). Kemuel is called “the father of Aram”, the forebear of an Aramean clan.

Bethuel fathered Rebekah. The only granddaughter named in the list. Rebekah is introduced ahead of chapter 24: on the far side of the desert, Isaac’s bride is already being prepared.

His concubine, whose name was Reumah. A secondary wife, of lower standing. Genesis records the arrangement without approving it (see the note on 16:1–3). With her four sons Nahor has twelve, as Ishmael (25:13–16) and Jacob will have.

For us. God’s provision is usually in place long before we look up and see it. While Abraham was climbing Moriah, Rebekah was growing up in Mesopotamia.
verseByVerse.note: Rebekah is the granddaughter of Abraham’s brother Nahor.

22.theology:
A Substitute Provided. The ram dies in Isaac's place. Isaac was no more guilty than any other boy, but like every child of Adam he could not stand before God on his own, and he was spared by a life given for his. The sacrificial system is built on this pattern, and it is fulfilled at the cross. The Lamb of God does not merely provide a substitute; he is the substitute, offered by the Father and giving himself.

Resurrection Faith. Hebrews 11:19 names the reason for Abraham’s obedience: he "considered that God was able even to raise him from the dead, from which, figuratively speaking, he did receive him back." He trusted the God who had made the impossible promise to keep it even through death. This is the faith that justifies: not certainty about outcomes but trust in the God of resurrection.
22.examples:
Then: 2 Chronicles 3:1 places Solomon's temple on Mount Moriah, so the place of Abraham's great act of faith became the place of Israel's sacrifices, all pointing to a provision still to come. On this one mountain the whole story of redemption comes together.

Now: Begin with grace: God did not spare his own Son for us. Only then hear the chapter's question: is there anything we love so much that it has quietly moved from gift to god? If you have clutched your Isaac, as most of us have, the way back is to look again at the God who provides, and open your hands. And if you have lost someone you love, this chapter does not mean God took them to test whether you loved them too much. Our losses are not God weighing our love. Abraham received Isaac back, and in Christ we shall receive our own back too.

keyVerse.quote: Abraham said, “God will provide for himself the lamb for a burnt offering, my son.”
keyVerse.note: Isaac’s question, “where is the lamb?”, is the question every altar in Israel would ask, and Abraham’s answer is faith speaking before it can see. God provided a ram that day, but the full answer came when John pointed to Jesus and said, “Behold, the Lamb of God.” The God who asked Abraham for his son gave his own.

22.reflection:
Abraham had to choose between holding on to God’s gift and trusting the Giver (vv. 1–3). What gifts in your life are most likely to move quietly from gift to god? What would it mean to hold them with open hands?

Abraham told his servants, “I and the boy will … come again to you” (v. 5), and Hebrews says he believed God could raise the dead (Hebrews 11:19). How does belief in the resurrection change the way you face loss or costly obedience?

Trace the likenesses between this chapter and the cross: the only son, the wood, the third day, the lamb, the substitute. Where does the story differ, and why does that difference matter so much?

Abraham named the place “The LORD will provide” (v. 14). Share a time when God provided what you needed, perhaps not what you expected. How does Romans 8:32 help you trust him for what you cannot yet see?

23.title: A Burial Place for Sarah
23.text: <sup>1</sup>Sarah lived 127 years; these were the years of the life of Sarah.<sup>2</sup>And Sarah died at Kiriath-arba (that is, Hebron) in the land of Canaan, and Abraham went in to mourn for Sarah and to weep for her.<sup>3</sup>And Abraham rose up from before his dead and said to the Hittites,<sup>4</sup>"I am a sojourner and foreigner among you; give me property among you for a burying place, that I may bury my dead out of my sight."<sup>5</sup>The Hittites answered Abraham,<sup>6</sup>"Hear us, my lord; you are a prince of God among us. Bury your dead in the choicest of our tombs. None of us will withhold from you his tomb to hinder you from burying your dead."<sup>7</sup>Abraham rose and bowed to the Hittites, the people of the land.<sup>8</sup>And he said to them, "If you are willing that I should bury my dead out of my sight, hear me and entreat for me Ephron the son of Zohar,<sup>9</sup>that he may give me the cave of Machpelah, which he owns; it is at the end of his field. For the full price let him give it to me in your presence as property for a burying place."<sup>10</sup>Now Ephron was sitting among the Hittites, and Ephron the Hittite answered Abraham in the hearing of the Hittites, of all who went in at the gate of his city,<sup>11</sup>"No, my lord, hear me: I give you the field, and I give you the cave that is in it. In the sight of the sons of my people I give it to you. Bury your dead."<sup>12</sup>Then Abraham bowed down before the people of the land.<sup>13</sup>And he said to Ephron in the hearing of the people of the land, "But if you will, hear me: I give the price of the field. Accept it from me, that I may bury my dead there."<sup>14</sup>Ephron answered Abraham,<sup>15</sup>"My lord, listen to me: a piece of land worth four hundred shekels of silver, what is that between you and me? Bury your dead."<sup>16</sup>Abraham listened to Ephron, and Abraham weighed out for Ephron the silver that he had named in the hearing of the Hittites, four hundred shekels of silver, according to the weights current among the merchants.<sup>17</sup>So the field of Ephron in Machpelah, which was to the east of Mamre, the field with the cave that was in it and all the trees that were in the field, throughout its whole area, was made over<sup>18</sup>to Abraham as a possession in the presence of the Hittites, before all who went in at the gate of his city.<sup>19</sup>After this, Abraham buried Sarah his wife in the cave of the field of Machpelah east of Mamre (that is, Hebron) in the land of Canaan.<sup>20</sup>The field and the cave that is in it were made over to Abraham as property for a burying place by the Hittites.
23.overview:
Where we are. Years have passed since Moriah. Sarah was ninety when Isaac was born, so when she dies at 127 he is thirty-seven. Abraham, living again near Hebron, still owns “not even a foot’s length” of the land God promised him (Acts 7:5).

The message. Faith grieves, and faith buys a grave. Abraham weeps for Sarah; then, a landless foreigner, he buys a burial place in Canaan at full price and with clear title, so that his wife lies in the land God promised and not in a borrowed tomb. The first piece of the promised land Abraham owns is a grave, a pledge that God’s promise reaches beyond death.

Why it was said. Israel, on its way to Canaan, needed to know that it was not seizing a stranger’s land but coming home to a promise its fathers had believed to the grave (see the introduction). The cave of Machpelah, bought and witnessed, was their first title deed, and their fathers’ bones were already waiting there (49:29–32; 50:13).

How the chapter makes its case. Sarah dies, and Abraham mourns and weeps (vv. 1–2). He rises and asks the Hittites for a burial place, calling himself a sojourner; they honour him as “a prince of God” and offer any tomb (vv. 3–6). He asks for Ephron’s cave at full price, and Ephron publicly offers to give it (vv. 7–11). Abraham insists on paying, Ephron names a high price, and Abraham weighs out the silver before witnesses (vv. 12–16). The field and cave are deeded to him, and he buries Sarah there (vv. 17–20).

Where it leads. By the need it exposes, and by promise. Abraham died owning only a grave, “not having received the things promised, but having seen them and greeted them from afar” (Hebrews 11:13). Death is the enemy every promise of God must overcome, and Genesis can only bury its dead in hope. Christ is the answer: he was laid in a borrowed tomb he needed for only three days, and he has been raised as “the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (1 Corinthians 15:20). So God “is not ashamed to be called their God, for he has prepared for them a city” (Hebrews 11:16).

For us. Grief is not unbelief; weep freely. But Christians bury their dead as people who expect to see them again, and how we honour the body, deal honestly with outsiders and live as sojourners all show what we believe about the future.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–20 — The Death of Sarah and the Purchase of Machpelah
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Abraham’s grief and his careful purchase belong together: the man who weeps for Sarah buys a grave in the land of promise, at full price and before witnesses, as an act of hope. Sarah dies, and Abraham mourns (vv. 1–2). Then he rises and, as a landless foreigner, asks the Hittites for a burial place (vv. 3–6). The courteous bargaining at the city gate (vv. 7–16) ends in a public sale: Abraham refuses a gift, pays four hundred shekels and receives the field and cave as his own (vv. 17–20). The only part of the promised land he ever owns is a grave, where Isaac, Rebekah, Leah and Jacob will one day lie beside him (49:29–32).
verseByVerse.theology: A sojourner with no land, Abraham asks the Hittites for a burial place, refuses Ephron's gift, and pays in public for the cave of Machpelah, the only part of the promised land he ever owns.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Abraham, Isaac, Rebekah, Leah and Jacob will all be laid there (49:29–32). Now: believers too are buried in hope of God’s promise.

verseByVerse.quote: Sarah lived 127 years; these were the years of the life of Sarah. And Sarah died at Kiriath-arba (that is, Hebron) in the land of Canaan, and Abraham went in to mourn for Sarah and to weep for her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sarah dies at 127 at Hebron, and Abraham mourns and weeps for her: the man of faith grieves openly.

Sarah lived 127 years. The age at death of Sarah is recorded as Abraham’s, Isaac’s and Jacob’s are: she is a mother of the nation, the woman through whom the promise came. She lived to see her son a grown man of thirty-seven.

Kiriath-arba (that is, Hebron). “The city of Arba”, named after a great man among the Anakim (Joshua 14:15), was its old name; the narrator adds the name his readers knew. Hebron lay in the hill country near Mamre, where Abraham had lived and built an altar (13:18).

Abraham went in to mourn for Sarah and to weep for her. Probably he went into the tent where she lay. To mourn was the public, customary lament for the dead (see Mourning Customs); to weep is personal grief. Abraham does both. The man who climbed Moriah without a recorded tear weeps at his wife’s side.

Faith grieves. Faith grieves, not without hope, but truly: Paul does not forbid grief, only grieving “as others do who have no hope” (1 Thessalonians 4:13). Jesus wept at the tomb of Lazarus moments before he raised him (John 11:35). It is right to weep for those you love, and faith does not ask you to hurry your tears.

When grief does not lift. Grief takes time, often far longer than friends expect. But if it settles into a darkness that does not lift for months, talk to your pastor or a biblical counsellor and see your doctor; medicine, where it is needed, is no failure of faith. If you have thoughts of ending your life, get help the same day.
verseByVerse.note: Sarah is the only woman in the Bible whose age at death is recorded.

verseByVerse.quote: And Abraham rose up from before his dead and said to the Hittites, "I am a sojourner and foreigner among you; give me property among you for a burying place, that I may bury my dead out of my sight." The Hittites answered Abraham, "Hear us, my lord; you are a prince of God among us. Bury your dead in the choicest of our tombs. None of us will withhold from you his tomb to hinder you from burying your dead."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abraham, a foreigner who owns no land, asks the Hittites for a burial place of his own, and they answer with honour, offering him the best of their tombs.

Abraham rose up from before his dead. Grief has its time, and then love has work to do. He rises and sees to the next thing.

The Hittites. Literally “the sons of Heth”, descendants of Heth, a son of Canaan (10:15), living in the hill country around Hebron. They are probably not the same as the great Hittite empire far to the north, though they may have been related.

I am a sojourner and foreigner among you. After some sixty years in the land Abraham owns none of it. He is a resident foreigner, allowed to live there but with no right to buy land without the community’s consent, which is why he asks the whole assembly. Hebrews sees in his words the confession of faith: “they were strangers and exiles on the earth” (Hebrews 11:13). David will pray the same: “I am a sojourner with you, a guest, like all my fathers” (Psalm 39:12).

Give me property among you for a burying place. The word for “property” means a lasting holding, the same word God used when he promised Abraham “all the land of Canaan, for an everlasting possession” (17:8). Abraham asks for a tiny first piece of it.

That I may bury my dead out of my sight. Not coldness. In that heat burial followed death quickly (see Burial Customs and Tombs), and love saw to it with care.

Bury your dead in the choicest of our tombs. A generous offer, and an honour to Abraham. But a tomb in someone else’s burial ground would leave his family as guests even in death. He wants a grave that is his.

Uncertain wording. “A prince of God” may mean a prince blessed by God, as the Hittites could see (compare 21:22). But Hebrew sometimes uses the word “God” to make a superlative, so it may simply mean “a mighty prince”, as the ESV note allows. Either way, his neighbours hold the landless foreigner in great respect.
verseByVerse.note: The Hittites here are “sons of Heth” (ESV note), a people living in Canaan.

verseByVerse.quote: Abraham rose and bowed to the Hittites, the people of the land. And he said to them, "If you are willing that I should bury my dead out of my sight, hear me and entreat for me Ephron the son of Zohar, that he may give me the cave of Machpelah, which he owns; it is at the end of his field. For the full price let him give it to me in your presence as property for a burying place." Now Ephron was sitting among the Hittites, and Ephron the Hittite answered Abraham in the hearing of the Hittites, of all who went in at the gate of his city, "No, my lord, hear me: I give you the field, and I give you the cave that is in it. In the sight of the sons of my people I give it to you. Bury your dead."
verseByVerse.commentary:
With great courtesy Abraham asks for Ephron’s cave of Machpelah at full price, and Ephron, before everyone at the city gate, offers to give him the field and the cave.

Abraham rose and bowed to the Hittites. He treats the people of the land with respect. Faith in God’s promise of their land does not make him rude or grasping towards them; he is gracious and patient with those he lives among.

Entreat for me Ephron the son of Zohar. He asks the assembly to speak for him, as custom required: a sale of land was a matter for the whole community, not a private deal.

The cave of Machpelah … at the end of his field. Abraham asks only for the cave on the edge of the field. Ephron offers the whole field, perhaps to sell more than was asked. Machpelah may mean “double”, perhaps a cave with two chambers.

For the full price. Literally “for full silver”. Centuries later David will use the same words at the threshing floor of Araunah (Ornan), the site of the temple on Mount Moriah: “I will buy them for the full price. I will not take for the LORD what is yours” (1 Chronicles 21:24).

In the hearing of … all who went in at the gate of his city. The city gate was where the elders sat and where business was witnessed (compare Ruth 4:1–11). Every word is said in public, so every word carries legal weight.

I give you the field. Ephron’s “I give it to you” is polite bargaining, the courteous opening of a sale, not a real offer. And had Abraham accepted a gift, the gift could be taken back, or leave him in Ephron’s debt. He wants clear legal title.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Abraham bowed down before the people of the land. And he said to Ephron in the hearing of the people of the land, "But if you will, hear me: I give the price of the field. Accept it from me, that I may bury my dead there." Ephron answered Abraham, "My lord, listen to me: a piece of land worth four hundred shekels of silver, what is that between you and me? Bury your dead." Abraham listened to Ephron, and Abraham weighed out for Ephron the silver that he had named in the hearing of the Hittites, four hundred shekels of silver, according to the weights current among the merchants.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abraham insists on paying; Ephron names his price as if it were nothing, four hundred shekels of silver, and Abraham weighs it out at once, without haggling, before witnesses.

Abraham bowed down before the people of the land. A second bow: courtesy all the way through.

I give the price of the field. Accept it from me. Abraham will not receive the land as a Canaanite’s gift, any more than he would let the king of Sodom say, “I have made Abram rich” (14:23). The land is God’s to give. What Abraham takes now he pays for, so that no one can claim his family’s place there was a favour from the people of the land.

Four hundred shekels of silver, what is that between you and me? Ephron names his price under cover of politeness, and it is high. Centuries later Jeremiah paid seventeen shekels for a field (Jeremiah 32:9), and David fifty for Araunah’s threshing floor and oxen (2 Samuel 24:24). Prices varied greatly from age to age, but four hundred was a great deal of money.

Abraham weighed out for Ephron the silver. There were no coins yet. A shekel was a weight, and silver was weighed on scales against stones of agreed weight, “the weights current among the merchants” (see Weights and Scales). Abraham pays the price named, in full, in public, at once. He could have bargained; he does not want his wife’s grave to be the subject of a quarrel.

Honest dealing. An open, witnessed transaction, with the price stated and paid in full, is a pattern for business. “A false balance is an abomination to the LORD, but a just weight is his delight” (Proverbs 11:1). Get agreements clear, put them on record, and pay what you agreed.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians must never bargain. Abraham had reasons of his own for paying without question, and fair negotiation is no sin; deceit and taking advantage are.
verseByVerse.note: Four hundred shekels was about 10 pounds of silver (a shekel was about 2/5 ounce, ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: So the field of Ephron in Machpelah, which was to the east of Mamre, the field with the cave that was in it and all the trees that were in the field, throughout its whole area, was made over to Abraham as a possession in the presence of the Hittites, before all who went in at the gate of his city. After this, Abraham buried Sarah his wife in the cave of the field of Machpelah east of Mamre (that is, Hebron) in the land of Canaan. The field and the cave that is in it were made over to Abraham as property for a burying place by the Hittites.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The field, the cave and every tree in it are made over to Abraham before all the townspeople, and he buries Sarah there: the first piece of the promised land he owns is a grave.

The field … the cave … all the trees … throughout its whole area. The wording reads like a title deed, listing the land, its boundaries and even its trees, and naming the witnesses, “all who went in at the gate of his city”. Nothing is left open to dispute.

Abraham buried Sarah his wife. The long negotiation was for this sentence. Sarah, who left Ur and Harran with him, is laid to rest in the land of promise.

A family grave. Abraham will be buried here (25:9), and Isaac, Rebekah, Leah and Jacob after him (49:29–32). Jacob made his sons swear to carry his body back from Egypt to this cave (50:13): he wanted to be buried where God had promised his family a future. The traditional site in Hebron, beneath a great enclosure built by Herod the Great, is still revered by Jews, Christians and Muslims.

A first instalment. Stephen reminded his hearers that God gave Abraham “no inheritance in it, not even a foot’s length, but promised to give it to him as a possession” (Acts 7:5). The grave was a first instalment of the promise, held by faith. The patriarchs’ care for burial shows their hope that God would keep his promise beyond death, the hope that grows into the resurrection of the body.

The tomb that could not hold him. Christ too was buried in a rich man’s tomb, a borrowed grave cut in the rock (Matthew 27:57–60), and he needed it for only three days. Because he rose, the graves of his people are not the end of the promise but places where bodies rest until the day he raises them. Every Christian burial is a little Machpelah: a claim staked on the future.

Does it matter how Christians bury their dead? Scripture lays down no law about burial or cremation, and God can raise a body from ashes as easily as from dust. But burial has long been the Christian custom, following the burial of the patriarchs and of Christ himself, because it pictures the body sown in hope (see the note on 1 Corinthians 15:35–36).
verseByVerse.note: The cave of Machpelah lay at Hebron.

23.theology:
Grief and Faith. Genesis 23 refuses to separate real grief from real faith. Abraham mourns and weeps; he also rises and acts. The psalms of lament do the same: honest pain before God, then the refrain of trust. The New Testament does not abolish grief but frames it: "that you may not grieve as others do who have no hope" (1 Thess. 4:13). The hope of resurrection does not suppress the tears of loss; it tells us they will not last for ever. Death is still an enemy, and the weeping now is real; but the resurrection morning will be more real still.

The Pilgrim Posture. Abraham's self-description as "a sojourner and foreigner" (v. 4) becomes the identity of the people of God throughout Scripture: "I urge you as sojourners and exiles to abstain from the passions of the flesh" (1 Peter 2:11). Those who know they are passing through have a particular freedom. They can be generous because they are not accumulating, bold because they are not protecting a permanent stake, and they can love their neighbours without needing them to be their home.
23.examples:
Then: The negotiation at the city gate before witnesses, which some scholars compare to Hittite land law, was needed to establish permanent ownership rather than a lease. A gift could be reclaimed; a legal purchase could not (vv. 11–13). Abraham secured the first instalment of the promise in the most durable form available.

Now: The modern West has largely hidden death from view and handed it to hospitals, losing both honest grief and the faith that gives it meaning. Abraham weeps for Sarah, not for death in general, then acts purposefully, trusting the promise. The church that recovers honest, hopeful grief for particular people will serve its culture better than one that either covers grief with clichés or drowns in it without hope.

keyVerse.quote: I am a sojourner and foreigner among you; give me property among you for a burying place, that I may bury my dead out of my sight.
keyVerse.note: Abraham, heir of the whole land by God’s promise, has to ask for a grave as a foreigner. The verse holds the tension of the life of faith: owning nothing yet, sure of everything. Hebrews takes up his words as the confession of all God’s people, who look for the city God has prepared, made sure by the risen Christ.

23.reflection:
Abraham mourned and wept for Sarah (v. 2), and then rose to do what needed doing (v. 3). How has your church helped, or failed to help, people who grieve? What does grieving “with hope” look like in practice?

Abraham called himself “a sojourner and foreigner” (v. 4). In what ways do you feel at home in this world, and in what ways like a stranger? How should that shape what you invest in?

Abraham insisted on paying the full price, openly and before witnesses (vv. 13–16). What would that kind of integrity look like in your work, your finances or your dealings with neighbours who do not share your faith?

The only land Abraham ever owned was a grave. How does Christ’s resurrection change the way you think about death, burial and the promises of God that are not yet fulfilled?

24.title: A Wife for Isaac
24.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Abraham was old, well advanced in years. And the LORD had blessed Abraham in all things.<sup>2</sup>And Abraham said to his servant, the oldest of his household, who had charge of all that he had, "Put your hand under my thigh,<sup>3</sup>that I may make you swear by the LORD, the God of heaven and God of the earth, that you will not take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites, among whom I dwell,<sup>4</sup>but will go to my country and to my kindred, and take a wife for my son Isaac."<sup>5</sup>The servant said to him, "Perhaps the woman may not be willing to follow me to this land. Must I then take your son back to the land from which you came?"<sup>6</sup>Abraham said to him, "See to it that you do not take my son back there.<sup>7</sup>The LORD, the God of heaven, who took me from my father's house and from the land of my kindred, and who spoke to me and swore to me, 'To your offspring I will give this land,' he will send his angel before you, and you shall take a wife for my son from there.<sup>8</sup>But if the woman is not willing to follow you, then you will be free from this oath of mine; only you must not take my son back there."<sup>9</sup>So the servant put his hand under the thigh of Abraham his master and swore to him concerning this matter.<sup>10</sup>Then the servant took ten of his master's camels and departed, taking all sorts of choice gifts from his master; and he arose and went to Mesopotamia to the city of Nahor.<sup>11</sup>And he made the camels kneel down outside the city by the well of water at the time of evening, the time when women go out to draw water.<sup>12</sup>And he said, "O LORD, God of my master Abraham, please grant me success today and show steadfast love to my master Abraham.<sup>13</sup>Behold, I am standing by the spring of water, and the daughters of the men of the city are coming out to draw water.<sup>14</sup>Let the young woman to whom I shall say, 'Please let down your jar that I may drink,' and who shall say, 'Drink, and I will water your camels'—let her be the one whom you have appointed for your servant Isaac. By this I shall know that you have shown steadfast love to my master."<sup>15</sup>Before he had finished speaking, behold, Rebekah, who was born to Bethuel the son of Milcah, the wife of Nahor, Abraham's brother, came out with her water jar on her shoulder.<sup>16</sup>The young woman was very attractive in appearance, a maiden whom no man had known. She went down to the spring and filled her jar and came up.<sup>17</sup>Then the servant ran to meet her and said, "Please give me a little water to drink from your jar."<sup>18</sup>She said, "Drink, my lord." And she quickly let down her jar upon her hand and gave him a drink.<sup>19</sup>When she had finished giving him a drink, she said, "I will draw water for your camels also, until they have finished drinking."<sup>20</sup>So she quickly emptied her jar into the trough and ran again to the well to draw water, and she drew for all his camels.<sup>21</sup>The man gazed at her in silence to learn whether the LORD had prospered his journey or not.<sup>22</sup>When the camels had finished drinking, the man took a gold ring weighing a half shekel, and two bracelets for her arms weighing ten gold shekels,<sup>23</sup>and said, "Please tell me whose daughter you are. Is there room in your father's house for us to spend the night?"<sup>24</sup>She said to him, "I am the daughter of Bethuel the son of Milcah, whom she bore to Nahor."<sup>25</sup>She added, "We have plenty of both straw and fodder, and room to spend the night."<sup>26</sup>The man bowed his head and worshiped the LORD<sup>27</sup>and said, "Blessed be the LORD, the God of my master Abraham, who has not forsaken his steadfast love and his faithfulness toward my master.
