As for me, the LORD has led me in the way to the house of my master's kinsmen."<sup>28</sup>Then the young woman ran and told her mother's household about these things.<sup>29</sup>Rebekah had a brother whose name was Laban. Laban ran out toward the man, to the spring.<sup>30</sup>As soon as he saw the ring and the bracelets on his sister's arms, and heard the words of Rebekah his sister, "Thus the man spoke to me," he went to the man. And behold, he was standing by the camels at the spring.<sup>31</sup>He said, "Come in, O blessed of the LORD. Why do you stand outside? For I have prepared the house and a place for the camels."<sup>32</sup>So the man came to the house and unharnessed the camels, and gave straw and fodder to the camels, and there was water to wash his feet and the feet of the men who were with him.<sup>33</sup>Then food was set before him to eat. But he said, "I will not eat until I have said what I have to say." He said, "Speak on."<sup>34</sup>So he said, "I am Abraham's servant.<sup>35</sup>The LORD has greatly blessed my master, and he has become great. He has given him flocks and herds, silver and gold, male servants and female servants, camels and donkeys.<sup>36</sup>And Sarah my master's wife bore a son to my master when she was old, and to him he has given all that he has.<sup>37</sup>My master made me swear, saying, 'You shall not take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites, in whose land I dwell,<sup>38</sup>but you shall go to my father's house and to my clan and take a wife for my son.'<sup>39</sup>I said to my master, 'Perhaps the woman will not follow me.'<sup>40</sup>But he said to me, 'The LORD, before whom I have walked, will send his angel with you and prosper your way. You shall take a wife for my son from my clan and from my father's house.<sup>41</sup>Then you will be free from my oath, when you come to my clan. And if they will not give her to you, you will be free from my oath.'<sup>42</sup>"I came today to the spring and said, 'O LORD, the God of my master Abraham, if now you are prospering the way that I go,<sup>43</sup>behold, I am standing by the spring of water. Let the virgin who comes out to draw water, to whom I shall say, "Please give me a little water from your jar to drink,"<sup>44</sup>and who will say to me, "Drink, and I will draw for your camels also," let her be the woman whom the LORD has appointed for my master's son.'<sup>45</sup>"Before I had finished speaking in my heart, behold, Rebekah came out with her water jar on her shoulder, and she went down to the spring and drew water. I said to her, 'Please let me drink.'<sup>46</sup>She quickly let down her jar from her shoulder and said, 'Drink, and I will give your camels drink also.' So I drank, and she gave the camels drink also.<sup>47</sup>Then I asked her, 'Whose daughter are you?' She said, 'The daughter of Bethuel, Nahor's son, whom Milcah bore to him.' So I put the ring on her nose and the bracelets on her arms.<sup>48</sup>Then I bowed my head and worshiped the LORD and blessed the LORD, the God of my master Abraham, who had led me by the right way to take the daughter of my master's kinsman for his son.<sup>49</sup>Now then, if you are going to show steadfast love and faithfulness to my master, tell me; and if not, tell me, that I may turn to the right hand or to the left."<sup>50</sup>Then Laban and Bethuel answered and said, "The thing has come from the LORD; we cannot speak to you bad or good.<sup>51</sup>Behold, Rebekah is before you; take her and go, and let her be the wife of your master's son, as the LORD has spoken."<sup>52</sup>When Abraham's servant heard their words, he bowed himself to the earth before the LORD.<sup>53</sup>And the servant brought out jewelry of silver and of gold, and garments, and gave them to Rebekah. He also gave to her brother and to her mother costly ornaments.<sup>54</sup>And he and the men who were with him ate and drank, and they spent the night there. When they arose in the morning, he said, "Send me away to my master."<sup>55</sup>Her brother and her mother said, "Let the young woman remain with us a while, at least ten days; after that she may go."<sup>56</sup>But he said to them, "Do not delay me, since the LORD has prospered my way. Send me away that I may go to my master."<sup>57</sup>They said, "Let us call the young woman and ask her."<sup>58</sup>And they called Rebekah and said to her, "Will you go with this man?" She said, "I will go."<sup>59</sup>So they sent away Rebekah their sister and her nurse, and Abraham's servant and his men.<sup>60</sup>And they blessed Rebekah and said to her, "Our sister, may you become thousands of ten thousands, and may your offspring possess the gate of those who hate him!"<sup>61</sup>Then Rebekah and her young women arose and rode on the camels and followed the man. Thus the servant took Rebekah and went his way.<sup>62</sup>Now Isaac had returned from Beer-lahai-roi and was dwelling in the Negeb.<sup>63</sup>And Isaac went out to meditate in the field toward evening. And he lifted up his eyes and saw, and behold, there were camels coming.<sup>64</sup>And Rebekah lifted up her eyes, and when she saw Isaac, she dismounted from the camel<sup>65</sup>and said to the servant, "Who is that man, walking in the field to meet us?" The servant said, "It is my master." So she took her veil and covered herself.<sup>66</sup>And the servant told Isaac all the things that he had done.<sup>67</sup>Then Isaac brought her into the tent of Sarah his mother and took Rebekah, and she became his wife, and he loved her. So Isaac was comforted after his mother's death.
24.overview:
Where we are. Sarah has died and been buried in the land (chapter 23), and Abraham is old. Isaac is about forty (25:20) and unmarried, and the promise of countless offspring through him waits on a wife. This is the last thing Abraham does for the promise, told in the longest chapter of Genesis.

The message. The God who made the promise guides the steps of those who serve it, through ordinary means: an oath, a journey, a prayer, a well, a kind young woman, a family’s consent. The chapter’s key word is “steadfast love” (vv. 12, 14, 27, 49): what looks like coincidence is God’s loyal love to Abraham, carrying his covenant into the next generation. And Rebekah’s “I will go” (v. 58) is faith answering God’s leading as Abraham once did.

Why it was said. Israel would be tempted to marry into the peoples of Canaan and drift into their gods (Deuteronomy 7:3–4); this chapter showed why the covenant family must not (see the introduction). It also taught them that the God who called Abraham was not distant: he hears prayer and leads his servants in the way.

How the chapter makes its case. Abraham makes his oldest servant swear to find Isaac a wife from his kindred and never to take Isaac back there (vv. 1–9). At the well outside Nahor’s city the servant prays for a sign that would reveal a generous heart, and before he finishes Rebekah does exactly that (vv. 10–21); learning who she is, he worships (vv. 22–27). At her family’s house he tells the whole story again (vv. 28–49), the family agrees that “the thing has come from the LORD”, and Rebekah says, “I will go” (vv. 50–61). Isaac meets his bride in the field at evening, takes her into Sarah’s tent and loves her (vv. 62–67).

Where it leads. By promise, and by the character of God revealed in Christ. The promised offspring needs a mother, and God guards the line that leads to Christ through a marriage he arranges himself. The “steadfast love and faithfulness” the servant praises (v. 27) came in person in Jesus, “full of grace and truth” (John 1:14). Some readers also hear in the servant sent to a far country to bring a bride for his master’s son a picture of the Spirit gathering the church for Christ; that is a fitting application, not the chapter’s direct meaning.

For us. God’s guidance is usually found through prayer, faithfulness and attention to his hand in ordinary things, and recognised looking back: “the LORD has led me in the way” (v. 27). Marry in the Lord. And when God’s way is clear, say with Rebekah, “I will go.”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — Abraham's Commission to His Servant
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Abraham’s last act for the promise is to secure a wife for Isaac who will neither draw him into the gods of Canaan nor take him back to Mesopotamia. The LORD has blessed Abraham in everything, but the promise needs another generation (v. 1). He binds his most trusted servant by a solemn oath: the bride must come from his own kindred, not from the Canaanites (vv. 2–4). When the servant asks what to do if she will not come, Abraham’s answer rests on God’s promise: the God who called him and swore to give the land will send his angel ahead. But Isaac must never go back (vv. 5–9).
verseByVerse.theology: Abraham makes his servant swear not to take a wife for Isaac from the Canaanites but from his kindred, and never to take Isaac back there.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the household of promise was not to be absorbed into the religion of the land (Deut. 7:3–4). Now: the principle still stands for God's people.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Abraham was old, well advanced in years. And the LORD had blessed Abraham in all things. And Abraham said to his servant, the oldest of his household, who had charge of all that he had, "Put your hand under my thigh, that I may make you swear by the LORD, the God of heaven and God of the earth, that you will not take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites, among whom I dwell, but will go to my country and to my kindred, and take a wife for my son Isaac."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Old and richly blessed, Abraham binds his chief servant by a solemn oath to find Isaac a wife from his own kindred and not from the Canaanites, so that the covenant family is not drawn into the gods of the land.

Abraham was old … And the LORD had blessed Abraham in all things. God’s promise of blessing (12:2) has come true in Abraham’s own life. But the promise reaches beyond him, and it now hangs on Isaac’s marriage. Abraham thinks his end is near; in fact he will live another thirty-five years (25:7).

His servant, the oldest of his household, who had charge of all that he had. The steward of the whole estate. He may be Eliezer of Damascus, named decades earlier (15:2), but the chapter never names him: he is simply “the servant”, and his master’s business is his whole identity.

Put your hand under my thigh. A solemn form of oath, near the source of life. It probably bound the servant by Abraham’s offspring, the very thing the oath protects; Jacob asks the same of Joseph about his burial (47:29).

The LORD, the God of heaven and God of the earth. Not a local god of Canaan but the Lord of everywhere, including the far country to which the servant must go.

Not … from the daughters of the Canaanites. The reason is faith, not race. The Canaanites’ religion and morals were already corrupt and would grow worse (15:16), and a wife from them would draw the family of promise into their gods. Abraham’s relatives in Mesopotamia were no saints (Joshua 24:2; Genesis 31:19), but they were kin who knew the name of the LORD (vv. 31, 50). Esau’s Hittite wives later show what Abraham feared: they “made life bitter for Isaac and Rebekah” (26:35).

Marry in the Lord. The principle continues: a believer should marry only a believer, “only in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 7:39; 2 Corinthians 6:14). Marriage is too close a bond, and too strong an influence on faith and on children, to be shared with someone who does not share your Lord.

What it does not mean. Not separation by race or nation. Rahab the Canaanite and Ruth the Moabite came into the line of Christ by faith (Matthew 1:5). Nor does it tell a believer already married to an unbeliever to leave; Paul says the opposite (1 Corinthians 7:12–14).
verseByVerse.note: Putting a hand “under the thigh”, near the source of offspring, was a solemn form of oath.

verseByVerse.quote: The servant said to him, "Perhaps the woman may not be willing to follow me to this land. Must I then take your son back to the land from which you came?" Abraham said to him, "See to it that you do not take my son back there. The LORD, the God of heaven, who took me from my father's house and from the land of my kindred, and who spoke to me and swore to me, 'To your offspring I will give this land,' he will send his angel before you, and you shall take a wife for my son from there. But if the woman is not willing to follow you, then you will be free from this oath of mine; only you must not take my son back there." So the servant put his hand under the thigh of Abraham his master and swore to him concerning this matter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The servant asks what to do if the woman will not come; Abraham answers that God will send his angel ahead, but that on no account may Isaac go back to Mesopotamia.

Perhaps the woman may not be willing. A sensible question. Her willingness will matter, and in the end she will be asked (v. 58).

See to it that you do not take my son back there. Said twice (vv. 6, 8). To take Isaac back would undo the call that brought Abraham out (12:1). The heir of the land must stay in the land, even unmarried, rather than return.

The LORD … who took me from my father’s house … and who spoke to me and swore to me. Abraham reasons from what God has done and said. The God who called him and promised, “To your offspring I will give this land” (12:7), will not let the promise fail for want of a wife. Faith remembers.

He will send his angel before you. God will go ahead of the servant, as he later promised to send his angel before Israel “to bring you to the place that I have prepared” (Exodus 23:20).

Then you will be free from this oath of mine. Abraham’s confidence is not presumption. He does not dictate how God must keep his word; if the woman will not come, the servant is released. These are Abraham’s last recorded words in Genesis: trust in God’s promise, and concern that his son stay in the land of promise.

For us. We may trust God to go ahead of us into tasks we cannot control, without demanding to know in advance how he will work.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–27 — The Servant's Journey and Prayer
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The servant’s prayer at the well is answered before he has finished praying, and he answers with worship. He travels to Nahor’s city with ten camels and gifts, and at evening, when the women come to draw water, he asks God for success and for a sign: a young woman who will offer water to him and to his camels (vv. 10–14). Rebekah arrives and does exactly that, running back and forth to water all ten camels (vv. 15–21). When he learns she is from Abraham’s own family, he bows and blesses the LORD, who has not forsaken his steadfast love and faithfulness and has led him in the way (vv. 22–27).
verseByVerse.theology: She is Bethuel's daughter, and the servant bows and blesses the LORD for his steadfast love and faithfulness.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the sign he asked for revealed character, and he asked it trusting a promise God had already given (v. 7). Now: guidance is usually recognised afterwards.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the servant took ten of his master's camels and departed, taking all sorts of choice gifts from his master; and he arose and went to Mesopotamia to the city of Nahor. And he made the camels kneel down outside the city by the well of water at the time of evening, the time when women go out to draw water. And he said, "O LORD, God of my master Abraham, please grant me success today and show steadfast love to my master Abraham.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The servant travels with gifts to the city of Nahor, waits by the well at evening when the women come to draw water, and begins with prayer for God’s steadfast love to his master.

Ten of his master’s camels … all sorts of choice gifts. A string of ten camels marked great wealth, and the gifts show that the servant comes to arrange a marriage in earnest. The journey to northern Mesopotamia, where Nahor’s family lived near Harran (27:43), was some five hundred miles, several weeks of travel.

Were there camels in Abraham’s day? Camels were not common in Canaan until later centuries, and some have taken their mention here as a sign that the story was written late. But camels were known and used in the wider region much earlier, and a rich man’s string of ten would have been a rare and striking sign of wealth, which is exactly how the story uses them.

Outside the city by the well of water at the time of evening. A sensible plan: in the cool of the evening the young women came out to draw water for their households, so the well was the place to meet them. Wells are where Jacob meets Rachel (29:9–12) and Moses meets Zipporah (Exodus 2:15–21).

O LORD, God of my master Abraham. He prays to his master’s God. By the end of the scene he can say, “the LORD has led me” (v. 27): his own faith grows on the journey.

Please grant me success today and show steadfast love to my master. Before he acts, he prays. “Steadfast love” is ḥesed, God’s loyal, covenant love, the love that keeps its promises. It is the key word of the chapter (vv. 12, 14, 27, 49): the servant is not asking for luck, but for God to be faithful to what he promised Abraham.
verseByVerse.note: Mesopotamia is “Aram-naharaim” (ESV note), “Aram of the two rivers,” in the north. A string of ten camels marked great wealth.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, I am standing by the spring of water, and the daughters of the men of the city are coming out to draw water. Let the young woman to whom I shall say, 'Please let down your jar that I may drink,' and who shall say, 'Drink, and I will water your camels'—let her be the one whom you have appointed for your servant Isaac. By this I shall know that you have shown steadfast love to my master."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The servant asks God for a particular sign: a young woman who, asked for a drink, will offer to water his camels too, a sign that would reveal a generous, hard-working heart.

Drink, and I will water your camels. The sign he asks for is a test of character. He does not ask for something random; he asks God to show him a woman who will do far more than she is asked, for a stranger, at hard labour. Ten camels after a desert journey could drink a great deal. Such a woman would fit the family of the man who ran to serve three strangers in the heat of the day (18:1–8).

Let her be the one whom you have appointed. He believes God has already chosen her; he asks only to recognise her.

Another meeting at a well. Centuries later, at another well, a weary traveller asked a woman for a drink: “Give me a drink” (John 4:7). But there the roles were turned round. The one who asked for water was the one who gives living water, and the bridegroom (John 3:29) had come to seek a people for himself.

Where Christians differ: asking for signs today. Some Christians “put out a fleece”, asking God for a sign, as Gideon did (Judges 6:36–40), and point to this servant as a model. Others note that the servant was not deciding a moral question, that he asked within a promise God had already given (v. 7), and that the sign he chose tested character. This commentary’s view: God guides chiefly through his word, prayer, wisdom and godly counsel. He may arrange circumstances, and we may ask him for help, but believers should not demand signs to decide what Scripture has already made plain, or let a sign override wisdom.

verseByVerse.quote: Before he had finished speaking, behold, Rebekah, who was born to Bethuel the son of Milcah, the wife of Nahor, Abraham's brother, came out with her water jar on her shoulder. The young woman was very attractive in appearance, a maiden whom no man had known. She went down to the spring and filled her jar and came up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before the servant has finished praying, Rebekah, the granddaughter of Abraham’s own brother, comes to the spring: God’s answer was on its way before the prayer was spoken.

Before he had finished speaking. God answers before the servant has finished asking: “Before they call I will answer; while they are yet speaking I will hear” (Isaiah 65:24). Rebekah had set out with her jar before he began.

Rebekah, who was born to Bethuel the son of Milcah. The reader knows from 22:23 what the servant does not yet: Rebekah is from Abraham’s own family, exactly what his master asked for.

Very attractive in appearance, a maiden whom no man had known. The narrator notes her beauty and that she was a virgin, free to marry. But the servant’s test looks for character, not looks: “Charm is deceitful, and beauty is vain, but a woman who fears the LORD is to be praised” (Proverbs 31:30).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the servant ran to meet her and said, "Please give me a little water to drink from your jar." She said, "Drink, my lord." And she quickly let down her jar upon her hand and gave him a drink. When she had finished giving him a drink, she said, "I will draw water for your camels also, until they have finished drinking." So she quickly emptied her jar into the trough and ran again to the well to draw water, and she drew for all his camels. The man gazed at her in silence to learn whether the LORD had prospered his journey or not.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rebekah gives the stranger a drink and then, unasked, runs again and again to water all his camels, while the servant watches in silence to see whether God has answered.

Drink, my lord. She treats a stranger with courtesy and gives at once, “quickly”. The narrator piles up words of speed: she hurried, she emptied her jar, she ran again. This is hospitality with energy.

I will draw water for your camels also, until they have finished drinking. Watering ten thirsty camels could mean well over a hundred gallons, carried up from the spring one jar at a time, at the end of the day, for a man she had never met. She does exactly what the servant prayed for, and more, without being asked.

The man gazed at her in silence. He does not jump to conclusions or interrupt; he waits and watches to see what God will do. Wisdom does not rush to read God’s hand.

For us. Character shows in small kindnesses to strangers, done quickly and cheerfully when no one is checking. “Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers, for thereby some have entertained angels unawares” (Hebrews 13:2). Rebekah entertained, unawares, the messenger of her own future.

verseByVerse.quote: When the camels had finished drinking, the man took a gold ring weighing a half shekel, and two bracelets for her arms weighing ten gold shekels, and said, "Please tell me whose daughter you are. Is there room in your father's house for us to spend the night?" She said to him, "I am the daughter of Bethuel the son of Milcah, whom she bore to Nahor." She added, "We have plenty of both straw and fodder, and room to spend the night." The man bowed his head and worshiped the LORD and said, "Blessed be the LORD, the God of my master Abraham, who has not forsaken his steadfast love and his faithfulness toward my master. As for me, the LORD has led me in the way to the house of my master's kinsmen."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The servant rewards Rebekah with gold, learns that she is Abraham’s own kin and that her family can take them in, and bows to worship the LORD, who has kept his steadfast love and led him in the way.

A gold ring weighing a half shekel, and two bracelets … weighing ten gold shekels. Rich gifts (on weights, see Shekel). The ring was for her nose (v. 47). When he retells the story he puts the question first and the gift after (v. 47), the order that mattered to her family.

We have plenty of both straw and fodder, and room. Again Rebekah offers more than she is asked: not only room for the men but food for the animals.

The man bowed his head and worshiped the LORD. His first response to answered prayer is worship, not self-congratulation. He will bow again (v. 52).

Steadfast love and faithfulness. In Hebrew ḥesed and ’emet, the pair God uses of himself when he passes before Moses: “abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness” (Exodus 34:6). The right woman at the right well at the right time is not luck but the loyal love of a God who keeps his word.

Full of grace and truth. John takes up the same pair to describe Jesus: “we have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1:14). The steadfast love and faithfulness that led the servant to Rebekah’s door came in person in Christ.

As for me, the LORD has led me in the way. He set out and kept walking, and found that God was leading. Guidance is usually recognised looking back, by those who were already on the road in obedience. “In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make straight your paths” (Proverbs 3:6).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 28–67 — The Servant's Report, Rebekah's Consent, and the Marriage
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The servant’s faithful report wins the family’s consent, Rebekah freely chooses to go, and the chapter ends in love and comfort. At Laban’s house the servant will not eat until he has told his errand (vv. 28–33), and he tells it all again, giving God the credit at every step (vv. 34–49). Laban and Bethuel agree that “the thing has come from the LORD” (vv. 50–54). Asked to wait, the servant presses to leave, and Rebekah herself answers, “I will go” (vv. 55–58). Blessed by her family, she leaves her home as Abraham once left his (vv. 59–61). Isaac meets her at evening, takes her into his mother’s tent and loves her (vv. 62–67).
verseByVerse.theology: Laban and Bethuel agree that the thing is from the LORD. Rebekah says, "I will go," and Isaac meets her in the field at evening.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Rebekah's leaving echoes Abraham's own call to leave country and kindred. Now: the servant who is never named shows faithfulness that needs no supervising (cf. Matt. 6:3–4).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the young woman ran and told her mother's household about these things. Rebekah had a brother whose name was Laban. Laban ran out toward the man, to the spring. As soon as he saw the ring and the bracelets on his sister's arms, and heard the words of Rebekah his sister, "Thus the man spoke to me," he went to the man. And behold, he was standing by the camels at the spring. He said, "Come in, O blessed of the LORD. Why do you stand outside? For I have prepared the house and a place for the camels." So the man came to the house and unharnessed the camels, and gave straw and fodder to the camels, and there was water to wash his feet and the feet of the men who were with him. Then food was set before him to eat. But he said, "I will not eat until I have said what I have to say." He said, "Speak on."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rebekah runs home with the news, her brother Laban hurries out, his eye on the gold, to welcome the stranger, and the servant refuses to eat until he has told his errand.

Her mother’s household. Probably the women’s part of the home. Her father Bethuel barely appears (v. 50); her brother Laban and her mother take the lead.

As soon as he saw the ring and the bracelets. The narrator lets us see Laban noticing the gold before he hurries out. It is a first glimpse of the man who will later cheat Jacob for twenty years (chapters 29–31).

Come in, O blessed of the LORD. Laban uses the LORD’s name: the family knew of Abraham’s God, though they also kept household gods (31:19, 30). His welcome is warm, with water for the men’s feet and straw and fodder for the camels.

I will not eat until I have said what I have to say. Food is set before him, but the servant puts his master’s business before his own hunger. Jesus said the same of his own mission: “My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work” (John 4:34).

verseByVerse.quote: So he said, "I am Abraham's servant. The LORD has greatly blessed my master, and he has become great. He has given him flocks and herds, silver and gold, male servants and female servants, camels and donkeys. And Sarah my master's wife bore a son to my master when she was old, and to him he has given all that he has.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The servant introduces himself only as Abraham’s servant, tells how richly the LORD has blessed his master, and presents Isaac as the heir of everything.

I am Abraham’s servant. No name, no titles. He was a slave (see Slavery in the Ancient World), yet trusted with everything his master had, and he speaks of his master, not himself: a faithful steward (1 Corinthians 4:2).

The LORD has greatly blessed my master. He gives God the credit for Abraham’s wealth, not Abraham’s skill. In a household with idols on the shelf, he bears witness to the living God.

To him he has given all that he has. Isaac is the sole heir (25:5), which is part of the case for the marriage. Christians hear an echo of a greater Father and Son: “The Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand” (John 3:35).

verseByVerse.quote: My master made me swear, saying, 'You shall not take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites, in whose land I dwell, but you shall go to my father's house and to my clan and take a wife for my son.' I said to my master, 'Perhaps the woman will not follow me.' But he said to me, 'The LORD, before whom I have walked, will send his angel with you and prosper your way. You shall take a wife for my son from my clan and from my father's house. Then you will be free from my oath, when you come to my clan. And if they will not give her to you, you will be free from my oath.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The servant repeats Abraham’s charge and the oath, including the release if the woman will not come.

My master made me swear. The story is told a second time, and the repetition underlines God’s guidance. Hebrew storytelling often retells events in a character’s own words, and small differences show the character’s mind.

A tactful retelling. The servant leaves out Abraham’s double warning never to take Isaac back (vv. 6, 8), which might sound to the family like contempt for their country. And he puts the possible refusal gently: “if they will not give her to you” (v. 41).

The LORD, before whom I have walked. A phrase not in the first telling: Abraham’s life has been a walk in God’s presence, as God told him, “walk before me, and be blameless” (17:1). The servant presents his master as a man who walks with God.

verseByVerse.quote: "I came today to the spring and said, 'O LORD, the God of my master Abraham, if now you are prospering the way that I go, behold, I am standing by the spring of water. Let the virgin who comes out to draw water, to whom I shall say, "Please give me a little water from your jar to drink," and who will say to me, "Drink, and I will draw for your camels also," let her be the woman whom the LORD has appointed for my master's son.' "Before I had finished speaking in my heart, behold, Rebekah came out with her water jar on her shoulder, and she went down to the spring and drew water. I said to her, 'Please let me drink.' She quickly let down her jar from her shoulder and said, 'Drink, and I will give your camels drink also.' So I drank, and she gave the camels drink also.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The servant tells of his silent prayer at the spring and how Rebekah answered it word for word before he had finished.

Before I had finished speaking in my heart. His prayer was spoken only in his heart, as Hannah’s would be (1 Samuel 1:13), and it was answered: God hears silent prayers.

Word for word. The family hears that Rebekah said exactly what the servant had asked God for. The detail is the evidence: they can judge for themselves that this was not chance.

Let the virgin who comes out. The word here, ‘almah, is the one used in Isaiah 7:14, “the virgin shall conceive”. Here it plainly describes an unmarried young woman, whom the narrator has called “a maiden whom no man had known” (v. 16).

verseByVerse.quote: Then I asked her, 'Whose daughter are you?' She said, 'The daughter of Bethuel, Nahor's son, whom Milcah bore to him.' So I put the ring on her nose and the bracelets on her arms. Then I bowed my head and worshiped the LORD and blessed the LORD, the God of my master Abraham, who had led me by the right way to take the daughter of my master's kinsman for his son. Now then, if you are going to show steadfast love and faithfulness to my master, tell me; and if not, tell me, that I may turn to the right hand or to the left."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having confirmed her family, the servant gave Rebekah the jewellery and worshipped; now he asks the family for a straight answer: will they show steadfast love to his master, or not?

I put the ring on her nose. Nose rings were a common ornament for women (Isaiah 3:21).

Who had led me by the right way. Literally “the way of truth”: the true road, the one God laid out.

If you are going to show steadfast love and faithfulness to my master. The same words he used of God (v. 27). He asks the family to answer God’s loyal love with loyalty of their own. Human kindness at its best reflects God’s.

That I may turn to the right hand or to the left. If they say no, he will look elsewhere. He asks for a clear answer, not a polite delay. Plain dealing is a kindness to everyone involved.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Laban and Bethuel answered and said, "The thing has come from the LORD; we cannot speak to you bad or good. Behold, Rebekah is before you; take her and go, and let her be the wife of your master's son, as the LORD has spoken." When Abraham's servant heard their words, he bowed himself to the earth before the LORD. And the servant brought out jewelry of silver and of gold, and garments, and gave them to Rebekah. He also gave to her brother and to her mother costly ornaments. And he and the men who were with him ate and drank, and they spent the night there. When they arose in the morning, he said, "Send me away to my master."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Laban and Bethuel recognise God’s hand and give their consent; the servant bows to the ground before the LORD, gives rich gifts, and at last sits down to eat.

The thing has come from the LORD; we cannot speak to you bad or good. An idiom: “we can say nothing either way” (compare 31:24). They see that God has decided, and they will not resist.

He bowed himself to the earth before the LORD. At each step the servant turns first to God (vv. 26, 52). Answered prayer leads him not to relax but to worship.

Jewelry of silver and of gold, and garments … costly ornaments. Gifts to the bride and to her family were part of arranging a marriage (compare 34:12; see Weddings and Betrothal). They honoured the family and showed the groom’s seriousness.

Send me away to my master. Only now does he eat and rest, and the next morning he is ready to go. His errand is not finished until the bride is home.

verseByVerse.quote: Her brother and her mother said, "Let the young woman remain with us a while, at least ten days; after that she may go." But he said to them, "Do not delay me, since the LORD has prospered my way. Send me away that I may go to my master." They said, "Let us call the young woman and ask her." And they called Rebekah and said to her, "Will you go with this man?" She said, "I will go."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The family asks for delay, the servant presses to leave, and when they ask Rebekah herself she gives her own consent: “I will go.”

Let the young woman remain with us a while. A natural wish: they may never see her again, and as far as we know they never did.

Do not delay me, since the LORD has prospered my way. When God has made the way plain, delay is no virtue.

Let us call the young woman and ask her. Rebekah is asked, which was not always the custom in her world, and she gives her own consent. A marriage God arranges is not forced on her.

I will go. In Hebrew a single word. Like Abraham, who was told to leave “your country and your kindred and your father’s house” (12:1), she leaves everything she knows for a land she has never seen and a husband she has never met, on the strength of a testimony to what God has done. That is faith.

Loving one we have not seen. Every Christian is a little like Rebekah: called through someone else’s testimony to a Bridegroom not yet seen. “Though you have not seen him, you love him” (1 Peter 1:8).

What it does not mean. Not that every quick decision is a mark of faith. Rebekah went after hearing a full and credible account, with her family’s consent and blessing. When God’s call is clear there is no need to delay; when it is not, wisdom takes counsel and time.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of v. 55 reads literally “days or ten”. It probably means “a few days, say ten” (ESV “at least ten days”), though some older Jewish interpreters took it as “a year, or ten months”. Either way, the family wanted time; the servant wanted to go at once.

verseByVerse.quote: So they sent away Rebekah their sister and her nurse, and Abraham's servant and his men. And they blessed Rebekah and said to her, "Our sister, may you become thousands of ten thousands, and may your offspring possess the gate of those who hate him!" Then Rebekah and her young women arose and rode on the camels and followed the man. Thus the servant took Rebekah and went his way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rebekah’s family sends her off with her nurse and her maids, blessing her with words that echo God’s promise to Abraham, and she rides away with the servant.

Their sister and her nurse. Her childhood nurse goes with her for the rest of her life; we later learn her name, Deborah, when Jacob’s household mourns her (35:8).

May you become thousands of ten thousands. The family’s blessing echoes God’s oath to Abraham, “your offspring shall possess the gate of his enemies” (22:17). Without knowing it, Laban’s household pronounces over Rebekah the blessing God had already sworn. On the gate, see the note on 22:15–19.

Rode on the camels and followed the man. She does not go alone; her maids go with her. But she follows a servant she met yesterday to a man she has never seen.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Isaac had returned from Beer-lahai-roi and was dwelling in the Negeb. And Isaac went out to meditate in the field toward evening. And he lifted up his eyes and saw, and behold, there were camels coming.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Isaac, now living in the Negeb near Beer-lahai-roi, has gone out into the field at evening to meditate when he sees the camels coming.

Isaac had returned from Beer-lahai-roi. Hagar’s well, named for the God who saw her (16:13–14). Isaac will settle there (25:11).

Toward evening. The same hour at which the servant prayed at the well (v. 11). At both ends of the journey someone was waiting before God.

He lifted up his eyes and saw. As Abraham lifted up his eyes on Moriah and saw the ram (22:13), Isaac looks up and sees what God has provided.

Uncertain wording. The verb translated “meditate” (lasuaḥ) is found only here, and its meaning is not certain. It may mean to meditate or pray, to walk or stroll, or, with a related word, to grieve or lament. Since he was still mourning his mother (v. 67), it may have been all three: a man walking alone at evening, thinking and praying through his loss.

verseByVerse.quote: And Rebekah lifted up her eyes, and when she saw Isaac, she dismounted from the camel and said to the servant, "Who is that man, walking in the field to meet us?" The servant said, "It is my master." So she took her veil and covered herself. And the servant told Isaac all the things that he had done. Then Isaac brought her into the tent of Sarah his mother and took Rebekah, and she became his wife, and he loved her. So Isaac was comforted after his mother's death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rebekah sees Isaac and veils herself as a bride; the servant reports everything; and Isaac takes Rebekah into his mother’s tent as his wife, loves her, and is comforted after Sarah’s death.

Who is that man, walking in the field to meet us? Rebekah gets down from her camel at once, a mark of respect. The servant now calls Isaac “my master”, for everything is his (v. 36).

She took her veil and covered herself. A bride wore a veil until the wedding; it explains how Jacob could be deceived on his own wedding night (29:23–25). See Weddings and Betrothal.

The servant told Isaac all the things that he had done. His last act. Then he disappears from the story, never named, his work done. Faithfulness that needs no credit is beautiful to God (Matthew 6:3–4).

Into the tent of Sarah his mother. Rebekah takes Sarah’s place as mother of the family of promise.

She became his wife, and he loved her. This is the first time the Bible says that a man loved his wife. Marriage came first and love grew within it, deep and lasting. God’s pattern for a husband is a love that keeps giving, “as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:25).

So Isaac was comforted after his mother’s death. Sarah had died three years before (23:1; 25:20). Isaac’s grief was long, and God’s comfort came through a new love. The book that began with a man alone and given a wife (2:18–24) shows God still providing companionship for the lonely.

What it does not mean. Not that arranged marriage is God’s only pattern, or that feelings do not matter. Nor that a spouse can fill a place only God can fill, or that marriage is the cure for grief or for loneliness. Singleness and marriage are both gifts from God, and neither is the holier.

A fitting application. Some see in the servant a picture of the Spirit, sent to a far country to bring a bride for the Father’s Son, who speaks not of himself but of his master and his master’s son. That is a fitting application, not the direct meaning.

24.theology:
Providence in the Particular. Genesis 24 is the Bible’s most detailed account of God’s providence, his rule over all that happens, at work in an ordinary, if important, decision. The servant prays, watches, interprets and gives thanks, treating each moment of the journey as possibly significant. This is not superstition but trust: the God who made and sustains the universe is also present in the details, as near as "before he had finished speaking" (v. 15).

Steadfast Love (Hesed). The servant's prayer and thanksgiving turn on hesed: the covenant loyalty, faithful love and unfailing commitment of God to his promises. The word appears more than two hundred times in the Old Testament and is its chief description of God’s attitude to his people. It is the ground of the Psalms' confidence (Ps. 136: "his steadfast love endures forever," 26 times) and of Lamentations' hope ("the steadfast love of the LORD never ceases," Lam. 3:22). In the New Testament the same loyal love is seen most fully in the gift of the Son.
24.examples:
Then: Marriage through a family go-between was standard practice in the ancient Near East, and the stakes here were the continuation of the covenant line. That Rebekah's own willingness mattered, not merely her family's agreement, was notable.

Now: The servant's way of seeking guidance is neither to sit and wait for God to act, nor to decide for himself without prayer. He acts, prays and pays attention: doing the work of the mission while watching for the hand of God in it. And what looks like luck or coincidence is the steadfast love of a God whose faithfulness is the most reliable thing in the universe.

keyVerse.quote: Blessed be the LORD, the God of my master Abraham, who has not forsaken his steadfast love and his faithfulness toward my master. As for me, the LORD has led me in the way to the house of my master’s kinsmen.
keyVerse.note: The servant’s prayer of thanks names what the whole chapter is about: not luck or good planning, but God’s “steadfast love and faithfulness” keeping his covenant into a new generation. And it shows how guidance is usually known: by someone already walking in obedience, who looks back and sees that God was leading. That same love and faithfulness came in person in Jesus Christ.

24.reflection:
Abraham insisted that Isaac marry within the family of faith (vv. 3–4). Why does Scripture take this so seriously? How can a church support single Christians in this without making them feel second-class?

The servant prayed before he acted, watched in silence, and worshipped when God answered (vv. 12–27). Which of these do you find hardest when you are facing a decision, and why?

Rebekah’s generous, unhurried kindness to a stranger turned out to be the moment her life changed (vv. 17–20). What small, unseen acts of kindness is God calling you to, and how might he use them?

Rebekah said, “I will go” (v. 58), leaving everything for a future she could not see. Where is God asking you to step out in trust, and what holds you back?

25.title: Two Nations in Your Womb
25.text: <sup>1</sup>Abraham took another wife, whose name was Keturah.<sup>2</sup>She bore him Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak, and Shuah.<sup>3</sup>Jokshan fathered Sheba and Dedan. The sons of Dedan were Asshurim, Letushim, and Leummim.<sup>4</sup>The sons of Midian were Ephah, Epher, Hanoch, Abida, and Eldaah. All these were the children of Keturah.<sup>5</sup>Abraham gave all he had to Isaac.<sup>6</sup>But to the sons of his concubines Abraham gave gifts, and while he was still living he sent them away from his son Isaac, eastward to the east country.<sup>7</sup>These are the days of the years of Abraham's life, 175 years.<sup>8</sup>Abraham breathed his last and died in a good old age, an old man and full of years, and was gathered to his people.<sup>9</sup>Isaac and Ishmael his sons buried him in the cave of Machpelah, in the field of Ephron the son of Zohar the Hittite, east of Mamre,<sup>10</sup>the field that Abraham purchased from the Hittites. There Abraham was buried, with Sarah his wife.<sup>11</sup>After the death of Abraham, God blessed Isaac his son. And Isaac settled at Beer-lahai-roi.<sup>12</sup>These are the generations of Ishmael, Abraham's son, whom Hagar the Egyptian, Sarah's servant, bore to Abraham.<sup>13</sup>These are the names of the sons of Ishmael, named in the order of their birth: Nebaioth, the firstborn of Ishmael; and Kedar, Adbeel, Mibsam,<sup>14</sup>Mishma, Dumah, Massa,<sup>15</sup>Hadad, Tema, Jetur, Naphish, and Kedemah.<sup>16</sup>These are the sons of Ishmael and these are their names, by their villages and by their encampments, twelve princes according to their tribes.<sup>17</sup>(These are the years of the life of Ishmael: 137 years. He breathed his last and died, and was gathered to his people.)<sup>18</sup>They settled from Havilah to Shur, which is opposite Egypt in the direction of Assyria. He settled over against all his kinsmen.<sup>19</sup>These are the generations of Isaac, Abraham's son: Abraham fathered Isaac,<sup>20</sup>and Isaac was forty years old when he took Rebekah, the daughter of Bethuel the Aramean of Paddan-aram, the sister of Laban the Aramean, to be his wife.<sup>21</sup>And Isaac prayed to the LORD for his wife, because she was barren. And the LORD granted his prayer, and Rebekah his wife conceived.<sup>22</sup>The children struggled together within her, and she said, "If it is thus, why is this happening to me?" So she went to inquire of the LORD.<sup>23</sup>And the LORD said to her, "Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples from within you shall be divided; the one shall be stronger than the other, the older shall serve the younger."<sup>24</sup>When her days to give birth were completed, behold, there were twins in her womb.<sup>25</sup>The first came out red, all his body like a hairy cloak, so they called his name Esau.<sup>26</sup>Afterward his brother came out with his hand holding Esau's heel, so his name was called Jacob. Isaac was sixty years old when she bore them.<sup>27</sup>When the boys grew up, Esau was a skillful hunter, a man of the field, while Jacob was a quiet man, dwelling in tents.<sup>28</sup>Isaac loved Esau because he ate of his game, but Rebekah loved Jacob.<sup>29</sup>Once when Jacob was cooking stew, Esau came in from the field, and he was exhausted.<sup>30</sup>And Esau said to Jacob, "Let me eat some of that red stew, for I am exhausted!" (Therefore his name was called Edom.)<sup>31</sup>Jacob said, "Sell me your birthright now."<sup>32</sup>Esau said, "I am about to die; of what use is a birthright to me?"<sup>33</sup>Jacob said, "Swear to me now." So he swore to him and sold his birthright to Jacob.<sup>34</sup>Then Jacob gave Esau bread and lentil stew, and he ate and drank and rose and went his way. Thus Esau despised his birthright.
25.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 25 is a hinge. It closes the story of Abraham, begun in 12:1, and opens the story of Isaac’s sons, which runs to the end of chapter 35. Isaac has been given his wife (chapter 24), and the promise must now pass to a third generation.

The message. God carries his promise forward by his own free choice, not by human custom or merit. Abraham dies in peace and Ishmael is blessed as God said, but the promise passes to Isaac and then, by God’s word before the twins are born, to the younger son. The chosen son is a schemer and the other despises God’s gift; God’s purpose stands on grace, not on the worth of either.

Why it was said. Israel, descended from Jacob, lived beside Edom, descended from Esau, and beside Arabian peoples descended from Ishmael and Keturah (see the introduction). This chapter told them why the blessing came to them and not to their larger, stronger neighbours: not because Jacob was better, but because God chose.

How the chapter makes its case. Abraham’s other sons are provided for and sent away, so that everything goes to Isaac (vv. 1–6). Abraham dies “full of years” and is buried by both his sons, and God blesses Isaac (vv. 7–11). Ishmael’s twelve princes show God keeping his word even to the son outside the covenant line (vv. 12–18). Then the story of Isaac’s family begins: twenty years of barrenness are answered by prayer (vv. 19–21); the twins fight in the womb and God declares that the older shall serve the younger (vv. 22–23); their births and characters set up the conflict (vv. 24–28); and Esau sells his birthright for a bowl of stew (vv. 29–34).

Where it leads. By promise and by pattern. Paul takes this oracle as the clearest picture of God’s free election: chosen “though they were not yet born and had done nothing either good or bad” (Romans 9:11), so that salvation rests on “him who calls”. The pattern of the barren wife opening to a child of promise runs on to the virgin birth. And Esau, who traded his birthright for a meal, is the opposite of Christ, the true firstborn, who in the wilderness, starving, would not trade his sonship for bread (Matthew 4:3–4), and who shares his inheritance freely with those who have nothing to bring.

For us. If God chose you, it was not for anything in you, so there is no room for pride and every reason for worship. And the same chapter warns against Esau’s folly: no appetite of this afternoon is worth the inheritance Christ gives. Value what God values, and keep praying for what he has promised, even when the answer takes twenty years.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–18 — Abraham's Final Years and Death
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Abraham’s life closes with everything in order: the promise and the inheritance go to Isaac, and the other sons are blessed but sent away. Abraham’s six sons by Keturah receive gifts and are sent east, so that nothing will rival Isaac (vv. 1–6). Abraham dies at 175, satisfied with his days, and Isaac and Ishmael bury him beside Sarah in the one piece of the land he owned; then God blesses Isaac (vv. 7–11). Ishmael’s twelve princes, his age and his territory follow (vv. 12–18), showing that God kept his word to Hagar and to Abraham even about the son outside the covenant line. Before the story moves on, every loose thread is tied.
verseByVerse.theology: Abraham has six more sons by Keturah and sends them east with gifts. He dies at 175, and Isaac and Ishmael bury him at Machpelah. Ishmael dies at 137.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: God kept his word to Hagar and to Abraham about Ishmael (21:18). Now: Abraham "died in faith, not having received the things promised" (Heb. 11:13), and the rest of the Bible is God keeping them.

verseByVerse.quote: Abraham took another wife, whose name was Keturah. She bore him Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak, and Shuah. Jokshan fathered Sheba and Dedan. The sons of Dedan were Asshurim, Letushim, and Leummim. The sons of Midian were Ephah, Epher, Hanoch, Abida, and Eldaah. All these were the children of Keturah. Abraham gave all he had to Isaac. But to the sons of his concubines Abraham gave gifts, and while he was still living he sent them away from his son Isaac, eastward to the east country.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abraham’s six sons by Keturah become the fathers of desert peoples, but the inheritance and the promise go to Isaac alone, and the other sons are provided for and sent away east.

Abraham took another wife, whose name was Keturah. Hebrew narrative does not always tell events in order, and the text does not say when this marriage took place. It may have been after Sarah’s death, when Abraham was well over a hundred (Hebrews 11:12 calls him “as good as dead” when Isaac was conceived). Or Keturah may have been taken earlier, while Sarah lived, and the story placed here to round off Abraham’s life. 1 Chronicles 1:32 calls her “Abraham’s concubine”, and v. 6 speaks of his concubines, so she had the lower standing of a secondary wife, as Hagar had.

Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak, and Shuah. These are the founders of tribes in the deserts east and south of Canaan. Midian is the best known: Moses fled to Midian and married the daughter of its priest, Jethro (Exodus 2:15–21), and Midianite traders carried Joseph to Egypt (37:28, 36). Sheba and Dedan were Arabian trading peoples (Ezekiel 27:20–22). Shuah may be the home of Job’s friend Bildad “the Shuhite” (Job 2:11). Abraham becomes the father of many nations in the plain sense too (17:4–5).

Abraham gave all he had to Isaac. The heir of the promise receives the whole estate. The servant had already told Laban as much (24:36). God had said, “through Isaac shall your offspring be named” (21:12), and Abraham acts on it.

To the sons of his concubines Abraham gave gifts. They are not cast off empty-handed. Abraham provides for them while he is alive, and sends them away “eastward to the east country”, the deserts of Arabia and beyond, whose tribes are later called “the people of the East” (Judges 6:3; Job 1:3). As with Ishmael (21:10–14), the separation protects the son of promise from rivals for the inheritance and the land.

Kindness beyond the covenant line. God’s choice of Isaac did not make Abraham careless of his other sons. God’s people are to do good to those outside the household of faith too (Galatians 6:10). And in the end these peoples were not forgotten: Isaiah sees the camels “of Midian and Ephah” and all those from Sheba coming to Zion with gold and frankincense to “bring good news, the praises of the LORD” (Isaiah 60:6), a picture fulfilled as the nations come to Abraham’s greater Son.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the days of the years of Abraham's life, 175 years. Abraham breathed his last and died in a good old age, an old man and full of years, and was gathered to his people. Isaac and Ishmael his sons buried him in the cave of Machpelah, in the field of Ephron the son of Zohar the Hittite, east of Mamre, the field that Abraham purchased from the Hittites. There Abraham was buried, with Sarah his wife. After the death of Abraham, God blessed Isaac his son. And Isaac settled at Beer-lahai-roi.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abraham dies at 175, at peace and satisfied with his life, as God had promised; his two sons bury him beside Sarah, and God’s blessing passes to Isaac.

175 years. Abraham left Harran at 75 (12:4), so he lived a hundred years as a foreigner in the land of promise. Isaac was 75 when his father died, and Jacob and Esau were fifteen (21:5; 25:26): Abraham lived to see his grandsons, though the story tells of his death first, to close his part before theirs begins.

In a good old age, an old man and full of years. God had promised, “you shall go to your fathers in peace; you shall be buried in a good old age” (15:15), and here it is, word for word. “Full of years” means not only many years but enough of them: Abraham dies satisfied. The man who left Ur not knowing where he was going (Hebrews 11:8), who failed and believed and obeyed, ends his life content.

Was gathered to his people. This is not the same as burial, for it comes before it, and Abraham’s ancestors lay far away in Mesopotamia. It means joining those who had died before him. It is a quiet hint, early in the Bible, that death is not the end of a person. Jesus draws it out: God still calls himself “the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” long after their deaths, and “He is not God of the dead, but of the living” (Matthew 22:32).

Isaac and Ishmael his sons buried him. The brothers separated in childhood (21:14) stand together at their father’s grave. They lay him in the cave of Machpelah, the field he had bought for Sarah (23:17–20; see Burial Customs and Tombs). Abraham owned only a grave in the land, and he is buried in it as a pledge that God would keep his word.

After the death of Abraham, God blessed Isaac his son. The blessing does not die with Abraham. God himself carries it to the next generation, as he promised (17:19, 21). Isaac settles at Beer-lahai-roi, “the well of the Living One who sees me”, where God once met the runaway Hagar (16:13–14), a place Isaac already knew (24:62).

Died in faith. Abraham died “not having received the things promised, but having seen them and greeted them from afar” (Hebrews 11:13). He held only a grave and one son, yet he died content, because he trusted the God who promised. Christ has made the end of the believer’s life a gathering, not a loss: to be away from the body is to be “at home with the Lord” (2 Corinthians 5:8). A Christian may hope to die as Abraham did, not with everything done, but at peace.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the generations of Ishmael, Abraham's son, whom Hagar the Egyptian, Sarah's servant, bore to Abraham. These are the names of the sons of Ishmael, named in the order of their birth: Nebaioth, the firstborn of Ishmael; and Kedar, Adbeel, Mibsam, Mishma, Dumah, Massa, Hadad, Tema, Jetur, Naphish, and Kedemah. These are the sons of Ishmael and these are their names, by their villages and by their encampments, twelve princes according to their tribes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ishmael’s twelve sons become princes of tribes, just as God promised: the son outside the covenant line is not forgotten.

These are the generations of Ishmael. Genesis is built on these headings (see the introduction). A side line, such as Cain’s (4:17–24) or Ishmael’s here, is told briefly before the story returns to the chosen line, which is told at length. The order teaches: the families of the world are not ignored, but the promise runs through one line, for the sake of them all (12:3).

Whom Hagar the Egyptian, Sarah’s servant, bore to Abraham. The narrator recalls Ishmael’s origin in Abraham and Sarah’s plan to get the promised child their own way (16:1–4). Yet God’s kindness to Ishmael did not depend on how he came to be born.

Nebaioth … Kedar … Dumah … Tema. Several of these names belong to Arabian tribes and oases known from later history. Kedar became a byword for the desert tribes with their black tents (Psalm 120:5; Song of Solomon 1:5), Tema and Dumah were oasis towns (Isaiah 21:11–14; Job 6:19), and Nebaioth and Kedar appear together as herding peoples (Isaiah 60:7).

By their villages and by their encampments, twelve princes according to their tribes. They lived partly in settlements, partly in tent camps. God had said, “He shall father twelve princes, and I will make him into a great nation” (17:20; compare 21:13, 18), and he kept his word to the letter. Twelve tribes of Ishmael come before the twelve tribes of Israel (35:22–26).

Ishmael’s sons in Zion. Isaiah foresees “All the flocks of Kedar” and “the rams of Nebaioth” brought to God’s altar (Isaiah 60:7). The peoples sent away from Isaac are not shut out for ever: they are among the nations blessed in Abraham’s offspring, who is Christ (Galatians 3:16). At Pentecost “Cretans and Arabians” heard the mighty works of God in their own tongues (Acts 2:11).
verseByVerse.note: Several of these names belong to Arabian tribes known from later records.

verseByVerse.quote: (These are the years of the life of Ishmael: 137 years. He breathed his last and died, and was gathered to his people.) They settled from Havilah to Shur, which is opposite Egypt in the direction of Assyria. He settled over against all his kinsmen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ishmael dies at 137 and joins his people; his descendants spread across the desert between Egypt and Mesopotamia, living apart from and often against their kin, as was foretold.

137 years … gathered to his people. Ishmael’s death is recorded with the same words as his father’s (v. 8). He shared Abraham’s blood and Abraham’s burial of his father; the narrator treats him with respect.

From Havilah to Shur, which is opposite Egypt. Shur was the desert on Egypt’s eastern frontier, where Hagar had first fled (16:7); Havilah was probably in Arabia. Ishmael’s descendants roamed the wide desert lands south and east of Canaan.

He settled over against all his kinsmen. The angel had told Hagar that Ishmael would be “a wild donkey of a man” and “shall dwell over against all his kinsmen” (16:12). His people lived independent of their relatives, and often at odds with them.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew says literally that he “fell” over against all his kinsmen. In this setting “fell” most likely means “settled”, as the ESV takes it, but it could mean that he “attacked” or “lived in hostility to” them. Either way it echoes 16:12. “In the direction of Assyria” is also unclear: it may mean the great empire of Asshur far to the north-east, or a local Arabian people of a similar name (compare Asshurim, v. 3).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–34 — The Birth of Jacob and Esau; the Birthright
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s word before the twins are born sets the course of the whole Jacob story: the promise is carried forward not by birth order but by God’s free choice. Rebekah is barren, like Sarah, and the promise waits twenty years on Isaac’s prayer (vv. 19–21). The twins fight in the womb, and the LORD tells Rebekah that two nations are within her and the older shall serve the younger (vv. 22–23). At birth Jacob already grips Esau’s heel (vv. 24–26); as men they are hunter and tent-dweller, each the favourite of one parent (vv. 27–28). Then Esau sells his birthright for a bowl of stew (vv. 29–34). The chosen one is a schemer, the rejected one a despiser of God’s gift: grace, not merit, decides.
verseByVerse.theology: After twenty years of prayer Rebekah conceives twins. The parents take sides, and Esau sells his birthright to Jacob for a bowl of stew.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul uses this word from God to show that God's choice is "not because of works but because of him who calls" (Rom. 9:11–12). Now: the eternal is still traded for the immediate on an ordinary afternoon.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the generations of Isaac, Abraham's son: Abraham fathered Isaac, and Isaac was forty years old when he took Rebekah, the daughter of Bethuel the Aramean of Paddan-aram, the sister of Laban the Aramean, to be his wife. And Isaac prayed to the LORD for his wife, because she was barren. And the LORD granted his prayer, and Rebekah his wife conceived.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Isaac’s story begins as Abraham’s did, with a barren wife: the promise again waits on God, and after twenty years Isaac’s prayer is answered.

These are the generations of Isaac. This heading opens the longest section of Genesis so far (25:19–35:29). It is called Isaac’s, but its hero is Jacob: the “generations” of a man are what came from him.

Bethuel the Aramean of Paddan-aram … Laban the Aramean. Rebekah came from Abraham’s kin who stayed in the region of Harran (24:10, 15). The word “Aramean” is repeated, a reminder that Israel’s mothers came from there; every Israelite would later confess at the harvest, “A wandering Aramean was my father” (Deuteronomy 26:5).

Isaac was forty years old. He was sixty when the twins were born (v. 26), so the couple waited twenty years.

Isaac prayed to the LORD for his wife, because she was barren. The word for “prayed” means to plead earnestly, and “for his wife” may mean “facing her” or “on her behalf”: the husband carries his wife’s grief to God as his own. Sarah had been barren (11:30), Rebekah is, and Rachel will be (29:31). Each time the family of promise cannot continue by its own strength; each time the child comes as God’s gift.

And the LORD granted his prayer. The same verb is used: Isaac pleaded, and the LORD let himself be pleaded with. The sentence is short, but it covers twenty years. Long-delayed answers are still answers.

The barren womb and the virgin’s womb. The pattern runs through Scripture: Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, Hannah (1 Samuel 1), Elizabeth (Luke 1:7). It reaches its climax in a birth with no human father at all, when the angel says, “nothing will be impossible with God” (Luke 1:37). The line that leads to Christ is God’s work from start to finish.

Keep praying. Isaac did not stop praying because the answer was slow, and he did not, like his father, take matters into his own hands (16:1–4). Childlessness is a deep grief, and God does not always give children; but no grief is too large or too long to bring to him, and he hears (Luke 18:1).
verseByVerse.note: Paddan-aram is the region of Haran in northern Mesopotamia.

verseByVerse.quote: The children struggled together within her, and she said, "If it is thus, why is this happening to me?" So she went to inquire of the LORD. And the LORD said to her, "Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples from within you shall be divided; the one shall be stronger than the other, the older shall serve the younger."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The twins fight within Rebekah, and when she asks the LORD why, he tells her that two nations are in her womb and that the older shall serve the younger.

The children struggled together within her. The verb is strong: they crushed or shoved one another. The rivalry of their whole lives, and of their nations, begins before birth.

If it is thus, why is this happening to me? After twenty years of praying for a child, the pregnancy brings pain and fear. Rebekah does not simply endure it; she takes her question to God.

She went to inquire of the LORD. We are not told how. Perhaps she prayed at an altar Abraham or Isaac had built (12:7–8; 26:25); perhaps she asked a prophet. Abraham, whom God called a prophet (20:7), was still alive. What matters is that she goes to the right place with her trouble, and that God answers her personally.

Two nations are in your womb. The answer is a short poem of four lines. The two boys will father two peoples, Israel and Edom, divided from birth. One “shall be stronger than the other”, and against all custom, which gave the firstborn the leading place (see Inheritance and the Firstborn), “the older shall serve the younger.”

As it worked out. Edom was settled and had kings long before Israel (36:31). But David subdued it, “and all the Edomites became David’s servants” (2 Samuel 8:14), until in a later reign Edom broke free (2 Kings 8:20–22), as Isaac would foretell (27:40). The rivalry lasted to the time of Christ: Herod the Great, who tried to kill the infant Jesus, was an Idumean, a descendant of Edom. The son of Esau set himself against the true King from Jacob’s line, and lost.

Chosen before birth. Paul sees here the heart of the gospel. The choice was made “though they were not yet born and had done nothing either good or bad … not because of works but because of him who calls” (Romans 9:11–12). God’s saving purpose rests on his mercy, not on what we are or do. That is humbling: there was nothing in Jacob to deserve it. It is also comforting: what God’s grace did not begin by our goodness, it will not abandon for our failures.

What it does not mean. Not that God is unjust, or that Esau was a puppet. Esau freely despised his birthright (v. 34) and is held responsible (Hebrews 12:16). Nor does God’s choice excuse Jacob’s scheming, which Genesis exposes without mercy. Scripture holds together God’s free choice and human responsibility without explaining how, and Paul answers objections not by softening election but by bowing before God’s right to have mercy (Romans 9:14–24).

Where Christians differ: election. Paul quotes this oracle, with Malachi’s “I have loved Jacob but Esau I have hated” (Malachi 1:2–3), to show God’s choice before birth, “not because of works” (Romans 9:10–13). Some say both passages concern nations and their roles in history, not individuals and salvation; Arminians add that God chooses those he foresees will believe. This commentary’s view: Paul applies it to individuals and their place in God’s saving purpose, as well as to the nations they founded, for his whole argument in Romans 9 concerns why some Israelites are saved and others not. Election is by grace, not merit. “Hated” means not chosen, as a comparison with love (compare Luke 14:26), though Malachi also has Edom’s real wickedness in view; God passes by others for their sin without being its author.

Uncertain wording. Rebekah’s words are very compressed in Hebrew, literally “If so, why this I?” They may mean “why is this happening to me?” (ESV), or “why am I still alive?”, or “why did I want this?”. Her distress is plain; its exact words are not. In the oracle Hebrew poetry does not always mark which noun is the subject, and a few have suggested the last line could be read the other way round; but the story that follows and Paul’s quotation (Romans 9:12) confirm the ESV.

verseByVerse.quote: When her days to give birth were completed, behold, there were twins in her womb. The first came out red, all his body like a hairy cloak, so they called his name Esau. Afterward his brother came out with his hand holding Esau's heel, so his name was called Jacob. Isaac was sixty years old when she bore them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Esau is born first, red and hairy, and Jacob follows gripping his brother’s heel: the names given at birth sum up the men they will become.

The first came out red, all his body like a hairy cloak. Each word is a pun on a later name. “Red” (admoni) sounds like Edom, Esau’s other name (v. 30), and “hairy” (se‘ar) sounds like Seir, the hill country where his people would live (32:3). The same word “ruddy” is used of David (1 Samuel 16:12), so it need not be an insult. His hairiness will matter in chapter 27.

So they called his name Esau. The meaning of “Esau” is not explained and is not known for certain.

His hand holding Esau’s heel, so his name was called Jacob. Jacob (Ya‘aqov) sounds like “heel” (‘aqev). To grab the heel came to mean to trip up, supplant or cheat, and Esau will make the bitter pun: “Is he not rightly named Jacob? For he has cheated me these two times” (27:36). Hosea remembered it centuries later: “In the womb he took his brother by the heel, and in his manhood he strove with God” (Hosea 12:3). The grasping that begins at birth will end only when God wrestles him into a new name, Israel (32:28).

Isaac was sixty years old. Twenty years after the wedding (v. 20). God was not late; he was making plain that these children were his gift.

Uncertain wording. Genesis links Jacob’s name with “heel”. Similar names outside the Bible seem to be short for a prayer meaning “May God protect”, so the name may have had a good meaning that Jacob’s conduct turned into a bad one. Genesis is concerned with how the name fitted the man.
verseByVerse.note: “Jacob” means “he takes by the heel” or “he cheats” (ESV note). “Hairy” (se‘ar) sounds like Seir, the hill country of Edom where Esau’s descendants lived.

verseByVerse.quote: When the boys grew up, Esau was a skillful hunter, a man of the field, while Jacob was a quiet man, dwelling in tents. Isaac loved Esau because he ate of his game, but Rebekah loved Jacob.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The boys grow into very different men, and each parent takes a favourite: the family is divided, and the trouble of chapter 27 is already being prepared.

Esau was a skilful hunter, a man of the field. Esau is the outdoor man, restless and strong. Genesis has met one other famous hunter, Nimrod, the founder of Babel (10:8–10), and hunting is never the work of the chosen line in Genesis; nothing is wrong with it, but it marks Esau as a man of his own appetites and his own strength.

Jacob was a quiet man, dwelling in tents. Jacob stays at home with the flocks and the camp, the settled life of a shepherd (compare 4:2, 20; see Shepherds and Sheepfolds). He is not the warrior but the thinker, and as the next verses show, the planner.

Isaac loved Esau because he ate of his game. Literally, “because game was in his mouth”. Isaac’s love is tied to his appetite, and his appetite will drive chapter 27 (27:4). Father and son share a weakness: both are ruled by the stomach.

But Rebekah loved Jacob. No reason is given. Perhaps she remembered the word of v. 23; perhaps she simply preferred the son who stayed near. Either way the parents are divided, each with a favourite, and the family is heading for deception and exile.

Favouritism in a family is never harmless. Jacob, the favoured son, will grow up to favour Rachel over Leah (29:30) and Joseph over his brothers (37:3–4), with terrible results. Children notice which of them is preferred, and wounds of that kind can last a lifetime and pass to the next generation. God loves his children with a love that is not won by being the easiest to like, and Christian parents must ask him for that kind of love.

Uncertain wording. “Quiet” translates tam, which elsewhere usually means “blameless” or “complete” (Job 1:1). Jacob is plainly not blameless in the sense of sinless, so here it probably means settled, orderly or even-tempered, in contrast with the wild hunter. Some think the narrator chose the word with irony.

verseByVerse.quote: Once when Jacob was cooking stew, Esau came in from the field, and he was exhausted. And Esau said to Jacob, "Let me eat some of that red stew, for I am exhausted!" (Therefore his name was called Edom.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Esau comes in exhausted and demands Jacob’s red stew, and the name Edom, “red”, sticks to him and to his people.

Jacob was cooking stew. A simple stew of lentils (v. 34), a red-brown dish. Jacob is at home and at hand, Esau out in the field and back with nothing.

He was exhausted. The word means faint, worn out with hunger and fatigue. Esau’s need is real, and the hunter has caught nothing.

Let me eat some of that red stew. His words are crude and hurried, literally “Let me gulp some of the red, this red”. He does not even name the food. Esau lives for the moment, and the moment says “now”.

Therefore his name was called Edom. “Edom” sounds like the Hebrew for red. The people descended from Esau, the Edomites, lived to Israel’s south-east in the red sandstone hills of Seir. They were a brother nation (Deuteronomy 23:7) and often a bitter enemy (Numbers 20:14–21; Obadiah 10–12), and this story told Israel how the rivalry began.

Uncertain wording. The verb Esau uses appears only here in the Bible. From related languages it seems to mean to swallow greedily or to feed an animal, which is why many translate “let me gulp down”. Its exact flavour is uncertain, but it is clearly not polite.
verseByVerse.note: “Edom” sounds like the Hebrew for red (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: Jacob said, "Sell me your birthright now." Esau said, "I am about to die; of what use is a birthright to me?" Jacob said, "Swear to me now." So he swore to him and sold his birthright to Jacob. Then Jacob gave Esau bread and lentil stew, and he ate and drank and rose and went his way. Thus Esau despised his birthright.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jacob takes advantage of his brother’s hunger to buy his birthright, and Esau sells it for one meal: the narrator’s verdict is that Esau despised it.

Sell me your birthright now. “Now” is literally “as the day”, today, at once. Jacob has evidently thought about this before; he offers no kindness, only a deal. The birthright was the firstborn son’s right to lead the family after his father and to a double share of the inheritance (Deuteronomy 21:17; see Inheritance and the Firstborn). In this family it carried far more: the promise God gave Abraham.

I am about to die; of what use is a birthright to me? He was hungry, not dying, and his exaggeration shows his values: the future is worth nothing if the stomach is empty now. Ancient records show that inheritance rights could be traded; one tablet from Nuzi in Mesopotamia records a man selling his inheritance share to his brother for three sheep. But to sell such a thing for one bowl of stew was folly any reader would see.

Swear to me now. Jacob makes it binding with an oath. He knows the value of what he is buying, and he does not trust his brother to remember the bargain on a full stomach.

He ate and drank and rose and went his way. Five quick verbs. There is no pause, no regret, no second thought. Esau eats, gets up and goes, as if nothing had happened.

Thus Esau despised his birthright. The narrator rarely comments, so this verdict is weighty. To despise is to treat as worth little. Esau’s sin was not hunger but contempt for what God had attached to his birth. Hebrews makes him a warning: let no one be “sexually immoral or unholy like Esau, who sold his birthright for a single meal” (Hebrews 12:16). He was “unholy” because he treated a holy thing as common.

The Son who would not sell. Jesus too was hungry in the wilderness, after forty days, and was tempted to use his sonship to make bread. He answered, “Man shall not live by bread alone” (Matthew 4:3–4). Where Esau traded his birthright for food, the true firstborn, “the firstborn of all creation” (Colossians 1:15), would not. Where Jacob grasped at a birthright by scheming, Christ “did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped” (Philippians 2:6) but gave himself. And he shares his birthright with his people, so that the church is “the assembly of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven” (Hebrews 12:23). We cannot buy that inheritance; it is a gift.

The bowl of stew today. The pattern is always the same: the present need feels more real than the promised future. It may be a relationship that offers intimacy at the cost of faithfulness, work that crowds out worship, or a comfort that dulls the appetite for God. Ask what you are tempted to trade, and stay close to Christ, who satisfies more deeply than any meal.

What it does not mean. God’s choice of Jacob does not excuse Jacob’s methods. He exploits his brother’s weakness, and his own grasping will bring him years of fear, exile and being cheated in turn (29:25). God fulfils his word through Jacob in spite of his scheming, not because of it.
