Can a person sell his birthright beyond recall? Hebrews says that later Esau “found no chance to repent, though he sought it with tears” (Hebrews 12:17). That does not mean God turns away anyone who truly repents. Esau wept for the lost blessing (27:34, 38), not for his sin, and he could not undo the consequence or change his father’s word. The warning is to value Christ now; the promise is that whoever comes to him he will never cast out (John 6:37).
verseByVerse.note: The birthright gave the firstborn a double share of the inheritance and headship of the family.

25.theology:
God's Free Choice. Romans 9:10–13 uses Jacob and Esau as its main illustration of election: God’s choice of Jacob over Esau was made “though they were not yet born and had done nothing either good or bad—in order that God’s purpose of election might continue, not because of works but because of him who calls.” Election does not rest on faith or merit that God foresaw in us, but on his free, gracious purpose. It is not arbitrary, for God’s purposes are wise and good, but it is free, depending on nothing in us.

Despising the Birthright. Esau's bargain is the Bible's classic picture of trading the eternal for the immediate, and Hebrews makes it a warning for the church: do not exchange your inheritance for the bowl of stew the present world offers. The inheritance is ours by grace, not by our grip on it; but the Spirit trains our desires through prayer, God's word and his people, so that we learn to value the unseen promise over the visible satisfaction.
25.examples:
Then: The firstborn received a double portion of the inheritance and carried the family's leadership. To sell that for a meal was a transaction any ancient reader would have found scandalous, and Esau simply "rose and went his way" (v. 34), indifferent to what he had traded.

Now: The bowl of stew takes a thousand forms: the relationship that offers immediate intimacy at the cost of faithfulness, the career that offers success at the cost of family and faith, the entertainment that crowds out attention to God. The pattern is always the same: the present need feels more real than the promised future. The remedy is to stay close to Christ, who is more real than any bowl of stew.

keyVerse.quote: Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples from within you shall be divided; the one shall be stronger than the other, the older shall serve the younger.
keyVerse.note: God’s word before the twins are born sets the course of the whole Jacob story and of two nations after them. It overturns the rule of the firstborn to show that his promise moves by his free choice, not by birth or merit. Paul makes it his chief example of election by grace (Romans 9:10–13), the grace that saves sinners in Christ.

25.reflection:
Abraham gave everything to Isaac but did not forget his other sons (vv. 5–6), and God kept his promise to bless Ishmael (vv. 12–16). What does this show about God’s kindness to those outside his covenant people, and how should it shape the way we treat them?

Isaac and Rebekah waited twenty years for children, and Isaac prayed (vv. 20–21, 26). What have you been praying about for a long time? What helps you to keep praying when the answer is slow?

Isaac loved Esau and Rebekah loved Jacob (v. 28). Where have you seen favouritism do damage in a family, a church or a workplace? How does God’s love in Christ give us a better way?

Esau traded what was lasting for what was immediate (vv. 32–34). What “bowl of stew” most tempts you to neglect what God has given you in Christ? What would it look like this week to value the inheritance more?

26.title: The LORD Is with You
26.text: <sup>1</sup>Now there was a famine in the land, besides the former famine that was in the days of Abraham. And Isaac went to Gerar to Abimelech king of the Philistines.<sup>2</sup>And the LORD appeared to him and said, "Do not go down to Egypt; dwell in the land of which I shall tell you.<sup>3</sup>Sojourn in this land, and I will be with you and will bless you, for to you and to your offspring I will give all these lands, and I will establish the oath that I swore to Abraham your father.<sup>4</sup>I will multiply your offspring as the stars of heaven and will give to your offspring all these lands. And in your offspring all the nations of the earth shall be blessed,<sup>5</sup>because Abraham obeyed my voice and kept my charge, my commandments, my statutes, and my laws."<sup>6</sup>So Isaac settled in Gerar.<sup>7</sup>When the men of the place asked him about his wife, he said, "She is my sister," for he feared to say, "My wife," thinking, "lest the men of the place should kill me because of Rebekah," because she was attractive in appearance.<sup>8</sup>When he had been there a long time, Abimelech king of the Philistines looked out of a window and saw Isaac laughing with Rebekah his wife.<sup>9</sup>So Abimelech called Isaac and said, "Behold, she is your wife. How then could you say, 'She is my sister'?" Isaac said to him, "Because I thought, 'Lest I die because of her.'"<sup>10</sup>Abimelech said, "What is this you have done to us? One of the people might easily have lain with your wife, and you would have brought guilt upon us."<sup>11</sup>So Abimelech warned all the people, saying, "Whoever touches this man or his wife shall surely be put to death."<sup>12</sup>And Isaac sowed in that land and reaped in the same year a hundredfold. The LORD blessed him,<sup>13</sup>and the man became rich, and gained more and more until he became very wealthy.<sup>14</sup>He had possessions of flocks and herds and many servants, so that the Philistines envied him.<sup>15</sup>(Now the Philistines had stopped and filled with earth all the wells that his father's servants had dug in the days of Abraham his father.)<sup>16</sup>And Abimelech said to Isaac, "Go away from us, for you are much mightier than we."<sup>17</sup>So Isaac departed from there and encamped in the Valley of Gerar and settled there.<sup>18</sup>And Isaac dug again the wells of water that had been dug in the days of Abraham his father, which the Philistines had stopped after the death of Abraham. And he gave them the names that his father had given them.<sup>19</sup>But when Isaac's servants dug in the valley and found there a well of spring water,<sup>20</sup>the herdsmen of Gerar quarreled with Isaac's herdsmen, saying, "The water is ours." So he called the name of the well Esek, because they contended with him.<sup>21</sup>Then they dug another well, and they quarreled over that also, so he called its name Sitnah.<sup>22</sup>And he moved from there and dug another well, and they did not quarrel over it. So he called its name Rehoboth, saying, "For now the LORD has made room for us, and we shall be fruitful in the land."<sup>23</sup>From there he went up to Beersheba.<sup>24</sup>And the LORD appeared to him the same night and said, "I am the God of Abraham your father. Fear not, for I am with you and will bless you and multiply your offspring for my servant Abraham's sake."<sup>25</sup>So he built an altar there and called upon the name of the LORD and pitched his tent there. And there Isaac's servants dug a well.<sup>26</sup>When Abimelech went to him from Gerar with Ahuzzath his adviser and Phicol the commander of his army,<sup>27</sup>Isaac said to them, "Why have you come to me, seeing that you hate me and have sent me away from you?"<sup>28</sup>They said, "We see plainly that the LORD has been with you. So we said, let there be a sworn pact between us, between you and us, and let us make a covenant with you,<sup>29</sup>that you will do us no harm, just as we have not touched you and have done to you nothing but good and have sent you away in peace. You are now the blessed of the LORD."<sup>30</sup>So he made them a feast, and they ate and drank.<sup>31</sup>In the morning they rose early and exchanged oaths. And Isaac sent them on their way, and they departed from him in peace.<sup>32</sup>That same day Isaac's servants came and told him about the well that they had dug and said to him, "We have found water."<sup>33</sup>He called it Shibah; therefore the name of the city is Beersheba to this day.<sup>34</sup>When Esau was forty years old, he took Judith the daughter of Beeri the Hittite to be his wife, and Basemath the daughter of Elon the Hittite,<sup>35</sup>and they made life bitter for Isaac and Rebekah.
26.overview:
Where we are. Abraham is dead, and God has blessed Isaac (25:11). This is the only chapter in Genesis given wholly to Isaac, and it reads like an echo of his father’s life: a famine, a wife passed off as a sister, great wealth, quarrels over wells and a treaty at Beersheba. Most of it probably happened before the twins were born, for no children are mentioned.

The message. The blessing of Abraham passes to Isaac not because Isaac is better than his father but because God keeps his word. God repeats to Isaac every promise he made to Abraham; Isaac repeats his father’s sin. Yet the LORD is with him, protects him, prospers him and makes room for him, until even his enemies have to confess, “the LORD has been with you” (v. 28).

Why it was said. Israel, a people of flawed sons of flawed fathers, needed to know that the promise did not die with Abraham, and that it rested on God’s faithfulness, not theirs (see the introduction). Living among envious neighbours, they could learn from Isaac to wait for God to make room.

How the chapter makes its case. In famine God forbids Isaac to go to Egypt and gives him the oath he swore to Abraham (vv. 1–6). Isaac, afraid, calls Rebekah his sister, and a pagan king rebukes him and protects her (vv. 7–11). God blesses Isaac with a hundredfold harvest and great wealth, and the envious Philistines drive him out (vv. 12–16). He reopens his father’s wells and gives way in two quarrels until the LORD makes room (vv. 17–22). At Beersheba God says “Fear not” and Isaac builds an altar (vv. 23–25). His enemies come seeking peace, and the day the oaths are sworn his servants find water (vv. 26–33). The chapter ends with Esau’s marriages, a cloud over the family (vv. 34–35).

Where it leads. By promise and by pattern. The promise that “in your offspring all the nations of the earth shall be blessed” (v. 4) is fulfilled in one offspring, Christ (Galatians 3:16). And twice God blesses Isaac because of another man’s obedience, “for my servant Abraham’s sake” (vv. 5, 24). That is the shape of the gospel: sinners are blessed not for their own record but for the sake of another, “by the one man’s obedience the many will be made righteous” (Romans 5:19).

For us. God does not abandon his people when they repeat old sins, though he does expose them. Bring your fears to the God who says “Fear not, for I am with you” (v. 24), give way rather than grab, and trust him to make room.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — Isaac and Abimelech: The Covenant Repeated
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God renews to Isaac the promise he made to Abraham and keeps it, even though Isaac repeats his father’s failure. In a famine the LORD forbids Isaac to go down to Egypt and binds himself to him with the oath sworn to Abraham (vv. 1–6). In Gerar, afraid for his life, Isaac calls Rebekah his sister, as Abraham had done twice; a pagan king discovers the truth, rebukes him and protects them both (vv. 7–11). Then God gives Isaac a hundredfold harvest and great wealth, and the Philistines, envious, stop up his father’s wells and send him away (vv. 12–16). Blessing does not depend on Isaac’s goodness, but it does not spare him the trouble of living among others.
verseByVerse.theology: In a famine God forbids Isaac to go to Egypt and renews to him the promise made to Abraham. In Gerar Isaac says Rebekah is his sister, and is found out; Abimelech protects them. Isaac reaps a hundredfold, and the envious Philistines send him away.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the son repeats a sin he had only heard about, and God blesses him while he lives with the consequences. Now: family sins are passed on by what children hear as well as see.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was a famine in the land, besides the former famine that was in the days of Abraham. And Isaac went to Gerar to Abimelech king of the Philistines. And the LORD appeared to him and said, "Do not go down to Egypt; dwell in the land of which I shall tell you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When famine comes, the LORD forbids Isaac to go down to Egypt: the heir of the promise must stay in the promised land, even when staying looks foolish.

Besides the former famine that was in the days of Abraham. The narrator points us back to 12:10, where Abraham went down to Egypt in a famine and lied about his wife. We are meant to watch whether the son will do the same.

Isaac went to Gerar to Abimelech king of the Philistines. Gerar lay in the south-west of Canaan, between Gaza and Beersheba, on the way to Egypt. Abraham had lived there and dealt with a king called Abimelech (chapter 20; 21:22–34). This may be the same man, now old, or more likely a son, for some seventy years have passed and “Abimelech” (“my father is king”) may have been a royal name, as Pharaoh was a title.

Do not go down to Egypt. Egypt, watered by the Nile, did not depend on rain as Canaan did, and in famine it was the obvious place to go (12:10; 42:1–2). But the LORD tells Isaac, “dwell in the land of which I shall tell you”, the very words he used to send Abraham out (12:1). Isaac never leaves the land of promise in his life. Faith stays where God puts it, even when sense says to leave.

Were there Philistines in Isaac’s day? The great Philistine settlement on the coast, from the Aegean region, came around 1200 BC, long after Isaac. Some therefore call the name an anachronism. But there were earlier waves of settlers from Caphtor (probably Crete) and the islands (Deuteronomy 2:23; Amos 9:7), and Gerar’s people, unlike the later Philistines, are peaceable herdsmen under a king. Either these were earlier settlers of the same stock, or the narrator calls them by the name his readers knew for the people of that region, as he uses later names for places (23:2).

verseByVerse.quote: Sojourn in this land, and I will be with you and will bless you, for to you and to your offspring I will give all these lands, and I will establish the oath that I swore to Abraham your father. I will multiply your offspring as the stars of heaven and will give to your offspring all these lands. And in your offspring all the nations of the earth shall be blessed, because Abraham obeyed my voice and kept my charge, my commandments, my statutes, and my laws."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God gives Isaac, in his own name, every promise he made to Abraham, and binds himself to keep the oath he swore: Isaac is blessed for his father’s sake.

Sojourn in this land, and I will be with you and will bless you. Isaac is to live as a resident foreigner, owning nothing, as his father did (Hebrews 11:9). But he has God’s presence, “I will be with you”, the first time Genesis gives this promise, and the heart of all the rest (28:15; Exodus 3:12; Matthew 28:20).

I will establish the oath that I swore to Abraham your father. On Moriah God swore by himself (22:16–18). The promises of land, offspring as many as the stars, and blessing for all nations (12:2–3; 15:5) now pass to Isaac by God’s own word. The covenant is not renegotiated for the new generation; it is renewed.

In your offspring all the nations of the earth shall be blessed. The promise is not only for Isaac’s family but for the world. Paul notes that the word “offspring” is singular and finds its final meaning in one person: “And to your offspring,” who is Christ (Galatians 3:16). Every nation blessed by the gospel is this promise kept.

Because Abraham obeyed my voice and kept my charge. The four words, “my charge, my commandments, my statutes, and my laws”, are the language of the law of Moses (Deuteronomy 11:1). Israel at Sinai is shown that its father Abraham lived the life of trusting obedience the law would later describe, centuries before it was written.

For another’s sake. Isaac receives blessing because of his father’s obedience (also v. 24). That is a small picture of a far greater gift. Believers are blessed, forgiven and accepted not for their own obedience but for the sake of Christ’s: “by the one man’s obedience the many will be made righteous” (Romans 5:19). When we pray “for Jesus’ sake”, we are standing where Isaac stood.

Thank God for those who went before. Many Christians owe much to the faith of parents, grandparents or the people who first taught them. Thank God for them, and for the God who kept faith with them, without imagining that their faith can stand in for yours.

Where Christians differ: did Abraham earn the promise? Some Jewish tradition taught that Abraham kept the whole law before it was given, and that his merit earned blessing for his descendants; some Christians speak of a store of merit from the saints. Others take v. 5 to mean that the promise depended on Abraham’s works. This commentary’s view: the promise was given freely before Abraham had done anything (12:1–3), and he was counted righteous by faith (15:6). His obedience was the fruit of that faith, which God was pleased to honour (22:16–18; Hebrews 11:8), as James says, “faith was completed by his works” (James 2:22). The only merit that blesses others is Christ’s.

verseByVerse.quote: So Isaac settled in Gerar. When the men of the place asked him about his wife, he said, "She is my sister," for he feared to say, "My wife," thinking, "lest the men of the place should kill me because of Rebekah," because she was attractive in appearance. When he had been there a long time, Abimelech king of the Philistines looked out of a window and saw Isaac laughing with Rebekah his wife. So Abimelech called Isaac and said, "Behold, she is your wife. How then could you say, 'She is my sister'?" Isaac said to him, "Because I thought, 'Lest I die because of her.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Afraid for his life, Isaac tells the men of Gerar that Rebekah is his sister, the same lie his father told twice, and it is exposed when the king sees him with her as a husband.

She is my sister. Abraham had said this in Egypt (12:13) and in this very town (20:2). Isaac was not yet born when either happened, yet he repeats the lie, perhaps because he had heard the story told. Unlike Abraham’s half-truth (20:12), Isaac’s is simply false; Rebekah was his cousin’s daughter.

For he feared. Fear is the root. He thinks the men of the place may kill him to take his beautiful wife, as Abraham had feared (20:11). To protect himself he exposes his wife to another man. That is not the protection Scripture permits; no one had threatened him, and he puts Rebekah, and the promise of offspring through her, at risk to save his own skin.

When he had been there a long time. The lie held for a while, but lies tend to come out.

Laughing with Rebekah his wife. The word is a play on Isaac’s own name, which means “he laughs” (21:6). It plainly describes behaviour that only a husband would show his wife, and the king draws the obvious conclusion.

How then could you say, “She is my sister”? The pagan king asks the question the man of God cannot answer well. Isaac can only admit his fear.

Sins pass down in families. Children learn what they see and what they hear about. Isaac’s lie shows how a father’s sin can reappear in a son, and Jacob will become the greatest deceiver of them all (chapter 27). But the God who kept faith with Isaac through his lie can break the pattern. Ask his Spirit to make you new where your family has gone wrong, and be honest with your children about your own failures, so they learn repentance as well as sin.

Uncertain wording. The word translated “laughing” can mean to laugh, to play or to jest. Here it probably means caressing or fondling, intimate play between husband and wife, and many translations say so. The narrator chooses the word for its echo of Isaac’s name.
verseByVerse.note: Isaac repeats his father’s lie.

verseByVerse.quote: Abimelech said, "What is this you have done to us? One of the people might easily have lain with your wife, and you would have brought guilt upon us." So Abimelech warned all the people, saying, "Whoever touches this man or his wife shall surely be put to death."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abimelech rebukes Isaac for endangering his people with guilt, and puts the couple under his own protection: God uses an outsider to guard the promise.

What is this you have done to us? The same question God asked Eve (3:13) and Pharaoh asked Abraham (12:18). The man of the world has a clearer conscience about adultery than the man of God has about lying.

You would have brought guilt upon us. Abimelech knows adultery is a serious sin, bringing guilt on a whole people, even if committed in ignorance (compare 20:9). He understands what Isaac’s fear made him forget.

Whoever touches this man or his wife shall surely be put to death. The king’s decree does what Isaac’s lie could not: it keeps Rebekah safe. For the third time in Genesis a pagan ruler protects the mother of the promise. God guards his promise even through those who do not know him.

Grace that exposes. God does not wink at Isaac’s lie. He lets it be found out and rebuked by a pagan, to Isaac’s shame. But he does not cancel his promise either. That is how grace treats believers: it does not leave us in our sin, nor abandon us for it.

What it does not mean. The story does not approve of Isaac’s lie because things turned out well. Genesis tells the patriarchs’ failures plainly, and the reader must weigh what they did against what God said (see the introduction). Scripture forbids deceiving one’s neighbour (Leviticus 19:11), and Isaac’s lie came from fear, not faith.

verseByVerse.quote: And Isaac sowed in that land and reaped in the same year a hundredfold. The LORD blessed him, and the man became rich, and gained more and more until he became very wealthy. He had possessions of flocks and herds and many servants, so that the Philistines envied him. (Now the Philistines had stopped and filled with earth all the wells that his father's servants had dug in the days of Abraham his father.) And Abimelech said to Isaac, "Go away from us, for you are much mightier than we."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In a famine year God gives Isaac a hundredfold harvest and great wealth, and the blessing provokes the Philistines’ envy until they drive him away.

Isaac sowed in that land and reaped in the same year a hundredfold. Isaac, a herdsman, sows a crop, as semi-nomads sometimes did, and in a time of famine reaps a hundred times what he sowed. A good harvest might be thirty or sixty times (compare Matthew 13:8). The narrator gives the reason: “The LORD blessed him.” The promise of v. 3 is already being kept.

The man became rich, and gained more and more. The Hebrew piles up the word “great”: he grew great, and kept growing, until he was very great. His wealth was in flocks, herds and many servants, the riches of a herdsman chief.

So that the Philistines envied him. Blessing often provokes envy, and envy turns to hostility. They “stopped and filled with earth” the wells Abraham’s servants had dug. In dry country a well meant life for people and flocks (see Wells and Cisterns), and wells marked a claim to the land around them, so to fill one in was an act of hostility.

Go away from us, for you are much mightier than we. Abimelech fears Isaac’s growing power. Later a Pharaoh will say the same of Israel in Egypt (Exodus 1:9), and the people God blesses will again be treated as a threat.

What it does not mean. Not that God always rewards faith with wealth. Isaac’s riches were part of God’s promise to bless the patriarchs in the land, a foretaste of the inheritance, and they brought him trouble as well. Many believers are poor, and the New Testament promises them a richer inheritance (James 2:5). Wealth is a gift to be held open-handed, never a measure of God’s favour.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–35 — Wells, Beersheba, and the Covenant with Abimelech
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God makes room for Isaac, and those who drove him out come to make peace, because they can see that the LORD is with him. Isaac reopens his father’s wells and calls them by their old names (vv. 17–18). He gives way when the herdsmen of Gerar quarrel over two new wells, and at the third, uncontested, he says that the LORD has made room (vv. 19–22). At Beersheba God appears, says “Fear not”, and Isaac builds an altar (vv. 23–25). Abimelech comes to make a treaty, and on the day of the oaths water is found (vv. 26–33). But Esau’s two Hittite marriages bring bitterness into the family (vv. 34–35), preparing the crisis of chapter 27.
verseByVerse.theology: Isaac re-digs his father's wells and yields two disputed wells until at Rehoboth the LORD makes room. At Beersheba God appears to him, and he builds an altar. Abimelech comes to make peace, and Esau marries two Hittite women.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the Philistines could account for Isaac only by saying, "the LORD has been with you." Now: "so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all" (Rom. 12:18).

verseByVerse.quote: So Isaac departed from there and encamped in the Valley of Gerar and settled there. And Isaac dug again the wells of water that had been dug in the days of Abraham his father, which the Philistines had stopped after the death of Abraham. And he gave them the names that his father had given them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Driven out, Isaac reopens the wells his father dug and gives them their old names: he does not pioneer, he recovers.

Encamped in the Valley of Gerar. Isaac moves away from the town but stays in the region, in a valley or wadi where water could be found beneath the dry riverbed.

Isaac dug again the wells of water. The Philistines had stopped them “after the death of Abraham”, perhaps thinking his claim had died with him. Isaac clears them out. A well dug by his father was part of his inheritance, and Abraham had once made a treaty to secure one (21:25–31).

He gave them the names that his father had given them. He is not trying to make his own name. He is continuing his father’s faith in his father’s God, and the old names claim the wells again as part of the promise.

Re-dig the old wells. Every generation of the church must recover the wells of grace that earlier generations opened, and that worldliness, compromise and neglect can stop up: the Scriptures, prayer, worship and the gospel itself. Reformation is not invention but recovery. The water is not new, and it has never run dry.

verseByVerse.quote: But when Isaac's servants dug in the valley and found there a well of spring water, the herdsmen of Gerar quarreled with Isaac's herdsmen, saying, "The water is ours." So he called the name of the well Esek, because they contended with him. Then they dug another well, and they quarreled over that also, so he called its name Sitnah. And he moved from there and dug another well, and they did not quarrel over it. So he called its name Rehoboth, saying, "For now the LORD has made room for us, and we shall be fruitful in the land."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Twice the herdsmen of Gerar claim a new well, and twice Isaac gives way and moves on, until he digs a third that no one disputes and names it for the room the LORD has made.

A well of spring water. Literally “living water”, a spring rather than a pit, the most valuable kind of well.

The water is ours. The local herdsmen claim it, probably because it lay in land they grazed. Isaac does not fight, though he was “much mightier” (v. 16).

Esek … Sitnah. He names the wells after what happened there: Esek means “contention” and Sitnah “enmity” (ESV notes). Sitnah comes from the same root as the word “Satan”, the adversary, the accuser.

Rehoboth … For now the LORD has made room for us. Rehoboth means “broad places” or “room”. When no one quarrels, Isaac gives the credit to God. The room he did not take by force, God gave him, and he looks ahead in faith: “we shall be fruitful in the land.”

The meekness that inherits. Isaac, the stronger party, gave way instead of grabbing, and God gave him room. He is a picture of what Jesus promised: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth” (Matthew 5:5). Jesus himself, “gentle and lowly in heart” (Matthew 11:29), did not grasp, and God gave him the nations as his inheritance. Paul puts it as a rule for believers: “If possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all” (Romans 12:18).

What it does not mean. Not that a Christian must give up every right or never stand firm. Isaac did not abandon the land God promised; he gave up particular wells for the sake of peace. Paul used his legal rights when the gospel or justice required it (Acts 16:37; 25:11). Giving way is right when it is a matter of our own advantage; when others are being wronged, love may need to stand firm.
verseByVerse.note: Esek means “contention,” Sitnah “enmity,” and Rehoboth “broad places” or “room” (ESV notes).

verseByVerse.quote: From there he went up to Beersheba. And the LORD appeared to him the same night and said, "I am the God of Abraham your father. Fear not, for I am with you and will bless you and multiply your offspring for my servant Abraham's sake." So he built an altar there and called upon the name of the LORD and pitched his tent there. And there Isaac's servants dug a well.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At Beersheba the LORD appears to Isaac at night, tells him not to fear and renews his promise for Abraham’s sake; Isaac answers by building an altar and calling on his name.

From there he went up to Beersheba. Beersheba, in the south of the land on the edge of the Negeb desert, was where Abraham had made a treaty, planted a tamarisk tree and called on the LORD (21:31–33).

The LORD appeared to him the same night. After the envy, the expulsion and the quarrels, God comes to Isaac at once. This is the second time God appears to him (v. 2).

I am the God of Abraham your father. God introduces himself by his relationship with Abraham. His faithfulness runs from one generation to the next, and he means to be Isaac’s God as he was Abraham’s.

Fear not, for I am with you. Isaac lied in Gerar because he “feared” (v. 7). Now God speaks to that fear. He does not promise that nothing will threaten Isaac; he promises himself. “I am with you” answers fear better than any reason why there is nothing to be afraid of.

For my servant Abraham’s sake. Isaac’s blessing rests on God’s commitment to another. God calls Abraham “my servant”, a title of honour later given to Moses, David and the prophets, and finally to the Servant who is Christ (Isaiah 42:1; Acts 3:13).

He built an altar there and called upon the name of the LORD. Isaac answers promise with worship, as his father did (12:7–8; 13:18). Altar, tent and well: worship, home and provision, all at the place where God met him. Praise is the right reply to promise.

The God who is with us. “I am with you” runs through the whole Bible, until God is with us in person, Immanuel (Matthew 1:23), and the risen Christ tells his disciples, “I am with you always, to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20). Whatever you fear, he does not leave.

verseByVerse.quote: When Abimelech went to him from Gerar with Ahuzzath his adviser and Phicol the commander of his army, Isaac said to them, "Why have you come to me, seeing that you hate me and have sent me away from you?" They said, "We see plainly that the LORD has been with you. So we said, let there be a sworn pact between us, between you and us, and let us make a covenant with you, that you will do us no harm, just as we have not touched you and have done to you nothing but good and have sent you away in peace. You are now the blessed of the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The men who drove Isaac away now come to him seeking a treaty, because they can see plainly that the LORD is with him.

Abimelech … with Ahuzzath his adviser and Phicol the commander of his army. A formal delegation: the king, his counsellor and his general. “Adviser” is literally “friend”, a court title, like the “king’s friend” in Solomon’s court (1 Kings 4:5). A Phicol had also come with Abimelech to Abraham (21:22); it may be the same man, or a title passed down.

Why have you come to me, seeing that you hate me and have sent me away? Isaac speaks plainly. He has given way, but he is not naive about what was done.

We see plainly that the LORD has been with you. Outsiders can see what Isaac was slow to trust: the LORD is with him. His blessing is so obvious that his enemies would rather have him as an ally than an enemy. This is a small foretaste of God’s promise that the nations would seek blessing through Abraham’s family (12:3).

We … have done to you nothing but good and have sent you away in peace. This is a generous account of what they did. Filling in wells and driving a man out are not “nothing but good”. Isaac does not argue; he lets it go for the sake of peace.

You are now the blessed of the LORD. The Philistines say it in their own words. God’s people are meant to be seen to be blessed, not by their wealth but by God’s evident presence with them. “By this all people will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13:35).

verseByVerse.quote: So he made them a feast, and they ate and drank. In the morning they rose early and exchanged oaths. And Isaac sent them on their way, and they departed from him in peace. That same day Isaac's servants came and told him about the well that they had dug and said to him, "We have found water." He called it Shibah; therefore the name of the city is Beersheba to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Isaac seals the peace with a feast and an oath, and that same day his servants find water: the place is named Shibah, and the city Beersheba.

So he made them a feast, and they ate and drank. In the ancient world a shared meal sealed an agreement (31:46, 54) and turned enemies into guests (see Hospitality). Isaac does not demand an apology before making peace; he provides the meal.

They rose early and exchanged oaths … and they departed from him in peace. The word “peace” closes the account. The man who was told to go away now sends his visitors on their way.

We have found water. On the very day of the oath God provides a new well. Peace with neighbours and provision from God arrive together.

He called it Shibah; therefore the name of the city is Beersheba. Shibah sounds like the Hebrew for “oath” (ESV note), and Beersheba means “well of the oath” or “well of seven” (21:31).

Did Beersheba get its name twice? Abraham had already named the place (21:31). As Isaac gave his father’s wells their old names again (v. 18), so here he renews the name with a new oath at a new well. The name is confirmed by a second event, in the next generation.
verseByVerse.note: “Shibah” sounds like the Hebrew for “oath” (ESV note), which is how Beersheba got its name.

verseByVerse.quote: When Esau was forty years old, he took Judith the daughter of Beeri the Hittite to be his wife, and Basemath the daughter of Elon the Hittite, and they made life bitter for Isaac and Rebekah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Esau marries two Hittite women, outside the family of promise, and they make life bitter for his parents: another sign that he does not value what God has given his family.

When Esau was forty years old. The same age as Isaac when he married Rebekah (25:20). But Isaac’s marriage was arranged with prayer and care, so that he would not take a wife from the Canaanites (24:3–4). Esau chooses for himself, and takes two wives at once.

Judith … Basemath … the Hittite. The Hittites were among the peoples of Canaan (10:15; 23:3), whose ways God would judge (15:16). Abraham had made his servant swear not to take a wife for Isaac from them (24:3). Esau ignores this, as he ignored the worth of the birthright (Hebrews 12:16).

They made life bitter for Isaac and Rebekah. Literally, they were “bitterness of spirit” to them. The marriages bring grief into the home, and Rebekah will later use that grief to send Jacob away (27:46). The scene is set for the crisis of chapter 27.

Marry in the Lord. The issue is faith, not race: Rahab the Canaanite and Ruth the Moabite were welcomed into God’s people because they trusted Israel’s God. The New Testament says a believer is free to marry “only in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 7:39), and warns, “Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers” (2 Corinthians 6:14). Marriage shapes everything, including faith and the children who grow up in it.

When children marry outside the faith. Isaac and Rebekah’s grief is common among Christian parents. Pray for your children’s choices long before they make them. If they choose against your hopes, grieve honestly, but keep loving them and their spouses, and keep praying; bitterness helps no one, and God’s grace reaches into many families that began badly.

Uncertain wording. Esau’s wives are listed again in 36:2–3 with different names and fathers: there Basemath is Ishmael’s daughter, and Adah the daughter of Elon. Women sometimes had two names, and Esau also took a third wife (28:9), but how the two lists fit together is not certain.
verseByVerse.note: Esau’s Hittite marriages showed the same disregard for the promise as the sold birthright, and grieved his parents.

26.theology:
Genesis 26 is a chapter about the passing on of grace. Isaac repeats his father’s sin; God repeats his promise unchanged. The covenant rests on the Giver, not the receiver.

Blessing is the key to the chapter. It flows despite sin, through life as a foreigner and quarrels over wells, until the Philistines themselves confess that the LORD is with this man. This anticipates Paul’s argument in Romans 4: Abraham’s children inherit not through law-keeping but through faith in the God who gives life to the dead (Rom 4:17).
26.examples:
Every generation of the church must re-dig the wells of grace (the gospel, the Scriptures, prayer and worship) that earlier generations opened but that worldliness, compromise or neglect can stop up. Reformation is not invention; it is recovery.

Isaac’s persistence through Esek and Sitnah to Rehoboth shows the patience of faith. The “room” did not come at once; it came through sustained trust in the God who promised it. The Christian life is like that: not a straight line upward, but a journey through opposition toward the room only God provides.

keyVerse.quote: I am the God of Abraham your father. Fear not, for I am with you and will bless you and multiply your offspring for my servant Abraham’s sake.
keyVerse.note: Isaac lied because he was afraid (v. 7), and quarrels and envy have followed him; now God meets his fear with his own presence. The promise rests on God’s faithfulness to Abraham, not on Isaac’s worth, which is exactly how God blesses sinners now, for the sake of his obedient Son. “I am with you” is the heart of every covenant promise, fulfilled in Immanuel.

26.reflection:
Isaac repeated the very sin his father had committed (v. 7). What patterns of sin or fear can you see passed down in your own family? How does the gospel give hope that they can be broken?

Twice God blesses Isaac “for my servant Abraham’s sake” (vv. 5, 24). How does this help you understand what it means to be blessed for Christ’s sake? How should it affect the way you pray?

Isaac gave way over two wells before he found room (vv. 19–22). When is it right to give way in a dispute, and when is it right to stand firm? Where might God be asking you to trust him to make room?

Abimelech said, “We see plainly that the LORD has been with you” (v. 28). What would make the people around you say that of you or your church?

27.title: Jacob Receives the Blessing
27.text: <sup>1</sup>When Isaac was old and his eyes were dim so that he could not see, he called Esau his older son and said to him, "My son"; and he answered, "Here I am."<sup>2</sup>He said, "Behold, I am old; I do not know the day of my death.<sup>3</sup>Now then, take your weapons, your quiver and your bow, and go out to the field and hunt game for me,<sup>4</sup>and prepare for me delicious food, such as I love, and bring it to me so that I may eat, that my soul may bless you before I die."<sup>5</sup>Now Rebekah was listening when Isaac spoke to his son Esau. So when Esau went to the field to hunt for game and bring it,<sup>6</sup>Rebekah said to her son Jacob, "I heard your father speak to your brother Esau,<sup>7</sup>'Bring me game and prepare for me delicious food, that I may eat it and bless you before the LORD before I die.'<sup>8</sup>Now therefore, my son, obey my voice as I command you.<sup>9</sup>Go to the flock and bring me two good young goats, so that I may prepare from them delicious food for your father, such as he loves.<sup>10</sup>And you shall bring it to your father to eat, so that he may bless you before he dies."<sup>11</sup>But Jacob said to Rebekah his mother, "Behold, my brother Esau is a hairy man, and I am a smooth man.<sup>12</sup>Perhaps my father will feel me, and I shall seem to be mocking him and bring a curse upon myself and not a blessing."<sup>13</sup>His mother said to him, "Let your curse be on me, my son; only obey my voice, and go, bring them to me."<sup>14</sup>So he went and took them and brought them to his mother, and his mother prepared delicious food, such as his father loved.<sup>15</sup>Then Rebekah took the best garments of Esau her older son, which were with her in the house, and put them on Jacob her younger son.<sup>16</sup>And the skins of the young goats she put on his hands and on the smooth part of his neck.<sup>17</sup>And she put the delicious food and the bread, which she had prepared, into the hand of her son Jacob.<sup>18</sup>So he went in to his father and said, "My father." And he said, "Here I am. Who are you, my son?"<sup>19</sup>Jacob said to his father, "I am Esau your firstborn. I have done as you told me; now sit up and eat of my game, that your soul may bless me."<sup>20</sup>But Isaac said to his son, "How is it that you have found it so quickly, my son?" He answered, "Because the LORD your God granted me success."<sup>21</sup>Then Isaac said to Jacob, "Please come near, that I may feel you, my son, to know whether you are really my son Esau or not."<sup>22</sup>So Jacob went near to Isaac his father, who felt him and said, "The voice is Jacob's voice, but the hands are the hands of Esau."<sup>23</sup>And he did not recognize him, because his hands were hairy like his brother Esau's hands. So he blessed him.<sup>24</sup>He said, "Are you really my son Esau?" He answered, "I am."<sup>25</sup>Then he said, "Bring it near to me, that I may eat of my son's game and bless you." So he brought it near to him, and he ate; and he brought him wine, and he drank.<sup>26</sup>Then his father Isaac said to him, "Come near and kiss me, my son."<sup>27</sup>So he came near and kissed him. And Isaac smelled the smell of his garments and blessed him and said, "See, the smell of my son is as the smell of a field that the LORD has blessed!<sup>28</sup>May God give you of the dew of heaven and of the fatness of the earth and plenty of grain and wine.<sup>29</sup>Let peoples serve you, and nations bow down to you. Be lord over your brothers, and may your mother's sons bow down to you. Cursed be everyone who curses you, and blessed be everyone who blesses you!"<sup>30</sup>As soon as Isaac had finished blessing Jacob, when Jacob had scarcely gone out from the presence of Isaac his father, Esau his brother came in from his hunting.<sup>31</sup>He also prepared delicious food and brought it to his father. And he said to his father, "Let my father arise and eat of his son's game, that you may bless me."<sup>32</sup>His father Isaac said to him, "Who are you?" He answered, "I am your son, your firstborn, Esau."<sup>33</sup>Then Isaac trembled very violently and said, "Who was it then that hunted game and brought it to me, and I ate it all before you came, and I have blessed him? Yes, and he shall be blessed."<sup>34</sup>As soon as Esau heard the words of his father, he cried out with an exceedingly great and bitter cry and said to his father, "Bless me, even me also, O my father!"<sup>35</sup>But he said, "Your brother came deceitfully, and he has taken away your blessing."<sup>36</sup>Esau said, "Is he not rightly named Jacob? For he has cheated me these two times. He took away my birthright, and behold, now he has taken away my blessing." Then he said, "Have you not reserved a blessing for me?"<sup>37</sup>Isaac answered and said to Esau, "Behold, I have made him lord over you, and all his brothers I have given to him for servants, and with grain and wine I have sustained him. What then can I do for you, my son?"<sup>38</sup>Esau said to his father, "Have you but one blessing, my father? Bless me, even me also, O my father." And Esau lifted up his voice and wept.<sup>39</sup>Then Isaac his father answered and said to him: "Behold, away from the fatness of the earth shall your dwelling be, and away from the dew of heaven on high.<sup>40</sup>By your sword you shall live, and you shall serve your brother; but when you grow restless you shall break his yoke from your neck."<sup>41</sup>Now Esau hated Jacob because of the blessing with which his father had blessed him, and Esau said to himself, "The days of mourning for my father are approaching; then I will kill my brother Jacob."<sup>42</sup>But the words of Esau her older son were told to Rebekah. So she sent and called Jacob her younger son and said to him, "Behold, your brother Esau comforts himself about you by planning to kill you.<sup>43</sup>Now therefore, my son, obey my voice. Arise, flee to Laban my brother in Haran<sup>44</sup>and stay with him a while, until your brother's fury turns away—<sup>45</sup>until your brother's anger turns away from you, and he forgets what you have done to him. Then I will send and bring you from there. Why should I be bereft of you both in one day?"<sup>46</sup>Then Rebekah said to Isaac, "I loathe my life because of the Hittite women. If Jacob marries one of the Hittite women like these, one of the women of the land, what good will my life be to me?"
27.overview:
Where we are. Years have passed since Esau sold his birthright (25:29–34) and married two Hittite women (26:34–35). Isaac is old and blind, and he thinks he is dying. The question left hanging since the twins’ birth now comes to a head: who will receive the father’s blessing, the older son or the younger?

The message. God’s purpose stands, even when every person in the story sins. Isaac sets out to bless the son God did not choose; Rebekah and Jacob deceive him to get the blessing God had already promised; Esau weeps for what he despised. Yet the blessing goes exactly where God said it would (25:23). God works through human sin without approving it, and each one reaps what he sowed.

Why it was said. Israel needed to know that it held the blessing not because Jacob was honest or deserving, for he was neither, but because God had chosen him (see the introduction). The chapter also explained the long, bitter story of Israel and Edom, brothers who became enemies.

How the chapter makes its case. Isaac plans a private blessing for Esau over a meal of game (vv. 1–4). Rebekah overhears and plots to put Jacob in his place, and Jacob agrees once she takes the risk on herself (vv. 5–17). Dressed in Esau’s clothes and goatskins, Jacob lies to his blind father again and again, even using God’s name, and receives the blessing of fruitfulness and lordship (vv. 18–29). Esau returns; Isaac trembles but confirms the blessing, and Esau’s bitter cry wins only a lesser word (vv. 30–40). Esau plans murder, and Rebekah sends Jacob away to her brother, with a pretext for Isaac (vv. 41–46).

Where it leads. By the need it exposes, and by contrast. Everyone here grasps at blessing, and no one can secure it by scheming. Rebekah says to Jacob, “Let your curse be on me” (v. 13), but she cannot carry it. Christ can and did: he “redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us … so that in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles” (Galatians 3:13–14). Jacob gained his father’s blessing by wearing his elder brother’s clothes under false pretences. Believers receive the Father’s blessing clothed in Christ, their elder brother, who gives his robe freely, before a Father who is not deceived but sees them truly and blesses them still.

For us. God’s promises never need our lies to help them along. Trust him enough to do right and wait for him. And when you have sinned and reaped bitter consequences, as everyone in this tent did, the God of Jacob is still the God of grace to those who come to him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s purpose to bless the younger son comes about through a tangle of sin in which no one behaves well. Isaac means to bless Esau in private, against what God had said (vv. 1–4). Rebekah plots to put Jacob in his brother’s place, and Jacob goes along with it once she takes the risk on herself (vv. 5–17). Disguised in Esau’s clothes and goatskins, Jacob lies to his blind father repeatedly and receives the blessing (vv. 18–29). Then Esau comes in; Isaac trembles and confirms that the blessing stands, and Esau’s bitter tears win only a lesser word about living by the sword (vv. 30–40). The promise is kept exactly as God said, but every person in the family will pay for the way it was grasped.
verseByVerse.theology: Blind Isaac sets out to bless Esau in private. Rebekah dresses Jacob in Esau's clothes and goatskins, and Jacob lies four times and invokes God to cover it. Isaac blesses him with dew, grain and lordship; then Esau comes in, Isaac trembles and confirms, “he shall be blessed,” and Esau weeps and receives a lesser blessing.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Hebrews commends Isaac's faith in this moment (Heb. 11:20) and warns that Esau "found no chance to repent, though he sought it with tears" (Heb. 12:17). Now: God's word never needed a lie to protect it, and grief over consequences is not repentance.

verseByVerse.quote: When Isaac was old and his eyes were dim so that he could not see, he called Esau his older son and said to him, "My son"; and he answered, "Here I am." He said, "Behold, I am old; I do not know the day of my death. Now then, take your weapons, your quiver and your bow, and go out to the field and hunt game for me, and prepare for me delicious food, such as I love, and bring it to me so that I may eat, that my soul may bless you before I die."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Old, blind and expecting death, Isaac plans to give Esau his blessing over a meal of game, though God had said the older would serve the younger.

His eyes were dim so that he could not see. Isaac’s blindness will make the deception possible. It is also a picture: the man who could not see with his eyes will not see God’s will either, until he trembles at it (v. 33). He lived many years after this (35:28–29), though he expected to die soon.

My son … Here I am. The same words passed between Abraham and Isaac on the road to Moriah (22:7). The echo makes the contrast sharp: then a father and son walked together in obedience; now a father is about to act against God’s word.

Take your weapons … and hunt game for me. Isaac sends Esau out with his hunting gear, and wants “delicious food, such as I love”. As before, his appetite shapes his choices (25:28): he loves Esau “because he ate of his game”.

That my soul may bless you before I die. A father’s blessing before his death was a solemn act, spoken “before the LORD” (v. 7), and believed to be binding and to shape the future (compare 48:1–20; 49:1–28). Usually it was given with the family present. Isaac plans it privately, with only Esau, perhaps knowing that Rebekah, and God’s word, were against him.

Did Isaac know what God had said? Almost certainly. The oracle had been given to Rebekah before the twins were born (25:23), and Esau had sold his birthright and married outside the family. Isaac seems to be following his own preference, not God’s revealed will. Yet Hebrews commends his faith: “By faith Isaac invoked future blessings on Jacob and Esau” (Hebrews 11:20). His faith shows when, at the end, he submits and confirms what God has done (v. 33), and in his trust that his words, spoken in God’s name, would come true.
verseByVerse.note: A father’s deathbed blessing was believed to be binding and irreversible.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Rebekah was listening when Isaac spoke to his son Esau. So when Esau went to the field to hunt for game and bring it, Rebekah said to her son Jacob, "I heard your father speak to your brother Esau, 'Bring me game and prepare for me delicious food, that I may eat it and bless you before the LORD before I die.' Now therefore, my son, obey my voice as I command you. Go to the flock and bring me two good young goats, so that I may prepare from them delicious food for your father, such as he loves. And you shall bring it to your father to eat, so that he may bless you before he dies."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rebekah overhears and plots to have Jacob take the blessing instead, using deception to bring about what God had promised.

Rebekah was listening. The family no longer speaks openly. The father plans in private, the mother listens at the tent door, and each works for a favourite son (25:28).

Bless you before the LORD. In repeating Isaac’s words, Rebekah adds “before the LORD”. She knows how solemn the blessing is, and that once given in God’s presence it cannot be undone.

Now therefore, my son, obey my voice as I command you. She gives Jacob orders, and will repeat them (vv. 13, 43). Two young goats, well prepared, could pass for game; she knows exactly what her husband likes.

God’s ends do not need our crooked means. Rebekah knew what God had promised, and she was right that Jacob should have the blessing. Her sin was not in her goal but in her method: she did not trust God to do what he had said. Abraham and Sarah had done the same with Hagar (16:1–4). Paul rejects the idea outright: “And why not do evil that good may come?” (Romans 3:8). God did not need her plot. He could have opened Isaac’s eyes, or turned his heart, as later he turned Jacob’s own hands when Jacob blessed Joseph’s sons (48:14–19).

What it does not mean. Not that a wife should never oppose a husband who is doing wrong, or that Rebekah should have stayed silent. She could have gone to Isaac and reminded him openly of God’s word, as Abigail spoke boldly to stop David’s sin (1 Samuel 25:23–31). The fault was deception, not her concern.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jacob said to Rebekah his mother, "Behold, my brother Esau is a hairy man, and I am a smooth man. Perhaps my father will feel me, and I shall seem to be mocking him and bring a curse upon myself and not a blessing." His mother said to him, "Let your curse be on me, my son; only obey my voice, and go, bring them to me." So he went and took them and brought them to his mother, and his mother prepared delicious food, such as his father loved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jacob objects only that he might be caught, not that the plan is wrong, and Rebekah takes any curse upon herself.

My brother Esau is a hairy man, and I am a smooth man. Jacob sees the practical problem at once (25:25). He is the planner of the family.

I shall seem to be mocking him. Literally, “I shall be in his eyes as a deceiver”. Jacob fears being seen as a deceiver, not being one. To trick a blind man was a cruel thing; the law would later say, “You shall not curse the deaf or put a stumbling block before the blind” (Leviticus 19:14).

And bring a curse upon myself and not a blessing. Jacob knows that if he is caught his father might curse him instead, and he believes a father’s words carry real weight.

Let your curse be on me, my son. Rebekah takes the risk on herself. In a sense the curse does fall on her: she sends Jacob away for “a while” (v. 44), and as far as Genesis tells, she never sees him again. Her death is not even recorded; we learn only of her nurse’s death (35:8) and where she was buried (49:31).

The one who bore the curse. Rebekah could offer to carry her son’s curse, but she could not take it away. Christ did what no mother could: he “redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13). On the cross he bore the curse we earned, so that the blessing of Abraham would come to us by faith (Galatians 3:14).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Rebekah took the best garments of Esau her older son, which were with her in the house, and put them on Jacob her younger son. And the skins of the young goats she put on his hands and on the smooth part of his neck. And she put the delicious food and the bread, which she had prepared, into the hand of her son Jacob.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rebekah prepares the meal and disguises Jacob in Esau’s best clothes and goatskins, so that he will feel and smell like his brother.

His mother prepared delicious food, such as his father loved. She knows her husband’s tastes well, and uses that knowledge against him.

The best garments of Esau. Probably festive clothes kept for special occasions, perhaps the garments of the firstborn, kept in Rebekah’s care. They would carry the smell of the fields (v. 27). Dressed in Esau’s clothes, Jacob takes his brother’s place.

The skins of the young goats … on his hands and on the smooth part of his neck. The hair of some eastern goats is coarse and dark, enough to fool a blind man’s touch.

What he sowed, he reaped. The goatskins have a sequel. Years later Jacob’s sons will deceive him with a goat’s blood on Joseph’s robe (37:31–33), and Laban will deceive him with one sister dressed as another (29:23–25). The deceiver is deceived by the same means: clothing, a goat, a substitution in the dark. “Whatever one sows, that will he also reap” (Galatians 6:7).

verseByVerse.quote: So he went in to his father and said, "My father." And he said, "Here I am. Who are you, my son?" Jacob said to his father, "I am Esau your firstborn. I have done as you told me; now sit up and eat of my game, that your soul may bless me." But Isaac said to his son, "How is it that you have found it so quickly, my son?" He answered, "Because the LORD your God granted me success."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jacob lies to his father outright, claiming to be Esau, and when questioned, he uses God’s name to cover the lie.

Who are you, my son? From the first moment Isaac is unsure. That question runs through the scene and will be asked again when Esau comes in (v. 32).

I am Esau your firstborn. A flat lie, the first of several. He claims not only Esau’s name but his birth rank, “your firstborn”, the very thing he had bought (25:33).

Because the LORD your God granted me success. Asked how he hunted so quickly, Jacob brings God into the lie. Notice “your God”, not “my God”: Jacob does not yet call the LORD his own. He will only do so after God meets him at Bethel (28:21).

Never bring God’s name into a lie. To use God’s name to cover sin is to take it in vain (Exodus 20:7), as when people say “God told me” or “God knows I am telling the truth” to win an argument. Where you have done this, the God who kept his promise to Jacob the liar still forgives the one who confesses (1 John 1:9).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Isaac said to Jacob, "Please come near, that I may feel you, my son, to know whether you are really my son Esau or not." So Jacob went near to Isaac his father, who felt him and said, "The voice is Jacob's voice, but the hands are the hands of Esau." And he did not recognize him, because his hands were hairy like his brother Esau's hands. So he blessed him. He said, "Are you really my son Esau?" He answered, "I am." Then he said, "Bring it near to me, that I may eat of my son's game and bless you." So he brought it near to him, and he ate; and he brought him wine, and he drank.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Isaac is suspicious and tests the son before him by touch, but trusts his hands over his ears; asked outright, Jacob lies again and the meal is served.

Please come near, that I may feel you. Isaac checks with his hands what his ears doubt.

The voice is Jacob’s voice, but the hands are the hands of Esau. The one sense that told the truth is overruled by the rest. The deception works on every sense Isaac has left: touch, taste and smell all say “Esau”; only hearing says “Jacob”. Isaac trusts the evidence that suits what he wants.

So he blessed him. This seems to sum up what follows in vv. 26–29: having decided, Isaac goes on to bless him.

Are you really my son Esau? He answered, “I am.” One word in Hebrew, and a second flat lie. Each lie makes the next easier.

He brought him wine, and he drank. The meal is the setting of the blessing, as Isaac planned it, a solemn occasion eaten together.

verseByVerse.quote: Then his father Isaac said to him, "Come near and kiss me, my son." So he came near and kissed him. And Isaac smelled the smell of his garments and blessed him and said, "See, the smell of my son is as the smell of a field that the LORD has blessed! May God give you of the dew of heaven and of the fatness of the earth and plenty of grain and wine. Let peoples serve you, and nations bow down to you. Be lord over your brothers, and may your mother's sons bow down to you. Cursed be everyone who curses you, and blessed be everyone who blesses you!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Isaac kisses Jacob, smells Esau’s clothes and pronounces the blessing: fruitful land, rule over peoples and over his brothers, and Abraham’s promise that those who bless him will be blessed.

Come near and kiss me, my son. The kiss that seals the blessing is also a final test, and a final deception. Jacob kisses the father he is deceiving.

The smell of my son is as the smell of a field that the LORD has blessed! Esau’s clothes carry the scent of the open country. Isaac takes it as a picture of the blessing itself: a land rich and fragrant with God’s favour.

The dew of heaven and … the fatness of the earth. In a land with little rain, the heavy dew of the dry season mattered greatly for crops. Isaac asks God for fertile land, “plenty of grain and wine”, the good things of Canaan (Deuteronomy 33:28).

Let peoples serve you … Be lord over your brothers. Isaac means to give Esau leadership, but his words confirm what God had foretold: “the older shall serve the younger” (25:23). The blessing looks beyond Jacob to the kingship that will come from his line, to David, under whom “all the Edomites became David’s servants” (2 Samuel 8:14), and finally to the Son of David, at whose name “every knee should bow” (Philippians 2:10).

Cursed be everyone who curses you, and blessed be everyone who blesses you! These words echo God’s promise to Abraham (12:3). Without realising whom he is blessing, Isaac passes on Abraham’s blessing to the son God chose. The fuller promises of land and offspring Isaac will give knowingly, as Jacob leaves home (28:3–4).

Clothed in the elder brother’s garments. Many Christian teachers have seen a picture of the gospel here, but it is a picture by contrast. Jacob received the blessing wearing his brother’s clothes and pretending to be someone he was not. Believers receive the Father’s blessing clothed in Christ, their elder brother: “as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Galatians 3:27). But nothing here is stolen or false. The elder brother gives his robe freely, and the Father is not deceived; he knows exactly who we are and blesses us “in Christ with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 1:3).

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as Isaac had finished blessing Jacob, when Jacob had scarcely gone out from the presence of Isaac his father, Esau his brother came in from his hunting. He also prepared delicious food and brought it to his father. And he said to his father, "Let my father arise and eat of his son's game, that you may bless me." His father Isaac said to him, "Who are you?" He answered, "I am your son, your firstborn, Esau." Then Isaac trembled very violently and said, "Who was it then that hunted game and brought it to me, and I ate it all before you came, and I have blessed him? Yes, and he shall be blessed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moments after Jacob leaves, Esau arrives with his meal; Isaac trembles violently as he realises what has happened, and confirms that the blessing stands.

As soon as Isaac had finished blessing Jacob. The timing is close: Jacob has barely left when Esau comes in. A few minutes earlier and the plot would have failed.

Who are you? … I am your son, your firstborn, Esau. Esau uses the very words Jacob had used falsely (v. 19), but his are true.

Isaac trembled very violently. Literally, “trembled a great trembling, exceedingly”. It is more than shock at being tricked. Isaac sees that God’s will has overruled his own: he had set out to bless the son God had not chosen, and God had prevented it.

Yes, and he shall be blessed. Isaac does not curse Jacob or try to take the blessing back. He accepts it. In that world a father’s blessing, spoken “before the LORD” (v. 7), was a solemn and binding act, not a wish to be withdrawn when the trick came to light. Isaac now acts in faith, submitting to what God had said (Hebrews 11:20). “Many are the plans in the mind of a man, but it is the purpose of the LORD that will stand” (Proverbs 19:21).

Irrevocable. If a father’s word could not be revoked, how much more God’s. Paul says of God’s promises to his people, “the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (Romans 11:29). The blessing God gives in Christ is not at the mercy of human schemes, or of our failures.

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as Esau heard the words of his father, he cried out with an exceedingly great and bitter cry and said to his father, "Bless me, even me also, O my father!" But he said, "Your brother came deceitfully, and he has taken away your blessing." Esau said, "Is he not rightly named Jacob? For he has cheated me these two times. He took away my birthright, and behold, now he has taken away my blessing." Then he said, "Have you not reserved a blessing for me?" Isaac answered and said to Esau, "Behold, I have made him lord over you, and all his brothers I have given to him for servants, and with grain and wine I have sustained him. What then can I do for you, my son?" Esau said to his father, "Have you but one blessing, my father? Bless me, even me also, O my father." And Esau lifted up his voice and wept.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Esau cries out bitterly and begs for a blessing too, blaming Jacob for taking what he himself had sold; his grief is for what he has lost, not for what he despised.

An exceedingly great and bitter cry. Esau’s grief is real and painful to read. The man who once shrugged off his birthright (25:34) now wants the blessing desperately.

Your brother came deceitfully. Isaac names what Jacob did. The Bible does not hide it or call it clever.

Is he not rightly named Jacob? For he has cheated me these two times. Esau makes a bitter pun: “Jacob” sounds like “he cheats” (25:26). And there is a second wordplay: “birthright” (bekorah) and “blessing” (berakah) sound alike in Hebrew. But Esau is not fair: he sold his birthright freely, under oath (25:33).

Have you but one blessing, my father? Isaac had already given Jacob lordship and plenty (v. 37); what was left to give? The tragedy is real, and the narrator lets us feel it.

Esau lifted up his voice and wept. Hebrews uses this moment as a warning: “afterward, when he desired to inherit the blessing, he was rejected, for he found no chance to repent, though he sought it with tears” (Hebrews 12:17). He wanted the blessing, but he did not repent of despising it. The tears were for the loss, not the sin. “Worldly grief produces death”, while godly grief “produces a repentance that leads to salvation” (2 Corinthians 7:10).

More than one blessing. Esau’s question has a different answer in the gospel. God’s blessing in Christ is not one gift for one son that leaves the others empty. There is enough for everyone who comes, and no one who comes to Christ in true repentance is turned away (John 6:37).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Isaac his father answered and said to him: "Behold, away from the fatness of the earth shall your dwelling be, and away from the dew of heaven on high. By your sword you shall live, and you shall serve your brother; but when you grow restless you shall break his yoke from your neck."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Isaac gives Esau a lesser word: his descendants will live in harsh country by the sword and serve his brother, but one day they will throw off his yoke.

Away from the fatness of the earth shall your dwelling be. Esau’s people, Edom, settled in the rugged, dry hills south-east of the Dead Sea, in Seir (32:3; 36:8), far less fertile than Canaan.

By your sword you shall live. Edom lived by raiding and war, and by controlling the trade routes through its land.

You shall serve your brother. The oracle of 25:23 is confirmed. Edom was conquered by Saul and David (1 Samuel 14:47; 2 Samuel 8:14) and remained under Judah for generations.

When you grow restless you shall break his yoke from your neck. This came true when Edom rebelled in the days of King Jehoram of Judah and set up its own king (2 Kings 8:20–22). The bitterness between the nations lasted for centuries, and the prophets condemned Edom for gloating when Jerusalem fell (Obadiah 10–14; Psalm 137:7).

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of v. 39 is the same small word used in Jacob’s blessing, “of the dew of heaven” (v. 28). It can mean “of” or “away from”. Older translations read Esau’s blessing as like Jacob’s (“thy dwelling shall be the fatness of the earth”). Most modern translations, like the ESV, read “away from”, which fits Edom’s barren land and the contrast Isaac is drawing. The verb in v. 40, “grow restless”, is rare and uncertain: it may mean to roam, to break loose or to grow strong. The general sense is clear: Edom will one day throw off Israel’s rule.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 41–46 — Esau's Rage and Jacob's Flight
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The deception that secured the blessing breaks the family apart. Esau consoles himself with plans to kill Jacob once their father is dead (v. 41). Rebekah hears of it and sends Jacob away to her brother Laban in Harran, for “a while” that will become twenty years (vv. 42–45). Then she persuades Isaac to send Jacob, using her genuine grief over Esau’s Hittite wives as the reason, without mentioning the threat (v. 46). Each pays: Rebekah loses the son she loved, Jacob loses his home, Esau loses his brother and Isaac is deceived once more. Yet even here God is at work, for Jacob’s flight will bring him to Bethel and to the God of his fathers (chapter 28).
verseByVerse.theology: Esau plans to kill Jacob once Isaac is dead. Rebekah sends Jacob to Laban "a while," and gives Isaac the Hittite wives as the reason.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: nobody in the tent got away with anything. Now: the blessing would have come without one word of the scheme; God's promises never need our sins to help them along.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Esau hated Jacob because of the blessing with which his father had blessed him, and Esau said to himself, "The days of mourning for my father are approaching; then I will kill my brother Jacob." But the words of Esau her older son were told to Rebekah. So she sent and called Jacob her younger son and said to him, "Behold, your brother Esau comforts himself about you by planning to kill you. Now therefore, my son, obey my voice. Arise, flee to Laban my brother in Haran and stay with him a while, until your brother's fury turns away— until your brother's anger turns away from you, and he forgets what you have done to him. Then I will send and bring you from there. Why should I be bereft of you both in one day?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Esau plans to kill Jacob once their father dies, and Rebekah, hearing it, sends Jacob away to her brother Laban until his brother’s anger cools.

Esau hated Jacob. The word suggests a grudge nursed over time. Like Cain (4:5–8), Esau turns grief and envy into a plan to kill his brother.

The days of mourning for my father are approaching; then I will kill my brother. He will wait until Isaac dies, perhaps not wanting to grieve his father further. In fact Isaac lived on for many years (35:28–29), and by then the brothers were reconciled and buried him together (33:4; 35:29).

Your brother Esau comforts himself about you by planning to kill you. Hatred can become a kind of comfort, a fantasy of revenge that eases a wound. It always corrupts the one who feeds it (Matthew 5:21–22; 1 John 3:15).

Flee to Laban my brother in Haran and stay with him a while. Literally “a few days”. Rebekah thinks it will be short; it became twenty years (31:38, 41). The deceiver will be sent to the house of a greater deceiver.

Why should I be bereft of you both in one day? If Esau killed Jacob, she would lose Jacob to death and Esau to the penalty for murder (9:6), or to exile. Compare the widow’s plea in 2 Samuel 14:6–7. Her scheme has put both her sons in danger.

Deception damages families for years. The trick in the tent took minutes. Its fruit was murderous hatred, a mother’s lifelong separation from her son, and twenty years of exile. Few sins stay small. Christians who have done such damage can find forgiveness in Christ, and sometimes, by God’s grace, reconciliation, as Jacob and Esau finally did (33:4).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Rebekah said to Isaac, "I loathe my life because of the Hittite women. If Jacob marries one of the Hittite women like these, one of the women of the land, what good will my life be to me?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rebekah gives Isaac a real but partial reason for sending Jacob away, her grief over Esau’s Hittite wives, without mentioning Esau’s threat.

I loathe my life because of the Hittite women. Her complaint is true: Esau’s wives had made life bitter for her and Isaac (26:34–35). But it is also a pretext. She does not tell her husband that Esau plans to kill Jacob, perhaps to spare him, perhaps to keep her own part hidden.

If Jacob marries one of the Hittite women … what good will my life be to me? She frames it so that Isaac will make the decision himself, and he does (28:1–2). The managing of others continues to the end.

God at work in a broken family. Yet God brings real good out of it. Jacob is sent away with his father’s full and knowing blessing (28:1–4), to find a wife among his own people, and on the road he will meet God at Bethel. God works his good purposes through this broken family, as he still does through ours. That never excuses the breaking, but it gives hope to families that are broken.

27.theology:
Genesis 27 makes readers face a hard truth: God accomplishes his purposes through human sin without approving the sin. Jacob’s deception is never praised and its consequences are severe, yet the blessing passes to Jacob exactly as God said. God’s rule works through human choices without cancelling responsibility for them.

Paul draws on Esau and Jacob in Romans 9 to argue that God’s choice does not depend on works but on God who calls (Rom 9:11–12). God is not indifferent to morality, but his purpose does not wait on human goodness. The heir of promise is not the more deserving son; he is the chosen one. This is the radical grace that the stories of the patriarchs are told to show.

Isaac cannot take back the spoken blessing (v. 33). Far more surely, “the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (Rom 11:29).
27.examples:
Every reader recognises these family patterns: favourite children, rivalry for approval, schemes hatched in whispers, words that cannot be unsaid. The patriarchs’ family is a mirror, not a flattering portrait, and the grace God works through it is our grace too.

Jacob is not chosen because he is good; he is made good (slowly, through much suffering) because he is chosen. The grace that overruled Jacob’s deception is open to every deceiver who comes to the God of Jacob in faith.

keyVerse.quote: Who was it then that hunted game and brought it to me, and I ate it all before you came, and I have blessed him? Yes, and he shall be blessed.
keyVerse.note: Isaac’s violent trembling is the moment he realises that God’s purpose has overruled his own. He does not try to undo it, but confirms what God said before the twins were born. Every scheme in the chapter fails or rebounds; God’s word stands, and the blessing that comes to the nations in Christ cannot be revoked (Romans 11:29).

27.reflection:
Every person in this chapter does wrong: Isaac, Rebekah, Jacob and Esau. Which of them do you find it easiest to understand, and why? What does this suggest about the kind of people God works through?

Rebekah and Jacob tried to bring about God’s promise by deception (vv. 5–17). Where are you tempted to “help” God by doing wrong for a good result? What would trusting him look like instead?

Esau wept bitterly over the lost blessing but did not repent of despising it (vv. 34–38; Hebrews 12:17). What is the difference between grief over consequences and true repentance?

Jacob received the blessing wearing his elder brother’s clothes. How does the gospel picture of being clothed with Christ (Galatians 3:27) both resemble and differ from what happened in Isaac’s tent?

28.title: Surely the LORD Is in This Place
28.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Isaac called Jacob and blessed him and directed him, "You must not take a wife from the Canaanite women.<sup>2</sup>Arise, go to Paddan-aram to the house of Bethuel your mother's father, and take as your wife from there one of the daughters of Laban your mother's brother.<sup>3</sup>God Almighty bless you and make you fruitful and multiply you, that you may become a company of peoples.<sup>4</sup>May he give the blessing of Abraham to you and to your offspring with you, that you may take possession of the land of your sojournings that God gave to Abraham!"<sup>5</sup>Thus Isaac sent Jacob away. And he went to Paddan-aram, to Laban, the son of Bethuel the Aramean, the brother of Rebekah, Jacob's and Esau's mother.<sup>6</sup>Now Esau saw that Isaac had blessed Jacob and sent him away to Paddan-aram to take a wife from there, and that as he blessed him he directed him, "You must not take a wife from the Canaanite women,"<sup>7</sup>and that Jacob had obeyed his father and his mother and gone to Paddan-aram.<sup>8</sup>So when Esau saw that the Canaanite women did not please Isaac his father,<sup>9</sup>Esau went to Ishmael and took as his wife, besides the wives he had, Mahalath the daughter of Ishmael, Abraham's son, the sister of Nebaioth.<sup>10</sup>Jacob left Beersheba and went toward Haran.<sup>11</sup>And he came to a certain place and stayed there that night, because the sun had set. Taking one of the stones of the place, he put it under his head and lay down in that place to sleep.<sup>12</sup>And he dreamed, and behold, there was a ladder set up on the earth, and the top of it reached to heaven. And behold, the angels of God were ascending and descending on it!<sup>13</sup>And behold, the LORD stood above it and said, "I am the LORD, the God of Abraham your father and the God of Isaac.
