The land on which you lie I will give to you and to your offspring.<sup>14</sup>Your offspring shall be like the dust of the earth, and you shall spread abroad to the west and to the east and to the north and to the south, and in you and your offspring shall all the families of the earth be blessed.<sup>15</sup>Behold, I am with you and will keep you wherever you go, and will bring you back to this land. For I will not leave you until I have done what I have promised you."<sup>16</sup>Then Jacob awoke from his sleep and said, "Surely the LORD is in this place, and I did not know it."<sup>17</sup>And he was afraid and said, "How awesome is this place! This is none other than the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven."<sup>18</sup>So early in the morning Jacob took the stone that he had put under his head and set it up for a pillar and poured oil on the top of it.<sup>19</sup>He called the name of that place Bethel, but the name of the city was Luz at the first.<sup>20</sup>Then Jacob made a vow, saying, "If God will be with me and will keep me in this way that I go, and will give me bread to eat and clothing to wear,<sup>21</sup>so that I come again to my father's house in peace, then the LORD shall be my God,<sup>22</sup>and this stone, which I have set up for a pillar, shall be God's house. And of all that you give me I will give a full tenth to you."
28.overview:
Where we are. Jacob has stolen his brother’s blessing (chapter 27), and Esau has sworn to kill him once their father dies. So the deceiver leaves home for his uncle Laban in Haran, far to the north, with nothing but a staff (32:10).

The message. God meets the undeserving with promise before they have changed. On his first night alone, the LORD gives a cheat on the run, freely and without conditions, everything he promised Abraham and Isaac, and adds what Jacob needs most: “I am with you … I will not leave you” (v. 15).

Why it was said. Israel bore Jacob’s name, and like him they were often far from home, in Egypt and in the wilderness, with little to show that God was with them (see the introduction). Bethel told them that their life as a people began with a promise God made to a fugitive, not with anything they had earned.

How the chapter makes its case. Isaac now blesses Jacob knowingly, passing on “the blessing of Abraham”, and sends him to find a wife among his mother’s people (vv. 1–5). Esau, seeing it, tries to please his father by marrying a daughter of Ishmael (vv. 6–9). Jacob sleeps in the open at “the place”, and in a dream sees a stairway joining earth and heaven, with angels on it and the LORD above it (vv. 10–12). The LORD speaks: land, offspring, blessing for all the families of the earth, and his own unfailing presence (vv. 13–15). Jacob wakes in awe, sets up his stone as a pillar and names the place Bethel, “house of God” (vv. 16–19), then vows that the LORD will be his God and promises a tenth (vv. 20–22).

Where it leads. By promise and by pattern, and Jesus himself makes the link. He told Nathanael, “you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man” (John 1:51). Jesus is the stairway: the one meeting place of heaven and earth, the true house of God (John 2:19–21) and the way to the Father (John 14:6). And the promise “I am with you” is fulfilled in the one called Immanuel, who says to every disciple, “behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20).

For us. God’s grace comes to us as it came to Jacob: before we have changed, when we have nothing to offer. Wherever you are, alone, at fault, far from home, the way to heaven is open in Christ. And the God who promised “I will not leave you” keeps his word to the end.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — Isaac's Blessing and Jacob's Dream at Bethel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Grace finds the fugitive: God gives Jacob the covenant promise freely, before Jacob has changed at all. The chapter opens with Isaac’s open, knowing blessing, which confirms what was stolen in chapter 27 and passes on “the blessing of Abraham” (vv. 1–5). Esau’s attempt to win his father’s approval with a new marriage shows the opposite way, outward effort without a changed heart (vv. 6–9). Then, at a nameless place on the road, God takes the initiative: the stairway to heaven, the LORD standing above it, and promises of land, offspring, blessing for the nations and his own presence (vv. 10–15). Jacob’s awe, his pillar and his vow (vv. 16–22) are the response of a young faith to a grace that came first.
verseByVerse.theology: Isaac knowingly blesses Jacob with the blessing of Abraham and sends him to Paddan-aram. Esau adds a daughter of Ishmael to his wives. At a nameless place Jacob sleeps on a stone and sees a stairway to heaven with angels on it; the LORD promises land, offspring and his presence. Jacob names the place Bethel and vows a tenth.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: God bound himself by promise to a fugitive, without a single condition. Now: the promise comes to us the same way, before we have anything to offer.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Isaac called Jacob and blessed him and directed him, "You must not take a wife from the Canaanite women. Arise, go to Paddan-aram to the house of Bethuel your mother's father, and take as your wife from there one of the daughters of Laban your mother's brother. God Almighty bless you and make you fruitful and multiply you, that you may become a company of peoples. May he give the blessing of Abraham to you and to your offspring with you, that you may take possession of the land of your sojournings that God gave to Abraham!" Thus Isaac sent Jacob away. And he went to Paddan-aram, to Laban, the son of Bethuel the Aramean, the brother of Rebekah, Jacob's and Esau's mother.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This time Isaac blesses Jacob openly and knowingly, passes on to him the covenant promises God gave Abraham, and sends him to find a wife among his mother’s people.

Then Isaac called Jacob and blessed him. The man who was deceived in chapter 27 now blesses the deceiver with his eyes open. He does not revoke the blessing he gave in error; he confirms it and adds to it, having accepted that God’s purpose stands (27:33). Hebrews counts this as faith: “By faith Isaac invoked future blessings on Jacob and Esau” (Hebrews 11:20).

You must not take a wife from the Canaanite women. The same charge Abraham gave about Isaac (24:3–4). The concern is not race but faith: the Canaanites worshipped other gods, and Esau’s Hittite wives had already made Isaac and Rebekah’s life bitter (26:34–35; 27:46). Paddan-aram, probably “the plain of Aram”, was the region around Haran in the far north, where Abraham’s relatives had stayed.

God Almighty bless you. “God Almighty” is El Shaddai (see the note), the name by which God revealed himself to Abraham when the promise of a son seemed impossible (17:1). Isaac commits Jacob to the God who does what nature cannot. God will use the same name when he renews this blessing at Bethel on Jacob’s return (35:11), and the old Jacob will remember: “God Almighty appeared to me at Luz in the land of Canaan and blessed me” (48:3).

That you may become a company of peoples. The word for “company” is the Hebrew qahal, which later describes Israel gathered as an assembly before the LORD. From one fleeing man God will make a great assembly, and in Christ that assembly will draw in people from every nation (Revelation 7:9).

The blessing of Abraham … the land of your sojournings. Now the heart of it is named: land and offspring, the promises of 12:1–3 and 17:1–8. Yet Isaac calls Canaan “the land of your sojournings”, the land where they live as foreigners. The patriarchs held it by promise, not by possession; as Hebrews says, they “acknowledged that they were strangers and exiles on the earth” (Hebrews 11:13), looking for a better country.

Laban, the son of Bethuel the Aramean. The family is called Aramean, from the region of Aram. Israel would later confess at the harvest, “A wandering Aramean was my father” (Deuteronomy 26:5), most likely remembering Jacob, the wanderer who went to Aram with nothing and came back with a family. The verse ends by naming Rebekah as “Jacob’s and Esau’s mother”: as far as Genesis tells, she never saw her favourite son again (see the note on 27:11–14).

Blessing given in the right way. In chapter 27 the blessing was grabbed in the dark by disguise and lies; here it is given in the open, with father and son face to face. The contrast teaches that God’s gifts are meant to be received, not stolen. Everything Jacob schemed for, he could have had as a gift.
verseByVerse.note: “God Almighty” translates El Shaddai (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: Now Esau saw that Isaac had blessed Jacob and sent him away to Paddan-aram to take a wife from there, and that as he blessed him he directed him, "You must not take a wife from the Canaanite women," and that Jacob had obeyed his father and his mother and gone to Paddan-aram. So when Esau saw that the Canaanite women did not please Isaac his father, Esau went to Ishmael and took as his wife, besides the wives he had, Mahalath the daughter of Ishmael, Abraham's son, the sister of Nebaioth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Esau, seeing that his Canaanite wives displease his father, tries to win Isaac’s approval by marrying a daughter of Ishmael, an outward change that misses what really mattered.

Esau saw … that Jacob had obeyed his father and his mother. Esau notices three things: the blessing, the charge about Canaanite wives, and Jacob’s obedience. For the first time it seems to dawn on him how much his marriages had grieved his parents (26:34–35).

Esau went to Ishmael and took as his wife … Mahalath the daughter of Ishmael. He goes to the family of his uncle Ishmael, probably to Ishmael’s clan rather than to the man himself, for by the usual reckoning of the dates Ishmael had already died (25:17). It looks like a step towards his father’s wishes: a wife from Abraham’s family, not a Canaanite. But Ishmael’s was the line God had set aside when he chose Isaac (17:19–21; 21:12), and Esau adds her “besides the wives he had”, so the Hittite wives remain.

Outward change without a changed heart. Esau responds to his father’s displeasure, not to God. He changes his behaviour to regain approval but does not grasp what the blessing was about: covenant faith in the LORD. Hebrews calls him “unholy”, a man who sold his birthright for a meal and later found no chance to repent though he sought the blessing with tears (Hebrews 12:16–17). Religion can be like this: adjusting the outside to please people while the heart stays where it was.

Why is she called Basemath in chapter 36? In 36:3 Esau’s wife from Ishmael is “Basemath, Ishmael’s daughter, the sister of Nebaioth”, and the names of his other wives differ too (26:34; 36:2–3). People in the ancient world often had more than one name, and the lists may also reflect different sources or later names. The same woman is clearly meant, since both passages make her Ishmael’s daughter and Nebaioth’s sister.

verseByVerse.quote: Jacob left Beersheba and went toward Haran. And he came to a certain place and stayed there that night, because the sun had set. Taking one of the stones of the place, he put it under his head and lay down in that place to sleep. And he dreamed, and behold, there was a ladder set up on the earth, and the top of it reached to heaven. And behold, the angels of God were ascending and descending on it!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Alone and in the open on his first night as a fugitive, Jacob dreams of a stairway joining earth and heaven, with God’s angels going up and down on it.

Jacob left Beersheba and went toward Haran. Jacob sets out on a journey of some five hundred miles (see Roads and Travel). He is not a youth: by the usual reckoning of Genesis’s dates he was in his seventies. He travels alone, with only a staff (32:10), without the camels and gifts Abraham’s servant had taken on the same road to find Isaac a wife (24:10).

He came to a certain place. Literally “the place”, a word repeated six times in vv. 11–19 (“the place”, “that place”, “this place”). It was not a shrine, just a spot on the road where night fell. The narrator lets us feel the irony: Jacob stops at an ordinary place, and it turns out to be the house of God. Later Israel would use “the place” for the sanctuary God chooses (Deuteronomy 12:5).

Because the sun had set. The sun sets as Jacob leaves the land of promise; twenty years later, when he returns limping from his wrestling with God, “the sun rose upon him” (32:31). His exile is framed by darkness and dawn.

Taking one of the stones of the place, he put it under his head. Not a pillow for comfort but perhaps for protection, or simply what lay at hand. The point is his poverty: the heir of the promise sleeps on the ground with a stone for a headrest.

A ladder set up on the earth, and the top of it reached to heaven. The word is probably better rendered “stairway” or “ramp” (see Uncertain wording below). Such stairways ran up the stepped temple-towers (ziggurats) of Mesopotamia, which were thought to link earth and the gods. The phrase “its top in the heavens” recalls Babel, where people tried to build a tower with “its top in the heavens” (11:4). Babel was humanity climbing up to make a name for itself; Bethel is God opening the way down from his side.

The angels of God were ascending and descending on it! The ascending comes first, as though the angels were already on earth around Jacob, keeping him, and going up and down between him and the LORD. Jacob is not as alone as he thinks. Angels meet him again on his way home (32:1–2), so God’s messengers frame his whole exile.

The stairway is Christ. Jesus took this verse for himself. Meeting Nathanael (Bartholomew), “an Israelite indeed, in whom there is no deceit!” (John 1:47), a true son of Israel without the guile of Jacob, he said, “you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man” (John 1:51). The traffic between heaven and earth now runs on a person. Jesus is the stairway: God come down to us and the way by which we come to God (John 14:6). No one needs to find a holy spot to reach heaven; everyone needs to come to him.

What it does not mean. Not that we should seek visions, sleep at holy sites, or expect God to guide us by dreams as he did here. God spoke to the patriarchs in dreams while Scripture was still being given; now he has spoken finally in his Son (Hebrews 1:1–2), and impressions and dreams must be tested by his word.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew word for “ladder”, sullam, occurs only here in the Old Testament. It is probably related to a verb meaning “to heap up”, as in building a raised road, so many scholars prefer “stairway” or “ramp”, which also fits angels going up and down in both directions. The exact picture is uncertain, but the meaning is clear: a connection set up by God between earth and heaven.
verseByVerse.note: The “ladder” may be a stairway (ESV: “a flight of steps”).

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, the LORD stood above it and said, "I am the LORD, the God of Abraham your father and the God of Isaac. The land on which you lie I will give to you and to your offspring. Your offspring shall be like the dust of the earth, and you shall spread abroad to the west and to the east and to the north and to the south, and in you and your offspring shall all the families of the earth be blessed. Behold, I am with you and will keep you wherever you go, and will bring you back to this land. For I will not leave you until I have done what I have promised you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD himself stands over the sleeping fugitive and gives him, freely and without a single condition, the covenant promises of land, offspring and blessing for the nations, with the promise of his own presence until all is done.

The LORD stood above it. The vision is not chiefly about the stairway or the angels but about the LORD who stands at its head and speaks. For Jacob, everything depends on what God says.

I am the LORD, the God of Abraham your father and the God of Isaac. God introduces himself through the family’s history. He calls Abraham Jacob’s “father”, for Jacob is the heir of Abraham’s promise. But he does not yet call himself “the God of Jacob”: that is still to be settled in Jacob’s own heart (v. 21). Jesus used this title to prove the resurrection: God “is not God of the dead, but of the living” (Matthew 22:32).

The land on which you lie I will give to you and to your offspring. The ground under the homeless man is his by promise. These are the words spoken to Abraham (13:14–17) and to Isaac (26:3–4), now spoken directly to Jacob for the first time. Every promise in these verses repeats what Abraham heard: land (12:7), offspring as the dust (13:16), spreading to every point of the compass (13:14), and blessing to “all the families of the earth” (12:3).

In you and your offspring shall all the families of the earth be blessed. The promise is not only for Jacob’s family but through it for the world. Paul says that in this promise Scripture “preached the gospel beforehand to Abraham” (Galatians 3:8), and that its offspring is ultimately Christ (Galatians 3:16), in whom people of every nation are blessed.

Behold, I am with you and will keep you wherever you go. Here is the new note, the promise suited to a man in flight. God had promised his presence to Isaac (26:3, 24); now he gives it to Jacob, and adds three things: he will keep (guard) him, he will bring him back, and he will not leave him until he has done all he promised. Jacob is afraid of Esau behind him and of the unknown ahead; God answers both fears with himself. Twenty years later Jacob could say, “God … has been with me wherever I have gone” (35:3).

Pure grace. Notice what God does not say. There is no rebuke for the lie in Isaac’s tent and no condition about reforming first. These promises are spoken to a cheat on the run. That is grace: God’s undeserved kindness, choosing and keeping a man for his own purpose (Romans 9:10–13). Jacob will be disciplined by what he has done, but he will not be abandoned.

Immanuel. The promise “I am with you” runs through the whole Bible until it takes flesh in Jesus, called “Immanuel (which means, God with us)” (Matthew 1:23). His last words in Matthew renew it to every disciple: “behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20). And Hebrews gives every believer the same assurance: “I will never leave you nor forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5).

For us. Christians are not promised a trouble-free journey; Jacob’s next twenty years were hard. We are promised God’s presence in it and his faithfulness to finish what he began (Philippians 1:6).

Uncertain wording. The words translated “stood above it” can also mean “stood beside him” (ESV note). The Hebrew pronoun could refer either to the stairway or to Jacob. If “above it”, the LORD stands at the top of the stairway, in heaven; if “beside him”, he has come down and stands over the sleeping Jacob. Both fit the context, and either way the LORD is present and speaks; “beside him” would make the nearness even more striking, and it matches v. 16: “Surely the LORD is in this place”.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jacob awoke from his sleep and said, "Surely the LORD is in this place, and I did not know it." And he was afraid and said, "How awesome is this place! This is none other than the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jacob wakes to the discovery that the LORD was present in a place he thought was empty, and it fills him with awe.

Surely the LORD is in this place, and I did not know it. Jacob may have thought that the God of his fathers belonged at home, at the family altars in Beersheba, and that he had left him behind. Now he learns that the LORD is present on the road, at night, in a nameless place. God is not confined to the places where we expect him.

And he was afraid. Not the terror of a man in danger but the holy fear of a sinner in the presence of God, the fear that is “the beginning of wisdom” (Proverbs 9:10). Jacob had feared Esau; now he meets someone far greater, and finds him gracious.

This is none other than the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven. Jacob gives the place two names: the house where God lives and the gate through which heaven is entered. Babylon’s name was popularly understood as “gate of god”, and Babel tried to build such a gate from below (11:4–9); here God sets one up himself. In the end there is only one such house and gate: Jesus spoke of his body as the temple (John 2:19–21), and called himself “the door” (John 10:9). Through him believers have “the new and living way that he opened for us” into God’s presence (Hebrews 10:20).

God in the ordinary place. Many Christians have found their Bethel in a hospital corridor, a lonely flat or a place they fled to in shame: the place where they discovered that God was there all along. The presence of God is not something we produce by finding the right spot or feeling, but something he gives. Through Christ he is with his people wherever they are.

verseByVerse.quote: So early in the morning Jacob took the stone that he had put under his head and set it up for a pillar and poured oil on the top of it. He called the name of that place Bethel, but the name of the city was Luz at the first.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jacob sets up the stone he slept on as a memorial pillar, consecrates it with oil, and names the place Bethel, “house of God”.

Jacob took the stone … and set it up for a pillar. A standing stone (Hebrew matstsevah) marked a place where something important had happened (compare 31:45; 35:20). Jacob wants the place remembered: here God spoke.

And poured oil on the top of it. Oil was a precious part of a traveller’s supplies (see Olive Tree and Olive Oil), and pouring it out set the stone apart for God. The same act would later consecrate the tabernacle and its furnishings (Exodus 30:25–29). God later reminds Jacob of this morning: “I am the God of Bethel, where you anointed a pillar and made a vow to me” (31:13).

He called the name of that place Bethel. “Bethel” means “house of God” (see the note). The town nearby was then called Luz. Bethel lay in the hill country north of Jerusalem and became one of the most important places in Israel’s story: Jacob returned to worship there (35:1–15), and the ark was there in the time of the judges (Judges 20:26–27).

A holy place that became a snare. Centuries later Jeroboam set up one of his golden calves at Bethel (1 Kings 12:28–29), and the place of Jacob’s meeting with God became a centre of false worship. The prophets mocked it as “Beth-aven”, “house of wickedness” (Hosea 4:15), and Amos warned, “Bethel shall come to nothing” (Amos 5:5). Hosea still remembered the true meaning: “He met God at Bethel, and there God spoke with us” (Hosea 12:4). Places where God once met his people can become idols if we trust the place instead of the God.

Was the pillar an idol? No. Standing stones were common in Canaanite religion, and once they were used in pagan worship the law forbade Israel to set them up: “you shall not set up a pillar, which the LORD your God hates” (Deuteronomy 16:22). Jacob’s pillar, long before that law, was not an object of worship or a home for a god, but a memorial of what the LORD had said there.
verseByVerse.note: “Bethel” means “the house of God” (ESV note). It lay about 12 miles north of Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jacob made a vow, saying, "If God will be with me and will keep me in this way that I go, and will give me bread to eat and clothing to wear, so that I come again to my father's house in peace, then the LORD shall be my God, and this stone, which I have set up for a pillar, shall be God's house. And of all that you give me I will give a full tenth to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jacob answers God’s promise with a vow: if God keeps him and brings him home, the LORD will be his God, the pillar will be God’s house, and he will give God a tenth of all he receives.

Then Jacob made a vow. A vow was a solemn promise to God, often made in a time of need, and binding once made (Numbers 30:2; Ecclesiastes 5:4–5). This is the first vow recorded in the Bible.

If God will be with me and will keep me in this way that I go. Jacob’s conditions simply repeat what God has just promised: presence, keeping, return (v. 15). He adds only the bare necessities of a traveller, “bread to eat and clothing to wear”, and to come home “in peace”. He is not asking for riches; he is asking God to do what he said.

Then the LORD shall be my God. Up to now the LORD has been “the God of Abraham … and the God of Isaac” (v. 13). Jacob looks for the day when he will call him his own. He does: on his return he builds an altar at Shechem and names it “El-Elohe-Israel”, “God, the God of Israel” (33:20), and he goes back to Bethel to worship the God “who answers me in the day of my distress” (35:3).

And of all that you give me I will give a full tenth to you. Abraham had given a tenth to Melchizedek (14:20); the law would later require a tenth of produce and flocks for the LORD (Leviticus 27:30–32). Notice Jacob’s words, “all that you give me”: even before he has anything, he acknowledges that whatever he gains will be God’s gift.

A young faith. Jacob’s “if” is the voice of a faith that is real but still immature, still in the habit of making deals. God had promised all this without conditions, and Jacob turns it into terms. Yet God does not withdraw. He is patient with weak faith and keeps his word before our faith is grown. The story ahead is God’s long work of turning a bargainer into a man who clings to him (32:26).

For us. Many people first come to God like this, with conditions and half-understood promises. God does not despise the beginning. But a faith that keeps saying “if” has more to learn: God has already promised in Christ, and “all the promises of God find their Yes in him” (2 Corinthians 1:20). We do not trust him because he has met our terms, but because he has already proved himself at the cross.

Where Christians differ. On Jacob’s vow. Some read it as unbelief, a bargain that puts God on trial. Others note that vows in the Bible were normally conditional in form (Numbers 21:2; 1 Samuel 1:11), and that Jacob’s conditions only echo God’s own promise, so that he is taking God at his word. On the tithe, some Christians hold that believers are still bound to give exactly a tenth; others that the New Testament commands generous, proportionate giving without fixing a percentage.

This commentary’s view. Jacob’s vow is genuine faith in an immature form: it rests on God’s promise, but its bargaining tone fits the man Jacob still was. On giving, no fixed percentage is commanded for Christians, but regular, proportionate, generous and cheerful giving (1 Corinthians 16:2; 2 Corinthians 9:7); the tithe is a helpful benchmark, and many should give more.

Uncertain wording. It is not certain where Jacob’s condition ends and his promise begins. The ESV reads “then the LORD shall be my God” as the first thing Jacob promises. Some scholars read that phrase as the last of the conditions (“and if the LORD will be my God”), so that the promise begins only with the pillar and the tithe in v. 22. The Hebrew allows either. The overall sense is the same: Jacob commits himself to the LORD in response to his promise.

28.theology:
The stairway of Bethel finds its fulfilment in Christ, the true house of God (John 2:19–21). Jacob said “how awesome is this place” of a patch of desert; the Christian says it of Christ, in whom “the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily” (Col 2:9). The holy places of the Old Testament (Bethel, Sinai, Zion, the temple) lead to a holy Person in the New. Jesus is the true Bethel: the place where God and humanity meet, permanently and finally.

Bethel also shows the order of grace: God moves first. Jacob has not repented or reformed, yet God appears. The promise comes before the change, and grace comes before the faith it awakens. This is the order of the gospel.
28.examples:
Jacob asleep on a stone with heaven opened above him is the lasting picture of grace finding us where we are: not in the temple, but in the wilderness, at night, in flight from our own sins. The God of Jacob meets people in their wilderness. He met Augustine in his restlessness, Luther in the terror of a thunderstorm, and Wesley when his heart was “strangely warmed” on hearing the gospel explained.

The Christian life begins not with achievement but with discovery: “Surely the LORD is in this place, and I did not know it.” The gospel is not a way for us to climb to God; it is the news that God has already come down, in the incarnation and in the Spirit who dwells within, and that we are already held by the God we did not know was there.

keyVerse.quote: Behold, I am with you and will keep you wherever you go, and will bring you back to this land. For I will not leave you until I have done what I have promised you.
keyVerse.note: This is the promise a fugitive most needed, and God gave it without conditions to a man who deserved nothing. It holds the whole chapter together: God’s presence, his protection, and his faithfulness to finish what he began. It finds its fulfilment in Jesus, Immanuel, who promises his people, “I am with you always” (Matthew 28:20).

28.reflection:
Jacob met God on the night he had lost everything, before he had repented or changed. What does this teach about how God’s grace works? Has God ever met you in a similar way?

Jesus said he is the stairway between heaven and earth (John 1:51). How does that change the way you think about prayer, worship and “holy places”?

“Surely the LORD is in this place, and I did not know it” (v. 16). Where in your ordinary life do you most need to remember that God is present?

Jacob answered God’s unconditional promise with an “if” (vv. 20–22). In what ways do we try to bargain with God? What would it look like to trust his promises in Christ without conditions, including in our giving?

29.title: Jacob, Leah, and Rachel
29.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Jacob went on his journey and came to the land of the people of the east.<sup>2</sup>As he looked, he saw a well in the field, and behold, three flocks of sheep lying beside it, for out of that well the flocks were watered. The stone on the well's mouth was large,<sup>3</sup>and when all the flocks were gathered there, the shepherds would roll the stone from the mouth of the well and water the sheep, and put the stone back in its place over the mouth of the well.<sup>4</sup>Jacob said to them, "My brothers, where do you come from?" They said, "We are from Haran."<sup>5</sup>He said to them, "Do you know Laban the son of Nahor?" They said, "We know him."<sup>6</sup>He said to them, "Is it well with him?" They said, "It is well; and see, Rachel his daughter is coming with the sheep!"<sup>7</sup>He said, "Behold, it is still high day; it is not time for the livestock to be gathered together. Water the sheep and go, pasture them."<sup>8</sup>But they said, "We cannot until all the flocks are gathered together and the stone is rolled from the mouth of the well; then we water the sheep."<sup>9</sup>While he was still speaking with them, Rachel came with her father's sheep, for she was a shepherdess.<sup>10</sup>Now as soon as Jacob saw Rachel the daughter of Laban his mother's brother, and the sheep of Laban his mother's brother, Jacob came near and rolled the stone from the well's mouth and watered the flock of Laban his mother's brother.<sup>11</sup>Then Jacob kissed Rachel and wept aloud.<sup>12</sup>And Jacob told Rachel that he was her father's kinsman, and that he was Rebekah's son, and she ran and told her father.<sup>13</sup>As soon as Laban heard the news about Jacob, his sister's son, he ran to meet him and embraced him and kissed him and brought him to his house. Jacob told Laban all these things,<sup>14</sup>and Laban said to him, "Surely you are my bone and my flesh!" And he stayed with him a month.<sup>15</sup>Then Laban said to Jacob, "Because you are my kinsman, should you therefore serve me for nothing? Tell me, what shall your wages be?"<sup>16</sup>Now Laban had two daughters. The name of the older was Leah, and the name of the younger was Rachel.<sup>17</sup>Leah's eyes were weak, but Rachel was beautiful in form and appearance.<sup>18</sup>Jacob loved Rachel. And he said, "I will serve you seven years for your younger daughter Rachel."<sup>19</sup>Laban said, "It is better that I give her to you than that I should give her to any other man; stay with me."<sup>20</sup>So Jacob served seven years for Rachel, and they seemed to him but a few days because of the love he had for her.<sup>21</sup>Then Jacob said to Laban, "Give me my wife that I may go in to her, for my time is completed."<sup>22</sup>So Laban gathered together all the people of the place and made a feast.<sup>23</sup>But in the evening he took his daughter Leah and brought her to Jacob, and he went in to her.<sup>24</sup>(Laban gave his female servant Zilpah to his daughter Leah to be her servant.)<sup>25</sup>And in the morning, behold, it was Leah! And Jacob said to Laban, "What is this you have done to me? Did I not serve with you for Rachel? Why then have you deceived me?"<sup>26</sup>Laban said, "It is not so done in our country, to give the younger before the firstborn.<sup>27</sup>Complete the week of this one, and we will give you the other also in return for serving me another seven years."<sup>28</sup>Jacob did so, and completed her week. Then Laban gave him his daughter Rachel to be his wife.<sup>29</sup>(Laban gave his female servant Bilhah to his daughter Rachel to be her servant.)<sup>30</sup>So Jacob went in to Rachel also, and he loved Rachel more than Leah, and served Laban for another seven years.<sup>31</sup>When the LORD saw that Leah was hated, he opened her womb, but Rachel was barren.<sup>32</sup>And Leah conceived and bore a son, and she called his name Reuben, for she said, "Because the LORD has looked upon my affliction; for now my husband will love me."<sup>33</sup>She conceived again and bore a son, and said, "Because the LORD has heard that I am hated, he has given me this son also." And she called his name Simeon.<sup>34</sup>Again she conceived and bore a son, and said, "Now this time my husband will be attached to me, because I have borne him three sons." Therefore his name was called Levi.<sup>35</sup>And she conceived again and bore a son, and said, "This time I will praise the LORD." Therefore she called his name Judah. Then she ceased bearing.
29.overview:
Where we are. Jacob has fled from Esau, whose blessing he stole by deceiving their blind father (chapter 27). On the way, at Bethel, God met the fugitive in a dream and promised, “I am with you and will keep you wherever you go” (28:15). Now he arrives in Haran, at the house of his mother’s brother Laban.

The message. God keeps his promise to be with Jacob, but being with him includes disciplining him. The deceiver is deceived, in the dark, by a substitution, and learns from the inside what it is to be cheated. And in the same household the LORD sees the wife nobody wanted: he opens Leah’s womb, and from her come the priests and the kings of Israel. God is not impressed by what impresses us.

Why it was said. Israel heard here how their twelve tribes began, in a household of rivalry and favouritism, not of heroes (see the introduction). They also heard their own story in Leah’s: “the LORD has looked upon my affliction” (v. 32) is the language God used when he saw his people’s affliction in Egypt (Exodus 3:7).

How the chapter makes its case. Providence brings Jacob to the right well on the right day, and he meets Rachel (vv. 1–12). Laban welcomes him, then turns a nephew into a hired man (vv. 13–15). Jacob loves Rachel and serves seven years for her, but on the wedding night Laban gives him Leah, and the man who once claimed to be the firstborn is lectured on the rights of the firstborn (vv. 16–28). Jacob marries Rachel too and loves her more (vv. 29–30). Then the LORD sees the unloved Leah and gives her four sons, whose names trace her journey from longing for her husband’s love to praising God (vv. 31–35).

Where it leads. By promise and by the character of God. From Leah’s fourth son, Judah, comes the line of David and of Jesus, “the Lion of the tribe of Judah” (Revelation 5:5); from Levi, the priesthood that pointed to him. And the God who saw Leah is the God revealed in Christ, who went looking for the overlooked and passed by the people the world admired.

For us. God may let us taste what we have done to others, not to destroy us but to change us. If you are the one who is not chosen, the one in the background of someone else’s love story, the LORD sees you. And when the thing we were sure would make life right turns out, in the morning, to be Leah, it is time to say with her, “This time I will praise the LORD.”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–30 — Jacob in Haran: Laban's Daughters
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The deceiver is deceived, and God uses it to begin changing him. Providence brings Jacob straight to Laban’s family at a well, as it brought Abraham’s servant (chapter 24), and he meets Rachel (vv. 1–12). Laban’s warm welcome soon becomes a question of wages (vv. 13–15). Jacob serves seven years for the woman he loves, but on the wedding night, in the dark, Laban substitutes the older daughter for the younger, just as Jacob once passed himself off as the older son before his blind father (vv. 16–25). Laban’s excuse about the firstborn stings, and Jacob serves seven more years (vv. 26–30). What Jacob sowed, he now reaps.
verseByVerse.theology: Jacob comes to a well in Haran, rolls away the stone for Rachel, and weeps. Laban welcomes him, and Jacob serves seven years for Rachel that seem but a few days. On the wedding night Laban substitutes Leah; Jacob serves seven more years for Rachel, and loves her more than Leah.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Jacob's own crime is played back to him. Now: "whatever one sows, that will he also reap" (Gal. 6:7), and God uses even that to teach.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jacob went on his journey and came to the land of the people of the east. As he looked, he saw a well in the field, and behold, three flocks of sheep lying beside it, for out of that well the flocks were watered. The stone on the well's mouth was large, and when all the flocks were gathered there, the shepherds would roll the stone from the mouth of the well and water the sheep, and put the stone back in its place over the mouth of the well.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jacob reaches the land of his mother’s family, and God’s quiet providence brings him straight to the well where Laban’s flocks are watered.

Then Jacob went on his journey. The Hebrew says that Jacob “lifted up his feet”. After the dream at Bethel the fugitive walks on with fresh heart: the God of his fathers has promised to be with him (28:15), and nothing in the journey that follows happens by chance.

The land of the people of the east. The region east of Canaan, here northern Mesopotamia around Haran, over four hundred miles from Beersheba, where Abraham’s brother Nahor had settled (24:10; 27:43).

A well in the field … the stone on the well’s mouth was large. In dry country a well was precious and shared. A heavy stone kept out dirt and animals and stopped any one shepherd from taking more than his share; by local custom it was rolled away only when all the flocks had gathered, so that everyone watered together. The detail matters for what Jacob does next (v. 10).

A well again. Abraham’s servant found Rebekah at a well (24:11–20), and Moses will find his wife at one (Exodus 2:15–21). The pattern tells Israel that God is at work in the meeting. Centuries later, beside the well that bore Jacob’s name, a weary traveller asked a woman for a drink, and offered her “living water” (John 4:10). The Samaritan woman asked, “Are you greater than our father Jacob?” (John 4:12). He was: the true Bridegroom had come, not to find a wife who pleased him, but to seek a people who did not.

verseByVerse.quote: Jacob said to them, "My brothers, where do you come from?" They said, "We are from Haran." He said to them, "Do you know Laban the son of Nahor?" They said, "We know him." He said to them, "Is it well with him?" They said, "It is well; and see, Rachel his daughter is coming with the sheep!" He said, "Behold, it is still high day; it is not time for the livestock to be gathered together. Water the sheep and go, pasture them." But they said, "We cannot until all the flocks are gathered together and the stone is rolled from the mouth of the well; then we water the sheep."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first shepherds Jacob meets know Laban, and his daughter is already on her way: Jacob is being guided, though he does not yet see it.

My brothers, where do you come from? A friendly greeting from a stranger. “We are from Haran”: the very place he was sent to find (27:43).

Is it well with him? Literally, “Is there peace (shalom) to him?” The ordinary greeting of the East, asking after a person’s whole welfare.

See, Rachel his daughter is coming with the sheep! The timing is the point. Jacob has not had to search; as with Abraham’s servant, the right person arrives while he is still speaking (24:15).

Water the sheep and go, pasture them. Jacob is already a shepherd who knows his trade. It is the middle of the day, too early to pen the flocks, so why are these men idling by the well? Perhaps he also wants them gone before Rachel arrives. Their reply is the local rule: the stone stays put until all the flocks are gathered.

verseByVerse.quote: While he was still speaking with them, Rachel came with her father's sheep, for she was a shepherdess. Now as soon as Jacob saw Rachel the daughter of Laban his mother's brother, and the sheep of Laban his mother's brother, Jacob came near and rolled the stone from the well's mouth and watered the flock of Laban his mother's brother. Then Jacob kissed Rachel and wept aloud. And Jacob told Rachel that he was her father's kinsman, and that he was Rebekah's son, and she ran and told her father.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jacob meets Rachel, rolls away the great stone single-handed to water her flock, and weeps aloud as he tells her who he is.

Rachel came with her father’s sheep, for she was a shepherdess. Rachel means “ewe”: a shepherdess with a shepherd’s name. Daughters often kept the family flocks before they married (Exodus 2:16).

Laban his mother’s brother. Three times in one verse. Jacob sees not just a lovely girl but his mother’s family: the end of his search and a link to the home he lost.

Rolled the stone from the well’s mouth. A stone that usually needed several shepherds is moved by one man, against local custom. The “quiet man, dwelling in tents” (25:27) shows unexpected strength, as Moses later sprang up to water the flock of seven sisters (Exodus 2:17). Love and relief make him bold.

Jacob kissed Rachel and wept aloud. A kiss of greeting between relatives, not yet of romance. The tears are the first we see Jacob shed: the end of a lonely, frightened journey, and a sign that God has brought him to safety as he promised.

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as Laban heard the news about Jacob, his sister's son, he ran to meet him and embraced him and kissed him and brought him to his house. Jacob told Laban all these things, and Laban said to him, "Surely you are my bone and my flesh!" And he stayed with him a month. Then Laban said to Jacob, "Because you are my kinsman, should you therefore serve me for nothing? Tell me, what shall your wages be?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Laban welcomes his nephew warmly, but within a month he has turned family into business.

He ran to meet him and embraced him and kissed him. Laban ran in just this way years before, when he saw the gold on his sister’s arms (24:29–30). This time the visitor has come with nothing but a staff (32:10), and the welcome cools.

Surely you are my bone and my flesh! The language of close kinship (2:23; 2 Samuel 5:1). It is truer than Laban knows: he and Jacob are alike in cunning, and Jacob is about to meet his match.

Should you therefore serve me for nothing? … what shall your wages be? It sounds generous, but it quietly changes the relationship. The kinsman becomes a hired worker, and from now on Laban deals with Jacob by contract. “Wages” will be the sore point of the next twenty years (31:7, 41).

verseByVerse.quote: Now Laban had two daughters. The name of the older was Leah, and the name of the younger was Rachel. Leah's eyes were weak, but Rachel was beautiful in form and appearance.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Laban has two daughters, the older plain Leah and the younger beautiful Rachel, and the contrast sets up the conflict of the next two chapters.

The older … the younger. Older and younger again. Jacob is the younger who took the older brother’s place (25:23); now he will be caught by the same distinction (v. 26).

Rachel was beautiful in form and appearance. The same words are later used of her son Joseph (39:6). Scripture does not despise beauty, but it warns that “man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart” (1 Samuel 16:7), and this chapter will show it.

Uncertain wording. The word translated “weak” (rakkot) usually means “soft” or “tender”. It may be a kindness, gentle or delicate eyes, or a contrast, eyes without sparkle or with poor sight, set beside Rachel’s striking looks. The sentence clearly ranks Leah below her sister in looks; just how is uncertain. The meaning of Leah’s name is also uncertain (“cow” and “weary” have been suggested); Rachel means “ewe”.

verseByVerse.quote: Jacob loved Rachel. And he said, "I will serve you seven years for your younger daughter Rachel." Laban said, "It is better that I give her to you than that I should give her to any other man; stay with me." So Jacob served seven years for Rachel, and they seemed to him but a few days because of the love he had for her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jacob loves Rachel and, having no bride-price to give, offers seven years of work for her; love makes the years seem like days.

Jacob loved Rachel. Plainly said. It is the first time Genesis says a man loved a woman before marriage; Isaac’s love for Rebekah came after (24:67).

I will serve you seven years. A bridegroom normally paid the bride’s family a bride-price (34:12; Exodus 22:16–17). Jacob, who left home with nothing, offers labour instead, and a generous amount of it. The prophet remembered: “there Israel served for a wife, and for a wife he guarded sheep” (Hosea 12:12).

It is better that I give her to you than … to any other man. Laban sounds agreeable, but he never actually says “Rachel”. His careful words leave room for the trick to come.

They seemed to him but a few days because of the love he had for her. Love turns long service into gladness. That is also the best description of service to Christ: it grows light not when the work grows less, but when love grows more.

A greater Bridegroom. Jacob laboured years for a beautiful bride. Christ came for a bride with nothing to commend her and paid with his life: he “loved the church and gave himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:25), “who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross” (Hebrews 12:2). Jacob served for what he found lovely; Christ serves to make his bride lovely (Ephesians 5:27).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jacob said to Laban, "Give me my wife that I may go in to her, for my time is completed." So Laban gathered together all the people of the place and made a feast. But in the evening he took his daughter Leah and brought her to Jacob, and he went in to her. (Laban gave his female servant Zilpah to his daughter Leah to be her servant.) And in the morning, behold, it was Leah! And Jacob said to Laban, "What is this you have done to me? Did I not serve with you for Rachel? Why then have you deceived me?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the wedding night Laban secretly gives Jacob the older daughter, and the man who deceived his blind father is himself deceived in the dark.

Give me my wife. The seven years are up, and Jacob is blunt. He has kept his side of the bargain.

Laban gathered together all the people of the place and made a feast. A wedding feast (literally a “drinking”) for the whole town. With many witnesses present, Jacob would find it hard to undo the marriage afterwards.

In the evening he took his daughter Leah and brought her to Jacob. A bride came to her husband veiled (24:65), at night, after a long feast with wine; in the dark Jacob had no way to tell. Leah could not have done this without her father’s orders, and perhaps her own silence. Whatever she felt, she is wronged too: given to a man who wanted her sister.

Laban gave his female servant Zilpah to his daughter Leah. A wealthy father gave his daughter a maid as part of her dowry. The aside matters later: Zilpah will bear two of Jacob’s sons (30:9–13).

In the morning, behold, it was Leah! The narrator lets us share Jacob’s shock as daylight reveals the face beside him.

Why then have you deceived me? The Hebrew word is the one Isaac used when he told Esau, “Your brother came deceitfully” (27:35). Jacob, who dressed up as his brother in his blind father’s tent, has been deceived by a woman dressed up as her sister in the dark. He tastes his own medicine, and the narrator does not need to point it out. “Whatever one sows, that will he also reap” (Galatians 6:7). Yet this is discipline, not destruction: “the Lord disciplines the one he loves” (Hebrews 12:6).

In the morning, it is always Leah. Jacob had poured everything into Rachel. Seven years of work “seemed to him but a few days” (v. 20), because he believed that if he could only have her, his restless, cheated life would finally come right. Then the morning came. Timothy Keller often pointed out that this is what every idol does: we go to bed with what we think is Rachel, and in the morning it is always Leah. The promotion, the house, the partner, the recognition, even the child we long for, are good gifts, but none of them can be what we hoped once we have asked it to be our salvation. That is not cynicism about love; it is a diagnosis of the weight we put on it. The disappointment is not proof that life is a cheat. It is a sign that we were made for a love no human being can give. Leah, the woman nobody wanted in the morning, comes to see it first: “This time I will praise the LORD” (v. 35). And the one Bridegroom who never disappoints was born of her son Judah’s line.
verseByVerse.note: Jacob, the younger, took the elder’s place; Laban gives the elder in place of the younger.

verseByVerse.quote: Laban said, "It is not so done in our country, to give the younger before the firstborn. Complete the week of this one, and we will give you the other also in return for serving me another seven years." Jacob did so, and completed her week. Then Laban gave him his daughter Rachel to be his wife.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Laban defends the trick with a lecture on the rights of the firstborn, and sells Rachel to Jacob for seven more years.

It is not so done in our country, to give the younger before the firstborn. The words sting. The man who once said, “I am Esau your firstborn” (27:19), is told that in decent places the firstborn comes first. Laban may be stating a real custom, but if so he could have said it seven years earlier.

Complete the week of this one. A wedding feast lasted seven days (Judges 14:12). Jacob must honour Leah’s marriage week in full; then Rachel will be given to him too, and he will pay for her afterwards with another seven years’ work, fourteen in all.

Jacob did so. The schemer, out-schemed, has no answer. He takes both sisters. The law of Moses would later forbid exactly this: “you shall not take a woman as a rival wife to her sister” (Leviticus 18:18). The next chapter shows why.

verseByVerse.quote: (Laban gave his female servant Bilhah to his daughter Rachel to be her servant.) So Jacob went in to Rachel also, and he loved Rachel more than Leah, and served Laban for another seven years.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jacob marries Rachel too and loves her more than Leah, and the favouritism that marred his own childhood enters his marriage.

Laban gave his female servant Bilhah to his daughter Rachel. Rachel too receives a maid, who will bear two of Jacob’s sons (30:3–8).

He loved Rachel more than Leah. Isaac loved Esau and Rebekah loved Jacob (25:28), and the family was torn apart. Jacob has learned nothing from it: he will love Rachel more than Leah, and later Joseph more than his brothers (37:3), with the same results.

Does the Bible approve of Jacob’s two wives? Scripture records polygamy without approving it, and shows its pain. God’s design from the beginning was one man and one woman becoming “one flesh” (2:24), and Jesus reached back to it: “from the beginning it was not so” (Matthew 19:8). Every household in Genesis with more than one wife is a place of rivalry and grief, and this one is the clearest example (see the note on 30:9–13).

Served Laban for another seven years. Jacob came to Haran to “stay with him a while” (27:44). He has now committed fourteen years, and it will be twenty before he leaves (31:41).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 31–35 — Leah's Children: The LORD Sees the Unloved
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The LORD sees the wife her husband overlooks. Jacob loves Rachel, but God opens the womb of the unloved Leah and closes Rachel’s (v. 31). Leah’s first three sons carry names full of hope that her husband will at last love her: Reuben, “the LORD has looked upon my affliction”; Simeon, “the LORD has heard”; Levi, “now this time my husband will be attached to me” (vv. 32–34). With the fourth her eyes turn from Jacob to God: “This time I will praise the LORD,” and she calls him Judah (v. 35). From the rejected wife come the priestly tribe and the royal one.
verseByVerse.theology: The LORD sees that Leah is unloved and opens her womb, while Rachel is barren. Leah names Reuben, Simeon and Levi in hope that her husband will love her; at Judah she says, "This time I will praise the LORD."
verseByVerse.examples: Then: God gave the unloved wife sons and a song. Now: God is drawn to the one nobody is attending to (Ps. 113:7–9).

verseByVerse.quote: When the LORD saw that Leah was hated, he opened her womb, but Rachel was barren. And Leah conceived and bore a son, and she called his name Reuben, for she said, "Because the LORD has looked upon my affliction; for now my husband will love me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD sees that Leah is unloved and gives her a son, but her hope that this will win her husband’s love goes unfulfilled.

When the LORD saw that Leah was hated. Until now the chapter has been about what Jacob and Laban see and want; now, for the first time, the LORD acts, and he acts for the woman nobody was looking at. “Hated” here means “loved less” (v. 30): the same comparison appears in the law about a man with two wives, “the one loved and the other unloved” (Deuteronomy 21:15), which protected the unloved wife’s son. It is not that Jacob despised Leah, but that she always came second.

He opened her womb, but Rachel was barren. In Genesis the LORD alone opens and closes the womb (20:18; 30:2, 22). Rachel is barren like Sarah and Rebekah before her; the wife who has her husband’s love lacks what the unloved wife is given.

She called his name Reuben. Reuben sounds like “See, a son”, and Leah hears in it, “the LORD has looked upon my affliction”. Hagar called the LORD “a God of seeing” (16:13); later Israel in Egypt would hear God say, “I have surely seen the affliction of my people” (Exodus 3:7). The LORD sees the afflicted. Leah uses God’s covenant name, the LORD: she knows the God of Abraham.

For now my husband will love me. A painful hope, and it is not fulfilled. A child cannot make a husband love his wife, and it is a heavy burden for a child to carry.

If you feel unloved. If you are the one who always comes second, in a marriage, a family or a church, the LORD who saw Leah sees you. Being unloved is not the measure of your worth. And if neglect in a marriage has become cruelty, threats or violence, that is abuse: seek safety first and tell someone who can help, such as a pastor or the police; God does not ask anyone to endure it in silence.
verseByVerse.note: “Reuben” means “See, a son” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: She conceived again and bore a son, and said, "Because the LORD has heard that I am hated, he has given me this son also." And she called his name Simeon. Again she conceived and bore a son, and said, "Now this time my husband will be attached to me, because I have borne him three sons." Therefore his name was called Levi. And she conceived again and bore a son, and said, "This time I will praise the LORD." Therefore she called his name Judah. Then she ceased bearing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Leah’s sons trace her journey from longing for Jacob’s love to praising God, and from this unloved wife come the priests and the kings of Israel.

Because the LORD has heard that I am hated … Simeon. Simeon sounds like “heard”. She knows that God listens; she is still hoping that her husband will.

Now this time my husband will be attached to me … Levi. Levi sounds like “attached”. A third son, and the same longing. From Levi came the tribe of priests and Levites, Moses and Aaron among them.

This time I will praise the LORD … Judah. Judah sounds like “praise”. Notice “this time” again, but now the sentence does not mention Jacob at all. Nothing in her circumstances has changed; what has changed is where she is looking. She has found in the LORD what she could not find in her husband.

Then she ceased bearing. A pause that sets up the struggles of the next chapter (30:9).

The leftover wife and the Lion of Judah. From Judah came David’s royal line, and from it Jesus: “our Lord was descended from Judah” (Hebrews 7:14; compare 49:10; Matthew 1:2). The Messiah came not from the beloved Rachel but from the woman nobody chose. That is how God works: “God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong” (1 Corinthians 1:27). And it is what Jesus did: he noticed the woman who touched his garment in the crowd, the tax collector up the tree, the sinner the host despised. In the end Jacob himself chose to be buried beside Leah, not Rachel: “there I buried Leah” (49:31), and Israel remembered both sisters as the women “who together built up the house of Israel” (Ruth 4:11).
verseByVerse.note: Simeon sounds like “heard,” Levi like “attached,” Judah like “praise” (ESV notes). From Levi came the priests.

29.theology:
God’s compassion for Leah is one of the Bible’s most tender reversals. Her husband does not love her, but God sees her, opens her womb, and gives her children the leading place in the line of promise.

This is the pattern of God’s choosing: he chooses the weak to shame the strong and the despised to bring to nothing what the world prizes (1 Cor 1:26–29). The line of the Messiah runs through Leah, the leftover wife, because God is not impressed by what impresses us.
29.examples:
Leah’s journey from “now my husband will love me” (v. 32) to “this time I will praise the LORD” (v. 35) is the story of every soul learning that no human love can fill the longing God made for himself. Leah’s heart is the restless heart Augustine described. What heals her is not Jacob’s love but that the LORD sees her, and that frees us to stop demanding from human relationships what only God can supply. It does not make her loneliness less real; God met her in it.

Jacob the deceiver is deceived: we reap what we sow. God lets us taste the results of our sin, not to destroy us but to change us: Jacob must become Israel, the man who clings to God (32:28).

keyVerse.quote: And she conceived again and bore a son, and said, “This time I will praise the LORD.” Therefore she called his name Judah. Then she ceased bearing.
keyVerse.note: Leah’s first three sons were named in hope of winning Jacob’s love; with the fourth she turns from her husband to the LORD, though nothing in her circumstances has changed. That turn is the heart of the chapter: what no human love could give, she finds in God. And from this son of the unloved wife came David, and David’s greater Son.

29.reflection:
Laban deceives Jacob in the dark much as Jacob deceived his father (vv. 23–26). Have you ever been on the receiving end of something you once did to others? How can God use that kind of experience to change us rather than simply punish us?

Jacob believed that if he could only have Rachel, life would come right (v. 20). What “Rachels” are people around you looking to for that kind of fulfilment, and what happens when the morning comes?

The chapter says that “the LORD saw” the unloved Leah (v. 31). Who in your church, family or workplace is easily overlooked, and how could you notice them as God does?

Leah’s names for her sons move from “now my husband will love me” to “this time I will praise the LORD” (vv. 32–35). What helps a person make that move, and why is it so hard?

30.title: The LORD Remembered Rachel
30.text: <sup>1</sup>When Rachel saw that she bore Jacob no children, she envied her sister. She said to Jacob, "Give me children, or I shall die!"<sup>2</sup>Jacob's anger was kindled against Rachel, and he said, "Am I in the place of God, who has withheld from you the fruit of the womb?"<sup>3</sup>Then she said, "Here is my servant Bilhah; go in to her, so that she may give birth on my behalf, that even I may have children through her."<sup>4</sup>So she gave him her servant Bilhah as a wife, and Jacob went in to her.<sup>5</sup>And Bilhah conceived and bore Jacob a son.<sup>6</sup>Then Rachel said, "God has judged me, and has also heard my voice and given me a son." Therefore she called his name Dan.<sup>7</sup>Rachel's servant Bilhah conceived again and bore Jacob a second son.<sup>8</sup>Then Rachel said, "With mighty wrestlings I have wrestled with my sister and have prevailed." So she called his name Naphtali.<sup>9</sup>When Leah saw that she had ceased bearing children, she took her servant Zilpah and gave her to Jacob as a wife.<sup>10</sup>Then Leah's servant Zilpah bore Jacob a son.<sup>11</sup>And Leah said, "Good fortune has come!" so she called his name Gad.<sup>12</sup>Leah's servant Zilpah bore Jacob a second son.<sup>13</sup>And Leah said, "Happy am I! For women have called me happy." So she called his name Asher.<sup>14</sup>In the days of wheat harvest Reuben went and found mandrakes in the field and brought them to his mother Leah. Then Rachel said to Leah, "Please give me some of your son's mandrakes."<sup>15</sup>But she said to her, "Is it a small matter that you have taken away my husband? Would you take away my son's mandrakes also?" 30.overview:
Where we are. Jacob is married to two sisters and serving Laban for the second seven years. The LORD has given the unloved Leah four sons, while Jacob’s beloved Rachel is barren (29:31–35). This chapter completes the family that will become Israel and then turns to the flocks that will make Jacob rich.

The message. Children and wealth are God’s gifts, not prizes won by human scheming. The sisters compete through their servants, bargain with mandrakes and name their sons like scores in a contest, but every birth is credited to God, and the turning point is one quiet sentence: “Then God remembered Rachel” (v. 22). In the same way Jacob’s cunning with the flocks is real, but it is God who makes him prosper, as he promised at Bethel.

Why it was said. Israel learned here where its twelve tribes came from: not from an ideal family, but from envy, rivalry and favouritism, held together only by God’s faithfulness (see the introduction). Every tribe carried a name that remembered a mother’s tears, boasts or prayers. And a people later enslaved in Egypt heard that the God who blessed Jacob under a grasping master could make them prosper under Pharaoh.

How the chapter makes its case. Rachel, desperate and envious, gives her servant Bilhah to Jacob, and names her sons Dan and Naphtali as verdicts in her war with her sister (vv. 1–8). Leah replies through Zilpah with Gad and Asher (vv. 9–13). The sisters trade mandrakes for a night with Jacob, but it is Leah, who gave the mandrakes away, whom God hears: Issachar, Zebulun and Dinah are born (vv. 14–21). At last God remembers Rachel, and Joseph is born (vv. 22–24). Then Jacob asks to go home; Laban, who knows he has been blessed because of Jacob, keeps him by offering wages (vv. 25–34). Laban cheats at once, Jacob breeds his flocks with peeled sticks and careful selection, and Jacob grows very rich (vv. 35–43).

Where it leads. By pattern, and by the need it exposes. This tangled household cannot secure its worth or its future by its own schemes; everything depends on the God who hears, remembers and gives. And from it come the twelve tribes whose story leads to Christ, and Joseph, the beloved son who will one day save the brothers who sold him, a living picture of the greater Son who saves those who rejected him. The God who “remembered Rachel” is the God who in Christ came “to remember his holy covenant” (Luke 1:72).

For us. Envy and comparison poison families and churches, and no child, possession or success will settle our worth. God gives, in his time, and he hears prayers no one else knows about. Work hard and honestly, even for an unfair master, and look for God’s hand behind what you receive.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–24 — The Birth of Jacob's Children
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The sisters fight for worth through their children, yet every child is God’s gift, and God remembers the barren. Rachel envies Leah and gives Jacob her servant Bilhah, and her names for Bilhah’s sons, Dan and Naphtali, announce a contest won (vv. 1–8). Leah answers through Zilpah, naming Gad and Asher (vv. 9–13). The mandrakes Rachel buys do nothing, while God listens to Leah, who bears Issachar, Zebulun and Dinah (vv. 14–21). Then, after long waiting, “God remembered Rachel”, and she bears Joseph (vv. 22–24). The twelve tribes of Israel come from this rivalry-torn household, held together only by God’s grace.
verseByVerse.theology: Rachel envies her sister and gives Bilhah to Jacob; Leah answers with Zilpah; the sisters trade mandrakes for a night with Jacob. Leah bears Issachar, Zebulun and Dinah. Then God remembers Rachel, listens to her and opens her womb, and she names her son Joseph.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: every conception is credited to God, not to the mandrakes or the scheming. Now: God hears prayers that no one else ever knows about.

verseByVerse.quote: When Rachel saw that she bore Jacob no children, she envied her sister. She said to Jacob, "Give me children, or I shall die!" Jacob's anger was kindled against Rachel, and he said, "Am I in the place of God, who has withheld from you the fruit of the womb?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rachel, childless and envious of her sister, demands children from Jacob, and he answers her anguish with anger, though what he says is true: only God gives children.

When Rachel saw that she bore Jacob no children, she envied her sister. Each sister has what the other wants: Leah has sons, Rachel has Jacob’s love. Envy is grief at another’s good, and it sours them both. “Envy makes the bones rot” (Proverbs 14:30).

Give me children, or I shall die! A cry of real anguish in a world where a childless wife was pitied and often scorned (v. 23). There is a painful irony in it: when Rachel does have a second son, she dies giving birth to him (35:16–18).

Am I in the place of God? True: Jacob cannot open her womb, and her demand was unreasonable. But true words spoken in anger can still be unkind. Isaac had prayed for barren Rebekah (25:21); we are not told that Jacob prayed for Rachel. Compare Elkanah’s clumsy but tender, “Am I not more to you than ten sons?” (1 Samuel 1:8).

In everyday life. When someone you love is in anguish, the right answer is rarely a correct statement of doctrine delivered in irritation. “Weep with those who weep” (Romans 12:15), and pray for them.

verseByVerse.quote: Then she said, "Here is my servant Bilhah; go in to her, so that she may give birth on my behalf, that even I may have children through her." So she gave him her servant Bilhah as a wife, and Jacob went in to her. And Bilhah conceived and bore Jacob a son.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rachel gives Jacob her servant Bilhah so that she may have children through her, repeating Sarah’s mistake with Hagar.

Here is my servant Bilhah; go in to her. Almost the very words of Sarah: “Go in to my servant; it may be that I shall obtain children by her” (16:2). Ancient marriage contracts show that a childless wife might give her slave to her husband in this way, and the child would count as hers. It was legal and customary; it was not God’s way, and it led to grief for Sarah, and will for Rachel.

So that she may give birth on my behalf. Literally “on my knees”. Placing a newborn on someone’s knees was a sign of claiming it as one’s own (compare 50:23).

As a wife. Bilhah’s place is lower than Rachel’s, but she is no longer simply a maid. A slave woman with no say in the matter becomes a mother of two tribes of Israel. Scripture records what was done to her without approving it.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “give birth on my behalf” is literally “on my knees.”

verseByVerse.quote: Then Rachel said, "God has judged me, and has also heard my voice and given me a son." Therefore she called his name Dan. Rachel's servant Bilhah conceived again and bore Jacob a second son. Then Rachel said, "With mighty wrestlings I have wrestled with my sister and have prevailed." So she called his name Naphtali.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rachel names Bilhah’s sons as verdicts in her contest with her sister: Dan, “God has judged me”, and Naphtali, “I have wrestled … and have prevailed.”

God has judged me, and has also heard my voice … Dan. Dan sounds like “judged”: here, “vindicated”, “judged in my favour”. Rachel has been praying, and she sees the son as God’s answer, though the way she pursued it was her own.

With mighty wrestlings I have wrestled with my sister and have prevailed … Naphtali. Naphtali sounds like “wrestling”. This is a family at war, and Rachel claims a round. The words anticipate her husband’s own night of wrestling: Jacob will strive with God and prevail (32:28), and learn that the only contest worth winning is the one that ends in being blessed.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew says “wrestlings of God”. This is probably a way of saying “mighty wrestlings”, as the ESV takes it, since “God” can work as a superlative in Hebrew; but it may mean “wrestlings before God”, that is, in prayer, or a struggle over God’s favour. The overall sense, a fierce contest Rachel believes she has won, is clear.
verseByVerse.note: Dan sounds like “judged,” Naphtali like “wrestling” (ESV notes).

verseByVerse.quote: When Leah saw that she had ceased bearing children, she took her servant Zilpah and gave her to Jacob as a wife. Then Leah's servant Zilpah bore Jacob a son. And Leah said, "Good fortune has come!" so she called his name Gad. Leah's servant Zilpah bore Jacob a second son. And Leah said, "Happy am I! For women have called me happy." So she called his name Asher.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Leah answers in kind through her servant Zilpah, and her names for the boys, “good fortune” and “happy”, sound like a scoreboard.

When Leah saw that she had ceased bearing children. Leah had come to praise the LORD at Judah’s birth (29:35). Now, with no more children, she is drawn back into the contest. Spiritual progress is seldom a straight line.

Good fortune has come! … Gad. Gad sounds like “good fortune”. Leah, who once named her sons for the LORD, now speaks of luck.

Happy am I! For women have called me happy … Asher. Asher sounds like “happy”. Her joy is measured by what other women say. The children have become weapons in the sisters’ rivalry.

Does the Bible approve of the patriarchs’ marriages? Readers ask it from opposite directions. A sceptic sees two wives, two slave women and a house full of rival sons, and concludes that “biblical marriage” is a myth. Some religious readers have quietly assumed that whatever the patriarchs did must have been allowed. Genesis disappoints both. It seldom stops to pass verdicts; it shows. And what it shows is that every household in the book with more than one wife is a battlefield: Lamech’s song of revenge, Sarah and Hagar, now two sisters keeping score with babies. The pattern was set at the beginning, one man and one woman becoming one flesh (2:24), and Jesus reached back past Moses to it: “from the beginning it was not so” (Matthew 19:8). So the Bible is neither a gallery of moral heroes nor a manual of family values. It is the story of a God who keeps his promise through families like this one, and builds the twelve tribes of Israel out of its rivalries. That is good news for anyone whose family is no model: the church is made not of tidy households but of people from broken ones, given a new family in Christ.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of v. 11 can be read either as “good fortune has come” (followed by modern translations) or as “a troop comes” (the King James Version). Either way the name Gad is explained by a play on its sound; “good fortune” is the likelier sense.
verseByVerse.note: Gad sounds like “good fortune,” Asher like “happy” (ESV notes).

verseByVerse.quote: In the days of wheat harvest Reuben went and found mandrakes in the field and brought them to his mother Leah. Then Rachel said to Leah, "Please give me some of your son's mandrakes." But she said to her, "Is it a small matter that you have taken away my husband? Would you take away my son's mandrakes also?" Rachel said, "Then he may lie with you tonight in exchange for your son's mandrakes." When Jacob came from the field in the evening, Leah went out to meet him and said, "You must come in to me, for I have hired you with my son's mandrakes." So he lay with her that night.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rachel buys Reuben’s mandrakes, thought to help a woman conceive, with a night of Jacob’s company, and Leah gets the night.

In the days of wheat harvest Reuben … found mandrakes. Wheat was harvested in late spring. The mandrake has a fragrant yellow fruit (Song of Songs 7:13), and its Hebrew name sounds like the word for “love”; it was widely believed to arouse desire and help conception. Reuben, a boy by now, brings them to his mother, perhaps knowing what she longed for.

Is it a small matter that you have taken away my husband? Leah’s bitterness spills out. Rachel did not take Jacob away; Laban gave Leah to a man who wanted her sister. But that is how it feels to Leah after years of coming second.

Then he may lie with you tonight in exchange for your son’s mandrakes. Jacob is traded between his wives like a commodity. Laban treated his daughters as goods (31:15); now they treat their husband the same way.

I have hired you with my son’s mandrakes. The word “hired” (sakar) will give Issachar his name (v. 18). It is a sad sentence for a wife to have to say to her husband.

What it does not mean. The mandrakes did nothing. Rachel got them and still had no child; Leah gave them up and conceived (v. 17). God, not superstition, opens the womb. That is no criticism of medicine: a couple who seek medical help in childlessness are using God’s gifts, not distrusting him. The point is that the life is his to give, and that charms and bargains cannot force his hand.
verseByVerse.note: Mandrakes were thought to help a woman conceive.

verseByVerse.quote: And God listened to Leah, and she conceived and bore Jacob a fifth son. Leah said, "God has given me my wages because I gave my servant to my husband." So she called his name Issachar. And Leah conceived again, and she bore Jacob a sixth son. Then Leah said, "God has endowed me with a good endowment; now my husband will honor me, because I have borne him six sons." So she called his name Zebulun. Afterward she bore a daughter and called her name Dinah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God listens to Leah, and the least-loved wife bears a fifth and sixth son and a daughter.

And God listened to Leah. Leah had been praying. The narrator does not credit the mandrakes or the bargain, but God. “Children are a heritage from the LORD” (Psalm 127:3).

God has given me my wages because I gave my servant to my husband … Issachar. Issachar sounds like “wages”, echoing “hired” in v. 16. Leah reads God’s gift as payment for giving Zilpah to Jacob. The narrator records her reasoning; he does not endorse it. Children are gifts, not wages, and God was being kind to her, not settling an account.

God has endowed me with a good endowment; now my husband will honor me … Zebulun. Zebulun sounds like “honour”, and there is a play on “endowed”. Even after six sons, Leah’s ache is the same as at the start: “now my husband will…” (29:32, 34). Nothing human fills that space.

Afterward she bore a daughter and called her name Dinah. Jacob had other daughters (37:35; 46:7), but Dinah alone is named, because of what happens to her in chapter 34. Her name comes from the same root as Dan, “judged”: a name of justice, for a girl who will suffer a great injustice.
verseByVerse.note: Issachar sounds like “wages,” Zebulun like “honor” (ESV notes).

verseByVerse.quote: Then God remembered Rachel, and God listened to her and opened her womb. She conceived and bore a son and said, "God has taken away my reproach." And she called his name Joseph, saying, "May the LORD add to me another son!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
After years of waiting, God remembers Rachel and gives her a son, Joseph, the son through whom he will one day save the whole family.

Then God remembered Rachel. When God “remembers” in Scripture it does not mean he had forgotten; it marks the moment he acts after a season of waiting, keeping faith with his own (8:1; 19:29; 1 Samuel 1:19). Rachel’s years of waiting were not abandonment: God’s silence is not absence.

God listened to her and opened her womb. Rachel too had been praying. Her bargains and her servant had not given her a child of her own; God did. Like Sarah, Rebekah and later Hannah, she receives a son as a pure gift, because the line of promise rests on God’s power, not human ability.

God has taken away my reproach. Her “reproach” is the shame of childlessness in a culture that counted it disgrace. Elizabeth used the same words when God gave her John the Baptist: “to take away my reproach among people” (Luke 1:25).

She called his name Joseph, saying, “May the LORD add to me another son!” Joseph means “may he add”, and sounds like “taken away”. Rachel speaks of “God” as she rejoices, and then of “the LORD”, God’s covenant name, as she prays. The prayer will be answered with Benjamin, at the cost of her life (35:16–18).

The son who will save. Joseph, born last of the eleven and loved most, will be hated and sold by his brothers and then raised up to save them (50:20). Genesis gives no clearer picture of the beloved Son, rejected by his own and exalted to save them (Acts 7:9–14).
verseByVerse.note: “Joseph” means “may he add” and sounds like “taken away” (ESV note).
