verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Laban cheats, Jacob schemes, and God keeps his word by making Jacob prosper. With Joseph born, Jacob asks to go home, but Laban, who knows the LORD has blessed him because of Jacob, keeps him by offering wages (vv. 25–30). Jacob asks only for the rare speckled and dark animals, a deal anyone can check (vv. 31–34). Laban removes every such animal that same day and sends them three days away (vv. 35–36). Jacob uses peeled sticks and careful breeding, and his flocks grow strong and many (vv. 37–43). Later he will say plainly that it was God who gave them to him (31:9).
verseByVerse.theology: Jacob asks to go home; Laban, who has learned by divination that the LORD blessed him through Jacob, asks him to name his wages. Jacob asks for the speckled and spotted animals; Laban removes them all that day. Jacob uses peeled rods and selective breeding, and grows exceedingly rich.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Laban cheated, and Jacob schemed, and God still kept his word. Now: God keeps faith with people still full of schemes, and settles accounts no human court would settle.

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as Rachel had borne Joseph, Jacob said to Laban, "Send me away, that I may go to my own home and country. Give me my wives and my children for whom I have served you, that I may go, for you know the service that I have given you." But Laban said to him, "If I have found favor in your sight, I have learned by divination that the LORD has blessed me because of you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Once Rachel has a son, Jacob asks to go home; Laban, who has learned that the LORD blessed him because of Jacob, wants him to stay.

As soon as Rachel had borne Joseph. With the beloved wife’s son born and fourteen years served, Jacob is ready to go home to Canaan, the land of promise.

Give me my wives and my children for whom I have served you. Jacob insists that he has paid for his family in full. He has to ask, because Laban would claim them as his (31:43).

I have learned by divination that the LORD has blessed me because of you. Divination, reading omens to learn the will of the gods, was common in Laban’s world and forbidden to Israel (Deuteronomy 18:10). Laban’s gods are not the LORD (31:30), but even he can see what God is doing. God had promised Abraham, “in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed” (12:3); here a pagan admits that the blessing has reached him through Abraham’s grandson. The same will happen in Potiphar’s house: “the LORD blessed the Egyptian’s house for Joseph’s sake” (39:5).

Uncertain wording. The verb translated “learned by divination” normally has that meaning, but some scholars connect it with a similar word for “growing rich” and read, “I have grown rich, and the LORD has blessed me because of you.” The usual translation is more likely, and either way Laban admits that his prosperity has come from Jacob’s God.

verseByVerse.quote: Name your wages, and I will give it." Jacob said to him, "You yourself know how I have served you, and how your livestock has fared with me. For you had little before I came, and it has increased abundantly, and the LORD has blessed you wherever I turned. But now when shall I provide for my own household also?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Laban offers Jacob any wages he names, and Jacob reminds him that his own work, blessed by God, has made Laban rich while Jacob still has nothing of his own.

Name your wages, and I will give it. It sounds generous, but Laban has already shown what his promises are worth (29:25), and he will change Jacob’s wages ten times (31:7).

You had little before I came, and it has increased abundantly. The word for “increased” means “burst out”. It is the word God used at Bethel when he promised that Jacob’s offspring would “spread abroad” in every direction (28:14), and it comes again at the end of the chapter (v. 43). The promise is already at work.

The LORD has blessed you wherever I turned. Literally “at my foot”: wherever Jacob went, blessing followed. He credits the LORD, not his own skill.

When shall I provide for my own household also? A fair question. A man must provide for his family (1 Timothy 5:8), and Jacob’s labour has gone into another man’s pocket for fourteen years.

In everyday life. Work faithfully, even for a difficult employer: you are serving the Lord Christ, who sees and repays (Colossians 3:23–24). And employers should remember that God hears when wages are withheld (James 5:4).

verseByVerse.quote: He said, "What shall I give you?" Jacob said, "You shall not give me anything. If you will do this for me, I will again pasture your flock and keep it: let me pass through all your flock today, removing from it every speckled and spotted sheep and every black lamb, and the spotted and speckled among the goats, and they shall be my wages. So my honesty will answer for me later, when you come to look into my wages with you. Every one that is not speckled and spotted among the goats and black among the lambs, if found with me, shall be counted stolen." Laban said, "Good! Let it be as you have said."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jacob asks for no wages except the rare speckled, spotted and dark animals, a modest deal that anyone can check.

You shall not give me anything. Jacob will not take a gift from Laban that Laban could later claim back. He wants only what God will give him through the flock.

Every speckled and spotted sheep and every black lamb, and the spotted and speckled among the goats. In that region sheep were usually white and goats dark brown or black. Animals with unusual markings were a small minority, so the request looks small, and Laban jumps at it (v. 34).

So my honesty will answer for me later. Literally “my righteousness”. Any plain-coloured animal found in Jacob’s flock can be counted stolen, so the arrangement is easy to inspect. There is irony in the word: Jacob has not always been a man of honest dealing. In this contract, at least, he is.

verseByVerse.quote: But that day Laban removed the male goats that were striped and spotted, and all the female goats that were speckled and spotted, every one that had white on it, and every lamb that was black, and put them in the charge of his sons. And he set a distance of three days' journey between himself and Jacob, and Jacob pastured the rest of Laban's flock.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Laban cheats at once, removing every marked animal that very day and sending them three days’ journey away, so that Jacob begins with nothing.

That day Laban removed the male goats that were striped and spotted. Before Jacob can even separate his wages, Laban takes them all, including any animal with a trace of white, and gives them to his sons. Jacob is left to tend a flock of plain-coloured animals that would rarely produce marked young.

He set a distance of three days’ journey between himself and Jacob. Laban makes sure no marked animal can wander back. Humanly speaking, Jacob’s wages are now in the hands of chance; in fact they are in the hands of God, who has seen all that Laban is doing (31:12).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jacob took fresh sticks of poplar and almond and plane trees, and peeled white streaks in them, exposing the white of the sticks. He set the sticks that he had peeled in front of the flocks in the troughs, that is, the watering places, where the flocks came to drink. And since they bred when they came to drink, the flocks bred in front of the sticks and so the flocks brought forth striped, speckled, and spotted. And Jacob separated the lambs and set the faces of the flocks toward the striped and all the black in the flock of Laban. He put his own droves apart and did not put them with Laban's flock.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jacob peels white streaks in fresh sticks and sets them where the flocks breed, and the flocks bear striped, speckled and spotted young.

Fresh sticks of poplar and almond and plane trees … exposing the white. A clever play on words runs through this. The Hebrew for “poplar” (livneh) and “white” (lavan) sound like Laban’s name, which means “white”: “Mr White” is outwitted with white sticks. And “almond” (luz) was the old name of Bethel (28:19), where God promised to be with Jacob.

The flocks bred in front of the sticks. Many in the ancient world believed that what a mother saw at conception could mark her offspring, and Jacob may have believed it too.

He set the faces of the flocks toward the striped and all the black in the flock of Laban. Jacob also turns the breeding animals towards the marked ones he now has, and keeps his own flocks apart, building up his herd with care.

Where Christians differ: how did it work? Some see in the sticks only a folk belief, some a primitive form of selective breeding, and some suggest the peeled wood had a physical effect on the animals. This commentary’s view: Jacob himself later says that God gave him the animals, and that God showed him in a dream that the males mating with the flock were striped, spotted and mottled (31:9–12). Whatever Jacob thought the sticks were doing, they did not cause the result; God’s blessing did.
verseByVerse.note: Peeled sticks placed before breeding animals reflect a folk belief of the time.

verseByVerse.quote: Whenever the stronger of the flock were breeding, Jacob would lay the sticks in the troughs before the eyes of the flock, that they might breed among the sticks, but for the feebler of the flock he would not lay them there. So the feebler would be Laban's, and the stronger Jacob's. Thus the man increased greatly and had large flocks, female servants and male servants, and camels and donkeys.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jacob breeds the strongest animals for himself and leaves the weaker to Laban, and grows very rich, as God promised.

Whenever the stronger of the flock were breeding. Jacob’s breeding is selective as well as colourful: the sturdy animals produce marked young that belong to him, the feeble produce plain young for Laban. It is shrewd, and within the letter of the agreement. After twenty years of being cheated, Jacob is a match for his uncle.

Thus the man increased greatly. The word again means “burst out”, the word of God’s promise at Bethel (28:14; see the note on vv. 28–30). Female and male servants, camels and donkeys: Jacob, who arrived with a staff, now has great wealth. God is keeping his promise to be with him (28:15).

God’s gifts, not ours. Jacob schemed, Laban cheated, and God still kept his word. Our cleverness is not the reason we prosper, and others’ dishonesty cannot finally rob those God means to bless. “Neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but only God who gives the growth” (1 Corinthians 3:7).

In everyday life. Look for God’s hand behind your own provision, and thank him, even when others cheat you. Wealth is not proof of God’s approval (Jacob’s methods were not spotless), but whatever we have, we have received.

30.theology:
Throughout Genesis God’s “remembering” marks the turn from waiting to acting (8:1; 19:29; 30:22). The time before it is not empty, even when those who wait cannot see what God is doing.

Rachel’s son Joseph becomes the great picture of Christ in Genesis 37–50: the beloved son, hated and sold by his brothers, raised to the ruler’s right hand, and made the saviour of the brothers who rejected him. God’s remembering Rachel is the beginning of the story that will end with all Jacob’s sons bowing before Joseph and being fed by his hand.
30.examples:
The mandrake bargain shows how little our own schemes can do. What is true of children is true of every blessing we try to engineer: spiritual life, godly character, peace of heart. We plant and water; God gives the growth (1 Cor 3:7). This is no rebuke to those who seek medical help in childlessness, only a reminder of who finally gives life, and that those who wait are not forgotten.

Even while naming Joseph, “May he add”, Rachel asks for another son. After years of pain her longing is understandable, but it reminds us all to give thanks for what God has given before reaching for the next thing.

keyVerse.quote: Then God remembered Rachel, and God listened to her and opened her womb.
keyVerse.note: In a chapter crowded with human schemes, servants, mandrakes and peeled sticks, this sentence shows who is really at work. God’s “remembering” is the moment he acts after long waiting, and the son born here is Joseph, through whom God will one day save the whole family. What we cannot win by bargaining, God gives by grace.

30.reflection:
Rachel envied her sister, and Leah measured her happiness by what other women said (vv. 1, 13). Where do envy and comparison show up in your life, and what do they do to relationships?

Jacob answered Rachel’s anguish with a true statement spoken in anger (v. 2). How can we respond better to people in deep distress, such as childlessness, grief or disappointment?

“Then God remembered Rachel” (v. 22). What does it mean that God’s silence is not his absence? How can we encourage someone who is still waiting?

Laban cheated and Jacob schemed, but God made Jacob prosper (vv. 35–43; 31:9). How should Christians work for an unfair employer, and where do you need to see God’s hand behind your own provision?

31.title: Return to the Land
31.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Jacob heard that the sons of Laban were saying, "Jacob has taken all that was our father's, and from what was our father's he has gained all this wealth."<sup>2</sup>And Jacob saw that Laban did not regard him with favor as before.<sup>3</sup>Then the LORD said to Jacob, "Return to the land of your fathers and to your kindred, and I will be with you."<sup>4</sup>So Jacob sent and called Rachel and Leah into the field where his flock was<sup>5</sup>and said to them, "I see that your father does not regard me with favor as he did before. But the God of my father has been with me.<sup>6</sup>You know that I have served your father with all my strength,<sup>7</sup>yet your father has cheated me and changed my wages ten times. But God did not permit him to harm me.<sup>8</sup>If he said, 'The spotted shall be your wages,' then all the flock bore spotted; and if he said, 'The striped shall be your wages,' then all the flock bore striped.<sup>9</sup>Thus God has taken away the livestock of your father and given them to me.<sup>10</sup>In the breeding season of the flock I lifted up my eyes and saw in a dream that the goats that mated with the flock were striped, spotted, and mottled.<sup>11</sup>Then the angel of God said to me in the dream, 'Jacob,' and I said, 'Here I am!'<sup>12</sup>And he said, 'Lift up your eyes and see, all the goats that mate with the flock are striped, spotted, and mottled, for I have seen all that Laban is doing to you.<sup>13</sup>I am the God of Bethel, where you anointed a pillar and made a vow to me. Now arise, go out from this land and return to the land of your kindred.'"<sup>14</sup>Then Rachel and Leah answered and said to him, "Is there any portion or inheritance left to us in our father's house?<sup>15</sup>Are we not regarded by him as foreigners? For he has sold us, and he has indeed devoured our money.<sup>16</sup>All the wealth that God has taken away from our father belongs to us and to our children. Now then, whatever God has said to you, do."<sup>17</sup>So Jacob arose and set his sons and his wives on camels.<sup>18</sup>He drove away all his livestock, all his property that he had gained, the livestock in his possession that he had acquired in Paddan-aram, to go to the land of Canaan to his father Isaac.<sup>19</sup>Laban had gone to shear his sheep, and Rachel stole her father's household gods.<sup>20</sup>And Jacob tricked Laban the Aramean, by not telling him that he intended to flee.<sup>21</sup>He fled with all that he had and arose and crossed the Euphrates, and set his face toward the hill country of Gilead.<sup>22</sup>When it was told Laban on the third day that Jacob had fled,<sup>23</sup>he took his kinsmen with him and pursued him for seven days and followed close after him into the hill country of Gilead.<sup>24</sup>But God came to Laban the Aramean in a dream by night and said to him, "Be careful not to say anything to Jacob, either good or bad."<sup>25</sup>And Laban overtook Jacob. Now Jacob had pitched his tent in the hill country, and Laban with his kinsmen pitched tents in the hill country of Gilead.<sup>26</sup>And Laban said to Jacob, "What have you done, that you have tricked me and driven away my daughters like captives of the sword?<sup>27</sup>Why did you flee secretly and trick me, and did not tell me, so that I might have sent you away with mirth and songs, with tambourine and lyre?<sup>28</sup>And why did you not permit me to kiss my sons and my daughters farewell? Now you have done foolishly.<sup>29</sup>It is in my power to do you harm. But the God of your father spoke to me last night, saying, 'Be careful not to say anything to Jacob, either good or bad.'<sup>30</sup>And now you have gone away because you longed greatly for your father's house, but why did you steal my gods?"<sup>31</sup>Jacob answered and said to Laban, "Because I was afraid, for I thought that you would take your daughters from me by force.<sup>32</sup>Anyone with whom you find your gods shall not live. In the presence of our kinsmen point out what I have that is yours, and take it." Now Jacob did not know that Rachel had stolen them.<sup>33</sup>So Laban went into Jacob's tent and into Leah's tent and into the tent of the two female servants, but he did not find them. And he went out of Leah's tent and entered Rachel's.<sup>34</sup>Now Rachel had taken the household gods and put them in the camel's saddle and sat on them. Laban felt all about the tent, but did not find them.<sup>35</sup>And she said to her father, "Let not my lord be angry that I cannot rise before you, for the way of women is upon me." So he searched but did not find the household gods.<sup>36</sup>Then Jacob became angry and berated Laban. Jacob said to Laban, "What is my offense? What is my sin, that you have hotly pursued me?<sup>37</sup>For you have felt through all my goods; what have you found of all your household goods? Set it here before my kinsmen and your kinsmen, that they may decide between us two.<sup>38</sup>These twenty years I have been with you. Your ewes and your female goats have not miscarried, and I have not eaten the rams of your flocks.<sup>39</sup>What was torn by wild beasts I did not bring to you. I bore the loss of it myself. From my hand you required it, whether stolen by day or stolen by night.<sup>40</sup>There I was: by day the heat consumed me, and the cold by night, and my sleep fled from my eyes.<sup>41</sup>These twenty years I have been in your house. I served you fourteen years for your two daughters, and six years for your flock, and you have changed my wages ten times.<sup>42</sup>If the God of my father, the God of Abraham and the Fear of Isaac, had not been on my side, surely now you would have sent me away empty-handed. God saw my affliction and the labor of my hands and rebuked you last night."<sup>43</sup>Then Laban answered and said to Jacob, "The daughters are my daughters, the children are my children, the flocks are my flocks, and all that you see is mine. But what can I do this day for these my daughters or for their children whom they have borne?<sup>44</sup>Come now, let us make a covenant, you and I. And let it be a witness between you and me."<sup>45</sup>So Jacob took a stone and set it up as a pillar.<sup>46</sup>And Jacob said to his kinsmen, "Gather stones." And they took stones and made a heap, and they ate there by the heap.<sup>47</sup>Laban called it Jegar-sahadutha, but Jacob called it Galeed.<sup>48</sup>Laban said, "This heap is a witness between you and me today." Therefore he named it Galeed,<sup>49</sup>and Mizpah, for he said, "The LORD watch between you and me, when we are out of one another's sight.<sup>50</sup>If you oppress my daughters, or if you take wives besides my daughters, although no one is with us, see, God is witness between you and me."<sup>51</sup>Then Laban said to Jacob, "See this heap and the pillar, which I have set between you and me.<sup>52</sup>This heap is a witness, and the pillar is a witness, that I will not pass over this heap to you, and you will not pass over this heap and this pillar to me, to do harm.<sup>53</sup>The God of Abraham and the God of Nahor, the God of their father, judge between us." So Jacob swore by the Fear of his father Isaac,<sup>54</sup>and Jacob offered a sacrifice in the hill country and called his kinsmen to eat bread. They ate bread and spent the night in the hill country.<sup>55</sup>Early in the morning Laban arose and kissed his grandchildren and his daughters and blessed them. Then Laban departed and returned home.
31.overview:
Where we are. Jacob has served Laban twenty years, and God has given him a large family and made him rich in spite of Laban’s cheating (chapter 30). Now Laban’s family turns against him, and the God who promised at Bethel to bring him home says it is time to go (28:15).

The message. The God who promised to be with Jacob has kept his word: he has seen how Jacob was treated, protected him from a stronger and dishonest master, and brings him out with all he gave him. Jacob’s wealth, his safety and his freedom come from God, not from Jacob’s cleverness or Laban’s goodwill. Laban can chase and complain, but he cannot harm the man God is keeping, and his gods cannot even protect themselves.

Why it was said. Israel heard its own story here in small (see the introduction). Jacob serves hard years in a foreign land under a master who exploits him, God sees his affliction, and he leaves with the master’s wealth and is pursued, as Israel would leave Egypt with its silver and gold and be chased by Pharaoh (Exodus 12:35–36; 14:5–9).

How the chapter makes its case. Laban’s sons grumble, his face turns cold, and the LORD says, “Return … and I will be with you” (vv. 1–3). Jacob tells his wives how God protected and enriched him, and they agree to go (vv. 4–16). The family slips away while Laban is shearing, and Rachel steals his household gods (vv. 17–21). Laban catches them in Gilead, but God has warned him in a dream not to touch Jacob (vv. 22–30). His search for his gods fails, because Rachel is sitting on them (vv. 31–35). Jacob pours out twenty years of grievance and credits God with his deliverance (vv. 36–42). The two men make a covenant of separation at a heap of stones and part in peace (vv. 43–55).

Where it leads. By pattern, and by God’s character revealed in Christ. Jacob’s escape is a small exodus, and every exodus points to the great one, when Christ brought his people out of a far worse bondage. Jacob the shepherd bore the loss of torn sheep himself; Christ, the good shepherd, bore the loss of his own life for the sheep (John 10:11). And the heap at Mizpah could only keep two hostile men apart, while Christ “is our peace” and breaks down the wall between enemies (Ephesians 2:14).

For us. God sees how we are treated, at work and at home, and no one can do us harm beyond what he allows. We can work faithfully for a hard master, leave when God opens the door, and give him the credit for what we carry away. And we should leave our old idols behind rather than pack them for the journey.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God keeps his promise to bring Jacob home, and Jacob at last sees that God, not his own cleverness, has carried him through. Laban’s family turns against him and the LORD tells him to return (vv. 1–3). Jacob explains to Rachel and Leah that God has protected him from Laban’s cheating, given him the flocks and called him back as the God of Bethel (vv. 4–13). The sisters, united for once, agree that their father has wronged them and urge obedience (vv. 14–16). So the family leaves, though Jacob slips away by stealth and Rachel carries her father’s household gods with her (vv. 17–21).
verseByVerse.theology: Laban's sons resent Jacob, Laban's face changes, and the LORD tells Jacob to return, promising, "I will be with you." Jacob tells his wives how God overruled ten changes of wages; they agree, and the household leaves while Laban is shearing. Rachel steals her father's household gods.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Rachel left Haran with her father's gods in her saddle. Now: a person can leave an old life behind and still carry its idols in the luggage (35:2–4).

verseByVerse.quote: Now Jacob heard that the sons of Laban were saying, "Jacob has taken all that was our father's, and from what was our father's he has gained all this wealth." And Jacob saw that Laban did not regard him with favor as before. Then the LORD said to Jacob, "Return to the land of your fathers and to your kindred, and I will be with you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
As resentment rises in Laban’s household, the LORD tells Jacob to go home and renews the promise he made at Bethel: “I will be with you.”

Jacob has taken all that was our father’s. Laban’s sons see only their inheritance shrinking. They do not mention the years their father cheated Jacob, or the blessing Jacob brought (30:27, 30). Envy is never short of reasons.

Laban did not regard him with favour as before. Literally, Laban’s face was not toward him as yesterday and the day before. The warmth of a useful relationship has cooled now that Jacob is the one growing rich.

Return to the land of your fathers … and I will be with you. The trouble at home is the push; God’s word is the call. Jacob does not leave because life became uncomfortable but because God told him to, and he goes with the very promise he was given when he fled (28:15). Twenty years on, God has not forgotten it.

In everyday life. Hostility and closing doors are not themselves a word from God, but God often uses them to move us. We weigh them with his word, with prayer and with wise counsel, and we go where we can take his promise with us.

verseByVerse.quote: So Jacob sent and called Rachel and Leah into the field where his flock was and said to them, "I see that your father does not regard me with favor as he did before. But the God of my father has been with me. You know that I have served your father with all my strength, yet your father has cheated me and changed my wages ten times. But God did not permit him to harm me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jacob gathers his wives in private and tells them that, though Laban has cheated him again and again, the God of his father has been with him and kept him from harm.

Into the field where his flock was. Jacob calls Rachel and Leah out to the open country, where no one in Laban’s household can overhear. Rachel is named first, as the beloved wife, but both are consulted: Jacob will not take them away without their consent.

But the God of my father has been with me. This is the heart of his speech, set against Laban’s cold face: Laban is no longer for me, but God is. Jacob now speaks of God far more than he did in chapter 30.

Changed my wages ten times. “Ten times” probably means “again and again” rather than an exact count (compare Numbers 14:22, “these ten times”). Each time Laban saw which animals were thriving, he changed the terms (v. 8).

But God did not permit him to harm me. Laban was free to scheme, but not free to ruin Jacob. God does not always stop wrongs being attempted; he sets limits on what they can do. Compare “you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good” (50:20).

verseByVerse.quote: If he said, 'The spotted shall be your wages,' then all the flock bore spotted; and if he said, 'The striped shall be your wages,' then all the flock bore striped. Thus God has taken away the livestock of your father and given them to me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whatever terms Laban set, God made the flocks breed in Jacob’s favour: the wealth came from God, not from Jacob’s tricks.

If he said, ‘The spotted shall be your wages’ … then all the flock bore spotted. Laban kept moving the goalposts, and the flocks kept following Jacob’s wages. Whatever Laban chose, the outcome went against him.

Thus God has taken away the livestock of your father and given them to me. In chapter 30 the narrator described Jacob’s peeled sticks and careful breeding (30:37–43). Here Jacob gives the true explanation. Peeled sticks cannot change the colour of lambs; whatever skill Jacob had as a breeder, it was God who gave the increase. Jacob has learned to see the hand behind his own hands.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God approved all Laban’s or Jacob’s methods, or that wealth proves God’s favour. It means God was just to a wronged worker and faithful to his promise, and that Jacob had to learn to credit God rather than his own cunning. Compare “The blessing of the LORD makes rich, and he adds no sorrow with it” (Proverbs 10:22).

verseByVerse.quote: In the breeding season of the flock I lifted up my eyes and saw in a dream that the goats that mated with the flock were striped, spotted, and mottled. Then the angel of God said to me in the dream, 'Jacob,' and I said, 'Here I am!' And he said, 'Lift up your eyes and see, all the goats that mate with the flock are striped, spotted, and mottled, for I have seen all that Laban is doing to you. I am the God of Bethel, where you anointed a pillar and made a vow to me. Now arise, go out from this land and return to the land of your kindred.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jacob tells his wives of a dream in which the angel of God showed him that God had seen Laban’s injustice, and called himself the God of Bethel, commanding him to go home.

In the breeding season of the flock … in a dream. We are not told when this dream came, perhaps early in the six years, explaining what God was doing with the flocks; the call to leave in v. 13 may belong to the same dream or to the word of v. 3. Jacob draws them together to show his wives that both the wealth and the departure come from God.

The angel of God said to me … ‘Jacob,’ and I said, ‘Here I am!’ The answer of a servant ready to listen, the same answer Abraham gave on Moriah (22:1, 11).

For I have seen all that Laban is doing to you. Nothing done to Jacob in twenty years was hidden from God. The same God would later say of Israel in Egypt, “I have surely seen the affliction of my people” (Exodus 3:7).

I am the God of Bethel, where you anointed a pillar and made a vow to me. The angel speaks as God himself, and takes Jacob back to the night he fled with nothing and God promised to keep him and bring him back (28:10–22). Jacob had vowed that if God did so, the LORD would be his God. Now God has kept his side, and calls Jacob home to keep his.

Christ in the passage. The messenger who speaks with God’s own voice and claims God’s own acts is one of the Old Testament’s quiet hints that God is more than one Person. Jesus said that the Son is sent by the Father, yet “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9).

In everyday life. God sees how you are treated at work, as he saw all that Laban did to Jacob. That is a comfort to the wronged and a warning to the one doing wrong.

Where Christians differ. Who is “the angel of God” who says “I am the God of Bethel”? Many Christian interpreters, from the early church on, have seen the Son of God appearing before his incarnation. Others see a created angel who speaks God’s words in God’s name, as an ambassador speaks for his king.

This commentary’s view. The angel who speaks and acts as God himself is best read as the Son appearing before his incarnation, the one who later wrestles with Jacob at the Jabbok (32:24–30; compare Hosea 12:3–4). But the passage does not depend on this: either way, it is God himself who sees, speaks and keeps his promise.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Rachel and Leah answered and said to him, "Is there any portion or inheritance left to us in our father's house? Are we not regarded by him as foreigners? For he has sold us, and he has indeed devoured our money. All the wealth that God has taken away from our father belongs to us and to our children. Now then, whatever God has said to you, do."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rachel and Leah, united for once, agree that their father has treated them as goods to be sold, and they tell Jacob to do whatever God has said.

Is there any portion or inheritance left to us in our father’s house? The sisters have nothing to stay for. By custom a daughter would expect a share of her family’s wealth, especially at marriage, but their father has kept it all.

Are we not regarded by him as foreigners? For he has sold us. Laban treated his daughters like foreign women bought and sold, not like his own flesh. Jacob’s fourteen years of labour were in effect the bride price (see wages and value), and a father was expected to hold at least part of such a gift for his daughter’s security.

He has indeed devoured our money. Laban spent what should have been theirs. So the sisters see the transfer of flocks as justice: what God took from their father he gave back to them and their children (v. 16).

Now then, whatever God has said to you, do. The rivals who fought over Jacob in chapter 30 stand together behind God’s word. It is the clearest expression of faith in this household so far, though Rachel’s next act shows how mixed it still is (v. 19).

In everyday life. Parents can treat children as assets, valued for what they bring. God’s word measures fathers by how they give, not by what they get (2 Corinthians 12:14).

verseByVerse.quote: So Jacob arose and set his sons and his wives on camels. He drove away all his livestock, all his property that he had gained, the livestock in his possession that he had acquired in Paddan-aram, to go to the land of Canaan to his father Isaac.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jacob sets out for Canaan with his family and all the wealth God has given him, going home to his father Isaac.

So Jacob arose. He obeys at once, resting on the promise “I will be with you” (v. 3). This is the first time Jacob moves simply because God told him to.

He drove away all his livestock, all his property that he had gained. The narrator piles up the words for possessions. The man who arrived with only a staff (32:10) leaves with a great household and flocks. As God would later bring Israel out of Egypt with great possessions, he brings Jacob out of Paddan-aram rich (15:14).

To the land of Canaan to his father Isaac. Isaac is still alive, though old and blind; Jacob will see him again before he dies (35:27–29). Rebekah is not mentioned, and the reader may sense that the mother who sent him away for “a while” (27:44) has not lived to see him return.

verseByVerse.quote: Laban had gone to shear his sheep, and Rachel stole her father's household gods. And Jacob tricked Laban the Aramean, by not telling him that he intended to flee. He fled with all that he had and arose and crossed the Euphrates, and set his face toward the hill country of Gilead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
While Laban is away shearing, Rachel steals his household gods, Jacob slips away without telling him, and the family crosses the Euphrates and heads for the hill country of Gilead.

Laban had gone to shear his sheep. Shearing was a busy, festive time that took the owner away from home for days (compare 1 Samuel 25:2–8; 2 Samuel 13:23). Laban’s flocks were kept three days’ journey from Jacob’s (30:36), giving Jacob his head start (v. 22).

Rachel stole her father’s household gods. These were teraphim, small figures of family gods, kept in the home (see the note on the verse). We are not told why she took them. Perhaps she wanted their protection on the journey, or wanted to spite her father, or still half believed in them. Some scholars once argued from ancient tablets that holding the household gods gave a claim to the family inheritance; that reading is now widely doubted, though Rachel may still have thought of them as a token of her rights. Whatever her motive, she has left her father’s house without fully leaving her father’s religion. Joshua would later remind Israel that their fathers “lived beyond the Euphrates … and they served other gods” (Joshua 24:2).

And Jacob tricked Laban the Aramean. The Hebrew says he “stole Laban’s heart”, that is, he deceived him. So Rachel steals the gods and Jacob steals the heart: it is still a family of thieves and deceivers, even as it obeys God. Jacob had God’s command to leave; he did not need to leave by stealth, but fear (v. 31) made him do it the old way.

Laban the Aramean. The label stresses that Laban belongs to another people. Yet Israel later confessed of Jacob himself, “A wandering Aramean was my father” (Deuteronomy 26:5).

Crossed the Euphrates, and set his face toward the hill country of Gilead. Gilead is the high, wooded country east of the Jordan, on the edge of the promised land. Jacob has set his face toward home.

In everyday life. What old idols are you carrying with you? People can leave a former life and still pack its gods: the security of money, the approval of others, old superstitions. God will in time bring Jacob’s household to bury theirs (35:2–4), and he calls us to do the same (1 John 5:21).
verseByVerse.note: The household gods are teraphim in Hebrew. “The Euphrates” is “the River” in Hebrew (ESV note).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–55 — Laban's Pursuit and the Covenant at Mizpah
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God controls the confrontation with Laban: the stronger man can chase, complain and search, but he cannot harm the man God protects. Warned in a dream, Laban plays the injured father and accuses Jacob of stealing his gods (vv. 22–30). His search fails because Rachel hides the gods under herself, a scene that mocks idols that cannot even save themselves (vv. 31–35). Jacob answers with twenty years of faithful, ill-rewarded work and confesses that God alone was on his side (vv. 36–42). The two make a covenant at a heap of stones, each calling God to watch the other, and Laban goes home and leaves the story (vv. 43–55).
verseByVerse.theology: Laban pursues for seven days, but God warns him in a dream not to harm Jacob. He searches for his gods; Rachel sits on them. Jacob recounts twenty years of faithful service and says God rebuked Laban. They make a covenant at a heap of witness called Galeed and Mizpah, and Laban goes home.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: God warned Laban in a dream before he could lay a hand on Jacob. Now: much of what never happens to God's people never happens because he stopped it.

verseByVerse.quote: When it was told Laban on the third day that Jacob had fled, he took his kinsmen with him and pursued him for seven days and followed close after him into the hill country of Gilead. But God came to Laban the Aramean in a dream by night and said to him, "Be careful not to say anything to Jacob, either good or bad." And Laban overtook Jacob. Now Jacob had pitched his tent in the hill country, and Laban with his kinsmen pitched tents in the hill country of Gilead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Laban pursues Jacob for a week and catches him in Gilead, but God appears to Laban in a dream and forbids him to do anything to Jacob.

On the third day … pursued him for seven days. Laban hears the news late, because he was three days away (30:36). He gathers his kinsmen, a small private army, and gives chase. Jacob’s flocks and young children slowed him down, and Laban catches up in the hill country of Gilead.

God came to Laban the Aramean in a dream by night. As he came to Abimelech to protect Sarah (20:3), God speaks to an outsider to protect his chosen. Jacob did not know this was happening; God was guarding him before the danger arrived.

Be careful not to say anything to Jacob, either good or bad. An idiom meaning “do not interfere with him at all”: neither threats nor smooth persuasion to bring him back. Laban had used the same phrase himself when Rebekah left: “we cannot speak to you bad or good” (24:50). He does still speak, and at length, but he dare not act.

verseByVerse.quote: And Laban said to Jacob, "What have you done, that you have tricked me and driven away my daughters like captives of the sword? Why did you flee secretly and trick me, and did not tell me, so that I might have sent you away with mirth and songs, with tambourine and lyre? And why did you not permit me to kiss my sons and my daughters farewell? Now you have done foolishly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Laban plays the injured father, complaining that Jacob has carried off his daughters like captives and robbed him of a proper farewell.

Driven away my daughters like captives of the sword. In fact the daughters chose to go, and complained that their father had sold them (vv. 14–15). Laban recasts himself as the victim.

So that I might have sent you away with mirth and songs, with tambourine and lyre. A lavish farewell feast, and the reader smiles: this is the man who changed Jacob’s wages ten times and would not let him go (30:25–28). The feast he describes would never have happened.

Why did you not permit me to kiss my sons and my daughters farewell? There is perhaps real feeling here, for Laban does kiss them in the end (v. 55). But it sits alongside a lifetime of treating them as property. People who wrong their families often speak most of their family feelings.

Now you have done foolishly. Laban has a point: Jacob’s secret flight was fearful and unnecessary when God had told him to go. But the man scolding him is no judge of honest dealing.

verseByVerse.quote: It is in my power to do you harm. But the God of your father spoke to me last night, saying, 'Be careful not to say anything to Jacob, either good or bad.' And now you have gone away because you longed greatly for your father's house, but why did you steal my gods?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Laban admits he could harm Jacob but dare not, because Jacob’s God has warned him, yet he still demands to know why Jacob stole his gods.

It is in my power to do you harm. He has the men and the strength. What he lacks is permission: “But the God of your father spoke to me last night.” The stronger man is restrained by the God of the weaker one.

The God of your father. Laban speaks of him as Jacob’s family God, not his own. He has heard from the true God and obeyed him out of fear, yet still clings to the gods in his house.

Why did you steal my gods? There is something absurd in the question. Gods that can be stolen, carried off and must be searched for are not gods worth having. Isaiah would later mock idols that must be carried: “it cannot move from its place. If one cries to it, it does not answer or save him from his trouble” (Isaiah 46:7). By contrast the true God says, “I have made, and I will bear; I will carry and will save” (Isaiah 46:4).

In everyday life. The test of any god, whether money, a career, a relationship or a reputation, is whether it can carry you, or whether you must carry it. Only the living God carries his people.

verseByVerse.quote: Jacob answered and said to Laban, "Because I was afraid, for I thought that you would take your daughters from me by force. Anyone with whom you find your gods shall not live. In the presence of our kinsmen point out what I have that is yours, and take it." Now Jacob did not know that Rachel had stolen them. So Laban went into Jacob's tent and into Leah's tent and into the tent of the two female servants, but he did not find them. And he went out of Leah's tent and entered Rachel's. Now Rachel had taken the household gods and put them in the camel's saddle and sat on them. Laban felt all about the tent, but did not find them. And she said to her father, "Let not my lord be angry that I cannot rise before you, for the way of women is upon me." So he searched but did not find the household gods.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jacob, not knowing Rachel took the gods, rashly swears that the thief shall die, and Laban searches every tent in vain, because Rachel sits on them and pleads her period.

Because I was afraid. Jacob admits it honestly: he fled in secret because he feared Laban would take his wives by force. Fear, not faith, set the manner of his leaving, though God had set its time.

Anyone with whom you find your gods shall not live. A rash oath. Jacob does not know he is pronouncing sentence on the wife he loves best. Some readers see a shadow of it in Rachel’s death on the road a few years later (35:16–19), though Genesis does not draw the link. Rash words spoken in anger can put those we love in danger (compare Jephthah, Judges 11:30–35).

Laban went into Jacob’s tent and into Leah’s tent and into the tent of the two female servants. The search is told slowly, tent by tent, building the suspense until he reaches Rachel’s.

Put them in the camel’s saddle and sat on them. The saddle was probably a cushioned seat with a basket frame, used by women riding camels, which could hide small objects. “Laban felt all about the tent”: the word is the one used when blind Isaac felt Jacob to find out who he was (27:12, 21–22). Jacob deceived a father who felt for the truth; now Jacob’s wife deceives her father the same way.

The way of women is upon me. Rachel says she is having her period and cannot get up. Whether or not it was true, the scene is a deliberate mockery of idols. Laban’s gods lie hidden under a woman who says she is ceremonially unclean; later law would say, “Everything also on which she sits shall be unclean” (Leviticus 15:20). The gods of Laban’s house cannot save themselves, cannot speak to reveal where they are, and end up as a seat cushion.

What it does not mean. The story does not commend Rachel’s theft or her lie. It shows God protecting his chosen family through, and in spite of, their sins, while it laughs at the idols. Nor does it treat a woman’s monthly cycle as shameful: the later laws on uncleanness concerned approaching the holy tabernacle, not a woman’s worth.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jacob became angry and berated Laban. Jacob said to Laban, "What is my offense? What is my sin, that you have hotly pursued me? For you have felt through all my goods; what have you found of all your household goods? Set it here before my kinsmen and your kinsmen, that they may decide between us two. These twenty years I have been with you. Your ewes and your female goats have not miscarried, and I have not eaten the rams of your flocks. What was torn by wild beasts I did not bring to you. I bore the loss of it myself. From my hand you required it, whether stolen by day or stolen by night. There I was: by day the heat consumed me, and the cold by night, and my sleep fled from my eyes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the search finds nothing, twenty years of grievance pour out of Jacob: he has been an honest and long-suffering shepherd, bearing losses that were not his to bear.

What is my offense? What is my sin? Jacob, who for once is innocent of what he is accused, turns the tables. He invites both families to judge between them, as in a court.

Your ewes and your female goats have not miscarried. Under Jacob’s care the flocks flourished (see sheep and goats), and he never helped himself to a ram from Laban’s flock for his own table.

What was torn by wild beasts I did not bring to you. I bore the loss of it myself. By the custom of the time, a shepherd could bring the remains of an animal killed by a beast as proof, and the owner bore the loss; ancient law codes such as Hammurabi’s say so, and so would Israel’s law: “If it is torn by beasts, let him bring it as evidence. He shall not make restitution” (Exodus 22:13). Laban made Jacob pay even for animals stolen by day or by night, beyond what was fair (see shepherds).

By day the heat consumed me, and the cold by night. The life of a shepherd in the open country, scorching days and freezing nights, often without sleep, guarding the flock from predators and thieves.

Christ in the passage. Jacob’s complaint describes a faithful shepherd who bore the loss himself. It finds its fullness in the good shepherd who bore not the loss of a few animals but the cost of his own life: “The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10:11). Jacob paid for what wild beasts tore; Christ was torn for his flock.

In everyday life. Jacob is a model of faithful work under an unjust employer: diligent, honest with what was not his, enduring hardship. “Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men” (Colossians 3:23).

verseByVerse.quote: These twenty years I have been in your house. I served you fourteen years for your two daughters, and six years for your flock, and you have changed my wages ten times. If the God of my father, the God of Abraham and the Fear of Isaac, had not been on my side, surely now you would have sent me away empty-handed. God saw my affliction and the labor of my hands and rebuked you last night."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jacob sums up twenty years of exploitation and confesses that only God’s being on his side kept him from being sent away with nothing.

Fourteen years for your two daughters, and six years for your flock. Twenty years in all, as the note on the verse explains. The man who once took his brother’s blessing by a trick has paid in long years of labour under a trickster.

If the God of my father … had not been on my side. Compare Psalm 124:1, “If it had not been the LORD who was on our side”. Jacob does not claim his own cleverness saved him. He began in Haran bargaining and scheming; he ends confessing that God alone made the difference. That is real growth.

Surely now you would have sent me away empty-handed. Israel’s law would later forbid sending a freed servant away empty-handed (Deuteronomy 15:13); God enforced that justice for Jacob before it was written.

God saw my affliction and the labor of my hands. The same God who “saw” Hagar (16:13) and would see Israel’s affliction in Egypt (Exodus 3:7) saw Jacob’s. And he “rebuked you last night”: the dream was God judging between them.

In everyday life. God sees your toil and the wrongs done to you, even when no one else does. You may not see justice as quickly as Jacob did, but it is certain, and “If God is for us, who can be against us?” (Romans 8:31).

Uncertain wording. “The Fear of Isaac” (also v. 53) is a rare title for God, found only in this chapter. Most take it to mean the God whom Isaac feared and worshipped, perhaps recalling Isaac’s trembling when he learned that God’s blessing had overruled his own plans (27:33), or the God who strikes fear into Isaac’s enemies. A few scholars have suggested “the Kinsman of Isaac” from a similar word in related languages, but that is less likely. The basic sense, the God of Isaac who is to be feared, is clear.
verseByVerse.note: Twenty years: fourteen for his wives and six for flocks.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Laban answered and said to Jacob, "The daughters are my daughters, the children are my children, the flocks are my flocks, and all that you see is mine. But what can I do this day for these my daughters or for their children whom they have borne? Come now, let us make a covenant, you and I. And let it be a witness between you and me." So Jacob took a stone and set it up as a pillar. And Jacob said to his kinsmen, "Gather stones." And they took stones and made a heap, and they ate there by the heap. Laban called it Jegar-sahadutha, but Jacob called it Galeed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Laban still claims everything as his, but he cannot keep it, so he proposes a covenant, and the two men mark it with a pillar and a heap of stones and a shared meal.

The daughters are my daughters … and all that you see is mine. Laban’s greed shows to the end, and his claim is hollow: everything he calls his is about to leave with Jacob. He cannot say what God has said, so he says what he wishes.

But what can I do this day for these my daughters? A grudging admission that he is beaten. He turns to the only course left: a treaty.

Jacob took a stone and set it up as a pillar. As he did at Bethel (28:18). Standing stones marked holy places and agreements; this one will witness the covenant.

They ate there by the heap. A shared meal sealed agreements in the ancient world: those who ate together were bound to keep faith.

Laban called it Jegar-sahadutha, but Jacob called it Galeed. Both names mean “heap of witness”, one in Aramaic and one in Hebrew (see the note on the verse). These are the only words of Aramaic in Genesis. One heap, two languages: the families of Abraham and Nahor are becoming two peoples.
verseByVerse.note: Laban names the heap in Aramaic, Jacob in Hebrew; both mean “heap of witness” (ESV notes).

verseByVerse.quote: Laban said, "This heap is a witness between you and me today." Therefore he named it Galeed, and Mizpah, for he said, "The LORD watch between you and me, when we are out of one another's sight. If you oppress my daughters, or if you take wives besides my daughters, although no one is with us, see, God is witness between you and me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Laban names the place Mizpah, “watchpost”, calling on the LORD to watch Jacob when they are apart and to judge him if he mistreats Laban’s daughters.

The LORD watch between you and me, when we are out of one another’s sight. In context these words are not a tender blessing but a wary threat: since I cannot keep an eye on you, may God do it for me. Two men who do not trust each other call on God to police the border.

If you oppress my daughters, or if you take wives besides my daughters. There is irony in this. The man who tricked Jacob into marrying two sisters now protests at the thought of more wives. Yet the concern is real, and God does care how husbands treat their wives.

Although no one is with us, see, God is witness. What Laban meant as a threat is still true. “The eyes of the LORD are in every place, keeping watch on the evil and the good” (Proverbs 15:3). That is a warning to anyone who mistreats a spouse in private, and a comfort to anyone mistreated where no one else sees.

What it does not mean. The “Mizpah benediction” is often engraved on jewellery or spoken at partings as a sweet farewell. Christians can rightly pray for God to keep those they love when apart, but that is not what these words meant on Laban’s lips.
verseByVerse.note: “Mizpah” means “watchpost” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Laban said to Jacob, "See this heap and the pillar, which I have set between you and me. This heap is a witness, and the pillar is a witness, that I will not pass over this heap to you, and you will not pass over this heap and this pillar to me, to do harm. The God of Abraham and the God of Nahor, the God of their father, judge between us." So Jacob swore by the Fear of his father Isaac, and Jacob offered a sacrifice in the hill country and called his kinsmen to eat bread. They ate bread and spent the night in the hill country. Early in the morning Laban arose and kissed his grandchildren and his daughters and blessed them. Then Laban departed and returned home.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The heap becomes a boundary neither man will cross to harm the other; Laban swears by his gods and Jacob by the Fear of Isaac, and after a sacrifice and a meal they part in peace.

I will not pass over this heap to you, and you will not pass over this heap … to do harm. This is peace by separation, a non-aggression treaty. The heap stood in Gilead, east of the Jordan, the borderland where Israel and the Arameans of Damascus would later face each other (compare 1 Kings 22:3), so Israel probably heard in it the beginning of an old frontier.

The God of Abraham and the God of Nahor, the God of their father, judge between us. Laban puts Abraham’s God alongside the gods of Nahor and Terah, who “served other gods” (Joshua 24:2). The verb “judge” is plural in Hebrew, which suggests Laban is thinking of more than one god.

So Jacob swore by the Fear of his father Isaac. Jacob will not blend his God with Laban’s. He swears by the one God of his father alone.

Jacob offered a sacrifice in the hill country and called his kinsmen to eat bread. A sacrifice to the LORD and a covenant meal. Jacob, the man who once fled with nothing, now acts as the head of a household hosting the meal.

Laban arose and kissed his grandchildren and his daughters and blessed them. The last we see of Laban is a kiss and a blessing, and then he goes home and leaves the story. The God who met Jacob as a fugitive at Bethel has brought him safely out of a hard place, as he promised (28:15).

Christ in the passage. The best this covenant could do was keep two suspicious men apart. The gospel does far more: Christ “himself is our peace, who has made us both one and has broken down in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility” (Ephesians 2:14). He does not merely separate enemies; he reconciles them to God and to one another.

In everyday life. Sometimes, with people who will not deal honestly, the most peaceable course is a clear boundary kept in good faith (Romans 12:18). But the Christian always hopes and prays for more than a truce.

31.theology:
Jacob’s years in Haran (chapters 29–31) foreshadow the exodus, and God’s protection of Jacob on the road is a pledge of his care for the nation that will bear Jacob’s name.

The stolen household gods remind us that leaving the world behind is rarely complete in one move; the journey out of idolatry takes a lifetime. Jacob, who met God at Bethel and returns at his command, still has a household whose worship is impure. God does not wait for perfect pilgrims; he leads his imperfect people and purifies them along the way.
31.examples:
Rightly used, the Mizpah words still call on the LORD who sees all things to hold people to the promises they make when no one else is watching. In the end everyone answers to him.

When Jacob tells Leah and Rachel his story (vv. 5–13), he tells it in terms of what God has done. He does not say, “I worked hard and prospered despite Laban.” He says that God was with him, God did not permit Laban to harm him, and God took away their father’s livestock and gave them to him. When we tell our own story as the story of what God has done, our faith grows.

keyVerse.quote: If the God of my father, the God of Abraham and the Fear of Isaac, had not been on my side, surely now you would have sent me away empty-handed. God saw my affliction and the labor of my hands and rebuked you last night.
keyVerse.note: Jacob, who began in Haran bargaining and scheming, ends by confessing that God alone made the difference. The verse gathers up the whole chapter: God saw what was done to Jacob, protected him from a stronger man, and brought him out with all he had given him, as he would later bring Israel out of Egypt.

31.reflection:
Laban’s sons resented Jacob’s success, and Laban’s face turned cold (vv. 1–2). How do we tell the difference between a closing door and a word from God, and how did Jacob know it was time to go?

Jacob said, “God did not permit him to harm me” (v. 7) and “If the God of my father … had not been on my side” (v. 42). Where can you look back and see God limiting harm or providing for you when others treated you unfairly?

Rachel stole her father’s gods, and Laban could not find them because she sat on them (vv. 19, 34–35). What “household gods” do people carry with them into the Christian life, and what does this story suggest about them?

Jacob worked faithfully under a dishonest employer and bore losses himself (vv. 38–40). What would faithful work look like in your situation, and how does Christ the good shepherd shape the way you serve others?

32.title: I Have Seen God Face to Face
32.text: <sup>1</sup>Jacob went on his way, and the angels of God met him.<sup>2</sup>And when Jacob saw them he said, "This is God's camp!" So he called the name of that place Mahanaim.<sup>3</sup>And Jacob sent messengers before him to Esau his brother in the land of Seir, the country of Edom,<sup>4</sup>instructing them, "Thus you shall say to my lord Esau: Thus says your servant Jacob, 'I have sojourned with Laban and stayed until now.<sup>5</sup>I have oxen, donkeys, flocks, male servants, and female servants. I have sent to tell my lord, in order that I may find favor in your sight.'"<sup>6</sup>And the messengers returned to Jacob, saying, "We came to your brother Esau, and he is coming to meet you, and there are four hundred men with him."<sup>7</sup>Then Jacob was greatly afraid and distressed. He divided the people who were with him, and the flocks and herds and camels, into two camps,<sup>8</sup>thinking, "If Esau comes to the one camp and attacks it, then the camp that is left will escape."<sup>9</sup>And Jacob said, "O God of my father Abraham and God of my father Isaac, O LORD who said to me, 'Return to your country and to your kindred, that I may do you good,'<sup>10</sup>I am not worthy of the least of all the deeds of steadfast love and all the faithfulness that you have shown to your servant, for with only my staff I crossed this Jordan, and now I have become two camps.<sup>11</sup>Please deliver me from the hand of my brother, from the hand of Esau, for I fear him, that he may come and attack me, the mothers with the children.<sup>12</sup>But you said, 'I will surely do you good, and make your offspring as the sand of the sea, which cannot be numbered for multitude.'"<sup>13</sup>So he stayed there that night, and from what he had with him he took a present for his brother Esau,<sup>14</sup>two hundred female goats and twenty male goats, two hundred ewes and twenty rams,<sup>15</sup>thirty milking camels and their calves, forty cows and ten bulls, twenty female donkeys and ten male donkeys.<sup>16</sup>These he handed over to his servants, every drove by itself, and said to his servants, "Pass on ahead of me and put a space between drove and drove."<sup>17</sup>He instructed the first, "When Esau my brother meets you and asks you, 'To whom do you belong? Where are you going? And whose are these ahead of you?'<sup>18</sup>then you shall say, 'They belong to your servant Jacob. They are a present sent to my lord Esau. And moreover, he is behind us.'"<sup>19</sup>He likewise instructed the second and the third and all who followed the droves, "You shall say the same thing to Esau when you find him,<sup>20</sup>and you shall say, 'Moreover, your servant Jacob is behind us.'" For he thought, "I may appease him with the present that goes ahead of me, and afterward I shall see his face. Perhaps he will accept me."<sup>21</sup>So the present passed on ahead of him, and he himself stayed that night in the camp.<sup>22</sup>The same night he arose and took his two wives, his two female servants, and his eleven children, and crossed the ford of the Jabbok.<sup>23</sup>He took them and sent them across the stream, and everything else that he had.<sup>24</sup>And Jacob was left alone. And a man wrestled with him until the breaking of the day.<sup>25</sup>When the man saw that he did not prevail against Jacob, he touched his hip socket, and Jacob's hip was put out of joint as he wrestled with him.<sup>26</sup>Then he said, "Let me go, for the day has broken." But Jacob said, "I will not let you go unless you bless me."<sup>27</sup>And he said to him, "What is your name?" And he said, "Jacob."<sup>28</sup>Then he said, "Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel, for you have striven with God and with men, and have prevailed."<sup>29</sup>Then Jacob asked him, "Please tell me your name." But he said, "Why is it that you ask my name?" And there he blessed him.<sup>30</sup>So Jacob called the name of the place Peniel, saying, "For I have seen God face to face, and yet my life has been delivered."<sup>31</sup>The sun rose upon him as he passed Penuel, limping because of his hip.<sup>32</sup>Therefore to this day the people of Israel do not eat the sinew of the thigh that is on the hip socket, because he touched the socket of Jacob's hip on the sinew of the thigh.
32.overview:
Where we are. Jacob has escaped Laban and made peace with him in Gilead (chapter 31). Ahead lies the promised land, and between him and it stands Esau, the brother he cheated twenty years ago and who swore to kill him (27:41). This is the night before they meet.

The message. Before Jacob can face his brother, he must face God. The man who has spent his life grasping, scheming and running is brought to a place where he can neither scheme nor run, and God himself wrestles him to the end of his own strength. Crippled, Jacob clings to God and begs for his blessing, and receives it, with a new name and a lifelong limp. God’s blessing is received not by those who are strong, but by those who have been broken and hold on.

Why it was said. Israel bore this name, and every Israelite who heard the story learned what it meant to be “Israel”: a people named after a cheat whom God had wrestled into dependence and blessed (see the introduction). Their own history would repeat the pattern of fear, scheming, crisis and grace, and the meal custom at the end kept the night at the Jabbok in their memory (v. 32).

How the chapter makes its case. Angels meet Jacob as he returns, a sign that God’s camp surrounds his (vv. 1–2). Hearing that Esau is coming with four hundred men, he divides his camp in terror (vv. 3–8), then prays, confessing his unworthiness and pleading God’s promise (vv. 9–12). He sends wave after wave of gifts ahead to soften his brother (vv. 13–21). Then, alone at the Jabbok, a man wrestles him until dawn, puts his hip out of joint, and, at Jacob’s plea, blesses him and renames him (vv. 22–30). The sun rises on Jacob limping across the stream (vv. 31–32).

Where it leads. By promise, pattern, and God revealed in Christ. The one who wrestled Jacob is God himself, and this commentary reads him as the Son appearing before his incarnation. Jacob saw “God face to face” and lived; in Christ, God has made himself fully known (John 1:18), and we see “the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6). The God who wounded Jacob in order to bless him would one day be wounded himself, and by his wounds we are healed. And the name Israel finds its meaning in Christ, the true Israel.

For us. God often brings us to the end of our own resources before he blesses us, and the limp is part of the gift. Pray as Jacob prayed, unworthy yet holding God to his promises. Face the people you have wronged, but first face God, who alone can change the heart of the one you fear and your own.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–21 — Jacob's Fear and His Prayer
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jacob comes home afraid, and learns to pray before he meets the brother he wronged. Angels meet him at Mahanaim, a reminder that God’s camp surrounds his own (vv. 1–2). He sends Esau a humble message, and the news that Esau is coming with four hundred men throws him into terror and frantic planning (vv. 3–8). Then he prays: he confesses he is unworthy of God’s steadfast love and pleads God’s own promises (vv. 9–12). Still afraid, he sends a huge present ahead in separate droves, hoping to cover his brother’s face and be accepted (vv. 13–21). Prayer and planning stand side by side, but the plans are not yet free of fear.
verseByVerse.theology: The angels of God meet Jacob at Mahanaim. His messengers return with news that Esau is coming with four hundred men; Jacob, greatly afraid, divides his camp and prays: "I am not worthy of the least of all the deeds of steadfast love." Then he sends ahead droves of animals as a present.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the prayer stands on God's own command and promise: "But you said." Now: seeing God's army on Monday does not stop fear on Tuesday; what we do next shows whether faith or fear is in charge.

verseByVerse.quote: Jacob went on his way, and the angels of God met him. And when Jacob saw them he said, "This is God's camp!" So he called the name of that place Mahanaim.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As Jacob nears the land, God’s angels meet him, a sign that God’s own camp surrounds his, and Jacob names the place Mahanaim, “two camps”.

The angels of God met him. Angels met Jacob at Bethel as he left the land (28:12); now, twenty years later, angels meet him as he returns. The journey is framed by God’s care at both ends.

This is God’s camp! Jacob sees an army of heaven encamped beside his own. He calls the place Mahanaim, “two camps”: God’s and his. Sadly, by v. 7 he has divided his own people into “two camps” out of fear, as if the protection he had just seen were not enough. Fear makes us forget what God has just shown us.

In everyday life. God’s people are surrounded by more than they can see. When Elisha’s servant panicked at the enemy army, Elisha prayed, “O LORD, please open his eyes that he may see”, and the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire (2 Kings 6:17). That is no promise that nothing hard will happen, but it is a reason not to be ruled by fear.
verseByVerse.note: Mahanaim lay east of the Jordan, near the Jabbok.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jacob sent messengers before him to Esau his brother in the land of Seir, the country of Edom, instructing them, "Thus you shall say to my lord Esau: Thus says your servant Jacob, 'I have sojourned with Laban and stayed until now. I have oxen, donkeys, flocks, male servants, and female servants. I have sent to tell my lord, in order that I may find favor in your sight.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jacob sends messengers ahead to Esau, calling him “my lord” and himself “your servant”, the very reverse of the blessing he once stole.

To Esau his brother in the land of Seir, the country of Edom. Esau has settled in the rugged country south-east of the Dead Sea (see the note on the verse). Jacob must pass near his territory to reach Canaan, and he cannot go home without facing the past.

My lord Esau … your servant Jacob. The stolen blessing had said, “Be lord over your brothers” (27:29). Now Jacob calls Esau “lord” and himself “servant”. Whether this is real humility, careful diplomacy, or both, it shows Jacob is no longer trying to hold on to what he took.

I have oxen, donkeys, flocks. Jacob tells Esau he is wealthy. He may mean, “I have not come to claim our father’s property”, or he may be hinting that he can pay for peace (vv. 13–15).

In order that I may find favor in your sight. The word for “favour” (chen) is the word for grace. Jacob is asking for what he cannot earn, though he does not yet quite believe he can receive it freely.
verseByVerse.note: Seir is the hill country of Edom, south-east of the Dead Sea.

verseByVerse.quote: And the messengers returned to Jacob, saying, "We came to your brother Esau, and he is coming to meet you, and there are four hundred men with him." Then Jacob was greatly afraid and distressed. He divided the people who were with him, and the flocks and herds and camels, into two camps, thinking, "If Esau comes to the one camp and attacks it, then the camp that is left will escape."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The messengers report that Esau is coming with four hundred men, and Jacob, terrified, divides his people and flocks into two camps so that one might escape.

He is coming to meet you, and there are four hundred men with him. Four hundred men is a war band; Abraham rescued Lot with 318 (14:14). The messengers bring no word from Esau, only the news of his coming, and silence leaves room for fear. A guilty conscience expects the worst.

Then Jacob was greatly afraid and distressed. Both words are strong. The man who outwitted everyone has met a problem he cannot outwit.

He divided the people … into two camps. A sensible plan, and sensible plans are not wrong. But note the order: Jacob divides his camp first and prays second. The “two camps” of fear echo the “two camps” of God he named at Mahanaim (v. 2).

verseByVerse.quote: And Jacob said, "O God of my father Abraham and God of my father Isaac, O LORD who said to me, 'Return to your country and to your kindred, that I may do you good,' I am not worthy of the least of all the deeds of steadfast love and all the faithfulness that you have shown to your servant, for with only my staff I crossed this Jordan, and now I have become two camps. Please deliver me from the hand of my brother, from the hand of Esau, for I fear him, that he may come and attack me, the mothers with the children. But you said, 'I will surely do you good, and make your offspring as the sand of the sea, which cannot be numbered for multitude.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jacob prays, calling on the God of his fathers, confessing that he is unworthy of all God’s steadfast love, and pleading God’s own promises for rescue from Esau.

O God of my father Abraham and God of my father Isaac, O LORD. This is Jacob’s first recorded prayer, and it begins with who God is: the covenant God of his family, the LORD who has made promises.

Who said to me, ‘Return to your country.’ Jacob reminds God that he is only here because God sent him (31:3, 13). He prays on the ground of God’s command.

I am not worthy of the least of all the deeds of steadfast love and all the faithfulness that you have shown to your servant. For the first time Jacob speaks with real humility. “Steadfast love and faithfulness” are the great words of God’s covenant loyalty, the words God would use of himself at Sinai (Exodus 34:6). Jacob, who once bargained with God (28:20–22), now admits he deserves none of it.

With only my staff I crossed this Jordan, and now I have become two camps. Twenty years ago he crossed alone with a walking stick; now he has a family and great flocks. Everything he has, God gave.

For I fear him, that he may come and attack me, the mothers with the children. An honest confession of fear. “The mothers with the children” describes total slaughter (compare Hosea 10:14). Jacob fears for everyone he loves.

But you said, ‘I will surely do you good.’ Jacob ends by holding God to his word (28:13–15; compare 22:17). This makes the prayer a model for ours. It praises God for who he is, rests on his command, confesses unworthiness, asks plainly, and pleads his promises. We may pray God’s promises back to him, not to inform him, but because faith takes hold of what he has said.

Christ in the passage. Jacob could plead the promise that his offspring would be “as the sand of the sea”. Christians plead promises that have all found their “Yes” in Christ (2 Corinthians 1:20), and pray in the name of the one who makes the unworthy welcome.

verseByVerse.quote: So he stayed there that night, and from what he had with him he took a present for his brother Esau, two hundred female goats and twenty male goats, two hundred ewes and twenty rams, thirty milking camels and their calves, forty cows and ten bulls, twenty female donkeys and ten male donkeys.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jacob takes a huge present from his flocks for Esau, over five hundred animals chosen to build a herd, offering back something of what God had given him.

So he stayed there that night. Having prayed, Jacob also plans. Prayer and planning belong together, though his planning is not yet free of fear.

Two hundred female goats and twenty male goats. The gift is huge, over five hundred animals. The proportions are those of breeding herds: many females, few males, and milking camels with their young (see sheep and goats). This is wealth that would go on growing, taken from the flocks God had given Jacob in Haran (31:9).

A present for his brother Esau. The word “present” (minchah) is used elsewhere both for tribute paid to a superior (Judges 3:15) and for the grain offering (Leviticus 2:1). When the brothers meet, Jacob will press Esau to accept it as “my blessing” (33:11): many see here a man trying to hand back something of the blessing he once stole. On the word “appease” in v. 20, see the note on vv. 20–21.

verseByVerse.quote: These he handed over to his servants, every drove by itself, and said to his servants, "Pass on ahead of me and put a space between drove and drove." He instructed the first, "When Esau my brother meets you and asks you, 'To whom do you belong? Where are you going? And whose are these ahead of you?' then you shall say, 'They belong to your servant Jacob. They are a present sent to my lord Esau. And moreover, he is behind us.'" He likewise instructed the second and the third and all who followed the droves, "You shall say the same thing to Esau when you find him,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jacob sends the gifts in separate droves, each with the same humble message, so that Esau meets wave after wave of generosity before he meets Jacob.

Put a space between drove and drove. Each drove arrives on its own, so Esau meets wave after wave of gifts, each carrying the same message. The words Jacob puts in his servants’ mouths keep the humble address of his first message, “your servant Jacob” and “my lord Esau” (see the note on vv. 3–5).

Moreover, he is behind us. Jacob does not mean to hide; he is coming to face his brother. But he keeps the gifts between himself and Esau.

In everyday life. Making amends is right, and Jesus tells us to go and be reconciled to a brother before we bring our gift to God (Matthew 5:23–24). Restoring what we took is part of true repentance (Luke 19:8). But no gift can buy forgiveness, which can only be given.

verseByVerse.quote: and you shall say, 'Moreover, your servant Jacob is behind us.'" For he thought, "I may appease him with the present that goes ahead of me, and afterward I shall see his face. Perhaps he will accept me." So the present passed on ahead of him, and he himself stayed that night in the camp.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jacob hopes his present will “cover” Esau’s face so that Esau will accept him, but the face he must meet first that night is God’s.

I may appease him … and afterward I shall see his face. The Hebrew word for “face” (panim) runs through this verse: “appease him” is literally “cover his face”, the present goes “ahead of me”, literally “before my face”, and “he will accept me” is literally “he will lift up my face”. The verb for “cover” is the one the Law later uses for covering guilt, making atonement. Jacob is dreading one face. That night he will see “God face to face” at Peniel (v. 30), and the next day he will tell Esau, “I have seen your face, which is like seeing the face of God” (33:10).

He himself stayed that night in the camp. The gift goes ahead and Jacob stays behind, but the meeting he most needs that night is not with Esau. Before he can face his brother he must face God, alone at the Jabbok (vv. 22–32). And when Esau comes, he runs to embrace him (33:4): grace outruns the plan.

Christ in the passage. Jacob hoped a gift would cover his guilt before his brother’s face. Before God’s face no gift of ours could do that. Christ is the one offering that covers our sin and lets us be “accepted” before God (Hebrews 10:14).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Alone at night by the Jabbok, Jacob is met by God himself, wrestled to the end of his strength, wounded, and blessed. A man wrestles him until dawn and with one touch puts his hip out of joint (vv. 22–25). Jacob, unable to fight, clings and will not let go without a blessing; asked his name, he must confess “Jacob”, and he is renamed Israel (vv. 26–28). God will not give his own name on demand, but he blesses Jacob, who realises he has seen God face to face and lived (vv. 29–30). The sun rises on a limping, changed man, and Israel remembers the night at every meal (vv. 31–32).
