verseByVerse.theology: Left alone at the Jabbok, Jacob wrestles with a man until daybreak. His hip is put out of joint, but he will not let go without a blessing. Asked his name, he says "Jacob," and is renamed Israel. He names the place Peniel and limps into the sunrise.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Jacob prevailed by clinging, not by strength. Now: God makes us own who we are and gives a new name (Rev. 2:17), and the weakness he leaves is a sign that he met us (2 Cor. 12:9–10).

verseByVerse.quote: The same night he arose and took his two wives, his two female servants, and his eleven children, and crossed the ford of the Jabbok. He took them and sent them across the stream, and everything else that he had. And Jacob was left alone. And a man wrestled with him until the breaking of the day. When the man saw that he did not prevail against Jacob, he touched his hip socket, and Jacob's hip was put out of joint as he wrestled with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jacob sends his family and possessions across the Jabbok and is left alone, and a man wrestles with him until dawn and, with a single touch, puts his hip out of joint.

The same night he arose … and crossed the ford of the Jabbok. The Jabbok runs west through a deep gorge into the Jordan (see the note on the verse). Crossing a ford with women, children and flocks in the dark shows how restless Jacob was. He sends everyone and everything across, and stays behind.

And Jacob was left alone. Everything Jacob relied on has gone ahead: his family, his wealth, his gifts, his plans. God meets him when he is alone and weakest. Twenty years earlier God met him alone at Bethel (28:11).

And a man wrestled with him until the breaking of the day. The opponent is first simply “a man”. Only gradually does Jacob, and the reader, understand who he is (vv. 28, 30). Jacob has wrestled all his life, with Esau in the womb (25:22–26), with his father, with Laban; now he wrestles with God, and every other struggle comes into the light.

When the man saw that he did not prevail against Jacob. This does not mean God was too weak. The struggle lasts as long as God allows. In the mystery of his grace, God lets himself be held.

He touched his hip socket, and Jacob’s hip was put out of joint. One touch ends the contest as a fight: his opponent could have ended it at any moment. Jacob’s strength, his greatest asset, is broken. Now he cannot fight; he can only cling.

Christ in the passage. The God who came to Jacob in human form, wrestling hand to hand in the dark, would one day take human flesh for good. And the God who wounded Jacob in order to bless him was himself wounded to bless us: “by his wounds you have been healed” (1 Peter 2:24).

Where Christians differ. Who is the man? Hosea calls him an angel: “He strove with the angel and prevailed” (Hosea 12:4). Jacob says he has seen God face to face (v. 30). Some therefore see a created angel acting for God; many, from the early church on, see God himself, the Son appearing before his incarnation.

This commentary’s view. God himself came to Jacob in human form. Hosea’s “angel” fits the commentary’s reading of the angel of the LORD who speaks and acts as God (see the note on 31:10–13): this is best read as the Son appearing before his incarnation.
verseByVerse.note: The Jabbok is a tributary flowing west into the Jordan. A sound-play runs through the scene: Jacob (Ya‘aqov) wrestles (ye’aveq) at the Jabbok (Yabboq).

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said, "Let me go, for the day has broken." But Jacob said, "I will not let you go unless you bless me." And he said to him, "What is your name?" And he said, "Jacob." Then he said, "Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel, for you have striven with God and with men, and have prevailed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Crippled, Jacob clings and will not let go without a blessing; made to confess his name, “Jacob”, he is given a new one, Israel.

Let me go, for the day has broken. Perhaps the visitor will not let Jacob see him in full daylight, since no one may see God’s face and live (Exodus 33:20); or the night’s work is simply done. Either way, Jacob now holds the one who could leave at will.

I will not let you go unless you bless me. Crippled and weak, Jacob clings. All his life he has grasped for blessing by trickery; now, at last, he grasps the right thing, the One who alone can give it, and he asks for it openly. Hosea says he “wept and sought his favor” (Hosea 12:4). This is not wrestling God into submission, but the desperate, persistent prayer that Jesus commends (Luke 18:1–8).

What is your name? … Jacob. The last time Jacob was asked who he was, by his blind father, he lied: “I am Esau your firstborn” (27:19). Now he tells the truth, and the name is a confession. Esau had said, “Is he not rightly named Jacob? For he has cheated me these two times” (27:36). Before God can bless him, Jacob must own what he has been.

Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel. A new name meant a new identity and calling, as when Abram became Abraham (17:5). The new name will be confirmed at Bethel (35:10), and it will become the name of a nation. Yet Genesis keeps calling him Jacob too, as if he grows into the new name slowly.

For you have striven with God and with men, and have prevailed. With men: Esau and Laban. With God: this night. He prevailed not by strength, for his strength was broken, but by clinging to God and pleading for his blessing. God’s blessing goes to those who know they cannot win and hold on to him anyway (James 4:6).

Christ in the passage. “Israel” was a people that failed to live up to its name, until one Israelite was faithful where Israel had failed. Jesus is the true Israel, God’s Son called out of Egypt (Matthew 2:15), and all who are joined to him by faith share the new name and the blessing.

In everyday life. Hold on to God in prayer when you have nothing left to hold. He is the one who came to Jacob first, and he delights to bless those who come to him empty.

Uncertain wording. The ESV note gives “Israel” as “he strives with God” or “God strives”. Genesis explains the name by the sound of the verb “strive” (sarah), a rare word whose exact sense is debated; some have suggested “God rules” or “God persists”. Hebrew names normally make God the subject, which favours “God strives” or “God rules” as the bare meaning of the name, while the story itself gives it the sense “one who has striven with God”. The point of the passage is clear either way.
verseByVerse.note: “Israel” means “he strives with God” or “God strives” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jacob asked him, "Please tell me your name." But he said, "Why is it that you ask my name?" And there he blessed him. So Jacob called the name of the place Peniel, saying, "For I have seen God face to face, and yet my life has been delivered."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The visitor will not give his name, but he blesses Jacob, and Jacob names the place Peniel, “face of God”, amazed that he has seen God face to face and lived.

Please tell me your name. To know a name was, in some sense, to know and perhaps to call on its owner. Jacob, given a new name, wants his opponent’s.

Why is it that you ask my name? God makes himself known as he chooses, not on demand. The angel of the LORD answers Manoah the same way: “Why do you ask my name, seeing it is wonderful?” (Judges 13:18). Jacob does not need the name; he needs the blessing, and he gets it.

And there he blessed him. The blessing is given freely, not won by wrestling. Jacob, who once took a blessing by deceit, now receives one by grace.

For I have seen God face to face, and yet my life has been delivered. Jacob realises who his opponent was, and is astonished to be alive, for “man shall not see me and live” (Exodus 33:20). He saw God veiled in human form, in the dark. God did not destroy him; he blessed him.

Christ in the passage. “No one has ever seen God; God the only Son, who is at the Father’s side, he has made him known” (John 1:18). What Jacob glimpsed in the night, we see in the light of the gospel: “the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6). And because of Christ, sinners can stand before God’s face and live.
verseByVerse.note: “Peniel” means “the face of God” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: The sun rose upon him as he passed Penuel, limping because of his hip. Therefore to this day the people of Israel do not eat the sinew of the thigh that is on the hip socket, because he touched the socket of Jacob's hip on the sinew of the thigh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sun rises on Jacob limping across the stream, blessed and marked by weakness for life, and Israel remembers the night by a custom at every meal.

The sun rose upon him as he passed Penuel. When Jacob fled the land, the sun set on him at Bethel (28:11); now it rises as he returns. Penuel is another spelling of Peniel. A long night in Jacob’s life is over.

Limping because of his hip. Jacob is blessed but marked by weakness, and he will limp for the rest of his life: God’s “power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9). Every step he takes towards Esau, he takes leaning on God.

Therefore to this day the people of Israel do not eat the sinew of the thigh. A custom that kept the story alive: at every meal of meat Israel remembered that their father had been touched by God. Jews still observe it today.

Isn’t faith a crutch? The charge is familiar: religion is for people who cannot cope, a prop for the weak. Jacob is an awkward example for it. He was not weak. He was the most capable man in Genesis, a self-made schemer who had outwitted his brother, his father and Laban, and who had wanted God mainly as a backer for his plans (28:20–22). God did not hand him a crutch at the Jabbok. He put his hip out of joint, and Jacob walked into the sunrise leaning on God because he could no longer stand on himself. That is the Christian answer. Faith is not a crutch for people who happen to be weak; it is what happens when people discover they were weaker than they thought. And everyone leans on something: a reputation, a bank balance, a relationship, their own judgment. The only question is whether it will bear the weight. Christ “was crucified in weakness, but lives by the power of God” (2 Corinthians 13:4), and those who lean on him find that the limp is where the blessing came in.

Uncertain wording. Which part of the body “the sinew of the thigh” means is not certain. Jewish tradition identifies it with the sciatic nerve, which runs down the back of the thigh and is removed from meat before it is eaten; others think of a tendon or muscle near the hip. The custom, not the anatomy, is the point.

32.theology:
The wrestling at the Jabbok is one of the Bible’s richest pictures of prayer and faith. Hosea says Jacob “strove with the angel and prevailed; he wept and sought his favor” (Hos 12:4). Jacob does not win by strength. He prevails by desperate, clinging faith that will not let God go until blessing comes. Jesus commends the same persistence in the parables of the persistent widow (Luke 18:1–8) and the friend at midnight (Luke 11:5–8): to keep on asking is not a lack of faith; it is what faith does under pressure.

The new name marks the change that is the goal of Jacob’s whole story. The deceiver who grasped at everything becomes the man who clings to God. The old Jacob does not vanish; he is the same person, renamed by meeting God. That is how God sanctifies, or makes holy, his people.

If, as many Christian readers have thought, the wrestler is the Son of God before his incarnation, then the scene foreshadows the incarnation: God takes human form, enters the struggle, and lets himself be held by the faith of his people.
32.examples:
The Jabbok is a picture of the believer’s darkest night: stripped of support, facing what feels like destruction, alone. Luther knew seasons of spiritual assault; John of the Cross wrote of the dark night of the soul; Spurgeon wrestled with depression. God meets us in the desolation, and the blessing comes on the other side, marked by the wound.

Jacob’s “I will not let you go” gives warrant for bold, persistent prayer, what older writers called “holy importunity”, a refusal to stop asking. God let himself be wrestled with and called Jacob’s refusal to give up “prevailing”: he invites this kind of prayer. The limp afterward is not a sign of failure; it is the mark of one who has been with God in the night.

keyVerse.quote: Then he said, “Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel, for you have striven with God and with men, and have prevailed.”
keyVerse.note: Jacob must first confess his old name, “Jacob”, the cheat, before God gives him a new one. He prevails not by strength, which God has just broken, but by clinging to God for his blessing. The name of the whole nation was born in this night, and it tells every believer how God’s blessing is received.

32.reflection:
Jacob saw God’s camp at Mahanaim and then divided his own people into two camps out of fear (vv. 1–2, 7). Why do we so quickly forget God’s care when a new threat appears?

Jacob’s prayer praises God, confesses unworthiness, asks plainly and pleads God’s promises (vv. 9–12). Which of God’s promises could you pray back to him this week?

Before God blessed him, Jacob had to say his name, “Jacob” (v. 27). What does it mean to own honestly what we have been before God, and why does blessing come that way?

Jacob left Peniel blessed but limping (v. 31). Where has God used weakness, loss or failure in your life to make you lean on him, and how does Christ’s own weakness on the cross help you see it?

33.title: Jacob and Esau Reconcile
33.text: <sup>1</sup>And Jacob lifted up his eyes and looked, and behold, Esau was coming, and four hundred men with him. So he divided the children among Leah and Rachel and the two female servants.<sup>2</sup>And he put the servants with their children in front, then Leah with her children, and Rachel and Joseph last of all.<sup>3</sup>He himself went on before them, bowing himself to the ground seven times, until he came near to his brother.<sup>4</sup>But Esau ran to meet him and embraced him and fell on his neck and kissed him, and they wept.<sup>5</sup>And when Esau lifted up his eyes and saw the women and children, he said, "Who are these with you?" Jacob said, "The children whom God has graciously given your servant."<sup>6</sup>Then the servants drew near, they and their children, and bowed down.<sup>7</sup>Leah likewise and her children drew near and bowed down. And last Joseph and Rachel drew near, and they bowed down.<sup>8</sup>Esau said, "What do you mean by all this company that I met?" Jacob answered, "To find favor in the sight of my lord."<sup>9</sup>But Esau said, "I have enough, my brother; keep what you have for yourself."<sup>10</sup>Jacob said, "No, please, if I have found favor in your sight, then accept my present from my hand. For I have seen your face, which is like seeing the face of God, and you have accepted me.<sup>11</sup>Please accept my blessing that is brought to you, because God has dealt graciously with me, and because I have enough." Thus he urged him, and he took it.<sup>12</sup>Then Esau said, "Let us journey on our way, and I will go ahead of you."<sup>13</sup>But Jacob said to him, "My lord knows that the children are frail, and that the nursing flocks and herds are a care to me. If they are driven hard for one day, all the flocks will die.<sup>14</sup>Let my lord pass on ahead of his servant, and I will lead on slowly, at the pace of the livestock that are ahead of me and at the pace of the children, until I come to my lord in Seir."<sup>15</sup>So Esau said, "Let me leave with you some of the people who are with me." But he said, "What need is there? Let me find favor in the sight of my lord."<sup>16</sup>So Esau returned that day on his way to Seir.<sup>17</sup>But Jacob journeyed to Succoth, and built himself a house and made booths for his livestock. Therefore the name of the place is called Succoth.<sup>18</sup>And Jacob came safely to the city of Shechem, which is in the land of Canaan, on his way from Paddan-aram, and he camped before the city.<sup>19</sup>And from the sons of Hamor, Shechem's father, he bought for a hundred pieces of money the piece of land on which he had pitched his tent.<sup>20</sup>There he erected an altar and called it El-Elohe-Israel.
33.overview:
Where we are. Twenty years after he fled from Esau’s threat to kill him (27:41), Jacob is coming home. He has heard that Esau is on the way with four hundred men (32:6), sent wave after wave of gifts ahead to soften him, and spent the night wrestling with God at the Jabbok, where he was lamed, blessed and renamed Israel (32:22–32). Now, limping, he sees his brother coming.

The message. The God who has met Jacob also goes before him: the meeting Jacob feared most becomes an embrace, because God has answered his prayer (32:11). Jacob, who once grabbed the blessing, now confesses that everything he has is grace, and gives back to Esau what he can. Peace with God has opened the way to peace with his brother, though the old habits of the heart are not yet all gone.

Why it was said. Israel would live beside Edom, Esau’s nation, for centuries, often in bitter conflict (see the introduction). This chapter told them that the two peoples began as brothers who wept on each other’s necks; Moses would later command, “You shall not abhor an Edomite, for he is your brother” (Deuteronomy 23:7). It also showed Israel that their father came into the land not by his own scheming but because God kept his word to bring him back “in peace” (28:21).

How the chapter makes its case. Jacob arranges his family, his favouritism on show, but goes ahead of them himself, bowing like a vassal before a king (vv. 1–3). Esau runs, embraces and kisses him, and they weep (v. 4). Jacob presents his family as gifts of God’s grace (vv. 5–7), then presses his present on Esau as “my blessing”, saying that seeing his face is like seeing the face of God (vv. 8–11). He politely declines Esau’s escort and promises to follow him to Seir, a promise he does not keep (vv. 12–17). He arrives at Shechem in peace, buys land and builds an altar to “God, the God of Israel” (vv. 18–20).

Where it leads. By pattern and by need. Esau’s running welcome is the picture Jesus borrowed for the father who ran to his returning son (Luke 15:20), and it shows how freely the God Jacob met at Peniel receives sinners. But Jacob’s gifts also expose a need: he tried to buy his way into his brother’s favour, as sinners try with God. Only Christ settles that: “while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son” (Romans 5:10), and he is the one who makes estranged brothers one (Ephesians 2:14).

For us. Reconciliation with those we have wronged starts with God: those who have been received by him can go humbly, admit the wrong, and make what amends they can. And when we have arrived “safely”, the right response is the one Jacob made: an altar, and the confession that this God is my God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The brother Jacob feared becomes the brother who welcomes him, because God has gone ahead. Jacob walks out in front of his family and bows to the ground, and Esau runs to embrace him (vv. 1–4). Jacob speaks of his children, his gifts and his very life as God’s grace, and urges Esau to take “my blessing”, as if to give back what he stole (vv. 5–11). The brothers part in peace, though Jacob, cautious and evasive, does not follow Esau to Seir (vv. 12–17). The chapter ends with Jacob safely in Canaan, buying a piece of the promised land and naming his altar for “God, the God of Israel” (vv. 18–20).
verseByVerse.theology: Jacob arranges his family, goes ahead, and bows seven times; Esau runs to meet him, embraces him and weeps. Jacob presses his gift, his "blessing", on Esau, promises to follow to Seir, then goes to Succoth and Shechem, buys land, and builds an altar, El-Elohe-Israel.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Esau ran to meet the brother who had wronged him. Now: when someone forgives what you actually did, you have seen something of the face of God.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jacob lifted up his eyes and looked, and behold, Esau was coming, and four hundred men with him. So he divided the children among Leah and Rachel and the two female servants. And he put the servants with their children in front, then Leah with her children, and Rachel and Joseph last of all. He himself went on before them, bowing himself to the ground seven times, until he came near to his brother.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Facing the brother he wronged, Jacob arranges his family by his favourites, but this time he goes ahead of them himself and comes to Esau bowing low.

Esau was coming, and four hundred men with him. Nothing has changed since the messengers’ report (32:6). The night of prayer has not removed the danger; it has changed the man who faces it. Four hundred men was a war band (compare 1 Samuel 22:2; 30:10).

He divided the children. The order is a ranking of love. The servants and their children go first, then Leah and hers, and “Rachel and Joseph last of all”, furthest from danger. Jacob loves as his father did, by preference (25:28), and everyone in the family can see it. The seed of the jealousy that will sell Joseph into Egypt is sown here in plain sight (37:3–4).

He himself went on before them. The night before, Jacob had sent his gifts ahead and kept himself at the back (32:16–21). Now the limping man walks out in front. The wrestling at the Jabbok has not made him perfect, but it has made him brave enough to face what he has done.

Bowing himself to the ground seven times. This was how a subject approached a king. Letters from Canaanite rulers to the pharaoh of Egypt, a few centuries later, open by saying that they fall at the king’s feet seven times and seven times. Isaac’s stolen blessing had said, “Be lord over your brothers, and may your mother’s sons bow down to you” (27:29). Now the man who received it bows seven times to the brother he took it from, calling him “my lord” and himself “your servant” (vv. 5, 8, 13–14).

What it does not mean. Jacob is not giving up God’s promise. The covenant blessing is still his (35:11–12). What he lays down is the grasping and the pride: he refuses to stand over his brother on the strength of a blessing he won by deceit.

In everyday life. Going to someone we have wronged is frightening, and it does not get easier by waiting twenty years. Jacob went first and went low. It is still the way.

verseByVerse.quote: But Esau ran to meet him and embraced him and fell on his neck and kissed him, and they wept.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Instead of attacking, Esau runs to Jacob, throws his arms around him and kisses him, and the brothers weep together: God has answered Jacob’s prayer.

But Esau ran to meet him. The “but” overturns everything Jacob feared. He came bowing; Esau came running. In that world a grown man of rank did not run; Esau forgets his dignity in his eagerness. The same four verbs reappear in Jesus’ parable of the lost son: the father “ran and embraced him and kissed him” (Luke 15:20).

Fell on his neck and kissed him. The last kiss between these brothers was the false kiss Jacob gave his blind father while dressed in Esau’s clothes (27:26–27). Now there is a true one. “Fell on his neck” is a full embrace, the way Joseph will later greet Benjamin (45:14).

And they wept. Twenty years of fear and anger come out in tears. Esau’s fury has turned away, as Rebekah had hoped it would (27:44–45), though Genesis never tells us that she sent for him.

God changed Esau. Jacob prayed, “Please deliver me from the hand of my brother” (32:11), and this is the answer. Jacob’s gifts may have helped, but the narrator has already shown us the decisive meeting: the night before, with God. “When a man’s ways please the LORD, he makes even his enemies to be at peace with him” (Proverbs 16:7). The God who turned Laban back in a dream (31:24) has turned Esau’s heart.

The welcome of the one who was wronged. In the end it is Esau, the injured brother, who makes peace possible by running. That is the gospel shape of every true reconciliation: it costs the one who was wronged. Jesus used this picture for God himself. We come rehearsing our speeches and calculating our gifts; the Father has been watching the road and comes running, and the welcome begins before the confession is finished (Luke 15:20–22). It can be so because the Son bore the cost of our wrongs himself.

Textual note. In the traditional Hebrew text the word “kissed him” is marked with a row of special dots. No one knows for certain why. Some later Jewish interpreters took the dots to suggest that Esau’s kiss was not sincere, but nothing in the story supports that: Esau’s generosity in the following verses is real.

verseByVerse.quote: And when Esau lifted up his eyes and saw the women and children, he said, "Who are these with you?" Jacob said, "The children whom God has graciously given your servant." Then the servants drew near, they and their children, and bowed down. Leah likewise and her children drew near and bowed down. And last Joseph and Rachel drew near, and they bowed down. Esau said, "What do you mean by all this company that I met?" Jacob answered, "To find favor in the sight of my lord." But Esau said, "I have enough, my brother; keep what you have for yourself." Jacob said, "No, please, if I have found favor in your sight, then accept my present from my hand. For I have seen your face, which is like seeing the face of God, and you have accepted me. Please accept my blessing that is brought to you, because God has dealt graciously with me, and because I have enough." Thus he urged him, and he took it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jacob presents his family as gifts of God’s grace and presses his present on Esau as a giving back of the blessing he stole; Esau’s gracious welcome reminds him of the face of God he has just seen.

Who are these with you? Esau left a brother with nothing but a staff (32:10); he meets a man with four wives, eleven sons and a daughter.

The children whom God has graciously given your servant. The man who once took what he wanted now speaks of what God has graciously given. The Hebrew word is the root of “grace” or “favour”, and it runs through the whole conversation: Jacob wants “to find favor” (v. 8), asks again “if I have found favor” (v. 10), and says “God has dealt graciously with me” (v. 11). The word Jacob has learned in twenty years is grace.

They bowed down. One group after another, the whole family bows: servants, Leah, and finally Joseph with Rachel. The order of v. 2 is still on display, and the boy who goes last and safest, Joseph, will one day have his brothers bowing before him in Egypt (42:6).

What do you mean by all this company that I met? Literally, “all this camp”, the same word as in Mahanaim, “two camps” (32:2, 7–10). Esau has been met by drove after drove of goats, sheep, camels, cows and donkeys (32:13–21).

To find favor in the sight of my lord. Jacob is honest about it: the gift was meant to win Esau over. The night before he had thought, “I may appease him with the present” (32:20); “appease him” is literally “cover his face”, from the same root Israel would later use for the atoning covering of sin. Jacob was trying to cover his guilt with a gift.

I have enough, my brother. Esau needs nothing. And he says “my brother”, where Jacob keeps saying “my lord”. The man Hebrews calls “unholy” for despising his birthright (Hebrews 12:16) is, in this scene, the more generous of the two. Scripture is honest about the covenant family: the unbeliever can shame the believer by his kindness.

For I have seen your face, which is like seeing the face of God. The night before, at Peniel (“the face of God”), Jacob said, “I have seen God face to face, and yet my life has been delivered” (32:30). He came expecting a face of judgment and found a face of grace, first God’s and now his brother’s. It is not flattery: the welcome in Esau’s face is God’s answer to his prayer, and the kindness of the one he wronged reminds him of the kindness of the God he wronged.

And you have accepted me. He had hoped, “Perhaps he will accept me” (32:20). He is accepted, but not because of the cattle: Esau welcomed him before he took a single gift.

Please accept my blessing that is brought to you. Jacob calls the present “my blessing”, the very word Esau used of what Jacob stole: “he has taken away my blessing” (27:36). It is as near as he can come to saying, “I took your blessing; let me give you a blessing back.” He cannot hand over the covenant promise, which was God’s to give (25:23), but he can make what restitution he is able to. Zacchaeus did the same when grace found him: “if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold” (Luke 19:8).

Because God has dealt graciously with me, and because I have enough. Esau said, “I have enough”; Jacob’s words are literally “I have everything”. The grasping younger brother is finally content. He can give generously because he has stopped believing that he must take.

Thus he urged him, and he took it. In that world, accepting a gift sealed a friendship; refusing it could leave an enmity open. When Esau takes it, the peace is made.

Christ, the gift that covers. Jacob sent gift after gift to “cover the face” of an angry brother, and found in the end that grace had run ahead of his gifts. Sinners still try to buy God’s favour with offerings of religion, effort and good works. But God himself has provided the covering: Christ “is the propitiation for our sins” (1 John 2:2). We do not send droves ahead to soften God; we come behind the one offering he has accepted, and are welcomed for his sake. “All this is from God, who through Christ reconciled us to himself” (2 Corinthians 5:18).

Gifts, not achievements. Our children, and all we have, are not achievements to show off but gifts we have been given. Saying so out loud, as Jacob did, teaches them where every good thing comes from.

In everyday life. Is there someone you need to be reconciled to? Jesus says not to wait: “First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift” (Matthew 5:24). Go as one God has already received, admit the wrong plainly, and where something was taken, give back what you can. You cannot control the welcome you get; Jacob could not. Paul says, “If possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all” (Romans 12:18).

What it does not mean. Reconciliation does not mean pretending the wrong never happened, and it does not always mean returning to closeness. Where there has been abuse or danger, forgiveness can be real while safety and boundaries remain wise and necessary. Even here, as the next verses show, the brothers made peace and then lived apart.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Esau said, "Let us journey on our way, and I will go ahead of you." But Jacob said to him, "My lord knows that the children are frail, and that the nursing flocks and herds are a care to me. If they are driven hard for one day, all the flocks will die. Let my lord pass on ahead of his servant, and I will lead on slowly, at the pace of the livestock that are ahead of me and at the pace of the children, until I come to my lord in Seir." So Esau said, "Let me leave with you some of the people who are with me." But he said, "What need is there? Let me find favor in the sight of my lord."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jacob politely declines to travel with Esau and promises to follow him to Seir, a promise he never keeps.

Let us journey on our way, and I will go ahead of you. Esau means it kindly: he offers to escort his brother home to Seir, the hill country south-east of the Dead Sea.

My lord knows that the children are frail. The reason is true. Joseph was about six, there were young lambs and calves, and a herdsman knows that “if they are driven hard for one day, all the flocks will die”. A good shepherd moves at the pace of the weakest.

Until I come to my lord in Seir. But Jacob does not go to Seir. As soon as Esau leaves, he turns the other way, north-west to Succoth (v. 17). The brothers will meet again only at their father’s grave (35:29).

Let me leave with you some of the people who are with me. Esau offers an armed guard; Jacob refuses that too. He does not want to be under Esau’s protection, or in his debt.

The shepherd who goes at the pace of the lambs. Jacob’s words describe, better than he knew, the way God leads his people. Isaiah says of the LORD, “He will tend his flock like a shepherd; he will gather the lambs in his arms; he will carry them in his bosom, and gently lead those that are with young” (Isaiah 40:11). Jesus is that shepherd: “a bruised reed he will not break” (Matthew 12:20). He never drives his weak ones harder than they can bear.

Where Christians differ. Was Jacob wise or deceitful here? Some see only prudence: Esau’s moods had been murderous before (27:41), and the two households could not live together (36:6–7). Others see the old Jacob, saying what pleases and then doing what he likes.

This commentary’s view. Probably both. Keeping his family apart from Esau’s was sensible, and fitting for the family of promise. But he did not need to promise a visit he did not intend to make. The man renamed Israel still carries some of Jacob in him, as every believer still fights the old self. Honesty would have served him better: “Let what you say be simply ‘Yes’ or ‘No’” (Matthew 5:37).

verseByVerse.quote: So Esau returned that day on his way to Seir. But Jacob journeyed to Succoth, and built himself a house and made booths for his livestock. Therefore the name of the place is called Succoth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The brothers part in peace: Esau goes home to Seir, and Jacob settles for a time at Succoth.

So Esau returned that day on his way to Seir. Esau goes back to the country that will bear his name, Edom (36:8). His part in the covenant story is over, though God will keep his word to him too (25:23; 36:1–43).

Built himself a house and made booths for his livestock. Jacob, who had lived in tents, builds a house: he means to stay a while. “Booths” were rough shelters of branches.

Therefore the name of the place is called Succoth. Succoth means “booths”. The town lay east of the Jordan, near where the Jabbok joins it (compare Judges 8:5). The same word later named the Feast of Booths, when Israel lived in shelters to remember the wilderness journey (Leviticus 23:42–43).

Peace without closeness. The quarrel is ended, but the brothers live apart. That is sometimes the best a broken relationship can come to in this life, and it is still peace. The full reconciliation of all God’s people, every wall of hostility gone, waits for the new creation (Ephesians 2:14–16; Revelation 7:9).
verseByVerse.note: “Succoth” means “booths” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: And Jacob came safely to the city of Shechem, which is in the land of Canaan, on his way from Paddan-aram, and he camped before the city. And from the sons of Hamor, Shechem's father, he bought for a hundred pieces of money the piece of land on which he had pitched his tent. There he erected an altar and called it El-Elohe-Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jacob arrives in Canaan in peace, as God promised, buys a piece of the land, and builds an altar confessing the God of Israel as his own God.

And Jacob came safely to the city of Shechem. “Safely” is the word for peace and wholeness. At Bethel, as a fugitive, Jacob had vowed, “If God will be with me … so that I come again to my father’s house in peace, then the LORD shall be my God” (28:20–21). God has kept every part of his side. Shechem lay in the hill country between Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim; it was where God first appeared to Abraham in the land and promised it to his offspring (12:6–7).

He bought for a hundred pieces of money the piece of land. Like Abraham at Hebron (23:16–20), Jacob pays for a plot in the land God has promised him. He owns a field, not a country; he is still living by faith in a promise (Hebrews 11:9). This field became important. Joseph’s bones were buried in it (Joshua 24:32), and near it was the well where Jesus sat, tired, and spoke with the Samaritan woman about living water: “near the field that Jacob had given to his son Joseph” (John 4:5).

Did Abraham or Jacob buy it? Stephen says the tomb at Shechem was bought by Abraham (Acts 7:16). Most likely he compresses Genesis’s two purchases, Abraham’s at Hebron and Jacob’s at Shechem, into one phrase as he races through the history (see the note on Acts 7:15–16).

There he erected an altar. Like Abraham, Jacob marks his arrival in the land with worship (12:7).

And called it El-Elohe-Israel. “God, the God of Israel.” Jacob uses his new name, given at the Jabbok (32:28). It is a confession: the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac is now, by his own choice, the God of Israel. “The LORD shall be my God,” he had vowed (28:21); here he says it.

Christ. The God who would not let the deceiver go has made him his own, and Jacob’s field became the place where, centuries later, the God of Israel came in person and sat by Jacob’s well. The Samaritan woman asked, “Are you greater than our father Jacob?” (John 4:12). He was: the one who gives water that ends thirst for ever, and in whom all Jacob’s children, and the nations with them, find the true place of worship (John 4:21–24).

A stop short of Bethel. Jacob’s vow had a second part: the stone at Bethel would be “God’s house” (28:22). Jacob settles at Shechem instead and stays some years; by the next chapter Dinah, a child here, is a young woman. What follows there is the darkest episode in his family’s story, and only afterwards does God say, “Arise, go up to Bethel” (35:1). Half-kept promises leave room for trouble.

In everyday life. When God brings you through what you feared, do not only feel relieved: give thanks out loud, as Jacob did, and finish what you promised him in the hard days.

Uncertain wording. Two phrases here are uncertain. The coins are literally “a hundred qesitah”, a unit of money whose weight and value are unknown (perhaps a lamb’s worth; compare Job 42:11). And the word translated “safely” in v. 18 can also be read as a place name; older versions such as the King James have “Shalem, a city of Shechem”. Most modern translations read “safely” (or “in peace”), which fits the echo of Jacob’s vow (28:21) and is probably right.
verseByVerse.note: “El-Elohe-Israel” means “God, the God of Israel” (ESV note).

33.theology:
Esau’s running embrace is one of the most powerful pictures of grace in the Old Testament. In Jesus’ parable the father sees the returning son “while he was still a long way off” and runs, not waiting for the confession to be finished before the welcome begins: that is how God receives sinners.

Jacob can face Esau at all because he has first faced God at the Jabbok. Those who have truly reckoned with God, confessed, wrestled and been renamed, find a new capacity to be reconciled with those they have wronged. As John says, whoever does not love the brother he has seen cannot love God whom he has not seen (1 John 4:20).
33.examples:
This reconciliation is a pattern for any that involves real wrongdoing. Jacob does not walk back into Esau’s life as if nothing happened; he prepares, prays, humbles himself and goes first. His gifts are no longer only meant to win Esau over (32:20) but also repayment, an admission that his wealth came partly at Esau’s expense. Reconciliation that costs nothing has not taken the offence seriously.

And the order matters: God had to humble Jacob at the Jabbok before Jacob could humble himself before Esau.

keyVerse.quote: But Esau ran to meet him and embraced him and fell on his neck and kissed him, and they wept.
keyVerse.note: This is the moment the whole Jacob story has been dreading for twenty years, and it turns out to be an embrace. God has answered Jacob’s prayer by changing his brother’s heart, and the scene is so full of grace that Jesus used its very words for the Father welcoming the lost son home (Luke 15:20).

33.reflection:
Jacob went out ahead of his family and bowed low before the brother he had wronged (v. 3). What makes it so hard to go to someone we have hurt, and what had happened to Jacob the night before (32:22–32) that made him able to do it?

Esau ran, embraced and kissed his brother before Jacob had made a single speech (v. 4). How does Jesus use this picture in Luke 15:20, and what does it tell you about how God receives those who come back to him?

Jacob called his present “my blessing” and urged Esau to take it (v. 11). Where might God be asking you to make amends for a wrong, not to earn forgiveness but because you have been forgiven?

Jacob promised to follow Esau to Seir and then went elsewhere (vv. 14–17). How do we tell the difference between wise boundaries in a broken relationship and simple evasion? What does honesty look like in that situation?

34.title: Dinah and the Shechemites
34.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Dinah the daughter of Leah, whom she had borne to Jacob, went out to see the women of the land.<sup>2</sup>And when Shechem the son of Hamor the Hivite, the prince of the land, saw her, he seized her and lay with her and humiliated her.<sup>3</sup>And his soul was drawn to Dinah the daughter of Jacob. He loved the young woman and spoke tenderly to her.<sup>4</sup>So Shechem spoke to his father Hamor, saying, "Get me this girl for my wife."<sup>5</sup>Now Jacob heard that he had defiled his daughter Dinah. But his sons were with his livestock in the field, so Jacob held his peace until they came.<sup>6</sup>And Hamor the father of Shechem went out to Jacob to speak with him.<sup>7</sup>The sons of Jacob had come in from the field as soon as they heard of it, and the men were indignant and very angry, because he had done an outrageous thing in Israel by lying with Jacob's daughter, for such a thing must not be done.<sup>8</sup>But Hamor spoke with them, saying, "The soul of my son Shechem longs for your daughter. Please give her to him to be his wife.<sup>9</sup>Make marriages with us. Give your daughters to us, and take our daughters for yourselves.<sup>10</sup>You shall dwell with us, and the land shall be open to you. Dwell and trade in it, and get property in it."<sup>11</sup>Shechem also said to her father and to her brothers, "Let me find favor in your eyes, and whatever you say to me I will give.<sup>12</sup>Ask me for as great a bride-price and gift as you will, and I will give whatever you say to me. Only give me the young woman to be my wife."<sup>13</sup>The sons of Jacob answered Shechem and his father Hamor deceitfully, because he had defiled their sister Dinah.<sup>14</sup>They said to them, "We cannot do this thing, to give our sister to one who is uncircumcised, for that would be a disgrace to us.<sup>15</sup>Only on this condition will we agree with you—that you will become as we are by every male among you being circumcised.<sup>16</sup>Then we will give our daughters to you, and we will take your daughters to ourselves, and we will dwell with you and become one people.<sup>17</sup>But if you will not listen to us and be circumcised, then we will take our daughter, and we will be gone."<sup>18</sup>Their words pleased Hamor and Hamor's son Shechem.<sup>19</sup>And the young man did not delay to do the thing, because he delighted in Jacob's daughter. Now he was the most honored of all his father's house.<sup>20</sup>So Hamor and his son Shechem came to the gate of their city and spoke to the men of their city, saying,<sup>21</sup>"These men are at peace with us; let them dwell in the land and trade in it, for behold, the land is large enough for them. Let us take their daughters as wives, and let us give them our daughters.<sup>22</sup>Only on this condition will the men agree to dwell with us to become one people—when every male among us is circumcised as they are circumcised.<sup>23</sup>Will not their livestock, their property and all their beasts be ours? Only let us agree with them, and they will dwell with us."<sup>24</sup>And all who went out of the gate of his city listened to Hamor and his son Shechem, and every male was circumcised, all who went out of the gate of his city.<sup>25</sup>On the third day, when they were sore, two of the sons of Jacob, Simeon and Levi, Dinah's brothers, took their swords and came against the city while it felt secure and killed all the males.<sup>26</sup>They killed Hamor and his son Shechem with the sword and took Dinah out of Shechem's house and went away.<sup>27</sup>The sons of Jacob came upon the slain and plundered the city, because they had defiled their sister.<sup>28</sup>They took their flocks and their herds, their donkeys, and whatever was in the city and in the field.<sup>29</sup>All their wealth, all their little ones and their wives, all that was in the houses, they captured and plundered.<sup>30</sup>Then Jacob said to Simeon and Levi, "You have brought trouble on me by making me stink to the inhabitants of the land, the Canaanites and the Perizzites. My numbers are few, and if they gather themselves against me and attack me, I shall be destroyed, both I and my household."<sup>31</sup>But they said, "Should he treat our sister like a prostitute?"
34.overview:
Where we are. Jacob has come home in peace and settled outside the Canaanite city of Shechem (33:18–20), instead of going on to Bethel, where he had vowed to worship (28:22). Some years have passed: Dinah, Leah’s daughter, is now a young woman.

The message. When God’s people settle down among the world on the world’s terms, the world’s evil comes into their own house, and they answer it with evil of their own. Dinah is violated; her abuser bargains for her as property; her father is silent; her brothers lie, abuse the sign of God’s covenant, and slaughter a town. God is not named once. The chapter shows, without comment, how badly the family of promise needs God to intervene, and how unable it is to bring justice by itself.

Why it was said. Israel was about to enter Canaan, where the pull to intermarry and “become one people” with the nations (v. 16) would be constant (Deuteronomy 7:3–4). This chapter showed them the danger, and it explained why the tribes of Simeon and Levi were scattered in Israel (49:5–7). It also told Israel the truth about its fathers: their place in God’s plan was never earned by their goodness.

How the chapter makes its case. Shechem, the prince of the land, seizes and violates Dinah, then wants to marry her (vv. 1–4). Jacob holds his peace, while his sons are rightly enraged (vv. 5–7). Hamor proposes intermarriage and trade, and Shechem offers any bride-price (vv. 8–12). The brothers answer deceitfully, demanding that every male be circumcised (vv. 13–17). Hamor and Shechem sell the deal to their city with an appeal to greed (vv. 18–24). On the third day Simeon and Levi kill every male, and the brothers plunder the city, taking its women and children (vv. 25–29). Jacob complains only of the danger to himself; the brothers have the last, unanswered word (vv. 30–31).

Where it leads. By the need it exposes. Neither a passive father nor vengeful sons could give Dinah justice; the family needed a king who would “defend the cause of the poor” and “crush the oppressor” (Psalm 72:4), and judge without partiality or cruelty. Christ is that king. He will judge the world in righteousness (Acts 17:31); he himself was stripped and shamed by violent men, so that the violated have a Saviour who knows; and his grace reached even Levi’s sword, turning the violent tribe into the priestly one.

For us. Do not settle comfortably on the world’s terms, and do not be silent when the vulnerable are wronged. Seek justice God’s way, through truth and lawful authority, not revenge. And if you have been abused, know that God calls it an outrage, that it was not your fault, and that he is near to the brokenhearted.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–31 — The Defilement of Dinah and the Vengeance of Simeon and Levi
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Without God, the family of promise can neither protect the weak nor bring justice. Dinah is violated by the prince of Shechem, who then wants her as his wife (vv. 1–4). Jacob says nothing; his sons are furious (vv. 5–7). Hamor offers the family intermarriage, land and trade, the very assimilation that would end Israel as God’s distinct people (vv. 8–12). The brothers answer with a lie, using circumcision, the sign of God’s covenant, as a trap (vv. 13–24). Simeon and Levi massacre the men of the city, and the brothers plunder it, taking captive its women and children (vv. 25–29). Jacob complains only about his own danger, and the brothers’ question hangs unanswered (vv. 30–31). God is not mentioned until he speaks again in 35:1.
verseByVerse.theology: Shechem the Hivite prince seizes and violates Dinah, then asks his father to get her for him as wife. Jacob holds his peace. Hamor proposes intermarriage and trade; Jacob's sons answer deceitfully, demanding circumcision, and on the third day Simeon and Levi kill every male in the city while the others plunder it.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Jacob's deathbed words on their anger (49:5–7) are the book's verdict. Now: a real injustice does not make every response to it right, and when a father stays silent, others, often worse, act in his place.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Dinah the daughter of Leah, whom she had borne to Jacob, went out to see the women of the land. And when Shechem the son of Hamor the Hivite, the prince of the land, saw her, he seized her and lay with her and humiliated her. And his soul was drawn to Dinah the daughter of Jacob. He loved the young woman and spoke tenderly to her. So Shechem spoke to his father Hamor, saying, "Get me this girl for my wife."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Shechem, the prince of the land, seizes Dinah and violates her, and then, having used her, decides that he wants her as his wife.

Now Dinah the daughter of Leah. Dinah is Leah’s daughter, Jacob’s only daughter named in Genesis (30:21). She is the full sister of Simeon and Levi, which explains why they act (v. 25). She is probably in her teens; the chapter never lets her speak.

Went out to see the women of the land. To visit the local women, perhaps her own age. There is nothing wrong in it. The family has settled beside a Canaanite city (33:18), and the meeting of the two peoples has begun.

The son of Hamor the Hivite, the prince of the land. Shechem has the same name as his city. The Hivites were one of the peoples of Canaan (10:17). He is the prince: the most powerful young man in the place, used to taking what he wants.

He seized her and lay with her and humiliated her. Three verbs, one after another, with no pause for her consent. “Seized” is literally “took”, the verb used of the sons of God who “took as their wives any they chose” (6:2). “Humiliated” means violated, the word used when Amnon raped his sister Tamar: “being stronger than she, he violated her and lay with her” (2 Samuel 13:14). The rest of the chapter calls it defiling (vv. 5, 13, 27) and treating her “like a prostitute” (v. 31).

And his soul was drawn to Dinah. Only afterwards does Shechem speak of love and speak “tenderly” (literally, “to her heart”). Desire is real in him, but it began with taking, and it is still self-centred: “Get me this girl for my wife.” He speaks of her as a purchase. And while the negotiations go on, she is kept in his house (v. 26).

What it does not mean. Dinah is not to blame for going out. Some older interpreters blamed her curiosity, but the text does not; the sin is Shechem’s alone. A victim of abuse is never responsible for the abuser’s choice.

If this has happened to you. God sees what was done in secret, as he saw Hagar in the wilderness, who called him “a God of seeing” (16:13). Scripture names sexual violence as an outrage (v. 7), not a misunderstanding. It was not your fault, and you are not defiled in God’s eyes: “The LORD is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit” (Psalm 34:18). If you are in danger, get to safety now. Report the abuse to the police; church leaders must report it too, and never handle it quietly. Tell a trusted pastor and seek a biblical counsellor who understands abuse, and see a doctor for a medical check-up. If fear, sleeplessness or despair overwhelm you, tell your doctor; using medicine is no failure of faith. If you are thinking of ending your life, get help the same day.

Uncertain wording. The word translated “humiliated” means to afflict, humble or violate. It is used of rape (2 Samuel 13:12–14; Judges 19:24), but a few scholars argue that here it means sex that dishonoured her by bypassing her father and marriage, not necessarily by force. What is certain is that Scripture treats it as a grave wrong done to her. The order of the verbs, with “seized” first, and the parallel with Tamar make force the most likely meaning, and this commentary reads it so.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Jacob heard that he had defiled his daughter Dinah. But his sons were with his livestock in the field, so Jacob held his peace until they came. And Hamor the father of Shechem went out to Jacob to speak with him. The sons of Jacob had come in from the field as soon as they heard of it, and the men were indignant and very angry, because he had done an outrageous thing in Israel by lying with Jacob's daughter, for such a thing must not be done.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jacob hears and says nothing, while his sons, rightly outraged, come in from the fields burning with anger.

Now Jacob heard that he had defiled his daughter Dinah. The narrator calls it defilement: Dinah has been treated as unclean by what was done to her. The fault lies with the one who did it.

So Jacob held his peace until they came. There may be prudence in waiting for his sons, but there is not a word of grief, comfort or protest. Jacob wept loudly over Rachel’s sons (37:34–35); over Leah’s daughter he is silent. The favouritism of 33:2 has consequences. King David, many centuries later, did the same when his daughter Tamar was raped: “he was very angry” (2 Samuel 13:21), and did nothing, and another brother took revenge.

And Hamor the father of Shechem went out to Jacob to speak with him. Hamor comes to negotiate, not to apologise.

He had done an outrageous thing in Israel. The word means folly in the moral sense: a disgraceful, senseless act against God’s order. It becomes a fixed phrase in Israel’s story (Deuteronomy 22:21; Judges 20:6), and Tamar uses it as she pleads with Amnon: “for such a thing is not done in Israel; do not do this outrageous thing” (2 Samuel 13:12). Here, for the first time, the family is called by its new name: “Israel”. A wrong against Dinah is a wrong against the people God has made.

For such a thing must not be done. The brothers are right. Their anger at a real atrocity is not sin; what they do with it will be (Ephesians 4:26).

In everyday life. Do not stay silent when the vulnerable are wronged, least of all in your own family or church. Silence often protects the powerful. Speak, protect the one who was harmed, and bring the matter to those God has given authority to deal with it.

verseByVerse.quote: But Hamor spoke with them, saying, "The soul of my son Shechem longs for your daughter. Please give her to him to be his wife. Make marriages with us. Give your daughters to us, and take our daughters for yourselves. You shall dwell with us, and the land shall be open to you. Dwell and trade in it, and get property in it." Shechem also said to her father and to her brothers, "Let me find favor in your eyes, and whatever you say to me I will give. Ask me for as great a bride-price and gift as you will, and I will give whatever you say to me. Only give me the young woman to be my wife."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hamor makes no apology but offers a merger: intermarriage, land and trade, and Shechem will pay any price for Dinah.

The soul of my son Shechem longs for your daughter. Hamor speaks of his son’s feelings, not of the wrong done. There is no confession, and Dinah is still in Shechem’s house (v. 26).

Make marriages with us. Hamor proposes not one marriage but a merging of the two peoples. That was the danger Abraham had guarded against when he made his servant swear not to take a wife for Isaac “from the daughters of the Canaanites” (24:3), and that Isaac and Rebekah guarded against for Jacob (28:1). If the family of promise dissolved into Canaan, there would be no distinct people through whom the promised offspring would come.

Dwell and trade in it, and get property in it. The offer is tempting: the very land God promised, available now on easy terms. But it would come as a gift from Canaan, at the price of becoming Canaanite. Abraham had refused even “a sandal strap” from the king of Sodom so that no one could say, “I have made Abram rich” (14:23). God’s promises are not to be received on the world’s terms.

Ask me for as great a bride-price and gift as you will. The bride-price was the payment from the groom’s family to the bride’s that sealed a marriage (see Weddings and Betrothal). Israel’s later law required a man who seduced or violated an unbetrothed young woman to pay it and marry her, unless her father refused (Exodus 22:16–17; Deuteronomy 22:28–29). In a world where a woman who was not a virgin might never marry, those laws laid the cost on the man and protected the woman’s future. Shechem offers to pay whatever is asked, as though the wrong could be priced.

What it does not mean. Scripture does not teach that a victim must marry her abuser. The law of Exodus gave the father the right to refuse, and no one in this chapter, not even her brothers, asks what Dinah wants. God’s law always aims to protect the weak; it never requires the abused to bind themselves to the one who harmed them.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Jacob answered Shechem and his father Hamor deceitfully, because he had defiled their sister Dinah. They said to them, "We cannot do this thing, to give our sister to one who is uncircumcised, for that would be a disgrace to us. Only on this condition will we agree with you—that you will become as we are by every male among you being circumcised. Then we will give our daughters to you, and we will take your daughters to ourselves, and we will dwell with you and become one people. But if you will not listen to us and be circumcised, then we will take our daughter, and we will be gone."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jacob’s sons answer with a lie, using circumcision, the sign of God’s covenant, as the bait for a trap.

The sons of Jacob answered … deceitfully. The narrator says it plainly. The family trait passes down: Jacob deceived his father (27:35), Laban deceived Jacob (29:25), and now Jacob’s sons deceive their neighbours. They will deceive their father again over Joseph (37:31–33).

Because he had defiled their sister Dinah. The motive is stated alongside the deceit: grief and fury at what was done to her. Real wrongs breed real anger, and anger that does not look to God looks for its own way.

To give our sister to one who is uncircumcised. Circumcision was the sign of God’s covenant with Abraham (17:10–14): it marked a family set apart to belong to the LORD. The brothers turn it into a tribal custom anyone can adopt, and then into a weapon. They do not call the men of Shechem to the God of Abraham; they demand only a cut in the flesh.

You will become as we are … and become one people. This is the very assimilation Hamor proposed, offered back as bait. The brothers do not mean it, but the words show how lightly they hold their calling.

We will take our daughter, and we will be gone. A threat, since Dinah is still in Shechem’s house (v. 26).

The sign without the heart. A sign of belonging to God can be used for the opposite of what it means. Paul says that circumcision without obedience counts for nothing: “circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit, not by the letter” (Romans 2:29). The same is true of baptism, church membership and Christian vocabulary when they are used to manipulate or to gain.

verseByVerse.quote: Their words pleased Hamor and Hamor's son Shechem. And the young man did not delay to do the thing, because he delighted in Jacob's daughter. Now he was the most honored of all his father's house. So Hamor and his son Shechem came to the gate of their city and spoke to the men of their city, saying, "These men are at peace with us; let them dwell in the land and trade in it, for behold, the land is large enough for them. Let us take their daughters as wives, and let us give them our daughters. Only on this condition will the men agree to dwell with us to become one people—when every male among us is circumcised as they are circumcised. Will not their livestock, their property and all their beasts be ours? Only let us agree with them, and they will dwell with us." And all who went out of the gate of his city listened to Hamor and his son Shechem, and every male was circumcised, all who went out of the gate of his city.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hamor and Shechem agree at once, and sell the deal to their city as a way to take over Jacob’s wealth.

The young man did not delay to do the thing. Shechem’s eagerness is real. He was “the most honored of all his father’s house”, and his word carried the city.

Came to the gate of their city. The city gate was the place of public business and decisions.

These men are at peace with us. Hamor tells his townsmen a different story from the one Jacob’s family heard. He says nothing of Dinah or of the wrong, and presents the circumcision as a small price for a good bargain.

Will not their livestock, their property and all their beasts be ours? Here is the real offer to the men of the city: absorb Jacob’s family and its wealth. Greed is on both sides of the negotiation. The brothers plan to kill; the Shechemites plan to swallow.

And every male was circumcised. The whole city submits, for profit. It is a sad irony: the sign of the covenant received not in faith but as a business arrangement, and by men about to die because of it.

verseByVerse.quote: On the third day, when they were sore, two of the sons of Jacob, Simeon and Levi, Dinah's brothers, took their swords and came against the city while it felt secure and killed all the males. They killed Hamor and his son Shechem with the sword and took Dinah out of Shechem's house and went away. The sons of Jacob came upon the slain and plundered the city, because they had defiled their sister. They took their flocks and their herds, their donkeys, and whatever was in the city and in the field. All their wealth, all their little ones and their wives, all that was in the houses, they captured and plundered.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Simeon and Levi kill every man in the defenceless city, and the brothers plunder it, carrying off its women and children: vengeance becomes a far greater atrocity than the crime it avenged.

On the third day, when they were sore. The men were in pain and unable to fight. The brothers planned it so.

Simeon and Levi, Dinah’s brothers. Both were sons of Leah, like Dinah. Their zeal for their sister is real; so is their cruelty. Levi is the ancestor of Moses, Aaron and all Israel’s priests.

Killed all the males. Not only Shechem, but his father and every man in the city, most of whom had done nothing to Dinah. God’s law would later insist that each person dies “for his own sin” (Deuteronomy 24:16).

Took Dinah out of Shechem’s house. Only here do we learn that she had been in his house all along. She is rescued, but nobody speaks to her or of her again in this chapter.

The sons of Jacob came upon the slain and plundered the city. The other brothers join in, and the plunder is total: flocks, herds, donkeys, wealth, “all their little ones and their wives”. They avenge the taking of one woman by taking all the women of the city. Their righteous anger has turned into the sin it claimed to punish.

Jacob’s verdict. On his deathbed Jacob will say, “Simeon and Levi are brothers; weapons of violence are their swords … Cursed be their anger, for it is fierce, and their wrath, for it is cruel! I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel” (49:5, 7). Simeon’s tribe was later absorbed within Judah’s territory (Joshua 19:1, 9).

Grace for Levi. But God did something astonishing with Levi. When Israel worshipped the golden calf, the sons of Levi alone stood “on the LORD’s side” (Exodus 32:26), and their scattering became a blessing: they had no tribal land but were spread through Israel as its priests and teachers (Deuteronomy 33:8–10; see Priests and Levites). The tribe of the sword became the tribe of the altar. That is what God does in Christ: he took Saul the persecutor, “a blasphemer, persecutor, and insolent opponent” (1 Timothy 1:13), and made him an apostle of peace. No one is too violent for grace.

What it does not mean. Scripture records the massacre; it does not approve it. Jacob’s curse in 49:5–7 is the Bible’s own verdict on it. Nor does it mean that wrongs like Dinah’s should go unpunished. Grave crimes call for justice, and God has given the sword to lawful authority, which is “an avenger who carries out God’s wrath on the wrongdoer” (Romans 13:4), not to private revenge.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jacob said to Simeon and Levi, "You have brought trouble on me by making me stink to the inhabitants of the land, the Canaanites and the Perizzites. My numbers are few, and if they gather themselves against me and attack me, I shall be destroyed, both I and my household." But they said, "Should he treat our sister like a prostitute?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jacob complains only that his sons have endangered him; they reply that their sister could not be treated as a prostitute, and the question is left hanging.

You have brought trouble on me. Jacob speaks at last, and it is about himself: “me … me … I shall be destroyed, both I and my household.” He says nothing of Dinah, nothing of the murdered men, nothing of God. His fear is real, for “my numbers are few”, and the danger is real, but his concern is his reputation and safety, not justice.

By making me stink to the inhabitants of the land. That is, making him hateful to the Canaanites and Perizzites around him. The family meant to bless the nations (12:3) has become a stench among them.

Should he treat our sister like a prostitute? The brothers have the last word, and it is a fair question. Shechem did treat her as a body to be had and then paid for. But their answer to the question, deceit and slaughter, was wrong. The chapter leaves both Jacob’s cowardice and the sons’ cruelty standing, with no one in the right.

God is silent, but not absent. God is not mentioned in the whole chapter: this is a family acting without him. Yet the next chapter begins, “God said to Jacob, ‘Arise, go up to Bethel’” (35:1), and “a terror from God” keeps the surrounding cities from avenging Shechem (35:5). God’s grace to this family was never because they deserved it.

Christ, the king this family needed. Dinah needed a father who would act, brothers who would not sin in their anger, and a judge who could give real justice. Israel’s psalm prays for such a king: “May he defend the cause of the poor of the people, give deliverance to the children of the needy, and crush the oppressor!” (Psalm 72:4). Jesus is that king. He welcomed women whom others used or despised, and he will judge every hidden wrong with perfect justice and no cruelty. He was himself stripped, mocked and shamed by violent men (Matthew 27:28–31), and he bore the sins of the violent so that even they could be forgiven. In him the violated find a Saviour who understands, and the violent find the only way back.

Where Christians differ. Were the brothers right? Some ancient Jewish writings praised Simeon and Levi as heroes zealous for purity, and some modern readers think the narrator sides with them, since they have the last word. Most Christian interpreters have read the chapter as a condemnation of the massacre, while affirming the brothers’ outrage.

This commentary’s view. Their outrage was right; their deceit, their slaughter of the innocent and their plunder were wicked, as Jacob’s dying words declare (49:5–7). Their final question stands as a rebuke to their father’s passivity, but the answer to it was never revenge.

In everyday life. When you have been wronged, or someone you love has, the anger is not wrong, but it must not rule you. “Never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God, for it is written, ‘Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord’” (Romans 12:19). Use the lawful means God has given, the police, the courts and the church’s discipline, and pray for victims of abuse and for the justice only God can give.

34.theology:
Genesis 34 follows from Jacob’s settling at Shechem, a city of Canaanites, when he had vowed to return to God at Bethel (28:20–22). The New Testament warns of the same danger in other words: do not be conformed to this world (Rom 12:2); come out from them and be separate (2 Cor 6:17). God’s people are to be in the world but not absorbed by it.

The chapter raises the hardest questions about violence, trauma and justice. Dinah’s violation is real, her suffering is real, and her brothers are right to be outraged. Yet vigilante massacre does not restore justice; it multiplies death. The chapter ends with nothing put right. It shows the need for justice that truly punishes wrong yet is carried out lawfully, not in rage. The law will begin to supply it, and the New Testament roots it in the cross, where God’s justice and mercy meet.
34.examples:
Any application of Genesis 34 must begin with Dinah, whose story is told almost entirely through other people’s reactions. She is neither defended by her father nor consulted, and she simply disappears from the narrative. The text exposes every failure of the church to hear victims of sexual violence, grieve with them and protect their dignity. The silence of the men around her is not God’s silence: he sees the wronged and will judge every wrong.

Jacob’s passivity warns every leader who puts reputation (“you have made me stink”) before justice for those in their care. A good altar at Shechem (33:20) was not enough protection for a family embedded in a world that did not share its values. The call to Bethel in chapter 35 is a call back to the God who named him Israel.

keyVerse.quote: The sons of Jacob had come in from the field as soon as they heard of it, and the men were indignant and very angry, because he had done an outrageous thing in Israel by lying with Jacob’s daughter, for such a thing must not be done.
keyVerse.note: This verse names the wrong for what it is: an outrage against God’s people, a thing that must not be done. It also holds the chapter’s tragedy, for the brothers’ anger is right, but what they do with it, without God, turns one atrocity into another.

34.reflection:
Jacob held his peace when he heard what had happened to Dinah (v. 5), and later spoke only of the danger to himself (v. 30). Why do people, and churches, sometimes stay silent when the vulnerable are wronged? What would it have looked like for Jacob to act rightly?

Hamor offered land, trade and marriages if Jacob’s family would “become one people” with the city (vv. 9–10, 16). In what ways are Christians tempted to receive good things on the world’s terms, at the cost of their distinctiveness?

The brothers’ anger was right, but their deceit and slaughter were wicked (vv. 13, 25–29; 49:5–7). How can we tell the difference between righteous anger and revenge, and what does Romans 12:19 ask of us when we or those we love are wronged?

God took Levi, the tribe of the violent sword, and made it the tribe of priests. What does that tell you about the reach of grace, and how does Christ meet both the person who has been wronged and the person who has done wrong?

35.title: Return to Bethel
35.text: <sup>1</sup>God said to Jacob, "Arise, go up to Bethel and dwell there. Make an altar there to the God who appeared to you when you fled from your brother Esau."<sup>2</sup>So Jacob said to his household and to all who were with him, "Put away the foreign gods that are among you and purify yourselves and change your garments.<sup>3</sup>Then let us arise and go up to Bethel, so that I may make there an altar to the God who answers me in the day of my distress and has been with me wherever I have gone."<sup>4</sup>So they gave to Jacob all the foreign gods that they had, and the rings that were in their ears. Jacob hid them under the terebinth tree that was near Shechem.<sup>5</sup>And as they journeyed, a terror from God fell upon the cities that were around them, so that they did not pursue the sons of Jacob.<sup>6</sup>And Jacob came to Luz (that is, Bethel), which is in the land of Canaan, he and all the people who were with him,<sup>7</sup>and there he built an altar and called the place El-bethel, because there God had revealed himself to him when he fled from his brother.<sup>8</sup>And Deborah, Rebekah's nurse, died, and she was buried under an oak below Bethel. So he called its name Allon-bacuth.<sup>9</sup>God appeared to Jacob again, when he came from Paddan-aram, and blessed him.<sup>10</sup>And God said to him, "Your name is Jacob; no longer shall your name be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name." So he called his name Israel.<sup>11</sup>And God said to him, "I am God Almighty: be fruitful and multiply. A nation and a company of nations shall come from you, and kings shall come from your own body.<sup>12</sup>The land that I gave to Abraham and Isaac I will give to you, and I will give the land to your offspring after you."<sup>13</sup>Then God went up from him in the place where he had spoken with him.<sup>14</sup>And Jacob set up a pillar in the place where he had spoken with him, a pillar of stone. He poured out a drink offering on it and poured oil on it.<sup>15</sup>So Jacob called the name of the place where God had spoken with him Bethel.<sup>16</sup>Then they journeyed from Bethel. When they were still some distance from Ephrath, Rachel went into labor, and she had hard labor.<sup>17</sup>And when her labor was at its hardest, the midwife said to her, "Do not fear, for you have another son."<sup>18</sup>And as her soul was departing (for she was dying), she called his name Ben-oni; but his father called him Benjamin.<sup>19</sup>So Rachel died, and she was buried on the way to Ephrath (that is, Bethlehem),<sup>20</sup>and Jacob set up a pillar over her tomb. It is the pillar of Rachel's tomb, which is there to this day.<sup>21</sup>Israel journeyed on and pitched his tent beyond the tower of Eder.<sup>22</sup>While Israel lived in that land, Reuben went and lay with Bilhah his father's concubine. And Israel heard of it. Now the sons of Jacob were twelve.<sup>23</sup>The sons of Leah: Reuben (Jacob's firstborn), Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun.<sup>24</sup>The sons of Rachel: Joseph and Benjamin.<sup>25</sup>The sons of Bilhah, Rachel's servant: Dan and Naphtali.<sup>26</sup>The sons of Zilpah, Leah's servant: Gad and Asher. These were the sons of Jacob who were born to him in Paddan-aram.<sup>27</sup>And Jacob came to his father Isaac at Mamre, or Kiriath-arba (that is, Hebron), where Abraham and Isaac had sojourned.<sup>28</sup>Now the days of Isaac were 180 years.<sup>29</sup>And Isaac breathed his last, and he died and was gathered to his people, old and full of days. And his sons Esau and Jacob buried him.
35.overview:
Where we are. After the disgrace and bloodshed at Shechem (chapter 34), Jacob’s family is hated by its neighbours and in danger. God has been silent through all of it. Now he speaks again, and sends Jacob back to Bethel, where he first met him as a fugitive and where Jacob vowed to worship him if he brought him home (28:10–22).

The message. God calls his people back to himself, and they must come cleansed of their idols; when they do, he renews his promises. At Bethel God confirms Jacob’s new name, Israel, and passes on to him the whole blessing of Abraham: a nation, kings, and the land. But the road of promise runs through grief. The chapter closes an era with the deaths of Deborah, Rachel and Isaac, and with Reuben’s sin, and yet it also completes the twelve sons from whom Israel will come. God’s promises go forward through death and failure, not around them.

Why it was said. Israel heard this on the edge of Canaan, a land full of other gods (see the introduction). Joshua would gather them at Shechem, under perhaps the same tree, and say, “put away the foreign gods that are among you” (Joshua 24:23). This chapter told them their father had done the same before them. It also told the twelve tribes where they came from, and why Reuben, the firstborn, did not lead them.

How the chapter makes its case. God tells Jacob to go to Bethel, and Jacob orders his household to bury their idols and purify themselves (vv. 1–4). A terror from God protects them on the road; Jacob builds the altar, and Rebekah’s old nurse dies (vv. 5–8). God appears, confirms the name Israel, and gives him the covenant promises in the name God Almighty (vv. 9–12). Jacob sets up a pillar and pours out an offering (vv. 13–15). Rachel dies giving birth to Benjamin near Bethlehem (vv. 16–20). Reuben sleeps with his father’s concubine (vv. 21–22). The twelve sons are listed (vv. 23–26), and Isaac dies and is buried by his two sons (vv. 27–29).

Where it leads. By promise and by pattern. “Kings shall come from your own body” (v. 11) is fulfilled in David and finally in Jesus, “the son of David” and the King of Israel (Matthew 1:1; John 1:49). Bethel, “the house of God”, where heaven touched earth, finds its fulfilment in Christ, on whom the angels of God ascend and descend (John 1:51). And near Bethlehem a son of sorrow becomes the son of the right hand: a faint outline of the man of sorrows born in Bethlehem who now sits at God’s right hand.

For us. When God calls you back, bury your idols; do not carry them with you into his presence. His promises are renewed to those who return. And when the road brings grief, as it will, remember that it still leads home: the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob “is not God of the dead, but of the living” (Matthew 22:32).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–29 — Return to Bethel; Deaths and Births
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God brings Jacob back to Bethel, renews the covenant with him, and carries his promise forward through death and failure. Called back by God, Jacob leads his household in burying their idols and goes up to worship, protected on the way by a terror from God (vv. 1–8). At Bethel God confirms the name Israel and gives him the promise of nations, kings and land in the name God Almighty, and Jacob marks the place again with a pillar (vv. 9–15). Then come sorrows: Rachel dies giving birth to Benjamin, Reuben defiles his father’s bed, and Isaac dies, buried by both his sons (vv. 16–29). Between them stands the list of the twelve sons, the founders of Israel (vv. 23–26).
verseByVerse.theology: God sends Jacob to Bethel; the household buries its foreign gods, and a terror from God keeps the cities from pursuing. God renews the name Israel and the promises; Jacob sets up a pillar with a drink offering.
