Rachel dies bearing Benjamin near Bethlehem, Reuben lies with Bilhah, the twelve sons are listed, and Isaac dies at 180.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the twelve names will be on the high priest's breastpiece and on the gates of the city (Exod. 28:21; Rev. 21:12). Now: real repentance gives something up for good, and God tells his people more than once who they now are.

verseByVerse.quote: God said to Jacob, "Arise, go up to Bethel and dwell there. Make an altar there to the God who appeared to you when you fled from your brother Esau." So Jacob said to his household and to all who were with him, "Put away the foreign gods that are among you and purify yourselves and change your garments. Then let us arise and go up to Bethel, so that I may make there an altar to the God who answers me in the day of my distress and has been with me wherever I have gone." So they gave to Jacob all the foreign gods that they had, and the rings that were in their ears. Jacob hid them under the terebinth tree that was near Shechem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God calls Jacob back to Bethel to worship, and Jacob leads his household in getting rid of their idols before they go.

Arise, go up to Bethel and dwell there. After the silence of chapter 34, God speaks first. He does not rebuke Jacob for Shechem; he calls him to the place of his first meeting. Jacob had vowed at Bethel that the LORD would be his God and the stone would be “God’s house” (28:20–22). He has been home for years and has not gone. God reminds him.

Make an altar there to the God who appeared to you when you fled from your brother Esau. God reminds Jacob who he was when God first met him: a fugitive with nothing (28:10–15). Remembering where grace found us is the start of every renewal.

Put away the foreign gods that are among you. There were idols in Jacob’s camp: Rachel’s stolen household gods (31:19, 34), and very likely images among the plunder and captives from Shechem (34:29). Jacob has known about at least some of them and done nothing. Now, for the first time, he leads his family spiritually. Worship of the true God cannot share a tent with other gods.

Purify yourselves and change your garments. Outward washing and clean clothes expressed inward preparation to meet God, as Israel later washed their garments before God came down at Sinai (Exodus 19:10). After Shechem, the family is stained with blood and plunder; they must come clean. Paul uses the same picture of clothes: “put off your old self … and to put on the new self” (Ephesians 4:22–24).

The God who answers me in the day of my distress and has been with me wherever I have gone. This is Jacob’s testimony, spoken to his household. God answered him when he fled (28:15), when Laban pursued (31:24), and when Esau came (32:11; 33:4). God kept his promise, “I am with you and will keep you wherever you go” (28:15), word for word.

And the rings that were in their ears. Earrings were often worn as charms linked with the gods; the prophets later linked rings and jewellery with the worship of Baal (Hosea 2:13), and Israel would make the golden calf out of its earrings (Exodus 32:2–4). Anything tied to the old gods had to go.

Jacob hid them under the terebinth tree that was near Shechem. He buried them, not to keep them for later but to be done with them. Centuries later, at Shechem, Joshua set up a stone “under the terebinth that was by the sanctuary of the LORD” and told Israel to “put away the foreign gods” (Joshua 24:23, 26), perhaps at the very same tree. Every generation has to make the same choice.

Christ. The call to Bethel is a call to come to God through the one he has appointed. Believers in Thessalonica did what Jacob’s household did: they “turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God” (1 Thessalonians 1:9). They could, because God had first turned to them in Christ. Notice the order here too: God called Jacob while the idols were still in his camp. His call does not wait for us to be clean; it is what makes us able to bury our idols.

In everyday life. What idols must you bury? Not only statues, but whatever you look to for the security, worth or comfort that only God can give: money, approval, success, a relationship. Name them, and get rid of whatever feeds them. And lead your household, as Jacob did at last; children learn more from what we put away than from what we say. “Little children, keep yourselves from idols” (1 John 5:21).

verseByVerse.quote: And as they journeyed, a terror from God fell upon the cities that were around them, so that they did not pursue the sons of Jacob. And Jacob came to Luz (that is, Bethel), which is in the land of Canaan, he and all the people who were with him, and there he built an altar and called the place El-bethel, because there God had revealed himself to him when he fled from his brother. And Deborah, Rebekah's nurse, died, and she was buried under an oak below Bethel. So he called its name Allon-bacuth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God protects the family on the road, Jacob builds the altar he promised, and the faithful old nurse of Rebekah dies and is mourned.

A terror from God fell upon the cities. After the massacre at Shechem, the surrounding towns had every reason to attack. Jacob had feared exactly that (34:30). God holds them back. The protection is grace pure and simple; the family had done nothing to earn it.

Luz (that is, Bethel). Luz was the city’s older name; Jacob had named the place Bethel, “house of God”, after his dream (28:19).

Called the place El-bethel. “God of Bethel.” At first Jacob named the place; now he names its God. The emphasis has moved from where he met God to the God he met.

Deborah, Rebekah’s nurse, died. She had come from Haran with Rebekah more than a century before (24:59). That she is now with Jacob suggests that Rebekah herself has died; Genesis never records her death, only that she was buried at Machpelah (49:31). The mother who loved Jacob and schemed for him did not see him come home.

Allon-bacuth. “Oak of weeping.” A servant woman is mourned and remembered by name, and the place is named for the tears shed for her (see Mourning Customs). God’s book notices faithful lives that the world overlooks.

In everyday life. Honour the people who have served your family quietly for years, and grieve them openly when they die. In God’s eyes there are no unimportant lives.
verseByVerse.note: “El-bethel” means “God of Bethel”; “Allon-bacuth” means “oak of weeping” (ESV notes).

verseByVerse.quote: God appeared to Jacob again, when he came from Paddan-aram, and blessed him. And God said to him, "Your name is Jacob; no longer shall your name be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name." So he called his name Israel. And God said to him, "I am God Almighty: be fruitful and multiply. A nation and a company of nations shall come from you, and kings shall come from your own body. The land that I gave to Abraham and Isaac I will give to you, and I will give the land to your offspring after you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God appears to Jacob again at Bethel, confirms his new name, Israel, and gives him the whole covenant blessing of Abraham: a nation, kings and the land.

God appeared to Jacob again … and blessed him. At Bethel the first time, God spoke to Jacob in a dream (28:12–15). Now he appears to him, back in the land, and blesses him in person.

No longer shall your name be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name. God confirms the name he gave at Peniel (32:28). There it was given after the wrestling; here it is confirmed in the land, at the place of worship, as the family’s official name. Yet Genesis goes on calling him both Jacob and Israel, as if to show that the new man and the old still live together in him until the end.

I am God Almighty. The name by which God revealed himself to Abraham when he gave him the sign of circumcision and promised a son (17:1), and the name Isaac used when he blessed Jacob on his way to Haran (28:3). It is the name of the God who does what is humanly impossible.

Be fruitful and multiply. These are the words God spoke to Adam and Eve (1:28) and again to Noah after the flood (9:1). Jacob’s family is God’s new start for humanity: through them the first blessing on mankind is to be restored.

A nation and a company of nations shall come from you. Israel would be one nation from twelve tribes; but “company of nations” points further. Paul says that all who belong to Christ, from every nation, are Abraham’s offspring: “if you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to promise” (Galatians 3:29).

And kings shall come from your own body. Promised to Abraham (17:6) and now to Jacob. It was fulfilled in David and his line, and finally in Jesus, the son of David, whom Nathanael greeted as “the King of Israel” (John 1:49). Contrast chapter 36: Esau’s line will have kings long before Israel (36:31). God’s promised king is worth the wait.

The land that I gave to Abraham and Isaac I will give to you. The promise of the land passes to Jacob and to his offspring. He will die in Egypt owning only a field and a grave, but he dies believing it (Hebrews 11:13, 21).

In everyday life. God does not give his promises once and leave us to remember them. He renews them, at the Lord’s Table, in his word, in the fellowship of his people. Come back to the place of worship, and hear them again.

Uncertain wording. The meaning of the Hebrew name El Shaddai, “God Almighty”, is not certain. The translation “Almighty” goes back to the ancient Greek and Latin versions and fits the way the name is used, at moments when God promises what only his power can do. Scholars have also suggested links with words for “mountain” or for “sufficient”, but none is proven. “God Almighty” remains the best guide to its meaning in Genesis.

verseByVerse.quote: Then God went up from him in the place where he had spoken with him. And Jacob set up a pillar in the place where he had spoken with him, a pillar of stone. He poured out a drink offering on it and poured oil on it. So Jacob called the name of the place where God had spoken with him Bethel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jacob marks the place where God spoke with him with a stone pillar, pours out an offering on it, and names it Bethel again: the vow of his youth is kept.

Then God went up from him. The same words are used when God finished speaking with Abraham (17:22). This was a real meeting with God, who came down and then went up.

In the place where he had spoken with him. The phrase comes three times in two verses. What made Bethel holy was not the stone or the view but that God had spoken there.

A pillar of stone. He poured out a drink offering on it and poured oil on it. As at his first visit, Jacob anoints a stone pillar (28:18). This time he adds a drink offering, wine poured out to God, the first in the Bible, a gift wholly given away. Some thirty years after the night of the ladder, Jacob stands in the same place, with a lifetime of God’s faithfulness behind him.

So Jacob called the name of the place … Bethel. “House of God.” The vow is kept: the stone has become God’s house (28:22).

Christ, the true Bethel. At Bethel Jacob saw a ladder joining earth and heaven, with angels going up and down (28:12). Jesus told Nathanael that this is what he is: “you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man” (John 1:51). Jacob had to travel to Bethel to meet God; in Christ the house of God has come to us. He is the meeting place of God and man, and where he is, his people worship (John 4:21–24).

verseByVerse.quote: Then they journeyed from Bethel. When they were still some distance from Ephrath, Rachel went into labor, and she had hard labor. And when her labor was at its hardest, the midwife said to her, "Do not fear, for you have another son." And as her soul was departing (for she was dying), she called his name Ben-oni; but his father called him Benjamin. So Rachel died, and she was buried on the way to Ephrath (that is, Bethlehem), and Jacob set up a pillar over her tomb. It is the pillar of Rachel's tomb, which is there to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the road near Bethlehem Rachel dies giving birth to her second son; she names him “son of my sorrow”, but Jacob names him Benjamin, “son of the right hand”.

Rachel went into labor, and she had hard labor. The scene is told slowly, with the hardest word repeated. Rachel once said to Jacob, “Give me children, or I shall die!” (30:1). Now the child she longed for costs her her life.

Do not fear, for you have another son. When Joseph was born, Rachel named him with a prayer: “May the LORD add to me another son!” (30:24). The midwife’s words tell her that the prayer has been answered, in the hour of her death.

She called his name Ben-oni; but his father called him Benjamin. Rachel names her son for her grief, “son of my sorrow”. Jacob will not let the boy carry his mother’s death as his name, and calls him “son of the right hand”, the side of strength, favour and honour. He does not deny the grief; he refuses to let it define the child. Benjamin is the only one of the twelve born in the promised land.

Some readers ask. Did Rachel die because Jacob had said of the stolen gods, “Anyone with whom you find your gods shall not live” (31:32)? Some readers have wondered. Genesis does not draw that line, and we should not insist on it.

Buried on the way to Ephrath (that is, Bethlehem). Jacob does not bury her in the family grave at Machpelah, where Leah will lie (49:31), but by the road where she died, and marks the tomb with a pillar. Years later he still remembers the place with pain (48:7).

Rachel weeping for her children. Rachel’s tomb became a symbol. Jeremiah heard “Rachel … weeping for her children” as Israel went into exile, and then heard God’s answer: “There is hope for your future, declares the LORD” (Jeremiah 31:15, 17). Matthew hears the same weeping when Herod slaughters the boys of Bethlehem (Matthew 2:18).

Christ, from sorrow to the right hand. Near Bethlehem a son of sorrow is renamed son of the right hand. It is not a prophecy, but it is a pattern God loves to repeat. In Bethlehem the true Son was born, who became “a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief” (Isaiah 53:3), and who now sits at God’s right hand (Psalm 110:1; Hebrews 1:3). Because of him the weeping of Rachel is answered, and sorrow will not have the last word over God’s children.

In everyday life. Grief is real, and death is still an enemy; Scripture tells Rachel’s death with tenderness, not with a quick moral. But God can bring a son of the right hand out of sorrow. Do not let the worst day of your life be the name of everything that came out of it.

Uncertain wording. “Ben-oni” is usually taken as “son of my sorrow”, but the Hebrew word can also mean strength or vigour, so it may mean “son of my strength”, perhaps her last strength (ESV note). The context of death makes “sorrow” the more natural reading, and Jacob’s change of name suggests it. The site of the tomb is also uncertain: 1 Samuel 10:2 places it “in the territory of Benjamin”, north of Jerusalem, while the traditional site is just outside Bethlehem. “On the way to Ephrath” may mean that she died some distance before reaching it.
verseByVerse.note: Ben-oni could mean “son of my sorrow” or “son of my strength” (ESV note). Ephrath is Bethlehem.

verseByVerse.quote: Israel journeyed on and pitched his tent beyond the tower of Eder. While Israel lived in that land, Reuben went and lay with Bilhah his father's concubine. And Israel heard of it. Now the sons of Jacob were twelve.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Reuben, Jacob’s firstborn, sleeps with his father’s concubine, a bid for his father’s place, and Israel hears of it and says nothing.

Pitched his tent beyond the tower of Eder. “Tower of the flock”, a watchtower for shepherds, near Bethlehem. The phrase appears again in Micah 4:8, “And you, O tower of the flock … to you shall it come, the former dominion shall come, kingship for the daughter of Jerusalem”, a promise of the king to come. Whether Micah means the same place is uncertain.

Reuben went and lay with Bilhah his father’s concubine. Bilhah was Rachel’s servant and the mother of Dan and Naphtali. With Rachel dead, Reuben may also have meant to stop Bilhah taking Rachel’s place over his own mother Leah. But taking a father’s concubine was above all a claim to the father’s position: Absalom did it publicly to show he had seized David’s throne (2 Samuel 16:21–22). Reuben, the firstborn, is grasping at the headship before his time.

And Israel heard of it. And that is all. As with Dinah (34:5), Jacob hears and is silent. But it is not forgotten. On his deathbed he will say to Reuben, “Unstable as water, you shall not have preeminence, because you went up to your father’s bed” (49:4), and the rights of the firstborn passed to Joseph’s sons (1 Chronicles 5:1; see Inheritance and the Firstborn).

Now the sons of Jacob were twelve. Right after this sin comes the statement that the family is complete. God builds his people out of sinners.

What it does not mean. The silence of Genesis is not approval. Scripture often tells a sin without comment and judges it later. God’s law would call this act a deep wrong (Leviticus 18:8).

In everyday life. Grasping at a place God has not yet given, in a family, a church or a workplace, often costs what we already have. The firstborn who reached for his father’s place lost his own.
verseByVerse.note: Bilhah was Rachel’s servant and the mother of Dan and Naphtali.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Leah: Reuben (Jacob's firstborn), Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun. The sons of Rachel: Joseph and Benjamin. The sons of Bilhah, Rachel's servant: Dan and Naphtali. The sons of Zilpah, Leah's servant: Gad and Asher. These were the sons of Jacob who were born to him in Paddan-aram.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here are the twelve sons of Jacob, grouped by their mothers: the founders of the twelve tribes of Israel.

The sons of Leah … The sons of Rachel … The sons of Bilhah … The sons of Zilpah. The twelve sons are listed by mother, Leah first. The rivalry of chapters 29 and 30 lies behind the list, and the jealousies between the groups will drive the Joseph story.

Reuben (Jacob’s firstborn). Still named as the firstborn, just after the sin that would cost him the firstborn’s rights (v. 22).

These were the sons of Jacob who were born to him in Paddan-aram. Benjamin was born in Canaan (v. 18), so this is a general summary of the group, not a precise statement about each son, a common way of speaking in Genesis (compare 46:15).

Christ and the twelve. Israel grew from these twelve, and their names will be written on the gates of the new Jerusalem (Revelation 21:12). When Jesus came to restore Israel, he chose twelve apostles and promised that they would sit “on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew 19:28). He was building a renewed people of God around himself, with the twelve tribes of Jacob as its pattern.

In everyday life. Look at the list and remember the stories behind the names: a violent pair, a son who defiled his father’s bed, brothers who would sell their brother. God built his people from them. He is not put off by your family’s history, or yours.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jacob came to his father Isaac at Mamre, or Kiriath-arba (that is, Hebron), where Abraham and Isaac had sojourned. Now the days of Isaac were 180 years. And Isaac breathed his last, and he died and was gathered to his people, old and full of days. And his sons Esau and Jacob buried him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jacob comes home to his father at Hebron before Isaac dies, full of days, and the two estranged brothers bury him together.

Jacob came to his father Isaac at Mamre … (that is, Hebron). Hebron is where Abraham lived and was buried (13:18; 25:9–10). Jacob comes back to the family home. His vow was that he would “come again to my father’s house in peace” (28:21); he has.

Now the days of Isaac were 180 years. Isaac lived longer than Abraham (175, 25:7). His death is recorded here to close his story before Joseph’s begins, but it took place later. Isaac was 60 when Jacob was born (25:26), so he died when Jacob was 120; Jacob was 130 when he went down to Egypt (47:9). Isaac was therefore still alive when Joseph was sold, and lived through most of Joseph’s years in Egypt.

Breathed his last … and was gathered to his people. The same words as at Abraham’s death (25:8). Being “gathered to his people” is not the same as being buried, for it is said before the burial. It speaks of joining those who have gone before. Jesus taught that God calls himself “the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob”, and “He is not God of the dead, but of the living” (Matthew 22:32).

Old and full of days. A long life, finished. Isaac, the quietest of the patriarchs, deceived by his son and wife and slow to see God’s purpose, still ends as a man who “died in faith, not having received the things promised, but having seen them and greeted them from afar” (Hebrews 11:13).

And his sons Esau and Jacob buried him. The twins who fought in the womb stand together at their father’s grave, as Isaac and Ishmael did at Abraham’s (25:9). The reconciliation of chapter 33 has held. Esau’s name comes first; he is the elder still in the world’s eyes. With this burial the story of Isaac’s family closes, and the next chapter gives Esau’s line before the story turns to Jacob’s sons.

Christ. Isaac, the son of promise who once lay on the altar at Moriah and was given back (22:1–14), dies at last. The promise still waits. The resurrection of Christ is the answer to every patriarch’s grave: because he lives, “the God of Isaac” is the God of a living Isaac.

In everyday life. Death in a family can open old wounds or heal them. Esau and Jacob show that estranged brothers can stand together at a graveside. If there is someone you need to stand with, do not wait for a funeral to make peace.

35.theology:
The command to “put away the foreign gods” is an Old Testament picture of growing in holiness. The call to Bethel is a call not to let the old life slowly fade but to bury it. Paul uses the same decisive language: “put off your old self” (Eph 4:22).

Rachel dies at Bethlehem, and that place of weeping becomes the birthplace of Benjamin, then the city of David, and at last the birthplace of the Son of David. The pilgrim road does not go around sorrow and death; it goes through them. The gospel does not remove suffering from the path, but it changes what suffering means: it is the road to glory, not the end of the story (Rom 8:17–18).
35.examples: The man who manipulated his family is beginning to lead them. The change is not complete, for he will still favour Joseph, but the direction is new. Suffering received in faith produced in Jacob what comfort never could.

keyVerse.quote: Then let us arise and go up to Bethel, so that I may make there an altar to the God who answers me in the day of my distress and has been with me wherever I have gone.
keyVerse.note: This is Jacob’s testimony at the turning point of his life. Everything God promised at Bethel, “I am with you and will keep you wherever you go” (28:15), has come true, and Jacob now leads his whole household back to worship the God who kept his word.

35.reflection:
Before going to Bethel, Jacob told his household to put away their foreign gods and change their clothes (vv. 2–4). What are the “foreign gods” Christians most often keep in their tents today, and what would it look like to bury them rather than simply hide them?

God confirmed Jacob’s new name and renewed all his promises (vv. 9–12), yet Genesis keeps calling him both Jacob and Israel. How does that encourage you in your own struggle between the old self and the new?

Rachel named her son for her sorrow; Jacob renamed him “son of the right hand” (v. 18). How does the gospel change what our griefs are allowed to say about us and those we love?

The chapter is full of failure and death: idols in the camp, Reuben’s sin, the deaths of Deborah, Rachel and Isaac. Yet the promise goes forward and the twelve sons are named. Where do you need to trust that God’s purposes are moving forward through loss and failure?

36.title: The Generations of Esau
36.text: <sup>1</sup>These are the generations of Esau (that is, Edom).<sup>2</sup>Esau took his wives from the Canaanites: Adah the daughter of Elon the Hittite, Oholibamah the daughter of Anah the daughter of Zibeon the Hivite,<sup>3</sup>and Basemath, Ishmael's daughter, the sister of Nebaioth.<sup>4</sup>And Adah bore to Esau, Eliphaz; Basemath bore Reuel;<sup>5</sup>and Oholibamah bore Jeush, Jalam, and Korah. These are the sons of Esau who were born to him in the land of Canaan.<sup>6</sup>Then Esau took his wives, his sons, his daughters, and all the members of his household, his livestock, all his beasts, and all his property that he had acquired in the land of Canaan. He went into a land away from his brother Jacob.<sup>7</sup>For their possessions were too great for them to dwell together. The land of their sojournings could not support them because of their livestock.<sup>8</sup>So Esau settled in the hill country of Seir. (Esau is Edom.)<sup>9</sup>These are the generations of Esau the father of the Edomites in the hill country of Seir.<sup>10</sup>These are the names of Esau's sons: Eliphaz the son of Adah the wife of Esau, Reuel the son of Basemath the wife of Esau.<sup>11</sup>The sons of Eliphaz were Teman, Omar, Zepho, Gatam, and Kenaz.<sup>12</sup>(Timna was a concubine of Eliphaz, Esau's son; she bore Amalek to Eliphaz.) These are the sons of Adah, Esau's wife.<sup>13</sup>These are the sons of Reuel: Nahath, Zerah, Shammah, and Mizzah. These are the sons of Basemath, Esau's wife.<sup>14</sup>These are the sons of Oholibamah the daughter of Anah the daughter of Zibeon, Esau's wife: she bore to Esau Jeush, Jalam, and Korah.<sup>15</sup>These are the chiefs of the sons of Esau. The sons of Eliphaz the firstborn of Esau: the chiefs Teman, Omar, Zepho, Kenaz,<sup>16</sup>Korah, Gatam, and Amalek; these are the chiefs of Eliphaz in the land of Edom; these are the sons of Adah.<sup>17</sup>These are the sons of Reuel, Esau's son: the chiefs Nahath, Zerah, Shammah, and Mizzah; these are the chiefs of Reuel in the land of Edom; these are the sons of Basemath, Esau's wife.<sup>18</sup>These are the sons of Oholibamah, Esau's wife: the chiefs Jeush, Jalam, and Korah; these are the chiefs born of Oholibamah the daughter of Anah, Esau's wife.<sup>19</sup>These are the sons of Esau (that is, Edom), and these are their chiefs.<sup>20</sup>These are the sons of Seir the Horite, the inhabitants of the land: Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah,<sup>21</sup>Dishon, Ezer, and Dishan; these are the chiefs of the Horites, the sons of Seir in the land of Edom.<sup>22</sup>The sons of Lotan were Hori and Hemam; and Lotan's sister was Timna.<sup>23</sup>These are the sons of Shobal: Alvan, Manahath, Ebal, Shepho, and Onam.<sup>24</sup>These are the sons of Zibeon: Aiah and Anah; he is the Anah who found the hot springs in the wilderness, as he pastured the donkeys of Zibeon his father.<sup>25</sup>These are the children of Anah: Dishon and Oholibamah the daughter of Anah.<sup>26</sup>These are the sons of Dishon: Hemdan, Eshban, Ithran, and Cheran.<sup>27</sup>These are the sons of Ezer: Bilhan, Zaavan, and Akan.<sup>28</sup>These are the sons of Dishan: Uz and Aran.<sup>29</sup>These are the chiefs of the Horites: the chiefs Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah,<sup>30</sup>Dishon, Ezer, and Dishan; these are the chiefs of the Horites, chief by chief in the land of Seir.<sup>31</sup>These are the kings who reigned in the land of Edom, before any king reigned over the Israelites.<sup>32</sup>Bela the son of Beor reigned in Edom, the name of his city being Dinhabah.<sup>33</sup>Bela died, and Jobab the son of Zerah of Bozrah reigned in his place.<sup>34</sup>Jobab died, and Husham of the land of the Temanites reigned in his place.<sup>35</sup>Husham died, and Hadad the son of Bedad, who defeated Midian in the country of Moab, reigned in his place, the name of his city being Avith.<sup>36</sup>Hadad died, and Samlah of Masrekah reigned in his place.<sup>37</sup>Samlah died, and Shaul of Rehoboth on the Euphrates reigned in his place.<sup>38</sup>Shaul died, and Baal-hanan the son of Achbor reigned in his place.<sup>39</sup>Baal-hanan the son of Achbor died, and Hadar reigned in his place, the name of his city being Pau; his wife's name was Mehetabel, the daughter of Matred, daughter of Mezahab.<sup>40</sup>These are the names of the chiefs of Esau, according to their clans and their dwelling places, by their names: the chiefs Timna, Alvah, Jetheth,<sup>41</sup>Oholibamah, Elah, Pinon,<sup>42</sup>Kenaz, Teman, Mibzar,<sup>43</sup>Magdiel, and Iram; these are the chiefs of Edom (that is, Esau, the father of Edom), according to their dwelling places in the land of their possession.
36.overview:
Where we are. Isaac is dead, buried by both his sons (35:29). Before Genesis turns to Jacob’s family and the long story of Joseph (“These are the generations of Jacob”, 37:2), it gives one chapter to Esau, just as it gave a short list to Ishmael before turning to Isaac (25:12–18).

The message. God kept his word to Esau too: the brother outside the covenant line became a nation, with chiefs and kings, settled in his own land long before Israel had any of these. But worldly greatness is not the same as the promise. Esau possessed his land at once; Jacob “lived in the land of his father’s sojournings” (37:1) and waited. God’s blessings in this world reach many, but the blessing through which the world will be saved runs, slowly and in weakness, through Jacob.

Why it was said. On their way to Canaan the Israelites would ask Edom for passage and be refused (Numbers 20:14–21), and God would forbid them to take Edom’s land: “I have given Mount Seir to Esau as a possession” (Deuteronomy 2:5). Amalek, who attacked them in the wilderness, came from Esau too (Exodus 17:8–16). This chapter told Israel who these neighbours were: brothers, under God’s hand, with their own history and their own land (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. Esau’s wives and sons born in Canaan, and his move to Seir because the land could not hold both brothers (vv. 1–8). His sons and grandsons in Seir, and the clan chiefs descended from them, among them Amalek (vv. 9–19). The Horites, the earlier people of Seir, with whom Esau’s family intermarried (vv. 20–30). The kings who reigned in Edom “before any king reigned over the Israelites” (vv. 31–39). A final list of Edom’s chiefs by their territories (vv. 40–43).

Where it leads. By promise, and by the long story of the two brothers. Balaam foresaw a star from Jacob and a sceptre from Israel before whom Edom would be dispossessed (Numbers 24:17–18). Isaiah saw the Lord coming from Edom’s capital, Bozrah, in garments red from victory (Isaiah 63:1–3). When the King was born in Bethlehem, Herod, a king of Edomite descent, tried to kill him (Matthew 2:16); yet soon crowds from Idumea, Edom’s land, came to hear him (Mark 3:8). The promised King conquers by grace, and Amos foresaw “the remnant of Edom and all the nations” called by God’s name (Amos 9:12; Acts 15:16–17).

For us. Do not measure God’s blessing by worldly success: Esau had kings while Israel had a promise. Be patient with God’s timing, and look for “an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading” (1 Peter 1:4). And remember that no family or nation is beyond the reach of the King who came from Jacob.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God gives Esau what he promised him, a nation and a land, but the story of salvation does not run through Esau. Esau’s family grows in Canaan and then moves to Seir, because the land cannot hold both brothers’ flocks (vv. 1–8). His sons become the chiefs of Edom, Amalek among them (vv. 9–19). The Horites, Seir’s earlier inhabitants, are listed, for Esau’s family married into them and absorbed them (vv. 20–30). Edom has a line of kings long before Israel (vv. 31–39), and its chiefs are settled in their own territories (vv. 40–43). Then, with Esau’s line complete, Genesis turns to Jacob, still a sojourner, still waiting.
verseByVerse.theology: The descendants of Esau: his wives, sons and chiefs, the Horite clans he displaced in Seir, and eight kings who reigned in Edom before any king reigned over Israel. Esau leaves Canaan to his brother because the land cannot hold them both.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Amalek, Israel's long enemy, comes from this line (v. 12). Now: the world has its kings and cities early, and God's people have a promise and a tent; and God is not mentioned once in Esau's forty-three verses.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the generations of Esau (that is, Edom). Esau took his wives from the Canaanites: Adah the daughter of Elon the Hittite, Oholibamah the daughter of Anah the daughter of Zibeon the Hivite, and Basemath, Ishmael's daughter, the sister of Nebaioth. And Adah bore to Esau, Eliphaz; Basemath bore Reuel; and Oholibamah bore Jeush, Jalam, and Korah. These are the sons of Esau who were born to him in the land of Canaan. Then Esau took his wives, his sons, his daughters, and all the members of his household, his livestock, all his beasts, and all his property that he had acquired in the land of Canaan. He went into a land away from his brother Jacob. For their possessions were too great for them to dwell together. The land of their sojournings could not support them because of their livestock. So Esau settled in the hill country of Seir. (Esau is Edom.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Esau’s family grows in Canaan, and then he leaves the land of promise for Seir, because the brothers’ wealth is too great for them to live together.

These are the generations of Esau (that is, Edom). “These are the generations of” marks a new section of Genesis (see the introduction). Esau’s other name, Edom (“red”), came from the red stew for which he sold his birthright (25:30). Three times the chapter says, “Esau is Edom” (vv. 1, 8, 19): the man has become a nation.

Esau took his wives from the Canaanites. Marrying Canaanites had grieved his parents (26:34–35; 27:46), and he later married a daughter of Ishmael to please his father (28:8–9). Esau’s family was a blend of peoples from the start, the very thing Abraham had guarded Isaac against (24:3).

Why do the names of Esau’s wives differ? Earlier Esau’s wives are Judith the daughter of Beeri, Basemath the daughter of Elon, and Mahalath the daughter of Ishmael (26:34; 28:9); here they are Adah the daughter of Elon, Oholibamah, and Basemath the daughter of Ishmael. People in the ancient world often had more than one name, and women sometimes took a new name at marriage; Esau may also have had more wives than either list gives. We do not know the exact explanation, and nothing in the story depends on it.

These are the sons of Esau who were born to him in the land of Canaan. Five sons, all born in the land of promise, all to grow up outside it.

He went into a land away from his brother Jacob. Like Abraham and Lot, the brothers part because “the land … could not support them” (13:6). Esau had already spent time in Seir (32:3); now he moves his whole household there. Lot chose the well-watered plain and lost everything; Esau chooses Seir and prospers, but in both cases the one who leaves is the one outside the line of promise. Jacob stays in Canaan as a sojourner (37:1).

So Esau settled in the hill country of Seir. Seir is the rugged mountain country south-east of the Dead Sea. God had told Rebekah, “Two nations are in your womb” (25:23), and Isaac had told Esau, “By your sword you shall live” (27:40). Both words come true: Esau is a nation, settled in a harsh land, and God himself will defend his right to it (Deuteronomy 2:5).

In everyday life. God is good to people outside his covenant family, giving them homes, families and success (Matthew 5:45). That kindness is real, and it should lead them to repentance (Romans 2:4). But it is not the same as belonging to him.

Uncertain wording. In v. 2 (and v. 14) Oholibamah is “the daughter of Anah the daughter of Zibeon”, while v. 24 names Anah as Zibeon’s son. Some ancient translations read “son of Zibeon” in v. 2 as well, and that is probably the meaning: Oholibamah was the daughter of Anah, who was the son of Zibeon.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the generations of Esau the father of the Edomites in the hill country of Seir. These are the names of Esau's sons: Eliphaz the son of Adah the wife of Esau, Reuel the son of Basemath the wife of Esau. The sons of Eliphaz were Teman, Omar, Zepho, Gatam, and Kenaz. (Timna was a concubine of Eliphaz, Esau's son; she bore Amalek to Eliphaz.) These are the sons of Adah, Esau's wife. These are the sons of Reuel: Nahath, Zerah, Shammah, and Mizzah. These are the sons of Basemath, Esau's wife. These are the sons of Oholibamah the daughter of Anah the daughter of Zibeon, Esau's wife: she bore to Esau Jeush, Jalam, and Korah. These are the chiefs of the sons of Esau. The sons of Eliphaz the firstborn of Esau: the chiefs Teman, Omar, Zepho, Kenaz, Korah, Gatam, and Amalek; these are the chiefs of Eliphaz in the land of Edom; these are the sons of Adah. These are the sons of Reuel, Esau's son: the chiefs Nahath, Zerah, Shammah, and Mizzah; these are the chiefs of Reuel in the land of Edom; these are the sons of Basemath, Esau's wife. These are the sons of Oholibamah, Esau's wife: the chiefs Jeush, Jalam, and Korah; these are the chiefs born of Oholibamah the daughter of Anah, Esau's wife. These are the sons of Esau (that is, Edom), and these are their chiefs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Esau’s sons and grandsons become the founding chiefs of Edom’s clans, and among them is Amalek, the ancestor of Israel’s bitterest enemy.

Esau the father of the Edomites in the hill country of Seir. A second heading: the first list (vv. 1–5) belonged to Canaan, this one to Seir. Esau’s family has become a people with a territory.

The sons of Eliphaz were Teman. Teman gave his name to a district of Edom famous for wisdom: “Is wisdom no more in Teman?” asks Jeremiah (49:7). Job’s friend “Eliphaz the Temanite” (Job 2:11) bears the names of both Esau’s firstborn and his grandson, and Job’s homeland, Uz, is a name from this chapter (v. 28; Lamentations 4:21). Job’s story may well be set in or near Edom.

Timna was a concubine of Eliphaz … she bore Amalek to Eliphaz. Timna was a Horite, the sister of the chief Lotan (v. 22). Her son Amalek founded the people who attacked Israel from behind in the wilderness, picking off “those who were lagging behind you” (Deuteronomy 25:18), and against whom the LORD swore war “from generation to generation” (Exodus 17:16). One concubine’s son in a list of names becomes a nation of enemies. Genesis records the seed of later history.

These are the chiefs of the sons of Esau. The word “chief” probably means the head of a clan. Fourteen chiefs (vv. 15–19) from three wives: Esau’s family is organised, powerful and growing, while Jacob’s twelve sons still live in tents.

God at work in a list of names. Lists like this are easy to skip, but they say something. God keeps track of every family, including those outside the covenant line. He promised Esau a nation, and here it is, name by name. The God who “determined allotted periods and the boundaries of their dwelling place” for every nation (Acts 17:26) is the same God who will draw people from every nation to Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the sons of Seir the Horite, the inhabitants of the land: Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah, Dishon, Ezer, and Dishan; these are the chiefs of the Horites, the sons of Seir in the land of Edom. The sons of Lotan were Hori and Hemam; and Lotan's sister was Timna. These are the sons of Shobal: Alvan, Manahath, Ebal, Shepho, and Onam. These are the sons of Zibeon: Aiah and Anah; he is the Anah who found the hot springs in the wilderness, as he pastured the donkeys of Zibeon his father. These are the children of Anah: Dishon and Oholibamah the daughter of Anah. These are the sons of Dishon: Hemdan, Eshban, Ithran, and Cheran. These are the sons of Ezer: Bilhan, Zaavan, and Akan. These are the sons of Dishan: Uz and Aran. These are the chiefs of the Horites: the chiefs Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah, Dishon, Ezer, and Dishan; these are the chiefs of the Horites, chief by chief in the land of Seir.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Horites, the earlier people of Seir, are listed because Esau’s family married into them and took over their land.

These are the sons of Seir the Horite, the inhabitants of the land. Seir was a man’s name before it was a region’s. The Horites lived there in Abraham’s time (14:6). Esau’s descendants later “dispossessed them and destroyed them from before them and settled in their place” (Deuteronomy 2:12). Moses adds that it was the LORD who “destroyed the Horites before them” (Deuteronomy 2:22): God gives lands to nations outside Israel too.

Lotan’s sister was Timna. The concubine of Eliphaz (v. 12), so Amalek was half Horite. And Oholibamah, Esau’s wife, was a Horite too, Anah’s daughter (vv. 2, 25). Edom is Esau’s family absorbed into the people of Seir, the mingling Jacob’s family was tempted to at Shechem (34:9, 16).

He is the Anah who found the hot springs in the wilderness. A small personal detail, preserved in a list: a young man pasturing his father’s donkeys made a discovery people remembered. Scripture is full of real, local life.

The sons of Dishan: Uz and Aran. Uz is the name of Job’s homeland (Job 1:1), which Lamentations links with Edom: “O daughter of Edom, you who dwell in the land of Uz” (Lamentations 4:21).

In everyday life. Whole peoples rise and disappear in this list; the Horites are remembered mainly because Esau married into them. Nations and empires are in God’s hands, and none lasts for ever but his kingdom (Daniel 2:44).

Uncertain wording. The word translated “hot springs” occurs only here, and its meaning is not known. Older translations such as the King James Version have “mules”, following later Jewish tradition; the ancient Latin version has “hot waters”, followed by the ESV. There are hot springs in the region, south-east of the Dead Sea, which makes that the likeliest meaning, but it is not certain.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the kings who reigned in the land of Edom, before any king reigned over the Israelites. Bela the son of Beor reigned in Edom, the name of his city being Dinhabah. Bela died, and Jobab the son of Zerah of Bozrah reigned in his place. Jobab died, and Husham of the land of the Temanites reigned in his place. Husham died, and Hadad the son of Bedad, who defeated Midian in the country of Moab, reigned in his place, the name of his city being Avith. Hadad died, and Samlah of Masrekah reigned in his place. Samlah died, and Shaul of Rehoboth on the Euphrates reigned in his place. Shaul died, and Baal-hanan the son of Achbor reigned in his place. Baal-hanan the son of Achbor died, and Hadar reigned in his place, the name of his city being Pau; his wife's name was Mehetabel, the daughter of Matred, daughter of Mezahab.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Edom had a line of kings long before Israel had any: the older brother’s nation reached greatness first, while the line of promise had to wait for God’s time.

These are the kings who reigned in the land of Edom, before any king reigned over the Israelites. God had just promised Jacob, “kings shall come from your own body” (35:11). Edom gets there first: eight kings in succession while Israel is still a family of shepherds, and then slaves in Egypt, and then wanderers. Israel’s first king, Saul, would reign some centuries later. The line God chose was not the quickest to grow.

Bela the son of Beor reigned in Edom, the name of his city being Dinhabah. Notice that no king is succeeded by his son, and almost every king has a different home city. Edom’s crown passed from one house to another, perhaps by choice of the clan chiefs, perhaps by strength. There was kingship, but no dynasty and no promise.

Jobab the son of Zerah of Bozrah. Bozrah became Edom’s chief city. Isaiah pictured the LORD coming as a warrior from there: “Who is this who comes from Edom, in crimsoned garments from Bozrah … ‘It is I, speaking in righteousness, mighty to save’” (Isaiah 63:1). An ancient addition to the Greek translation of Job identified Job with this Jobab, but there is no good reason to accept it.

Hadad the son of Bedad, who defeated Midian in the country of Moab. Another small piece of history: a battle otherwise unknown, between peoples who will all appear in Israel’s later story.

Shaul of Rehoboth on the Euphrates. The name Shaul is the same as Saul, Israel’s first king.

Edom and Israel’s King. David would subdue Edom (2 Samuel 8:14), fulfilling the word that “the older shall serve the younger” (25:23), and Balaam had foreseen it: “a star shall come out of Jacob, and a scepter shall rise out of Israel … Edom shall be dispossessed” (Numbers 24:17–18). The story of the two brothers ran on to the end. When Jesus was born King of the Jews, the king in Jerusalem was Herod the Great, of Edomite descent, and he tried to kill the child (Matthew 2:16). But the true King conquers in another way. Isaiah’s warrior from Bozrah is red with the blood of his enemies; Christ’s robe is “dipped in blood” (Revelation 19:13), and the blood that won his victory was first his own. Soon people from Idumea, Edom’s land, were coming to hear him (Mark 3:8), and the apostles saw Amos’s promise, that God’s people would possess “the remnant of Edom and all the nations who are called by my name” (Amos 9:12), fulfilled as Gentiles came to Christ (Acts 15:16–17).

In everyday life. It can be hard to watch others reach what God has promised you long before you do, or to see the ungodly flourish while you wait. Edom’s kings came first; Israel’s King was worth waiting for. “Fret not yourself because of evildoers” (Psalm 37:1): God’s timing is not slow, and his promises are not small.

Where Christians differ. Who wrote “before any king reigned over the Israelites”? The phrase seems to have been written after Israel had kings, and some take it as evidence that Genesis was written long after Moses (see the introduction).

This commentary’s view. Moses is the author of the Pentateuch in substance (John 5:46), and a later inspired editor may have added notes like this one. Inspiration covers the whole. Others read it as Moses’ own forward look, since God had already promised Israel kings (17:6; 35:11); that is possible, but the plainer reading is a later note.

Uncertain wording. “Rehoboth on the Euphrates” is literally “Rehoboth of the River”. In the Old Testament “the River” usually means the Euphrates, as the ESV takes it, but the Euphrates is far from Edom, and some think a local river is meant. The exact place is unknown.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the names of the chiefs of Esau, according to their clans and their dwelling places, by their names: the chiefs Timna, Alvah, Jetheth, Oholibamah, Elah, Pinon, Kenaz, Teman, Mibzar, Magdiel, and Iram; these are the chiefs of Edom (that is, Esau, the father of Edom), according to their dwelling places in the land of their possession.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Edom’s chiefs are listed by their territories, settled in their own land, and with that Esau’s story ends and Genesis turns to Jacob.

According to their clans and their dwelling places. This last list may name the districts of Edom by the clans that held them in a later period; several names repeat earlier ones (Timna, Oholibamah, Kenaz, Teman). Either way, it shows Edom organised and settled.

In the land of their possession. This is the last phrase about Esau, and it is pointed. Esau has his land, his “possession”. The very next verse says, “Jacob lived in the land of his father’s sojournings” (37:1). Esau possesses; Jacob sojourns and waits. Jacob’s descendants would wait four hundred years and more for their land (15:13–16).

Christ, the inheritance worth waiting for. The patriarchs lived in tents because “he was looking forward to the city that has foundations, whose designer and builder is God” (Hebrews 11:10). Esau’s possession was real, but it passed: Edom disappeared from history. Those who belong to Christ wait for “an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, kept in heaven for you” (1 Peter 1:4). The one who sold his birthright for a single meal (Hebrews 12:16) is a warning to us not to trade the promised inheritance for what we can have now.

What it does not mean. Esau’s line is not written off as worthless. God gave Edom its land and forbade Israel to take it (Deuteronomy 2:5), and Israel was told, “You shall not abhor an Edomite, for he is your brother” (Deuteronomy 23:7). When Malachi says, “I have loved Jacob but Esau I have hated” (Malachi 1:2–3), and Paul quotes it (Romans 9:13), it speaks of God’s free choice of the line through which the Saviour would come, not of contempt for every Edomite.

In everyday life. Do not envy those who seem to have everything now. Ask instead whether you are holding on to the promise. And pray for those outside God’s family as people he made, sustains and can still bring in.

36.theology:
God’s choice of one people does not mean contempt for others. Esau is not chosen for the covenant line, yet his descendants fill Seir with chiefs, kings and clans. God’s kindness to all people, what theologians call common grace, reaches those outside the covenant too. When Romans 9 quotes “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (from Malachi 1:2–3), it speaks of God’s free choice, made before the twins were born and resting on his purpose, not their works (Rom 9:11–13). Esau’s line lives on, though outside the family line through which the Messiah will come.

The kings of Edom remind us that the world’s kingdoms grow by power and numbers, while God’s kingdom advances in another way: through barren women, younger sons, suffering servants and a crucified King. Edom, with its kings, looks the stronger; a family of landless sojourners produces the Lion of Judah.
36.examples:
God’s silence about someone in this history is not indifference to them. Those who feel outside the main story of what God is doing are not outside his care. The God who numbers the hairs of his people’s heads is also the God who notes that Anah found hot springs in the wilderness.

Human kingdoms come and go; the kingdom of God cannot be shaken (Heb 12:28). The lasting King will come from Judah, Leah’s son, the unloved wife’s son, by a grace that overturns every human reckoning of worth.

keyVerse.quote: These are the kings who reigned in the land of Edom, before any king reigned over the Israelites.
keyVerse.note: The verse sums up the chapter’s quiet point. Esau’s line had kings first; the line of promise waited centuries for its king, and longer still for the King. God’s choice is not measured by who gets there first, and his promised King was worth the wait.

36.reflection:
Genesis gives Esau’s family a whole chapter before turning to Jacob. What does this chapter show about God’s care for people outside his covenant family, and how should that shape the way we think about our unbelieving neighbours?

Edom had chiefs and kings long before Israel had any (v. 31), and Esau possessed his land while Jacob still sojourned (v. 43; 37:1). Where are you tempted to envy those who seem to have everything now, and how does Hebrews 11:10 help?

A single name in this list, Amalek (v. 12), became a nation of enemies to Israel. What does that suggest about the long effects of choices made in one generation?

The story of Jacob and Esau runs on to Herod’s attack on the child in Bethlehem and to people from Edom coming to hear Jesus (Matthew 2:16; Mark 3:8). How does Christ fulfil God’s promises to Jacob while also opening the door to Esau’s descendants?

37.title: Joseph's Dreams
37.text: <sup>1</sup>Jacob lived in the land of his father's sojournings, in the land of Canaan.<sup>2</sup>These are the generations of Jacob. Joseph, being seventeen years old, was pasturing the flock with his brothers. He was a boy with the sons of Bilhah and Zilpah, his father's wives. And Joseph brought a bad report of them to their father.<sup>3</sup>Now Israel loved Joseph more than any other of his sons, because he was the son of his old age. And he made him a robe of many colors.<sup>4</sup>But when his brothers saw that their father loved him more than all his brothers, they hated him and could not speak peacefully to him.<sup>5</sup>Now Joseph had a dream, and when he told it to his brothers they hated him even more.<sup>6</sup>He said to them, "Hear this dream that I have dreamed:<sup>7</sup>Behold, we were binding sheaves in the field, and behold, my sheaf arose and stood upright. And behold, your sheaves gathered around it and bowed down to my sheaf."<sup>8</sup>His brothers said to him, "Are you indeed to reign over us? Or are you indeed to rule over us?" So they hated him even more for his dreams and for his words.<sup>9</sup>Then he dreamed another dream and told it to his brothers and said, "Behold, I have dreamed another dream. Behold, the sun, the moon, and eleven stars were bowing down to me."<sup>10</sup>But when he told it to his father and to his brothers, his father rebuked him and said to him, "What is this dream that you have dreamed? Shall I and your mother and your brothers indeed come to bow ourselves to the ground before you?"<sup>11</sup>And his brothers were jealous of him, but his father kept the saying in mind.<sup>12</sup>Now his brothers went to pasture their father's flock near Shechem.<sup>13</sup>And Israel said to Joseph, "Are not your brothers pasturing the flock at Shechem? Come, I will send you to them." And he said to him, "Here I am."<sup>14</sup>So he said to him, "Go now, see if it is well with your brothers and with the flock, and bring me word." So he sent him from the Valley of Hebron, and he came to Shechem.<sup>15</sup>And a man found him wandering in the fields. And the man asked him, "What are you seeking?"<sup>16</sup>"I am seeking my brothers," he said. "Tell me, please, where they are pasturing the flock."<sup>17</sup>And the man said, "They have gone away, for I heard them say, 'Let us go to Dothan.'" So Joseph went after his brothers and found them at Dothan.<sup>18</sup>They saw him from afar, and before he came near to them they conspired against him to kill him.<sup>19</sup>They said to one another, "Here comes this dreamer.<sup>20</sup>Come now, let us kill him and throw him into one of the pits. Then we will say that a fierce animal has devoured him, and we will see what will become of his dreams."<sup>21</sup>But when Reuben heard it, he rescued him out of their hands, saying, "Let us not take his life."<sup>22</sup>And Reuben said to them, "Shed no blood; throw him into this pit here in the wilderness, but do not lay a hand on him"— that he might rescue him out of their hand to restore him to his father.<sup>23</sup>So when Joseph came to his brothers, they stripped him of his robe, the robe of many colors that he wore.<sup>24</sup>And they took him and threw him into a pit. The pit was empty; there was no water in it.<sup>25</sup>Then they sat down to eat. And looking up they saw a caravan of Ishmaelites coming from Gilead, with their camels bearing gum, balm, and myrrh, on their way to carry it down to Egypt.<sup>26</sup>Then Judah said to his brothers, "What profit is it if we kill our brother and conceal his blood?<sup>27</sup>Come, let us sell him to the Ishmaelites, and let not our hand be upon him, for he is our brother, our own flesh." And his brothers listened to him.<sup>28</sup>Then Midianite traders passed by. And they drew Joseph up and lifted him out of the pit, and sold him to the Ishmaelites for twenty shekels of silver. They took Joseph to Egypt.<sup>29</sup>When Reuben returned to the pit and saw that Joseph was not in the pit, he tore his clothes<sup>30</sup>and returned to his brothers and said, "The boy is gone, and I, where shall I go?"<sup>31</sup>Then they took Joseph's robe and slaughtered a goat and dipped the robe in the blood.<sup>32</sup>And they sent the robe of many colors and brought it to their father and said, "This we have found; please identify whether it is your son's robe or not."<sup>33</sup>And he identified it and said, "It is my son's robe. A fierce animal has devoured him. Joseph is without doubt torn to pieces."<sup>34</sup>Then Jacob tore his garments and put sackcloth on his loins and mourned for his son many days.<sup>35</sup>All his sons and all his daughters rose up to comfort him, but he refused to be comforted and said, "No, I shall go down to Sheol to my son, mourning." Thus his father wept for him.<sup>36</sup>Meanwhile the Midianites had sold him in Egypt to Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh, the captain of the guard.
37.overview:
Where we are. Jacob is home in Canaan at last. He has wrestled with God, been renamed Israel, made peace with Esau and buried Rachel (chapters 32–35). The heading “These are the generations of Jacob” (v. 2) opens the last and longest section of Genesis, the story of his sons, and above all of Joseph.

The message. God has spoken his purpose, and no human hatred can stop it. Joseph’s brothers try to kill his dreams by getting rid of the dreamer, and every step they take to bury the dream carries it forward: the pit, the caravan and the slave market all lead to Egypt, where the dreams will come true. God is not named once in the chapter, yet he is at work in every line of it.

Why it was said. Israel in the wilderness needed to know how their family came to be slaves in Egypt (see the introduction). The answer begins here, and it is humbling: with favouritism, envy and a brother sold for silver. The tribes learned that their nation was born not from heroes but from God’s faithfulness to sinners.

How the chapter makes its case. Jacob’s favouritism and a special robe make the brothers hate Joseph (vv. 1–4). Joseph dreams twice that his family will bow to him, and their hatred turns to jealousy (vv. 5–11). Sent by his father to check on them, he follows them to Dothan (vv. 12–17). They plot to kill him; Reuben talks them into a pit instead (vv. 18–22). They strip him, throw him in, and sit down to eat (vv. 23–25). Judah proposes selling him, and he is sold for twenty shekels (vv. 26–28). Reuben finds the pit empty (vv. 29–30); the brothers deceive their father with a bloodied robe, and Jacob refuses to be comforted (vv. 31–35). Meanwhile Joseph is sold to Potiphar in Egypt (v. 36).

Where it leads. By pattern, and by the character of God. Joseph is not a symbol but a real man, yet God shaped his life into a foreshadowing of his Son: the father’s beloved son, sent to his brothers, hated without cause, stripped, sold for silver, handed to Gentiles, and in the end raised to rule and to save the very people who rejected him. Jesus told the same story of himself (Matthew 21:38). And the God who turned the brothers’ crime into the saving of many lives turned the worst crime of all, the cross, into salvation for the world (Acts 2:23).

For us. Favouritism, envy and contempt can tear a family apart, and this chapter does not pretend otherwise. But no one can sin God’s purposes out of existence. If you are in the pit, wronged by those closest to you, God is not absent because he is silent; and if you are among the brothers, the God who later forgave them offers you the same mercy in Christ.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Joseph’s dreams of rule set his brothers against him, and their attempt to destroy the dreamer becomes the road by which God will fulfil the dreams. Favouritism and a special robe breed hatred (vv. 1–4); two dreams of bowing sheaves and stars turn hatred into jealousy (vv. 5–11). Sent to check on his brothers, Joseph is seen far off at Dothan, plotted against, stripped, thrown into a dry pit and sold for twenty shekels, while Reuben’s secret rescue comes too late (vv. 12–30). The bloodied robe deceives Jacob, who refuses to be comforted, and the chapter closes with one word of hope: “meanwhile” Joseph is already in Egypt, in the house of Pharaoh’s officer (vv. 31–36).
verseByVerse.theology: Jacob loves Joseph more than his brothers and makes him a robe; Joseph dreams of sheaves and stars bowing to him. Sent to his brothers, he is stripped and thrown into a dry pit while they eat, then sold for twenty shekels to traders. The brothers show Jacob the robe dipped in goat's blood, and he refuses comfort; Joseph is sold to Potiphar.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the beloved son sent to his brothers is rejected, as Christ "came to his own, and his own people did not receive him" (John 1:11). Now: God is not mentioned once in the chapter, yet he is at work in every line of it (50:20).

verseByVerse.quote: Jacob lived in the land of his father's sojournings, in the land of Canaan. These are the generations of Jacob. Joseph, being seventeen years old, was pasturing the flock with his brothers. He was a boy with the sons of Bilhah and Zilpah, his father's wives. And Joseph brought a bad report of them to their father. Now Israel loved Joseph more than any other of his sons, because he was the son of his old age. And he made him a robe of many colors. But when his brothers saw that their father loved him more than all his brothers, they hated him and could not speak peacefully to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jacob settles in Canaan, and the story turns to his sons, where his open favouritism for Joseph, marked by a special robe, makes the brothers hate him.

Jacob lived in the land of his father’s sojournings. Isaac had lived in Canaan as a resident foreigner, owning only a grave. Jacob lives there the same way: the land is promised, not yet possessed. In contrast, Esau’s line has just settled in its own land with its own chiefs (36:6–8, 43).

These are the generations of Jacob. This heading opens the last of the ten sections of Genesis (see the introduction). Though it is Jacob’s “generations”, the story centres on Joseph, with Judah as the other main character, for these two sons will carry the family’s future.

Joseph brought a bad report of them to their father. The sons of Bilhah and Zilpah were the servant-wives’ sons, perhaps already treated as second rank. Joseph’s report may have been honest, and the brothers’ later conduct suggests there was plenty to report, but it was unwise, and the word used usually describes an unfavourable, even slanted, report. A seventeen-year-old reporting on his older brothers to a father who already favours him is not a recipe for peace.

Israel loved Joseph more than any other of his sons. Jacob repeats his parents’ mistake: Isaac loved Esau and Rebekah loved Jacob (25:28). Joseph was “the son of his old age” and, more to the point, the firstborn of Rachel, the wife Jacob loved (29:30). The love passed from mother to son.

He made him a robe. Whatever its exact form (see below), the robe was a public sign of favour, perhaps of a rank above his brothers, and it marked Joseph out every day. Clothing becomes a thread through the Joseph story: the robe is stripped and dipped in blood (vv. 23, 31), a garment is left in the hands of Potiphar’s wife (39:12), and Pharaoh clothes him in fine linen (41:42).

They hated him and could not speak peacefully to him. Literally they could not speak to him “for peace” (shalom): not even a civil greeting. Hatred has settled into the family before any dream is told.

In everyday life. Favouritism breeds hatred in families. Parents often feel more drawn to one child than another; what this chapter warns against is showing it, rewarding it and building the family around it. And children who have been passed over need to know that the heavenly Father has no favourites among his children (Romans 2:11), and loves each one fully in Christ.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew for Joseph’s robe (ketonet passim) is uncertain, as the note on the verse says. The older translations, following the Greek, have “many colors”; many modern scholars think the word refers to its length: a robe reaching to the wrists and ankles, with long sleeves. Either way it was a costly garment, unsuited to work in the fields: the same phrase is used of the robe worn by King David’s daughters (2 Samuel 13:18).
verseByVerse.note: The meaning of the Hebrew for Joseph’s robe is uncertain: perhaps “of many colors” or “with long sleeves” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: Now Joseph had a dream, and when he told it to his brothers they hated him even more. He said to them, "Hear this dream that I have dreamed: Behold, we were binding sheaves in the field, and behold, my sheaf arose and stood upright. And behold, your sheaves gathered around it and bowed down to my sheaf." His brothers said to him, "Are you indeed to reign over us? Or are you indeed to rule over us?" So they hated him even more for his dreams and for his words. Then he dreamed another dream and told it to his brothers and said, "Behold, I have dreamed another dream. Behold, the sun, the moon, and eleven stars were bowing down to me." But when he told it to his father and to his brothers, his father rebuked him and said to him, "What is this dream that you have dreamed? Shall I and your mother and your brothers indeed come to bow ourselves to the ground before you?" And his brothers were jealous of him, but his father kept the saying in mind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God gives Joseph two dreams that his family will bow to him; Joseph tells them, his brothers hate him all the more, and his father rebukes him but does not forget.

Joseph had a dream. The dreams are from God and they will come true: the brothers will bow before him in Egypt (42:6; 43:26; 50:18). In Genesis God often speaks by dreams (20:3; 28:12; 31:24), and dreams come in pairs in the Joseph story: Joseph’s two, the cupbearer’s and baker’s, Pharaoh’s two. Joseph will later explain why: “the doubling of Pharaoh’s dream means that the thing is fixed by God” (41:32).

Hear this dream that I have dreamed. Was Joseph wrong to tell it? He may simply have been passing on what God showed him, but the eager “Hear this” and the repeated “Behold” sound like youthful pride, and telling it to brothers who already hated him showed little wisdom. God’s purpose did not depend on Joseph’s good judgment; it went ahead in spite of his immaturity, and in time humbled and matured him.

Are you indeed to reign over us? The brothers understand the dream at once: rule. Their question, meant as mockery, states exactly what God intends. They hate him “for his dreams and for his words”, both what he dreamed and how he told it.

The sun, the moon, and eleven stars were bowing down to me. The second dream raises the stakes: not only the brothers but the parents will bow. Jacob reads it that way at once.

Shall I and your mother …? Rachel has died (35:19). Jacob may be thinking of Leah or Bilhah as the mother of the household, or treating the dream’s pictures as standing for the whole family. Dreams are pictures, not photographs, and the point is plain: the whole house of Israel will one day depend on Joseph.

His brothers were jealous of him, but his father kept the saying in mind. Jealousy and pondering are two ways of hearing God’s word. Jacob rebukes Joseph aloud, yet he “kept the saying in mind”, much as Mary later treasured up what she was told about her son and pondered it (Luke 2:19). Stephen named the brothers’ jealousy as the root of what followed: “the patriarchs, jealous of Joseph, sold him into Egypt; but God was with him” (Acts 7:9).

In everyday life. What God has given us, whether gifts, calling or blessing, can be held humbly or flaunted. Joseph had to learn the difference in a pit and a prison. If God has shown you something good, you do not have to announce it to those who already resent you.

verseByVerse.quote: Now his brothers went to pasture their father's flock near Shechem. And Israel said to Joseph, "Are not your brothers pasturing the flock at Shechem? Come, I will send you to them." And he said to him, "Here I am." So he said to him, "Go now, see if it is well with your brothers and with the flock, and bring me word." So he sent him from the Valley of Hebron, and he came to Shechem. And a man found him wandering in the fields. And the man asked him, "What are you seeking?" "I am seeking my brothers," he said. "Tell me, please, where they are pasturing the flock." And the man said, "They have gone away, for I heard them say, 'Let us go to Dothan.'" So Joseph went after his brothers and found them at Dothan.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jacob sends Joseph, willing and unsuspecting, to see how his brothers are, and a stranger who happens to know where they went points him on to Dothan.

Near Shechem. Shechem was where Simeon and Levi had massacred the men of the city (chapter 34). Jacob may have had reason to worry about his sons pasturing there, and the city lay some fifty miles north of Hebron, several days’ walk.

Come, I will send you to them. Jacob seems blind to the danger, sending the hated son alone, wearing the robe (v. 23), to brothers who cannot speak a civil word to him. He sends him to ask whether it is “well” (shalom) with them, the very thing they could not offer him (v. 4).

Here I am. Joseph’s “Here I am” is willing obedience, the same reply Abraham gave when God called him to Moriah (22:1, 11). The father sends the son he loves, and the son goes.

A man found him wandering in the fields. A stranger who happens to be in the right place and happens to have overheard the brothers keeps the story moving. Some have thought him an angel, but the text says only “a man”. That is the point: providence works in small, ordinary details, in a chance meeting in a field.

Let us go to Dothan. Dothan lay about fifteen miles further north, beside the trade route from Gilead down to the coast and Egypt (v. 25). Had Joseph turned home at Shechem, there would have been no pit and no caravan.

verseByVerse.quote: They saw him from afar, and before he came near to them they conspired against him to kill him. They said to one another, "Here comes this dreamer. Come now, let us kill him and throw him into one of the pits. Then we will say that a fierce animal has devoured him, and we will see what will become of his dreams." But when Reuben heard it, he rescued him out of their hands, saying, "Let us not take his life." And Reuben said to them, "Shed no blood; throw him into this pit here in the wilderness, but do not lay a hand on him"— that he might rescue him out of their hand to restore him to his father.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seeing Joseph far off, the brothers plot to kill him and so put an end to his dreams, but Reuben persuades them to throw him alive into a pit, meaning to rescue him later.

They saw him from afar. The robe would be recognisable at a distance. Before he even reaches them, they have decided.

Here comes this dreamer. Literally “this master of dreams”, a sneer. The contempt has grown from hatred to murder, exactly the path Jesus traced: anger in the heart is murder in seed (Matthew 5:21–22), and “everyone who hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3:15).

Come now, let us kill him. Generations later Jesus told a parable about a vineyard owner who sent his beloved son to the tenants, and they said, “This is the heir. Come, let us kill him and have his inheritance” (Matthew 21:38). The echo is unmistakable. Those who refuse a son’s right to rule over them try to remove him, and God overturns their plan.

We will see what will become of his dreams. The mocking words are exactly what God will answer. The rest of Genesis is the reply: they will see what becomes of his dreams, as they bow before him in Egypt.

But when Reuben heard it, he rescued him. Reuben, the firstborn, carried responsibility for the brothers. He may also have been hoping to recover his standing with his father after sleeping with Bilhah (35:22). His plan is secret: he does not openly oppose the others but steers them toward a pit, “that he might rescue him out of their hand”.

Shed no blood. Shedding a brother’s blood was the sin of Cain (4:10–11) and carried God’s judgment (9:6). The brothers grasp at a way to be rid of him without blood on their hands, as if leaving a man to die in a pit were different.
verseByVerse.note: The “pits” were cisterns (ESV note) cut into rock to store rainwater.

verseByVerse.quote: So when Joseph came to his brothers, they stripped him of his robe, the robe of many colors that he wore. And they took him and threw him into a pit. The pit was empty; there was no water in it. Then they sat down to eat. And looking up they saw a caravan of Ishmaelites coming from Gilead, with their camels bearing gum, balm, and myrrh, on their way to carry it down to Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The brothers strip Joseph of his robe, throw him into a dry cistern, and calmly sit down to eat while he pleads for his life.

They stripped him of his robe. The robe, the sign of his father’s favour, is the first thing they attack. Stripping a man was also a deliberate humiliation. The beloved son is stripped before he is sold, as Jesus was stripped before he was crucified (Matthew 27:28, 35).

The pit was empty; there was no water in it. A cistern cut into the rock to store rainwater (see the note on vv. 18–22), bell-shaped and impossible to climb out of. With no water, a man would not drown, but he would die slowly of thirst. Prisoners were sometimes held in such pits: Jeremiah was let down into a muddy one (Jeremiah 38:6).

Then they sat down to eat. The coldness is chilling. We learn later that Joseph was pleading with them from the pit: “we saw the distress of his soul, when he begged us and we did not listen” (42:21). Centuries later Amos rebuked the comfortable rulers of Israel who feasted “but are not grieved over the ruin of Joseph” (Amos 6:6), using Joseph’s name for the northern tribes, and perhaps remembering this meal.

A caravan of Ishmaelites coming from Gilead. Dothan lay near the trade road that ran from Gilead, east of the Jordan, down to the coast and on to Egypt, so a caravan was a likely sight. Its gum, balm and myrrh were valued in Egypt for medicine and embalming. Its arrival at that very moment is one more ordinary event God uses.
verseByVerse.note: Gilead lay east of the Jordan; caravans carried spices to Egypt.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Judah said to his brothers, "What profit is it if we kill our brother and conceal his blood? Come, let us sell him to the Ishmaelites, and let not our hand be upon him, for he is our brother, our own flesh." And his brothers listened to him. Then Midianite traders passed by. And they drew Joseph up and lifted him out of the pit, and sold him to the Ishmaelites for twenty shekels of silver. They took Joseph to Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah proposes selling Joseph instead of killing him, and Joseph is sold to the traders for twenty shekels of silver and taken to Egypt.

What profit is it if we kill our brother and conceal his blood? Judah’s argument is greed, not mercy. Killing Joseph would gain them nothing; selling him would gain them silver, and they would be rid of him just the same. “He is our brother, our own flesh” sounds tender, but it is used to justify selling him into slavery. Judah will need to change, and the next chapter begins to show how.

Midianite traders … sold him to the Ishmaelites. The traders are called both Ishmaelites and Midianites; the terms overlapped, and in Judges the Midianites are said to wear gold earrings “because they were Ishmaelites” (Judges 8:24). “Ishmaelites” may describe their way of life, travelling traders, more than their ancestry.

Twenty shekels of silver. Twenty shekels was about the going price for a young slave at the time, and later the value Moses’ law put on a boy of Joseph’s age (Leviticus 27:5). Jesus would be sold for thirty pieces of silver (Matthew 26:15), the price of a slave in the law (Exodus 21:32). Both beloved sons were priced as slaves by those who should have loved them.

They took Joseph to Egypt. Joseph goes down to Egypt as a slave. Seven chapters later his whole family will follow him there, and their descendants will become slaves in Egypt too (Exodus 1). God had already told Abraham that his offspring would be “sojourners in a land that is not theirs” and would be afflicted there (15:13).

Who sold Joseph? Verse 28 could be read to say that the Midianites, not the brothers, pulled Joseph out and sold him. Some scholars take this as a sign of two stories stitched together. But “they” most naturally means the brothers, who had just agreed to Judah’s plan, and Joseph himself later says plainly, “I am your brother, Joseph, whom you sold into Egypt” (45:4).
verseByVerse.note: Twenty shekels was about 8 ounces of silver (ESV note: a shekel was about 2/5 ounce).

verseByVerse.quote: When Reuben returned to the pit and saw that Joseph was not in the pit, he tore his clothes and returned to his brothers and said, "The boy is gone, and I, where shall I go?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Reuben comes back to rescue Joseph and finds the pit empty; his secret plan has failed, and he is left in despair.

He tore his clothes. Tearing one’s clothes was the sign of grief and horror (v. 34; 44:13; see mourning customs).

The boy is gone, and I, where shall I go? Reuben returns too late. He had planned a secret rescue, not open opposition, and half-hearted courage fails. As the firstborn he expected to answer to his father, and his cry is partly for Joseph and partly for himself. Yet he goes along with the cover-up that follows.

In everyday life. Good intentions kept private are no substitute for standing up openly for what is right. Reuben meant well and achieved nothing; it is often in the moment, before the group, that courage counts.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they took Joseph's robe and slaughtered a goat and dipped the robe in the blood. And they sent the robe of many colors and brought it to their father and said, "This we have found; please identify whether it is your son's robe or not." And he identified it and said, "It is my son's robe. A fierce animal has devoured him. Joseph is without doubt torn to pieces." Then Jacob tore his garments and put sackcloth on his loins and mourned for his son many days. All his sons and all his daughters rose up to comfort him, but he refused to be comforted and said, "No, I shall go down to Sheol to my son, mourning." Thus his father wept for him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The brothers deceive their father with Joseph’s robe dipped in goat’s blood, and Jacob, believing Joseph torn by a wild animal, mourns and refuses all comfort.

They took Joseph’s robe and slaughtered a goat. Jacob once deceived his blind father with a goat’s skins and his brother’s clothing (27:9, 15–16); now his own sons deceive him with a goat’s blood and his son’s clothing. What he sowed, he reaps, and the deceit passes down a generation.

Please identify whether it is your son’s robe or not. They do not tell a lie in words; they let the bloodied robe speak, and let their father draw the conclusion. Deceiving by implication is still deceiving. The same word, “identify”, will return in the next chapter, when Tamar sends Judah his own pledge and says, “Please identify whose these are” (38:25).
