A fierce animal has devoured him. Jacob says exactly what the brothers planned to say (v. 20). They never have to say it themselves.

Jacob tore his garments and put sackcloth on his loins. Sackcloth, a rough cloth of goat’s hair, was the dress of mourning. He “mourned for his son many days”: his grief will last more than twenty years, until Joseph is found alive (45:26–28).

All his sons and all his daughters rose up to comfort him. Only one daughter, Dinah, is named, so “daughters” probably includes his sons’ wives. The sons who caused the grief now offer comfort, keeping their secret, and must live with it for twenty years (42:21–22).

He refused to be comforted. Jacob’s grief is real and the story does not rebuke it. Jeremiah would later picture Rachel, Joseph’s mother, weeping for her lost children and refusing “to be comforted for her children” (Jeremiah 31:15), and Matthew hears that cry again at Bethlehem (Matthew 2:18).

I shall go down to Sheol to my son, mourning. Sheol is the Old Testament name for the place of the dead (see the note on the verse). Jacob expects to grieve until he dies. He will say the same again when Benjamin is threatened (42:38).

In everyday life. The sins we commit can come back through our children. But God can break the pattern, as he will in this family, where the brothers who sold Joseph will one day bow before him, confess, and be forgiven (50:17–21).
verseByVerse.note: Sheol is the Old Testament name for the place of the dead.

verseByVerse.quote: Meanwhile the Midianites had sold him in Egypt to Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh, the captain of the guard.
verseByVerse.commentary:
While Jacob mourns, Joseph is already in Egypt, sold to Potiphar, one of Pharaoh’s officers: God is at work in the “meanwhile”.

Meanwhile. While Jacob mourns, God is already at work in Egypt, as he works in the “meanwhile” of every believer’s life. The verse ties the story to chapter 39, which picks it up again after the account of Judah (39:1).

Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh, the captain of the guard. Joseph has not been sold to any household but to a high official of Pharaoh’s court. “Captain of the guard” is literally “chief of the slaughterers”, perhaps the commander of the royal bodyguard, and his house includes the prison where the king’s prisoners are kept (40:3). The road from the pit to the throne runs through exactly this house.

Joseph and Christ. Beloved of his father, hated by his brothers, sold for silver, exalted to save many: Joseph is a living foreshadowing of Christ. Stephen tells Joseph’s story in a way that points straight to Jesus: rejected by his brothers, yet “God was with him” (Acts 7:9–10).

Where Christians differ: is Joseph a picture of Christ? Many interpreters, ancient and modern, have seen Joseph as one of the clearest foreshadowings of Christ in the Old Testament. Others urge caution, because the New Testament never explicitly calls Joseph a type of Christ, and they read the story chiefly as a lesson in providence and character.

This commentary’s view. Joseph is a real man and his story is first about providence and repentance, but God so ordered his life that it foreshadows his Son, and Stephen’s retelling (Acts 7:9–14) invites us to see it. The likeness is in the pattern the story itself gives (the rejected brother who becomes the saviour), not in fanciful details.

37.theology:
Joseph is the fullest portrait of Christ in the Old Testament: the beloved son of his father (Matt 3:17), sent to his brothers (John 1:11), hated without cause (John 15:25), stripped of his garments (Matt 27:28), sold for silver, handed over to Gentiles, falsely accused, imprisoned, and finally raised to the ruler’s right hand, where he saves the brothers who rejected him (Acts 2:23, 36; Rom 11:11–15).

Joseph is not an allegory, a mere symbol of Christ. He is a real man, and God so ordered his real life that it foreshadowed the one who was to come, as God directs all history toward his Son. The pattern of the rejected brother who becomes the saviour runs through Scripture.

God’s silence in the story is itself a lesson. The caravan passes at the very moment needed; a nameless man knows where the brothers went; Reuben’s rescue fails at the crucial moment. God works through ordinary events and choices, not around them.
37.examples:
Joseph’s descent into the pit and into Egypt is the experience of every believer wronged by those closest to them, family, church or colleagues, who watches things get worse before God acts. This story is written for those in the pit: God is present there, even when he seems silent, and what looks like the end is the beginning of the journey toward the throne.

Joseph’s suffering is real; he weeps again and again (42:24; 45:2, 14; 46:29) and never pretends the pain away. Only at the end can he say, “you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good” (50:20). Those words cannot be said at the start of the story. In the middle, our calling is to stay faithful, held up by the God who was with Joseph (39:2) and is with us in the pit.

keyVerse.quote: “Come now, let us kill him and throw him into one of the pits. Then we will say that a fierce animal has devoured him, and we will see what will become of his dreams.”
keyVerse.note: The brothers mean to bury God’s word with the dreamer, and their mocking question is the one the rest of Genesis answers. Every step they take to destroy the dreams carries Joseph toward their fulfilment. It shows the pattern that reaches its height at the cross, where human hatred did its worst and God brought salvation out of it.

37.reflection:
Jacob’s favouritism and Joseph’s tactlessness both feed the brothers’ hatred (vv. 2–11). Where do you see similar patterns in families or churches, and how does the gospel speak to the favoured and the overlooked?

The brothers move from hatred, to jealousy, to plotting murder, to eating a meal beside the pit (vv. 4, 11, 18, 25). How does Jesus’ teaching on anger (Matthew 5:21–22) help us see where small resentments can lead?

God is never mentioned in this chapter, yet a stranger in a field and a passing caravan move the story on (vv. 15–17, 25). Where have you seen God at work through ordinary events you only understood later?

Joseph is the beloved son sent to his brothers, rejected and sold for silver (vv. 13, 28). How does his story help you see what Jesus suffered, and what he went on to do for those who rejected him?

38.title: Judah and Tamar
38.text: <sup>1</sup>It happened at that time that Judah went down from his brothers and turned aside to a certain Adullamite, whose name was Hirah.<sup>2</sup>There Judah saw the daughter of a certain Canaanite whose name was Shua. He took her and went in to her,<sup>3</sup>and she conceived and bore a son, and he called his name Er.<sup>4</sup>She conceived again and bore a son, and she called his name Onan.<sup>5</sup>Yet again she bore a son, and she called his name Shelah. Judah was in Chezib when she bore him.<sup>6</sup>And Judah took a wife for Er his firstborn, and her name was Tamar.<sup>7</sup>But Er, Judah's firstborn, was wicked in the sight of the LORD, and the LORD put him to death.<sup>8</sup>Then Judah said to Onan, "Go in to your brother's wife and perform the duty of a brother-in-law to her, and raise up offspring for your brother."<sup>9</sup>But Onan knew that the offspring would not be his. So whenever he went in to his brother's wife he would waste the semen on the ground, so as not to give offspring to his brother.<sup>10</sup>And what he did was wicked in the sight of the LORD, and he put him to death also.<sup>11</sup>Then Judah said to Tamar his daughter-in-law, "Remain a widow in your father's house, till Shelah my son grows up"—for he feared that he would die, like his brothers. So Tamar went and remained in her father's house.<sup>12</sup>In the course of time the wife of Judah, Shua's daughter, died. When Judah was comforted, he went up to Timnah to his sheepshearers, he and his friend Hirah the Adullamite.<sup>13</sup>And when Tamar was told, "Your father-in-law is going up to Timnah to shear his sheep,"<sup>14</sup>she took off her widow's garments and covered herself with a veil, wrapping herself up, and sat at the entrance to Enaim, which is on the road to Timnah. For she saw that Shelah was grown up, and she had not been given to him in marriage.<sup>15</sup>When Judah saw her, he thought she was a prostitute, for she had covered her face.<sup>16</sup>He turned to her at the roadside and said, "Come, let me come in to you," for he did not know that she was his daughter-in-law. She said, "What will you give me, that you may come in to me?"<sup>17</sup>He answered, "I will send you a young goat from the flock." And she said, "If you give me a pledge, until you send it—"<sup>18</sup>He said, "What pledge shall I give you?" She replied, "Your signet and your cord and your staff that is in your hand." So he gave them to her and went in to her, and she conceived by him.<sup>19</sup>Then she arose and went away, and taking off her veil she put on the garments of her widowhood.<sup>20</sup>When Judah sent the young goat by his friend the Adullamite to take back the pledge from the woman's hand, he did not find her.<sup>21</sup>And he asked the men of the place, "Where is the cult prostitute who was at Enaim at the roadside?" And they said, "No cult prostitute has been here."<sup>22</sup>So he returned to Judah and said, "I have not found her. Also, the men of the place said, 'No cult prostitute has been here.'"<sup>23</sup>And Judah replied, "Let her keep the things as her own, or we shall be laughed at. You see, I sent this young goat, and you did not find her."<sup>24</sup>About three months later Judah was told, "Tamar your daughter-in-law has been immoral. Moreover, she is pregnant by immorality." And Judah said, "Bring her out, and let her be burned."<sup>25</sup>As she was being brought out, she sent word to her father-in-law, "By the man to whom these belong, I am pregnant." And she said, "Please identify whose these are, the signet and the cord and the staff."<sup>26</sup>Then Judah identified them and said, "She is more righteous than I, since I did not give her to my son Shelah." And he did not know her again.<sup>27</sup>When the time of her labor came, there were twins in her womb.<sup>28</sup>And when she was in labor, one put out a hand, and the midwife took and tied a scarlet thread on his hand, saying, "This one came out first."<sup>29</sup>But as he drew back his hand, behold, his brother came out. And she said, "What a breach you have made for yourself!" Therefore his name was called Perez.<sup>30</sup>Afterward his brother came out with the scarlet thread on his hand, and his name was called Zerah.
38.overview:
Where we are. Joseph has just been sold into Egypt on Judah’s suggestion (37:26–28), and Jacob is mourning a son he believes dead. Before the story follows Joseph down to Egypt, it turns aside to follow Judah, the brother who proposed the sale. Its place between chapters 37 and 39 is deliberate.

The message. The family through whom God promised to bless the world is in moral collapse, and the son who will carry the royal line is the worst of it. Judah drifts from his brothers, marries into Canaan, breaks his word to his widowed daughter-in-law and sleeps with a woman he takes for a prostitute. Yet God does not abandon the line. He preserves it through a wronged woman’s desperate act and begins to change Judah through a humiliating confession: “She is more righteous than I.”

Why it was said. Judah became the leading tribe of Israel, the tribe of David’s kings (see the introduction). Its first hearers learned that their royal line began not in heroism but in scandal and grace, and that Perez, the ancestor of David (Ruth 4:18–22), was born of Judah’s sin and Tamar’s courage.

How the chapter makes its case. Judah leaves his brothers, marries a Canaanite and has three sons (vv. 1–5). The LORD puts the first two to death for their wickedness, Onan for refusing to give his dead brother an heir, and Judah sends Tamar home with a promise he does not mean to keep (vv. 6–11). Years later, seeing she has been abandoned, Tamar disguises herself by the road; Judah takes her for a prostitute and leaves his seal, cord and staff as a pledge (vv. 12–19). His friend cannot find her, and Judah drops the matter to save face (vv. 20–23). When Tamar is found pregnant, Judah orders her burned, until she produces his pledge, and he confesses (vv. 24–26). She bears twins, and the younger, Perez, breaks out first (vv. 27–30).

Where it leads. By promise, and by the need it exposes. The sceptre will be promised to Judah (49:10), and from Perez comes David and, in time, Jesus: Matthew names Tamar in the first lines of his genealogy (Matthew 1:3). The chapter shows how badly the royal line needed a better King, and how far God’s grace will stoop to bring him. And the change that begins in Judah here will lead to the day he offers himself as a substitute for his brother (44:33), a faint early shadow of the Son of Judah who gave himself for us.

For us. God does not wait for respectable people before he works, and our shameful chapters are not too dark for his grace. Be quick to own your sin before you condemn others’ sin. And if you have been failed by those who should have protected you, God sees, remembers, and can write even that into his story.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: While Joseph goes down to Egypt, Judah goes down from his brothers, and his failure, and the first sign of his change, threaten and then carry forward the line of promise. He marries a Canaanite and has three sons; the LORD puts the wicked Er and Onan to death, and Judah sends the widowed Tamar away with a hollow promise (vv. 1–11). Abandoned, Tamar disguises herself and conceives by Judah, keeping his seal, cord and staff (vv. 12–23). When he orders her burned, she produces the pledge, and Judah confesses, “She is more righteous than I” (vv. 24–26). Her twin sons end the chapter with the younger breaking out first: Perez, the ancestor of David and of Christ (vv. 27–30).
verseByVerse.theology: Judah goes down from his brothers and marries a Canaanite. God puts to death his wicked sons Er and Onan, and Judah sends Tamar home, withholding Shelah. Tamar veils herself by the road to Timnah; Judah takes her for a prostitute and leaves his seal, cord and staff. When he orders her burned, she asks him to identify them, and he says, "She is more righteous than I." She bears Perez and Zerah.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: "please identify" is the phrase Judah and his brothers used over Joseph's bloodied robe (37:32), and now it is turned on him. Now: God's line to the Messiah runs through this chapter, not around it.

verseByVerse.quote: It happened at that time that Judah went down from his brothers and turned aside to a certain Adullamite, whose name was Hirah. There Judah saw the daughter of a certain Canaanite whose name was Shua. He took her and went in to her, and she conceived and bore a son, and he called his name Er. She conceived again and bore a son, and she called his name Onan. Yet again she bore a son, and she called his name Shelah. Judah was in Chezib when she bore him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah leaves his brothers, settles among the Canaanites, marries a Canaanite woman and has three sons.

It happened at that time. The story is set just after the sale of Joseph. The chapter covers many years, enough for Judah’s sons to grow up and marry, so it runs alongside Joseph’s years in Egypt and perhaps begins a little earlier. The point of placing it here is the contrast: while Joseph is faithful as a slave (chapter 39), the free and prosperous Judah is falling apart.

Judah went down from his brothers. Joseph “had been brought down” to Egypt (39:1); Judah “went down” of his own accord. He is moving away from God’s people in heart as well as in place. Adullam lay in the lowlands south-west of Bethlehem, where David would later hide in a cave (1 Samuel 22:1).

The daughter of a certain Canaanite whose name was Shua. Abraham had made his servant swear not to take a wife for Isaac “from the daughters of the Canaanites” (24:3), and Isaac and Rebekah grieved over Esau’s Canaanite wives (26:34–35; 28:1). Judah ignores the family’s standard. “Saw … took … went in” is the language of appetite, as with Shechem (34:2). Her name is not given; she is remembered only as Shua’s daughter.

Er … Onan … Shelah. Three sons, the first two named in quick succession. The chapter will turn on what becomes of them. Chezib, where Shelah was born, is probably Achzib in the same lowland region (Joshua 15:44).

Was there time? Some readers wonder how all this fits into the twenty-two years before Jacob’s family goes down to Egypt, where Perez already has sons (46:12). It is tight but possible if Judah married young, as people did, and his sons too. The phrase “at that time” is a loose link, and Genesis often tells overlapping stories side by side.

verseByVerse.quote: And Judah took a wife for Er his firstborn, and her name was Tamar. But Er, Judah's firstborn, was wicked in the sight of the LORD, and the LORD put him to death. Then Judah said to Onan, "Go in to your brother's wife and perform the duty of a brother-in-law to her, and raise up offspring for your brother." But Onan knew that the offspring would not be his. So whenever he went in to his brother's wife he would waste the semen on the ground, so as not to give offspring to his brother. And what he did was wicked in the sight of the LORD, and he put him to death also. Then Judah said to Tamar his daughter-in-law, "Remain a widow in your father's house, till Shelah my son grows up"—for he feared that he would die, like his brothers. So Tamar went and remained in her father's house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD puts Judah’s two older sons to death for their wickedness, Onan for refusing to give his dead brother an heir; then Judah, fearing for his last son, sends Tamar away with a promise he does not intend to keep.

Her name was Tamar. Tamar means “palm tree”. Her family is not named; she was probably a Canaanite too. Judah arranges her marriage to Er, as fathers did.

Er … was wicked in the sight of the LORD, and the LORD put him to death. His sin is not described, but it was serious enough that the LORD himself acted. God is not absent from Judah’s household, even if Judah has forgotten him.

Perform the duty of a brother-in-law. When a man died childless, his brother had a duty to marry the widow and give his dead brother an heir, who would carry his name and inherit his share (see the note on the verse). The custom was later written into the law (Deuteronomy 25:5–6), and it lies behind the story of Ruth and the question the Sadducees put to Jesus (Ruth 4:5–10; Matthew 22:24). It protected the widow, who otherwise had no one to provide for her, and kept the family line alive.

Onan knew that the offspring would not be his. Onan slept with Tamar but made sure she could not conceive. A son would have counted as his brother’s heir and taken the share of the inheritance Onan wanted, for with Er dead, Onan stood to inherit the firstborn’s portion himself. He enjoyed the privileges of the duty while refusing its purpose, “whenever” he went in to her: not once, but repeatedly. He used Tamar and cheated his dead brother, and it was “wicked in the sight of the LORD”.

Remain a widow in your father’s house, till Shelah my son grows up. Judah, afraid of losing his last son too, sends Tamar home and withholds Shelah. He seems to blame her for his sons’ deaths, though the text has told us plainly why they died. Sent back to her father’s house, Tamar is neither free to remarry nor provided for: bound to Judah’s family by his promise, and left by it with nothing.

Where Christians differ: contraception. Roman Catholic teaching has cited Onan against contraception, and many Protestants once did the same.

This commentary’s view. Onan’s sin was selfish refusal of his duty to his brother’s widow, not contraception as such: the text says he acted “so as not to give offspring to his brother”. Christians may differ on family planning, while welcoming children as God’s gift (Psalm 127:3).
verseByVerse.note: This duty is often called “levirate marriage,” from the Latin for “brother-in-law.”

verseByVerse.quote: In the course of time the wife of Judah, Shua's daughter, died. When Judah was comforted, he went up to Timnah to his sheepshearers, he and his friend Hirah the Adullamite. And when Tamar was told, "Your father-in-law is going up to Timnah to shear his sheep," she took off her widow's garments and covered herself with a veil, wrapping herself up, and sat at the entrance to Enaim, which is on the road to Timnah. For she saw that Shelah was grown up, and she had not been given to him in marriage.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Years pass; Shelah is grown and Tamar has not been given to him, so when she hears Judah is going to the sheep-shearing she takes off her widow’s clothes, veils herself and waits by the road.

When Judah was comforted. Judah, now a widower, finishes mourning his wife. The contrast with his father is sharp: Jacob “refused to be comforted” for Joseph (37:35), a grief Judah caused.

Timnah to his sheepshearers. Sheep-shearing was a time of feasting and drinking (1 Samuel 25:2–8, 36; 2 Samuel 13:23–28), the kind of occasion when a man away from home might be careless.

She took off her widow’s garments. Tamar’s widow’s clothes announced her status to everyone; taking them off meant stepping out of the place Judah had left her in. Covered by a veil, she sits at the entrance to Enaim, a town whose name means “two springs” or “eyes”: Judah, of all people, will be the one who does not see.

She saw that Shelah was grown up, and she had not been given to him in marriage. Judah has broken his word, and Tamar is a widow with no future in that world: no husband, no son, no inheritance. Her desperation drives what follows. The narrator gives her reason before he tells what she did, so that we understand her even where we cannot approve her.

verseByVerse.quote: When Judah saw her, he thought she was a prostitute, for she had covered her face. He turned to her at the roadside and said, "Come, let me come in to you," for he did not know that she was his daughter-in-law. She said, "What will you give me, that you may come in to me?" He answered, "I will send you a young goat from the flock." And she said, "If you give me a pledge, until you send it—" He said, "What pledge shall I give you?" She replied, "Your signet and your cord and your staff that is in your hand." So he gave them to her and went in to her, and she conceived by him. Then she arose and went away, and taking off her veil she put on the garments of her widowhood.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah takes his veiled daughter-in-law for a prostitute and sleeps with her, leaving his seal, cord and staff as a pledge of payment; she conceives, and quietly returns to her widow’s clothes.

He thought she was a prostitute. Judah’s sin is plain: he uses a prostitute. He does not know she is his daughter-in-law, which later law would forbid in any case (Leviticus 18:15), but he knows enough to know he is sinning. A woman sitting alone and veiled by the road, out of her own district, could be read that way, and Judah does not hesitate.

What will you give me? Tamar bargains carefully. A young goat is promised, and a goat turns up again in a story of deceit, as when Jacob deceived Isaac (27:9) and the brothers deceived Jacob (37:31). The family keeps using goats to deceive, and now one is used on Judah.

Your signet and your cord and your staff. The signet was a personal seal, often a small cylinder carved with a design and worn on a cord round the neck, rolled or pressed into clay to sign agreements. The staff probably had its own carved top. Together they were Judah’s identity, something like handing over a passport and a bank card. Tamar asks for what cannot be denied.

She arose and went away … and put on the garments of her widowhood. She asks for no payment and takes nothing for herself. Her aim was never money but a child for her dead husband’s line, the right Judah had withheld. She returns to her widow’s clothes and waits.

What it does not mean. The story does not hold Tamar up as a model to copy, nor excuse Judah. Scripture tells what happened, and lets the confession in v. 26 give the verdict on who was more in the wrong.

verseByVerse.quote: When Judah sent the young goat by his friend the Adullamite to take back the pledge from the woman's hand, he did not find her. And he asked the men of the place, "Where is the cult prostitute who was at Enaim at the roadside?" And they said, "No cult prostitute has been here." So he returned to Judah and said, "I have not found her. Also, the men of the place said, 'No cult prostitute has been here.'" And Judah replied, "Let her keep the things as her own, or we shall be laughed at. You see, I sent this young goat, and you did not find her."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah tries to pay the woman and recover his pledge through his friend, but she cannot be found, and Judah drops the matter rather than be laughed at.

He did not find her. Judah sends his friend Hirah to do the awkward errand. He is careful about his property and his debts, and careless about his sin.

Where is the cult prostitute? Hirah asks for the “cult prostitute” (see the note on the verse), a more respectable word than the one used in v. 15: in public he dresses up what Judah did. No such woman is known there, for none was ever there.

Let her keep the things as her own, or we shall be laughed at. Judah would rather lose his seal and staff than his reputation. His concern is how it looks, not what he has done. The fear of being laughed at is a poor substitute for the fear of God.

Uncertain wording. The word for “cult prostitute” (qedeshah) means literally “consecrated woman”, and is used of women attached to pagan shrines, whom Israel’s law forbade (Deuteronomy 23:17). Scholars debate whether such women actually served as prostitutes in pagan worship or whether the word had another meaning, which the Bible pairs with prostitution (Hosea 4:14). Here it is clearly a politer word for the same thing Judah thought he had found.
verseByVerse.note: “Cult prostitute” is literally “sacred woman” (ESV note): a woman serving a pagan deity.

verseByVerse.quote: About three months later Judah was told, "Tamar your daughter-in-law has been immoral. Moreover, she is pregnant by immorality." And Judah said, "Bring her out, and let her be burned." As she was being brought out, she sent word to her father-in-law, "By the man to whom these belong, I am pregnant." And she said, "Please identify whose these are, the signet and the cord and the staff." Then Judah identified them and said, "She is more righteous than I, since I did not give her to my son Shelah." And he did not know her again.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Tamar is found pregnant, Judah orders her burned; she produces his own pledge, and Judah confesses publicly that she is more righteous than he.

Tamar your daughter-in-law has been immoral. Promised to Shelah, Tamar was still counted as belonging to Judah’s family, so her pregnancy was treated as unfaithfulness. Judah, the head of the family, acts as judge.

Bring her out, and let her be burned. The sentence is extreme, harsher than later law required for most such cases (Deuteronomy 22:23–24); burning was later reserved for a priest’s daughter who played the prostitute (Leviticus 21:9). It is also hypocrisy: Judah condemns in her what he did himself, and it would rid him of the widow he did not want.

Please identify whose these are. Tamar does not shame him in public. She sends the pledge privately and lets Judah decide. Her words, “please identify”, are the very words the brothers used when they brought Jacob the bloodied robe (37:32). Judah, who once made his father identify a robe, must now identify his own seal and staff. What he did to his father has come back to him.

She is more righteous than I. This is Judah’s turning point. The man who proposed selling Joseph begins to change, and the change will reach its height when he offers himself as a slave in Benjamin’s place (44:33). He gives his reason too: “since I did not give her to my son Shelah.” He owns the wrong that started it all.

And he did not know her again. Judah does not take Tamar as a wife; the relationship was not right, and he does not continue it. His confession is followed by changed conduct.

What it does not mean. Not that Tamar’s act was right, but that Judah’s wrong was greater: she was faithful to the duty to give her dead husband an heir; he was not.

In everyday life. Admit your own guilt before condemning others. With God, confession leads not to the fire but to mercy: “I acknowledged my sin to you … and you forgave the iniquity of my sin” (Psalm 32:5).

verseByVerse.quote: When the time of her labor came, there were twins in her womb. And when she was in labor, one put out a hand, and the midwife took and tied a scarlet thread on his hand, saying, "This one came out first." But as he drew back his hand, behold, his brother came out. And she said, "What a breach you have made for yourself!" Therefore his name was called Perez. Afterward his brother came out with the scarlet thread on his hand, and his name was called Zerah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Tamar bears twins, and the younger, Perez, breaks out ahead of his brother to become the ancestor of David and of Christ.

There were twins in her womb. God gives Tamar two sons in place of the two Judah lost. The birth recalls Rebekah’s twins, Esau and Jacob, where the younger also grasped at the older (25:24–26).

A scarlet thread on his hand. The midwife marks the first hand to appear, because the firstborn had special rights. But the hand draws back.

What a breach you have made for yourself! Once again the younger comes first. Perez means “a breach” (see the note on the verse): he breaks out ahead of his brother. As with Abel, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph and Ephraim, God’s choice does not follow the order of birth. Perez becomes an ancestor of David and of Christ (Ruth 4:18–22; Matthew 1:3), and in Ruth the people of Bethlehem bless Boaz’s house that it may be “like the house of Perez, whom Tamar bore to Judah” (Ruth 4:12).

Tamar in the family tree of Jesus. Tamar is one of four women Matthew names in Jesus’ genealogy, alongside Rahab, Ruth and “the wife of Uriah” (Matthew 1:3–6), all with irregular stories, and most of them outsiders to Israel. She is there not in spite of her story but because of it: the Messiah’s line runs through scandal, and God’s grace writes even our shameful chapters into his story. Jesus did not come from a respectable family tree; he came to save sinners, and he is not ashamed to call them his brothers (Hebrews 2:11).
verseByVerse.note: “Perez” means “a breach” (ESV note).

38.theology:
Genesis 38 shows God’s purposes running through morally tangled, even scandalous events without being stained by them and without approving them. God does not abandon Judah’s line because of Judah’s failures; he works through Tamar’s courage to preserve it.

Judah’s confession is the moment he faces his own sin honestly, and it prepares for his great speech in chapter 44. Judah must be broken before he can become the man who offers himself for Benjamin. The Joseph story is not only about Joseph; it is also about the change in Judah, and that change begins here, on the road to Timnah, when a veiled woman holds up his signet ring.
38.examples:
Set between Joseph’s sale and his rise, the Tamar story invites comparison. Joseph is faithful in Egypt despite unjust suffering; Judah fails in Canaan despite freedom and prosperity. Faithfulness is possible in the pit, and unfaithfulness in comfort.

Tamar risked everything to secure what was rightly hers, and God wrote her into Jesus’ family line. That is an encouragement to anyone failed by those who should have protected them: God sees and remembers. The irregular path of a desperate woman became the path by which the Messiah came into the world.

keyVerse.quote: Then Judah identified them and said, “She is more righteous than I, since I did not give her to my son Shelah.” And he did not know her again.
keyVerse.note: This is the first sign of change in the brother who sold Joseph: Judah stops defending himself and owns his sin publicly. The royal line survives not through Judah’s goodness but through his confession and God’s mercy, and the confession prepares for the day he offers himself for Benjamin (44:33).

38.reflection:
Judah “went down from his brothers” and drifted into the ways of the people around him (vv. 1–2). What are the small steps by which believers drift from God’s people today?

Judah was ready to have Tamar burned for the very sin he had committed (v. 24). Why is it so much easier to see others’ sins than our own, and what does it take to say, “She is more righteous than I”?

Tamar was failed by the men who should have protected her (vv. 11, 14). How should a church care for those who have been let down by family or leaders?

Matthew names Tamar in the family line of Jesus (Matthew 1:3). What does it tell you about Jesus that he came from a family like this, and what hope does it give you about your own story?

39.title: The LORD Was with Joseph
39.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Joseph had been brought down to Egypt, and Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh, the captain of the guard, an Egyptian, had bought him from the Ishmaelites who had brought him down there.<sup>2</sup>The LORD was with Joseph, and he became a successful man, and he was in the house of his Egyptian master.<sup>3</sup>His master saw that the LORD was with him and that the LORD caused all that he did to succeed in his hands.<sup>4</sup>So Joseph found favor in his sight and attended him, and he made him overseer of his house and put him in charge of all that he had.<sup>5</sup>From the time that he made him overseer in his house and over all that he had, the LORD blessed the Egyptian's house for Joseph's sake; the blessing of the LORD was on all that he had, in house and field.<sup>6</sup>So he left all that he had in Joseph's charge, and because of him he had no concern about anything but the food he ate. Now Joseph was handsome in form and appearance.<sup>7</sup>And after a time his master's wife cast her eyes on Joseph and said, "Lie with me."<sup>8</sup>But he refused and said to his master's wife, "Behold, because of me my master has no concern about anything in the house, and he has put everything that he has in my charge.<sup>9</sup>He is not greater in this house than I am, nor has he kept back anything from me except you, because you are his wife. How then can I do this great wickedness and sin against God?"<sup>10</sup>And as she spoke to Joseph day after day, he would not listen to her, to lie beside her or to be with her.<sup>11</sup>But one day, when he went into the house to do his work and none of the men of the house was there in the house,<sup>12</sup>she caught him by his garment, saying, "Lie with me." But he left his garment in her hand and fled and got out of the house.<sup>13</sup>And as soon as she saw that he had left his garment in her hand and had fled out of the house,<sup>14</sup>she called to the men of her household and said to them, "See, he has brought among us a Hebrew to laugh at us. He came in to me to lie with me, and I cried out with a loud voice.<sup>15</sup>And as soon as he heard that I lifted up my voice and cried out, he left his garment beside me and fled and got out of the house."<sup>16</sup>Then she laid up his garment by her until his master came home,<sup>17</sup>and she told him the same story, saying, "The Hebrew servant, whom you have brought among us, came in to me to laugh at me.<sup>18</sup>But as soon as I lifted up my voice and cried, he left his garment beside me and fled out of the house."<sup>19</sup>As soon as his master heard the words that his wife spoke to him, "This is the way your servant treated me," his anger was kindled.<sup>20</sup>And Joseph's master took him and put him into the prison, the place where the king's prisoners were confined, and he was there in prison.<sup>21</sup>But the LORD was with Joseph and showed him steadfast love and gave him favor in the sight of the keeper of the prison.<sup>22</sup>And the keeper of the prison put Joseph in charge of all the prisoners who were in the prison. Whatever was done there, he was the one who did it.<sup>23</sup>The keeper of the prison paid no attention to anything that was in Joseph's charge, because the LORD was with him. And whatever he did, the LORD made it succeed.
39.overview:
Where we are. The story returns to Joseph after the account of Judah (chapter 38). At the end of chapter 37 he was sold in Egypt to Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh; now we see what became of the seventeen-year-old slave. Judah fell in freedom; Joseph is about to be tested in slavery.

The message. The LORD is with his servant in the slave’s quarters and in the prison, and his presence does not depend on circumstances. Joseph rises, is tempted, refuses, is falsely accused and is thrown into prison, and the refrain sounds at both ends of the chapter: “the LORD was with Joseph.” Faithfulness to God may cost everything in the short run, but it is never wasted, because God is never absent.

Why it was said. Israel, slaves in Egypt and then wanderers in the wilderness, needed to know that the LORD was with his people even in a foreign land and under a foreign master (see the introduction). Joseph shows them that God can bless an Egyptian household through one faithful servant, as he promised Abraham (12:3), and that integrity before God matters most when no one is watching.

How the chapter makes its case. Bought by Potiphar, Joseph prospers because the LORD is with him, and the LORD blesses the Egyptian’s house for his sake (vv. 1–6). Potiphar’s wife presses him day after day; he refuses, because it would betray his master and be “sin against God” (vv. 7–10). When she seizes him, he runs, leaving his garment, and she uses it to accuse him (vv. 11–18). Potiphar puts him in the king’s prison (vv. 19–20). But there too the LORD is with Joseph, shows him steadfast love, and makes him the keeper’s right-hand man (vv. 21–23).

Where it leads. By pattern, and by the character of God. Joseph is the innocent man who resists temptation, is falsely accused and condemned, yet goes down only to be raised up; Jesus, “in every respect … tempted as we are, yet without sin” (Hebrews 4:15), went the whole way down to death under false charges and was raised to the right hand of God. And “the LORD was with Joseph” finds its fullest meaning in Immanuel, “God with us” (Matthew 1:23), who promises, “I am with you always, to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20).

For us. God is with you in the job you did not choose and the place you did not want to be. Faithfulness at work can bring blessing to those you work for. Run from sexual temptation rather than argue with it, and if you have failed, run to Christ, whose purity is counted as yours. And when doing right costs you dearly, remember that the LORD who was with Joseph in prison is with his people still.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The LORD is with Joseph in slavery and in prison, and his presence explains both of Joseph’s rises. Bought by Potiphar, Joseph prospers and becomes overseer of the house, and the LORD blesses the Egyptian for his sake (vv. 1–6). Day after day Potiphar’s wife presses him to lie with her; he refuses because it would betray his master and be sin against God, and when she seizes him he flees, leaving his garment (vv. 7–12). She uses the garment to accuse him, and he is thrown into the king’s prison (vv. 13–20). But the LORD is with him there too, showing him steadfast love, and the keeper puts everything in his charge (vv. 21–23).
verseByVerse.theology: The LORD is with Joseph in Potiphar's house, and he is put in charge of everything. Potiphar's wife presses him day after day; he refuses and flees, leaving his garment. She accuses him, and he is imprisoned, where the LORD is with him again and he is put in charge.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: that the LORD was with Joseph is said both in the great house and in the dungeon. Now: "Flee from sexual immorality" (1 Cor. 6:18) means run, and God's presence means he is with us in trouble, not that he will soon free us.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Joseph had been brought down to Egypt, and Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh, the captain of the guard, an Egyptian, had bought him from the Ishmaelites who had brought him down there. The LORD was with Joseph, and he became a successful man, and he was in the house of his Egyptian master. His master saw that the LORD was with him and that the LORD caused all that he did to succeed in his hands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joseph is bought as a slave by an Egyptian official, but the LORD is with him, and even his pagan master can see that the LORD makes all he does succeed.

Now Joseph had been brought down to Egypt. The verse picks up where 37:36 left off, after the story of Judah. Judah “went down” by choice (38:1); Joseph “had been brought down” against his will. Potiphar, “an Egyptian”, bought him: the word is repeated because Joseph is now a foreign slave in a foreign land, and the family that sold him is far away. Potiphar’s name is Egyptian, probably meaning “he whom Ra has given” (see the note on 37:36 on his office).

The LORD was with Joseph. This is the refrain of the chapter (vv. 2, 3, 21, 23), and it explains everything. The covenant name, the LORD, appears again and again in this chapter, though it is rare in the rest of Joseph’s story: the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob has not stayed behind in Canaan. God is with Joseph even as a slave; his presence does not depend on circumstances. Stephen sums it up: “the patriarchs, jealous of Joseph, sold him into Egypt; but God was with him” (Acts 7:9).

He became a successful man. Success here does not mean freedom or wealth: he is still a slave. It means that his work prospers. Even his Egyptian master, who does not know the LORD, can see that something beyond Joseph’s skill is at work.

In everyday life. God is with you in the job you did not choose. Joseph did not wait for better circumstances before serving faithfully; he served where he had been put, and that is where God blessed him.

Uncertain wording. The word translated “officer” (saris) can mean a eunuch, and in later books it often does, but it is also used of high court officials in general. Since Potiphar has a wife, most take it here to mean simply “official”. Whether the word hints at something more about his marriage cannot be known.

verseByVerse.quote: So Joseph found favor in his sight and attended him, and he made him overseer of his house and put him in charge of all that he had. From the time that he made him overseer in his house and over all that he had, the LORD blessed the Egyptian's house for Joseph's sake; the blessing of the LORD was on all that he had, in house and field. So he left all that he had in Joseph's charge, and because of him he had no concern about anything but the food he ate. Now Joseph was handsome in form and appearance.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Potiphar puts Joseph in charge of everything he owns, and the LORD blesses the Egyptian’s house and fields for Joseph’s sake; and Joseph, we are told, was handsome.

Joseph found favor in his sight. Joseph rises from household slave to personal attendant to overseer of the whole estate. Potiphar trusts him so completely that he pays attention to nothing but “the food he ate”, perhaps a way of saying he cared only for his own meals, or a reminder that, as an Egyptian, he would not let a Hebrew handle his food (43:32).

The LORD blessed the Egyptian’s house for Joseph’s sake. The LORD blesses the Egyptian’s house for Joseph’s sake: Abraham’s blessing is reaching the nations, as God promised: “in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed” (12:3). Laban had said the same of Jacob (30:27). God’s people are meant to be a blessing to those around them, even to those who own them.

Now Joseph was handsome in form and appearance. The same words were used of his mother Rachel (29:17). The note prepares for the temptation that follows. Good looks are a gift, but they can also bring danger.

In everyday life. Your faithfulness, too, can bring blessing to those you work for, believers or not. Paul tells Christian slaves to serve “as for the Lord and not for men” (Colossians 3:23), and the same holds for every employee.

verseByVerse.quote: And after a time his master's wife cast her eyes on Joseph and said, "Lie with me." But he refused and said to his master's wife, "Behold, because of me my master has no concern about anything in the house, and he has put everything that he has in my charge. He is not greater in this house than I am, nor has he kept back anything from me except you, because you are his wife. How then can I do this great wickedness and sin against God?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Potiphar’s wife tries to seduce Joseph, and he refuses, because it would betray the master who trusted him and, above all, be sin against God.

His master’s wife cast her eyes on Joseph and said, “Lie with me.” The temptation is strong: a young man, far from home, enslaved and alone, propositioned by a powerful woman who could make his life easy or miserable. Her words are blunt, two words in Hebrew: a command from a mistress to a slave. It is also harassment by someone with power over him.

He refused. Joseph does not hesitate. He gives his reasons, and they are worth noting: his master has trusted him with everything except her, and to take her would betray that trust. He calls it “this great wickedness”.

And sin against God. Joseph refuses out of loyalty to the master who trusted him, and above all because sin is first against God, as David would confess: “Against you, you only, have I sinned” (Psalm 51:4). Joseph sees what Judah did not (chapter 38): there is a God before whom all is done, whether or not anyone else ever knows.

Isn’t it only wrong if someone gets hurt? That is the working morality of our culture: between consenting adults, what happens in private is no one else’s business. Joseph’s situation came close to passing that test, for no one need ever have known. Yet his deepest reason is not the harm it would do, real as the betrayal of his master would be. He calls it sin against God. That sounds narrower to modern ears, but it is larger and kinder. It means right and wrong are not only a matter of managing damage, but of faithfulness to a Person who made us and loves us, so that sex, like everything else, carries a meaning that consent alone cannot give it. And it means something more. If sin is only against people, then when you have done wrong you are left with those you hurt, who may not forgive, and with yourself, who often cannot. If sin is first against God, there is somewhere to go, because the God we have sinned against has come looking for us: “God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8).

verseByVerse.quote: And as she spoke to Joseph day after day, he would not listen to her, to lie beside her or to be with her. But one day, when he went into the house to do his work and none of the men of the house was there in the house, she caught him by his garment, saying, "Lie with me." But he left his garment in her hand and fled and got out of the house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
She keeps pressing him day after day, and Joseph avoids her; when at last she seizes him alone in the house, he leaves his garment in her hand and runs.

As she spoke to Joseph day after day. Temptation is persistent, “day after day”. One refusal does not end it. Joseph not only refuses to lie with her; he refuses even “to be with her”, keeping out of her way as far as his duties allow.

None of the men of the house was there. She chooses her moment. Whether by chance or by her arrangement, Joseph is alone with her, and she seizes him.

He left his garment in her hand and fled. When she seizes him, he runs, as Paul would later command: “Flee from sexual immorality” (1 Corinthians 6:18; 2 Timothy 2:22). He would rather lose his garment, and his position, than his integrity. For the second time a garment of Joseph’s is used against him: first the robe dipped in blood (37:31), now this.

In everyday life. Do not argue with sexual temptation. Run, in the strength of the Spirit who now lives in you (Galatians 5:16), and arrange your life so that you are not often alone with what tempts you. Where you have not run, Christ’s purity is counted as yours, and the way back is confession (1 John 1:9).

verseByVerse.quote: And as soon as she saw that he had left his garment in her hand and had fled out of the house, she called to the men of her household and said to them, "See, he has brought among us a Hebrew to laugh at us. He came in to me to lie with me, and I cried out with a loud voice. And as soon as he heard that I lifted up my voice and cried out, he left his garment beside me and fled and got out of the house." Then she laid up his garment by her until his master came home, and she told him the same story, saying, "The Hebrew servant, whom you have brought among us, came in to me to laugh at me. But as soon as I lifted up my voice and cried, he left his garment beside me and fled out of the house."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rejected, Potiphar’s wife turns the garment into evidence and accuses Joseph of trying to assault her, first to the servants and then to her husband.

A Hebrew to laugh at us. Rejected lust turns to hatred, and she accuses him falsely. She stirs prejudice by calling him “a Hebrew”, a foreigner whom Egyptians held in contempt (43:32), and makes the servants feel insulted with her: “to laugh at us”. The word can also mean to toy with or take liberties with someone (26:8), and she means it in that sense.

He has brought among us. She even blames her husband: “he has brought among us” a Hebrew, and to Potiphar, “whom you have brought among us”. The accusation reaches everyone but herself.

He left his garment beside me. The garment left “in her hand” (v. 12) becomes, in her story, a garment left “beside me”. A small change of words turns evidence of her assault into evidence of his. She tells the same story twice, to the servants and to her husband, and the repetition makes it sound settled.

What it does not mean. This story does not mean accusations of assault should be dismissed. Every claim must be heard justly (Deuteronomy 19:15–19). Most such accusations are true, and anyone who has been assaulted or harassed, at work or anywhere, should get to safety and report it at once. The story warns against judging on one side’s word without inquiry, which is what Potiphar did.

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as his master heard the words that his wife spoke to him, "This is the way your servant treated me," his anger was kindled. And Joseph's master took him and put him into the prison, the place where the king's prisoners were confined, and he was there in prison.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Potiphar, angry, puts Joseph in the prison where the king’s prisoners are held: Joseph is punished for doing right.

His anger was kindled. We are not told whom his anger was against. An accused slave would normally have been executed; that Potiphar only imprisoned him may mean that he doubted his wife’s story, or valued Joseph too much to kill him. Either way, Joseph’s rise has ended in a cell.

The place where the king’s prisoners were confined. Not an ordinary jail but the prison for those who had offended Pharaoh, attached to the house of the captain of the guard (40:3). It is exactly where Joseph needs to be to meet Pharaoh’s cupbearer.

He was there in prison. The psalmist remembers it: “His feet were hurt with fetters; his neck was put in a collar of iron”, until God’s time came, and meanwhile “the word of the LORD tested him” (Psalm 105:18–19). Joseph is punished for doing right, the kind of suffering Peter says is “a gracious thing in the sight of God” (1 Peter 2:20).

Innocent and condemned. The narrator records no word of defence from Joseph. He goes down for doing right, and God will raise him. His Lord would one day stand falsely accused before rulers, and like a sheep before its shearers he did not open his mouth (Isaiah 53:7; Acts 8:32).

verseByVerse.quote: But the LORD was with Joseph and showed him steadfast love and gave him favor in the sight of the keeper of the prison. And the keeper of the prison put Joseph in charge of all the prisoners who were in the prison. Whatever was done there, he was the one who did it. The keeper of the prison paid no attention to anything that was in Joseph's charge, because the LORD was with him. And whatever he did, the LORD made it succeed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But even in prison the LORD is with Joseph, showing him steadfast love, and the keeper of the prison puts him in charge of everything.

But the LORD was with Joseph. The chapter ends as it began. The pit, the slave market and the prison could not separate Joseph from the LORD. Each step down is also a step toward the throne, by a route Joseph cannot see and cannot control. He can only be faithful in each place, and he is.

And showed him steadfast love. Hebrew hesed: God’s loyal, covenant-keeping love, which reaches into every prison. It is the love God promised to Abraham’s family, and Joseph, cut off from that family, still has it.

The keeper of the prison put Joseph in charge. The pattern of Potiphar’s house repeats itself (vv. 4–6). The keeper pays no attention to anything in Joseph’s charge, because the LORD makes it succeed. Joseph is learning to rule by learning to serve.

In everyday life. God does not guarantee comfort, but he does guarantee his presence. Nothing in all creation can separate us from the love of God in Christ (Romans 8:38–39). If you are in a place you did not choose and cannot leave, serve faithfully there; the LORD is with you there.

39.theology:
God’s presence with Joseph is not interrupted by slavery or imprisonment. This is the meaning of Immanuel, “God with us”: God does not guarantee comfort, but he does guarantee his presence. Jesus’ last promise, “I am with you always, to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20), carries the same promise to all his people.

The steadfast love God shows Joseph in prison (v. 21) runs through all his dealings with his people. Paul says the same: nothing in all creation can separate us from the love of God (Romans 8:38–39). The prison could not separate Joseph from it.
39.examples:
Joseph’s temptation was daily and private, and it came from a woman with power over him, an enslaved foreigner: no witness, no protection, nothing but the conviction that sin is sin against God whether or not anyone knows. Behind that conviction stood the God who was with him. Integrity grows from knowing whom we belong to.

Peter points sufferers to Christ, who “when he suffered, he did not threaten, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly” (1 Pet 2:23). Joseph is an early picture of that pattern. Faithfulness in unjust suffering is never wasted, even when, as for Joseph, the waiting is long.

keyVerse.quote: But the LORD was with Joseph and showed him steadfast love and gave him favor in the sight of the keeper of the prison.
keyVerse.note: The refrain of the chapter reaches into the darkest place yet. Joseph has done right and been condemned, but the LORD’s covenant love goes with him into the prison. It is the promise of God’s presence that every believer in Christ has, whatever the circumstances.

39.reflection:
“The LORD was with Joseph” in slavery and in prison (vv. 2, 21). How does this change the way you think about God’s presence in circumstances you did not choose?

Joseph refused Potiphar’s wife because it would be “sin against God” (v. 9). Why does it matter that sin is first against God, and how does that give both a higher standard and greater hope?

Joseph kept away from temptation and ran when it seized him (vv. 10–12). What practical steps help believers flee temptation today, and what should someone do who has not fled?

Joseph was punished for doing right (v. 20). How does Jesus’ own unjust suffering help you endure when faithfulness costs you?

40.title: The Cupbearer and the Baker
40.text: <sup>1</sup>Some time after this, the cupbearer of the king of Egypt and his baker committed an offense against their lord the king of Egypt.<sup>2</sup>And Pharaoh was angry with his two officers, the chief cupbearer and the chief baker,<sup>3</sup>and he put them in custody in the house of the captain of the guard, in the prison where Joseph was confined.<sup>4</sup>The captain of the guard appointed Joseph to be with them, and he attended them. They continued for some time in custody.<sup>5</sup>And one night they both dreamed—the cupbearer and the baker of the king of Egypt, who were confined in the prison—each his own dream, and each dream with its own interpretation.<sup>6</sup>When Joseph came to them in the morning, he saw that they were troubled.<sup>7</sup>So he asked Pharaoh's officers who were with him in custody in his master's house, "Why are your faces downcast today?"<sup>8</sup>They said to him, "We have had dreams, and there is no one to interpret them." And Joseph said to them, "Do not interpretations belong to God? Please tell them to me."<sup>9</sup>So the chief cupbearer told his dream to Joseph and said to him, "In my dream there was a vine before me,<sup>10</sup>and on the vine there were three branches. As soon as it budded, its blossoms shot forth, and the clusters ripened into grapes.<sup>11</sup>Pharaoh's cup was in my hand, and I took the grapes and pressed them into Pharaoh's cup and placed the cup in Pharaoh's hand."<sup>12</sup>Then Joseph said to him, "This is its interpretation: the three branches are three days.<sup>13</sup>In three days Pharaoh will lift up your head and restore you to your office, and you shall place Pharaoh's cup in his hand as formerly, when you were his cupbearer.<sup>14</sup>Only remember me, when it is well with you, and please do me the kindness to mention me to Pharaoh, and so get me out of this house.<sup>15</sup>For I was indeed stolen out of the land of the Hebrews, and here also I have done nothing that they should put me into the pit."<sup>16</sup>When the chief baker saw that the interpretation was favorable, he said to Joseph, "I also had a dream: there were three cake baskets on my head,<sup>17</sup>and in the uppermost basket there were all sorts of baked food for Pharaoh, but the birds were eating it out of the basket on my head."<sup>18</sup>And Joseph answered and said, "This is its interpretation: the three baskets are three days.<sup>19</sup>In three days Pharaoh will lift up your head—from you!—and hang you on a tree. And the birds will eat the flesh from you."<sup>20</sup>On the third day, which was Pharaoh's birthday, he made a feast for all his servants and lifted up the head of the chief cupbearer and the head of the chief baker among his servants.<sup>21</sup>He restored the chief cupbearer to his position, and he placed the cup in Pharaoh's hand.<sup>22</sup>But he hanged the chief baker, as Joseph had interpreted to them.<sup>23</sup>Yet the chief cupbearer did not remember Joseph, but forgot him.
40.overview:
Where we are. Joseph has been thrown into the king’s prison on a false charge, but the LORD is with him there, and the keeper has put him in charge of the other prisoners (39:20–23). Now two of Pharaoh’s own officials arrive in the same prison.

The message. God’s word is true, and God’s timing is his own. Joseph, who gives God the credit before he says a word, interprets two dreams, and both come true exactly, on the third day. Yet the man he helped forgets him, and the chapter ends with Joseph still in prison. God’s word can be trusted even when his servants are forgotten and his promises seem stalled.

Why it was said. Israel knew long years of waiting: in slavery in Egypt, in the wilderness, and later in exile (see the introduction). This chapter taught them that God’s silence is not his absence, that his word comes true to the letter, and that being forgotten by people is not being forgotten by God.

How the chapter makes its case. Pharaoh’s chief cupbearer and chief baker offend the king and are put in custody, and Joseph is assigned to serve them (vv. 1–4). Both dream on the same night; Joseph notices their troubled faces and points them to God, who gives interpretations (vv. 5–8). The cupbearer’s dream of a vine means restoration in three days (vv. 9–13), and Joseph asks only to be remembered (vv. 14–15). The baker’s dream of birds eating from his basket means death in three days (vv. 16–19). On Pharaoh’s birthday both come true exactly (vv. 20–22). But the cupbearer forgets Joseph (v. 23).

Where it leads. By pattern, and by the need it exposes. Joseph asks a forgiven man to “remember me”, and is forgotten. Centuries later a dying criminal said to another innocent man condemned beside him, “Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom”, and received the answer, “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:42–43). Joseph could only ask to be remembered; Christ is the King who remembers. And the one who, in his own suffering, noticed the troubled faces of others is a faint early picture of the Servant who came “not to be served but to serve” (Mark 10:45).

For us. Suffering need not turn us inward: notice the troubled faces around you. Give God the credit for any wisdom you have. And when people forget you and the waiting goes on, remember that the waiting is part of God’s plan, and that the Lord who remembered the thief on the cross has not forgotten you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–23 — Joseph Interprets the Dreams of the Cupbearer and Baker
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Two dreams, two interpretations that come true exactly, and a chapter that ends with Joseph still in prison, forgotten by the man he helped. Pharaoh’s chief cupbearer and chief baker are put in Joseph’s prison, and Joseph serves them (vv. 1–4). When both are troubled by dreams, Joseph points them to God and interprets: the cupbearer will be restored in three days, the baker executed (vv. 5–19). In between, Joseph asks only to be remembered, protesting his innocence without bitterness (vv. 14–15). On Pharaoh’s birthday it all happens as Joseph said (vv. 20–22), but the cupbearer forgets him (v. 23). God’s word proves true, and his timing is not yet.
verseByVerse.theology: Pharaoh's cupbearer and baker are put in the prison where Joseph serves. Seeing their downcast faces, he asks, and they tell him their dreams. In three days the cupbearer is restored and the baker hanged, as Joseph said, and the cupbearer forgets him.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: because the cupbearer forgot, Joseph was remembered two years later, the very morning Pharaoh needed him. Now: when God is at work in our suffering, we can still notice someone else's.

verseByVerse.quote: Some time after this, the cupbearer of the king of Egypt and his baker committed an offense against their lord the king of Egypt. And Pharaoh was angry with his two officers, the chief cupbearer and the chief baker, and he put them in custody in the house of the captain of the guard, in the prison where Joseph was confined. The captain of the guard appointed Joseph to be with them, and he attended them. They continued for some time in custody.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pharaoh’s chief cupbearer and chief baker offend him and are put in the same prison as Joseph, who is assigned to serve them.

The cupbearer of the king of Egypt and his baker. The cupbearer and baker were high officials, not kitchen servants. The cupbearer served the king his wine and stood close to him, so he became a trusted adviser, as Nehemiah later was to the king of Persia (Nehemiah 1:11). Both men had charge of what went into the king’s mouth, and in a court where poisoning was a real danger, an offence by either could be serious.

Committed an offense against their lord. We are not told how they had offended Pharaoh. The story is not interested in their crime, only in where it puts them.

In the prison where Joseph was confined. The captain of the guard (37:36) had charge of this prison, so the officials land in exactly the place where Joseph is. God’s providence is placing the right people in Joseph’s path.

The captain of the guard appointed Joseph to be with them. If the captain of the guard is still Potiphar, as 37:36 suggests, he is now trusting the slave he imprisoned with Pharaoh’s own officials, perhaps a sign that he never fully believed his wife. Joseph, the overseer of a household and then of a prison, now serves two prisoners. He “attended them”, the same word used of his service to Potiphar (39:4).

verseByVerse.quote: And one night they both dreamed—the cupbearer and the baker of the king of Egypt, who were confined in the prison—each his own dream, and each dream with its own interpretation. When Joseph came to them in the morning, he saw that they were troubled. So he asked Pharaoh's officers who were with him in custody in his master's house, "Why are your faces downcast today?" They said to him, "We have had dreams, and there is no one to interpret them." And Joseph said to them, "Do not interpretations belong to God? Please tell them to me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Both officials dream on the same night and are troubled; Joseph notices, asks why, and tells them that interpretations belong to God.

Each dream with its own interpretation. Two dreams on one night, each with its own meaning: God is speaking, though they do not know it. Dreams come in pairs in the Joseph story (37:5–9; 41:1–7).

He saw that they were troubled. Joseph notices their faces and asks, “Why are your faces downcast today?” He has every reason to be absorbed in his own injustice, yet suffering has not turned him inward. He sees, and he asks.

There is no one to interpret them. Egyptians took dreams very seriously and had trained interpreters who used written guides to the meaning of dreams. In prison the two officials had no access to such experts, and a dream left uninterpreted felt like a sentence hanging over them.

Do not interpretations belong to God? Joseph gives God the credit before he says a word about the dreams. He claims no technique and no power of his own, as Daniel would later tell Nebuchadnezzar that no wise man could show the king’s mystery, “but there is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries” (Daniel 2:27–28). Yet he is also confident: “Please tell them to me.” Humility and confidence sit together when they both rest on God.

In everyday life. Notice the troubled faces around you, as the God who saw you in your trouble has noticed yours. Those who have been through the pit are often the quickest to see it in others’ faces.
verseByVerse.note: The cupbearer and baker had offended Pharaoh; we are not told how.

verseByVerse.quote: So the chief cupbearer told his dream to Joseph and said to him, "In my dream there was a vine before me, and on the vine there were three branches. As soon as it budded, its blossoms shot forth, and the clusters ripened into grapes. Pharaoh's cup was in my hand, and I took the grapes and pressed them into Pharaoh's cup and placed the cup in Pharaoh's hand." Then Joseph said to him, "This is its interpretation: the three branches are three days. In three days Pharaoh will lift up your head and restore you to your office, and you shall place Pharaoh's cup in his hand as formerly, when you were his cupbearer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The cupbearer dreams of a vine with three branches whose grapes he presses into Pharaoh’s cup, and Joseph tells him that in three days he will be restored to his office.

A vine … three branches … clusters ripened into grapes. In the dream everything happens at once: the vine buds, blossoms and ripens in a moment, and the cupbearer presses the grapes straight into Pharaoh’s cup. The dream pictures his old work, done again, and done quickly.

The three branches are three days. “Three days” is a precise prediction that can be checked. Joseph is not speaking in vague generalities; he stakes his word, and God’s name, on a date.

Pharaoh will lift up your head. To “lift up the head” was an idiom for raising someone from disgrace, here for summoning a prisoner and restoring him (2 Kings 25:27). The cupbearer will stand again in Pharaoh’s presence, cup in hand.

Where Christians differ: interpreting dreams today. Some Christians seek God’s messages in dreams and expect him to speak through them today as he did to Joseph and Daniel. Others hold that such revelation belonged to the time when Scripture was being given.

This commentary’s view. God spoke through dreams in Scripture, and he can do so, but now he has spoken fully in his Son and his word (Hebrews 1:1–2). Dreams must be tested by Scripture, never added to it. Joseph’s gift served God’s plan to bring his family to Egypt and preserve the line of promise; it is not a pattern for seeking hidden meanings in our own dreams.

verseByVerse.quote: Only remember me, when it is well with you, and please do me the kindness to mention me to Pharaoh, and so get me out of this house. For I was indeed stolen out of the land of the Hebrews, and here also I have done nothing that they should put me into the pit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joseph asks the cupbearer to remember him to Pharaoh, protesting his innocence plainly but without bitterness.

Only remember me. “Remember me” is a natural human hope, and Joseph is not wrong to ask: trusting God does not rule out asking people for help. He asks the cupbearer to “do me the kindness”, the word is hesed, loyal love, the very love the LORD had shown him in prison (39:21). The cupbearer will not show it.

I was indeed stolen out of the land of the Hebrews. Joseph tells the truth about his past without accusing anyone by name. He names neither his brothers nor Potiphar’s wife, and shows no bitterness. He was “stolen”, kidnapped: later law made that a capital crime (Exodus 21:16).

Into the pit. The word for the prison is the same word used of the dry cistern his brothers threw him into (37:24). From one pit to another: Joseph’s life has been a series of pits, and he has done nothing to deserve either.

Remember me. Joseph asked a man to remember him, and the man forgot. A dying thief once asked the same of Jesus, “remember me when you come into your kingdom”, and was promised paradise that very day (Luke 23:42–43). Christ is the King who does not forget those who ask him.

verseByVerse.quote: When the chief baker saw that the interpretation was favorable, he said to Joseph, "I also had a dream: there were three cake baskets on my head, and in the uppermost basket there were all sorts of baked food for Pharaoh, but the birds were eating it out of the basket on my head." And Joseph answered and said, "This is its interpretation: the three baskets are three days. In three days Pharaoh will lift up your head—from you!—and hang you on a tree. And the birds will eat the flesh from you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Encouraged, the baker tells his dream of birds eating from the basket on his head, and Joseph tells him plainly that in three days Pharaoh will execute him.

When the chief baker saw that the interpretation was favorable. The baker speaks only after hearing good news for his colleague. He hopes for the same, and does not get it.

The birds were eating it out of the basket on my head. The difference from the cupbearer’s dream is ominous. The cupbearer is active, serving Pharaoh; the baker is passive, and what was meant for Pharaoh is taken by birds before it reaches him.

Pharaoh will lift up your head … from you! The same phrase as v. 13 turns grim: for the cupbearer “lift up your head” meant restoration, for the baker execution, his head lifted off. Joseph tells the baker the hard truth as plainly as he told the cupbearer the good news. A faithful messenger does not soften God’s word to please his hearers.

And hang you on a tree. And the birds will eat the flesh from you. His body will be displayed after death and left for the birds. For Egyptians, who took great care to preserve the body after death, this was a horror beyond execution. Later Israel’s law said that a man hanged on a tree was under God’s curse (Deuteronomy 21:22–23), and Paul says that Christ became a curse for us by being hanged on a tree, to redeem us from the curse (Galatians 3:13).

Uncertain wording. The “cake baskets” are, in Hebrew, sallei chori. The second word is rare. It may mean “white bread” (three baskets of white bread or pastries) or describe the baskets themselves, perhaps made of white wicker or open-work. Either way the picture is clear: baskets of baked goods for Pharaoh’s table, carried on the head as Egyptian bakers did.

verseByVerse.quote: On the third day, which was Pharaoh's birthday, he made a feast for all his servants and lifted up the head of the chief cupbearer and the head of the chief baker among his servants. He restored the chief cupbearer to his position, and he placed the cup in Pharaoh's hand. But he hanged the chief baker, as Joseph had interpreted to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the third day, Pharaoh’s birthday, everything happens exactly as Joseph said: the cupbearer is restored and the baker hanged.

Pharaoh’s birthday. It all happens on Pharaoh’s birthday, exactly as Joseph said: God’s word proves true. A royal birthday was an occasion for feasting and for deciding the fate of prisoners. The only other birthday feast in Scripture is Herod’s, where John the Baptist was beheaded (Matthew 14:6–10).

Lifted up the head of the chief cupbearer and the head of the chief baker. The narrator uses the double-edged phrase one last time. Both men are summoned before Pharaoh; one is restored, the other condemned. On the third day, the one who served Pharaoh’s cup is raised, and the other is hanged on a tree.

As Joseph had interpreted to them. The key words of the paragraph. Joseph’s word, which was God’s word, comes true to the detail. That will matter in the next chapter, when the cupbearer finally remembers him.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet the chief cupbearer did not remember Joseph, but forgot him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The restored cupbearer forgets Joseph, and Joseph is left in prison; but God has not forgotten him.

The chief cupbearer did not remember Joseph, but forgot him. The narrator says it twice: he did not remember, he forgot. The man who owed Joseph most did nothing. Joseph stays two more whole years in prison (41:1). The wise man who saved a city, the preacher observed, was likewise forgotten by everyone (Ecclesiastes 9:15).

But God has not forgotten. The waiting is part of God’s plan: the cupbearer will remember on the very morning Pharaoh needs Joseph (41:9–13). Had he remembered sooner, Joseph might have been released into obscurity, or sent home. God’s delays are not his denials, and his timing is better than ours.

In everyday life. When people forget you, God does not: “Can a woman forget her nursing child …? Even these may forget, yet I will not forget you” (Isaiah 49:15). Thank him that he remembers when others forget, and keep serving faithfully where you are, as Joseph did.

40.theology:
Genesis 40 is about the gap between promise and fulfilment. Joseph has dreams from God that he will be raised above his brothers (37:5–10), yet his story so far is one injustice after another: sold, falsely accused, imprisoned, and now forgotten. Where is God in the forgetting?

Genesis answers that God may go unmentioned in the events and still be at work in them. The forgetful cupbearer, the two-year wait, the imprisonment in exactly the right prison: all will be seen, looking back, as parts of God’s plan. “All things work together for good” (Romans 8:28) is true in the middle of the story, though it is often seen only at the end. Meanwhile the faithful way is Joseph’s: attention to others, confidence that God knows what it all means, and faithfulness where he has put us.
40.examples:
Many believers know the cupbearer’s kind of forgetting: they did the right thing, served faithfully, asked for fair help, and were forgotten by those who could have helped. The forgetting is not the end of the story; it is the dark before the dawn of chapter 41.

Joseph’s question, “Why are your faces downcast today?”, marks a man whose suffering has produced compassion instead of self-absorption. He is like the servant who came “not to be served but to serve” (Mark 10:45). Those who have been through the pit are often the quickest to see the pit in others’ faces. Suffering received in faith can equip us to help others.

keyVerse.quote: They said to him, “We have had dreams, and there is no one to interpret them.” And Joseph said to them, “Do not interpretations belong to God? Please tell them to me.”
keyVerse.note: Joseph, a forgotten prisoner, points two of Pharaoh’s officials to the God who knows the future and gives the meaning. He takes no credit for himself, yet speaks with confidence, because his trust is in God. The same confidence will carry him before Pharaoh in the next chapter.

40.reflection:
Joseph noticed the downcast faces of two fellow prisoners in the middle of his own suffering (vv. 6–7). What helps us notice others when we are hurting ourselves?

Joseph said, “Do not interpretations belong to God?” (v. 8). How can we give God the credit for whatever wisdom or gifts we have, without false modesty?

Joseph told the baker bad news as plainly as he told the cupbearer good news (vv. 12–19). Why is it hard to speak hard truths kindly, and why does it matter?

The cupbearer forgot Joseph for two years (v. 23; 41:1). How does the thief’s prayer, “Jesus, remember me” (Luke 23:42), comfort you when you feel forgotten?

41.title: Joseph Interprets Pharaoh's Dreams

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–57 — From Prison to Palace: Joseph Exalted
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God lifts his forgotten servant from the pit to the palace in a single day, and through him keeps the world alive. Pharaoh’s two dreams baffle Egypt’s experts, and the cupbearer finally remembers Joseph (vv. 1–13). Joseph gives God the credit, interprets the dreams as seven years of plenty and seven of famine fixed by God, and proposes a plan (vv. 14–36). Pharaoh recognises the Spirit of God in him and sets him over all Egypt (vv. 37–45). Joseph stores grain beyond measuring, names his sons for God’s kindness in affliction (vv. 46–52), and when famine strikes, all the earth comes to him for bread (vv. 53–57).
verseByVerse.theology: After two whole years Pharaoh dreams of cows and ears of grain, and his magicians fail. The cupbearer remembers; Joseph is brought from the pit, interprets seven years of plenty and seven of famine, and proposes a plan. Pharaoh sets him over Egypt; he stores grain, names his sons Manasseh and Ephraim, and all the earth comes to him for bread.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: "Go to Joseph. What he says to you, do" (v. 55; cf. John 2:5). Now: God raises the poor from the dust and seats them with princes (Ps. 113:7–8), in his time, not ours.
