verseByVerse.quote: After two whole years, Pharaoh dreamed that he was standing by the Nile, and behold, there came up out of the Nile seven cows, attractive and plump, and they fed in the reed grass. And behold, seven other cows, ugly and thin, came up out of the Nile after them, and stood by the other cows on the bank of the Nile. And the ugly, thin cows ate up the seven attractive, plump cows. And Pharaoh awoke. And he fell asleep and dreamed a second time. And behold, seven ears of grain, plump and good, were growing on one stalk. And behold, after them sprouted seven ears, thin and blighted by the east wind. And the thin ears swallowed up the seven plump, full ears. And Pharaoh awoke, and behold, it was a dream.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two years after the cupbearer forgot Joseph, Pharaoh dreams twice of plenty being swallowed by want: fat cows eaten by thin ones, full ears swallowed by blighted ones.

After two whole years. “Two whole years” after the cupbearer’s release (40:23), literally “two years of days”: the phrase makes the reader feel every day of Joseph’s wait. God had not forgotten him, but he was waiting for the right moment, when the king himself would need Joseph.

Standing by the Nile. The Nile was the life of Egypt. Rain hardly ever falls there; the yearly flood of the river watered the fields, and a low flood meant a poor harvest and hunger. So a dream about the Nile was a dream about the welfare of the whole kingdom. Cattle often stood in the river and grazed in the “reed grass” along its banks, so the scene is an ordinary one, until the thin cows eat the fat.

Seven ears … on one stalk. The second dream says the same thing in a different picture: from the herd to the harvest. Seven is the number of completeness in Scripture, and the doubling of the dream will matter (v. 32).

Blighted by the east wind. The east wind is the scorching wind off the desert that withers crops in a day (Hosea 13:15).

And behold, it was a dream. Pharaoh wakes and realises it was only a dream, yet he cannot shake it off. Egyptians believed dreams could carry messages from the gods, and a dream about the Nile was a dream about Pharaoh’s own duty, for he was thought to keep the order of the land.

verseByVerse.quote: So in the morning his spirit was troubled, and he sent and called for all the magicians of Egypt and all its wise men. Pharaoh told them his dreams, but there was none who could interpret them to Pharaoh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Egypt’s magicians and wise men cannot interpret the dreams: all the wisdom of the most learned court in the world fails before what God is saying.

His spirit was troubled. The most powerful man in the world lies awake worried by two dreams. Power cannot buy peace or knowledge of the future.

All the magicians of Egypt. The word for “magicians” probably comes from an Egyptian title for priests skilled in sacred writings and rituals. They were a professional class with written guides to the meaning of dreams, and the same word is used of the magicians who opposed Moses (Exodus 7:11). Their public failure is the point: the wisdom of Egypt fails, as Babylon’s will fail before Daniel (Daniel 2:10–11). “Has not God made foolish the wisdom of the world?” (1 Corinthians 1:20).

There was none who could interpret them. God has closed every door but one, so that when the answer comes, there will be no doubt where it came from.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the chief cupbearer said to Pharaoh, "I remember my offenses today. When Pharaoh was angry with his servants and put me and the chief baker in custody in the house of the captain of the guard, we dreamed on the same night, he and I, each having a dream with its own interpretation. A young Hebrew was there with us, a servant of the captain of the guard. When we told him, he interpreted our dreams to us, giving an interpretation to each man according to his dream. And as he interpreted to us, so it came about. I was restored to my office, and the baker was hanged."
verseByVerse.commentary:
At last the chief cupbearer remembers the young Hebrew who interpreted his dream in prison, and tells Pharaoh that everything happened exactly as he said.

I remember my offenses today. The cupbearer is careful: he reminds Pharaoh of an old offence only to explain how he met Joseph, and he may also be admitting the later fault of forgetting. Either way, the forgetting that seemed so cruel in 40:23 turns out to have been timed by God. Had the cupbearer remembered two years earlier, Joseph might have been released and gone home to Canaan; now he is remembered on the very morning when Pharaoh needs him.

A young Hebrew … a servant of the captain of the guard. The description is faintly dismissive: young, foreign, a slave. Yet the cupbearer’s witness is plain: “as he interpreted to us, so it came about.” Joseph’s word has been proved true.

In everyday life. People will forget what you did for them. God does not, and his timing is better than ours even when it is slower.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Pharaoh sent and called Joseph, and they quickly brought him out of the pit. And when he had shaved himself and changed his clothes, he came in before Pharaoh. And Pharaoh said to Joseph, "I have had a dream, and there is no one who can interpret it. I have heard it said of you that when you hear a dream you can interpret it." Joseph answered Pharaoh, "It is not in me; God will give Pharaoh a favorable answer."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joseph is rushed from the pit to the palace, and his first words to Pharaoh give all the credit to God.

They quickly brought him out of the pit. Joseph goes from the pit to the palace in a single day. The word “pit” is the same one used of the dry cistern his brothers threw him into (37:24), and Joseph used it of the prison (40:15): Joseph’s life has been one pit after another, and now God lifts him out.

When he had shaved himself and changed his clothes. Egyptians, unlike Hebrews, went clean-shaven, and a bearded foreigner would not be fit to stand before Pharaoh. Clothes keep marking the turns of Joseph’s story: the robe his brothers stripped from him (37:23), the garment left in the hand of Potiphar’s wife (39:12), and now new clothes for the court, with finer ones to come (v. 42).

I have heard it said of you that when you hear a dream you can interpret it. Pharaoh assumes Joseph has a skill he can use at will, as the magicians claimed to.

It is not in me; God will give Pharaoh a favorable answer. Standing before the most powerful man in the world, after thirteen years of slavery and prison, Joseph has every reason to sell himself. Instead his first words deny that the power is his: “It is not in me.” As in prison (40:8), humility and confidence sit together, because both rest on God. And he speaks of God to a king who thought himself a god, without apology.

In everyday life. Give God the credit for your gifts, especially when they are what people are praising you for.
verseByVerse.note: Egyptians were clean-shaven; Joseph is made presentable for court.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Pharaoh said to Joseph, "Behold, in my dream I was standing on the banks of the Nile. Seven cows, plump and attractive, came up out of the Nile and fed in the reed grass. Seven other cows came up after them, poor and very ugly and thin, such as I had never seen in all the land of Egypt. And the thin, ugly cows ate up the first seven plump cows, but when they had eaten them no one would have known that they had eaten them, for they were still as ugly as at the beginning. Then I awoke.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pharaoh retells his first dream to Joseph, adding how shockingly ugly the thin cows were and how they stayed thin after eating the fat ones.

Such as I had never seen in all the land of Egypt. Pharaoh adds vivid details of his own, as people do when retelling a dream that still disturbs them. He has never seen cows so ugly in all Egypt.

No one would have known that they had eaten them. This detail is not in the narrator’s account (vv. 3–4) but it matters: the famine will be so severe that the years of plenty will leave no trace, “and all the plenty will be forgotten” (v. 30).

verseByVerse.quote: I also saw in my dream seven ears growing on one stalk, full and good. Seven ears, withered, thin, and blighted by the east wind, sprouted after them, and the thin ears swallowed up the seven good ears. And I told it to the magicians, but there was no one who could explain it to me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pharaoh tells his second dream, of thin ears swallowing full ones, and admits that his magicians could not explain it.

Withered, thin, and blighted by the east wind. Pharaoh again adds a word, “withered”, to what the narrator told us. The hot desert wind dries the grain before it can fill.

There was no one who could explain it to me. Pharaoh openly admits the failure of his own experts to a foreign slave. The stage is set for God to speak.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Joseph said to Pharaoh, "The dreams of Pharaoh are one; God has revealed to Pharaoh what he is about to do. The seven good cows are seven years, and the seven good ears are seven years; the dreams are one. The seven lean and ugly cows that came up after them are seven years, and the seven empty ears blighted by the east wind are also seven years of famine. It is as I told Pharaoh; God has shown to Pharaoh what he is about to do.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joseph tells Pharaoh that the two dreams are one message from God, revealing what he is about to do: seven good years and seven years of famine.

The dreams of Pharaoh are one. Two pictures, one message. Joseph does not need to puzzle over the dream or consult a book; the meaning comes plainly and at once.

God has revealed to Pharaoh what he is about to do. Joseph names God again and again in his answer (vv. 16, 25, 28, 32). The coming famine is not chance or the whim of the Nile, which Egyptians worshipped as a god: the God of Joseph rules the seasons and the river, and he alone knows and declares the future (Isaiah 46:9–10). He tells Pharaoh in advance, not to frighten him, but so that lives can be saved.

verseByVerse.quote: There will come seven years of great plenty throughout all the land of Egypt, but after them there will arise seven years of famine, and all the plenty will be forgotten in the land of Egypt. The famine will consume the land, and the plenty will be unknown in the land by reason of the famine that will follow, for it will be very severe. And the doubling of Pharaoh's dream means that the thing is fixed by God, and God will shortly bring it about.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seven years of great plenty will be followed by seven years of famine so severe that the plenty will be forgotten, and the doubled dream shows that God has fixed it and will do it soon.

All the plenty will be forgotten. The repetition is deliberate: forgotten, unknown, consumed. Good times are quickly forgotten when hard times come, unless someone has prepared.

The thing is fixed by God, and God will shortly bring it about. A dream given twice means the matter is certain, as Joseph’s own two dreams had been (37:5–9). This is not blind fate, but the settled decision of a personal God who rules all things and does what he says. And God’s certainty is not a reason to do nothing: it is the reason for the plan Joseph is about to propose.

verseByVerse.quote: Now therefore let Pharaoh select a discerning and wise man, and set him over the land of Egypt. Let Pharaoh proceed to appoint overseers over the land and take one-fifth of the produce of the land of Egypt during the seven plentiful years. And let them gather all the food of these good years that are coming and store up grain under the authority of Pharaoh for food in the cities, and let them keep it. That food shall be a reserve for the land against the seven years of famine that are to occur in the land of Egypt, so that the land may not perish through the famine."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joseph advises Pharaoh to appoint a wise man to store a fifth of the harvest in the good years, so that the land will not perish in the famine.

A discerning and wise man. Joseph does not stop at interpretation; he gives counsel. Faith in God’s word does not make him passive; it leads him to wise, practical planning. Knowing what God will do is the reason to act, not a reason to sit still.

One-fifth of the produce. A fifth of the harvest, stored in the cities “under the authority of Pharaoh.” In the good years that is a bearable share; in the bad years it will be the difference between life and death. Later the fifth becomes a permanent arrangement (47:24, 26).

So that the land may not perish. The aim of the whole plan is life. God reveals the famine in order to save people from it.

In everyday life. Save in good times for hard times. “Go to the ant, O sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise” (Proverbs 6:6). Trusting God and planning ahead are not opposites.

verseByVerse.quote: This proposal pleased Pharaoh and all his servants. And Pharaoh said to his servants, "Can we find a man like this, in whom is the Spirit of God?" Then Pharaoh said to Joseph, "Since God has shown you all this, there is none so discerning and wise as you are. You shall be over my house, and all my people shall order themselves as you command. Only as regards the throne will I be greater than you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pharaoh sees that the Spirit of God is in Joseph and sets him over his house and all his people, second only to the throne.

In whom is the Spirit of God. A pagan king sees that Joseph’s wisdom is not merely human. Pharaoh would have meant something vaguer than the full truth about the Holy Spirit, perhaps “the spirit of the gods,” but the narrator lets his words stand: the wisdom that Egypt lacked was the gift of God. The same is said of Daniel by Babylonian kings (Daniel 4:8; 5:11).

There is none so discerning and wise as you are. Joseph had advised Pharaoh to find “a discerning and wise man” (v. 33), with no thought of himself; Pharaoh uses the same words of Joseph. Joseph does not push himself forward. God lifts him up.

Only as regards the throne will I be greater than you. The humiliated prisoner becomes the second man in the kingdom in one morning. “The king sent and released him … he made him lord of his house and ruler of all his possessions” (Psalm 105:20–21), and Stephen says that God “gave him favor and wisdom before Pharaoh” (Acts 7:10).

verseByVerse.quote: And Pharaoh said to Joseph, "See, I have set you over all the land of Egypt." Then Pharaoh took his signet ring from his hand and put it on Joseph's hand, and clothed him in garments of fine linen and put a gold chain about his neck. And he made him ride in his second chariot. And they called out before him, "Bow the knee!" Thus he set him over all the land of Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pharaoh installs Joseph with a signet ring, fine linen, a gold chain and the second chariot, and men cry before him, “Bow the knee!”

Pharaoh took his signet ring. The signet ring sealed documents in the king’s name, so giving it to Joseph meant giving him the king’s own authority. Fine linen was the clothing of Egypt’s nobles and priests, and a gold chain was a reward for high service, often pictured in Egyptian art.

Garments of fine linen. His brothers stripped Joseph of one robe (see clothing), and Potiphar’s wife held up another as false evidence. Now Pharaoh clothes him in honour. God has the last word over the garments too.

He made him ride in his second chariot. Joseph is paraded publicly as the king’s second, so that all Egypt will know who rules under Pharaoh.

“Bow the knee!” The young man whose dreams of others bowing to him made his brothers hate him (37:8) now has all Egypt commanded to bow before him. It is a picture of how every knee will bow to the exalted Christ: “so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow” (Philippians 2:10). So God lifts up the humble in his own time.

A picture, not a code. How far Joseph is a picture of Christ is discussed at 37:36. The likeness lies in the pattern the story itself gives, humiliation then exaltation, the rejected brother who becomes the saviour, not in pressing every detail.

Uncertain wording. The cry translated “Bow the knee!” is the Hebrew Abrek, which appears only here. It sounds like the Hebrew word for “kneel,” which is why the ESV translates it so, but it is probably a foreign word: suggestions include an Egyptian call for attention or an Akkadian title for a high official. The general sense is clear in any case: it was a public cry of honour before Joseph as he passed.
verseByVerse.note: “Bow the knee” renders Abrek, probably an Egyptian word that sounds like the Hebrew for “to kneel” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: Moreover, Pharaoh said to Joseph, "I am Pharaoh, and without your consent no one shall lift up hand or foot in all the land of Egypt." And Pharaoh called Joseph's name Zaphenath-paneah. And he gave him in marriage Asenath, the daughter of Potiphera priest of On. So Joseph went out over the land of Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pharaoh confirms Joseph’s total authority, gives him an Egyptian name, and marries him into a leading priestly family, and Joseph goes out over the land.

Without your consent no one shall lift up hand or foot. An idiom for complete authority: nothing in Egypt moves without Joseph. Behind Pharaoh’s grant, the narrator wants us to see God’s: the dreams of 37:5–9 are coming true.

Pharaoh called Joseph’s name Zaphenath-paneah. Giving a new name was a way of claiming someone for the court, as Babylon later renamed Daniel and his friends (Daniel 1:7). Joseph accepts the name, but not the gods behind it: his faith remains clear in the names he gives his own sons (vv. 51–52), and those sons will be counted in Israel (48:5).

Asenath, the daughter of Potiphera priest of On. On, later called Heliopolis, near modern Cairo, was the great centre of the worship of the sun god, so Joseph is joined to the heart of Egypt’s religious elite. The narrator neither praises nor blames the marriage; it was arranged by the king, and nothing suggests Joseph worshipped Egypt’s gods. His wife’s names, Asenath and Potiphera, probably honour Egyptian gods, which only shows how fully Joseph now lived inside Egypt while remaining the LORD’s.

Uncertain wording. The meaning of Zaphenath-paneah is not certain. It is an Egyptian name written in Hebrew letters, and the most common suggestion is “God speaks and he lives,” though others have been proposed. Whatever its exact sense, it marks Joseph as a man of the court.
verseByVerse.note: On was the city of the sun god, later called Heliopolis.

verseByVerse.quote: Joseph was thirty years old when he entered the service of Pharaoh king of Egypt. And Joseph went out from the presence of Pharaoh and went through all the land of Egypt. During the seven plentiful years the earth produced abundantly,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joseph is thirty when he enters Pharaoh’s service, and he goes straight to work across the land as the good years begin.

Joseph was thirty years old. He was seventeen when he was sold (37:2), so thirteen years have passed in slavery and prison. They were not wasted years: in Potiphar’s house and in the prison God was training a ruler (Psalm 105:19). David was also thirty when he began to reign (2 Samuel 5:4), and Jesus was “about thirty years of age” when he began his ministry (Luke 3:23).

Went through all the land of Egypt. Joseph does not enjoy his new status at court; he travels the country and starts the work at once.

The earth produced abundantly. The first half of God’s word comes true, which gives confidence that the second half will too.
verseByVerse.note: Joseph was 17 when sold (37:2) and 30 here: thirteen years as slave and prisoner.

verseByVerse.quote: and he gathered up all the food of these seven years, which occurred in the land of Egypt, and put the food in the cities. He put in every city the food from the fields around it. And Joseph stored up grain in great abundance, like the sand of the sea, until he ceased to measure it, for it could not be measured.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joseph stores the harvest of the good years in the cities, until there is so much grain that they stop measuring it.

He put in every city the food from the fields around it. Wise administration: the grain is stored near where it was grown and where it will be needed, not carried to one distant capital.

Like the sand of the sea. The phrase recalls God’s promise to Abraham that his offspring would be “as the sand that is on the seashore” (22:17). God’s blessing on Abraham’s family is overflowing even here, in Egypt, through one of Abraham’s great-grandsons.

Until he ceased to measure it. Joseph the careful administrator gives up counting: God’s provision is beyond measuring.

verseByVerse.quote: Before the year of famine came, two sons were born to Joseph. Asenath, the daughter of Potiphera priest of On, bore them to him. Joseph called the name of the firstborn Manasseh. "For," he said, "God has made me forget all my hardship and all my father's house." The name of the second he called Ephraim, "For God has made me fruitful in the land of my affliction."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joseph names his two sons for what God has done with his suffering: God has made him forget his hardship and made him fruitful in the land of his affliction.

Manasseh … God has made me forget. Manasseh sounds like “making to forget.” Joseph does not mean that he has lost his memory or disowned his family; he will weep at the sight of them (42:24). He means that the pain no longer rules him. The wounds of his father’s house have been healed by God’s kindness.

Ephraim … God has made me fruitful in the land of my affliction. Ephraim sounds like “making fruitful,” the word of God’s blessing from the beginning (1:28; 35:11). Yet Joseph still calls Egypt “the land of my affliction.” Healing has come, but this is not home, and faith still remembers the promises (50:24–25).

Two sons … before the year of famine came. Both names give God the credit. Joseph’s story is not that he overcame his past by his own strength, but that God made something fruitful of it.

In everyday life. God can make you fruitful in the place of your affliction, without asking you to pretend it was not affliction. If memories of past wrongs still hold you, talking them through with a wise pastor or biblical counsellor is not a failure of faith.
verseByVerse.note: Manasseh sounds like “making to forget,” Ephraim like “making fruitful” (ESV notes).

verseByVerse.quote: The seven years of plenty that occurred in the land of Egypt came to an end, and the seven years of famine began to come, as Joseph had said. There was famine in all lands, but in all the land of Egypt there was bread. When all the land of Egypt was famished, the people cried to Pharaoh for bread. Pharaoh said to all the Egyptians, "Go to Joseph. What he says to you, do."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The famine comes just as Joseph said, and when Egypt cries to Pharaoh for bread, Pharaoh sends everyone to Joseph.

As Joseph had said. The second half of God’s word comes true as surely as the first. In all lands there is famine; “but in all the land of Egypt there was bread,” because one man listened to God and acted.

Go to Joseph. What he says to you, do. The whole land must come to the one man Pharaoh has appointed, and do what he says. The words are echoed by Mary at Cana: “Do whatever he tells you” (John 2:5). There is only one place to find bread, and only one person to go to.

verseByVerse.quote: So when the famine had spread over all the land, Joseph opened all the storehouses and sold to the Egyptians, for the famine was severe in the land of Egypt. Moreover, all the earth came to Egypt to Joseph to buy grain, because the famine was severe over all the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joseph opens the storehouses, and Egypt and all the earth come to him to buy grain.

Joseph opened all the storehouses. Joseph sells the grain rather than giving it away; it was Pharaoh’s, and the system had to last seven years. Chapter 47 shows where this led.

All the earth came to Egypt to Joseph. “All the earth” comes to Joseph, and Abraham’s offspring becomes a blessing to the nations, as God promised: “in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed” (12:3). Here the blessing comes as sacks of grain for people who had never heard of Abraham. And “all the earth” will include Canaan and ten brothers who never expected to see Joseph again: the next chapter begins there.

The bread of life. Joseph fed the world for a few years; a greater Son of Abraham gives himself as bread for all nations for ever: “I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger” (John 6:35).

Then I awoke.<sup>22</sup>I also saw in my dream seven ears growing on one stalk, full and good.<sup>23</sup>Seven ears, withered, thin, and blighted by the east wind, sprouted after them,<sup>24</sup>and the thin ears swallowed up the seven good ears. And I told it to the magicians, but there was no one who could explain it to me."<sup>25</sup>Then Joseph said to Pharaoh, "The dreams of Pharaoh are one; God has revealed to Pharaoh what he is about to do.<sup>26</sup>The seven good cows are seven years, and the seven good ears are seven years; the dreams are one.<sup>27</sup>The seven lean and ugly cows that came up after them are seven years, and the seven empty ears blighted by the east wind are also seven years of famine.<sup>28</sup>It is as I told Pharaoh; God has shown to Pharaoh what he is about to do.<sup>29</sup>There will come seven years of great plenty throughout all the land of Egypt,<sup>30</sup>but after them there will arise seven years of famine, and all the plenty will be forgotten in the land of Egypt. The famine will consume the land,<sup>31</sup>and the plenty will be unknown in the land by reason of the famine that will follow, for it will be very severe.<sup>32</sup>And the doubling of Pharaoh's dream means that the thing is fixed by God, and God will shortly bring it about.<sup>33</sup>Now therefore let Pharaoh select a discerning and wise man, and set him over the land of Egypt.<sup>34</sup>Let Pharaoh proceed to appoint overseers over the land and take one-fifth of the produce of the land of Egypt during the seven plentiful years.<sup>35</sup>And let them gather all the food of these good years that are coming and store up grain under the authority of Pharaoh for food in the cities, and let them keep it.<sup>36</sup>That food shall be a reserve for the land against the seven years of famine that are to occur in the land of Egypt, so that the land may not perish through the famine."<sup>37</sup>This proposal pleased Pharaoh and all his servants.<sup>38</sup>And Pharaoh said to his servants, "Can we find a man like this, in whom is the Spirit of God?"<sup>39</sup>Then Pharaoh said to Joseph, "Since God has shown you all this, there is none so discerning and wise as you are.<sup>40</sup>You shall be over my house, and all my people shall order themselves as you command. Only as regards the throne will I be greater than you."<sup>41</sup>And Pharaoh said to Joseph, "See, I have set you over all the land of Egypt."<sup>42</sup>Then Pharaoh took his signet ring from his hand and put it on Joseph's hand, and clothed him in garments of fine linen and put a gold chain about his neck.<sup>43</sup>And he made him ride in his second chariot. And they called out before him, "Bow the knee!" Thus he set him over all the land of Egypt.<sup>44</sup>Moreover, Pharaoh said to Joseph, "I am Pharaoh, and without your consent no one shall lift up hand or foot in all the land of Egypt."<sup>45</sup>And Pharaoh called Joseph's name Zaphenath-paneah. And he gave him in marriage Asenath, the daughter of Potiphera priest of On. So Joseph went out over the land of Egypt.<sup>46</sup>Joseph was thirty years old when he entered the service of Pharaoh king of Egypt. And Joseph went out from the presence of Pharaoh and went through all the land of Egypt.<sup>47</sup>During the seven plentiful years the earth produced abundantly,<sup>48</sup>and he gathered up all the food of these seven years, which occurred in the land of Egypt, and put the food in the cities. He put in every city the food from the fields around it.<sup>49</sup>And Joseph stored up grain in great abundance, like the sand of the sea, until he ceased to measure it, for it could not be measured.<sup>50</sup>Before the year of famine came, two sons were born to Joseph. Asenath, the daughter of Potiphera priest of On, bore them to him.<sup>51</sup>Joseph called the name of the firstborn Manasseh. "For," he said, "God has made me forget all my hardship and all my father's house."<sup>52</sup>The name of the second he called Ephraim, "For God has made me fruitful in the land of my affliction."<sup>53</sup>The seven years of plenty that occurred in the land of Egypt came to an end,<sup>54</sup>and the seven years of famine began to come, as Joseph had said. There was famine in all lands, but in all the land of Egypt there was bread.<sup>55</sup>When all the land of Egypt was famished, the people cried to Pharaoh for bread. Pharaoh said to all the Egyptians, "Go to Joseph. What he says to you, do."<sup>56</sup>So when the famine had spread over all the land, Joseph opened all the storehouses and sold to the Egyptians, for the famine was severe in the land of Egypt.<sup>57</sup>Moreover, all the earth came to Egypt to Joseph to buy grain, because the famine was severe over all the earth.
41.overview:
Where we are. Joseph has been in prison for two more years since the chief cupbearer, restored to his office, forgot the young Hebrew who had interpreted his dream (40:23). Nothing seems to be happening. Then Pharaoh has two dreams.

The message. God rules the future, and he lifts up the humble in his own time. In a single morning the forgotten prisoner is raised to be second only to Pharaoh, and the chapter credits every step to God: God sends the dreams, God gives their meaning, God has fixed what will happen. And God puts his servant where he can feed the whole world in its hunger.

Why it was said. Israel came out of Egypt knowing it as the land of slavery (see the introduction). This chapter told them how they had come to be there at all: not by accident, but because God had sent Joseph ahead of them to keep them alive, and because the God of their fathers was wiser than all Egypt’s magicians and stronger than its famine.

How the chapter makes its case. Pharaoh dreams of seven fat cows eaten by seven thin ones, then of seven good ears swallowed by seven blighted ones (vv. 1–7). Egypt’s wise men cannot interpret them, and the cupbearer at last remembers Joseph (vv. 8–13). Joseph is brought from the pit and gives God the credit before he hears a word (vv. 14–16). Pharaoh tells the dreams (vv. 17–24); Joseph explains them as seven years of plenty followed by seven of famine, fixed by God (vv. 25–32), and advises a plan to store grain (vv. 33–36). Pharaoh sets Joseph over all Egypt (vv. 37–45). Joseph gathers grain beyond measuring (vv. 46–49), names his two sons for God’s kindness (vv. 50–52), and when the famine comes, Egypt and all the earth come to him for bread (vv. 53–57).

Where it leads. By pattern. The New Testament never calls Joseph a type, but the shape of his life is the shape of Christ’s: the rejected son, brought low through no fault of his own, raised in a day to the right hand of the throne, with every knee commanded to bow, and the hungry world told, “Go to Joseph.” Joseph stored grain to keep the body alive for a few years; Jesus says, “I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger” (John 6:35). The chapter also shows the character of God revealed in Christ, who “humbled himself” and whom “God has highly exalted” (Philippians 2:8–9).

For us. God’s delays are not his forgetfulness: “Humble yourselves, therefore, under the mighty hand of God so that at the proper time he may exalt you” (1 Peter 5:6). Give him the credit for every gift. Plan wisely in good times. And when the world is hungry, point people to the one who has the bread.
41.theology:
Providence in the ordinary workings of the world. There is no miracle in this chapter. A king sleeps badly, a servant remembers, an administrator has a good idea, and grain is stored. God governs by dreams and harvests, by a courtier’s memory and the failure of a guild of magicians, and each event helps to put the right man in the right office in the right year. Paul states it plainly: God “works all things according to the counsel of his will” (Eph. 1:11), not merely the religious things.

Exaltation after humiliation. The pit, the false accusation, the forgotten years, and then a throne he did not seek: this is the shape Scripture keeps returning to, and it reaches its true form in Christ, who “humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death... Therefore God has highly exalted him” (Phil. 2:8–9). Joseph is not Christ; he is a preview, and God intended the likeness.
41.examples:
Then: Egypt’s wealth depended on the Nile flood, and a run of low floods meant national famine. Egyptian records show foreigners rising high at court, so a Semitic outsider made vizier, given an Egyptian name and a wife from the priests of On, fits what is known of Egypt. That is how a Hebrew household came to be settled in Goshen.

Now: Two years of silence ended in a single morning, and nothing Joseph did shortened them; he was not released because he prayed harder or behaved better, but because the moment arrived. Those years also changed him. The teenager who announced his dreams at the family table has become a man who says “it is not in me” before the most powerful person on earth. Long obscurity is not wasted time; it is where God makes people who can be trusted with an answered prayer.

keyVerse.quote: Joseph answered Pharaoh, “It is not in me; God will give Pharaoh a favorable answer.”
keyVerse.note: After thirteen years as a slave and prisoner, Joseph stands before the most powerful man in the world and gives all the credit to God. The whole chapter rests on this: it is God who reveals, God who fixes the future, God who lifts up his servant. Joseph’s humility is the doorway through which God’s wisdom comes to Egypt.

41.reflection:
Joseph waited two more years after the cupbearer forgot him (40:23; 41:1). How does this chapter help you when God’s timing seems slow?

Joseph’s first words to Pharaoh were, “It is not in me” (v. 16). Where are you tempted to take credit for what God has given?

Joseph believed God’s word about the famine and planned carefully for it (vv. 33–36). How do trusting God and planning wisely fit together in your life?

Pharaoh told the hungry, “Go to Joseph” (v. 55). Who in your life is spiritually hungry, and how could you point them to Jesus, the bread of life?

42.title: Joseph's Brothers Come to Egypt

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–38 — The First Journey: Recognition and Testing
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God begins to bring the brothers’ old sin to light, through the brother they wronged and do not recognise. Famine drives ten sons of Jacob to Egypt, where they bow before Joseph as his dreams foretold (vv. 1–8). Joseph accuses them of spying, holds them for three days, and demands that they bring Benjamin, keeping Simeon as a hostage (vv. 9–24). In the middle of the test the brothers confess to one another their guilt over Joseph, and he turns away to weep. On the way home they find their money returned and tremble at what God is doing (vv. 25–28). Jacob, hearing it all, refuses to send Benjamin, and the chapter ends in grief and deadlock (vv. 29–38).
verseByVerse.theology: Jacob sends ten sons to Egypt for grain but keeps Benjamin. They bow before Joseph, who knows them and speaks roughly, accuses them of spying, holds them three days, and demands Benjamin. They confess to one another their guilt over their brother; Joseph turns away and weeps, binds Simeon, and returns their money. Jacob refuses to let Benjamin go.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the sheaves bow as the dream said (37:7). Now: a wrong that is never confessed does not fade with time; it waits.

verseByVerse.quote: When Jacob learned that there was grain for sale in Egypt, he said to his sons, "Why do you look at one another?" And he said, "Behold, I have heard that there is grain for sale in Egypt. Go down and buy grain for us there, that we may live and not die." So ten of Joseph's brothers went down to buy grain in Egypt. But Jacob did not send Benjamin, Joseph's brother, with his brothers, for he feared that harm might happen to him. Thus the sons of Israel came to buy among the others who came, for the famine was in the land of Canaan.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Famine forces Jacob to send ten of his sons to Egypt to buy grain, but he keeps Benjamin, Rachel’s other son, at home.

Why do you look at one another? The brothers stand frozen, each waiting for another to act. The narrator does not say why. Perhaps it is simple helplessness; perhaps guilt already hangs over any thought of Egypt, the land to which they sold Joseph.

That we may live and not die. The family is facing starvation. Jacob’s words will be echoed by Judah when the food runs out again (43:8), and they are the very thing God is doing through Joseph: keeping his people alive (45:5; 50:20).

Ten of Joseph’s brothers. The narrator calls them “Joseph’s brothers,” not “Jacob’s sons.” Their journey is not only about grain; it is about the brother they wronged.

Jacob did not send Benjamin. Jacob keeps Benjamin back “for he feared that harm might happen to him.” Benjamin is no child now, but he is Rachel’s other son, and Jacob’s favouritism has simply moved from Joseph to him. The brothers cannot have missed it.

Among the others who came. The sons of Israel, heirs of God’s promise to bless the nations, arrive as hungry foreigners in a queue. God’s people are not spared the famine; they are fed through God’s servant.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Joseph was governor over the land. He was the one who sold to all the people of the land. And Joseph's brothers came and bowed themselves before him with their faces to the ground. Joseph saw his brothers and recognized them, but he treated them like strangers and spoke roughly to them. "Where do you come from?" he said. They said, "From the land of Canaan, to buy food." And Joseph recognized his brothers, but they did not recognize him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The brothers bow to the ground before Joseph, fulfilling his dream; he recognises them at once, but they do not recognise him.

Joseph was governor over the land. The narrator reminds us who holds the grain, and the power, as the brothers walk in.

Bowed themselves before him with their faces to the ground. The sheaves bow to Joseph’s sheaf (37:7). The brothers had sold him to make sure his dreams never came true (37:20), and their very journey to escape death has brought them to fulfil them.

He recognized them, but he treated them like strangers. Hebrew plays on two words from the same root: Joseph “recognized” them, but “made himself strange” to them. The same verb “recognize” ran through the earlier story: the brothers asked Jacob to “identify” Joseph’s bloodied robe (37:32), and Tamar asked Judah to “identify” his seal and staff (38:25). The theme of recognition and deception comes back now on the brothers’ own heads.

They did not recognize him. Joseph was about seventeen when they last saw him (37:2); now he is a man of nearly forty, shaved, dressed and speaking as an Egyptian, and they think he is dead or a slave somewhere. They have no reason to look for him in the second man in Egypt.

Spoke roughly to them. Joseph speaks harshly, through an interpreter (v. 23), and keeps his distance. Whatever he feels, he has decided not to reveal himself yet.
verseByVerse.note: Joseph was about seventeen when they last saw him, and now dressed and spoke as an Egyptian.

verseByVerse.quote: And Joseph remembered the dreams that he had dreamed of them. And he said to them, "You are spies; you have come to see the nakedness of the land." They said to him, "No, my lord, your servants have come to buy food. We are all sons of one man. We are honest men. Your servants have never been spies." He said to them, "No, it is the nakedness of the land that you have come to see." And they said, "We, your servants, are twelve brothers, the sons of one man in the land of Canaan, and behold, the youngest is this day with our father, and one is no more."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Remembering his dreams, Joseph accuses the brothers of spying, and in defending themselves they tell him about their father, Benjamin, and the brother who “is no more.”

Joseph remembered the dreams. Seeing them bow, Joseph remembers his dreams and understands that God has been at work. The dreams were not about his own glory, but about what God would do; the second dream included his father and his whole family (37:9–10), and none of that has happened yet.

You are spies; you have come to see the nakedness of the land. “Nakedness” means its weak, unguarded places. The charge was a plausible one: Egypt’s north-eastern frontier, facing Canaan, was the border it watched most closely, and ten men from there could easily be scouts. Joseph uses it to put them under pressure and to learn about home.

We are all sons of one man. We are honest men. Every word is true and full of irony. “Sons of one man” includes the man they are speaking to. “Honest men” comes from brothers who sold their brother and lied to their father for twenty years.

One is no more. Their guilty secret, spoken to the very brother they mean. They still cannot say what happened to him; “no more” covers it.

verseByVerse.quote: But Joseph said to them, "It is as I said to you. You are spies. By this you shall be tested: by the life of Pharaoh, you shall not go from this place unless your youngest brother comes here. Send one of you, and let him bring your brother, while you remain confined, that your words may be tested, whether there is truth in you. Or else, by the life of Pharaoh, surely you are spies." And he put them all together in custody for three days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joseph repeats the charge and sets a test: one brother must fetch Benjamin while the rest stay in prison, and he locks them all up for three days.

By this you shall be tested. Joseph’s demand is a test, and Benjamin is at its centre. Are these still the men who could get rid of Rachel’s son and sit down to eat (37:25)? Will they treat Benjamin as they treated Joseph? He needs to know whether their words, and their hearts, are true: “whether there is truth in you.”

By the life of Pharaoh. An Egyptian official’s oath. Joseph is playing his part fully, and the brothers have no reason to suspect anything.

Custody for three days. The brothers taste a little of what they did to Joseph: thrown into a pit, at the mercy of a stranger, not knowing whether they will live. Three days of it does more than twenty years of silence.

Where Christians differ: was Joseph cruel? Some readers see revenge, or at least a man enjoying his power after years of suffering. Others see wisdom and love throughout.

This commentary’s view. Joseph weeps again and again in these chapters (v. 24; 43:30; 45:2), and his harshness serves a purpose: to bring his brothers to face what they did and to find out whether they have changed. A cheap reconciliation, with the sin never named, would have healed nothing. Yet Joseph is not a pattern for manipulating people: he holds a unique place in God’s plan, and the narrator shows his methods without holding them up for us to copy.

verseByVerse.quote: On the third day Joseph said to them, "Do this and you will live, for I fear God: if you are honest men, let one of your brothers remain confined where you are in custody, and let the rest go and carry grain for the famine of your households, and bring your youngest brother to me. So your words will be verified, and you shall not die." And they did so.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the third day Joseph softens his demand, because he fears God: only one brother will stay in prison while the rest take grain home and bring Benjamin back.

Do this and you will live, for I fear God. “I fear God” is a clue the brothers miss, an unexpected word from an Egyptian ruler. To fear God means to live as answerable to him, and so to deal justly with the weak, as the Hebrew midwives would later do in Egypt (Exodus 1:17). The brothers have power over no one now, and the one who has power over them fears God.

Let one of your brothers remain … let the rest go. Joseph changes his first plan out of mercy. Their families at home are hungry, so nine go back with grain and only one stays. The test remains, but the burden is lighter.

So your words will be verified. Bringing Benjamin will prove their story. It will also show whether they will bring Rachel’s son back safely, or abandon a brother again.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they said to one another, "In truth we are guilty concerning our brother, in that we saw the distress of his soul, when he begged us and we did not listen. That is why this distress has come upon us." And Reuben answered them, "Did I not tell you not to sin against the boy? But you did not listen. So now there comes a reckoning for his blood."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Faced with Joseph’s test, the brothers confess to one another that they are guilty concerning Joseph, and Reuben says that a reckoning for his blood has come.

In truth we are guilty concerning our brother. After more than twenty years, conscience wakes. No one has accused them of selling Joseph; the pressure of their situation brings it out of them. Like the psalmist, they have found that guilt kept silent does not go away: “For when I kept silent, my bones wasted away through my groaning all day long” (Psalm 32:3).

We saw the distress of his soul, when he begged us. We learn here something chapter 37 did not tell us: Joseph begged for his life from the pit, and they did not listen. They have remembered it for two decades. Hebrew uses the same word for his “distress” and for the “distress” that has come on them now: they see their trouble as measure for measure.

Did I not tell you not to sin against the boy? Reuben had tried to rescue Joseph (37:21–22, 29–30), and now he says, in effect, “I told you so.” It is true, but it does not help; he is clearing himself rather than standing with his brothers. “A reckoning for his blood” shows that they believe Joseph is dead, and that they know God requires an account for a brother’s life (9:5).

Misery is not yet repentance. The brothers have been miserable about Joseph for twenty years, but misery is not the same as repentance. Paul distinguishes “godly grief,” which “produces a repentance that leads to salvation,” from “worldly grief,” which “produces death” (2 Corinthians 7:10). Joseph is looking for the first kind: not just regret, but a change of heart that will show itself in how they treat Benjamin.

In everyday life. Unconfessed sin does not go away; confessed, it meets a God who forgives: “I acknowledged my sin to you, and I did not cover my iniquity … and you forgave the iniquity of my sin” (Psalm 32:5).

verseByVerse.quote: They did not know that Joseph understood them, for there was an interpreter between them. Then he turned away from them and wept. And he returned to them and spoke to them. And he took Simeon from them and bound him before their eyes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joseph, who has understood every word, turns away to weep, then comes back and has Simeon bound before their eyes.

There was an interpreter between them. Joseph has been speaking Egyptian and using an interpreter, so the brothers speak freely in Hebrew, thinking he cannot understand. He hears their confession, and he hears that Reuben tried to save him.

He turned away from them and wept. Joseph turns away and weeps, the first of many times he weeps in this story (43:30; 45:2, 14–15; 46:29; 50:1, 17). His heart is not hard; his harshness is a mask, worn for their good.

He took Simeon from them and bound him. Simeon was the second son. Joseph passes over Reuben, the eldest, perhaps because he has just learned that Reuben tried to save him, and takes the next in line. Simeon may also have been a leader in the plot, as he was in the massacre at Shechem (34:25), though the text does not say so. Binding him “before their eyes” makes them watch a brother taken from them, as Joseph once was.

verseByVerse.quote: And Joseph gave orders to fill their bags with grain, and to replace every man's money in his sack, and to give them provisions for the journey. This was done for them. Then they loaded their donkeys with their grain and departed. And as one of them opened his sack to give his donkey fodder at the lodging place, he saw his money in the mouth of his sack. He said to his brothers, "My money has been put back; here it is in the mouth of my sack!" At this their hearts failed them, and they turned trembling to one another, saying, "What is this that God has done to us?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joseph secretly returns their money with the grain, and when one brother finds his silver on the way home, they all tremble and ask what God has done to them.

To replace every man’s money in his sack. Joseph gives them the grain free and adds provisions for the journey. It is kindness, but it is also a further test: will they keep the silver, as they once took silver for Joseph (37:28)?

At the lodging place. A stopping place on the road, perhaps no more than a campsite with water. Travellers fed their donkeys and slept there.

My money has been put back. The returned money was Joseph’s kindness, but it terrifies them: they will be accused of theft, and the Egyptian lord already thinks them spies. A guilty conscience reads unexpected kindness as a threat.

What is this that God has done to us? For the first time in the story the brothers speak of God. They begin to see that God is calling them to account, and the narrator does not correct them: God does use circumstances to press on a guilty conscience. What they do not yet see is that the God who is confronting them is also preparing their rescue.

verseByVerse.quote: When they came to Jacob their father in the land of Canaan, they told him all that had happened to them, saying, "The man, the lord of the land, spoke roughly to us and took us to be spies of the land. But we said to him, 'We are honest men; we have never been spies. We are twelve brothers, sons of our father. One is no more, and the youngest is this day with our father in the land of Canaan.' Then the man, the lord of the land, said to us, 'By this I shall know that you are honest men: leave one of your brothers with me, and take grain for the famine of your households, and go your way. Bring your youngest brother to me. Then I shall know that you are not spies but honest men, and I will deliver your brother to you, and you shall trade in the land.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Back in Canaan, the brothers tell Jacob all that happened, softening the harshest parts, and explain that Benjamin must go to Egypt to free Simeon and prove them honest.

They told him all that had happened to them. This time the brothers tell their father the truth, a change from their lie over Joseph’s robe (37:32). Their account is accurate in substance, though they leave out the three days in prison and do not describe Simeon being bound; they are trying to spare their father, and perhaps themselves.

The man, the lord of the land. They twice call Joseph “the man, the lord of the land.” They do not know that “the man” is the son their father mourns.

You shall trade in the land. Joseph’s promise, as they report it, includes Simeon’s release and freedom to trade. The way back to Egypt is open, but only with Benjamin.

verseByVerse.quote: As they emptied their sacks, behold, every man's bundle of money was in his sack. And when they and their father saw their bundles of money, they were afraid. And Jacob their father said to them, "You have bereaved me of my children: Joseph is no more, and Simeon is no more, and now you would take Benjamin. All this has come against me." Then Reuben said to his father, "Kill my two sons if I do not bring him back to you. Put him in my hands, and I will bring him back to you." But he said, "My son shall not go down with you, for his brother is dead, and he is the only one left. If harm should happen to him on the journey that you are to make, you would bring down my gray hairs with sorrow to Sheol."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The money turns up in every sack, Jacob refuses to risk Benjamin, and Reuben’s rash offer of his own sons is turned down.

Every man’s bundle of money was in his sack. Now all of them, and their father, see it. Whatever one brother found on the road, this is no accident. They are afraid, and so is Jacob.

You have bereaved me of my children. Jacob speaks as if his sons are to blame for Joseph as well as Simeon. He does not know how close to the truth he is, and the brothers do.

All this has come against me. Jacob sees only loss. In fact God is already preparing the rescue of his whole family, and all of it is working for his good. “We know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to his purpose” (Romans 8:28).

Kill my two sons if I do not bring him back. Reuben means well but his offer is rash and useless: what grieving grandfather would be comforted by the death of his grandsons? Reuben, the firstborn who had lost his father’s trust (35:22), cannot lead the family. Judah will make a better pledge (43:8–9).

He is the only one left. Jacob speaks as though Benjamin were his only son, and ten others stand in front of him. The favouritism that tore the family apart is still there, and the brothers must live with it.

Bring down my gray hairs with sorrow to Sheol. Jacob expects to die of grief. Sheol is the Old Testament name for the place of the dead (see the note on 37:35). The chapter ends in deadlock: no grain for long, no Simeon, and no Benjamin.

In everyday life. When everything seems against you, God may be working for you, though from the inside you cannot yet see it. Jacob’s “all this has come against me” will become “It is enough; Joseph my son is still alive” (45:28).

And he said to them, "You are spies; you have come to see the nakedness of the land."<sup>10</sup>They said to him, "No, my lord, your servants have come to buy food.<sup>11</sup>We are all sons of one man. We are honest men. Your servants have never been spies."<sup>12</sup>He said to them, "No, it is the nakedness of the land that you have come to see."<sup>13</sup>And they said, "We, your servants, are twelve brothers, the sons of one man in the land of Canaan, and behold, the youngest is this day with our father, and one is no more."<sup>14</sup>But Joseph said to them, "It is as I said to you. You are spies.<sup>15</sup>By this you shall be tested: by the life of Pharaoh, you shall not go from this place unless your youngest brother comes here.<sup>16</sup>Send one of you, and let him bring your brother, while you remain confined, that your words may be tested, whether there is truth in you. Or else, by the life of Pharaoh, surely you are spies."<sup>17</sup>And he put them all together in custody for three days.<sup>18</sup>On the third day Joseph said to them, "Do this and you will live, for I fear God:<sup>19</sup>if you are honest men, let one of your brothers remain confined where you are in custody, and let the rest go and carry grain for the famine of your households,<sup>20</sup>and bring your youngest brother to me. So your words will be verified, and you shall not die." And they did so.<sup>21</sup>Then they said to one another, "In truth we are guilty concerning our brother, in that we saw the distress of his soul, when he begged us and we did not listen. That is why this distress has come upon us."<sup>22</sup>And Reuben answered them, "Did I not tell you not to sin against the boy? But you did not listen. So now there comes a reckoning for his blood."<sup>23</sup>They did not know that Joseph understood them, for there was an interpreter between them.<sup>24</sup>Then he turned away from them and wept. And he returned to them and spoke to them. And he took Simeon from them and bound him before their eyes.<sup>25</sup>And Joseph gave orders to fill their bags with grain, and to replace every man's money in his sack, and to give them provisions for the journey. This was done for them.<sup>26</sup>Then they loaded their donkeys with their grain and departed.<sup>27</sup>And as one of them opened his sack to give his donkey fodder at the lodging place, he saw his money in the mouth of his sack.<sup>28</sup>He said to his brothers, "My money has been put back; here it is in the mouth of my sack!" At this their hearts failed them, and they turned trembling to one another, saying, "What is this that God has done to us?"<sup>29</sup>When they came to Jacob their father in the land of Canaan, they told him all that had happened to them, saying,<sup>30</sup>"The man, the lord of the land, spoke roughly to us and took us to be spies of the land.<sup>31</sup>But we said to him, 'We are honest men; we have never been spies.<sup>32</sup>We are twelve brothers, sons of our father. One is no more, and the youngest is this day with our father in the land of Canaan.'<sup>33</sup>Then the man, the lord of the land, said to us, 'By this I shall know that you are honest men: leave one of your brothers with me, and take grain for the famine of your households, and go your way.<sup>34</sup>Bring your youngest brother to me. Then I shall know that you are not spies but honest men, and I will deliver your brother to you, and you shall trade in the land.'"<sup>35</sup>As they emptied their sacks, behold, every man's bundle of money was in his sack. And when they and their father saw their bundles of money, they were afraid.<sup>36</sup>And Jacob their father said to them, "You have bereaved me of my children: Joseph is no more, and Simeon is no more, and now you would take Benjamin. All this has come against me."<sup>37</sup>Then Reuben said to his father, "Kill my two sons if I do not bring him back to you. Put him in my hands, and I will bring him back to you."<sup>38</sup>But he said, "My son shall not go down with you, for his brother is dead, and he is the only one left. If harm should happen to him on the journey that you are to make, you would bring down my gray hairs with sorrow to Sheol."
42.overview:
Where we are. Joseph now rules Egypt, and the famine he foretold has spread to “all the earth” (41:57), including Canaan. More than twenty years after they sold him, his brothers come to buy grain from the brother they think is dead.

The message. God brings buried sin to the surface in order to heal it. The brothers bow before Joseph, and his boyhood dreams come true; but God is after more than their bowing. Through Joseph’s hard testing, through a few days in prison and through money that turns up in their sacks, he wakes the guilty conscience of men who had lived with a lie for two decades, and begins to lead them to repentance.

Why it was said. The tribes of Israel came from these brothers (see the introduction). Israel needed to know that their fathers were not heroes but guilty men, and that the nation began with God’s mercy to sinners who were brought to admit what they had done.

How the chapter makes its case. Jacob sends ten sons to Egypt, keeping Benjamin back (vv. 1–5). They bow before Joseph, who recognises them and treats them as strangers (vv. 6–8). He accuses them of spying and draws out their family story (vv. 9–13), then tests them, first holding all of them for three days (vv. 14–17), then keeping only one and demanding Benjamin (vv. 18–20). The brothers confess their guilt over Joseph to one another, not knowing he understands (vv. 21–22). Joseph weeps in secret and binds Simeon (vv. 23–24). He sends them home with grain and secretly returns their money, which fills them with dread (vv. 25–28). They tell Jacob everything (vv. 29–34), the money appears in every sack, and Jacob, in grief, refuses to let Benjamin go (vv. 35–38).

Where it leads. By pattern, and by the need it exposes. Like Jesus, who “came to his own, and his own people did not receive him” (John 1:11), Joseph stands before his brothers unrecognised, holding their lives in his hand, and loves them. His severity serves his love: he wants them changed, not merely sorry. The chapter also lays bare a need no one in it can meet. Misery does not wipe out guilt, and Reuben’s offer of his sons cannot pay for anything. The brothers need a mercy greater than their sin, and Joseph’s secret tears point to the heart of the one who would weep over the people who rejected him and then die for them.

For us. Buried sin does not stay buried, but God unearths it to heal, not to destroy. When conscience wakes, do not run from it; confess and turn to Christ. And do not read God’s kindness as a threat: “God’s kindness is meant to lead you to repentance” (Romans 2:4).
42.theology:
Remorse and repentance. What Joseph wants is not regret but change: will men who once gave up a favoured younger son do it again when the same choice is put in front of them? Chapter 44 gives the answer. God’s dealings with his people aim at something deeper than feeling bad.

Severity in the service of love. Joseph is not punishing his brothers; every hard thing he does aims to bring them to the point where the family can be whole. Scripture says the same of God’s discipline: it is painful at the time, but God disciplines “for our good, that we may share his holiness” (Heb. 12:10–11). Love that never makes anyone uncomfortable is not the love the Bible describes.
42.examples:
Then: Egypt kept grain reserves and sold to foreigners, and its eastern border was the one exposed to groups arriving from Canaan, so a charge of spying out “the nakedness of the land” would sound plausible. Officials used interpreters, which is why the brothers spoke freely in Hebrew in front of the governor.

Now: A secret buried for twenty-two years comes to the surface in one hard week. Time settles nothing; only confession and forgiveness do.

keyVerse.quote: Then they said to one another, “In truth we are guilty concerning our brother, in that we saw the distress of his soul, when he begged us and we did not listen. That is why this distress has come upon us.”
keyVerse.note: After more than twenty years, the brothers name their sin. Everything Joseph does in these chapters aims at this: not their humiliation, but their honest confession. It is the first step on the road from guilt to reconciliation.

42.reflection:
Joseph’s brothers lived with their secret for more than twenty years, but it came out under pressure (v. 21). Why is buried sin so heavy, and why is confession such a relief (Psalm 32:3–5)?

Joseph was harsh with his brothers, yet he wept in private (vv. 7, 24). When is it loving to make someone face what they have done, and how can we tell love from revenge?

The brothers read the returned money as a threat (v. 28). Have you ever misread God’s kindness? What helps us trust it?

Jacob said, “All this has come against me” (v. 36), when God was in fact preparing his rescue. How does Romans 8:28 help you in a season like that?

43.title: The Second Journey to Egypt

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–34 — Judah’s Pledge and the Feast with Joseph
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Judah’s pledge opens the way back to Egypt, and there the brothers, expecting punishment, are met with peace and a feast. The famine forces Jacob to face the demand for Benjamin, and Judah offers his own life as a guarantee, a real pledge unlike Reuben’s rash offer (vv. 1–10). Jacob relents, commending them to God Almighty (vv. 11–14). In Egypt the brothers fear a trap, but the steward speaks peace, returns their money and releases Simeon (vv. 15–23). Joseph greets them, is overcome at the sight of Benjamin and weeps in private (vv. 24–31), and then seats them in birth order at his table, where Benjamin receives five times as much (vv. 32–34).
verseByVerse.theology: When the grain runs out, Judah pledges himself for Benjamin, and Jacob lets him go. In Joseph's house the steward tells the frightened brothers their God put treasure in their sacks, and releases Simeon. Joseph sees Benjamin and weeps in private, then seats them in birth order and gives Benjamin five times as much.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the man who sold a brother offers himself as surety for one. Now: grace often has to be explained before it is recognised as grace.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the famine was severe in the land. And when they had eaten the grain that they had brought from Egypt, their father said to them, "Go again, buy us a little food." But Judah said to him, "The man solemnly warned us, saying, 'You shall not see my face unless your brother is with you.' If you will send our brother with us, we will go down and buy you food. But if you will not send him, we will not go down, for the man said to us, 'You shall not see my face, unless your brother is with you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the grain runs out, Jacob tells his sons to go again, but Judah insists that they cannot face the man in Egypt without Benjamin.

The famine was severe in the land. Nothing moves in this family until the food runs out. God will use an empty cupboard to move people whom argument cannot move.

Go again, buy us a little food. Jacob speaks as though nothing had changed, as if the problem could be solved without facing the Egyptian’s demand. “A little food” is a brave understatement in a famine.

But Judah said to him. Judah, the brother who proposed selling Joseph (37:26–27), now steps forward to lead. Reuben’s offer has failed (42:37–38), and from here on Judah speaks for the brothers. Since his confession to Tamar, “She is more righteous than I” (38:26), he has been a changed man.

You shall not see my face unless your brother is with you. Judah repeats the Egyptian’s warning twice. He will not pretend: there is no way forward that avoids Benjamin. Facing the truth is the start of his leadership.

verseByVerse.quote: Israel said, "Why did you treat me so badly as to tell the man that you had another brother?" They replied, "The man questioned us carefully about ourselves and our kindred, saying, 'Is your father still alive? Do you have another brother?' What we told him was in answer to these questions. Could we in any way know that he would say, 'Bring your brother down'?" And Judah said to Israel his father, "Send the boy with me, and we will arise and go, that we may live and not die, both we and you and also our little ones. I will be a pledge of his safety. From my hand you shall require him. If I do not bring him back to you and set him before you, then let me bear the blame forever. If we had not delayed, we would now have returned twice."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jacob complains that they ever mentioned Benjamin, and Judah answers by pledging his own life for the boy’s safe return.

Why did you treat me so badly? Jacob, called “Israel” here, looks for someone to blame. The brothers explain that the Egyptian questioned them closely; they could not have known what he would demand. For once, they are telling their father the plain truth.

Send the boy with me … that we may live and not die. Benjamin is called “the boy,” though he was a grown man with sons of his own by the time the family went down to Egypt (46:21). It is the language of a father’s protectiveness. Judah’s argument is simple: without Benjamin they will all starve, “both we and you and also our little ones.” Jacob is risking everyone to protect one.

I will be a pledge of his safety. Judah makes himself legally answerable for Benjamin, the guarantor who stands surety for another. “From my hand you shall require him” uses the language Reuben used of the reckoning for Joseph’s blood (42:22): Judah accepts that he will answer for his brother’s life. “Let me bear the blame forever” is literally “I will be a sinner before you all my days.” Unlike Reuben, who offered his sons’ lives (42:37), Judah offers his own.

If we had not delayed, we would now have returned twice. Judah’s impatience is a mark of his leadership: the family’s fear has cost time it did not have.

Judah and Christ. Judah’s pledge points to Jesus, the descendant of Judah (Hebrews 7:14) who became “the guarantor of a better covenant” (Hebrews 7:22). Judah offered himself for one brother; Christ pledged himself for all his people, and unlike every human guarantor, he did not fail.

In everyday life. Take responsibility for those in your care. And when your own faithfulness falls short, lean on his.

verseByVerse.quote: Then their father Israel said to them, "If it must be so, then do this: take some of the choice fruits of the land in your bags, and carry a present down to the man, a little balm and a little honey, gum, myrrh, pistachio nuts, and almonds. Take double the money with you. Carry back with you the money that was returned in the mouth of your sacks. Perhaps it was an oversight. Take also your brother, and arise, go again to the man. May God Almighty grant you mercy before the man, and may he send back your other brother and Benjamin. And as for me, if I am bereaved of my children, I am bereaved."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jacob gives in, sending gifts, double money and Benjamin, and commits them to God Almighty, ready to accept whatever comes.

If it must be so. Jacob yields to reality. There is no other way.

Carry a present down to the man. Jacob sends a present, as he once did to win Esau’s favour (32:13). The list is of luxuries from Canaan that Egypt did not grow, even in a famine: balm, honey, gum, myrrh, pistachios and almonds. Three of them, gum, balm and myrrh, are the very goods the caravan was carrying when Joseph was sold (37:25). The brothers are carrying the same goods to the same land, to the same brother.

Take double the money. Jacob insists on honesty: return the money that came back, and bring more for the new grain. “Perhaps it was an oversight.” Perhaps; but God was behind it (v. 23).

May God Almighty grant you mercy before the man. At the moment he has run out of ways to protect his family, Jacob calls on God Almighty, El Shaddai. That is the name God used when he gave Jacob the promises (35:11), and first when a son for Abraham seemed impossible (17:1). He asks for “mercy,” the same word used of Joseph’s “compassion” in verse 30: Jacob prays for mercy, and Joseph’s heart is already full of it.

If I am bereaved of my children, I am bereaved. This is not a shrug at fate but surrender, like Esther’s “if I perish, I perish” (Esther 4:16): a man letting go of what he cannot hold and putting it in God’s hands.

Uncertain wording. The phrase translated “choice fruits of the land” is unusual. The Hebrew word normally means “song,” so some take it as “the land’s famous products,” the things it is praised for; others think it is a different word meaning “best” or “choicest.” The sense, the finest produce of Canaan, is not in doubt. “Honey” may be bees’ honey or a thick syrup made from dates or grapes; the Hebrew word covers both.
verseByVerse.note: “God Almighty” is El Shaddai (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: So the men took this present, and they took double the money with them, and Benjamin. They arose and went down to Egypt and stood before Joseph. When Joseph saw Benjamin with them, he said to the steward of his house, "Bring the men into the house, and slaughter an animal and make ready, for the men are to dine with me at noon." The man did as Joseph told him and brought the men to Joseph's house. And the men were afraid because they were brought to Joseph's house, and they said, "It is because of the money, which was replaced in our sacks the first time, that we are brought in, so that he may assault us and fall upon us to make us servants and seize our donkeys."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The brothers return with Benjamin, and when Joseph orders a meal for them at his house, they are terrified that they are about to be seized as slaves.

When Joseph saw Benjamin with them. Benjamin’s presence changes everything for Joseph: his story was true, and Rachel’s son is alive and safe.

Slaughter an animal and make ready. Meat was a luxury, kept for honoured guests. Joseph is preparing a feast.

The men were afraid. Brought to the governor’s house, the brothers expect the worst: an accusation of theft, an ambush, slavery, even their donkeys taken. Their fear is ironic: to be made slaves is exactly what they did to Joseph. Guilt reads every kindness as a threat.

verseByVerse.quote: So they went up to the steward of Joseph's house and spoke with him at the door of the house, and said, "Oh, my lord, we came down the first time to buy food. And when we came to the lodging place we opened our sacks, and there was each man's money in the mouth of his sack, our money in full weight. So we have brought it again with us, and we have brought other money down with us to buy food. We do not know who put our money in our sacks." He replied, "Peace to you, do not be afraid. Your God and the God of your father has put treasure in your sacks for you. I received your money." Then he brought Simeon out to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The brothers explain about the returned money to Joseph’s steward, who tells them not to fear, says their God gave them the treasure, and brings Simeon out to them.

At the door of the house. They speak before they enter, wanting to clear themselves before anything happens inside. Their account is honest and complete: they found the money, brought it back, and brought more.

Peace to you, do not be afraid. It is an Egyptian steward who points them to God: “Your God and the God of your father has put treasure in your sacks for you.” He may have learned the words from his master. Grace is announced, though they cannot yet see it as grace. The money they feared would condemn them was a gift.

I received your money. The steward says, in effect, “Your account is settled; I was paid.” There is no debt to fear.

Then he brought Simeon out to them. The brother who was bound is set free. The family is whole again, apart from the one brother they still think is dead.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the man had brought the men into Joseph's house and given them water, and they had washed their feet, and when he had given their donkeys fodder, they prepared the present for Joseph's coming at noon, for they heard that they should eat bread there. When Joseph came home, they brought into the house to him the present that they had with them and bowed down to him to the ground.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The brothers are welcomed as honoured guests, and when Joseph comes home they present their gifts and bow down to him.

Given them water, and they had washed their feet. Water for dusty feet and fodder for the donkeys were the marks of hospitality (18:4; 24:32). Men who expected to be arrested are being treated as guests.

They heard that they should eat bread there. To eat bread with someone was to share fellowship, and the brothers can hardly believe it.

Bowed down to him to the ground. Again they bow down, and this time Benjamin is with them: all eleven brothers bow before Joseph, as in his second dream the eleven stars bowed to him (37:9).

verseByVerse.quote: And he inquired about their welfare and said, "Is your father well, the old man of whom you spoke? Is he still alive?" They said, "Your servant our father is well; he is still alive." And they bowed their heads and prostrated themselves. And he lifted up his eyes and saw his brother Benjamin, his mother's son, and said, "Is this your youngest brother, of whom you spoke to me? God be gracious to you, my son!" Then Joseph hurried out, for his compassion grew warm for his brother, and he sought a place to weep. And he entered his chamber and wept there. Then he washed his face and came out. And controlling himself he said, "Serve the food."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joseph asks after his father, blesses Benjamin, and is so overcome that he has to leave the room to weep before he can return and order the meal.

Is your father well … Is he still alive? Joseph’s first question is about his father. The word “well” is shalom, the peace the steward has just spoken over them. “Your servant our father” is their reply, and they bow again: without knowing it, they bow on behalf of their father too.

God be gracious to you, my son! Joseph’s first words to Benjamin are a blessing. “His mother’s son” reminds us that Benjamin is his only full brother, the son of Rachel.

His compassion grew warm for his brother. The Hebrew pictures deep, inward love growing hot. Joseph hurries out to weep in private, washes his face, and comes back “controlling himself.” His love is real, and so is his restraint: the test is not yet finished.

In everyday life. Deep love can coexist with wise restraint. Love sometimes waits for the right moment to show itself.

verseByVerse.quote: They served him by himself, and them by themselves, and the Egyptians who ate with him by themselves, because the Egyptians could not eat with the Hebrews, for that is an abomination to the Egyptians. And they sat before him, the firstborn according to his birthright and the youngest according to his youth. And the men looked at one another in amazement. Portions were taken to them from Joseph's table, but Benjamin's portion was five times as much as any of theirs. And they drank and were merry with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the meal the brothers find themselves seated in exact birth order, and Benjamin is given five times as much as the rest, yet they eat and drink freely with Joseph.

They served him by himself, and them by themselves. Three tables: Joseph alone, as befits his rank; the Egyptians; and the Hebrews. The separate tables are Egyptian custom, not a snub. Egyptians kept apart from foreigners at meals for reasons of religious purity, and shepherds in particular were looked down on (46:34). Joseph, a Hebrew at an Egyptian table by himself, belongs fully to neither.

The firstborn according to his birthright and the youngest according to his youth. The brothers are seated in exact birth order by a man who cannot possibly know it, and they look at one another in amazement. Someone here knows far more about them than they have told.

Benjamin’s portion was five times as much. A test of jealousy: will they resent the favoured brother, as they resented Joseph and his robe? This time there is no sign of it. “They drank and were merry with him”: the fear has gone, at least for now.

A table spread for sinners. They are feasting at the table of the brother they wronged, before they know who he is. It is a glimpse of the generous table God spreads for sinners: “You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies” (Psalm 23:5). And it anticipates the risen Jesus, who sat at table with two downcast disciples and was recognised as he broke the bread (Luke 24:30–31).
verseByVerse.note: Egyptians would not eat with foreigners, as verse 32 says, so the three separate tables are true to custom, not awkwardness on Joseph’s part.
