43.overview:
Where we are. Simeon is still bound in Egypt, Jacob has refused to let Benjamin go (42:38), and the grain from the first journey is running out. The family has to face what it has been avoiding.

The message. When God’s people come to the end of their own resources, they find themselves met by grace they did not expect and cannot yet understand. Judah, who once sold a brother, now pledges his own life for a brother. Jacob, out of options, entrusts Benjamin to God Almighty. And the brothers, braced for punishment, are welcomed with peace, given back their money, and seated at a feast in the house of the brother they wronged.

Why it was said. Israel’s tribes looked back to these men (see the introduction). Judah’s pledge showed the beginning of the leadership that would one day give his tribe the sceptre (49:10), and the whole chapter taught Israel that their God meets frightened, guilty people with undeserved kindness.

How the chapter makes its case. The famine forces the question, and Judah insists they cannot go back without Benjamin (vv. 1–5). When Jacob complains, Judah offers himself as a pledge for the boy (vv. 6–10). Jacob gives in, sending a present, double money and Benjamin, with a prayer to God Almighty (vv. 11–14). In Egypt Joseph has them brought to his house, and they fear a trap (vv. 15–18). They confess about the money; the steward answers, “Peace to you,” and brings out Simeon (vv. 19–23). They are welcomed as guests and bow before Joseph (vv. 24–26). Joseph asks after his father, blesses Benjamin, and leaves the room to weep (vv. 27–31). At the meal they are seated in birth order and Benjamin is given five times as much, and they feast with him (vv. 32–34).

Where it leads. By pattern. Judah, the brother who stands surety for another with his own life, points to the descendant of Judah who became “the guarantor of a better covenant” (Hebrews 7:22) and did not fail. And the brothers feasting at the table of the one they betrayed, before they even know who he is, are a picture of the grace of Christ, who meets disciples who had deserted him with “Peace be with you” (John 20:19), and who spreads a table for sinners.

For us. When all your options are gone, entrust what you love most to God Almighty. Take responsibility for others, as Judah did. And do not read God’s kindness as a trap: the peace offered in Christ is real, and it is offered to the guilty.
43.theology:
Substitution. Judah’s “I will be a pledge of his safety... let me bear the blame forever” is the turning point of his life. The man who sold a brother now offers to answer for one, and in chapter 44 he will offer to take his place outright. From the tribe of Judah came David, and from David the one who did not merely offer to bear the blame, but bore it.

Grace explained by a stranger. The brothers can only read the returned silver as a trap, until the steward tells them that their God put treasure in their sacks. A guilty conscience cannot see a gift as a gift until God makes it plain.
43.examples: Twenty-two years after the worst thing he ever did, Judah steps forward and risks himself for Benjamin, his father’s favourite, though he once hated Joseph for being exactly that. People do change. It may take years, but God does not give up on them.

keyVerse.quote: I will be a pledge of his safety. From my hand you shall require him. If I do not bring him back to you and set him before you, then let me bear the blame forever.
keyVerse.note: Judah, who once sold one brother for silver, now offers his own life as a guarantee for another. This pledge opens the way back to Egypt and prepares for his plea in chapter 44, the turning point of the whole story. It points to the descendant of Judah who became the guarantor of a better covenant (Hebrews 7:22).

43.reflection:
Jacob would not let Benjamin go until the food ran out (vv. 1–2). Why does God sometimes let us run out of options before we trust him?

Judah said, “I will be a pledge of his safety” (v. 9). What does it mean for you to take responsibility for someone else, and how does Christ’s pledge for us change the way we do it?

The brothers feared a trap, but were met with “Peace to you, do not be afraid” (v. 23). Why do guilty people find it hard to believe in grace?

Joseph held back his tears until the right time (vv. 30–31). When is it wise to wait before showing what we feel?

44.title: Judah's Plea for Benjamin

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–34 — The Silver Cup and Judah’s Substitution
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Joseph’s last test shows that his brothers are changed men, and Judah offers himself in Benjamin’s place. Joseph has his silver cup hidden in Benjamin’s sack and sends his steward after the brothers with the charge of theft (vv. 1–10). When the cup is found, they tear their clothes and all return (vv. 11–13). Judah confesses that God has found out their guilt, and Joseph offers to keep only Benjamin and send the rest home in peace (vv. 14–17). In one of the longest speeches in Genesis, Judah pleads for his father’s life and offers to remain as a slave instead of the boy (vv. 18–34).
verseByVerse.theology: Joseph has his silver cup put in Benjamin's sack. The steward overtakes the brothers; the cup is found, and every man tears his clothes and goes back. Judah says God has found out their guilt, and when Joseph offers to keep only Benjamin, Judah tells the whole story from his father's side and asks to remain as a slave instead of the boy.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the brothers face the same choice as twenty-two years before, and refuse it. Now: repentance is proved when the old sin is offered again and not taken.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he commanded the steward of his house, "Fill the men's sacks with food, as much as they can carry, and put each man's money in the mouth of his sack, and put my cup, the silver cup, in the mouth of the sack of the youngest, with his money for the grain." And he did as Joseph told him. As soon as the morning was light, the men were sent away with their donkeys. They had gone only a short distance from the city. Now Joseph said to his steward, "Up, follow after the men, and when you overtake them, say to them, 'Why have you repaid evil for good? Is it not from this that my lord drinks, and by this that he practices divination? You have done evil in doing this.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joseph has his silver cup hidden in Benjamin’s sack, then sends his steward after the brothers to accuse them of repaying evil for good.

Fill the men’s sacks with food, as much as they can carry. Joseph is generous again, and again the money goes back into the sacks. Kindness and testing go together to the end.

My cup, the silver cup. This is the final test. Joseph creates a situation exactly like the one twenty-two years before: Rachel’s son, the father’s favourite, can be left behind as a slave in Egypt, and the rest can go home free with an easy excuse. Will they abandon Benjamin, as they abandoned Joseph?

Why have you repaid evil for good? The charge is false about the cup, but it is true about Joseph: the brothers did repay his good with evil. The same words, evil and good, come back in Joseph’s great summary: “you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good” (50:20).

By this that he practices divination. Diviners in the ancient world poured water or oil into a cup and read omens in the patterns, so such a cup fits a great Egyptian household. The steward’s words make the cup sound precious and its theft serious.

Where Christians differ: did Joseph practise divination? Some think Joseph really did use the cup, as an Egyptian official might, before the law of Moses forbade it. Others think the claim was only part of his disguise, and the narrator never says Joseph practised divination.

This commentary’s view. The claim is probably part of his disguise as an Egyptian official, and nothing suggests he actually used the cup. Joseph consistently gives God the credit for his knowledge (40:8; 41:16), and divination was later forbidden to Israel (Deuteronomy 18:10). In any case, the text describes what Joseph said in his role; it does not commend divination.
verseByVerse.note: Diviners read omens in liquid poured into a cup, so such a cup fits an Egyptian household.

verseByVerse.quote: When he overtook them, he spoke to them these words. They said to him, "Why does my lord speak such words as these? Far be it from your servants to do such a thing! Behold, the money that we found in the mouths of our sacks we brought back to you from the land of Canaan. How then could we steal silver or gold from your lord's house? Whichever of your servants is found with it shall die, and we also will be my lord's servants." He said, "Let it be as you say: he who is found with it shall be my servant, and the rest of you shall be innocent."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Overtaken by the steward, the brothers protest their innocence and rashly offer death for the thief and slavery for themselves, and the steward lowers the penalty to slavery for the guilty one alone.

Far be it from your servants to do such a thing! This time the brothers really are innocent, and they point to their record: they brought back the money they found. Their honesty is real now.

Whichever of your servants is found with it shall die. The brothers make a rash vow, like Jacob’s over Laban’s gods: “Anyone with whom you find your gods shall not live” (31:32). Then too the stolen goods were hidden with a child of Rachel, though Jacob did not know it. The brothers are so sure of each other that they stake their lives on it.

He who is found with it shall be my servant, and the rest of you shall be innocent. The steward at once reduces the penalty to something survivable, and frees the others in advance. It is a first hint that the whole thing is staged. It also sets the trap: only one need suffer, and the rest may walk away.

verseByVerse.quote: Then each man quickly lowered his sack to the ground, and each man opened his sack. And he searched, beginning with the eldest and ending with the youngest. And the cup was found in Benjamin's sack. Then they tore their clothes, and every man loaded his donkey, and they returned to the city.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The search goes from eldest to youngest, the cup is found in Benjamin’s sack, and the brothers tear their clothes and all go back to the city.

Beginning with the eldest and ending with the youngest. The narrator slows the scene down. Ten sacks are opened and nothing is found; the tension rises with each one. Then the last sack, Benjamin’s.

They tore their clothes. Tearing clothes was the sign of overwhelming grief (see mourning customs). Reuben tore his clothes at the empty pit, and Jacob tore his at the sight of Joseph’s robe (37:29, 34). Now all the brothers tear theirs for Benjamin.

Every man loaded his donkey, and they returned to the city. They have been told they are free to go (v. 10). Nobody would blame them for leaving Benjamin, and they have told a cover story before. Instead every one of them goes back. They will not abandon Rachel’s son. In substance, the test is passed.

verseByVerse.quote: When Judah and his brothers came to Joseph's house, he was still there. They fell before him to the ground. Joseph said to them, "What deed is this that you have done? Do you not know that a man like me can indeed practice divination?" And Judah said, "What shall we say to my lord? What shall we speak? Or how can we clear ourselves? God has found out the guilt of your servants; behold, we are my lord's servants, both we and he also in whose hand the cup has been found." But he said, "Far be it from me that I should do so! Only the man in whose hand the cup was found shall be my servant. But as for you, go up in peace to your father."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah leads the brothers back to Joseph, confesses that God has found out their guilt and offers them all as slaves, but Joseph insists that only Benjamin must stay.

Judah and his brothers. The narrator now names Judah as the leader. They fall to the ground before Joseph, bowing yet again.

A man like me can indeed practice divination. Joseph keeps up the mask. His point is that nothing can be hidden from him; and indeed he knows far more about them than they imagine.

God has found out the guilt of your servants. Judah is not talking about the cup. They are innocent of the theft, and he does not argue the point, because everyone in the family knows what he means: Joseph. He does not blame Benjamin either. He speaks of “we”: the whole family is guilty before God, and they will share the punishment together. Sin can be found out long after everyone thought it buried: “be sure your sin will find you out” (Numbers 32:23).

Only the man in whose hand the cup was found shall be my servant. Joseph presses the test to its sharpest point: only the “guilty” one need stay; the rest may go home free. “Go up in peace to your father” is the cruellest line of the test, because there could be no peace for them, or for their father, if they left Benjamin behind.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Judah went up to him and said, "Oh, my lord, please let your servant speak a word in my lord's ears, and let not your anger burn against your servant, for you are like Pharaoh himself. My lord asked his servants, saying, 'Have you a father, or a brother?' And we said to my lord, 'We have a father, an old man, and a young brother, the child of his old age. His brother is dead, and he alone is left of his mother's children, and his father loves him.' Then you said to your servants, 'Bring him down to me, that I may set my eyes on him.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah steps forward and, with great respect and courage, begins to retell the story of how Benjamin came to be in Egypt.

Then Judah went up to him. Judah’s plea is one of the longest speeches in Genesis, and it takes courage: he is speaking to a man who could have him killed, a man “like Pharaoh himself.” He does not argue about the cup or plead innocence. He simply tells the truth about his father.

A young brother, the child of his old age. Judah describes Benjamin with the very words used of Joseph: Jacob loved Joseph “because he was the son of his old age” (37:3). Twenty-two years ago that love made the brothers hate Joseph. Now Judah says, “his father loves him,” without a trace of bitterness.

His brother is dead, and he alone is left of his mother’s children. Judah still believes Joseph is dead, and he says so to Joseph’s face.

That I may set my eyes on him. A phrase that normally means to look on someone with favour (Jeremiah 39:12; 40:4). Judah quotes Joseph’s own words back to him: you asked for him; surely you did not mean him harm.

verseByVerse.quote: We said to my lord, 'The boy cannot leave his father, for if he should leave his father, his father would die.' Then you said to your servants, 'Unless your youngest brother comes down with you, you shall not see my face again.' "When we went back to your servant my father, we told him the words of my lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah reminds Joseph that they warned him the boy could not leave his father, and that they told their father everything.

The boy cannot leave his father, for if he should leave his father, his father would die. The brothers who once did not care what their father suffered now plead for him. Twenty-two years ago they brought Jacob a bloodstained robe and watched him refuse to be comforted (37:31–35). Now his grief is the thing they cannot bear to cause.

We told him the words of my lord. Judah’s account is careful and true. He builds the case step by step so that Joseph will see what is at stake.

verseByVerse.quote: And when our father said, 'Go again, buy us a little food,' we said, 'We cannot go down. If our youngest brother goes with us, then we will go down. For we cannot see the man's face unless our youngest brother is with us.' Then your servant my father said to us, 'You know that my wife bore me two sons. One left me, and I said, "Surely he has been torn to pieces," and I have never seen him since. If you take this one also from me, and harm happens to him, you will bring down my gray hairs in evil to Sheol.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah reports his father’s words: Rachel bore him two sons, one is gone, and if this one is lost too, it will kill him.

You know that my wife bore me two sons. Jacob’s words, as Judah repeats them, count only Rachel as his wife and her two sons as his sons, as if Leah and her children did not exist. Judah is Leah’s son, yet he quotes the words without a trace of resentment. The favouritism that once drove the brothers to hatred is now simply accepted as part of the father they love.

Surely he has been torn to pieces. The lie the brothers told is still believed (37:33). Judah repeats it to the very brother it concerns, not knowing what Joseph is hearing.

You will bring down my gray hairs in evil to Sheol. Jacob means he will die in misery (42:38). Judah quotes it because he knows it is true.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now therefore, as soon as I come to your servant my father, and the boy is not with us, then, as his life is bound up in the boy's life, as soon as he sees that the boy is not with us, he will die, and your servants will bring down the gray hairs of your servant our father with sorrow to Sheol. For your servant became a pledge of safety for the boy to my father, saying, 'If I do not bring him back to you, then I shall bear the blame before my father all my life.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah explains that his father’s life is bound up with Benjamin’s, and that he himself is the guarantor for the boy’s safe return.

His life is bound up in the boy’s life. The phrase is strong: Jacob’s life is knotted together with Benjamin’s. The same verb describes the love of Jonathan for David: “the soul of Jonathan was knit to the soul of David” (1 Samuel 18:1). To lose the boy would be to kill the father.

Your servant became a pledge of safety for the boy. Judah keeps the pledge he made (43:9). His word to his father now binds him before the ruler of Egypt. A pledge is tested when it becomes costly, and Judah’s is about to cost him his freedom.

verseByVerse.quote: Now therefore, please let your servant remain instead of the boy as a servant to my lord, and let the boy go back with his brothers. For how can I go back to my father if the boy is not with me? I fear to see the evil that would find my father."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah offers to stay as a slave in Benjamin’s place, because he cannot bear to see the grief that losing the boy would bring on his father.

Let your servant remain instead of the boy. This is substitution, the clearest picture of it in Genesis after the ram at Moriah, which Abraham offered “instead of his son” (22:13); the Hebrew word is the same. The man who sold one brother into slavery for silver (37:26–27) offers himself as a slave for another, though he is innocent of the charge, so that a father will not be destroyed. He does not ask to share Benjamin’s fate; he asks to take it entirely.

How can I go back to my father if the boy is not with me? Judah’s motive is love for his father. Twenty-two years ago he went back to his father without Joseph and watched him grieve. He will not do it again.

A picture of Christ. Judah’s offer is a picture of Christ given in advance. From Judah’s line came the one who gave himself in our place (Hebrews 7:14): “For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45). Judah was guilty of much and offered his freedom; Jesus was guilty of nothing and gave his life. “Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13). He is “the Lion of the tribe of Judah” (Revelation 5:5).

In everyday life. True repentance shows in changed actions, the fruit of God’s long work in Judah, and of his Spirit in us. The proof that God has changed us is often found in how we treat the very people we once resented.
verseByVerse.note: “Pledge” means Judah made himself legally answerable for Benjamin (43:9).

I fear to see the evil that would find my father."
44.overview:
Where we are. The brothers have brought Benjamin, Simeon has been released, and they have feasted with the Egyptian lord who seated them in birth order and gave Benjamin five times as much (43:32–34). They set off for home with full sacks. Joseph has one more test to set.

The message. God has changed these men, and the proof is that they will not abandon a brother. Joseph recreates the choice they faced twenty-two years before: leave Rachel’s favoured son in Egypt as a slave and go home free. Instead they all go back, and Judah, who once sold Joseph, offers to become a slave in Benjamin’s place so that his father will not die of grief. Repentance has borne its fruit, and in Judah’s offer the gospel’s great word, substitution, sounds clearly.

Why it was said. Judah’s tribe would become the royal tribe of Israel (see the introduction), and this chapter shows why the sceptre would belong to him (49:10): not because he was the best of men, but because God turned a man who sold his brother into one who would give himself for his brother.

How the chapter makes its case. Joseph has his silver cup hidden in Benjamin’s sack (vv. 1–5). The steward overtakes the brothers, who swear their innocence and rashly offer the life of the guilty one (vv. 6–10). The cup is found in Benjamin’s sack; they tear their clothes and all return to the city (vv. 11–13). Judah confesses that God has found out their guilt, and Joseph offers to keep only Benjamin and let the rest go (vv. 14–17). Judah then pleads: he recounts the story (vv. 18–24), Jacob’s grief for the son he lost (vv. 25–29), and what losing Benjamin would do to him (vv. 30–32), and offers himself as a slave instead of the boy (vv. 33–34).

Where it leads. By pattern, and by promise. Judah offers himself “instead of the boy”, the same words used when Abraham offered the ram “instead of his son” (22:13). He stands in for one condemned, to spare a father’s grief. From Judah’s own line came the one who did that perfectly: wholly innocent, he gave himself not as a slave in Egypt but to death on a cross, “the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God” (1 Peter 3:18). Judah offered his freedom; Jesus gave his life “as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45).

For us. Real repentance shows in changed actions, especially toward the people we once wronged or resented. Love that costs us something is the mark of a heart God has changed. And at the centre of our faith stands the one who took our place, so that we could go home free.
44.theology:
Repentance is proved by the same choice, met again. God does not settle for regret. He puts these men in front of the identical decision (a favoured younger son, an easy way to be rid of him, and a father who will never know), and this time they refuse it. That is what a changed man looks like: not one who feels worse about the old sin, but one who is offered it again and will not take it.

Substitution, offered by a man. Judah offers his freedom for his brother’s. Out of his tribe came David, and out of David’s line the one of whom Judah is a small and true likeness, who did not only offer but gave his life for others.
44.examples: Judah’s speech has no protest of innocence and no attempt to shift the blame, only a description of what this will do to an old man, and an offer to take the consequence himself. If you have ever had to plead for somebody, a child, a friend, a colleague in trouble, this is how it is done: tell the truth about the cost, and be ready to bear it yourself.

keyVerse.quote: Now therefore, please let your servant remain instead of the boy as a servant to my lord, and let the boy go back with his brothers.
keyVerse.note: This is the turning point of the Joseph story. Judah, who once sold his brother into slavery, now offers to become a slave in his brother’s place. It shows that God has changed him, and it gives a clear picture of the substitution that lies at the heart of the gospel.

44.reflection:
Joseph’s test gave the brothers an easy way to abandon Benjamin, yet they all went back (v. 13). What does that show about how God had changed them?

Judah said, “God has found out the guilt of your servants” (v. 16), meaning their sin against Joseph. Why does old, hidden sin come back to the surface, and what should we do when it does?

Judah spoke of his father’s love for Benjamin without resentment (vv. 20, 27–29). Where do you need God to free you from bitterness about someone else being favoured?

Judah offered to stay “instead of the boy” (v. 33). How does his offer help you understand what Jesus did in taking your place?

45.title: Joseph Makes Himself Known

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–28 — The Great Revelation: ‘I Am Joseph’
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The brother they betrayed reveals himself, and instead of revenge he gives them forgiveness, a home and food in the famine, because God has been at work in their sin. Joseph weeps and makes himself known (vv. 1–3), then explains that God sent him ahead to preserve life (vv. 4–8). He sends for his father, promising Goshen and provision through the five years of famine still to come (vv. 9–13), and embraces his brothers until they can speak with him again (vv. 14–15). Pharaoh confirms the invitation with the best of the land and wagons for the journey (vv. 16–20). Joseph sends gifts and a warning not to quarrel (vv. 21–24), and Jacob’s numb heart revives at the news that his son is alive (vv. 25–28).
verseByVerse.theology: Joseph clears the room and weeps. He tells his terrified brothers that they sold him, and three times that God sent him to preserve life. He embraces Benjamin and all of them, and after that they talk with him. Pharaoh sends wagons, and Jacob's spirit revives.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Joseph sent his brothers home with wagons, provisions and a warning not to quarrel. Now: forgiveness names the wrong plainly and releases the wrongdoer anyway.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Joseph could not control himself before all those who stood by him. He cried, "Make everyone go out from me." So no one stayed with him when Joseph made himself known to his brothers. And he wept aloud, so that the Egyptians heard it, and the household of Pharaoh heard it. And Joseph said to his brothers, "I am Joseph! Is my father still alive?" But his brothers could not answer him, for they were dismayed at his presence.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Overcome by Judah’s plea, Joseph sends out his Egyptian attendants, weeps aloud and tells his brothers who he is; they are too terrified to answer.

Then Joseph could not control himself. Joseph has wept in secret twice already (42:24; 43:30), and both times he washed his face and went on with the test. Judah’s offer to take Benjamin’s place (44:33–34) is the proof he has been waiting for: the brothers who once sold Rachel’s son for silver will now give themselves for Rachel’s other son. The test is over, and so is Joseph’s self-control.

Make everyone go out from me. He clears the room of Egyptians. What he has to say is family business, and he will not shame his brothers in front of foreigners by exposing their crime publicly. Love covers, even while it tells the truth.

He wept aloud. Joseph weeps so loudly that the Egyptians outside, and the household of Pharaoh, hear it. Twenty-two years of grief, loneliness and longing come out at once.

I am Joseph! Is my father still alive? This is the sentence the whole story has been moving toward. He speaks it, it seems, in Hebrew, no longer through an interpreter (42:23). And he speaks as Joseph, not as Zaphenath-paneah, the Egyptian name Pharaoh gave him (41:45). His first question is about his father. He has already heard that his father is alive (43:27–28), but now he asks as a son, not as a governor.

They were dismayed at his presence. The brothers cannot answer. The word means terrified, thrown into panic. The man who holds their lives in his hand is the brother they threw into a pit, and the guilt they confessed to one another (42:21) is now standing in front of them. Every reason they had to fear him seems to have come true at once.

Joseph and Christ. Stephen notes that it was “on the second visit” that Joseph made himself known to his brothers (Acts 7:13), and goes on to show that Israel first rejected Moses too. He is pointing to Jesus, rejected by his own, who reveals himself as the wronged brother and the forgiving Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: So Joseph said to his brothers, "Come near to me, please." And they came near. And he said, "I am your brother, Joseph, whom you sold into Egypt. And now do not be distressed or angry with yourselves because you sold me here, for God sent me before you to preserve life. For the famine has been in the land these two years, and there are yet five years in which there will be neither plowing nor harvest. And God sent me before you to preserve for you a remnant on earth, and to keep alive for you many survivors. So it was not you who sent me here, but God. He has made me a father to Pharaoh, and lord of all his house and ruler over all the land of Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joseph draws his brothers close, names plainly what they did, and tells them three times that God sent him ahead of them to keep them alive.

Come near to me, please. The brothers have backed away in fear, and Joseph calls them close. Grace does not keep the guilty at a distance; it invites them in.

Your brother, Joseph, whom you sold into Egypt. Joseph does not pretend the sin never happened. He names it exactly: “you sold me”. True forgiveness is not saying “it doesn’t matter”. It says, “This is what you did, and I release you from it.”

Do not be distressed or angry with yourselves. Now he lifts the weight. He does not want them crushed by self-reproach. The wrong is real, but it does not have the last word.

God sent me before you to preserve life. Three times Joseph says that God sent him (vv. 5, 7, 8). He is not excusing their sin; in 50:20 he will say plainly, “you meant evil against me”. He is saying that behind their evil intention stood God’s good purpose. The same event had two authors with two opposite aims: they meant to get rid of him, God meant to save lives. This is the key to the whole Joseph story, and Psalm 105 tells it the same way: God “had sent a man ahead of them, Joseph, who was sold as a slave” (Psalm 105:17).

Two years … five years. The famine is only two years old. Without Joseph in Egypt, the family of promise, the line through which the world was to be blessed, would have starved in Canaan.

A remnant on earth. A remnant is what survives a disaster and carries life forward. The idea appears here near the start of the Bible and will run through the prophets: God always keeps a remnant through whom his promise goes on.

A father to Pharaoh. This was a title for the king’s most trusted adviser, possibly echoing an Egyptian court title. Joseph is “lord of all his house and ruler over all the land”, exactly what his dreams foretold (37:5–9), and God, not the brothers, put him there.

Where it leads. The cross is the supreme case of what Joseph describes. Peter told the crowd at Pentecost that Jesus was “delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God”, and in the same breath, “you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men” (Acts 2:23). The worst thing human beings ever did became, in God’s hand, the salvation of the world, offered first to those who rejected him (Acts 3:17–19).

In everyday life. When you look back on what others have done to you, you can say both things: they did wrong, and God was at work. That does not make the wrong good. It means that the wrong was not the strongest thing in the story. And when you look back on your own sins, you need not be destroyed by them; there is a God who works even through our failures for those who love him (Romans 8:28).

What it does not mean. Joseph’s forgiveness came after he had tested his brothers and seen real change (42:21; 44:16, 33). Forgiving someone in your heart does not require you to pretend, to trust at once, or to put yourself back in danger. If you have been abused, you are not required to restore a relationship with someone unsafe; seek safety first, and seek wise help from your pastor and, where needed, the authorities.

Where Christians differ: God and evil. How can God “send” Joseph through the brothers’ sin? Some say God merely permitted the sin and then made the best of it. Others say God ordained even the sinful act, without himself doing evil.

This commentary’s view. God ordains all things, including the sinful acts of people, without being the author of sin. The brothers were fully responsible for what they did, and God worked it for good (50:20; Acts 2:23).

verseByVerse.quote: Hurry and go up to my father and say to him, 'Thus says your son Joseph, God has made me lord of all Egypt. Come down to me; do not tarry. You shall dwell in the land of Goshen, and you shall be near me, you and your children and your children's children, and your flocks, your herds, and all that you have. There I will provide for you, for there are yet five years of famine to come, so that you and your household, and all that you have, do not come to poverty.' And now your eyes see, and the eyes of my brother Benjamin see, that it is my mouth that speaks to you. You must tell my father of all my honor in Egypt, and of all that you have seen. Hurry and bring my father down here."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joseph sends an urgent message to his father: God has made him lord of Egypt, and the whole family must come down to Goshen, where he will provide for them through the rest of the famine.

Hurry … do not tarry. The urgency is twofold: the famine has five more years to run, and Joseph has waited twenty-two years to see his father. He speaks with the authority of a ruler and the longing of a son.

Thus says your son Joseph. The phrase echoes the way a king’s or a prophet’s message was introduced. “Your son Joseph” is the message Jacob never expected to hear. The ruler of Egypt owns these shepherds as family, as Christ “is not ashamed to call them brothers” (Hebrews 2:11).

God has made me lord of all Egypt. Again the credit goes to God. Joseph’s position is not something to boast of; it is the means by which God will keep the family alive.

The land of Goshen … near me. Goshen was fertile pasture in the eastern Nile delta (see the note), good for flocks and close to the court. Joseph wants them near him: “you and your children and your children’s children”. He thinks in generations.

There I will provide for you. The brother they sold now promises to feed them. The word means to sustain, to keep supplied; he will use it again when he promises to provide for their little ones after Jacob’s death (50:21).

It is my mouth that speaks to you. He is no longer speaking through an interpreter (42:23). They can hear their own language from his own lips, and Benjamin, who never betrayed him, is a witness too. Jacob will need every proof they can bring.
verseByVerse.note: Goshen was fertile pasture in the eastern Nile delta, near the court but outside the Egyptian heartland.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he fell upon his brother Benjamin's neck and wept, and Benjamin wept upon his neck. And he kissed all his brothers and wept upon them. After that his brothers talked with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joseph embraces Benjamin and weeps, then kisses all his brothers, and at last they are able to talk with him.

He fell upon his brother Benjamin’s neck and wept. Benjamin was a small boy when Joseph was sold, the only other son of their mother Rachel. The two weep on each other’s necks. Benjamin had no part in the crime, and the reunion between them is simple joy.

He kissed all his brothers and wept upon them. Then Joseph does the harder thing: he kisses the brothers who threw him into the pit. A kiss in that culture was a sign of family affection and of peace. Joseph makes the first move, and keeps on making it.

After that his brothers talked with him. This small sentence closes a long wound. Years before, the brothers “hated him and could not speak peacefully to him” (37:4). Forgiveness has restored conversation. The brothers are slow to speak, because guilt makes people silent; but grace, once it is believed, opens the mouth.

In everyday life. Reconciliation often has to be expressed before it is fully felt. Joseph’s brothers may still have been afraid (50:15 shows that some fear lingered for years). Yet they talked with him. If you are the one who has been wronged and are able to forgive, you may need to make the first move more than once.

verseByVerse.quote: When the report was heard in Pharaoh's house, "Joseph's brothers have come," it pleased Pharaoh and his servants. And Pharaoh said to Joseph, "Say to your brothers, 'Do this: load your beasts and go back to the land of Canaan, and take your father and your households, and come to me, and I will give you the best of the land of Egypt, and you shall eat the fat of the land.' And you, Joseph, are commanded to say, 'Do this: take wagons from the land of Egypt for your little ones and for your wives, and bring your father, and come. Have no concern for your goods, for the best of all the land of Egypt is yours.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pharaoh is delighted at the news and adds his own invitation: the family is to come with wagons and receive the best of the land of Egypt.

It pleased Pharaoh and his servants. News of Joseph’s brothers spreads through the palace, and the response is pleasure, not suspicion. Joseph’s faithful service has made Pharaoh glad to welcome his family. God’s blessing on Joseph has become a blessing to Egypt, and now Egypt’s generosity flows back to Joseph’s family, as God promised Abraham (12:3).

The best of the land of Egypt … the fat of the land. Pharaoh offers more than Joseph asked. “The fat of the land” means its richest produce. The family that had come to buy a little grain is offered the best the land can give.

Take wagons from the land of Egypt. Wagons were rare in Canaan, where people travelled on foot or by donkey. Wagons sent from Egypt would be unmistakable evidence of where the message came from, and they make the journey possible for an old man, small children and their mothers. The wagons will be what finally convinces Jacob (v. 27).

Have no concern for your goods. Literally, “let not your eye pity your belongings”: do not worry about what you leave behind, for everything you need is waiting for you. Pharaoh’s generosity is a faint picture of the welcome God gives his people: whatever they leave behind, what is prepared for them is far better.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Israel did so: and Joseph gave them wagons, according to the command of Pharaoh, and gave them provisions for the journey. To each and all of them he gave a change of clothes, but to Benjamin he gave three hundred shekels of silver and five changes of clothes. To his father he sent as follows: ten donkeys loaded with the good things of Egypt, and ten female donkeys loaded with grain, bread, and provision for his father on the journey. Then he sent his brothers away, and as they departed, he said to them, "Do not quarrel on the way."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joseph sends his brothers home with wagons, provisions and rich gifts, and warns them not to quarrel on the way.

The sons of Israel did so. The narrator calls them “the sons of Israel”, the name of the nation they will become. A family reconciled is becoming a people.

A change of clothes. Clothing has marked every turning point in Joseph’s story: the robe his brothers stripped from him and dipped in blood (37:23, 31), the garment he left in the hand of Potiphar’s wife (39:12), the fine linen Pharaoh gave him (41:42), the clothes the brothers tore in grief (44:13). Now Joseph gives his brothers new clothes. The man they stripped clothes them.

To Benjamin … three hundred shekels of silver and five changes of clothes. Benjamin again receives far more than the rest, as he did at the meal (43:34). The brothers once hated Joseph because their father favoured him (37:4); now favour is shown openly to Rachel’s other son, and there is no sign of envy. The shekel was a weight of silver (see the note). The brothers sold Joseph for twenty shekels (37:28); Benjamin receives fifteen times that.

Ten donkeys … ten female donkeys. Joseph’s gifts for his father are generous and practical: the good things of Egypt, and grain and bread for the journey. He wants his father to travel in comfort and to see from the gifts how much he is wanted.

Do not quarrel on the way. This is the most practical sentence in the chapter. Ten men with a shared guilty past have a long journey in which to work out whose fault it was, and Reuben has already reminded them that he warned them (42:22). Joseph heads it off. Being forgiven does not by itself make peace among those who shared the guilt; that is a further work, and it often breaks down on the road home.

In everyday life. When God has forgiven a whole group of people, the temptation is to start sorting out among ourselves who was most to blame. Those who have been forgiven together need to walk together in peace.

Uncertain wording. The verb translated “quarrel” usually means to tremble or be stirred up, whether in anger or in fear. Most translations, including the ESV, take it here as “do not quarrel” or “do not get agitated with one another”. A few take it as “do not be afraid on the way”, that is, do not fear that I will turn on you. The first fits the brothers’ history best, but either way Joseph is speaking peace to them for the journey.
verseByVerse.note: Three hundred shekels was about 7½ pounds of silver (a shekel was about 2/5 ounce, ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: So they went up out of Egypt and came to the land of Canaan to their father Jacob. And they told him, "Joseph is still alive, and he is ruler over all the land of Egypt." And his heart became numb, for he did not believe them. But when they told him all the words of Joseph, which he had said to them, and when he saw the wagons that Joseph had sent to carry him, the spirit of their father Jacob revived. And Israel said, "It is enough; Joseph my son is still alive. I will go and see him before I die."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jacob cannot believe that Joseph is alive, until he hears all Joseph’s words and sees the wagons, and then his spirit revives and he resolves to go and see his son before he dies.

Joseph is still alive. For twenty-two years Jacob had believed Joseph was torn by a wild animal, and had refused to be comforted (37:33–35). The brothers who brought him the bloodstained robe must now tell him the truth, and in doing so they must also confess, at least implicitly, what they did.

His heart became numb. The Hebrew pictures the heart growing cold or faint, as if it stopped. The news is too good to take in, and Jacob simply does not believe them. Long grief can make good news feel impossible; this man has been disappointed too often.

When he saw the wagons. Words alone do not reach him. Then come “all the words of Joseph”, and the wagons, real evidence from Egypt, sent “to carry him”. Then “the spirit of their father Jacob revived”, as if from death to life.

And Israel said, “It is enough.” The narrator switches from “Jacob” to “Israel”, the covenant name God gave him (32:28), as the old man’s faith revives. He wants nothing more: “Joseph my son is still alive. I will go and see him before I die.”

Where it leads. The disciples, too, could not at first believe that the one they had lost was alive. The women’s words “seemed to them an idle tale” (Luke 24:11), until the risen Lord showed them his hands and his feet. The gospel is news of a Son who was dead and is alive, ruling at the right hand of the throne and sending for his people. It still brings numb, grieving hearts back to life.

In everyday life. If you find it hard to believe that the gospel is true for you, do what Jacob did: listen to all the words, and look at the evidence God has given. Faith is not a leap in the dark; it rests on testimony and on what God has done in history.

45.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Joseph could not control himself before all those who stood by him. He cried, "Make everyone go out from me." So no one stayed with him when Joseph made himself known to his brothers.<sup>2</sup>And he wept aloud, so that the Egyptians heard it, and the household of Pharaoh heard it.<sup>3</sup>And Joseph said to his brothers, "I am Joseph! Is my father still alive?" But his brothers could not answer him, for they were dismayed at his presence.<sup>4</sup>So Joseph said to his brothers, "Come near to me, please." And they came near. And he said, "I am your brother, Joseph, whom you sold into Egypt.<sup>5</sup>And now do not be distressed or angry with yourselves because you sold me here, for God sent me before you to preserve life.<sup>6</sup>For the famine has been in the land these two years, and there are yet five years in which there will be neither plowing nor harvest.<sup>7</sup>And God sent me before you to preserve for you a remnant on earth, and to keep alive for you many survivors.<sup>8</sup>So it was not you who sent me here, but God. He has made me a father to Pharaoh, and lord of all his house and ruler over all the land of Egypt.<sup>9</sup>Hurry and go up to my father and say to him, 'Thus says your son Joseph, God has made me lord of all Egypt. Come down to me; do not tarry.<sup>10</sup>You shall dwell in the land of Goshen, and you shall be near me, you and your children and your children's children, and your flocks, your herds, and all that you have.<sup>11</sup>There I will provide for you, for there are yet five years of famine to come, so that you and your household, and all that you have, do not come to poverty.'<sup>12</sup>And now your eyes see, and the eyes of my brother Benjamin see, that it is my mouth that speaks to you.<sup>13</sup>You must tell my father of all my honor in Egypt, and of all that you have seen. Hurry and bring my father down here."<sup>14</sup>Then he fell upon his brother Benjamin's neck and wept, and Benjamin wept upon his neck.<sup>15</sup>And he kissed all his brothers and wept upon them. After that his brothers talked with him.<sup>16</sup>When the report was heard in Pharaoh's house, "Joseph's brothers have come," it pleased Pharaoh and his servants.<sup>17</sup>And Pharaoh said to Joseph, "Say to your brothers, 'Do this: load your beasts and go back to the land of Canaan,<sup>18</sup>and take your father and your households, and come to me, and I will give you the best of the land of Egypt, and you shall eat the fat of the land.'<sup>19</sup>And you, Joseph, are commanded to say, 'Do this: take wagons from the land of Egypt for your little ones and for your wives, and bring your father, and come.<sup>20</sup>Have no concern for your goods, for the best of all the land of Egypt is yours.'"<sup>21</sup>The sons of Israel did so: and Joseph gave them wagons, according to the command of Pharaoh, and gave them provisions for the journey.<sup>22</sup>To each and all of them he gave a change of clothes, but to Benjamin he gave three hundred shekels of silver and five changes of clothes.<sup>23</sup>To his father he sent as follows: ten donkeys loaded with the good things of Egypt, and ten female donkeys loaded with grain, bread, and provision for his father on the journey.<sup>24</sup>Then he sent his brothers away, and as they departed, he said to them, "Do not quarrel on the way."<sup>25</sup>So they went up out of Egypt and came to the land of Canaan to their father Jacob.<sup>26</sup>And they told him, "Joseph is still alive, and he is ruler over all the land of Egypt." And his heart became numb, for he did not believe them.<sup>27</sup>But when they told him all the words of Joseph, which he had said to them, and when he saw the wagons that Joseph had sent to carry him, the spirit of their father Jacob revived.<sup>28</sup>And Israel said, "It is enough; Joseph my son is still alive. I will go and see him before I die."
45.overview:
Where we are. Joseph has tested his brothers for more than a year, and in chapter 44 the test reached its end: Judah, who once proposed selling Joseph, offered to stay in Egypt as a slave so that Benjamin could go home to their father (44:18–34). Joseph can hold back no longer.

The message. God rules even over the worst things people do, and turns them into salvation. The brothers really did sell Joseph, and Joseph says so; but three times he tells them that God sent him, “to preserve life”. The wronged brother, now ruler of the world’s greatest kingdom, uses his power to forgive, to gather and to provide. Grace names the sin and then lifts the guilt.

Why it was said. Israel in the wilderness needed to know how they came to be in Egypt (see the introduction). It was not an accident of famine or the fruit of their fathers’ crime alone: God had sent Joseph ahead to keep the family of promise alive.

How the chapter makes its case. Joseph clears the room, weeps aloud and says, “I am Joseph” (vv. 1–3). He draws his terrified brothers close, names what they did, and three times sets it inside God’s purpose (vv. 4–8). He sends for his father, promising Goshen and food (vv. 9–13). He embraces Benjamin and all his brothers, and at last they talk with him (vv. 14–15). Pharaoh adds his own generous invitation and wagons (vv. 16–20). Joseph loads them with gifts and warns them not to quarrel (vv. 21–24), and Jacob, numb with disbelief, is revived by the words and the wagons (vv. 25–28).

Where it leads. By pattern. Joseph is rejected and sold by his own brothers, raised from humiliation to the right hand of the throne, and becomes the means of life for the very people who betrayed him. In Christ the pattern is fulfilled and surpassed: he was handed over “according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God” by lawless hands (Acts 2:23), raised to the throne, and from there offers forgiveness to those who put him to death. And he too “is not ashamed to call them brothers” (Hebrews 2:11).

For us. No sin against us is outside God’s rule, and no sin of ours is beyond the reach of his grace. Those who have been forgiven much can name a wrong honestly and still release the one who did it. And the gospel, like the news Jacob heard, is often too good to believe until we see the evidence: the risen Son has sent for us.
45.theology:
Two hands on the same event. “You sold me” and “God sent me” are both true, and neither cancels the other. Joseph does not say his brothers meant well or that the wrong was small; he says twice that they sold him. He also says God was doing something through it they knew nothing about. Peter preached the same about a far greater crime: Jesus was “delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God,” and “you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men” (Acts 2:23): God’s plan and human guilt in one sentence.

Forgiveness without minimising. Real forgiveness does not pretend the thing was less than it was; it looks straight at it and releases the person anyway, as God in Christ has forgiven us (Ephesians 4:32).

A remnant preserved. “God sent me before you to preserve for you a remnant on earth.” The word “remnant”, the few God keeps alive when many are lost, will run through the prophets and into Paul’s argument in Romans 11. The line that carries the promise is repeatedly reduced to almost nothing and repeatedly kept alive, and here it is kept alive by the brother the family tried to be rid of.
45.examples: For anyone who has been told good news too large to take in, there is Jacob: his heart went numb, he did not believe it, and then he saw the wagons. God is patient with slow faith, and he gives evidence enough to rest on.

keyVerse.quote: And now do not be distressed or angry with yourselves because you sold me here, for God sent me before you to preserve life.
keyVerse.note: Joseph names the brothers’ sin plainly, yet sets it inside God’s saving purpose, and so releases them from crushing guilt. This is the heart of the Joseph story and will be repeated in 50:20. It points ahead to the cross, where human evil and God’s plan to save met in one event.

45.reflection:
Joseph said both “you sold me” and “God sent me” (vv. 4–5). How can we hold both truths about a wrong done to us, without excusing the wrong or forgetting God’s hand in it?

Before he forgave, Joseph saw clear evidence that his brothers had changed (44:16, 33–34). What is the difference between forgiving someone in our hearts and restoring trust in a relationship?

“After that his brothers talked with him” (v. 15). What helps forgiven people to speak freely again, with God and with one another?

Jacob could not believe the good news until he saw the wagons (vv. 26–27). What evidence has God given that helps you believe that Christ is alive and has sent for you?

46.title: Jacob Goes to Egypt

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–34 — The Descent to Egypt: God's Promise and the Family Register
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God sends Israel down into Egypt with his own promise to go with them and bring them back, and the small family of seventy becomes the seed of a nation. At Beersheba God tells Jacob not to fear, for he will make him a great nation in Egypt and bring him up again (vv. 1–4). The whole family goes down (vv. 5–7), and the register names the seventy, grouped by Jacob’s four wives (vv. 8–27). Judah leads the way, and Joseph and Jacob are reunited in Goshen after twenty-two years (vv. 28–30). Joseph then prepares his brothers to tell Pharaoh they are shepherds, so that they will be kept apart and not swallowed up by Egypt (vv. 31–34).
verseByVerse.theology: At Beersheba Jacob offers sacrifices, and God tells him not to fear going to Egypt: he will make him a great nation there, go down with him and bring him up again. Seventy persons of the house of Jacob go down. Joseph meets his father in Goshen and weeps on his neck a good while, and briefs his brothers to say they are shepherds.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the exodus is promised four centuries before it happens. Now: God's work often looks far too small at the start to become what he promised.

verseByVerse.quote: So Israel took his journey with all that he had and came to Beersheba, and offered sacrifices to the God of his father Isaac. And God spoke to Israel in visions of the night and said, "Jacob, Jacob." And he said, "Here I am." Then he said, "I am God, the God of your father. Do not be afraid to go down to Egypt, for there I will make you into a great nation. I myself will go down with you to Egypt, and I will also bring you up again, and Joseph's hand shall close your eyes."
verseByVerse.commentary:
At Beersheba, the last stop in the promised land, Jacob worships, and God tells him not to be afraid to go down to Egypt: God himself will go with him, make him a great nation there, and bring him up again.

He came to Beersheba, and offered sacrifices to the God of his father Isaac. Beersheba was the southern edge of Canaan, where Abraham had called on the name of the LORD (21:33) and Isaac had built an altar after God appeared to him (26:23–25). Jacob had every practical reason to hurry, yet he stops to offer sacrifices before he crosses the border. He does not take this step without asking God.

Visions of the night. God had appeared to Jacob at Bethel as he left the land the first time (28:12–15), and now speaks to him as he leaves it a second time. This is the last time God speaks directly to anyone in Genesis.

“Jacob, Jacob.” And he said, “Here I am.” The name is called twice, as God called “Abraham, Abraham” on Mount Moriah (22:11), and as he would call Moses and Samuel. “Here I am” is the answer of a servant ready to listen.

Do not be afraid to go down to Egypt. Jacob had reason to fear. Abraham had gone down to Egypt in a famine and got into trouble (12:10–20), and Isaac had been told not to go there (26:2). God had told Abraham that his descendants would be sojourners and slaves “in a land that is not theirs” (15:13). Leaving Canaan might look like abandoning the promise. God removes the fear: this time he is sending them.

There I will make you into a great nation. The promise to Abraham (12:2) will be fulfilled in Egypt of all places. Seventy people go down; a nation of hundreds of thousands will come out (Exodus 12:37). God grows his people in the least likely soil.

I myself will go down with you. This is the heart of the promise. God is not a local god tied to Canaan; he goes with his people into exile. Jacob is not leaving God behind at the border.

I will also bring you up again. This was fulfilled twice: for Jacob himself, when his body was carried back to Canaan and buried with his fathers (50:13), and for his descendants in the exodus, more than four hundred years later. God promised the exodus before Israel ever went down.

Joseph’s hand shall close your eyes. The son Jacob mourned as dead will be at his deathbed. It was a tender promise to an old man: he will not die alone or bereaved.

Where it leads. God’s “I myself will go down with you” finds its fulness in the Son of God, who came down to share the exile of his people. His name is Immanuel, “God with us” (Matthew 1:23), and his promise to his disciples is, “I am with you always” (Matthew 28:20).

In everyday life. Before a big move or decision, stop and worship, as Jacob did. God does not always remove the strangeness of where he leads, but he goes with you into it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jacob set out from Beersheba. The sons of Israel carried Jacob their father, their little ones, and their wives, in the wagons that Pharaoh had sent to carry him. They also took their livestock and their goods, which they had gained in the land of Canaan, and came into Egypt, Jacob and all his offspring with him, his sons, and his sons' sons with him, his daughters, and his sons' daughters. All his offspring he brought with him into Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole family, from Jacob down to his granddaughters, travels to Egypt in Pharaoh’s wagons, taking everything they have.

In the wagons that Pharaoh had sent to carry him. The old man is carried in the wagons that convinced him Joseph was alive (45:27). The sons who once deceived their father now carry him.

Their livestock and their goods, which they had gained in the land of Canaan. They take everything. This is not a short visit to buy grain; it is a migration. They leave nothing to come back to, except the promise and the graves of their fathers.

All his offspring he brought with him into Egypt. The text lists them with care: sons and sons’ sons, daughters and sons’ daughters. The whole covenant family goes down together, nobody left behind. God had promised Abraham that his offspring would be sojourners in a foreign land (15:13–14), and now it begins.

verseByVerse.quote: Now these are the names of the descendants of Israel, who came into Egypt, Jacob and his sons. Reuben, Jacob's firstborn, and the sons of Reuben: Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi. The sons of Simeon: Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Jachin, Zohar, and Shaul, the son of a Canaanite woman. The sons of Levi: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. The sons of Judah: Er, Onan, Shelah, Perez, and Zerah (but Er and Onan died in the land of Canaan); and the sons of Perez were Hezron and Hamul. The sons of Issachar: Tola, Puvah, Yob, and Shimron. The sons of Zebulun: Sered, Elon, and Jahleel. These are the sons of Leah, whom she bore to Jacob in Paddan-aram, together with his daughter Dinah; altogether his sons and his daughters numbered thirty-three. The sons of Gad: Ziphion, Haggi, Shuni, Ezbon, Eri, Arodi, and Areli. The sons of Asher: Imnah, Ishvah, Ishvi, Beriah, with Serah their sister. And the sons of Beriah: Heber and Malchiel. These are the sons of Zilpah, whom Laban gave to Leah his daughter; and these she bore to Jacob—sixteen persons. The sons of Rachel, Jacob's wife: Joseph and Benjamin. And to Joseph in the land of Egypt were born Manasseh and Ephraim, whom Asenath, the daughter of Potiphera the priest of On, bore to him. And the sons of Benjamin: Bela, Becher, Ashbel, Gera, Naaman, Ehi, Rosh, Muppim, Huppim, and Ard. These are the sons of Rachel, who were born to Jacob—fourteen persons in all. The son of Dan: Hushim. The sons of Naphtali: Jahzeel, Guni, Jezer, and Shillem. These are the sons of Bilhah, whom Laban gave to Rachel his daughter, and these she bore to Jacob—seven persons in all. All the persons belonging to Jacob who came into Egypt, who were his own descendants, not including Jacob's sons' wives, were sixty-six persons in all. And the sons of Joseph, who were born to him in Egypt, were two. All the persons of the house of Jacob who came into Egypt were seventy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The register lists Jacob’s descendants who went down to Egypt, grouped by their mothers, and counts them as seventy: the whole house of Israel, small enough to number by name.

These are the names of the descendants of Israel. Exodus opens with almost the same words (Exodus 1:1), so this list links Genesis to the story of the nation. It is the founding register of the twelve tribes, and the first hearers would have looked in it for their own ancestors.

Grouped by mothers. The sons of Leah come first (vv. 8–15), then of her servant Zilpah (vv. 16–18), then of Rachel (vv. 19–22), then of Rachel’s servant Bilhah (vv. 23–25). The rivalries of chapters 29 and 30 are still visible in the shape of the family, but now they all travel together.

Shaul, the son of a Canaanite woman. Simeon married a Canaanite, against the family’s practice (24:3; 28:1), and Judah too had married one (38:2). The note quietly shows how close the family came to being absorbed into Canaan. The move to Egypt, where they were kept apart as shepherds, preserved them.

Er and Onan died in the land of Canaan. The list remembers the sons whom the LORD put to death for their wickedness (38:7–10), and through Tamar it records Perez, from whose line David and Christ would come (Ruth 4:18–22; Matthew 1:3).

Asenath, the daughter of Potiphera the priest of On. Joseph’s Egyptian wife is named (41:45, 50), and her sons are counted among Israel. Outsiders are brought into the family of promise.

Seventy. The numbers add up carefully: thirty-three for Leah’s line (counting Jacob himself), sixteen for Zilpah’s, fourteen for Rachel’s, seven for Bilhah’s. Sixty-six travelled (v. 26); with Jacob, Joseph and his two sons already in Egypt the total is seventy (v. 27; see the note). Seventy also matches the seventy nations of Genesis 10, as if this small family stands for the blessing meant for all of them. Moses later reminded Israel how small they had been: “Your fathers went down to Egypt seventy persons, and now the LORD your God has made you as numerous as the stars of heaven” (Deuteronomy 10:22).

Were all these born before the journey? Benjamin was “a young brother, the child of his old age” (44:20), yet he has ten sons here, and Perez, a baby in chapter 38, already has two. Some of the names may belong to grandchildren born later in Egypt, listed here because the register records the founding families of Israel, those who “came into Egypt” in their father’s line. Ancient registers often worked this way. The list is not careless; it is counting the nation in its seed.

Where it leads. God’s great works often begin small enough to number by name. Jesus began with twelve, and his kingdom, “like a grain of mustard seed” (Matthew 13:31), will fill the earth.

Textual note. Stephen says seventy-five (Acts 7:14), following the Greek Old Testament, which counts additional descendants of Joseph. Both counts are ways of numbering the family.
verseByVerse.note: The total of seventy includes Jacob, Joseph and Joseph’s two sons.

verseByVerse.quote: He had sent Judah ahead of him to Joseph to show the way before him in Goshen, and they came into the land of Goshen. Then Joseph prepared his chariot and went up to meet Israel his father in Goshen. He presented himself to him and fell on his neck and wept on his neck a good while. Israel said to Joseph, "Now let me die, since I have seen your face and know that you are still alive."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah leads the family to Goshen, Joseph rides out to meet his father, and after twenty-two years they weep in each other’s arms; Jacob says he can now die content.

He had sent Judah ahead of him. The brother who proposed selling Joseph (37:26–27) and later offered himself in Benjamin’s place (44:33) is now the one Jacob trusts to lead the way. Judah has become the leader among the brothers, and in 49:8–10 he will receive the promise of the sceptre.

Joseph prepared his chariot and went up to meet Israel his father. The ruler of Egypt goes out to meet the old shepherd, not the other way round. The phrase “he presented himself to him” uses a verb most often used of God appearing to people. For Jacob, seeing Joseph’s face was like seeing someone return from the dead.

He fell on his neck and wept on his neck a good while. Twenty-two years of grief are released in one long embrace. Genesis rarely lingers over emotion, but here it does.

Now let me die, since I have seen your face. Jacob has nothing left to wish for. His words are like those of Simeon, who held the infant Jesus and said, “Lord, now you are letting your servant depart in peace, according to your word; for my eyes have seen your salvation” (Luke 2:29–30). Every reunion God gives is a foretaste of the greater one to come.

In everyday life. Some griefs are not healed in this life, and Genesis knows it: Rachel did not come back. But Jacob’s joy is a reminder that God can restore what we had given up for lost, and that for his people every parting is temporary.

verseByVerse.quote: Joseph said to his brothers and to his father's household, "I will go up and tell Pharaoh and will say to him, 'My brothers and my father's household, who were in the land of Canaan, have come to me. And the men are shepherds, for they have been keepers of livestock, and they have brought their flocks and their herds and all that they have.' When Pharaoh calls you and says, 'What is your occupation?' you shall say, 'Your servants have been keepers of livestock from our youth even until now, both we and our fathers,' in order that you may dwell in the land of Goshen, for every shepherd is an abomination to the Egyptians."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joseph prepares his family to tell Pharaoh honestly that they are shepherds, knowing that the Egyptians’ dislike of shepherds will keep them settled apart in Goshen.

I will go up and tell Pharaoh. Joseph handles the introduction himself. Having brought his family to Egypt, he takes responsibility for settling them wisely.

The men are shepherds. Joseph tells his brothers to be honest about their work. There is no pretence, no attempt to dress them up as something more respectable. Their honesty serves a purpose: it will place them where God wants them.

Every shepherd is an abomination to the Egyptians. Settled Egyptian farmers looked down on wandering herdsmen, as they already refused to eat with Hebrews (43:32; compare Exodus 8:26). Their contempt for shepherds would keep Israel apart, in Goshen, and not absorbed into Egypt. What looked like a disadvantage protected the family’s identity, as their marriages in Canaan had shown it needed protecting (v. 10; 38:2).

Where it leads. The great Shepherd of the sheep (Hebrews 13:20) was also despised and rejected (Isaiah 53:3). Those who belong to him should not be surprised to be looked down on by the world; it is part of being kept for him.

In everyday life. Do not be ashamed of honest work, and do not try to win acceptance by pretending to be what you are not. Being a little out of step with the world around you can be God’s way of keeping you his.

46.text: <sup>1</sup>So Israel took his journey with all that he had and came to Beersheba, and offered sacrifices to the God of his father Isaac.<sup>2</sup>And God spoke to Israel in visions of the night and said, "Jacob, Jacob." And he said, "Here I am."<sup>3</sup>Then he said, "I am God, the God of your father. Do not be afraid to go down to Egypt, for there I will make you into a great nation.<sup>4</sup>I myself will go down with you to Egypt, and I will also bring you up again, and Joseph's hand shall close your eyes."<sup>5</sup>Then Jacob set out from Beersheba. The sons of Israel carried Jacob their father, their little ones, and their wives, in the wagons that Pharaoh had sent to carry him.<sup>6</sup>They also took their livestock and their goods, which they had gained in the land of Canaan, and came into Egypt, Jacob and all his offspring with him,<sup>7</sup>his sons, and his sons' sons with him, his daughters, and his sons' daughters. All his offspring he brought with him into Egypt.<sup>8</sup>Now these are the names of the descendants of Israel, who came into Egypt, Jacob and his sons. Reuben, Jacob's firstborn,<sup>9</sup>and the sons of Reuben: Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi.<sup>10</sup>The sons of Simeon: Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Jachin, Zohar, and Shaul, the son of a Canaanite woman.<sup>11</sup>The sons of Levi: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari.<sup>12</sup>The sons of Judah: Er, Onan, Shelah, Perez, and Zerah (but Er and Onan died in the land of Canaan); and the sons of Perez were Hezron and Hamul.<sup>13</sup>The sons of Issachar: Tola, Puvah, Yob, and Shimron.<sup>14</sup>The sons of Zebulun: Sered, Elon, and Jahleel.<sup>15</sup>These are the sons of Leah, whom she bore to Jacob in Paddan-aram, together with his daughter Dinah; altogether his sons and his daughters numbered thirty-three.<sup>16</sup>The sons of Gad: Ziphion, Haggi, Shuni, Ezbon, Eri, Arodi, and Areli.<sup>17</sup>The sons of Asher: Imnah, Ishvah, Ishvi, Beriah, with Serah their sister. And the sons of Beriah: Heber and Malchiel.<sup>18</sup>These are the sons of Zilpah, whom Laban gave to Leah his daughter; and these she bore to Jacob—sixteen persons.<sup>19</sup>The sons of Rachel, Jacob's wife: Joseph and Benjamin.<sup>20</sup>And to Joseph in the land of Egypt were born Manasseh and Ephraim, whom Asenath, the daughter of Potiphera the priest of On, bore to him.<sup>21</sup>And the sons of Benjamin: Bela, Becher, Ashbel, Gera, Naaman, Ehi, Rosh, Muppim, Huppim, and Ard.<sup>22</sup>These are the sons of Rachel, who were born to Jacob—fourteen persons in all.<sup>23</sup>The son of Dan: Hushim.<sup>24</sup>The sons of Naphtali: Jahzeel, Guni, Jezer, and Shillem.<sup>25</sup>These are the sons of Bilhah, whom Laban gave to Rachel his daughter, and these she bore to Jacob—seven persons in all.<sup>26</sup>All the persons belonging to Jacob who came into Egypt, who were his own descendants, not including Jacob's sons' wives, were sixty-six persons in all.<sup>27</sup>And the sons of Joseph, who were born to him in Egypt, were two. All the persons of the house of Jacob who came into Egypt were seventy.<sup>28</sup>He had sent Judah ahead of him to Joseph to show the way before him in Goshen, and they came into the land of Goshen.<sup>29</sup>Then Joseph prepared his chariot and went up to meet Israel his father in Goshen. He presented himself to him and fell on his neck and wept on his neck a good while.<sup>30</sup>Israel said to Joseph, "Now let me die, since I have seen your face and know that you are still alive."<sup>31</sup>Joseph said to his brothers and to his father's household, "I will go up and tell Pharaoh and will say to him, 'My brothers and my father's household, who were in the land of Canaan, have come to me.<sup>32</sup>And the men are shepherds, for they have been keepers of livestock, and they have brought their flocks and their herds and all that they have.'<sup>33</sup>When Pharaoh calls you and says, 'What is your occupation?'<sup>34</sup>you shall say, 'Your servants have been keepers of livestock from our youth even until now, both we and our fathers,' in order that you may dwell in the land of Goshen, for every shepherd is an abomination to the Egyptians."
46.overview:
Where we are. Jacob has heard that Joseph is alive and ruler of Egypt, and has seen the wagons sent to carry him (45:25–28). Now the whole family sets out. But before they cross the border, Genesis stops at Beersheba.

The message. God goes with his people where he sends them. Israel does not drift into Egypt out of hunger and bad judgment: God sends them, promises to go down with them, to make them a great nation there, and to bring them up again. The move that looks like leaving the promise behind is the next step in keeping it.

Why it was said. The first hearers had just come out of Egypt (see the introduction). This chapter told them why their fathers had gone there, and that the exodus they had lived through was what God had promised Jacob on the night he left Canaan. The list of seventy names told each family where it came from.

How the chapter makes its case. At Beersheba Jacob worships, and God speaks to him for the last time in Genesis: do not be afraid, I will go with you and bring you up again (vv. 1–4). The whole family goes down in Pharaoh’s wagons (vv. 5–7). Their names are listed, seventy in all, the seed of the great nation (vv. 8–27). Judah leads the way to Goshen, and Joseph and his father meet at last and weep (vv. 28–30). Joseph prepares his family to tell Pharaoh honestly that they are shepherds, so that they will be settled apart in Goshen (vv. 31–34).

Where it leads. By promise and pattern. God’s “I myself will go down with you” is the promise of his presence that reaches its fulness in Immanuel, God with us, who came down to share our exile. And Israel’s going down into Egypt and coming up again is a pattern the Son himself would walk: Jesus was carried into Egypt as a child, so that Matthew could write, “Out of Egypt I called my son” (Matthew 2:15). The true Israel went down where his people had gone, and brings them up with him.

For us. God’s guidance does not always lead where we expect, and sometimes it leads into places that look like the opposite of his promise. But we never go alone. Stop to worship before the big decisions, take the next step he shows you, and trust him for the return journey.
46.theology:
God goes down with his people. “I will also bring you up again.” The covenant is not tied to a plot of ground. Whatever the years in Egypt would bring, and they would end in slavery, God’s people were never there without him. Centuries later he said it again to the exiles: “when you pass through the waters, I will be with you” (Isa. 43:2).

The exodus promised in advance. God had told Abraham the same thing in a night vision (15:12–14), and he keeps it in full at the Red Sea. Nothing about the four hundred years was outside the plan.

Seventy persons. The whole covenant people can be listed on one page, yet God had promised offspring like the stars and the sand.
46.examples:
Then: The delta was Egypt’s usual entry point for Semitic herdsmen, and Egyptian records mention such groups being let in during hard years. Goshen was pasture rather than farmland, which suited shepherds. Joseph turns Egyptian contempt for herdsmen to advantage, so that his family can remain a distinct people.

Now: This is the difference between the Jacob of chapter 27 and the Jacob of chapter 46: he now seeks God before a move that everything in him already wants to make. And the answer he gets is not advice about the journey. It is a promise that God will go with him.

keyVerse.quote: Do not be afraid to go down to Egypt, for there I will make you into a great nation. I myself will go down with you to Egypt, and I will also bring you up again, and Joseph’s hand shall close your eyes.
keyVerse.note: In the last words God speaks in Genesis, he turns a frightening move into a step of faith. The promise of his presence (“I myself will go down with you”) and of the exodus (“I will also bring you up again”) explains the whole move to Egypt and points to Immanuel, God with us.

46.reflection:
Jacob stopped at Beersheba to worship before he left the land (v. 1). How can we bring our big decisions to God before we make them, not afterward?

God promised, “I myself will go down with you” (v. 4). Where are you being asked to go that feels like leaving the promise behind, and how does God’s presence change it?

The nation began as seventy names (v. 27). How does God’s habit of beginning small encourage us about our church or our own small acts of faith?

The Egyptians’ contempt for shepherds kept Israel apart (v. 34). In what ways can being out of step with our culture help keep us faithful to Christ?

47.title: Jacob Settles in Goshen; Joseph's Administration

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–31 — Goshen Granted; Joseph's Famine Policy; Jacob's Last Request
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In Egypt God’s people are both blessed and a blessing, yet they never forget that they are only sojourners. Pharaoh welcomes Joseph’s brothers, honest shepherds, and grants them Goshen (vv. 1–6). Jacob blesses Pharaoh, and calls his 130 years a pilgrimage, few and evil (vv. 7–10). Joseph provides for his family (vv. 11–12), while across Egypt his famine policy exchanges money, livestock and finally land for food, saving the people’s lives and bringing all into Pharaoh’s hands (vv. 13–26). Israel is fruitful in Goshen (vv. 27–28), and Jacob, near death, makes Joseph swear to bury him with his fathers in Canaan (vv. 29–31).
verseByVerse.theology: Pharaoh grants Jacob's family the best of the land, and Jacob blesses Pharaoh twice, calling his 130 years few and evil. Through the famine Joseph takes Egypt's money, livestock and land for Pharaoh, and the people say, "You have saved our lives." Israel is fruitful in Goshen; after seventeen years Jacob makes Joseph swear to bury him in Canaan, and bows in worship.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the old shepherd is the greater man in the room. Now: grief can hide from a man how God has carried him, and faith can show in where he asks to be buried.

verseByVerse.quote: So Joseph went in and told Pharaoh, "My father and my brothers, with their flocks and herds and all that they possess, have come from the land of Canaan. They are now in the land of Goshen." And from among his brothers he took five men and presented them to Pharaoh. Pharaoh said to his brothers, "What is your occupation?" And they said to Pharaoh, "Your servants are shepherds, as our fathers were." They said to Pharaoh, "We have come to sojourn in the land, for there is no pasture for your servants' flocks, for the famine is severe in the land of Canaan. And now, please let your servants dwell in the land of Goshen." Then Pharaoh said to Joseph, "Your father and your brothers have come to you. The land of Egypt is before you. Settle your father and your brothers in the best of the land. Let them settle in the land of Goshen, and if you know any able men among them, put them in charge of my livestock."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joseph presents five of his brothers to Pharaoh, who tell him honestly that they are shepherds come to sojourn because of the famine, and Pharaoh grants them the best of the land in Goshen.
