From among his brothers he took five men. Joseph chooses a small delegation rather than overwhelming the king with the whole family. Throughout, he handles Pharaoh with tact and wisdom.

Your servants are shepherds, as our fathers were. They answer exactly as Joseph told them to (46:33–34), without pretending to be anything grander. Their honesty about a despised trade is what secures them a place apart in Goshen.

We have come to sojourn in the land. The brothers call themselves sojourners, resident foreigners with no rights of their own: they see Egypt as a temporary home. The word is the one God used to Abraham, “your offspring will be sojourners in a land that is not theirs” (15:13). They have come because the famine is severe, and they ask, rather than assume, to settle in Goshen.

The land of Egypt is before you. Pharaoh answers Joseph, not the brothers, and grants more than they asked: “the best of the land”. Then he offers the capable among them charge of his own livestock. The Egyptians may despise shepherds, but Pharaoh knows the value of a skilled herdsman. Honest work earns trust.

In everyday life. Be honest about who you are and what you do. Christians are sojourners too (1 Peter 2:11), and we can ask humbly for what we need from those in authority, without either grovelling or pretending.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Joseph brought in Jacob his father and stood him before Pharaoh, and Jacob blessed Pharaoh. And Pharaoh said to Jacob, "How many are the days of the years of your life?" And Jacob said to Pharaoh, "The days of the years of my sojourning are 130 years. Few and evil have been the days of the years of my life, and they have not attained to the days of the years of the life of my fathers in the days of their sojourning." And Jacob blessed Pharaoh and went out from the presence of Pharaoh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The aged shepherd Jacob blesses Pharaoh, the greatest king on earth, and tells him that his 130 years have been a short and hard pilgrimage.

Jacob blessed Pharaoh. A shepherd of no standing blesses the most powerful man on earth, twice (vv. 7, 10). By every visible measure Pharaoh outranks him; by the measure that matters, the old shepherd is the greater man in the room. As Hebrews says, “the inferior is blessed by the superior” (Hebrews 7:7): Jacob carries the promise that in Abraham’s family “all the families of the earth shall be blessed” (12:3), and through him the nations are beginning to be blessed.

How many are the days of the years of your life? Pharaoh’s question may be simple courtesy, or wonder at a man so old. Egyptians regarded 110 years as the ideal lifespan (Joseph will live exactly that, 50:26), and Jacob is already 130.

The days of the years of my sojourning. Jacob calls his whole life a sojourning, a pilgrimage, and Hebrews describes the whole family that way: they “acknowledged that they were strangers and exiles on the earth” (Hebrews 11:13). He has never owned more of Canaan than a field at Shechem and a family grave, and now he is a foreigner in Egypt.

Few and evil have been the days. His 130 years are “few” compared with Abraham’s 175 (25:7) and Isaac’s 180 (35:28), and “evil”, that is, full of trouble. He has known exile from home, deception by Laban, the death of Rachel, the shame of Dinah, and twenty-two years of grief for Joseph, much of it the harvest of his own deceit. It is an honest look at a hard life, though it is not his last word on it: by 48:15 he will call God “the God who has been my shepherd all my life long.”

In everyday life. You do not have to pretend that life has been easy. Honest lament is part of faith, and the Psalms are full of it. But do not let a hard look at your life be your last look: the same life seen from the end may show you how God shepherded you all the way. And your life is a journey toward a better country, one God has prepared for you (Hebrews 11:16).

Uncertain wording. The verb “blessed” can also describe a formal greeting or farewell, a blessing spoken on meeting or parting, and some translations have “greeted” in verse 7 or verse 10. But in Genesis, where blessing is the central theme, and coming from the bearer of God’s promise, it is likely that the narrator means more than politeness: the patriarch is blessing the king.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Joseph settled his father and his brothers and gave them a possession in the land of Egypt, in the best of the land, in the land of Rameses, as Pharaoh had commanded. And Joseph provided his father, his brothers, and all his father's household with food, according to the number of their dependents.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joseph settles his family in the best part of Egypt, as Pharaoh commanded, and feeds them all through the famine.

Gave them a possession in the land of Egypt. The word “possession” is a strong one: a holding, property of their own. Abraham’s family had owned only a burial plot in Canaan (23:20), and now they hold land in Egypt.

In the land of Rameses. “The land of Rameses” is Goshen, called by the name it bore in later days, after Rameses, the store city Israel would one day be forced to build there (Exodus 1:11). The land of welcome would become the land of slavery.

Joseph provided his father, his brothers, and all his father’s household with food. Joseph provides for the whole family, just as he promised (45:11). The brother they sold now feeds them, “according to the number of their dependents”, literally “according to the mouths of the little ones”: no child goes hungry.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was no food in all the land, for the famine was very severe, so that the land of Egypt and the land of Canaan languished by reason of the famine. And Joseph gathered up all the money that was found in the land of Egypt and in the land of Canaan, in exchange for the grain that they bought. And Joseph brought the money into Pharaoh's house. And when the money was all spent in the land of Egypt and in the land of Canaan, all the Egyptians came to Joseph and said, "Give us food. Why should we die before your eyes? For our money is gone." And Joseph answered, "Give your livestock, and I will give you food in exchange for your livestock, if your money is gone." So they brought their livestock to Joseph, and Joseph gave them food in exchange for the horses, the flocks, the herds, and the donkeys. He supplied them with food in exchange for all their livestock that year. And when that year was ended, they came to him the following year and said to him, "We will not hide from my lord that our money is all spent. The herds of livestock are my lord's. There is nothing left in the sight of my lord but our bodies and our land. Why should we die before your eyes, both we and our land? Buy us and our land for food, and we with our land will be servants to Pharaoh. And give us seed that we may live and not die, and that the land may not be desolate."
verseByVerse.commentary:
As the famine grows worse, the Egyptians spend all their money on grain, then trade their livestock, and finally offer their land and themselves to Pharaoh in exchange for food and seed.

No food in all the land. The famine is at its height and affects Canaan as well as Egypt. Only Joseph’s stored grain stands between the people and death.

Joseph gathered up all the money … into Pharaoh’s house. Joseph does not enrich himself. The money goes into Pharaoh’s treasury. His honesty matches his faithfulness in Potiphar’s house and in the prison (39:6, 22–23).

Give your livestock. When the money runs out, Joseph accepts livestock in payment. Taking the animals also relieved the people of having to feed them through the famine, and Joseph gave them food for a year in exchange.

There is nothing left … but our bodies and our land. In the second year the people themselves propose the next step: “Buy us and our land for food.” They ask for seed as well as food, so that the land will not become desolate. They are thinking about survival beyond the famine.

verseByVerse.quote: So Joseph bought all the land of Egypt for Pharaoh, for all the Egyptians sold their fields, because the famine was severe on them. The land became Pharaoh's. As for the people, he made servants of them from one end of Egypt to the other. Only the land of the priests he did not buy, for the priests had a fixed allowance from Pharaoh and lived on the allowance that Pharaoh gave them; therefore they did not sell their land. Then Joseph said to the people, "Behold, I have this day bought you and your land for Pharaoh. Now here is seed for you, and you shall sow the land. And at the harvests you shall give a fifth to Pharaoh, and four fifths shall be your own, as seed for the field and as food for yourselves and your households, and as food for your little ones." And they said, "You have saved our lives; may it please my lord, we will be servants to Pharaoh." So Joseph made it a statute concerning the land of Egypt, and it stands to this day, that Pharaoh should have the fifth; the land of the priests alone did not become Pharaoh's.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joseph buys all the land of Egypt for Pharaoh except the priests’ land, gives the people seed, and fixes a permanent rent of one fifth of the harvest; the people thank him for saving their lives.

The land became Pharaoh’s. By the end of the famine all Egypt’s farmland belongs to the crown, except the land of the priests, who already lived on an allowance from Pharaoh. The people work the land as tenants.

He made servants of them. The people become Pharaoh’s servants, bound to the land and owing him a share of the harvest. This was something like the serfdom of medieval Europe: hard, but a long way from the brutal slavery Israel would later suffer.

A fifth to Pharaoh, and four fifths shall be your own. Joseph had stored a fifth of the harvest in the years of plenty (41:34), and the same proportion now becomes a permanent tax. The people keep four fifths for seed and food. Twenty per cent was moderate by the standards of the ancient world.

You have saved our lives. The Egyptians themselves count Joseph’s policy as rescue, not oppression. The verb is the one Joseph used of God’s purpose: God sent him “to keep alive” many survivors (45:7), and he will say, “to bring it about that many people should be kept alive, as they are today” (50:20).

Where it leads. All the earth came to Joseph for bread (41:57), and paid for it with everything they had. Jesus is “the bread of life” (John 6:35), but he gives freely: “come, buy wine and milk without money and without price” (Isaiah 55:1). The people of Egypt offered themselves as Pharaoh’s servants to stay alive; those whom Christ saves become his willing servants, not to earn their bread, but because he has given himself for them.

Where Christians differ: Joseph’s policy. Some see harsh state control, a man of God helping a king gather the whole land into his hands. Others see a wise, merciful response to famine that kept a nation alive.

This commentary’s view. Genesis records it without praising or condemning. The terms (a fifth) were moderate by ancient standards, and lives were saved, but the concentration of power in Pharaoh’s hands would later be used to enslave Israel.

Textual note. In verse 21 the standard Hebrew text says that he moved the people into the cities from one end of Egypt to the other, perhaps to be near the grain stores. The ESV follows other ancient versions, “he made servants of them”, which fits the people’s offer in verse 19. Either way, the people’s land now belongs to Pharaoh.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus Israel settled in the land of Egypt, in the land of Goshen. And they gained possessions in it, and were fruitful and multiplied greatly. And Jacob lived in the land of Egypt seventeen years. So the days of Jacob, the years of his life, were 147 years.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In Goshen Israel gains possessions and multiplies greatly, as God promised; Jacob lives there seventeen years and dies at 147.

Thus Israel settled in the land of Egypt. “Israel” here means the people, not only the man. The contrast with the verses before is striking: the Egyptians have sold their land, while Israel “gained possessions in it”.

Fruitful and multiplied greatly. This is the blessing of creation (1:28) and God’s promise at Beersheba (46:3) coming true. Exodus picks up the story with the same words: “the people of Israel were fruitful and increased greatly; they multiplied” (Exodus 1:7).

Seventeen years. Jacob had Joseph with him for seventeen years before the boy was sold (37:2), and now Joseph has his father for seventeen years in Egypt. God gave back to him the years he thought were lost.
verseByVerse.note: Jacob lived 147 years.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the time drew near that Israel must die, he called his son Joseph and said to him, "If now I have found favor in your sight, put your hand under my thigh and promise to deal kindly and truly with me. Do not bury me in Egypt, but let me lie with my fathers. Carry me out of Egypt and bury me in their burying place." He answered, "I will do as you have said." And he said, "Swear to me"; and he swore to him. Then Israel bowed himself upon the head of his bed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As death approaches, Jacob makes Joseph swear a solemn oath not to bury him in Egypt but with his fathers in Canaan, and then bows in worship.

Put your hand under my thigh. This was a solemn form of oath, used by Abraham when he sent his servant to find a wife for Isaac (24:2–3; see the note). It bound the one who swore to the most serious promise.

Deal kindly and truly with me. Literally, “do hesed and truth with me”: loyal love and faithfulness, the qualities that describe God’s own covenant love (24:27; 32:10). Jacob asks his son to keep faith with him after death.

Do not bury me in Egypt, but let me lie with my fathers. Jacob will not be buried in Egypt, however well he has been treated there. He wants his body to lie in the cave of Machpelah, in the land God promised (49:29–32). It is an act of faith: he is sure that the promise outlasts his death, and that his descendants will return.

Then Israel bowed himself upon the head of his bed. Having received Joseph’s oath, Jacob bows in worship. Hebrews counts this among the acts of faith: “By faith Jacob, when dying, blessed each of the sons of Joseph, bowing in worship over the head of his staff” (Hebrews 11:21).

In everyday life. How we face death shows where our hope lies. Christians are not superstitious about burial, but we can make even our last wishes a witness that our home is with God, and that “our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3:20).

Textual note. In verse 31 the Hebrew consonants can be read “bed” or “staff”. The Greek Old Testament reads “staff”, followed by Hebrews 11:21. The ESV follows the Hebrew vowels, “bed”.
verseByVerse.note: Putting a hand under the thigh was a solemn form of oath (compare 24:2).

47.text: <sup>1</sup>So Joseph went in and told Pharaoh, "My father and my brothers, with their flocks and herds and all that they possess, have come from the land of Canaan. They are now in the land of Goshen."<sup>2</sup>And from among his brothers he took five men and presented them to Pharaoh.<sup>3</sup>Pharaoh said to his brothers, "What is your occupation?" And they said to Pharaoh, "Your servants are shepherds, as our fathers were."<sup>4</sup>They said to Pharaoh, "We have come to sojourn in the land, for there is no pasture for your servants' flocks, for the famine is severe in the land of Canaan. And now, please let your servants dwell in the land of Goshen."<sup>5</sup>Then Pharaoh said to Joseph, "Your father and your brothers have come to you.<sup>6</sup>The land of Egypt is before you. Settle your father and your brothers in the best of the land. Let them settle in the land of Goshen, and if you know any able men among them, put them in charge of my livestock."<sup>7</sup>Then Joseph brought in Jacob his father and stood him before Pharaoh, and Jacob blessed Pharaoh.<sup>8</sup>And Pharaoh said to Jacob, "How many are the days of the years of your life?"<sup>9</sup>And Jacob said to Pharaoh, "The days of the years of my sojourning are 130 years. Few and evil have been the days of the years of my life, and they have not attained to the days of the years of the life of my fathers in the days of their sojourning."<sup>10</sup>And Jacob blessed Pharaoh and went out from the presence of Pharaoh.<sup>11</sup>Then Joseph settled his father and his brothers and gave them a possession in the land of Egypt, in the best of the land, in the land of Rameses, as Pharaoh had commanded.<sup>12</sup>And Joseph provided his father, his brothers, and all his father's household with food, according to the number of their dependents.<sup>13</sup>Now there was no food in all the land, for the famine was very severe, so that the land of Egypt and the land of Canaan languished by reason of the famine.<sup>14</sup>And Joseph gathered up all the money that was found in the land of Egypt and in the land of Canaan, in exchange for the grain that they bought. And Joseph brought the money into Pharaoh's house.<sup>15</sup>And when the money was all spent in the land of Egypt and in the land of Canaan, all the Egyptians came to Joseph and said, "Give us food. Why should we die before your eyes? For our money is gone."<sup>16</sup>And Joseph answered, "Give your livestock, and I will give you food in exchange for your livestock, if your money is gone."<sup>17</sup>So they brought their livestock to Joseph, and Joseph gave them food in exchange for the horses, the flocks, the herds, and the donkeys. He supplied them with food in exchange for all their livestock that year.<sup>18</sup>And when that year was ended, they came to him the following year and said to him, "We will not hide from my lord that our money is all spent. The herds of livestock are my lord's. There is nothing left in the sight of my lord but our bodies and our land.<sup>19</sup>Why should we die before your eyes, both we and our land? Buy us and our land for food, and we with our land will be servants to Pharaoh. And give us seed that we may live and not die, and that the land may not be desolate."<sup>20</sup>So Joseph bought all the land of Egypt for Pharaoh, for all the Egyptians sold their fields, because the famine was severe on them. The land became Pharaoh's.<sup>21</sup>As for the people, he made servants of them from one end of Egypt to the other.<sup>22</sup>Only the land of the priests he did not buy, for the priests had a fixed allowance from Pharaoh and lived on the allowance that Pharaoh gave them; therefore they did not sell their land.<sup>23</sup>Then Joseph said to the people, "Behold, I have this day bought you and your land for Pharaoh. Now here is seed for you, and you shall sow the land.<sup>24</sup>And at the harvests you shall give a fifth to Pharaoh, and four fifths shall be your own, as seed for the field and as food for yourselves and your households, and as food for your little ones."<sup>25</sup>And they said, "You have saved our lives; may it please my lord, we will be servants to Pharaoh."<sup>26</sup>So Joseph made it a statute concerning the land of Egypt, and it stands to this day, that Pharaoh should have the fifth; the land of the priests alone did not become Pharaoh's.<sup>27</sup>Thus Israel settled in the land of Egypt, in the land of Goshen. And they gained possessions in it, and were fruitful and multiplied greatly.<sup>28</sup>And Jacob lived in the land of Egypt seventeen years. So the days of Jacob, the years of his life, were 147 years.<sup>29</sup>And when the time drew near that Israel must die, he called his son Joseph and said to him, "If now I have found favor in your sight, put your hand under my thigh and promise to deal kindly and truly with me. Do not bury me in Egypt,<sup>30</sup>but let me lie with my fathers. Carry me out of Egypt and bury me in their burying place." He answered, "I will do as you have said."<sup>31</sup>And he said, "Swear to me"; and he swore to him. Then Israel bowed himself upon the head of his bed.
47.overview:
Where we are. Jacob’s family has arrived in Goshen, and Joseph and his father have met after twenty-two years (46:28–30). Joseph now presents his family to Pharaoh, as he planned (46:31–34).

The message. God keeps his people alive and blesses the nations through them, even while they are strangers far from home. An old shepherd blesses the most powerful king on earth; the brother once sold for silver saves a whole country from starvation; and the family of promise, settled in the best of Egypt, grows and multiplies. Yet Egypt is not home, and Jacob makes sure that even his bones will go back to the land God promised.

Why it was said. The first hearers knew the Egypt of slavery (see the introduction). This chapter showed them that Egypt had once welcomed their fathers and been saved through one of them, and that their fathers had always regarded themselves as sojourners there, looking to Canaan.

How the chapter makes its case. Five brothers tell Pharaoh honestly that they are shepherds who have come to sojourn, and Pharaoh grants them Goshen (vv. 1–6). Jacob blesses Pharaoh and calls his long life a short and hard pilgrimage (vv. 7–10). Joseph settles and feeds the family (vv. 11–12). Meanwhile the famine deepens, and Joseph’s administration takes Egypt’s money, then its livestock, then its land and people for Pharaoh, in exchange for food and seed (vv. 13–26). Israel prospers in Goshen (vv. 27–28), and the dying Jacob makes Joseph swear to bury him in Canaan (vv. 29–31).

Where it leads. By pattern, and by contrast. Joseph is the one to whom the starving world must come for bread, and the Egyptians say to him, “You have saved our lives.” Jesus is the bread of life, who says, “whoever comes to me shall not hunger” (John 6:35); but where Joseph sold bread for everything people had, Christ gives it “without money and without price” (Isaiah 55:1), having paid the price himself. And Jacob, the sojourner who would not be buried in Egypt, is among those who “desire a better country, that is, a heavenly one” (Hebrews 11:16), which Christ has gone to prepare.

For us. We too are pilgrims, blessed in order to bless the world around us, even its powerful. Life may feel “few and evil” at times, and we may say so honestly; but our hope is not tied to where we now live. Live and die as people whose home is with God.
47.theology: Faith that makes arrangements about a grave. Jacob makes Joseph swear to bury him in Canaan, because the land God promised is not where he is living but it is where he intends to be laid. It is the same faith that bought a cave at Machpelah (ch. 23) and the same faith Joseph will show at 50:25: men staking their bones on a word from God.
47.examples:
Then: The famine policy in verses 13–26 fits what is known of Egyptian land-holding: the crown owned most of the land, the temples held theirs exempt, and a fifth of the harvest was a realistic rate.

Now: Reunited with a lost son and settled in the best land, Jacob sums up his life as “few and evil.” Long grief can change how a man reads his own life: God has carried him at every turn, and he cannot see it. Jacob could not see it that day. He could by chapter 48, and what changed was not his circumstances. If you cannot see God’s kindness in your story today, that does not mean it is not there.

keyVerse.quote: And Jacob said to Pharaoh, “The days of the years of my sojourning are 130 years. Few and evil have been the days of the years of my life, and they have not attained to the days of the years of the life of my fathers in the days of their sojourning.”
keyVerse.note: Standing before the most powerful king on earth, Jacob describes his whole life as a pilgrimage. Hebrews takes up this confession to describe all God’s people as strangers and exiles on the earth, seeking a better country (Hebrews 11:13–16).

47.reflection:
An old shepherd blessed the king of Egypt (vv. 7, 10). How can Christians be a blessing to those in power, without either fearing them or flattering them?

Jacob called his life “few and evil” (v. 9), but later called God “the God who has been my shepherd all my life long” (48:15). How does looking at your life from God’s side change the way you tell your story?

The Egyptians said to Joseph, “You have saved our lives” (v. 25). How is Christ’s gift of the bread of life different from Joseph’s sale of grain?

Jacob would not be buried in Egypt (vv. 29–30). What would it look like for you to live as a sojourner, serving gladly where God has put you without making this world your home?

48.title: Jacob Blesses Ephraim and Manasseh

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — The Adoption and Blessing of Joseph's Sons
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At the end of his life Jacob adopts Joseph’s two sons, crosses his hands to bless the younger above the elder, and confesses God as his shepherd and redeemer. Recalling God’s promise at Bethel, he claims Ephraim and Manasseh as his own sons, giving Joseph a double share (vv. 1–7). He embraces and blesses the boys, deliberately setting Ephraim first, in the name of the God of his fathers, his shepherd and redeemer (vv. 8–16). When Joseph objects, Jacob insists: the younger shall be greater (vv. 17–20). He ends with the promise that God will bring Joseph’s family back to the land of their fathers (vv. 21–22).
verseByVerse.theology: Dying, Jacob adopts Joseph's sons: "Ephraim and Manasseh shall be mine." He blesses them with crossed hands, naming "the God who has been my shepherd all my life long" and "the angel who has redeemed me from all evil," and sets Ephraim the younger before Manasseh. He promises that God will bring them back to the land.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: two boys born in Egypt became two tribes of Israel by a father's word. Now: God adopts outsiders as sons (Eph. 1:5).

verseByVerse.quote: After this, Joseph was told, "Behold, your father is ill." So he took with him his two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim. And it was told to Jacob, "Your son Joseph has come to you." Then Israel summoned his strength and sat up in bed. And Jacob said to Joseph, "God Almighty appeared to me at Luz in the land of Canaan and blessed me, and said to me, 'Behold, I will make you fruitful and multiply you, and I will make of you a company of peoples and will give this land to your offspring after you for an everlasting possession.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the dying Jacob hears that Joseph has come, he gathers his strength, sits up, and recalls God’s promise to him at Bethel.

After this, Joseph was told, “Behold, your father is ill.” Joseph comes at once and brings his two sons, now young men, born before the famine (41:50–52).

Israel summoned his strength and sat up in bed. The narrator uses the name “Israel” as the old man rises to act as the bearer of God’s covenant. He has something important to do before he dies, and faith gives him strength.

God Almighty appeared to me at Luz. Luz was the old name of Bethel (28:19). Jacob’s last thoughts go back to God’s word there, when God, as “God Almighty” (El Shaddai, see the note), renewed the promise of fruitfulness and land (35:9–12). Everything he is about to do rests on that promise.

A company of peoples … an everlasting possession. God promised to make Jacob a company or assembly of peoples, and to give the land to his offspring for ever. Jacob is in Egypt, but his mind is on Canaan. The promise, not his present circumstances, governs what he does next.
verseByVerse.note: “God Almighty” is El Shaddai (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: And now your two sons, who were born to you in the land of Egypt before I came to you in Egypt, are mine; Ephraim and Manasseh shall be mine, as Reuben and Simeon are. And the children that you fathered after them shall be yours. They shall be called by the name of their brothers in their inheritance. As for me, when I came from Paddan, to my sorrow Rachel died in the land of Canaan on the way, when there was still some distance to go to Ephrath, and I buried her there on the way to Ephrath (that is, Bethlehem)."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jacob adopts Joseph’s two sons as his own, ranking them with Reuben and Simeon, so that Joseph receives a double inheritance; then he remembers Rachel, who died on the way to Bethlehem.

Ephraim and Manasseh shall be mine, as Reuben and Simeon are. Jacob adopts his grandsons. They will not be counted as Joseph’s sons but as Jacob’s, with full and equal shares among the tribes. Naming them alongside Reuben and Simeon, his two eldest, may hint at what follows: Reuben lost the birthright by his sin with Bilhah (35:22), and the firstborn’s double portion goes to Joseph through his two sons (1 Chronicles 5:1–2).

The children that you fathered after them shall be yours. Any later sons of Joseph will be counted within the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh, not as separate tribes. That is why the tribes of Israel are twelve without a tribe of Joseph, and why Levi can be set apart for the priesthood without the number changing (see the note).

To my sorrow Rachel died. In the middle of a legal arrangement the old man’s grief breaks through. Rachel, the wife he loved, died young, giving birth to Benjamin (35:16–20), and had no more sons. By adopting her grandsons, Jacob in a sense gives Rachel the sons she did not live to bear. And he explains why she is not buried at Machpelah, where he himself wants to lie (47:30; 49:31).

Ephrath (that is, Bethlehem). Rachel’s grave lay near Bethlehem, the town from which, Micah said, a ruler would come for Israel (Micah 5:2). Matthew later heard Rachel “weeping for her children” in the grief of Bethlehem’s mothers when Herod sought the child Jesus (Matthew 2:18).

Uncertain wording. The phrase translated “when there was still some distance to go” (also in 35:16) is rare, and its exact meaning is not known. It describes a length of road, but how long is unclear; it may be a fixed measure of distance or simply “a stretch of country”. The point is plain enough: Rachel died on the road, short of her destination.
verseByVerse.note: That is why the tribes of Israel are twelve without a tribe of Joseph, and why Levi can be set apart for the priesthood without the number changing.

verseByVerse.quote: When Israel saw Joseph's sons, he said, "Who are these?" Joseph said to his father, "They are my sons, whom God has given me here." And he said, "Bring them to me, please, that I may bless them." Now the eyes of Israel were dim with age, so that he could not see. So Joseph brought them near him, and he kissed them and embraced them. And Israel said to Joseph, "I never expected to see your face; and behold, God has let me see your offspring also." Then Joseph removed them from his knees, and he bowed himself with his face to the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The nearly blind Jacob asks who the boys are, embraces and kisses them, and marvels that God has let him see not only Joseph but Joseph’s children; Joseph takes them from his knees and bows to his father.

Who are these? Jacob’s eyes are “dim with age”, like his father Isaac’s when Jacob deceived him (27:1). The question may also be part of the formal adoption: the father asks, the son identifies, and the father claims them.

They are my sons, whom God has given me here. Joseph, like Jacob before him (33:5), speaks of his children as God’s gift. “Here” is Egypt, the land of his affliction, where God made him fruitful (41:52).

I never expected to see your face. Jacob had given up hope of Joseph, and God gave him Joseph and Joseph’s sons too, far more than he could ask or think (Ephesians 3:20). That is not a promise that every grief ends this way; Genesis is honest about the ones that do not, like Rachel’s death a few verses earlier.

Joseph removed them from his knees. Placing children on the knees was a sign of claiming them as one’s own (compare 30:3; 50:23). The boys have been on Jacob’s knees, adopted; now Joseph takes them back and bows to the ground before his father. The ruler of Egypt bows before the head of the covenant family, fulfilling, in a way, his own early dream (37:9–10).

verseByVerse.quote: And Joseph took them both, Ephraim in his right hand toward Israel's left hand, and Manasseh in his left hand toward Israel's right hand, and brought them near him. And Israel stretched out his right hand and laid it on the head of Ephraim, who was the younger, and his left hand on the head of Manasseh, crossing his hands (for Manasseh was the firstborn). And he blessed Joseph and said, "The God before whom my fathers Abraham and Isaac walked, the God who has been my shepherd all my life long to this day, the angel who has redeemed me from all evil, bless the boys; and in them let my name be carried on, and the name of my fathers Abraham and Isaac; and let them grow into a multitude in the midst of the earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jacob crosses his hands to put his right hand on the younger son, and blesses Joseph through his sons in the name of the God who walked with his fathers, shepherded him all his life and redeemed him from all evil.

Ephraim in his right hand toward Israel’s left hand. Joseph positions the boys carefully so that his father’s right hand, the hand of the greater blessing, will fall on Manasseh, the firstborn. He is following custom.

Crossing his hands. Jacob crosses his hands and once again the younger is set over the elder, as Isaac over Ishmael, Jacob over Esau, and Joseph himself over his older brothers. Jacob is overruling custom on purpose.

He blessed Joseph. The blessing on the boys is a blessing on Joseph: his line is honoured in them.

The God before whom my fathers Abraham and Isaac walked. Jacob names God first as the God of his fathers, who walked before him in faithful obedience (17:1; 24:40). The blessing he passes on is not his own invention; it is the family promise.

The God who has been my shepherd all my life long. This is Jacob’s summary of his life, and the first time in Scripture anyone calls God his shepherd: a man who spent his life keeping sheep, driven from place to place, says God has kept him. Jacob will call God “the Shepherd, the Stone of Israel” (49:24); David would take it up (Psalm 23:1), Ezekiel would prophesy it (Ezekiel 34), and Jesus would say, “I am the good shepherd” (John 10:11). One chapter earlier Jacob called his life “few and evil” (47:9). Nothing has changed except that he is looking at it from the end.

The angel who has redeemed me from all evil. Jacob names this angel alongside God in a single blessing, with a singular verb: “bless the boys”. He is not a created angel but God himself appearing, the one with whom Jacob wrestled and of whom he said, “I have seen God face to face” (32:30).

What it means to be redeemed. This is the first time the Bible uses the verb “redeem”, and it is a family word. In Israel the redeemer (Hebrew go’el) was the nearest relative, who stepped in when one of the family had fallen into debt, slavery or ruin, and paid to buy him back (Leviticus 25:25; Ruth 4:14). So when Jacob says God “has redeemed me from all evil”, he is not describing a distant rescuer. God acted as next of kin to a man who had cheated his way through much of his life and could not buy himself out of anything. We like to think we need a helper, someone to top up our efforts; a redeemer is for people who belong to something else and cannot pay. That is why God’s Son became our kinsman, “born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law” (Galatians 4:4–5), paying not with silver or gold “but with the precious blood of Christ” (1 Peter 1:19). See Redemption in the Theological Dictionary.

In them let my name be carried on. Literally, “let my name be named on them”: they are to be called sons of Israel, bearing the family name and its promise. “Let them grow into a multitude” uses a rare verb related to the word for fish: let them teem like fish.

In everyday life. Look back on your own story as Jacob did, name the evils God has bought you out of, and thank him for each one. If your life feels “few and evil” now, ask God for the eyes to see it from the end, where his shepherding is plain.

Where Christians differ: the angel who redeemed. Some take the angel of verse 16 as a created angel acting on God’s behalf. Others, noting that Jacob sets him alongside God in one blessing and calls him the redeemer, see God himself, appearing as the angel of the LORD.

This commentary’s view. The angel who speaks and acts as God is best read as the Son appearing before his incarnation. Jacob’s redeemer is the one who would later become our kinsman in the flesh.

Hebrews 11:21. By faith Jacob, when dying, blessed Joseph’s sons. He could not see them clearly, but he saw the promise.

verseByVerse.quote: When Joseph saw that his father laid his right hand on the head of Ephraim, it displeased him, and he took his father's hand to move it from Ephraim's head to Manasseh's head. And Joseph said to his father, "Not this way, my father; since this one is the firstborn, put your right hand on his head." But his father refused and said, "I know, my son, I know. He also shall become a people, and he also shall be great. Nevertheless, his younger brother shall be greater than he, and his offspring shall become a multitude of nations." So he blessed them that day, saying, "By you Israel will pronounce blessings, saying, 'God make you as Ephraim and as Manasseh.'" Thus he put Ephraim before Manasseh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joseph tries to move his father’s right hand to the firstborn, but Jacob refuses, knowing that the younger will be greater, and blesses them with Ephraim first.

It displeased him. Joseph assumes his father, half-blind and dying, has made a mistake, and takes his hand to move it. It is the natural reaction of a man who respects order and custom.

I know, my son, I know. This is not a mistake but a prophecy. Isaac, blind and deceived, blessed the wrong son without knowing it (27:18–29); Jacob, dim-eyed but clear-sighted, knows exactly what he is doing. The deceiver has become a prophet.

He also shall become a people … Nevertheless, his younger brother shall be greater. Manasseh is not rejected; he too will be great. But Ephraim will be greater. Ephraim became the leading tribe of the north: Joshua came from it (Numbers 13:8), the tabernacle stood at Shiloh in its territory, and the prophets often call the whole northern kingdom simply “Ephraim” (Hosea 11:8). Moses’ blessing reflects the same order: “they are the ten thousands of Ephraim, and they are the thousands of Manasseh” (Deuteronomy 33:17).

A multitude of nations. Literally, “the fulness of the nations”: Ephraim’s descendants will be very many.

God make you as Ephraim and as Manasseh. The boys’ names will become a formula of blessing in Israel. Many Jewish fathers still bless their sons with these words.

Where it leads. God chooses freely, by grace, not by order of birth. Paul uses the same pattern to show that God’s choice “depends not on human will or exertion, but on God, who has mercy” (Romans 9:16): “The older will serve the younger” (Romans 9:12). Two boys born in Egypt to an Egyptian mother (41:50) became full sons of Israel by a father’s word, as those far off become sons of God through Christ.

What it does not mean. This does not mean that God despises the firstborn, or that parents should favour one child over another. Jacob’s own favouritism caused years of misery (37:3–4). God’s free choice is his alone, and it is always grace, never earned and never a licence for us to rank our children.
verseByVerse.note: Joseph’s two sons were born in Egypt to an Egyptian mother (41:50).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Israel said to Joseph, "Behold, I am about to die, but God will be with you and will bring you again to the land of your fathers. Moreover, I have given to you rather than to your brothers one mountain slope that I took from the hand of the Amorites with my sword and with my bow."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jacob assures Joseph that God will be with him and bring the family back to the land of their fathers, and gives Joseph an extra portion of land.

Behold, I am about to die, but God will be with you. Jacob’s death will not end God’s presence with his family. The promise God gave him at Beersheba, “I myself will go down with you … and I will also bring you up again” (46:4), passes to Joseph, who will repeat it to his own brothers as he dies (50:24).

Will bring you again to the land of your fathers. Egypt is not home. Even with his sons settled and prospering there, Jacob points them back to Canaan.

One mountain slope. The Hebrew for “mountain slope” is shekem, the name of Shechem (see the note), where Jacob bought land (33:19) and where Joseph’s bones would be buried in his sons’ inheritance (Joshua 24:32). Centuries later Jesus sat by Jacob’s well “near the field that Jacob had given to his son Joseph” (John 4:5) and offered a Samaritan woman living water.

In everyday life. Pass on to your children your confidence in God’s faithfulness, and thank God who is with each generation.

Uncertain wording. Two things are unclear. First, shekem means “shoulder”, hence a ridge or slope, or a “portion”, and it is also the town of Shechem; Jacob may mean either, or both by a play on words. Second, Genesis records no battle in which Jacob took land from the Amorites with sword and bow. At Shechem he bought land (33:19), and his sons Simeon and Levi attacked the city, which he condemned (34:30; 49:5–7). He may be referring to an event not otherwise recorded, or speaking of a future conquest as already done. Whichever it is, the gift marks Joseph out for a special share in the land.
verseByVerse.note: “Mountain slope” is shekem in Hebrew, which sounds like the town Shechem (ESV note).

48.text: <sup>1</sup>After this, Joseph was told, "Behold, your father is ill." So he took with him his two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim.<sup>2</sup>And it was told to Jacob, "Your son Joseph has come to you." Then Israel summoned his strength and sat up in bed.<sup>3</sup>And Jacob said to Joseph, "God Almighty appeared to me at Luz in the land of Canaan and blessed me,<sup>4</sup>and said to me, 'Behold, I will make you fruitful and multiply you, and I will make of you a company of peoples and will give this land to your offspring after you for an everlasting possession.'<sup>5</sup>And now your two sons, who were born to you in the land of Egypt before I came to you in Egypt, are mine; Ephraim and Manasseh shall be mine, as Reuben and Simeon are.<sup>6</sup>And the children that you fathered after them shall be yours. They shall be called by the name of their brothers in their inheritance.<sup>7</sup>As for me, when I came from Paddan, to my sorrow Rachel died in the land of Canaan on the way, when there was still some distance to go to Ephrath, and I buried her there on the way to Ephrath (that is, Bethlehem)."<sup>8</sup>When Israel saw Joseph's sons, he said, "Who are these?"<sup>9</sup>Joseph said to his father, "They are my sons, whom God has given me here." And he said, "Bring them to me, please, that I may bless them."<sup>10</sup>Now the eyes of Israel were dim with age, so that he could not see. So Joseph brought them near him, and he kissed them and embraced them.<sup>11</sup>And Israel said to Joseph, "I never expected to see your face; and behold, God has let me see your offspring also."<sup>12</sup>Then Joseph removed them from his knees, and he bowed himself with his face to the earth.<sup>13</sup>And Joseph took them both, Ephraim in his right hand toward Israel's left hand, and Manasseh in his left hand toward Israel's right hand, and brought them near him.<sup>14</sup>And Israel stretched out his right hand and laid it on the head of Ephraim, who was the younger, and his left hand on the head of Manasseh, crossing his hands (for Manasseh was the firstborn).<sup>15</sup>And he blessed Joseph and said, "The God before whom my fathers Abraham and Isaac walked, the God who has been my shepherd all my life long to this day,<sup>16</sup>the angel who has redeemed me from all evil, bless the boys; and in them let my name be carried on, and the name of my fathers Abraham and Isaac; and let them grow into a multitude in the midst of the earth."<sup>17</sup>When Joseph saw that his father laid his right hand on the head of Ephraim, it displeased him, and he took his father's hand to move it from Ephraim's head to Manasseh's head.<sup>18</sup>And Joseph said to his father, "Not this way, my father; since this one is the firstborn, put your right hand on his head."<sup>19</sup>But his father refused and said, "I know, my son, I know. He also shall become a people, and he also shall be great. Nevertheless, his younger brother shall be greater than he, and his offspring shall become a multitude of nations."<sup>20</sup>So he blessed them that day, saying, "By you Israel will pronounce blessings, saying, 'God make you as Ephraim and as Manasseh.'" Thus he put Ephraim before Manasseh.<sup>21</sup>Then Israel said to Joseph, "Behold, I am about to die, but God will be with you and will bring you again to the land of your fathers.<sup>22</sup>Moreover, I have given to you rather than to your brothers one mountain slope that I took from the hand of the Amorites with my sword and with my bow."
48.overview:
Where we are. Jacob has lived seventeen years in Egypt and has made Joseph swear to bury him in Canaan (47:28–31). Now he falls ill, and Joseph brings his two sons to his father’s bedside.

The message. God’s blessing comes by his free choice and his promise, not by birth order or human expectation. The dying Jacob adopts two Egyptian-born grandsons as his own sons, gives them full shares in Israel, and deliberately crosses his hands to put the younger first. And looking back over a life of trouble, he confesses that God has been his shepherd all his life and his redeemer from all evil.

Why it was said. The first hearers needed to know why there was no tribe of Joseph but two tribes, Ephraim and Manasseh, and why Ephraim, the younger, came to lead (see the introduction). Behind the tribal map lay a dying man’s faith in God’s promise of the land.

How the chapter makes its case. Jacob gathers his strength and recalls God’s promise at Bethel (vv. 1–4). On the strength of it he adopts Ephraim and Manasseh as his own, and remembers Rachel (vv. 5–7). He embraces the boys, marvelling that God has let him see not only Joseph but Joseph’s children (vv. 8–12). He crosses his hands and blesses them in the name of the God who shepherded and redeemed him (vv. 13–16). Joseph objects, but Jacob knows what he is doing: the younger will be greater (vv. 17–20). Finally he promises that God will bring them back to the land and gives Joseph an extra portion (vv. 21–22).

Where it leads. By promise, pattern and the character of God. Jacob’s Shepherd is the one Jesus claimed to be, “I am the good shepherd” (John 10:11). His redeemer is the kinsman who buys back those who cannot free themselves, which God’s Son became for us. And the adoption of two sons born outside the family, given full rights by the father’s word, is a picture of the grace by which God “predestined us for adoption to himself as sons through Jesus Christ” (Ephesians 1:5).

For us. We receive God’s blessing not by birth or merit but by his free choice. Look back on your life as Jacob did at the end: name the evils from which God has redeemed you, and confess him as your shepherd. Then pass that confidence on to the next generation.
48.theology:
Adoption. Two boys with no natural claim on the covenant are declared sons of Israel with a full inheritance alongside Reuben and Simeon. They did nothing; an old man said, “They are mine.” Paul uses the same picture for Gentiles brought into God’s family: “he predestined us for adoption as sons” (Eph. 1:5).

God’s free choice, again. Isaac over Ishmael, Jacob over Esau, Perez over Zerah, and now Ephraim over Manasseh. Jacob had once stolen a blessing meant for the elder; he now gives one to the younger in full daylight, with the boys’ father objecting. God’s choosing does not run by birth order, merit or seniority, and Genesis says so again and again before it ends.
48.examples:
Then: Adoptions and deathbed blessings had real legal force in the ancient Near East, and a patriarch’s spoken word about inheritance bound the family.

Now: At the end of his life Jacob discovers that God had been shepherding him through years he could only describe, while living them, as few and evil.

keyVerse.quote: The God before whom my fathers Abraham and Isaac walked, the God who has been my shepherd all my life long to this day, the angel who has redeemed me from all evil, bless the boys
keyVerse.note: At the end of a troubled life, Jacob sums up God as the faithful God of his fathers, his lifelong shepherd and his redeemer. It is the first time Scripture calls God a shepherd and the first use of the verb “redeem”, and both words find their fulfilment in Christ, the good shepherd who redeemed us with his blood.

48.reflection:
Jacob, who once called his life “few and evil” (47:9), now calls God “my shepherd all my life long” (v. 15). What evils has God redeemed you from, and where can you see his shepherding in your story?

Jacob crossed his hands and gave the greater blessing to the younger son (vv. 14, 19). What does this teach about the way God gives his grace, and how should it shape the way we treat one another?

Two boys born in Egypt were adopted as full sons of Israel (v. 5). How does this picture help you understand what it means to be adopted as a child of God in Christ?

Jacob’s last words to Joseph were about God’s presence and promise (v. 21). What do you want the next generation to know most about God?

49.title: Jacob's Blessings of His Twelve Sons

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–33 — The Blessing of the Twelve Tribes
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On his deathbed Jacob tells each of his twelve sons what lies ahead for him and his tribe, and the promise narrows to a coming King from Judah. The three eldest lose the leadership through their own sins (vv. 3–7). Judah, the brother who changed, is given the lion’s strength and the sceptre until the ruler comes to whom the peoples’ obedience belongs (vv. 8–12). The other sons each receive a future fitted to them, with a cry for the LORD’s salvation in the middle (vv. 13–21), and Joseph is blessed lavishly by the Mighty One of Jacob (vv. 22–26). Jacob then gives orders for his burial in the promised land, and dies in faith (vv. 27–33).
verseByVerse.theology: Jacob tells his sons what will happen in days to come. Reuben loses the firstborn's place; Simeon and Levi are scattered for their anger; Judah receives the lion and the sceptre "until tribute comes to him." The other tribes are sketched in a line or two, Joseph is blessed at length, and Benjamin is a wolf. Jacob asks to be buried at Machpelah, and dies.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: "I wait for your salvation, O LORD" (v. 18) breaks into the poem. Now: great gifts do not last without steady character (v. 4).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jacob called his sons and said, "Gather yourselves together, that I may tell you what shall happen to you in days to come. "Assemble and listen, O sons of Jacob, listen to Israel your father.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jacob gathers his sons to hear what God will do with them in the future, and speaks to them as Israel, the bearer of God’s promise. What follows is not a fond farewell but prophecy.

Gather yourselves together. All twelve sons stand around one bed, the whole future nation in one room. It is the first time they are addressed together as the family of promise.

What shall happen to you in days to come. The phrase, literally “in the latter days”, looks into the distant future. It is used later of Israel’s future under God’s hand (Numbers 24:14; Deuteronomy 31:29) and by the prophets for the days when the nations would stream to the LORD (Isaiah 2:2). Jacob speaks of his sons, but he sees through them to their tribes and beyond, to the ruler of verse 10.

Listen to Israel your father. He uses both his names, Jacob and Israel. The man who grasped at blessing all his life (27:36) now gives blessing, as the one God renamed (32:28).

A poem. From here to verse 27 Jacob speaks in poetry, some of the oldest Hebrew poetry we have, full of word-plays on the sons’ names, rare words and vivid animal pictures. Its words are shaped by the sons’ own conduct: what each has done helps decide what each will be. Moses would bless the tribes in a similar poem at the end of his life (Deuteronomy 33).

Is this genuine prediction? Many modern scholars think the poem was composed later, in the time of the judges or of David, and put into Jacob’s mouth, because it fits later tribal history so well. This commentary takes it as what it says it is: Jacob’s own prophetic word, recorded by Moses (see the introduction). The details are fulfilled over centuries, and verse 10 reaches beyond anything any writer in David’s day could have seen.

verseByVerse.quote: "Reuben, you are my firstborn, my might, and the firstfruits of my strength, preeminent in dignity and preeminent in power. Unstable as water, you shall not have preeminence, because you went up to your father's bed; then you defiled it—he went up to my couch!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Reuben, the firstborn, had every advantage, but he loses the leading place because he could not control himself and defiled his father’s bed. His sin was years old, but it had not gone away.

You are my firstborn, my might. Reuben was born first, to Leah (29:32), and as firstborn he should have received a double share and led the family. Jacob piles up his privileges: “the firstfruits of my strength, preeminent in dignity and preeminent in power”.

Unstable as water. Then one phrase undoes it all. The word describes water boiling over or rushing uncontrolled (see the box below). Reuben had good impulses: he tried to save Joseph from his brothers (37:21–22) and offered his own sons as a pledge for Benjamin (42:37). But he acted on impulse and could not be relied on. Water poured out cannot hold a shape.

Because you went up to your father’s bed. Reuben had slept with Bilhah, his father’s concubine (35:22). It was more than lust. In the ancient world taking a ruler’s concubine was a claim to his place, as when Absalom went in to David’s concubines (2 Samuel 16:21–22). Reuben grasped at the headship early, and lost it altogether. When it happened, Genesis says only that “Israel heard of it” (35:22). Jacob said nothing then; he speaks now. The birthright passed to Joseph, and leadership to Judah (1 Chronicles 5:1–2).

So it proved. No judge, prophet or king ever came from Reuben. The tribe chose land east of the Jordan for its cattle (Numbers 32:1–5); its leaders Dathan and Abiram rebelled against Moses (Numbers 16:1); in Deborah’s day Reuben debated at length and never came to the battle (Judges 5:15–16). Moses’ blessing is little more than a prayer that the tribe survive: “Let Reuben live, and not die, but let his men be few” (Deuteronomy 33:6).

The firstborn who did not grasp. Reuben reached for his father’s place and lost his own. The Son who is “the firstborn of all creation” (Colossians 1:15) did the opposite: he “did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself” (Philippians 2:6–7), and was given the name above every name. The way up in God’s kingdom runs down.

In everyday life. Gifts, position and natural advantages are not character, and they do not last without it. A moment of self-indulgence can cost a lifetime, and sins left unconfessed have a way of surfacing years later. Yet Reuben was not cut off: his name stands among the tribes to the end (Revelation 7:5). The God who forgives the confessing sinner is the one to run to (Psalm 51:1–2), and self-control is a fruit the Spirit grows in those who belong to Christ (Galatians 5:22–23).

What it does not mean. Not that forgiven sin is held against us before God. Reuben’s loss was of a position in history, not of his place in the covenant. Forgiveness does not always remove every earthly consequence, but in Christ there is no condemnation (Romans 8:1).

Uncertain wording. The word translated “unstable” is rare. Elsewhere it describes “reckless” men (Judges 9:4) and “fickle” prophets (Zephaniah 3:4), and a related word means wantonness. It may picture water boiling over, or water that cannot be held. The point is plain either way: Reuben was uncontrolled and unreliable.

verseByVerse.quote: "Simeon and Levi are brothers; weapons of violence are their swords. Let my soul come not into their council; O my glory, be not joined to their company. For in their anger they killed men, and in their willfulness they hamstrung oxen. Cursed be their anger, for it is fierce, and their wrath, for it is cruel! I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jacob refuses any share in Simeon and Levi’s cruelty at Shechem, curses their anger, and foretells that their tribes will be scattered through Israel. Yet God would turn Levi’s scattering into a blessing.

Simeon and Levi are brothers. Brothers in blood, and brothers in violence. When Shechem raped their sister Dinah, these two deceived the city into circumcision and then killed every male while they were still in pain (34:25–29). Jacob at the time objected only that they had made him hated and put the family in danger (34:30). Now he names the deeper wrong: “weapons of violence are their swords”.

Let my soul come not into their council. Jacob distances himself from their plans: “O my glory, be not joined to their company.” Their kind of zeal, family honour defended by treachery and slaughter, is not the way of Israel’s God.

They hamstrung oxen. Cutting an animal’s leg tendons crippled it for good. Genesis 34:28 says they took the flocks and herds; the detail here shows the wanton destructiveness of their rage, harming even what they did not need to.

Cursed be their anger. Jacob curses their anger, not the men themselves. He hates the sin and still calls them sons.

I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel. So it proved. Simeon’s towns lay inside Judah’s territory (Joshua 19:1, 9), and the tribe dwindled (from 59,300 fighting men in Numbers 1:23 to 22,200 in Numbers 26:14) and was largely absorbed; Moses’ blessing does not even mention it (Deuteronomy 33). Levi received no tribal land at all, only forty-eight towns scattered among the other tribes (Joshua 21:41).

Judgment turned to blessing. But Levi’s scattering became a gift. When Israel worshipped the golden calf, the Levites alone rallied to Moses, and were set apart for the LORD (Exodus 32:26–29). The tribe became Israel’s priests and teachers, spread through the land so that every region had them. Their old zeal, once used in cruelty, was turned to the service of God. The sentence was carried out, and then God made it the means of blessing to all Israel.

Christ and anger. When James and John wanted to call down fire on a Samaritan village that had refused Jesus, he turned and rebuked them (Luke 9:54–55). Jesus did not defend his honour by violence; he bore violence for the sake of those who wronged him. And our great high priest came not from Levi but from Judah (Hebrews 7:14), the priest who offered himself.

In everyday life. Anger at real wrong is not always sin, but anger that takes revenge into its own hands becomes cruelty, “for the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God” (James 1:20). Be honest about any fury you nurse on behalf of your family or your cause. Where wrong has been done, especially violence or abuse, the right path is to seek justice through proper authorities, not private vengeance (Romans 12:19; 13:4).

Uncertain wording. The word translated “swords” occurs only here. It may mean swords or weapons, or, by a different derivation, “their plans” or “their kinship arrangements”; the general sense, that their dealings were violent, is clear. “O my glory” is also unusual: it may mean “my honour”, or, as some suggest, by a slight change of vowels, “my liver”, the seat of feeling, in parallel with “my soul”.
verseByVerse.note: Levi had no territory of its own, and Simeon’s land lay inside Judah’s and was absorbed into it.

verseByVerse.quote: "Judah, your brothers shall praise you; your hand shall be on the neck of your enemies; your father's sons shall bow down before you. Judah is a lion's cub; from the prey, my son, you have gone up. He stooped down; he crouched as a lion and as a lioness; who dares rouse him? The scepter shall not depart from Judah, nor the ruler's staff from between his feet, until tribute comes to him; and to him shall be the obedience of the peoples.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah will lead his brothers like a lion, and the royal sceptre will stay in his line until the coming of the ruler to whom all peoples will give their obedience. This is the heart of the chapter, and one of the great promises of the Messiah.

Judah, your brothers shall praise you. A play on Judah’s name, which sounds like the Hebrew for “praise” (29:35). The brothers will bow to him, a startling word after Joseph’s dreams of the brothers bowing to Joseph (37:7–10). Joseph receives the double portion, but the kingship goes to Judah: “though Judah became strong among his brothers and a chief came from him, yet the birthright belonged to Joseph” (1 Chronicles 5:2).

Why Judah? Not because he was good. Judah proposed selling Joseph for silver (37:26–27), left his family, and treated his daughter-in-law Tamar shamefully (chapter 38). But God changed him. Judah came to say of Tamar, “She is more righteous than I” (38:26), and when Benjamin faced slavery, he offered himself in his brother’s place (44:33). The sceptre goes to the man who learned to give himself for another. Grace chose him, and grace remade him.

Judah is a lion’s cub. Jacob pictures Judah as a young lion that has gone up from its kill and now lies down in confident strength: “who dares rouse him?” Judah would march first among the tribes (Numbers 2:3; 10:14), go up first against the Canaanites (Judges 1:1–2), and produce David, who defended his flock from lions and became Israel’s great king.

The scepter shall not depart from Judah. The sceptre and the ruler’s staff are the signs of royal authority; the staff rests “between his feet” as the king sits enthroned. Rule will remain in Judah’s line, and it did, from David through four centuries of kings in Jerusalem, and after the exile the hope of the coming king fixed on David’s house.

Until tribute comes to him. The Hebrew of this line is difficult (see the box below), but every reading points forward to a coming one in whom Judah’s rule reaches its goal. “Until” does not mean that the sceptre then departs, but that it arrives where it was always heading. And his rule will not stop at Israel: “to him shall be the obedience of the peoples”. The promise to Abraham that all the families of the earth would be blessed in him (12:3) now has a royal face.

The Lion who is a Lamb. Israel’s kings rose and fell, and the line of David seemed to end in exile. Then Matthew’s Gospel opens: “Judah the father of Perez and Zerah by Tamar” (Matthew 1:3), and traces the line to Jesus. “It is evident that our Lord was descended from Judah” (Hebrews 7:14). In heaven John is told, “Weep no more; behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered”, and he turns to see “a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain” (Revelation 5:5–6). The Lion conquers by being slain. Like Judah before him, but infinitely more, he offered himself in his brothers’ place. And now the obedience of the peoples is being gathered to him, as the apostles were sent “to bring about the obedience of faith for the sake of his name among all the nations” (Romans 1:5).

In everyday life. Every human authority is temporary; this King’s is not. To bow to him is not humiliation but homecoming, for his rule is the rule of the one who died for his subjects. And no past is too dark for him to rewrite: if Judah could be made the royal tribe, there is hope for us.

How Jewish readers take it. The Aramaic Targum Onkelos renders the difficult line “until the Messiah comes, whose is the kingdom”, and the medieval commentator Rashi follows it; the Talmud (Sanhedrin 98b) counts Shiloh among the Messiah’s names. Many Jewish interpreters do not read the verse as setting a deadline that has already passed, and so still look for the Messiah to come. This commentary agrees that the ruler is the Messiah, and holds that the promise reaches its goal in Jesus of Judah’s line, the King whose rule now gathers the nations (Revelation 5:5).

Uncertain wording. The line the ESV translates “until tribute comes to him” is one of the most debated in the Old Testament. The Hebrew letters read literally “until Shiloh comes”. Some take Shiloh as a title of the Messiah; others as the town of Shiloh, where the tabernacle later stood (“until he comes to Shiloh”), though that makes poor sense of the promise. Many ancient translations read the letters slightly differently, as “until he comes to whom it belongs”, which matches Ezekiel 21:27: “until he comes, the one to whom judgment belongs”. The ESV divides the letters to read “tribute to him”, picturing the nations bringing gifts to a king (compare Psalm 72:10). The word for “obedience” is also rare (elsewhere only Proverbs 30:17). The readings differ in detail, but all of them describe a coming ruler from Judah with authority over the nations.
verseByVerse.note: “Until Shiloh comes” is the Hebrew as it stands; a slight change gives “until he comes to whom it belongs” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: Binding his foal to the vine and his donkey's colt to the choice vine, he has washed his garments in wine and his vesture in the blood of grapes. His eyes are darker than wine, and his teeth whiter than milk.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah’s coming king will bring an age of such overflowing abundance that vines are as common as hitching posts and wine as plentiful as washing water. The pictures are deliberately extravagant.

Binding his foal to the vine. No farmer would tie his donkey to a choice vine, because it would eat it. In this king’s day vines are so plentiful that it does not matter. He washes his clothes in wine, as if wine were as cheap as water, and his eyes and teeth shine with health and plenty.

His donkey’s colt. The king rides a donkey’s colt, not a war horse. The prophet Zechariah took up the picture: “Behold, your king is coming to you; righteous and having salvation is he, humble and mounted on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey” (Zechariah 9:9). On Palm Sunday Jesus sent for a donkey and her colt and rode into Jerusalem (Matthew 21:2–7), the King of Judah coming humbly to his city.

The blood of grapes. The plain meaning is abundance: wine so plentiful it is used like water. The prophets spoke of the messianic age in the same terms: “the mountains shall drip sweet wine” (Amos 9:13). Jesus’ first sign was to turn water into wine, well over a hundred gallons of it, at a wedding (John 2:1–11). From the second century, Christian writers such as Justin Martyr also saw in garments washed “in the blood of grapes” a hint of the King’s own blood. That is not the poem’s first meaning, but it is not a fanciful echo either: the abundance the King brings came through the cup he called “the new covenant in my blood” (Luke 22:20).

In everyday life. Christ’s kingdom is not thin or grudging. The God who gives his people the King gives them, with him, joy that overflows. When the Christian life feels dry, remember whose wine it is, and come back to his table.

Uncertain wording. The comparison in verse 12 can be read “darker than wine … whiter than milk” or “dark from wine … white from milk”. The word for “darker” is rare, and a related word describes eyes red from drinking (Proverbs 23:29). Either way the picture is of a king glowing with the health of a land overflowing with wine and milk.

verseByVerse.quote: "Zebulun shall dwell at the shore of the sea; he shall become a haven for ships, and his border shall be at Sidon. "Issachar is a strong donkey, crouching between the sheepfolds. He saw that a resting place was good, and that the land was pleasant, so he bowed his shoulder to bear, and became a servant at forced labor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Zebulun will live toward the sea and trade, and Issachar will settle for comfort and pay for it with forced labour. Two neighbouring tribes, two different futures.

Zebulun shall dwell at the shore of the sea. Zebulun’s land lay in lower Galilee, between the Sea of Galilee and the Mediterranean (Joshua 19:10–16), astride the coastal trade routes, with access toward the Phoenician ports of Sidon. Moses later blessed Zebulun to “draw from the abundance of the seas” (Deuteronomy 33:19). How far its border reached the coast itself is not clear, but its life faced the sea and its commerce.

Galilee of the nations. Centuries later the region of Zebulun and Naphtali was the first to fall to Assyria, and Isaiah promised that this very land of gloom would see a great light (Isaiah 9:1–2). Matthew notes that Jesus made his home in Capernaum, “in the territory of Zebulun and Naphtali”, and quotes Isaiah: “the people dwelling in darkness have seen a great light” (Matthew 4:13–16). The forgotten northern tribes were the first to hear the gospel.

Issachar is a strong donkey. Issachar received the fertile Jezreel valley (Joshua 19:17–23), the richest farmland in the land. Jacob pictures a sturdy donkey lying down between its loads. “He saw that a resting place was good, and that the land was pleasant”, so he bowed his shoulder and “became a servant at forced labor”. The fertile valley lay on the great trade and invasion route, and Issachar seems to have preferred paying overlords with labour to fighting for its freedom.

Not the whole story. Issachar also had its heroes. Its princes came with Deborah into battle (Judges 5:15), and in David’s day it supplied “men who had understanding of the times, to know what Israel ought to do” (1 Chronicles 12:32). Jacob’s word describes a tendency, not a fate no one could escape.

A better yoke. Issachar bowed to a master’s burden for the sake of rest. Jesus offers rest of another kind: “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart” (Matthew 11:28–29). Every life bows under some yoke. The only one that gives rest is his.

In everyday life. Comfort is a good gift and a bad master. Many have traded freedom, conscience or calling for an easy life, and ended up serving what they meant to enjoy. Ask what comforts you are unwilling to risk for Christ.

Uncertain wording. The word translated “sheepfolds” (also in Judges 5:16) is uncertain. It may mean sheepfolds, the two saddlebags of a pack donkey, or the hearths or ash-heaps of a settlement. Any of these gives the picture of a strong animal settling down to rest rather than rising to work or fight.

verseByVerse.quote: "Dan shall judge his people as one of the tribes of Israel. Dan shall be a serpent in the way, a viper by the path, that bites the horse's heels so that his rider falls backward. I wait for your salvation, O LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Dan, though small and born to a servant-wife, will have full standing and strike like a snake, and at the thought of the dangers ahead, Jacob cries out to the LORD for salvation. The prayer of verse 18 is the only prayer in the poem.

Dan shall judge his people. Another play on a name: Dan means “judged” or “vindicated”, the name Rachel gave him when God vindicated her (30:6). Dan was the son of Bilhah, Rachel’s servant, but he will judge “as one of the tribes of Israel”, with full and equal standing. The sons of the servant-wives are not second-class.

A serpent in the way. A small tribe that fights by ambush, like a snake by the path that bites a horse’s heel and throws its rider. Samson, the Danite judge (Judges 13:2), fought the Philistines alone, by cunning and surprise. Later the tribe, unable to hold its land, moved north and took the quiet town of Laish by surprise (Judges 18:27). There it set up a carved image and its own priesthood (Judges 18:30–31), and Dan became one of the two centres of Jeroboam’s golden calves (1 Kings 12:28–30). The snake struck Israel too.

Bites the horse’s heels. The image recalls the serpent of the garden, to whom God said, “he shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel” (3:15). The serpent bites at heels; the promised offspring crushes heads. Dan’s story, from Samson to the golden calf, shows that Israel’s own tribes could carry the serpent’s poison. Israel needed a deliverer as much as the nations did.

Missing from Revelation 7. Dan is the one tribe not named in the list of the sealed in Revelation 7:5–8 (Ephraim is also absent by name, perhaps included under Joseph). Revelation does not say why, and the guesses of early writers remain guesses. Its idolatry is the likeliest reason (see the note on Revelation 7).

I wait for your salvation, O LORD. In the middle of the blessings a dying man breaks off to pray. Jacob’s hope is in God, not his sons. It is the first time the word salvation appears in the Bible, and it means rescue from a danger you cannot escape on your own. To wait, in the Old Testament, is not to pass the time idly but to lean your whole weight on God before he has acted (Psalm 62:1). Facing a future he will not see, Jacob neither grabs the controls nor gives up; he hands the future to God.

Salvation with a name. The word Jacob prays shares its root with a name. The angel told Joseph of Nazareth, “you shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins” (Matthew 1:21), and old Simeon, holding the child in the temple, said, “my eyes have seen your salvation” (Luke 2:30). What Jacob waited for has a face. So whatever you are waiting on God for this week, bring it to him in Jacob’s words, knowing that the salvation that matters most has already come. See Salvation in the Theological Dictionary.
verseByVerse.note: “Dan shall judge” plays on Dan’s name, which sounds like the Hebrew for “judged.”

verseByVerse.quote: "Raiders shall raid Gad, but he shall raid at their heels. "Asher's food shall be rich, and he shall yield royal delicacies. "Naphtali is a doe let loose that bears beautiful fawns.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gad, Asher and Naphtali each receive a different future: Gad harassed but hitting back, Asher rich in food, Naphtali free and fruitful. Three short lines, each fitted to the tribe.

Raiders shall raid Gad. Almost every word in Hebrew plays on Gad’s name, which sounds like “raider” and “raid”. Gad settled east of the Jordan (Numbers 32), exposed to Ammonite, Moabite and desert raiders. But Gad would “raid at their heels”, chasing them off. In David’s time the Gadite warriors were men “whose faces were like the faces of lions and who were swift as gazelles upon the mountains” (1 Chronicles 12:8), and when Gad and its neighbours went to war, “they cried out to God in the battle, and he granted their urgent plea because they trusted in him” (1 Chronicles 5:20).

Asher’s food shall be rich. Asher received the fertile coastal plain in the north-west, olive country. Moses blessed him to “dip his foot in oil” (Deuteronomy 33:24). Asher would produce “royal delicacies”, food fit for a king’s table.

An old widow from Asher. The tribe is hardly mentioned again in Israel’s history, but in Luke’s Gospel a widow of eighty-four, Anna, “of the tribe of Asher”, who never left the temple, saw the infant Jesus and spoke of him “to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem” (Luke 2:36–38). The forgotten tribe had its share in the King after all.

Naphtali is a doe let loose. A deer set free, swift and graceful in the hills of upper Galilee. Barak, who led Israel to victory with Deborah, came from Kedesh in Naphtali, and Deborah praised Zebulun and Naphtali for risking their lives “on the heights of the field” (Judges 4:6; 5:18). Naphtali too would see the great light of Galilee (Matthew 4:13–16).

In everyday life. God’s people are not all alike, and God does not give them the same gifts or the same troubles. Some are always under pressure and must keep fighting back; some have plenty to give; some run free. Do not envy another’s portion. Each is given “the blessing suitable to him” (v. 28).

Uncertain wording. The last line of verse 21 can be read two ways. The ESV, taking the words as a continuation of the picture of the doe, has “that bears beautiful fawns”. The same letters, read as most older translations read them, give “he gives beautiful words”, perhaps of Naphtali’s eloquence or songs (compare Deborah’s song in Judges 5). Both readings are possible; the doe picture suits the line better.
verseByVerse.note: “Gad” sounds like the Hebrew for “raiders” and “raid” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: "Joseph is a fruitful bough, a fruitful bough by a spring; his branches run over the wall. The archers bitterly attacked him, shot at him, and harassed him severely, yet his bow remained unmoved; his arms were made agile by the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob (from there is the Shepherd, the Stone of Israel), by the God of your father who will help you, by the Almighty who will bless you with blessings of heaven above, blessings of the deep that crouches beneath, blessings of the breasts and of the womb. The blessings of your father are mighty beyond the blessings of my parents, up to the bounties of the everlasting hills. May they be on the head of Joseph, and on the brow of him who was set apart from his brothers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joseph, attacked by enemies but held steady by the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob, receives the richest blessing of all, overflowing from heaven and earth. Jacob’s longest words are for the son he thought he had lost.

Joseph is a fruitful bough. A vine or tree planted by a spring, its branches climbing over the wall. The word “fruitful” plays on Ephraim, the name Joseph gave his son because “God has made me fruitful in the land of my affliction” (41:52). His two sons will become two great tribes.

The archers bitterly attacked him. Joseph was a target from youth: hated and sold by his brothers (37:4, 28), falsely accused by Potiphar’s wife (39:14–18), forgotten in prison (40:23). Yet “his bow remained unmoved”: he did not fall apart, or take revenge, or abandon God.

By the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob. Joseph’s steadiness did not come from his own hardness but from God, whose hands held his. Jacob piles up names for the God who did it: “the Mighty One of Jacob” (used again in Psalm 132:2 and Isaiah 49:26), the Shepherd (as in 48:15), “the Stone of Israel”, “the God of your father”, “the Almighty” (Shaddai). Each name says that the God who held Jacob through his troubles will hold his sons too.

Blessings of heaven above. Rain from the sky and springs from “the deep that crouches beneath”, the fertility of the womb and the abundance of the hills: everything that makes land and family flourish. Moses’ blessing for Joseph echoes these words (Deuteronomy 33:13–16), and the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh received the fertile hill country at the heart of the land.
