Set apart from his brothers. The word is related to “Nazirite”, one consecrated or separated. Joseph was separated from his brothers by their hatred, and then set apart above them as their ruler and rescuer.

The Shepherd, the Stone of Israel. Joseph’s story has the shape of the gospel: the beloved son rejected by his brothers, sold for silver, unjustly condemned, then exalted to the right hand of the throne to save many, including those who betrayed him. Stephen told it that way to the council: “the patriarchs, jealous of Joseph, sold him into Egypt; but God was with him” (Acts 7:9), and went on to show how Israel always resisted the deliverers God sent. And the names Jacob gives to Joseph’s God belong to Christ: he is “the good shepherd” (John 10:11), and he is the living stone, “rejected by men but in the sight of God chosen and precious” (1 Peter 2:4).

In everyday life. When you are under attack, your steadiness will not come from toughness but from the hands that hold yours. Joseph’s steadiness did not mean staying in harm’s way: when Potiphar’s wife grabbed him, he ran (39:12). If someone is harming you, getting to safety and telling those with authority to protect you is not a failure of faith.

Uncertain wording. Several phrases here are hard. “A fruitful bough” is literally “a son of fruitfulness”; some translate “a wild colt”, keeping the animal pictures of the poem. “His branches” is literally “daughters”. “From there is the Shepherd” may mean “from there”, that is, from God’s hand, or “by the name of the Shepherd”. In verse 26 some translations, with a small change of vowels, read “the blessings of the eternal mountains” in place of “the blessings of my parents”, matching “the everlasting hills” (compare Deuteronomy 33:15). None of these affects the main sense: God has upheld Joseph and will bless him richly.
verseByVerse.note: “The Mighty One of Jacob,” “the Shepherd,” “the Stone of Israel” and “the Almighty” (Shaddai) are among the earliest titles for God in the Bible.

verseByVerse.quote: "Benjamin is a ravenous wolf, in the morning devouring the prey and at evening dividing the spoil." All these are the twelve tribes of Israel. This is what their father said to them as he blessed them, blessing each with the blessing suitable to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Benjamin, the youngest, will be a fierce fighter, and so Jacob ends twelve blessings, each one suited to the son who received it. Even the warnings were blessings, for they were spoken over sons who all remained in Israel.

Benjamin is a ravenous wolf. The protected youngest son will produce a tribe of fighters. Ehud, the left-handed deliverer, was a Benjaminite (Judges 3:15); the tribe had seven hundred left-handed slingers who “could sling a stone at a hair and not miss” (Judges 20:16); and its ferocity nearly destroyed it when it defended the men of Gibeah (Judges 20–21). From Benjamin came Saul, Israel’s first king, and Jonathan, and Mordecai in Esther’s day (Esther 2:5).

Morning and evening. Another Benjaminite was Saul of Tarsus, “of the tribe of Benjamin” (Philippians 3:5). Some early Christian writers, Tertullian among them, applied this verse to him: in the morning of his life he ravaged the church (Acts 8:3), and in its evening he gave out the riches of Christ (Ephesians 3:8). That is an application, not the verse’s meaning, but it shows the kind of thing God does with wolves.

All these are the twelve tribes of Israel. The first time the Bible speaks of the twelve tribes. The twelve sons stand at the head of the nation, and later Jesus chose twelve apostles to lead the renewed people of God (Matthew 19:28). The new Jerusalem bears the names of the twelve tribes on its gates and the twelve apostles on its foundations (Revelation 21:12–14): one people of God, old covenant and new.

Blessing each with the blessing suitable to him. Even Reuben, Simeon and Levi are counted as blessed. Their rebukes were part of their blessing, for they were spoken by a father to sons who remained his. That is how God disciplines his children: “the Lord disciplines the one he loves” (Hebrews 12:6).

In everyday life. God deals with each of his children personally, not in bulk. The word he has for you, whether comfort or rebuke, is fitted to you and given in love. Receive it as such.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he commanded them and said to them, "I am to be gathered to my people; bury me with my fathers in the cave that is in the field of Ephron the Hittite, in the cave that is in the field at Machpelah, to the east of Mamre, in the land of Canaan, which Abraham bought with the field from Ephron the Hittite to possess as a burying place. There they buried Abraham and Sarah his wife. There they buried Isaac and Rebekah his wife, and there I buried Leah— the field and the cave that is in it were bought from the Hittites." When Jacob finished commanding his sons, he drew up his feet into the bed and breathed his last and was gathered to his people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jacob charges all his sons to bury him in the family grave in Canaan, the one piece of the promised land the family owns, and then dies in faith. He is gathered to his people before he is laid in the cave.

Bury me with my fathers. Jacob had already made Joseph swear to bury him in Canaan (47:29–31); now he lays the charge on all the brothers. He describes the cave at Machpelah in legal detail: the field of Ephron the Hittite, east of Mamre, which Abraham “bought … to possess as a burying place” (23:17–20). It is the only part of the promised land the family owns, and Jacob wants his body there. His burial is an act of faith that God will keep his promise of the land.

There I buried Leah. Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Rebekah, and Leah. Rachel, the wife Jacob loved, lies by the road near Bethlehem (35:19). Jacob will lie beside Leah, the wife he did not choose and did not love as he should have. There is a quiet honour in his naming her here. And it was Leah, not Rachel, who bore Levi and Judah: the priestly and royal lines came from the unloved wife (29:31–35).

He drew up his feet into the bed. He had “summoned his strength and sat up in bed” to bless his sons (48:2); now, his work finished, he lies back and dies. He has given his blessing, settled his affairs and spoken his faith. It is a good death.

Gathered to his people. Jacob is “gathered to his people” before he is buried, and his burial is weeks away (50:1–13). The phrase means more than burial in a family grave: he has joined those who went before him. That is why Jesus could argue from God’s words, “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob”, that “He is not God of the dead, but of the living” (Matthew 22:32).

Died in faith. Jacob owned a grave in the promised land and nothing more. Hebrews says of the patriarchs, “These all died in faith, not having received the things promised, but having seen them and greeted them from afar” (Hebrews 11:13). Their hope was a better country, a heavenly one, and the guarantee of it is another tomb in that land, which was found empty. Christ has been raised, “the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (1 Corinthians 15:20).

In everyday life. How we die is the last sermon we preach. Jacob died with his affairs in order, his family blessed, and his hope fixed on God’s promise. Talk with those you love, while you can, about where your hope lies, and make plans that say what you believe.

For in their anger they killed men, and in their willfulness they hamstrung oxen.<sup>7</sup>Cursed be their anger, for it is fierce, and their wrath, for it is cruel! I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel.<sup>8</sup>"Judah, your brothers shall praise you; your hand shall be on the neck of your enemies; your father's sons shall bow down before you.<sup>9</sup>Judah is a lion's cub; from the prey, my son, you have gone up. He stooped down; he crouched as a lion and as a lioness; who dares rouse him?<sup>10</sup>The scepter shall not depart from Judah, nor the ruler's staff from between his feet, until tribute comes to him; and to him shall be the obedience of the peoples.<sup>11</sup>Binding his foal to the vine and his donkey's colt to the choice vine, he has washed his garments in wine and his vesture in the blood of grapes.<sup>12</sup>His eyes are darker than wine, and his teeth whiter than milk.<sup>13</sup>"Zebulun shall dwell at the shore of the sea; he shall become a haven for ships, and his border shall be at Sidon.<sup>14</sup>"Issachar is a strong donkey, crouching between the sheepfolds.<sup>15</sup>He saw that a resting place was good, and that the land was pleasant, so he bowed his shoulder to bear, and became a servant at forced labor.<sup>16</sup>"Dan shall judge his people as one of the tribes of Israel.<sup>17</sup>Dan shall be a serpent in the way, a viper by the path, that bites the horse's heels so that his rider falls backward.<sup>18</sup>I wait for your salvation, O LORD.<sup>19</sup>"Raiders shall raid Gad, but he shall raid at their heels.<sup>20</sup>"Asher's food shall be rich, and he shall yield royal delicacies.<sup>21</sup>"Naphtali is a doe let loose that bears beautiful fawns.<sup>22</sup>"Joseph is a fruitful bough, a fruitful bough by a spring; his branches run over the wall.<sup>23</sup>The archers bitterly attacked him, shot at him, and harassed him severely,<sup>24</sup>yet his bow remained unmoved; his arms were made agile by the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob (from there is the Shepherd, the Stone of Israel),<sup>25</sup>by the God of your father who will help you, by the Almighty who will bless you with blessings of heaven above, blessings of the deep that crouches beneath, blessings of the breasts and of the womb.<sup>26</sup>The blessings of your father are mighty beyond the blessings of my parents, up to the bounties of the everlasting hills. May they be on the head of Joseph, and on the brow of him who was set apart from his brothers.<sup>27</sup>"Benjamin is a ravenous wolf, in the morning devouring the prey and at evening dividing the spoil."<sup>28</sup>All these are the twelve tribes of Israel. This is what their father said to them as he blessed them, blessing each with the blessing suitable to him.<sup>29</sup>Then he commanded them and said to them, "I am to be gathered to my people; bury me with my fathers in the cave that is in the field of Ephron the Hittite,<sup>30</sup>in the cave that is in the field at Machpelah, to the east of Mamre, in the land of Canaan, which Abraham bought with the field from Ephron the Hittite to possess as a burying place.<sup>31</sup>There they buried Abraham and Sarah his wife. There they buried Isaac and Rebekah his wife, and there I buried Leah—<sup>32</sup>the field and the cave that is in it were bought from the Hittites."<sup>33</sup>When Jacob finished commanding his sons, he drew up his feet into the bed and breathed his last and was gathered to his people.
49.overview:
Where we are. Jacob has adopted Joseph’s two sons and blessed them with crossed hands (chapter 48). Now, on his deathbed in Egypt, he gathers all twelve sons to speak over each of them before he dies.

The message. God’s promise will go forward through this flawed family, and it will reach its goal in a King from Judah whom the nations will obey. Jacob’s words are honest: sin has lasting consequences, and three sons lose what they might have had. But grace has the last word. Every son remains in Israel, and the leading place goes to Judah, the brother who once sold Joseph and later offered himself in Benjamin’s place.

Why it was said. Israel coming out of Egypt (see the introduction) needed to know why the tribes stood where they did: why Reuben did not lead, why Levi had no land, why Judah marched first. This poem told them that their tribal history was the outworking of a prophetic word, and that the whole people was moving toward a coming ruler.

How the chapter makes its case. Jacob calls his sons to hear what will happen “in days to come” (vv. 1–2). The three eldest are passed over: Reuben for defiling his father’s bed (vv. 3–4), Simeon and Levi for their cruelty at Shechem (vv. 5–7). Judah receives the lion’s strength, the sceptre and a future of overflowing abundance (vv. 8–12). The other sons are sketched briefly, each with his own future (vv. 13–21), with a sudden prayer for the LORD’s salvation at the centre (v. 18). Joseph receives the richest blessing, from the Mighty One of Jacob (vv. 22–26), and Benjamin the wolf closes the list (vv. 27–28). Jacob then charges his sons to bury him in the cave at Machpelah, and dies (vv. 29–33).

Where it leads. Chiefly by promise. Verse 10 promises a ruler from Judah to whom “the obedience of the peoples” belongs, and the New Testament names him: “our Lord was descended from Judah” (Hebrews 7:14). John is told to behold “the Lion of the tribe of Judah”, and turns to see a Lamb that has been slain (Revelation 5:5–6). And by pattern: Judah received the sceptre after offering himself in his brother’s place, and the King who came from him gave himself for us. And the need is exposed: Jacob prays, “I wait for your salvation, O LORD,” and the salvation he waited for came with the name Jesus.

For us. Our sins have consequences, and God is honest about them, but he does not throw away his people. Whatever our past, the way forward is to bow to Judah’s King, who rules by dying for his enemies, and to face our own end as Jacob did, waiting for God’s salvation.
49.theology:
The promise of the Messiah. Verse 10 is one of the great Old Testament signposts. The rule stays in Judah’s line until someone comes to whom it belongs, and when he comes it is not Israel only but “the peoples” who obey him. David comes from Judah; so does the one John heard announced as “the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David.”

Sin has consequences that grace does not cancel. Reuben, Simeon and Levi stay in the covenant, and they lose things they will not get back. Forgiveness does not remove every effect of sin, and Genesis is honest about the difference. Yet God took Levi’s scattering and made it the priesthood: the sentence was carried out, and then turned into a blessing.

“I wait for your salvation, O LORD.” In the middle of the blessings a dying man breaks off to pray (v. 18). It is the first time the word salvation appears in the Bible, spoken by a man who has just described his sons’ futures and knows he will see none of it.
49.examples:
Then: Tribal poems describing the character and territory of clans are known from the ancient world, and the details here match later history: Zebulun toward the coast, Issachar in the fertile Jezreel valley under forced labour, Dan in the north on the invasion route, Gad exposed on the eastern frontier, Asher in the rich soil of the north-west. Jacob is describing tribes, not just temperaments.

Now: Reuben’s advantages were real, and he kept none of them, because he had no self-control. Gifts, position and natural advantage are not character. No one is steady by nature; it is the fruit the Spirit grows in those who belong to Christ (Galatians 5:22–23).

keyVerse.quote: The scepter shall not depart from Judah, nor the ruler’s staff from between his feet, until tribute comes to him; and to him shall be the obedience of the peoples.
keyVerse.note: This is the centre of Jacob’s blessings and one of the great messianic promises of the Old Testament. It sets the royal line in Judah and points to a coming ruler whose kingdom reaches all nations, fulfilled in Jesus, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, who conquered as the slain Lamb.

49.reflection:
Reuben had every advantage and lost the leading place through one act of self-indulgence (vv. 3–4). Why do gifts and position not last without character, and where do you most need the Spirit’s self-control?

Judah, who once sold his brother, was given the sceptre after offering himself in Benjamin’s place (vv. 8–10; 44:33). What does that teach about God’s grace, and about the kind of King Jesus is?

In the middle of the blessings Jacob prays, “I wait for your salvation, O LORD” (v. 18). What are you waiting on God for, and what would it look like to lean your whole weight on him while you wait?

Jacob died with his family blessed, his affairs settled and his hope fixed on God’s promise (vv. 29–33). What would you want to say to those you love about your hope, and is there anything you should do about it now?

50.title: Jacob's Burial; Joseph's Grace and Death

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–26 — Mourning, Burial, and Final Forgiveness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Genesis ends with a funeral, a final act of forgiveness and a coffin waiting for the exodus. Joseph mourns his father, and with Pharaoh’s leave a great Egyptian procession takes Jacob to be buried in the promised land, as he asked (vv. 1–14). When the brothers, afraid that Joseph will now repay them, beg for mercy, he weeps and reassures them: he is not in God’s place, and God meant their evil for good (vv. 15–21). Joseph lives to see his great-grandchildren, and dies confident that God will visit his people and bring them up to the land; he makes them swear to carry his bones with them (vv. 22–26).
verseByVerse.theology: Joseph weeps over his father, has him embalmed, and leads a great Egyptian procession to bury him at Machpelah. The brothers, afraid now, beg forgiveness; Joseph weeps and says, "Am I in the place of God? ... you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good." He dies at 110, making them swear to carry his bones out when God visits them.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Hebrews remembers Joseph for his directions about his bones (Heb. 11:22). Now: to forgive is to leave the judging to God, and God's purpose runs through the very evil men intend.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Joseph fell on his father's face and wept over him and kissed him. And Joseph commanded his servants the physicians to embalm his father. So the physicians embalmed Israel. Forty days were required for it, for that is how many are required for embalming. And the Egyptians wept for him seventy days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joseph grieves openly over his father, and has his body embalmed so that it can be carried home, while all Egypt mourns Jacob like royalty. Faith and grief are not enemies.

Joseph fell on his father’s face and wept over him and kissed him. God had promised Jacob, “Joseph’s hand shall close your eyes” (46:4), and it did. Joseph is the man in Genesis who weeps most often (42:24; 43:30; 45:2, 14; 46:29; 50:17), and he is not ashamed to weep now. Grief is not unbelief. Jesus wept at the grave of a friend he was about to raise (John 11:35). Christians grieve, but not “as others do who have no hope” (1 Thessalonians 4:13).

Joseph commanded his servants the physicians to embalm his father. Egyptians preserved the bodies of the dead by drying them in natron salt and wrapping them, a process tied in Egypt to beliefs about the afterlife. Joseph uses his own physicians, not the professional embalmers, perhaps to keep the religious rites away from his father’s body; the text does not say. The purpose here is practical: to embalm the body so it could be carried the long journey to Canaan. Jacob is the only Israelite in the Bible, with Joseph (v. 26), to be embalmed.

Forty days … seventy days. Embalming took forty days; the full period of public mourning was seventy, close to the honour Egypt gave a Pharaoh. Israel later mourned Aaron and Moses thirty days each (Numbers 20:29; Deuteronomy 34:8). The foreign shepherd whom Egypt once despised (46:34) is honoured by the whole nation, because of the son God raised up.

In everyday life. Do not be afraid to grieve, or ashamed of tears, when someone you love dies. Weep, and give thanks, and take your grief to the God who raises the dead. If grief settles into a darkness that will not lift, talk to your pastor or a biblical counsellor, and see your doctor too; there is no shame in getting help.
verseByVerse.note: Embalming took forty days, and the whole mourning period seventy.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the days of weeping for him were past, Joseph spoke to the household of Pharaoh, saying, "If now I have found favor in your eyes, please speak in the ears of Pharaoh, saying, 'My father made me swear, saying, "I am about to die: in my tomb that I hewed out for myself in the land of Canaan, there shall you bury me." Now therefore, let me please go up and bury my father. Then I will return.'" And Pharaoh answered, "Go up, and bury your father, as he made you swear."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joseph asks Pharaoh, through his court, for leave to keep his oath to bury his father in Canaan, and promises to return; Pharaoh agrees. Joseph honours his father and keeps faith with his king.

Joseph spoke to the household of Pharaoh. Joseph does not go to Pharaoh directly. He may still have been in mourning, unshaven and in mourning clothes, unfit to appear before the king (compare 41:14; Esther 4:2). Or he may have thought it wiser for others to plead his request. Either way he goes carefully.

My father made me swear. Joseph puts his request in terms Pharaoh would respect: a solemn oath to a dying father (47:29–31). He does not need to explain the promise of the land to an Egyptian king; the oath is enough.

In my tomb that I hewed out for myself. Jacob had evidently prepared his own place in the family burial cave at Machpelah (49:29–32).

Then I will return. The second most powerful man in Egypt asks permission and promises to come back. Joseph keeps faith with both his father and his king, and he does return (v. 14).

Go up, and bury your father, as he made you swear. Pharaoh’s answer is gracious. It is a far cry from a later Pharaoh, who would refuse again and again to let Israel go (Exodus 5:2).

In everyday life. Honouring our parents does not end when they die. Keep the promises you made them, as far as you rightly can. Jesus, dying on the cross, made sure his mother would be cared for (John 19:26–27).

Uncertain wording. The verb translated “hewed out” usually means to dig. In a few places a similar word means to buy (Deuteronomy 2:6; Hosea 3:2), and some translate “the tomb I bought for myself”. Since the cave was bought by Abraham (23:16–20), Jacob probably means a place he prepared within it, but the exact sense is not certain.

verseByVerse.quote: So Joseph went up to bury his father. With him went up all the servants of Pharaoh, the elders of his household, and all the elders of the land of Egypt, as well as all the household of Joseph, his brothers, and his father's household. Only their children, their flocks, and their herds were left in the land of Goshen. And there went up with him both chariots and horsemen. It was a very great company.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Egypt’s highest officials, Joseph’s whole family and a military escort go up together to bury Jacob, a state funeral fit for a king. The family’s children and flocks stay behind, a pledge that they will return.

All the servants of Pharaoh, the elders of his household, and all the elders of the land of Egypt. An extraordinary honour for the father of Egypt’s chief minister, and a public sign of what God had done through Joseph. The Canaanites would see it too (v. 11).

Only their children, their flocks, and their herds were left. The little ones and the livestock stay in Goshen. Egypt keeps a guarantee that the family will come back, and the family is not yet free to leave for good. Centuries later Pharaoh would try the same pressure, offering to let the men go but keep the children and flocks (Exodus 10:9–11, 24).

Both chariots and horsemen. An escort of honour. The next time Egypt’s chariots and horsemen go out after Jacob’s family, it will be to pursue and drag them back (Exodus 14:9). The same power that honours Israel now will later enslave it.

A foretaste of the exodus. Jacob’s body goes up out of Egypt to the promised land in a great procession: a picture in miniature of what God will do for his whole people. The book of Exodus will tell of a greater procession, and the gospel of a greater exodus still, when Christ by his death and resurrection led his people out of bondage to sin and death (Luke 9:31).

verseByVerse.quote: When they came to the threshing floor of Atad, which is beyond the Jordan, they lamented there with a very great and grievous lamentation, and he made a mourning for his father seven days. When the inhabitants of the land, the Canaanites, saw the mourning on the threshing floor of Atad, they said, "This is a grievous mourning by the Egyptians." Therefore the place was named Abel-mizraim; it is beyond the Jordan. Thus his sons did for him as he had commanded them, for his sons carried him to the land of Canaan and buried him in the cave of the field at Machpelah, to the east of Mamre, which Abraham bought with the field from Ephron the Hittite to possess as a burying place. After he had buried his father, Joseph returned to Egypt with his brothers and all who had gone up with him to bury his father.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At a threshing floor on the way, Joseph holds a week of great mourning, and then Jacob’s sons bury him in the cave at Machpelah, as he had commanded. Even the Canaanites notice, and name the place after Egypt’s grief.

The threshing floor of Atad. A threshing floor was a large, open, flattened space, a natural place for a public gathering, a ceremony or a lament. The mourning lasts seven days, the customary period (compare 1 Samuel 31:13; Job 2:13).

A grievous mourning by the Egyptians. The Canaanites, watching, saw only Egyptians, and named the place Abel-mizraim, a play on words: “mourning of Egypt”, or “meadow of Egypt”. Jacob had become so bound up with Egypt in their eyes that they did not recognise the family burying its own.

Thus his sons did for him as he had commanded them. The great procession escorts the body, but it is his sons who carry him into the land and bury him. For once, all twelve brothers act together in obedience to their father. The detailed description of the cave (compare 23:17–20; 49:29–32) is the last echo of Abraham’s purchase: the one piece of the promised land the family holds receives its third generation.

Joseph returned to Egypt. He keeps his word to Pharaoh (v. 5). The promise of the land is real, but the time has not yet come; God had told Abraham that his offspring would be sojourners in a land not their own for four hundred years (15:13–16).

Did Stephen get it wrong? In Acts 7:15–16 Stephen says that Jacob and “our fathers” were carried back to Shechem and laid in the tomb that Abraham bought from the sons of Hamor. Genesis says that Jacob was buried at Machpelah near Hebron, in a cave Abraham bought from Ephron, and that Jacob bought land at Shechem from the sons of Hamor (33:19), where Joseph was later buried (Joshua 24:32). Stephen is speaking quickly to a hostile council and compresses two burials and two purchases into one sentence, as speakers often do. He is summarising, not correcting Genesis, and his point stands: the patriarchs, dead in Egypt, were buried in the land God had promised.

Uncertain wording. Where the threshing floor of Atad lay is not known. The phrase “beyond the Jordan” usually means east of the river, which would mean the procession went the long way round, east of the Dead Sea, as Israel itself would later go. But “beyond the Jordan” depends on where the speaker stands, and could mean the western side to someone writing from the east. The site of Abel-mizraim has not been identified.
verseByVerse.note: “Abel-mizraim” means “mourning (or meadow) of Egypt” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: When Joseph's brothers saw that their father was dead, they said, "It may be that Joseph will hate us and pay us back for all the evil that we did to him." So they sent a message to Joseph, saying, "Your father gave this command before he died: 'Say to Joseph, "Please forgive the transgression of your brothers and their sin, because they did evil to you."' And now, please forgive the transgression of the servants of the God of your father." Joseph wept when they spoke to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With their father dead, Joseph’s brothers fear that his forgiveness was only for Jacob’s sake, and they send a message pleading for mercy; Joseph weeps. Seventeen years after they were forgiven, they still did not believe it.

It may be that Joseph will hate us and pay us back. Joseph’s brothers had lived seventeen years in Egypt (47:28), fed at his expense, and yet they assumed it had all been a performance for their father’s sake. Esau had once planned to kill Jacob as soon as their father died (27:41); perhaps they feared Joseph was waiting in the same way. A guilty conscience does not easily believe it is forgiven.

Your father gave this command before he died. Genesis records no such command. Jacob may have said it, but the message has the look of a story invented in fear, using the dead father’s authority as a shield. Even so, for the first time the brothers name their own deed fully: “the transgression of your brothers and their sin, because they did evil to you”.

The servants of the God of your father. They appeal to the faith they share with Joseph. They are not only his brothers; they belong to the same God.

Joseph wept when they spoke to him. Perhaps from grief that after all these years they still did not trust him; perhaps from pity at their fear; perhaps because at last he heard them confess it all. Probably all three. Forgiveness offered and not believed wounds the one who offers it.

An intercessor who does not die. The brothers thought their protection had died with Jacob. Our forgiveness does not depend on a go-between who might die and leave us exposed. Christ, who pleads for us, “always lives to make intercession” for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25). There is no day coming when the Father will drop the act, because it was never an act: it rests on the finished work of his Son.

In everyday life. Do you doubt that God has really forgiven you, and live waiting for the blow to fall? His forgiveness rests on Christ’s finished work, not on your performance, and it does not lapse when circumstances change: “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). And if you have forgiven someone, be patient when they find it hard to believe.

verseByVerse.quote: His brothers also came and fell down before him and said, "Behold, we are your servants." But Joseph said to them, "Do not fear, for am I in the place of God? As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring it about that many people should be kept alive, as they are today. So do not fear; I will provide for you and your little ones." Thus he comforted them and spoke kindly to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joseph will not take God’s place as judge, because God has turned his brothers’ evil into good for the saving of many lives; so he comforts them and promises to provide for them. This is the summit of the Joseph story and the theme of all Genesis.

Behold, we are your servants. The brothers fall down before him, as Joseph dreamed when he was seventeen (37:7–10). They had sold him as a slave; now they offer themselves as his slaves (compare 44:16). He does not accept the offer.

Do not fear, for am I in the place of God? Jacob used the same words to Rachel when she demanded children he could not give (30:2). Joseph means that judgment and vengeance belong to God, not to him, and also that God has already done with their sin what only God could do. To punish them now would be to take God’s seat. Paul gives the same ground for not avenging ourselves: “leave it to the wrath of God” (Romans 12:19).

You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good. The same verb in both halves: they planned it, and God planned it. Joseph does not soften what they did; “you meant evil” stands. But in the same events, through the same choices, God was at work for good. God’s rule over an evil act does not make the act less evil or the doers less guilty, and human wickedness does not put a single event outside his purpose.

To bring it about that many people should be kept alive. God’s purpose was bigger than Joseph’s comfort or even his family’s survival: Egypt and the surrounding nations were saved from famine (41:57), and the family through whom God would bless all nations was kept alive (45:5–7).

Does everything happen for a reason? People say it at hospital bedsides and funerals, meaning to help, and it often wounds, because it seems to say the loss was somehow fine. Others answer that nothing happens for a reason: the universe is blind, and suffering means nothing at all. Joseph says neither. He does not tell his brothers that what they did was secretly good, nor does he call his years in the pit and the prison meaningless. God was at work in the very same events, for a purpose bigger than Joseph. Biblical providence is not a slogan that explains everything. Joseph saw the purpose only after more than twenty years, and many of God’s people never see it in this life. It is trust in a Person.

Good Friday. The reason we can trust him is the event where this verse comes true most fully. At the cross men did the worst evil ever done, and God meant it for the salvation of the world: Jesus was “delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God”, and “crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men” (Acts 2:23). The guilty were guilty; the plan was God’s; and many people are kept alive. If God could do that with Good Friday, he can be trusted with what we cannot explain. That is the ground of the promise that “for those who love God all things work together for good” (Romans 8:28).

I will provide for you and your little ones. Forgiveness is shown in deeds. Joseph does not merely refrain from revenge; he takes responsibility for the welfare of those who wronged him and their children. “He comforted them and spoke kindly to them”, literally, “spoke to their hearts”, the phrase Isaiah uses for God’s tender words to his people (Isaiah 40:2). Joseph forgives as God forgives, and Christ, who bore the wrong we did him, is “not ashamed to call them brothers” (Hebrews 2:11).

What it does not mean. Joseph’s forgiveness does not mean calling evil good, or pretending it did not happen; he names it plainly. Nor did his trust come quickly: he tested his brothers for a long time before he made himself known (chapters 42–44), and the relationship was restored after they had changed. Forgiving someone who has harmed you means letting go of revenge and bitterness, and leaving judgment to God, but it does not mean returning to danger. Where there is abuse or a crime, reporting it to the authorities, and keeping yourself and others safe, is not a failure to forgive. Seek wise help from your pastor or a biblical counsellor.

Where Christians differ: did God plan the evil, or only use it? Many Christians, especially in the Arminian tradition, hold that God permits sinful choices and then overrules them for good, but does not ordain them. Reformed Christians hold that God ordains whatever comes to pass, including sinful acts, without being the author of sin or removing human guilt.

This commentary’s view. The Reformed view. Joseph uses the same verb for his brothers’ intention and God’s: God did not only react to their plan, he “meant it”. Yet the brothers are fully guilty, for they meant evil, and God meant good. The same pattern appears at the cross (Acts 2:23; 4:27–28). God’s plan includes human choices as real choices, and that is why we can trust him with ours.

verseByVerse.quote: So Joseph remained in Egypt, he and his father's house. Joseph lived 110 years. And Joseph saw Ephraim's children of the third generation. The children also of Machir the son of Manasseh were counted as Joseph's own.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joseph lives to a full old age in Egypt, sees his great-grandchildren, and welcomes them into the family as his own. God’s blessing rests on him to the end.

So Joseph remained in Egypt, he and his father’s house. The family stays, as God told Jacob it would (46:3–4). These quiet years are the years in which, as Exodus says, “the people of Israel were fruitful and increased greatly” (Exodus 1:7).

Joseph lived 110 years. Egyptian texts speak of a hundred and ten years as the ideal length of a full and blessed life. Joshua, who led Israel into the land, died at the same age (Joshua 24:29). Joseph lived fifty-four years after his father’s death.

Ephraim’s children of the third generation. Joseph lived to see his descendants through Ephraim to the third generation, a sign of God’s blessing: “May you see your children’s children!” (Psalm 128:6). The son whose name meant “God has made me fruitful” (41:52) became a fruitful line.

Counted as Joseph’s own. Literally, “born on Joseph’s knees”. Taking a child on one’s knees was a way of receiving him as one’s own, as Jacob had done with Ephraim and Manasseh (48:12; compare 30:3). Machir’s line became a leading clan of Manasseh, and settled Gilead (Numbers 32:39–40); in Deborah’s song, “from Machir marched down the commanders” (Judges 5:14).

In everyday life. Grandparents and great-grandparents have a place in God’s purposes. Take the children of your family on your knees, as Joseph did: welcome them, bless them, and pass on to them the faith that has carried you.

Uncertain wording. The phrase “children of the third generation” is not entirely clear. It may mean Ephraim’s great-grandchildren, or, counting Ephraim himself as the first generation, his grandchildren. Either way Joseph lived to see a long line of descendants.

verseByVerse.quote: And Joseph said to his brothers, "I am about to die, but God will visit you and bring you up out of this land to the land that he swore to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob." Then Joseph made the sons of Israel swear, saying, "God will surely visit you, and you shall carry up my bones from here." So Joseph died, being 110 years old. They embalmed him, and he was put in a coffin in Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joseph dies certain that God will keep his promise and bring Israel out of Egypt to the land, and he makes them swear to carry his bones with them. Genesis ends with a coffin in Egypt, waiting.

God will visit you. Joseph’s last words are faith in God’s promise. To “visit” here means to come and act: to attend to someone in order to keep a promise. God had promised the land to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and Joseph does not doubt that he will keep it. When God appeared to Moses, his message was the same word: “I have observed you” (Exodus 3:16), and when the people heard “that the LORD had visited the people of Israel … they bowed their heads and worshiped” (Exodus 4:31).

You shall carry up my bones from here. Joseph could have had a magnificent Egyptian tomb. Instead he asked to wait, unburied, until God brought Israel out. Four centuries later Moses “took the bones of Joseph with him” at the exodus (Exodus 13:19), and they were buried at Shechem, in the land Jacob had bought (Joshua 24:32). Out of Joseph’s whole remarkable career, Hebrews chooses this to remember him by: “By faith Joseph, at the end of his life, made mention of the exodus of the Israelites and gave directions concerning his bones” (Hebrews 11:22).

He was put in a coffin in Egypt. The word for coffin is the word later used for the ark of the covenant. Through the wilderness Israel would carry two chests: the ark, with God’s law and his presence, and the coffin with Joseph’s bones, a standing reminder that God keeps his word.

A coffin and a promise. Genesis began with God creating life in a garden; it ends with a dead man in a coffin in Egypt. Sin has brought death, as God said (2:17), and even the best of the patriarchs dies. The book leaves us waiting for God’s visit. It came: “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, for he has visited and redeemed his people” (Luke 1:68). Jesus spoke on the mountain of transfiguration of the departure, literally the exodus, “which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem” (Luke 9:31). And unlike Joseph, whose bones had to be carried out, Jesus walked out of his tomb, and will raise all who wait for him.

In everyday life. Live with your hope set on God’s promises, not your present address. Joseph spent almost his whole life in Egypt, yet his heart was in the land God promised. The God who has kept every promise so far will keep the rest. Make your plans, and even your funeral, say so.
verseByVerse.note: Joseph’s body, embalmed and laid in a coffin, could be kept until it was carried out four centuries later.

They embalmed him, and he was put in a coffin in Egypt.
50.overview:
Where we are. Jacob has blessed his twelve sons and died (chapter 49). Genesis closes with his funeral, the brothers’ last fear, and the death of Joseph.

The message. God rules over everything, even the evil people do, and turns it to good for the saving of many. That is why Joseph can forgive: he does not pretend his brothers did no wrong, but he will not take God’s place as their judge, because he has seen God’s purpose running through their sin. And the book ends looking forward. God has kept his promises so far, and he will keep the rest: “God will surely visit you.”

Why it was said. Israel, coming out of Egypt (see the introduction), needed to know that their slavery had not been an accident and that God had not forgotten them. Joseph’s last words were the promise their exodus fulfilled, and they carried his coffin out with them (Exodus 13:19).

How the chapter makes its case. Joseph mourns his father, and Egypt honours Jacob like a king (vv. 1–3). Pharaoh lets Joseph keep his oath (vv. 4–6), and a great procession carries Jacob to the cave at Machpelah, where his sons bury him (vv. 7–14). Then the brothers, afraid that Joseph will now take revenge, beg his forgiveness (vv. 15–17). Joseph weeps, refuses to put himself in God’s place, and declares that what they meant for evil God meant for good; he promises to provide for them (vv. 18–21). He lives to see his great-grandchildren (vv. 22–23), and dies certain that God will bring Israel out, making them swear to carry his bones with them (vv. 24–26).

Where it leads. By pattern, and by the need it leaves open. Joseph, rejected by his brothers and then exalted to save them, forgives those who wronged him and provides for them, as Christ does for us. Verse 20 comes truest at the cross, where men did the worst evil ever done “according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God” (Acts 2:23), for the saving of the world. And the book that began with life in a garden ends with a coffin in Egypt: death still reigns, and the promise waits. It waits for the day when “the Lord God of Israel … has visited and redeemed his people” (Luke 1:68), and for the one who accomplished a greater exodus and left his tomb empty.

For us. If God rules even over the wrongs done to us, we can leave judgment with him and forgive. If he has forgiven us in Christ, we need not live like the brothers, waiting for him to change his mind. And we can live and die as Joseph did, sure that God will keep every promise.
50.theology:
Genesis 50:20 and the two intentions. The same act is described twice: you meant evil and God meant it for good. The verb is the same in both halves: they planned it, and he planned it. God’s rule over an evil act does not make the act less evil or the doers less guilty, and human wickedness does not put a single event outside his purpose. This is what Paul means by “for those who love God all things work together for good,” and what Peter preached about the cross. Genesis states it long before anyone set it out as doctrine.

Forgiveness that refuses the judge’s seat. Paul gives the same ground for not avenging yourself: “leave it to the wrath of God.” Forgiveness does not pretend no wrong was done; it refuses to be the judge who punishes it.

Faith at the end of a life. Joseph dies certain of an exodus he will not see. Hebrews picks this, out of his whole extraordinary career, as the thing to remember him by: “By faith Joseph, at the end of his life, made mention of the exodus of the Israelites and gave directions concerning his bones” (Heb. 11:22).
50.examples: The brothers had been forgiven seventeen years earlier and had eaten at Joseph’s table ever since, yet the moment their father died they assumed it had all been a performance. People who have never really believed they are forgiven live like that, waiting for the other person to drop the act. Joseph’s tears are the answer: the forgiveness was real all along.

keyVerse.quote: As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring it about that many people should be kept alive, as they are today.
keyVerse.note: Joseph’s words sum up the whole of his story and the message of Genesis: God rules over human evil without excusing it, and works through it for the saving of many. The verse finds its deepest fulfilment at the cross, where the worst human evil became the salvation of the world.

50.reflection:
After seventeen years of kindness the brothers still feared Joseph would take revenge (vv. 15–17). Why is it so hard to believe we are forgiven, by God or by others, and what does Christ’s ever-living intercession (Hebrews 7:25) say to that fear?

Joseph asks, “Am I in the place of God?” (v. 19). How does leaving judgment to God set us free to forgive, and what is the difference between forgiving someone and pretending they did no wrong?

“You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good” (v. 20). Where have you seen God bring good out of evil, and how can you hold on to this truth when you cannot yet see the good?

Joseph died asking for his bones to be carried to the promised land (vv. 24–25). What would it look like for your plans and priorities to show that your hope is in God’s promises?
